before.justification: v1 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments on Multistage Reacher, Maze Navigation and Meta-World Manipulation, including baseline comparisons, ablations and per-task appendix results.

title: QMP: Q-switch Mixture of Policies for Multi-Task Behavior Sharing

C1.justification: The central claims about selective behavior sharing, sample efficiency, convergence, and complementarity remain the same. Off-policy applicability is emphasized more explicitly, but that scope was already stated in v2's introduction and method.

C2.justification: v3's conclusion explicitly states that QMP cannot use on-policy base algorithms such as PPO because sharing operates through off-policy data collection. This adds a concrete applicability limitation; existing interpretations and qualifications otherwise remain.

D1.justification: v3 adds a direct QMP source-code repository link in Section 6.2, supplementing the existing project/video link. Appendix H's implementation details, architectures, hardware, and hyperparameters are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same reaching, maze, Meta-World, Walker2D, and Kitchen settings. The three-versus-ten-task maze comparison and PCGrad benchmarks already appear in v2.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain the same methods, including sharing baselines, DnC variants, PCGrad, MCAL variants, and DECAF. Removing the UDS commentary from Section 7.2 does not remove its existing comparisons.

E3.justification: The PCGrad MT50 comparison changes from average return in v2's appendix Figure 9 to success rate in v3's Figure 15. Other stated experimental settings remain unchanged; shorter displayed training horizons do not establish changed training budgets or reruns.

E4.justification: Both retain the policy-mixture, action-expectation, exploration-entropy, and temporal-horizon ablations, plus per-task and behavior-sharing analyses. Reordered appendix material and the PCGrad summary table introduce no new analytical question.

E5.justification: Five-seed reporting, shaded standard deviations, and existing plus/minus results are retained. The new PCGrad table gives point estimates but introduces no stated change in run counts, statistical tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: v3 newly reports MT50 success-rate curves and Table 2's PCGrad/QMP+PCGrad values: Reacher 0.78/0.78, Maze 0.90/1.00, Kitchen 0.55/0.60, and MT50 0.35/0.42. These are additional summaries and changed-metric results, not demonstrated performance gains between versions. The main experimental results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Q-switch selection, Algorithm 1, and off-policy SAC training are unchanged. The practical approximations, conservative MT10 sharing, and temporally extended variant were already documented in v2.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the introductory behavior-sharing example, makes localized wording corrections, changes the publication header, and reorders the maze-scaling, data-sharing, and PCGrad appendix subsections. The overall narrative and section structure remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds Table 2, redraws and relocates the PCGrad panels with changed axes and shorter displayed horizons, and reorganizes appendix figures. It also resolves duplicate figure numbering and resizes some retained plots; most visual content is unchanged.

R1.justification: Schulman et al. (2017), Proximal Policy Optimization, is newly cited for the on-policy limitation. The related-work discussion and positioning against prior behavior-sharing approaches otherwise remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Definitions 4.1-4.2, Theorem 5.1, and the derivations, assumptions, and convergence proofs in Appendices B-C are unchanged. The introduction's expanded explanation of behavior adds no formal mathematical definition.

improvement.justification: v3 modestly improves usability through clearer applicability limits, direct code-access information, and repaired appendix numbering and references. The empirical addition is less clear: Table 2 reports Kitchen PCGrad as 0.55, whereas Figure 15's shortened curve ends below 0.20, without explaining checkpoints or aggregation. This limits the benefit of the new summary, but the documentation improvements support a small overall gain.

A1.justification: Both complete 29-page PDFs describe the same QMP research. The main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A-H support comparison, including matching material across appendix reordering and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and reports revised PCGrad comparison metrics and an additional numerical summary table.

before.justification: v2 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments, including the 2D reaching example, seven multi-task settings, baseline comparisons, and appendix ablations.

title: QMP: Q-switch Mixture of Policies for Multi-Task Behavior Sharing

C1.justification: The central claims of combating forgetting without task labels and approaching offline-oracle performance remain. V2 drops the three-solver contribution, adds an explicit small-buffer effectiveness claim and extends its comparative claim to model-based methods.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of MBPO's sampling bias and online EWC's adaptation–retention tradeoff, plus limitations concerning network capacity and more complex contexts requiring larger buffers. V1's explanations for surpassing offline policies and LCPO-P's weaker performance disappear. The exploration limitation is retained and expanded.

D1.justification: V2 adds a source-code URL, hardware and runtime information, tuning procedures, OOD sampling details and new-baseline hyperparameters. Software documentation changes from OpenAI Gym 0.26.2 to Gymnasium 0.29.1 and MuJoCo 3.1.1. Some earlier straggler specifications, including the full observation and reward description, are omitted.

E1.justification: V2 adds wind-driven InvertedPendulum-v4, InvertedDoublePendulum-v4, Hopper-v4 and Reacher-v4 evaluations. These substantially broaden the control tasks beyond v1's Pendulum-v1 and straggler mitigation. The grid-world example, four synthetic wind traces and two real workloads are retained.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated comparisons with MBCD, MBPO and online EWC alongside the retained A2C, TRPO, DDQN, SAC and offline-oracle comparisons. Appendix A.2 also compares against Ideal MBPO using ground-truth dynamics. MBPO is additionally included in the wind-free Pendulum validation.

E3.justification: V2 introduces normalized-return aggregation, limited-buffer settings, buffer-size sweeps, EWC tuning protocols and a ground-truth-model MBPO control. It also revises the stated straggler OOD thresholds from -5/-6/-7 to 5/6/7, with corresponding interpretation changes. This reported correction does not establish that the underlying implementation changed.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses of buffer-size sensitivity, EWC hyperparameter sensitivity, change-point detector sensitivity and whether model error explains MBPO's weakness. It removes v1's LCPO-S/D/P comparison while retaining the OOD-threshold sensitivity analysis. These changes substantially alter the diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: The stated seed counts rise from five to ten for straggler mitigation and the wind-free Pendulum validation; the main wind-driven control experiments remain at five. V2 explicitly reports 95% confidence bounds or ranges and latency uncertainty bands, whereas v1's result tables provide point estimates without confidence intervals.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive MuJoCo and diagnostic results and revises retained-task estimates. For example, Pendulum trace 3 changes from LCPO-S -194 in v1 Table 1 to LCPO -237 in v2 Table 2; revised settings prevent interpreting this as a controlled performance decline. The new Reacher results show DDQN and online EWC outperforming LCPO on all four traces.

M1.justification: V2 retains v1's LCPO-S procedure as LCPO, but removes the doubly constrained LCPO-D and proximal LCPO-P alternatives. It adds bounded reservoir sampling to the accumulating experience archive described in v1. Automatic entropy regularization was already used in v1; its explicit inclusion in v2's objective is not a new component.

P1.justification: V2 changes the title and replaces input terminology with context terminology throughout. It substantially rewrites the introduction and methodology, swaps Preliminaries and Related Work, reorganizes evaluation around comparisons and sensitivities, and adds separate Discussion and Limitations and Broader Impact sections. The appendices are also extensively reorganized.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the grid-world illustration into two modes and combines its two performance plots. It adds change-point, normalized-return, EWC and buffer-size figures; removes the Pendulum learning-curve figure; relocates trace and systems illustrations to the appendices; and substantially expands result tables and uncertainty displays.

R1.justification: V2 adds a dedicated latent-context literature discussion and substantially expands positioning within observed exogenous-context RL, citing works such as Zintgraf, Caccia, Chen, Feng and Sinclair. It also develops comparisons with model-based learning and online EWC. The LCPO-P relationship to editable neural networks and its Sinitsin citation disappear.

T1.justification: V1 Appendix A.1's dual/KKT derivation for the doubly constrained optimization problem, including Equations 5–12, is removed entirely. V2 retains the former LCPO-S trust-region formulation and explicitly states the existing policy-gradient and entropy objectives, but supplies no replacement derivation for the removed solver.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical coverage and limited diagnostic and uncertainty reporting. Additional control tasks, relevant baselines, memory and model-error controls, confidence ranges and reproducibility disclosures make the evidence much more informative. These gains outweigh the narrower solver coverage and some lost environment detail. The broad superiority wording nevertheless needs qualification given the Reacher exceptions in Table 2.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LCPO research, with matching core formulations and retained experiments. The main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: V2 reports original results across six evaluation environments, the grid-world illustration, and additional sensitivity and diagnostic experiments in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original grid-world, wind-driven Pendulum and straggler-mitigation experiments, plus action-space validation in Appendix B.

title: Online Reinforcement Learning in Non-Stationary Context-Driven Environments

C1.justification: The central contribution remains OOD-based policy anchoring to mitigate forgetting without task labels in observed exogenous-context environments. Both versions claim strong aggregate performance relative to online baselines and proximity to offline-trained policies. Expanded supporting evidence and oracle-to-prescient terminology do not redefine that contribution.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations for Sliding OGD, CLEAR, and PT-DQN failures and for LCPO-P's sensitivity to its penalty coefficient. It develops the causal-versus-prescient performance distinction, discusses OOD tuning requirements, and proposes forgetting sufficiently old contexts when network capacity becomes limiting.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds reservoir and OOD-sampling pseudocode and implementation detail. v3 also supplies new baseline/LCPO-P hyperparameters, warm-up details, software versions/licenses, and runtime information, and changes the code-access pointer. It newly discloses that the straggler environment and dataset are nonpublic and proprietary.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same grid-world example, five Gymnasium environments under four wind traces, and straggler mitigation on two production workloads. The added OOD and LCPO-P studies vary detector or optimizer configurations within this coverage.

E2.justification: v3 Tables 5–6 add evaluated Sliding OGD, CLEAR, BFDQN, and PT-DQN comparators. Appendix E.1 also compares LCPO-P. The buffer-size table replaces individually listed baseline columns with the best baseline per condition; the oracle-to-prescient renaming does not introduce a new comparator.

E3.justification: The grid-world diagnostic changes from up-action probability for one context to total-variation distance for both contexts. Added experiments specify OOD metric/threshold configurations and PPO settings for LCPO-P. Existing action discretization and main LCPO hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: OOD sensitivity testing expands beyond the retained straggler thresholds to Gymnasium threshold sweeps and a detector using joint state-context inputs without their separation. New analyses compare constrained anchoring with LCPO-P and examine forgetting in both grid-world modes. Existing buffer-size and ideal-model MBPO checks remain.

E5.justification: v3 reports 25 seeds for most main Gymnasium comparisons instead of five, retaining five for MBPO/MBCD and ten for straggler experiments. CDFs gain 95% confidence bands, and table captions explicitly define boldface through 95%-confidence superiority. Confidence intervals already existed in v2's tables.

E6.justification: Many Gymnasium estimates change alongside revised seed counts: LCPO on Pendulum trace 2 changes from -357 ±6.38 to -355 ±2.57. New comparator, OOD, LCPO-P, and runtime results substantially expand the evidence. Straggler Table 1 remains numerically unchanged; updated estimates do not establish an algorithmic performance gain.

M1.justification: The principal constrained LCPO algorithm is retained. Appendix E.1 introduces LCPO-P, an alternative that uses a cross-entropy anchoring penalty and repeated PPO updates instead of LCPO's hard anchoring constraint.

P1.justification: v3 reorganizes the illustration and methodology into subsections, moves detailed baseline explanations into Appendix D, rewrites the related-work narrative, and reverses the ordering of the two sensitivity sections. It adopts prescient terminology, adds reproducibility and acknowledgement sections, and removes the generic broader-impact section.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation. v3 merges and expands the grid-world figures, adds an LCPO architecture diagram and new analysis tables, splits the main benchmark table, and rearranges existing context and latency panels. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: Section 3 and new Appendix A substantially expand positioning against latent-context inference, meta-learning, multitask RL, stationary interference, and limited-buffer methods. New citations include Woo et al. (2022) and Anand and Precup (2023), with detailed discussion of how their approaches differ from LCPO.

T1.justification: v3 adds formal lifelong-average-return definitions, Lemma B.1 and Theorem B.2 with a tabular Q-learning convergence proof under restricted context assumptions, and binomial OOD-sampling analysis. These are absent from v2. The theorem's printed reward and learning-rate inequalities contain apparent sign errors.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v2's limited continual-learning comparator coverage and evidence for the anchoring design through additional baselines, Gymnasium OOD tests, and the LCPO-P comparison. More reported seeds, computational measurements, and implementation details strengthen empirical reliability and transparency. The new theorem's erroneous printed inequalities require correction, but this localized weakness does not outweigh the substantial validation and documentation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LCPO research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical evaluations and adds comparator results, OOD experiments, an LCPO-P comparison, and computational measurements in Section 5 and the appendices.

before.justification: v2 reports original grid-world, wind-driven Gymnasium, and straggler-mitigation experiments, including comparative results and ablations in Section 6 and Appendices A–B.

title: Online Reinforcement Learning in Non-Stationary Context-Driven Environments

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add the general noise–depth–purity relationship as a central contribution. The main learning guarantee narrows from O(poly log n) noisy-circuit depth in v1 Theorem 2 to O(log n) in v3 Theorem 3, while approximation accuracy becomes explicit. The central QML complexity-prediction claim remains.

C2.justification: v3 adds a substantive explanation for restricting pure-state approximation to logarithmic depth and interprets the new overlap bound as an applicability boundary. It also introduces a connection between circuit entanglement and noise spreading. The existing discussions of sampling advantages and prospective applications largely remain.

D1.justification: v1 Appendix D.4 supplies coarse coefficient-domain intervals. v3 Appendix E.3 additionally describes estimating their bounds through one-dimensional polynomial optimization, including kernel choices and approximation margins. This provides more explicit computational instructions without demonstrating a new implementation.

E1.justification: Neither version evaluates datasets or application tasks. Quantum phase classification and circuit learning remain theoretical applications; revised formal task boundaries are covered under T1 and C1.

E2.justification: Neither version reports evaluated comparison methods. References to classical simulation and other learning approaches provide theoretical context, not baseline experiments.

E3.justification: Neither PDF reports an experimental evaluation protocol. Changes to sample requirements and optimization budgets specify theoretical algorithms and guarantees, not performed evaluations.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, robustness tests or evaluated case studies. The added noise analysis is a theorem and proof, assessed under T1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports empirical runs, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The retained Gaussian-process uncertainty model and probabilistic regret guarantees are theoretical.

E6.justification: v3 Section III.B adds an analytical numerical illustration: n = 50 and local depolarizing strength p = 10^-3 give a stated depth bound of 46 log(1/eta). This is a newly reported calculation, not an empirical performance improvement.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 retain the shadow-based objective, Bayesian optimization and binary search. v3 makes epsilon an explicit input, replaces the 1/n acceptance threshold with epsilon, and changes the prescribed QNN sample count from LRn^4 to LRn^2/epsilon^2.

P1.justification: Existing passages in the introduction, noise setup, task statement and algorithm exposition are substantially rewritten. Section III is reorganized, Section IV gains a Metric Construction subsection, and the proof appendices are restructured. These changes recast the narrative beyond theorem renumbering; authorship and acknowledgments also change.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to identify the noisy-state shadow, show N sampled QNN circuits and label the loss connecting them. Its three-panel organization remains. Algorithm blocks shift within the layout, but no experimental plots or result tables are introduced.

R1.justification: v3 removes the Cerezo et al. cost-dependent barren-plateau reference and Anschuetz–Kiani traps reference from v1. It expands the introduction's discussion of Gibbs-ball simulation limits and AdS/CFT motivation using existing references. Appendix A's principal research positioning remains.

T1.justification: v3 removes v1's global-depolarizing rank argument and its supporting material in Appendix D.1–D.2. It adds Theorem 1 and Appendix E.1, deriving an expected pure/noisy-state overlap bound for general Kraus noise under independent unitary 2-design layers. It also revises SSAP and learning guarantees to explicit epsilon and logarithmic depth, and adds the coefficient-domain derivation in Appendix E.3. The local-depolarizing analysis is retained as Appendix D.

improvement.justification: The explicit error-dependent algorithms and new coefficient-domain construction make the method easier to assess, while Theorem 1 supplies a conditional noise–depth characterization absent from v1. These are useful gains in specificity. However, the new theorem is ensemble-averaged, and Section VI.B and Appendix A retain polylogarithmic scope wording despite Theorem 3's logarithmic restriction, limiting the improvement in overall clarity and rigor.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same structured-complexity-prediction work. Their text, equations, figure, algorithms and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial theoretical revisions.

after.justification: v3 remains theoretical. Its new 50-qubit numerical example illustrates an analytical bound rather than reporting an experiment or simulation.

before.justification: v1 presents algorithms, proofs and proposed applications, including phase classification, but no original experimental, simulation or data-analysis outcomes.

title: Learning the Complexity of Weakly Noisy Quantum States

C1.justification: v4 adds sample optimality with respect to circuit depth as a headline claim in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. Its decision guarantee now explicitly permits an indeterminate case. The efficient structured-complexity prediction claim remains, while v3's separate mixed-state approximation contribution and Corollary 1 are dropped.

C2.justification: v4 interprets the simulations as showing that complexity lower bounds need not increase with preparation depth and interprets the stress tests as supporting scalability. Appendices B–D add substantive discussion of gate-dependent noise as unresolved, local versus global noise applicability, and the absence of real-device testing.

D1.justification: v4 newly identifies PennyLane, a 64-vCPU server with 128 GiB memory, and the simulation's gate decomposition and parameter choices. Appendix C adds proposed hardware requirements of 50–100 noisy qubits, gate fidelity at least 0.99, and error-mitigated shadow preparation. Neither PDF provides a code release.

E1.justification: v3 has no empirical task coverage. v4 evaluates complexity lower bounds for noisy transverse-field Ising dynamics on a 3-by-4 lattice and on 1D chains of 6, 8, and 10 qubits. The prospective phase-classification applications in v3 were not evaluated datasets.

E2.justification: Neither version reports an empirical comparison against competing algorithms. The different preparation depths in v4 Figures 2 and 3 are target-state conditions, not baseline methods; cited learning methods are discussed without comparative evaluation.

E3.justification: v4 introduces an experimental protocol absent from v3: first-order Trotter dynamics, local depolarizing noise p = 0.001, target preparation depths 2 and 10, comparison-circuit depths 2 through 5, N = n^2 R sampled circuits, and epsilon = 0.01. These are settings for new experiments, not revisions to previously reported experiments.

E4.justification: v4 adds sensitivity evidence across five transverse-field settings in Figure 2. Appendix L introduces explicit stress tests across 6-, 8-, and 10-qubit chains, examining separation between depth conditions and stability of variability. v3 contains no corresponding empirical robustness analyses.

E5.justification: Section 6 newly reports means from ten independent experiments per plotted point and error bars described as 'standard variance.' v3 contains no empirical repetition counts or error bars. This adds basic uncertainty reporting without significance tests or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: All simulation results are new. Figure 2(b) reports LS-complexity lower bounds greater than 4L for preparation depth 2 and greater than 2L for depth 10, at LS error 0.125. Figure 3 adds analogous lower-bound separation on 1D chains. These are new findings, not same-setting performance improvements over v3.

M1.justification: The shadow-based Bayesian optimization and binary-search framework remains, but v4 changes optimization from joint (q, beta) parameters to beta with a sampling distribution q, introduces a nonnegative coefficient restriction, and adds separate epsilon/2epsilon decisions with an indeterminate outcome. Appendix I also replaces deliberately added unit-variance noise with snapshot-dependent measurement noise.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. QNN/SQNN terminology becomes QCA, the background is condensed, problem formulation is reorganized, and Bayesian optimization moves to Appendix I. The appendices are extensively restructured, beyond changes caused solely by adding experiments.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redesigned to depict data collection and classical learning. New multi-panel Figures 2 and 3 display simulations and stress tests. The document adopts the ICLR conference layout, with changed typography, headers, and algorithm placement. Neither version contains result tables.

R1.justification: Appendix A substantially revises research positioning, adding comparisons with circuit-learning work by Huang et al. (2024) and Landau and Liu (2024), and a detailed discussion of Schuster et al. (2024) and pseudorandomness. Noise-learning and error-mitigation references are added, while much of v3's broad variational-algorithm and chemistry coverage is removed.

T1.justification: v4 adds the sample-complexity lower bound and Appendix J proof, formal decision intervals, and explicit weak-Pauli-noise scaling. The intrinsic-structure bound acquires a log n factor and its derivation changes. v3's unitary-learning theorem, entropy warm-up analysis, and several auxiliary derivations are removed. The noise-overlap result is retained as Fact 1, corresponding to v3 Theorem 1.

improvement.justification: v4 adds useful simulations, repeated-run reporting, and clearer applicability discussions. However, its new headline optimality claim is not established by the displayed lower bound: under p = O(1/n) and depth O(log n), that bound falls below one sample. Appendix L also extrapolates 6–10-qubit tests to large-scale reliability. These concrete gains coexist with new gaps between evidence and claims, preventing a confident net-quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same structured quantum-state complexity prediction framework. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching retained results across renaming and relocation.

after.justification: v4 reports original transverse-field Ising simulations in Section 6 and Figure 2, with additional 1D simulations in Appendix L and Figure 3.

before.justification: v3 presents theoretical results, algorithms, and prospective applications, but no original experimental or simulation outcomes. Its numerical illustration of a theoretical noise bound is not an empirical study.

title: Learning the Complexity of Weakly Noisy Quantum States

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion preserve the same novelty, model-agnostic applicability, training-free valuation, and experimental-effectiveness claims.

C2.justification: The interpretations of RA1–RA3 and Section 6's proposed privacy, content-pricing, and intellectual-property applications are unchanged. No substantive limitation or applicability qualification is added.

D1.justification: Implementation and reproducibility information are unchanged. The new acknowledgment of an NVIDIA Hardware Award does not specify experimental hardware, hyperparameters, or code/data access.

E1.justification: Both retain the CIFAR-10 training-versus-nontraining comparisons and CelebA face-matching examples. The MNIST description is also unchanged; no dataset, task, domain, or test scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates competing data-valuation methods; methods such as Shapley valuation remain discussion-only. The same BigGAN, classifier-free guidance diffusion, and StyleGAN2 evaluations are retained.

E3.justification: Sections 5.1–5.3 retain the same CIFAR-10 partition design, generator choices, VGG-16 embeddings with t-SNE, and CelebA matching procedure. No experimental setting or evaluation procedure is revised.

E4.justification: The distribution visualization in Figure 2 and high-value versus low-value image case study in Figure 3 are unchanged. No ablation, sensitivity analysis, or robustness test is added or removed.

E5.justification: Section 5.3 and Table 1 retain the same hypothesis-testing procedure and significance-threshold reporting. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Table 1 retains training/nontraining means of 1.632352/0.319654 for BigGAN and 0.369565/0.030434 for classifier-free guidance diffusion, with identical p-values and t-statistics. Figures 2–3 and their reported findings are also unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Algorithm 1 retain the same product-quantization similarity matching, top-k selection, contribution scoring, and aggregation procedure. No method component changes.

P1.justification: v2 adds Section 8, Acknowledgments, between the conclusion and references, crediting NSERC, Public Safety Canada, and NVIDIA. The arXiv version/date stamp changes; the scientific prose and narrative structure otherwise remain unchanged.

P2.justification: The acknowledgments block shifts the reference layout on pages 9–10, moving entries 14–15 onto page 10. Other differences are minor text reflow; Figures 1–3, Table 1, and Algorithm 1 retain their displays and placement.

R1.justification: Section 2, all 30 cited works, and the positioning relative to prior data-valuation research remain unchanged. Reference relocation does not introduce additional literature.

T1.justification: The IID assumption, Wasserstein formulation, and scoring and aggregation definitions in Equations 1–6 are retained. No mathematical assumption, derivation, or proof is added or corrected.

improvement.justification: The added acknowledgments provide funding attribution, while the method, evidence, interpretations, and reproducibility information remain unchanged. The limited layout changes neither materially improve nor harm readability, leaving overall paper quality essentially unchanged.

A1.justification: Both readable ten-page PDFs describe the same GMValuator study, with corresponding equations, Algorithm 1, Figures 1–3, and Table 1. All pages were inspected; both documents end with references and contain no appendices.

after.justification: Section 5 retains the original CIFAR-10 analyses and CelebA image-matching results in Figure 2, Table 1, and Figure 3.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original CIFAR-10 distribution and data-value analyses (Figure 2 and Table 1), alongside CelebA image-matching examples (Figure 3).

title: GMValuator: Similarity-based Data Valuation for Generative Models

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same novelty and scope claims: a first model-agnostic, training-free, post-hoc valuation approach for generative models based on similarity matching.

C2.justification: Sections 5.3 and 6 retain the same interpretations linking similarity to contribution and the same proposed privacy, content-pricing and intellectual-property applications. No substantive limitation or applicability qualification is added.

D1.justification: The same matching details, VGG-16 embedding choice, dataset descriptions and generator choices are documented. No new hyperparameter, hardware, training-budget, code-access or data-access information is supplied.

E1.justification: The CIFAR-10 training-versus-held-out comparisons and CelebA face-matching evaluation are unchanged. Both versions also list MNIST without separately displaying its experimental results. No dataset, task or test scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: Neither version reports comparisons against competing data-valuation algorithms; LOO, Shapley and Banzhaf methods remain background discussion. BigGAN, StyleGAN2 and classifier-free guidance diffusion retain the same experimental roles.

E3.justification: Both retain the same nonoverlapping CIFAR-10 subsets, training on Xv1, VGG-16 embeddings with t-SNE visualization, valuation comparison against Xv2, and CelebA/StyleGAN2 evaluation. No reported evaluation setting or procedure changes.

E4.justification: The RA1–RA3 analyses remain the same: distribution visualization, training-versus-held-out valuation comparison, and high-/low-value face examples. Splitting v2 Figure 3 into v4 Figures 3 and 4 adds no new case study or analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same hypotheses, t-statistics, p-values and 0.01 significance level in Table 1, alongside unchanged threshold discussion in Section 5.3. Neither adds run counts, seeds, error bars or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: All Table 1 values match, including Xv1/Xv2 means of 1.632352/0.319654 for BigGAN and 0.369565/0.030434 for diffusion. The t-SNE plot, face examples and reported qualitative findings are also unchanged.

M1.justification: Sections 4.1–4.2 and Algorithm 1 retain the same product-quantization similarity matching, top-k selection, exponential distance weighting and aggregation over generated samples. No algorithmic component changes.

P1.justification: Prose and section order remain essentially unchanged. Limited edits include changing the author spelling from Wenglong Deng to Wenlong Deng, removing the keywords line, and updating punctuation and figure references.

P2.justification: The document is comprehensively reformatted from one column to two, changing typography and placement of figures, tables and Algorithm 1. Table 1 changes from side-by-side model columns to vertically stacked blocks, while Figure 3(a,b) becomes separate Figures 3 and 4 containing the same images.

R1.justification: Both retain the same 30 references and the same related-work discussion and novelty positioning. Citation-range compression and bibliographic formatting do not change the cited works.

T1.justification: The IID assumption, generative-model background, Wasserstein formulation and valuation definitions in Equations 1–6 are unchanged. No formal result, derivation or proof is added or revised.

improvement.justification: The extensive layout revision preserves readable access to the same method, evidence and claims. Existing issues also persist, including Section 5.3 stating that the p-value is greater than 0.05 despite Table 1 reporting extremely small p-values. The presentation changes and limited editorial edits produce no meaningful overall quality difference.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GMValuator work. Inspection of all pages establishes that the text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

after.justification: v4 retains the original CIFAR-10 results in Figure 2 and Table 1 and the CelebA/StyleGAN2 matching results, now displayed in Figures 3 and 4.

before.justification: v2 reports original CIFAR-10 visualization and statistical valuation results in Figure 2 and Table 1, plus CelebA/StyleGAN2 qualitative matching results in Figure 3.

title: GMValuator: Similarity-based Data Valuation for Generative Models

C1.justification: v5 narrows v4's broad claim of being the first generative-model data-valuation work to being the first model-agnostic, training-free approach, acknowledging existing model-specific methods. It also elevates image-quality calibration and four evaluation criteria into explicit contributions in the abstract and introduction.

C2.justification: v5 adds substantive explanations of equal-credit bias for poor generated images, accumulated contributions from distant samples, and the accuracy/runtime tradeoff of DreamSim. It attributes VAE-TracIn's weak CIFAR-10 results to possible underfitting and identifies other modalities as future validation. v4 mainly interprets training-set proximity and qualitative facial resemblance; its applications discussion survives in Appendix F.

D1.justification: v5 newly provides hardware specifications in Table I, expanded dataset and model information in Appendix E, and layer/latent specifications in Table VII, substantially extending v4's sparse implementation documentation. Reliability is limited by reversed CPU/GPU labels and apparently swapped BigGAN/beta-VAE headings. These disclosures do not establish changes to previously unspecified settings.

title: GMValuator: Similarity-based Data Valuation for Generative Models

C1.justification: The title, abstract, and introduction expand the principal claims from estimation MSE to both prediction and estimation risks, including trace-based variance characterization for both. v1's two-part contribution of general conditional bounds and more restrictive unconditional characterization is replaced by an emphasis on exact finite-sample variance factorization.

C2.justification: v2 narrows applicability to errors independent of the design, removing discussion of design-dependent heteroskedasticity and the conditional-bound argument for bias dominance. It extends the trace-only interpretation to prediction variance and newly asserts that prediction bias depends only on rank deficiency under its weighted random-effects assumption.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds a brief instruction to apply the existing Monte Carlo approach analogously to prediction variance. The Gaussian/Haar covariance construction and nested sampling recipe are otherwise retained, with no new code-access, hardware, or runtime information.

E1.justification: Both evaluate the same Gaussian-design linear-regression simulations with autoregressive and clustered errors and the same overparameterization scenarios. Prediction risk adds measurements on retained simulations. The removed heteroskedastic examples in Appendix A were theoretical examples, not evaluated datasets or scenarios.

E2.justification: Neither version benchmarks alternative estimators. Both compare simulated quantities with finite-sample theoretical expressions and asymptotic reference curves; the added prediction-risk expressions do not introduce a competing estimation method.

E3.justification: v2 adds covariance-weighted prediction variance and bias as evaluation quantities. Existing settings remain: n=50, p=100 for Figure 1; n=20, p=40 for Figure 2; and fixed n=50 with varying p/n for Figure 3. No revision to the retained simulation protocol is documented.

E4.justification: v2 extends the existing analyses to prediction risk: Figure 4 checks insensitivity to randomized within-cluster covariances, and Figure 3 examines behavior as p/n increases. These supplement the corresponding estimation-risk analyses already present in v1.

E5.justification: Figures 1 and 2 retain 100 design-matrix samples and 100 error samples per design realization. Neither version adds seed reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates for the Monte Carlo results.

E6.justification: Figures 1, 2, and 4 add empirical prediction-variance contours and corresponding theoretical values. Figure 3 adds prediction-variance and prediction-bias curves across p/n. These substantially expand reported outcomes and extend the reported trace-factorization and variance-descent findings; the earlier estimation-risk panels are retained.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same minimum-norm least-squares estimator computed through the Moore–Penrose inverse. v2's explicit constrained-minimization formulation does not change the estimation procedure.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, research questions, and contribution paragraphs are rewritten. Section 2 becomes a framework section; variance and bias receive separate sections organized by risk type; the former asymptotics section becomes Section 4.2.1. Clustered-error explanations are rewritten, and the former Appendix A content disappears.

P2.justification: Figures 1, 2, and 4 expand from two to four panels, and Figure 3 expands from one to two panels. Prediction results appear above retained estimation results, with revised legends and captions. Figure 3 is now placed after Appendix B begins.

R1.justification: The cited works are unchanged. v2 drops v1's explicit assertion that left-spherical symmetry had not been explored for ridgeless estimators and repositions the contribution from an estimation-MSE alternative to a joint finite-sample treatment of prediction and estimation risks.

T1.justification: v2 adds prediction-variance Theorem 3.2 with a singular-vector/Haar-averaging proof, weighted random-effects Assumption 4.2, and prediction-risk Corollary 4.1. It removes v1's conditional bounds, Theorem 2.2, covariance-dependence relaxation, and Appendix A examples, while strengthening error independence assumptions. Estimation-risk formulas and asymptotics largely survive renumbering. The new prediction-bias derivation in Equation (5) contains an invalid matrix-square step for general anisotropic covariance.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful prediction-variance theory and numerical evidence, but introduces a substantive error into its new full prediction-risk claim. Appendix C's proof of Equation (5) replaces a matrix–transpose product with the square of a generally nonsymmetric matrix. Consequently, the claimed rank-only prediction bias and Corollary 4.1 fail for general anisotropic covariance under the stated assumptions. v1's unweighted-bias derivation avoids this error. The damage to a central mathematical claim outweighs the expanded coverage.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ridgeless least-squares research. Their text, equations, figures, references, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite the revised title and substantial theoretical reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these simulations and adds empirical prediction-risk variance and bias results in Figures 1–4.

before.justification: v1 reports original Monte Carlo simulations with autoregressive and clustered errors, including empirical variance estimates and overparameterization curves in Figures 1–4.

title: Prediction Risk and Estimation Risk of the Ridgeless Least Squares Estimator under General Assumptions on Regression Errors

C1.justification: V3 drops the explicit abstract claim that adding many unimportant parameters reduces both risks and instead emphasizes applicability to clustered or serial dependence and time-series, panel and grouped data. It adds an interpretation of the ACS curves as suggesting broader dependence-insensitivity. Figure 4's caption also clarifies isotropic feature covariance, correcting v2 Figure 3's reference to isotropic error covariance.

The previous synthetic-generation and Monte Carlo documentation is retained.

E2.justification: No competing estimator is added or removed from the reported comparisons. The simulations retain comparisons against theoretical risk expressions; the ACS specifications vary features within the same estimator.

improvement.justification: V3 improves readability and scope qualification through direct theory–simulation overlays, a clearer proof presentation and an explicit design-assumption limitation. The net gains are useful but limited, with the theoretical results unchanged.

before.justification: V2 reports original simulations of prediction and estimation risk under AR(1) and clustered errors, including the supplementary experiment in Figure 4.

title: Prediction Risk and Estimation Risk of the Ridgeless Least Squares Estimator under General Assumptions on Regression Errors

It supplies the RNASolo snapshot date, A100 hardware, training time and state-dependent memory costs. These substantially expand reproducibility information; newly disclosed settings alone do not establish procedural changes.

The dedicated ensemble-size evaluation and theophylline case study from v1 are no longer reported. RNASolo remains the inverse-design data source.

E2.justification: v1 principally compares multi-state gRNAde with its single-state variant. v4 adds Rosetta and FARNA comparisons using published recovery values, plus fitness-ranking baselines that randomly select from all variants, single mutants, or single and double mutants. Appendix Table 2 additionally compares autoregressive and one-shot decoders.

It adds MCC/perplexity metrics and screening-budget evaluation, while changing encoder/decoder depth from 3 to 4 layers, training from 100 to at most 50 epochs, and initial learning rate from 0.001 to 0.0001.

The detailed theophylline case study in v1 Table 2 is removed.

The new fitness study extends uncertainty reporting through 10,000 simulations per randomized strategy and screening budget. Figure 7 specifies medians and interquartile ranges, although the surrounding text calls the intervals confidence intervals. This does not establish an increase in training runs.

E6.justification: The original splitwise and theophylline results are replaced by new benchmark, ablation and fitness-ranking findings. v4 Appendix Table 1 reports recovery of 0.5682 for gRNAde versus 0.45 for Rosetta and 0.32 for FARNA. In its multi-state split, one-to-five-state mean recovery rises from 0.4549 to 0.4722, while mean MCC falls from 0.5689 to 0.5488 (Appendix Table 2). Changed protocols prevent interpreting these as performance changes relative to v1.

M1.justification: The multi-state GVP encoder, conformer averaging and autoregressive decoder remain. Graph construction changes from C4' coordinates with 10 neighbors to three-bead centroids with 32 neighbors, and edge encodings increase from 16 to 32 channels. v4 also describes distance/angle/torsion features and evaluates a one-shot MLP decoder variant. These refine the retained architecture.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten. The method becomes a structured exposition of the problem, representation, architecture and metrics; results are organized into three application sections. Separate related-work and usage-FAQ appendices substantially reorganize and expand the narrative around retained technical material.

P2.justification: v4 changes the main layout from two columns to one, redraws the pipeline and adds feature, architecture, evaluation and tensor-symmetry diagrams. New benchmark, nucleotide-analysis and fitness plots accompany redesigned result tables. The dataset-statistics display is retained and updated as Figure 9; the theophylline structure/sequence-logo table is removed.

R1.justification: v4 adds a substantial related-work appendix covering energy-based inverse folding, backbone generation, structure prediction and RNA language models, including RNA FM, RiNaLMo and CodonBERT. It develops comparisons with Rosetta and positions gRNAde as a structure-conditioned language model, substantially extending v1's shorter RNA-versus-protein motivation.

T1.justification: v4 adds an explicit distinction between the SO(3)-equivariant encoder with dihedral inputs and its O(3)-equivariant GVP layers. Section 4.2 also introduces a numerical probability-averaging counterexample; it does not establish the accompanying criticism of logit averaging because it averages probabilities. The main pooling mathematics remains, without substantial new theorem or proof development.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens evidence previously centered on recovery against its own single-state baseline. Structural-cluster holdouts, comparisons with published Rosetta/FARNA results, controlled ablations and retrospective fitness analysis improve assessment of generalization and practical utility.
