These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: Rosetta runtime superiority is not established by controlled timing, and Figure 5's single-seed self-consistency benefit does not persist in the three-seed means in Appendix Table 2.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same gRNAde multi-state RNA design framework. Their main texts, appendices, equations, figures and tables are readable and support reliable comparison despite the changed title and expanded scope.

after.justification: v4 reports original gRNAde evaluations, ablations, nucleotide-level analyses and retrospective fitness-ranking simulations. Rosetta and FARNA results are explicitly attributed to prior work.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations across three data splits and a theophylline aptamer case study, including numerical sequence-recovery results in Tables 1–2.

title: gRNAde: Geometric Deep Learning for 3D RNA inverse design

C1.justification: The abstract and central design, speed, and multi-state claims remain stable. V5's conclusion adds the claim that perplexity correlates with structural recovery. The introduction stops foregrounding partial design as a contribution, although that capability remains described in Section 2.3.

C2.justification: V5 adds substantive interpretations of 3D designability, native-sequence predictions as a reference ceiling, transfer from ribosomal training data, and autoregressive modeling of paired nucleotide constraints. It expands guidance on predictor-dependent sequence selection. It also removes explicit statements about inability to modulate conformational propensities and random selection outperforming gRNAde at larger screening budgets; the latter behavior remains visible in revised Figure 7.

D1.justification: V5 specifies a 3,000-node minibatch limit for the reported GPU-memory figures and eight encoder layers for non-autoregressive models. It also supplies designed sequences with structural examples. These improve implementation and reproduction detail without establishing changes to the underlying retained experiments; code access remains unchanged.

E1.justification: V5 extends fitness-ranking evaluation from catalytic subunit 5TU to scaffolding subunit t1, covering 47,504 mutants in Figure 12. RNASolo coverage and the 14-RNA benchmark remain unchanged; the three structural case studies use RNAs already represented in v4.

E2.justification: V5 adds ViennaRNA to the 14-RNA comparison and both aggregate test splits, plus ground-truth-sequence and random-sequence controls in Table 1. These substantially broaden comparison beyond the retained Rosetta/FARNA results and model variants.

E3.justification: V5 adds RhoFold-based C4' RMSD, TM-score, GDT_TS, and designability-threshold percentages. Appendix A introduces evaluations using 100 designs per RNA at temperature 0.5, alongside the retained standard 16-design, temperature-0.1 protocol. Figure 7 revises screening budgets and extends them from 2,000 to 10,493. The stated 'All data' evaluation changes from the multi-state to single-state test set, and one training-length ablation changes from 2,000 to 2,500 nucleotides; these disclosures do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: V5 adds invariant-versus-equivariant GNN ablations, extends autoregressive/non-autoregressive comparisons to the single-state split, and evaluates existing ablations using 3D metrics. Figures 8–11 add structural case studies and perplexity-versus-structural-consistency analysis. Conversely, v4's three-state and five-state non-autoregressive ablation rows are absent from v5 Table 1.

E5.justification: Both versions report standard deviations across three consistent random seeds and summarize stochastic fitness-ranking strategies using medians and interquartile ranges from 10,000 simulations. Added results retain these practices; changed numerical uncertainties do not establish a change in statistical procedure.

E6.justification: V5 adds extensive 3D scores, baseline results, structural examples, and t1 fitness-ranking outcomes. Some retained aggregate values change beyond rounding: single-state, one-state AR recovery changes from 0.5271 to 0.530, and secondary-structure MCC from 0.5706 to 0.585 (v4 Table 2; v5 Table 1). The original 14-RNA gRNAde, Rosetta, and FARNA entries remain unchanged, with ViennaRNA added at 0.27 overall recovery. 'All data' results accompany a changed stated test split and cannot establish same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The proposed backbone featurization, multi-state GVP-GNN encoder, conformer pooling, autoregressive decoder, loss, and sampling procedure remain unchanged in Section 2 and Listing 1. The added invariant-GNN configurations are evaluated as ablations.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and section order are retained. V5 makes local language corrections, adds an author and affiliation, expands metric and FAQ explanations, and organizes appendix material into dedicated visualization, ablation, results, and figure sections.

P2.justification: V5 adds structural overlays, structural-score plots, and the t1 ranking figure; expands the aggregate table substantially; and adds ViennaRNA to Figure 4. It redraws and promotes the evaluation schematic, relocates the architecture diagram to the appendix, and merges existing multi-state recovery plots while dropping the separate secondary-consistency panel. These materially revise visual presentation beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: V5 adds Shen et al. (2022) for its structure-prediction evaluation and Vicens and Kieft (2022) for RNA structural interactions, while removing Maron et al. (2020). The related-work discussion and principal novelty positioning remain essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: The graph definitions, symmetry statements, and Equations 1–3 are retained. The illustrative argument against averaging single-state predictions moves into the FAQ. New empirical metrics and interpretive discussion introduce no formal derivations, proofs, or revised mathematical results.

improvement.justification: V4 evaluates a 3D design method mainly through sequence recovery and secondary structure. V5 addresses this important evidential gap with systematic 3D self-consistency measurements, native/random controls, and structural examples, while expanded ablations and a second fitness landscape strengthen assessment of applicability. Predictor limitations and selected examples constrain biological conclusions, and removing the explicit high-budget caveat weakens balance somewhat. Nevertheless, the added evidence substantially improves the paper's ability to demonstrate and expose limits of design fidelity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same gRNAde research. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V5 retains these original results and adds structural evaluations, expanded ablations, and retrospective fitness ranking for the t1 ribozyme subunit.

before.justification: V4 reports original gRNAde evaluations on single-state and multi-state RNA design, ablations, and retrospective simulations of ribozyme mutant selection.

title: gRNAde: Geometric Deep Learning for 3D RNA inverse design

C1.justification: The three headline contributions remain single-state design, multi-state design and zero-shot fitness ranking. v6's introduction makes the multi-state recovery claim quantitative at 5%, and its conclusion adds superiority over Rosetta in both computational and experimental performance. The latter wording is broader without a new direct experimental comparison against Rosetta.

C2.justification: v6 interprets equivariance as improving evaluation metrics, whereas v5 reported no significant differences beyond fitting the training distribution. It adds predictor-choice rationale and discussion of expensive molecular-dynamics validation, but removes the specific assay-noise caveat and the discussion of random mutagenesis as complementary local exploration. Most applicability limitations and the FAQs are retained.

D1.justification: v6 adds CPU inference timing of approximately 10 seconds and discloses over 2.8 million training nucleotides. It omits v5's explicit averaging rule for multi-state structural scores and the description of training all-data release checkpoints; this does not establish that checkpoint access was withdrawn. Core hyperparameters, pseudocode and the repository address remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same RNASolo collection of 4,223 sequences and 12,011 structures, the single-state and multi-state design benchmarks, and the 5TU/t1 ribozyme fitness landscapes. Additional state counts and model variants concern configurations within retained coverage.

E2.justification: v6 adds RDesign to the 14-RNA comparison in Figure 4 and Table 2, reporting mean recovery of 0.4296; v5 compares against ViennaRNA, FARNA and Rosetta. Appendix B also newly reports a qualitative comparison with NuPack's design tool, without numerical scores. Existing external comparators are retained.

E3.justification: The stated split construction, default training budget, metrics and sampling of 16 sequences at temperature 0.1 are retained. Within this framework, v6 adds two-/four-state evaluations, random-order decoding and additional model configurations, switches the multi-state training-length ablation from one-state to three-state models, and adds an RNAFold scoring control. The all-data training/evaluation configuration is removed.

E4.justification: The ablation evidence is substantially reworked: v6 adds random-decoding-order and DS/DSS-labelled comparisons, expands multi-state non-autoregressive evaluations, and tests sensitivity to replacing EternaFold with RNAFold. It removes the solvent-accessibility analysis from v5 Figure 6 and some multi-state invariant-model ablations. The structural design case studies remain in the appendices.

E5.justification: v6 Figure 4 newly quantifies the perplexity–recovery association with Pearson correlation -0.76 and Spearman correlation -0.67. Reporting standard deviations across three consistent seeds and interquartile ranges from 10,000 random-strategy simulations is unchanged; there is no stated increase in repetitions.

E6.justification: Table 1 substantially revises multi-state results: the reported one-/three-/five-state autoregressive recoveries change from 0.455/0.467/0.473 to 0.481/0.531/0.510, making three states best among these configurations. Several single-state ablation values also change, RDesign and new control results are added, and all-data results are removed. The 14-RNA gRNAde recovery of 0.5682 and ribozyme-ranking results remain unchanged. The PDFs do not explain the cause of the broad multi-state numerical revisions.

M1.justification: The documented featurization, GVP-GNN updates, Deep Set pooling, autoregressive loss and Listing 1 are unchanged; unordered decoding was already discussed in v5. However, v6 Table 1 introduces variants labelled DSS without defining their operations. The PDFs therefore do not establish whether these represent a substantive architectural adaptation.

P1.justification: The appendix organization is comprehensively reordered, with related work and ablations brought forward, FAQs moved to the end, and a contents list added. The inverse-folding problem subsection is merged into the opening of Section 2, and the ablation narrative is reorganized and expanded. Most main-text prose remains recognizable, but the document structure changes substantially.

P2.justification: v6 adopts different title, heading and page styling and extensively relocates displays. Figure 4 gains an RDesign bar, the multi-state figure changes from three to five state-count groups and loses its solvent-accessibility panel, and both tables are restructured. The duplicated main-text riboswitch visualization is removed while its appendix counterpart is retained.

R1.justification: v6 cites Tan et al. (2023) and positions RDesign as a concurrent GNN-based inverse-folding method. The cryo-EM future-work references to Kappel et al. (2020) and Bonilla and Kieft (2022) are removed. The related-work survey otherwise remains substantively unchanged despite relocation and bibliography restyling.

T1.justification: The multi-graph definitions, message-passing and pooling equations, and equivariance reasoning are retained. The numerical example concerning averaging single-state predictions also remains, moving from Appendix C to Appendix F. No new theorem, proof or mathematical correction is introduced.

improvement.justification: Adding a concurrent neural comparator and checks of decoding order and structure-predictor dependence modestly strengthens the empirical argument beyond v5. The benefit is limited by insufficient documentation of DSS variants, RDesign settings and the revised multi-state results. Removing the assay-noise caveat and broadening the conclusion also reduce caution, so the revision does not establish a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same gRNAde study. All 22 pages of v5 and 23 pages of v6, including equations, figures, tables, pseudocode and appendices, are readable and support comparison despite substantial appendix reordering.

after.justification: v6 retains original sequence-design and ribozyme-ranking results and reports revised multi-state experiments and additional comparisons and controls.

before.justification: v5 reports original gRNAde sequence-design experiments, architectural ablations and retrospective simulations of ribozyme mutant selection using published fitness data.

title: gRNAde: Geometric Deep Learning for 3D RNA inverse design

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add an explicit wet lab validation contribution, specifying ten backbones and approximately 50% success versus 35% for Rosetta. The broader superiority, multi-state novelty, and zero-shot ranking claims remain; v6's conclusion already asserted an advantage in experimental performance.

C2.justification: v7 adds interpretations of experimental scores as evidence of target folding, including the qualification that scores below 80 need not indicate failure. It also adds DSS expressivity/cost tradeoffs, a GPU-versus-CPU timing caveat, and substantial arguments about RDesign's sampling limitations and possible overfitting. The existing limitations concerning interacting chains and negative design remain.

D1.justification: v7 newly explains DSS update steps and discloses approximately 200,000 additional parameters and training iteration times of four versus eight minutes. It also explicitly identifies training/inference code, checkpoints, Colab notebooks, and tutorials. These expand documentation; the retained hyperparameters and pseudocode do not establish an implementation change.

E1.justification: Section 5 adds experimental validation on ten OpenKnot targets, including the SARS-CoV-2 frameshift element, HCV IRES, and synthetic kissing-loop RNA, using partial and full redesign tasks. The existing RNASolo benchmarks and ribozyme fitness datasets remain.

E2.justification: Figure 5a newly includes RDesign in the multi-state benchmark. The new wet lab comparison evaluates Rosetta HiRes and LoRes variants alongside wildtype controls. The original single-state comparator membership is unchanged, including RDesign despite its omission from v7 Table 2's caption.

E3.justification: v7 introduces SHAPE-based evaluation using a 0–100 OpenKnot score and a success threshold above 80, with ten partial and ten full gRNAde designs per target. Existing computational splits and training settings remain unchanged. The separate 100-design, temperature-0.5 RhoFold case-study protocol in v6 Appendix D is removed.

E4.justification: v6 Appendix D's dedicated analysis relating perplexity to 3D designability across three RNAs, together with nine illustrated designs, is removed entirely. Aggregate structural metrics and the architectural ablations remain. v7 additionally reports training-fit and computational-cost diagnostics for the already evaluated DS/DSS pooling variants.

E5.justification: Both versions report standard deviations across three consistent seeds and retain the 10,000-simulation uncertainty reporting for retrospective fitness ranking. The new wet lab figures report score distributions and success proportions without introducing confidence intervals, significance tests, or a new stated uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: New wet lab results report 52% success for partial designs and 49% for full designs, versus 35% and 31% for Rosetta HiRes and LoRes. Figure 5a adds RDesign recovery of 0.385 on the multi-state test set. DSS training-loss diagnostics are newly reported, while the standalone 3D case-study results disappear. Tables 1 and 2 retain their numerical values.

M1.justification: The backbone representation, multi-state GVP-GNN, pooling, autoregressive decoding, and training objective are retained. DSS pooling receives additional explanation, but DSS variants already appear in v6 Table 1. Partial redesign was also already described in v6.

P1.justification: Localized wording edits and expanded explanations accompany the new wet lab section and RDesign appendix. The visualization appendix is removed and later appendices are relabeled, but most existing prose, the main methodological sequence, and the FAQs remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v7 adds aggregate and per-target wet lab plots, adds a RDesign comparison scatterplot, and redraws Figure 5a to include RDesign. It removes v6 Figures 8–11 containing structural analyses and overlays. Retained architecture diagrams, dataset plots, and pseudocode are relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: New Appendix F expands RDesign from a briefly described contemporary baseline into a detailed discussion of publication priority, architectural differences, evaluation choices, and claimed reproducibility problems. Related work also expands its Rosetta explanation and adds references on RNAInvbench, DSS pooling, and cryo-EM.

T1.justification: The mathematical representations, equivariance statements, Equations 1–3, and the FAQ counterexample are retained. The expanded DSS description and assay-score explanation introduce no new formal result, derivation, or proof.

improvement.justification: Independent SHAPE validation of 200 generated sequences addresses v6's reliance on computational design metrics and retrospective mutant ranking, substantially strengthening experimental support for practical RNA design. Success remains assay-score based rather than direct determination of 3D structures. The gain outweighs the removed structural case studies and a new overstatement in Appendix F: its claim of beating RDesign on all 14 targets conflicts with Table 2's 354D values, 0.4410 versus 0.4458.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same gRNAde study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite additions, removals, and renumbering.

after.justification: v7 retains those original computational results and adds independent SHAPE assay results for 200 gRNAde-designed sequences across ten RNA backbones.

before.justification: v6 reports original single-state and multi-state design experiments, architectural ablations, and retrospective simulations evaluating ribozyme mutant ranking.

title: gRNAde: Geometric Deep Learning for 3D RNA inverse design

C1.justification: The central contribution remains approximation-tolerant alternating minimization with the same runtime and recovery guarantees in Theorem 5.6. The abstract adds a hardness qualification already discussed in v1's introduction; the main contribution claims and conclusion remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 3 retains the same explanations of backward versus forward error and applicability to other alternating-minimization problems. Section 6 retains the limitation that approximate regression is analyzed while approximate QR factorization is left for future work.

D1.justification: Some implementation guidance disappears with the deleted proofs, including Lemma 4.4's instruction to evaluate update products from right to left and Appendix C.5's explicit weighted-data rescaling construction. The pseudocode and algorithmic parameter choices remain documented.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or conducts benchmark evaluations. Weighted low-rank approximation remains the theoretical task, with the same application domains discussed.

E2.justification: No empirical comparison methods are added or removed. Table 2 retains the same theoretical comparisons with LLR16 under random and SVD initialization.

E3.justification: Neither version reports an empirical evaluation protocol, data splits, training budgets, or testing procedures. The mathematical iteration and accuracy parameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Neither version contains empirical ablations, sensitivity tests, robustness experiments, or case studies. The theoretical robust-update and initialization analyses in Appendices E–K are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated experiments, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The retained probabilistic guarantees concern randomized algorithms, rather than empirical uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: No empirical result entries are added, removed, or revised. Table 2 retains its runtime expressions, and the principal recovery and convergence bounds are unchanged.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–5 retain the same alternating regression updates, high-precision solver, clipping, QR steps, and random initialization. The revisions do not establish a new algorithmic procedure; changes to the precision of mathematical definitions are covered under T1.

P1.justification: Section 2 is rewritten, and several definitions and lemma statements in Section 4 and Appendix D are recast into shorter sentences. Appendix C's roadmap is shortened following removal of C.4–C.5. These are localized revisions within an otherwise retained narrative and section order.

P2.justification: Rewritten statements and removed proofs change equation spacing, algorithm placement, and page breaks; the acknowledgement occupies a separate, mostly empty page in v2. Tables 1–2 retain their content and structure, and no scientific figures are added or redesigned.

R1.justification: v2 adds GSYZ23, Low rank matrix completion via robust alternating minimization in nearly linear time, as the explicit source for Lemmas 4.4–4.7 and D.4–D.8. This refines attribution of supporting machinery; the broader related-work discussion and positioning against LLR16 remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 removes the proof of Lemma 4.4, Sections C.4–C.5, and the proofs of Lemmas D.4, D.5, D.7, and D.8, replacing their support with GSYZ23 citations while retaining the corresponding results. This substantially changes the supplied derivations. Rewritten definitions also introduce specification problems: Definition 4.1 loses the explicit random, exactly-one-entry sampling requirement, and Definition D.3 replaces column-orthogonality equations with dimensionally incompatible XX^T = YY^T = I_k for n-by-k matrices.

improvement.justification: v2 improves attribution through GSYZ23 and corrects the abstract's factorization to UV^T. However, its rewrites introduce incompatible orthogonality equations in Definition D.3 and make the SRHT sampling specification less precise in Definition 4.1. Together with reduced in-document proof detail, these modestly weaken precision and verifiability despite the attribution gains; the main algorithm and guarantees remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, algorithms, mathematical displays, tables, and appendices A–K are readable and support reliable matching of retained, rewritten, and removed material.

after.justification: v2 remains entirely theoretical. Its main text and appendices contain no original empirical outcomes, and Table 2 still reports theoretical runtime comparisons.

before.justification: v1 contains theoretical algorithms, guarantees, and proofs, including its appendices. Table 2 compares asymptotic runtimes; no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes are reported.

title: Efficient Alternating Minimization with Applications to Weighted Low Rank Approximation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion strengthen the central efficiency claim from dense-matrix dependence to dependence on the number of nonzero weights. The near-verification-time interpretation consequently extends to sparse weights. The central claim of robust approximate alternating minimization is retained.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive justifications of the recovery assumptions, discusses rectangular-matrix applicability and interprets anticipated speedups for large n/k. The conclusion replaces v2's discussion of approximate QR as an unresolved limitation with emphasis on cubic SVD initialization. Appendix K adds computational limits and interpretations of the timing/error results.

D1.justification: Appendix K adds synthetic-data generation rules, factor scaling, noise variance, weight construction, sketch choices and iteration budgets. These provide limited reproducibility guidance beyond the retained pseudocode; hardware, software, code access and the matrix experiments' error metric remain unspecified.

E1.justification: v3 adds actual evaluations on synthetic noisy matrix completion, dense weighted low-rank approximation and standalone least-squares regression. These cover Gaussian, Laplace and uniform matrix factors, plus power-law regression data; v2 contains no empirical evaluation.

E2.justification: Tables 4–5 newly evaluate the proposed algorithm against the exact alternating-minimization solver from LLR16. Table 6 adds an exact regression-solver comparison. LLR16 appeared only in theoretical comparisons in v2.

E3.justification: Appendix K introduces experimental protocols: n=800, k=100, CountSketch size 150 and 20 alternating iterations for the matrix experiments; n=10^6, k=500, sketch size 5500 and five iterations for regression. It reports execution times and explicitly defines solution infinity-norm error for regression. These are new protocols, not revisions of existing experiments.

E4.justification: Experiment 3 adds a focused study of the regression subroutine, motivated by whether acceleration increases when n greatly exceeds k. This provides limited component-level evidence; the different task and single configuration do not establish a controlled end-to-end scaling analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports empirical repeated-run counts, seeds, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. The theoretical failure probabilities are not experimental uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 4–6 add previously absent numerical results. Reported speedups are 12.39%–16.53% for matrix completion, 2.71%–10.84% for weighted approximation and 19.27%–29.45% for regression. Every matrix-experiment row reports higher error for the approximate solver than for the exact solver.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Algorithm 1 introduce a sparsity-aware adaptation that solves weighted regressions using the nonzero support of the weights. The alternating updates, preconditioned regression solver, clipping and QR procedures otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 extensively reorganizes and rewrites the exposition: expanded preliminaries, a unified results section, new explanations of the convergence argument, and a rewritten conclusion. Regression and subspace material move between the main text and reorganized appendices, and a contents list is added.

P2.justification: v3 adds three experimental result tables and an expanded main-text presentation of the existing notation table. It retains the appendix notation and runtime tables under new numbers, simplifies Algorithm 1 by removing analysis-only lines, and adds contents pages. These substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: New Section 4.4 substantially expands positioning against noisy and noiseless matrix-completion methods and nonconvex-landscape research. The introduction adds BRW21 and Dai23, while Appendix B broadens the sketching literature. GSYZ23 becoming GSYZ24 is a publication update, but its substantive comparison is expanded.

T1.justification: The runtime theorems replace n^2k with nnz(W)k, supported by a new support-size argument. The SRHT embedding row bound changes from log(n/delta) to log^2(n/delta). Most convergence proofs are retained, but new Lemma 4.5 gives an inverse-first-power incoherence bound where v2 Lemma E.8 and v3 Appendix D.9 use inverse-square dependence.

improvement.justification: v3 adds useful organization, a sparsity argument, broader context and empirical timing evidence. However, Tables 4–5 do not specify their error metric, and Experiment 2's stated Gaussian-perturbed weights can violate nonnegativity without a documented correction. Theorem 4.6 omits the explicit small-gamma restriction still required by Lemma J.1, and new Lemma 4.5 conflicts with Appendix D.9's incoherence bound. These benefits and new consistency problems prevent a reliable net quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, algorithms, equations, tables and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: Appendix K reports three original synthetic experiments, with measured runtimes and errors in Tables 4–6.

before.justification: v2 reports theoretical guarantees and proofs, but no original empirical results. Its tables summarize notation and theoretical runtimes.

title: Efficient Alternating Minimization with Applications to Weighted Low Rank Approximation

C1.justification: v2 explicitly claims a novel tracking algorithm and feature aggregator that ensure temporally consistent captions, strengthening v1's claim of reducing caption switches. The main contributions remain Dense VOC, disjoint supervision and transfer to grounding.

C2.justification: v2 explains the middle-frame baseline's weakness through insufficient temporal context and attributes improvements to association without compromising detection. v1's explanation that Aug-COCO provides no finetuning benefit is dropped. The explicit long-video limitation disappears, while single-caption-per-trajectory and temporal-grounding limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies a 0.5 inference proposal-score threshold and changes the promised code release to reported availability, with Appendix A.2 naming chota.py. Conversely, v1 Appendix B.1's padding/truncation to K=16 and association threshold of 0.7 disappear. These are documentation and access-statement changes; external code availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: The same COCO, Aug-COCO, Visual Genome, SMiT, VidSTG and VLN/UVO data support the same captioning and grounding tasks. UVO tracking pretraining and temporally untrimmed VidSTG grounding already appear in v1 Appendix C and remain in v2 Appendix B.

E2.justification: v1 Table 4 compares against a per-frame captioner with an IoU tracker. v2 Table 2 additionally evaluates FairMOT, ByteTrack and a middle-frame-caption/ByteTrack pipeline, substantially expanding the central comparison. The corresponding VLN tracking comparison disappears; grounding comparator membership in Tables 5, 6 and 11 remains unchanged.

E3.justification: The default VidSTG configuration changes from soft aggregation to hard aggregation. Table 7's frame-count sweep changes from four-dataset pretraining to Visual Genome pretraining. Numerical CapSwitch evaluation is removed and replaced by categorical caption-consistency indicators, changing how a central property is assessed. VLN Location-QA also stops reporting recall and precision separately.

E4.justification: v2 adds a middle-frame-caption control testing whether enforcing consistency sacrifices caption quality, and analyzes detection and association separately. It removes the VLN tracking ablation and the soft-aggregation comparison from Table 7's frame-count sweep. The disjoint-dataset and UVO-pretraining analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests, including in the appendices.

E6.justification: Captioning results change extensively. Full-model zero-shot CHOTA changes from 28.0/28.2 to 31.1/29.2, and finetuned CHOTA from 54.3/40.8 to 56.9/41.3 on VidSTG/VLN respectively (v1 Tables 2–3; v2 Tables 3–4). Aggregation and pretraining rankings also change. These are revised-setting results, not established same-setting gains. Grounding results in Tables 6 and 11 remain identical.

M1.justification: v2 Section 4.5 excludes the Visual Genome detection loss when training jointly with COCO; v1 Section 3.4 and Table 1 describe using both detection and captioning losses on Visual Genome without this exception. This revises the stated training objective. The architecture, greedy grouping algorithm and hard/soft aggregation procedures otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and method explanations are extensively rewritten, including an enumerated contribution list. Tracking analysis precedes disjoint-training results, Algorithm 1 moves into the main method, evaluation subsections are reorganized, and the appendices are reordered.

P2.justification: v2 adds the space–time–language diagram in Figure 2, redraws the model diagram, replaces illustrative clips and restructures the tracking and Location-QA tables. Algorithm 1 moves into the main text, and typography, margins, headers and captions are reformatted throughout.

R1.justification: v2 elaborates its distinction from GTR's post-processing, adds discussion of first-frame-guided single-object tracking/segmentation, and explicitly claims the first generative approach to this grounding task. References add works including ByteTrack, XMem, PaLI-X and Gemini. These refine positioning within the existing research areas.

T1.justification: The formal indicator-based CapSwitch definition in v1 Section 4.1.2 is removed. CHOTA, association and aggregation definitions, and the appendix loss mathematics otherwise remain substantively unchanged. Relocating Algorithm 1 does not introduce a new algorithm or proof.

improvement.justification: v2's FairMOT, ByteTrack and middle-frame controls strengthen evaluation of the central end-to-end design beyond v1's IoU-only comparison, and the reorganized presentation clarifies the method. These provide a limited net improvement, tempered by lost numerical consistency evidence and tracking hyperparameters. Numerical reporting also develops inconsistencies: v2 Table 4 gives VidSTG CapA 34.5 for row 0, whereas Table 10 gives 35.8.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Dense Video Object Captioning work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on VidSTG and VLN, expanded tracking comparisons, and supplementary experiments in Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original zero-shot, finetuning, tracking-ablation and grounding experiments, including additional results in Appendix C.

title: Dense Video Object Captioning from Disjoint Supervision

C1.justification: V3 adds a fifth introductory contribution claiming state-of-the-art semantic multi-object tracking on BenSMOT, including an 18.2-point HOTA advantage. The original task, architecture, disjoint-supervision, and grounding claims remain, and the abstract is substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 4.6 adds interpretations concerning pretraining, backbone capacity, tracking architecture, and the language-model-size explanation for OW-VISCap's captioning advantage. Appendix D adds annotation subjectivity and the need for rigorous annotation protocols. Its single-caption limitation and richer-dataset future work already appeared in v2's conclusion.

D1.justification: V2 specifies JAX/Scenic and TPUs; v3 describes a public-GRiT-based implementation and GPUs, identifying V100s for pretraining while retaining reported budgets and timings. V3 also discloses the 46-million-parameter language head, revises CHOTA code-location instructions, and omits VLN captioned-trajectory counts. The PDFs do not explain the platform revision or establish reruns.

E1.justification: V3 adds BenSMOT finetuning and evaluation, extending coverage to a dedicated person-tracking-and-captioning benchmark containing 3,292 videos (Sections 4.1 and 4.6). The existing pretraining datasets, VidSTG/VLN evaluations, and UVO experiment remain.

E2.justification: V3 adds direct comparisons with BeyondMOT (Li et al., 2024b) on BenSMOT and OW-VISCap on VidSTG in Tables 4–5. The OW-VISCap scores are explicitly attributed to the concurrent paper. Neither comparison appears in v2; the original tracking and grounding comparator sets remain.

E3.justification: The new BenSMOT experiment reuses VidSTG finetuning hyperparameters, evaluates HOTA, DetA, AssA, and CIDEr, and includes settings without disjoint pretraining and with a smaller backbone. Existing benchmark splits, frame sampling, training budgets, and evaluation metrics are retained, including the relocated mAP-METEOR evaluation.

E4.justification: V3 Table 4 adds a focused ablation testing whether BenSMOT gains persist after removing disjoint pretraining and then reducing backbone capacity. The existing pretraining-mixture, frame-sampling, UVO, qualitative-error, and spatiotemporal-grounding analyses remain substantively unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests for its experimental results.

title: Revisiting a Design Choice in Gradient Temporal Difference Learning

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same algorithmic, computational, and convergence claims. The conclusion removes its explicit assertion that experiments demonstrate advantages over GTD, while retaining the central contribution and preliminary-evidence qualification.

C2.justification: v3 removes the conjecture attributing favorable learning transients to eliminating the secondary weight vector. It also removes the two-entry memory example and recasts the gap-growth discussion as suggesting Assumption 4.4 may be overly conservative. The broader empirical limitations remain.

D1.justification: Deleting Appendix D removes explicit Baird transition, reward, discount, and initialization details, including discount 0.99 and the initial weight vector. v3 newly identifies Ghiassian et al. (2020)’s implementation as its basis and refers readers there for task, baseline, and metric details, reducing self-contained documentation.

E1.justification: v2 evaluates only Baird’s off-policy counterexample. v3 retains it and adds Boyan’s on-policy chain to both the algorithm comparison and gap-function study, substantially extending the evaluated policy regimes.

E2.justification: v2 compares against TD and GTD. v3 retains TD, removes GTD from the empirical comparison, and adds GTD2, TDC, Vtrace, HTD, and TDRC. Figure 1 confirms their participation; GTD2 is a distinct comparator, not a renaming of GTD.

E3.justification: Section 6 changes the metric from NEU to RMSPBE and the learning-rate grid from {0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.05} to powers of two from 2^-20 through 1. Baird’s plotted horizon changes from 10,000 steps to 25,000 for comparisons and 20,000 for sensitivity analysis. Figure 1 also changes the proposed method’s gap function by adding a 100-step offset.

E4.justification: v2 Figure 1 tests squared-logarithmic, logarithmic, doubly logarithmic, and triply logarithmic gaps on Baird. v3 Figure 2 replaces this with first, second, and third powers of logarithms, with task-specific offsets, on both tasks. This substantially revises the sensitivity study, removing evidence about extremely slowly growing gaps and adding faster-growth comparisons.

E5.justification: Reported replication changes from 30 independent runs in v2 Figure 1 to 10 random seeds in v3 Figures 1–2. Both versions retain mean curves with standard-error shading.

E6.justification: The empirical curves are replaced. v2 reports faster initial NEU reduction and less oscillation than GTD; v3 reports better final RMSPBE than GTD2 and TDC on Boyan, and comparable final error to GTD2, TDC, and TDRC on Baird despite slower transients. Gap-function results also change. Different metrics, comparators, and settings prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Sections 3 and 5 retain the same temporally separated-sample update and projected variant. Different gap functions used in the revised experiments are configurations of the existing method.

P1.justification: Section 6 is locally rewritten, the conclusion is shortened, and small wording edits appear elsewhere. v3 adds publication headers and acknowledgements and removes Appendix D, while retaining the overall section order and most prose.

P2.justification: v2’s mixed two-panel NEU figure becomes two larger two-panel RMSPBE figures, separating algorithm comparisons from gap-function analyses across both tasks. Axes, legends, and captions are revised, and the appendix’s Baird diagram is removed. This substantially changes the empirical presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds Boyan (2002), Espeholt et al. (2018), White and White (2016), and Liu et al. (2025), supporting the expanded experiments and stochastic-approximation discussion. The related-work argument and positioning relative to GTD otherwise remain stable.

T1.justification: Assumptions 4.1–4.4, the asymptotic and finite-sample theorems, and the lemmas and proofs in Appendices A–C are unchanged. Minor notation and explanatory wording edits do not revise the mathematical arguments.

improvement.justification: The expanded comparator set and added on-policy task make Section 6 more informative about practical competitiveness, revealing both competitive final errors and slower transients. The theoretical contribution remains unchanged. The empirical gain is tempered by reducing replication from 30 runs to 10 seeds and removing Appendix D’s explicit setup details, supporting a limited net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and are readable throughout, including equations, figures, and appendices. Appendices A–C match across versions; v2’s Appendix D is removed in v3.

after.justification: Section 6 and Figures 1–2 report original comparisons and gap-function experiments on Boyan’s chain and Baird’s counterexample, averaged over 10 random seeds.

before.justification: Section 6 and Figure 1 report original algorithm comparisons and gap-function experiments on Baird’s counterexample, averaged over 30 independent runs.

title: Revisiting a Design Choice in Gradient Temporal Difference Learning

C1.justification: The central contribution broadens from improving Llama-2 to improving multiple backbone families, with new claims about data efficiency and the importance of instruction evolution and process supervision. V1 acknowledges trailing GPT-4 and Claude 2; v2 claims superiority over early GPT-4 and other proprietary models and emphasizes strong performance from a 7B Mistral model.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations concerning complementary evolution directions, instruction-quality control, PRM's advantages on longer reasoning problems, and generalization across backbones and datasets. It attributes gains to evolved-data quality rather than contamination and discusses the accuracy-cost tradeoff of replacing GPT-4 with an open teacher. Appendix A.7 also explains DART-Math's advantage at small data scales.

D1.justification: Section 4.1 and Appendices A.1–A.5 add model-version information, learning rates, epoch counts, batch size, sequence length, data-construction details, and evolution, ranking, labeling and filtering prompts. Minimum-over-steps PRM reward aggregation is newly documented. V1's literal training/evaluation templates and explicit Hugging Face access pointer are omitted; this does not establish that resources became unavailable.

E1.justification: GSM8k and MATH remain, while v2 adds seven out-of-domain benchmarks: College Math, TAL, Math23k, Ape210k, GaokaoBench Math, AGIEval Gaokao Math and AGIEval SAT Math. Tables 7 and 18 extend evaluation to additional school, college and examination settings beyond v1's coverage.

E2.justification: The GSM8k/MATH comparisons drop older comparators such as Falcon, MPT and Vicuna and add MetaMath, DART-Math, Xwin-Math, MathScale, Skywork-Math and newer proprietary models. V2 also introduces reward and verification comparisons against ORM, PRM800k, Math-Shepherd and self-consistency in Tables 4–5 and Figure 3.

E3.justification: V1 reports eight evolution turns producing a 96k instruction corpus; v2 describes five-round evolution, 418k SFT examples and a separate 90k reward-training instruction set. V2 adds test-overlap filtering, multiple backbone families and scales from 0.1B to 70B, controlled data-size sweeps, and verification using 1–256 candidate solutions. Headline greedy CoT pass@1 evaluation is retained.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's subtopic breakdown and selected solution cases, v2 adds PRM/IRM ablations, upward/downward evolution ablations, data-scaling studies, reward-source comparisons, verifier sensitivity, out-of-domain testing and contamination checks. Appendix Tables 15–18 further examine synthesis methods and transfer of reward training to other SFT models. The original six solution-comparison cases are replaced with evolution and error-labeling examples.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent repeated-run counts, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. V2's multiple sampled solutions are inference budgets, not repeated experimental runs or uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces WizardMath-Llama2-70B's GSM8k/MATH results of 81.6/22.7 with 92.8/58.6 under revised training conditions. V2 adds many backbone, ablation and generalization results, including Mistral-7B scores of 90.7/55.4 and PRM verification scores of 95.2/64.7 with 256 candidates in Table 5. These are not controlled same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: V1 describes SFT on regenerated seed solutions followed by active evolution and PPO; v2 uses GPT-4-evolved problems for SFT. IRM ranking criteria change from definition, precision and integrity to difficulty and definition. V2 also introduces PRM-weighted answer aggregation at inference in Section 3.4. These substantially revise the training and inference procedures.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction and results narrative, moves related work before the method, and reorganizes method and experimental sections. The two-part solution-case appendix becomes a ten-part prompt and analysis appendix. Citation style, authorship and affiliations also change.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn, the original GSM8k leaderboard bar chart disappears, and new scaling, verification and similarity plots appear. Table 1 gains a backbone column and extensive grouping. Compact ablation tables and color-coded annotation cases replace the original long solution tables, with substantial changes to figure/table placement and surrounding layout.

R1.justification: V2 substantially updates positioning around mathematical data synthesis, modern math-specialized models and process supervision, adding discussion of MetaMath, DART-Math, Xwin-Math, Llemma and other newer work. It explicitly distinguishes its approach from Python-assisted reasoning and human-labeled supervision. V1's broad instruction-fine-tuning survey is removed.

T1.justification: V2 adds explicit mathematical definitions for IRM ranking loss, PRM step-label loss and PRM-weighted answer aggregation in Equations 1, 2 and 4. V1 specifies only the combined reward product. This is a limited addition of formal methodological definitions; no theoretical guarantees or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: V1 mainly supports its method through benchmark scores and selected solutions. V2 adds direct component ablations, stronger comparative evidence, seven-benchmark generalization tests, contamination checks and detailed training and annotation instructions. These substantially address attribution and reproducibility gaps. Numerical inconsistencies, such as Table 6 versus its discussion, and the unexplained binary-versus-ternary PRM labels in Equation 2 and Appendix A.3 weaken precision, but the stronger empirical support and documentation provide a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WizardMath and RLEIF, with identifiable correspondences in the methods and GSM8k/MATH experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: V2 reports original WizardMath benchmark results, component ablations, verifier experiments, out-of-domain evaluations and contamination analyses, including substantial appendix results.

before.justification: V1 reports original WizardMath benchmark results for 7B, 13B and 70B models, MATH subtopic scores, and generated solution cases in Appendix A.

title: WizardMath: Empowering Mathematical Reasoning for Large Language Models via Reinforced Evol-Instruct

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain their central method and performance claims. New Appendix A.13 strengthens novelty positioning through explicit first-to-propose claims for downward evolution, combined IRM/PRM training and AI annotation of step-level PRM data.

C2.justification: The new appendix discussion qualifies SFT performance against Xwin-Math and Skywork-Math through data-efficiency tradeoffs and discusses gains on math-specialized backbones. A.12 explicitly acknowledges GPT-4 labeling costs and the lack of ground-truth answers needed by Math-Shepherd, interpreting the alternative annotator as a potential cost-accuracy compromise.

D1.justification: A.7 adds comparison-specific training details, including four checkpoints per epoch and selection by highest GSM8k/MATH accuracy. Its reported batch size of 256 is not reconciled with Section 4.1's 512. These are documentation additions; the PDFs do not establish changed execution or resource availability.

E1.justification: Both versions use GSM8k, MATH and the same seven MWPBench out-of-domain tasks. The added base-model and annotator comparisons use existing benchmarks without expanding task or population coverage.

E2.justification: New Table 16 adds untreated Mathstral-7B, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B comparators; Qwen2.5-Math-7B was already included in v2 Table 14. Table 19 adds a Llama-3.1-405B-labeled PRM variant alongside the GPT-4-labeled PRM and SFT baseline.

E3.justification: Appendix A.12 adds a controlled annotator comparison using Llama-3.1-405B instead of GPT-4, with Mistral-7B and the same stated labeling prompts and training settings. Existing benchmark splits and metrics are retained; A.7's additional settings document comparisons already present in v2 and do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: New A.12/Table 19 tests sensitivity to the model providing PRM annotations. Existing evolution-turn, reward-component, data-scaling, verification and out-of-domain analyses remain; the expanded discussion of DART-Math comparisons mostly concerns evidence already in v2.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without documented independent repeated runs, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added results introduce no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 19 newly reports 85.8% GSM8k and 51.5% MATH for the Llama-labeled PRM, compared with retained GPT-4-labeled results of 87.2% and 52.7%. Table 16 adds three previously unreported base-model rows. Matched existing tables retain their scores, although new A.9 prose incorrectly gives 48.9 where Table 17 retains 48.7.

M1.justification: The instruction-evolution procedure, IRM and PRM objectives, reward combination, PPO training and verification remain unchanged. New Appendix A.6 explains the existing pipeline; the alternative PRM annotator is tested within that pipeline.

P1.justification: The appendix undergoes substantial narrative reorganization: the extended survey is replaced by a detailed pipeline walkthrough, existing comparisons receive extensive explanation, and previously heading-only subsections gain substantive prose. The main text receives only limited wording, cross-reference and publication-header edits.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 16 and 19, relocates Figure 4 beside the contamination discussion, and redistributes and renumbers existing appendix tables. Figure 1 gains an explanatory cross-reference, while existing graphics and table formats remain largely unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 removes the extended related-work appendix and many distinct references across language modeling, mathematical reasoning and reinforcement learning, including QLoRA, Orca-Math and MathCoder. Section 2 remains largely intact, while new appendix passages sharpen comparisons with data-synthesis methods and make explicit priority claims.

T1.justification: Equations (1)-(4), defining the reward-model losses, combined reward and answer aggregation, are unchanged. The added pipeline explanation introduces no new formal assumptions, derivations or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 makes previously unexplained appendix comparisons easier to assess, discloses checkpoint-selection details, and adds useful PRM-annotator evidence and explicit limitations. These provide a modest net benefit because the main method and existing results remain unchanged. Reduced literature coverage and new consistency errors, including A.9's 48.9 versus Table 17's 48.7 and the incorrect Table 19 reference in Section 4.3, temper the improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WizardMath and RLEIF. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results and adds an experiment using Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct to label PRM training data.

before.justification: v2 reports original WizardMath evaluations on GSM8k, MATH and MWPBench, together with reward-model ablations, data-scaling experiments and case studies.

title: WizardMath: Empowering Mathematical Reasoning for Large Language Models via Reinforced Evol-Instruct

C1.justification: The central claims that surface-only methods underperform and that graph/surface integration improves the tested Atom3d results remain. v2 extends the abstract and conclusion's state-of-the-art claim explicitly to ligand-binding pocket classification, without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds a substantial explanation attributing training instability to protein-scale variation, and explains hybrid design choices through complementary local/global processing and parameter allocation to message passing. v1 offered a briefer long-range-diffusion hypothesis. The conclusion also makes memory requirements an explicit limitation.

D1.justification: Sections 2.3–2.5 and Appendix A add task-specific depths and widths, encoder internals, BatchNorm placement, the 8-angstrom bipartite cutoff and implementation-library links. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to every disclosed setting. Conversely, v1's explicit Gaussian projection of atom features onto surface vertices is omitted; the project code/data link remains unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds MaSIF-ligand binding-site classification, predicting one of seven co-factors from a binding site. This introduces a distinct ligand-preference task and dataset beyond the retained protein interaction, mutation stability and structure-ranking tasks.

E2.justification: MaSIF and HMR, previously cited without scored comparisons, become evaluated comparators in the new binding-site experiment, Figure 3. This adds direct comparisons against specialist surface-learning methods. The existing Atom3d comparator sets and adapted HoloProt baseline remain.

E3.justification: The binding-site experiment introduces 1,634/202/418 training/validation/test instances, balanced accuracy, chemical and geometric features comparable to the baselines, and parameter-count matching to HMR. Existing Atom3d splits and metrics remain unchanged. The reported surface-model depth changes from 'three or four' blocks to consistently three; this does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds a PSR validation-convergence comparison between original and modified DiffusionNet, testing the combined adaptations' optimization benefit. The existing architecture, message-passing and depth ablations, together with the PIP qualitative examples, are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or other uncertainty estimates. The new convergence curves and binding-site scores likewise provide no stated run aggregation or uncertainty.

E6.justification: Figure 3 newly reports binding-site balanced accuracy of 0.88 for AtomSurf, 0.81 for HMR and 0.74 for MaSIF; Figure 5 adds PSR convergence results. Existing tables also contain substantive revisions, including surface PSR local R from 0.32 to 0.330 and three-block attention PIP AuROC from 0.791 to 0.792. The principal Atom3d rankings remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 2.3 introduces protein-scale-informed diffusion-time initialization using absolute samples from N(2,2). The core graph/surface architecture and residual bipartite GAT combination remain intact. Batching and BatchNorm were already described in v1 and are not new components.

P1.justification: The introduction and methods are extensively rewritten. The original two method subsections become five, separating graph modeling, surface modeling, scale adaptation, hybrid representation and architecture. The conclusion is rewritten around conclusions and limitations, and implementation/proof appendices create a substantially different explanatory structure.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, redraws the representation overview and architecture schematic, and removes the separate v1 Figure 2 graph/surface illustration. It adds binding-site and convergence charts. Existing tables and qualitative predictions are resized or relocated, with the qualitative content preserved.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations on geometric GNNs, sequence models, over-smoothing and heat/surface geometry, including Duval, Rao, Li, Bronstein–Kokkinos, Meyer and Sun, while removing Méndez-Lucio et al. The central positioning around Atom3d, DiffusionNet and hybrid representations remains, with more specific discussion of graph-based limitations.

T1.justification: v1 contains architectural equations but no scale proposition or proof. v2 introduces Proposition 2.1 on expected Brownian geodesic distance under uniform scaling, with an Appendix B derivation using eigenvalue, eigenfunction, heat-kernel and area scaling. This is substantive new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens weaknesses in v1's validation and reproducibility: Section 3.4 directly compares specialist surface methods under stated feature and parameter controls, while Appendix A supplies concrete architecture settings. The scale analysis and convergence evidence also make the adaptation rationale more assessable. These gains outweigh the omitted Gaussian-projection detail. Statistical uncertainty remains unreported, and the convergence comparison does not isolate individual modifications.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AtomSurf, with matching authors, core architecture and Atom3d experiments. The supplied text, figures, tables and equations support comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 adds readable Appendices A and B.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds binding-site classification results in Figure 3 and a DiffusionNet convergence comparison in Appendix B, Figure 5.

before.justification: v1 reports original surface and hybrid-model experiments on PIP, MSP and PSR, including quantitative comparisons, architectural ablations and qualitative predictions.

title: AtomSurf: Surface Representation for Learning on Protein Structures

C1.justification: v3 retains the central claim that integrating graph and surface representations improves protein learning, but expands the claimed contributions to antibody–antigen binding-site detection, richer sequence-informed representations and competitive computational throughput. Its conclusion claims state-of-the-art results across several benchmark tasks, whereas v2 claimed them across all benchmark tasks.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations of computational applicability: coarsening shifts the runtime bottleneck toward graph encoding, while variable mesh sizes cause memory spikes and restrict batching. It also attributes stronger competing PSR performance to explicit geometric priors and revises the explanation of sequential fusion's weakness from optimization difficulty toward inadequate simultaneous multiscale communication. The high-memory limitation remains.

D1.justification: v3 documents additional feature construction, mesh cleaning, neighborhood construction, a 0.1 coarsening rate and dynamic batching. Appendix D.3 newly reports hardware, training durations and aggregate training expenditure. The stated repository changes from atom2D to atomsurf, and pip-package availability is mentioned. Existing block widths and depths mostly move from Appendix A to Appendix C rather than becoming newly disclosed settings.

E1.justification: The three protein-only Atom3D tasks and MaSIF-ligand are retained. v3 additionally evaluates functional segmentation of 5S ribosomal RNA surfaces and antibody–antigen binding-site detection. These introduce a new molecular domain and distinct residue-level prediction requirements.

E2.justification: v3 Table 2 adds ProNet, GVP, GVP-ESM and GearNet-ESM comparisons on retained Atom3D tasks, and Table 3 adds ProNet to MaSIF-ligand. New evaluations compare against DGCNN, DeltaConv and GEP. The parallel fusion comparator disappears from the architectural ablation; HoloProt is the renamed v2 holo comparator.

E3.justification: v3 adds a richer 600k-parameter evaluation setting alongside the restricted benchmark model, plus antibody–antigen evaluation with a 186/49 train/test split, antibody scoring restricted to CDRs, and MCC reporting. Reported minimum mesh size changes from 128 to 256 vertices, and diffusion initialization changes from N(2,2) to N(10,5). Original dataset splits are retained in Appendix E. For MaSIF-ligand, the prose still specifies balanced accuracy while Table 3 says AuROC, so an actual metric switch cannot be established.

E4.justification: v3 adds RNA training-stability comparisons, diffusion-scale visualizations, learned-time distributions, memory profiling and distance-threshold sensitivity including out-of-memory failures. The existing PSR stabilization analysis is retained and supplemented with a results table. Qualitative protein examples are replaced, while the parallel-fusion and separate depth comparisons in v2 Table 3 are removed from v3 Table 4.

E5.justification: Neither version reports evaluation seed counts, replicated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. v3's approximately 100 model trainings describe aggregate computational expenditure across settings and failed experiments, not repeated-run statistical estimation.

E6.justification: The original hybrid benchmark scores are retained as AtomSurf-bench. New AtomSurf results include PIP 0.907, MSP 0.715 and PSR local/global correlations 0.613/0.861 under the richer configuration, rather than demonstrating same-setting gains over v2. New results include RNA accuracy of 84.1% versus original DiffusionNet's 80.9%, and antibody MCC of 0.47 versus GEP's 0.28. Additional baseline, sensitivity and computational results appear, while ablation entries are revised or removed.

M1.justification: Beyond naming the original benchmark hybrid AtomSurf-bench, v3 introduces a distinct AtomSurf variant using residue graphs, pretrained ESM features, ProNet graph encoding and GVP messages between representations. Reported bipartite connectivity changes from an 8-angstrom cutoff to 16 nearest neighbors, and dynamic batching is introduced. These are procedural additions and revisions, not merely expanded descriptions.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial introductory and methodological passages are rewritten. v3 introduces a dedicated Motivation and Contribution section, reorganizes the method presentation, distinguishes Surface Diff, AtomSurf-bench and AtomSurf, and moves detailed dataset descriptions and architectural alternatives into expanded appendices. These changes substantially reshape the narrative.

P2.justification: v3 changes the main text from two columns to one, redraws the architecture diagrams, consolidates and transposes the original benchmark tables, and replaces the ligand-classification bar chart with a table. It also replaces the qualitative prediction panels and adds binding-detection, diffusion-scale, memory and supplementary-result displays. These are substantial visual changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning around multimodal protein learning, discussing Lee et al., Pegoraro et al. and Xu et al. and contrasting their fusion or pretraining approaches with communication across intermediate layers. It also incorporates protein-language-model integration and newer geometric encoders. This extends the scientific comparison beyond v2's narrower treatment of surface methods and HoloProt.

T1.justification: The Brownian-motion scaling proposition and its proof are retained with renumbering. v3 corrects an eigenfunction index in the initial heat-kernel formula, although inconsistent indices remain later in the derivation. Appendix D.1 adds an auxiliary asymptotic runtime analysis of diffusion, graph encoding and bipartite message passing.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens v2's limited validation through contemporary competing methods, independent RNA and antibody–antigen tasks, and targeted diffusion, threshold and memory analyses. Separating restricted benchmarking from the richer model also makes the comparisons more informative, while computational disclosures improve practical assessability. These gains outweigh the loss of depth and parallel-fusion ablations and new reporting inconsistencies, notably Table 3's AuROC label despite balanced-accuracy prose and inconsistent model naming in the binding-detection discussion.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AtomSurf, with matching core benchmarks, hybrid representation framework and scaling proposition. All pages, including appendices, equations, tables and figures, are readable and support comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds evaluations of another model configuration, RNA segmentation, antibody–antigen binding-site detection, and computational and sensitivity analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original surface and hybrid-model experiments on PIP, MSP, PSR and MaSIF-ligand, architectural ablations, qualitative predictions and a PSR learning-curve comparison.

title: AtomSurf: Surface Representation for Learning on Protein Structures

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: adapting a surface encoder, benchmarking representations, integrating surface and graph features across layers, and achieving strong performance with computational efficiencies. Additional validation does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v4 substantially expands interpretation of generalization and feature dependence. It interprets PINDER results as evidence of robustness and tentatively links small ESM benefits under stricter splits to sequence memorization versus structural generalization. Appendix F.5 discusses optimization as a possible explanation for MSP failure without ESM, and the conclusion newly acknowledges the need for real-world validation.

D1.justification: Appendix E newly documents random RNA splitting, sequence-identity criteria for retained datasets, chronological PSR splitting, and unbound PIP test structures. PINDER composition and the unchanged-hyperparameter ESM ablation are also documented. Existing construction details are largely relocated, while architecture sizes, hardware, training-time information, and repository access remain essentially unchanged.

E1.justification: v4 adds the clustered PINDER dataset, containing approximately 42,000 structures, while retaining the earlier datasets. It introduces paired-residue interaction prediction and single-protein binding-site prediction evaluated on bound, unbound, and AlphaFold2-predicted structures, substantially expanding coverage.

E2.justification: Relative to v3 Table 2, v4 Table 3 adds explicit pretrained GVP and pretrained GearNet-ESM comparator rows. The existing comparator families remain; using ProNet on the new PINDER benchmark does not itself introduce another baseline method.

E3.justification: The added PINDER experiments introduce interface-similarity-based splitting and AUROC/accuracy evaluation across structural conditions. Appendix E specifies 1,955 test clusters, with 342 corresponding unbound and 1,747 predicted structures. The ESM ablation also introduces a control holding hyperparameters fixed. Newly documented split rules for retained datasets do not establish changes to their existing protocols.

E4.justification: v4 adds extensive ESM-removal analyses across the existing tasks and PINDER, testing dependence on pretrained sequence features. PINDER comparisons across bound, unbound, and predicted structures add robustness evidence. Earlier architecture, diffusion-stability, and distance-threshold analyses remain, although several are relocated.

E5.justification: Appendix F.2 and Supplementary Table 2 newly report means and standard errors over three replicates for Atom3D, AbAg, and MaSIF-ligand results. v3 provides no explicit per-result repeat counts or corresponding standard errors. This establishes new uncertainty reporting, not an increase from a previously specified run count; baseline replicates remain unavailable for formal significance tests.

E6.justification: New PINDER, ESM-ablation, and pretrained-comparator results substantially expand the evidence. Existing AtomSurf estimates also change: PIP AUROC is revised from 0.907 to 0.909 and PSR global correlation from 0.861 to 0.857 in the main comparison tables. AbAg antibody AUROC/MCC changes from 0.86/0.47 to 0.88/0.53, while antigen scores change from 0.73/0.18 to 0.673/0.143, below GEP's 0.72/0.18. The later AbAg values are explicitly reported as replicate means.

M1.justification: The modified DiffusionNet, layerwise surface–graph communication, AtomSurf-bench, and residue-based AtomSurf architecture remain unchanged. Representation-construction details move to Appendix C.1; the ESM-free variants are experimental ablations rather than revisions to the proposed method.

P1.justification: The organization changes substantially: representation-construction passages move into Appendix C.1; ligand classification and antibody prediction are reordered and grouped in Section 4.3; detailed architectural ablations move from the main text to Appendix F.4; and the supplementary-results section is reorganized. Conference headers, acknowledgements, funding, and a broader-impact statement are also added, although much scientific prose is retained.

P2.justification: v4 moves the representation illustration to the appendix, promotes the RNA learning curve and results table to the main text, and relocates the architectural-ablation table. It adds PINDER, uncertainty, and ESM-ablation tables and restructures the main comparison table to distinguish PLM use and additional pretraining. The MaSIF-ligand header is corrected to balanced accuracy, and Figure 3's display is updated.

R1.justification: v4 adds references to structure-informed protein language models by Bepler and Berger, Heinzinger and colleagues, and Su and colleagues, plus PINDER and structural-robustness references. The central positioning against surface-only approaches and early/late representation fusion remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The heat-equation formulation, scaling proposition and Appendix B proof, and computational-complexity derivation remain substantively unchanged. Renaming the appendix heading from 'Proposition' to 'Theorem' introduces no new mathematical result.

improvement.justification: PINDER evaluation under stricter splitting and varied structural conditions, ESM-removal controls, and three-replicate uncertainty estimates address important gaps in generalization, attribution of gains, and reliability present in v3. Some reporting weaknesses remain: MSP is 71.6 in Table 3 versus 71.5 in Supplementary Table 2, antigen performance is still described optimistically despite lower scores, and baseline uncertainty is unavailable. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AtomSurf and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–F. Corresponding content can be matched despite substantial relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds PINDER evaluations, ESM-feature ablations, and performance estimates over three replicates.

before.justification: v3 reports original experiments on RNA segmentation, Atom3D tasks, antibody–antigen binding-site prediction, and MaSIF-ligand, together with architectural and sensitivity analyses.

title: AtomSurf: Surface Representation for Learning on Protein Structures

C1.justification: The abstract revises its quoted ImageNet improvement figures from 0.55% and 1.9% to 0.40% and 1.9%. Applicability is explicitly framed as SSL and includes iBOT, while the central contribution remains unchanged; v1 already evaluated non-contrastive DINO and SimSiam.

C2.justification: V3 links zooming patterns to local-to-global correspondence and suggests multi-crop differences explain poor transfer of manual IoU policies between methods. Appendix H adds memory and efficiency qualifications. Appendix J acknowledges mostly similar attention maps while suggesting occasional differences in object shape and contextual attention.

The gains remain limited by selected qualitative examples and missing hybrid-guidance implementation details; the stronger claim that previous methods cannot perform the editing is not supported by a direct editing-baseline comparison.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe IPDreamer and have readable text, equations, figures, and references throughout. Neither contains an appendix. v2 refers to separate supplementary material that is absent from the supplied PDFs; its contents cannot be assessed.

after.justification: v2 reports original generation and texture-editing outputs, a single-image-to-3D comparison, and component analyses in Figures 1 and 3–8.

before.justification: v1 reports original qualitative 3D-generation results in Figures 1 and 3 and a comparison with four text-to-3D methods in Figure 4.

title: IPDreamer: Appearance-Controllable 3D Object Generation with Complex Image Prompts

C1.justification: The central IPSD, appearance-control, and high-quality generation claims remain. v3 extends the stated applicability to guidance by arbitrary complex images and makes limitations of existing single-image-to-3D methods an explicit central motivation, broadening v2's predominantly text-to-3D framing.

C2.justification: v2 stresses dependence on initial NeRF quality and warns that IPSD alone cannot fully preserve reference identity. v3 instead emphasizes that a basic coarse NeRF suffices and presents IPSD as improving existing single-image methods, omitting that explicit identity warning. Appendix D newly documents hours-long optimization and incomplete style control, supported by the failure in Figure D.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-repository link and substantial implementation documentation in Appendix C: A100 hardware, 5k/10k/15k optimization steps, timestep schedules, batch size 1, rendering resolution 512, memory requirements, and attention/joint-loss details. It also supplies a prompt list. These are newly disclosed settings, not evidence that retained experiments changed their training budgets.

E1.justification: The same text-to-3D, image-guided editing, and single-image-to-3D tasks remain. v3 modestly extends tested input conditions through deliberately extreme reference/coarse-object mismatches in Figure 5 and the failed doll example in Figure D. Complex-image guidance itself was already demonstrated in v2.
