It introduces an 80-volunteer, 16-prompt, 1,280-pair preference study with image prompts generated without scribble guidance, plus image-image CLIP evaluation of the geometry prompt difference. These substantially expand v2's visual evaluation protocols.

E4.justification: The visual geometry-prompt-difference ablation in v2 Figure 8 is replaced by an aggregate alignment ablation in v3 Table 3, while the normal-map ablation is retained. v3 also adds a stagewise optimization example, a joint-loss comparison in Figure C, and a failed style-transfer case in Figure D, substantially expanding component and failure analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v3's new scores and preference percentages remain point estimates; its volunteer and comparison counts describe evaluation sample sizes rather than repeated-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: v3 adds numerical results absent from v2: IPDreamer obtains FID 257.17 and CLIP score 0.2859 in Table 1, 58.35% preference against ProlificDreamer in Table 2, and image-alignment scores of 0.8228 without versus 0.8389 with the geometry prompt difference in Table 3. Additional qualitative comparisons and failure outcomes also appear. These are newly reported results, not measured improvements over v2.

M1.justification: The NeRF-to-mesh pipeline, IPSD geometry and texture optimization, geometry prompt difference, and main Equations (1)–(10) are retained. Combining IPSD with Zero-1-to-3 for single-image generation was already described in v2 Section 4.4; v3 supplies further documentation rather than establishing a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: Selected passages in the abstract, introduction, method overview, NeRF discussion, and conclusion are rewritten around complex-image guidance. Experimental subsections are reorganized and 'embeddings' often becomes 'features'. The main section hierarchy and much of the related-work and technical exposition remain unchanged.

P2.justification: The two-column layout becomes single-column, the pipeline illustration is simplified, and several figure panels are substantially rearranged, including v2 Figure 3 becoming v3 Figure 4. New quantitative tables and appendix displays expand the presentation. Portions of v2 Figure 4 reappear in v3 Figure 7 and Figure B rather than being wholly removed.

R1.justification: v3 adds InstantID, SSR-Encoder, ConsistNet, and references supporting CLIP evaluation, FID, and optimization. Most related-work discussion remains intact, with additional positioning around image-prompt adaptation and existing single-image methods' difficulty handling complex images.

T1.justification: Main Equations (1)–(10) remain unchanged. Appendix C adds explicit decoupled-attention and weighted joint IPSD/Zero-1-to-3 gradient definitions in Equations (A.1)–(A.4), providing a limited expansion of the mathematical specification without new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens v2's qualitative-only validation through quantitative baseline comparisons, human preferences, and an aggregate ablation, while providing essential training details and explicit failure limitations. These additions address important evidential and reproducibility gaps. Reporting remains imperfect: Table 2's Fantasia3D percentages sum to 98%, and Table A lists 20 prompts under a user-study caption although Section 4.3 specifies 16. These inconsistencies limit confidence but do not outweigh the substantial gains in support and documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of IPDreamer with matching methods and experiments. The supplied v2 ends after its references; v3 includes Appendices A–E, which are assessed as newly supplied content.

after.justification: v3 retains original generation experiments and adds quantitative comparisons, a user study, quantitative ablation results, and appendix experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original generated 3D objects, qualitative baseline comparisons, and geometry and texture ablations in Section 4.

title: IPDreamer: Appearance-Controllable 3D Object Generation with Complex Image Prompts

C1.justification: v4 adds LEPI as an explicit principal contribution, claiming successful editing when image prompts differ substantially from the initial NeRF. This extends the contribution beyond v3's IPSD framework and general controllable-generation claims. The central claims concerning high-quality, appearance-controllable 3D synthesis remain.

C2.justification: v4 explains complex-image guidance through attention-based spatial alignment and attributes severe-mismatch failures to inadequate localization. LEPI is presented as addressing that mechanism. The limitations discussion changes from v3's demonstrated doll-editing failure and incomplete style control to residual appearance/color inconsistency and deployment speed.

D1.justification: Appendix F.3 adds a substantial implementation workflow: GPT-4v analysis, SAM segmentation, user-adjustable partial prompts, ControlNet enhancement with a specified checkpoint, and local followed by global optimization. Existing hardware, iteration counts, timestep schedules, memory requirements, and code access remain unchanged. However, v3's explicit several-hours-per-model runtime description disappears.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate text-to-3D generation, single-image-to-3D generation, and complex-image-guided texture editing. Severe prompt–NeRF mismatch was already tested in v3's failed doll example. The additional LEPI examples and single-image example extend results within this coverage without introducing a distinct task or dataset.

E2.justification: The new LEPI comparisons explicitly use IPDreamer without LEPI as an internal comparator, including Table 5 and Figures 3, 7, and 10. External comparator membership remains unchanged: DreamFusion, Magic3D, Fantasia3D, and ProlificDreamer for text-to-3D, and Zero-1-to-3 and SyncDreamer for the corresponding image-based comparisons.

E3.justification: v4 adds a paired with/without-LEPI evaluation using image prompts from Figures 3, 7, 10, and 11, assessed through CLIP scores and user preferences. The original 20-prompt benchmark, 80-volunteer study with 1,280 comparisons, and stated optimization budgets remain unchanged. LEPI-specific participant and trial counts are not separately specified.

E4.justification: v4 adds substantial evidence testing whether LEPI preserves object semantics under strong appearance mismatch: the revisited doll failure, bird and cottage ablations, additional controlled examples, quantitative comparisons, and localization-mask visualization. The existing geometry-loss, geometry-prompt-difference, and combined-supervision analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed evaluations, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. v4's additional CLIP scores and preference percentages follow the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: v4 adds a substantial block of LEPI findings. Table 5 reports CLIP scores of 0.2041 without LEPI and 0.2189 with LEPI, with preference rates of 24.363% and 75.637%, respectively. New qualitative comparisons demonstrate improved semantic preservation, and Figure 14 adds a single-image example. The original benchmark, baseline-preference, and geometry-prompt ablation numbers are unchanged.

M1.justification: v4 introduces optional Local Editing with Partial Images (LEPI). It uses partial image prompts and localization words to construct spatially masked attention, followed by global texture optimization using combined prompt features. This substantially extends the procedure beyond v3's global image-prompt guidance; the original NeRF and IPSD components remain.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized around LEPI. The original user study, single-image generation, and Zero-1-to-3 comparison move into expanded appendices; attention explanation enters the main method section, and VSD preliminaries are shortened. The introduction, contribution list, limitations, title, and author block are also revised.

P2.justification: v4 changes the page format and extensively rearranges displays. It redraws the teaser and pipeline, transposes Table 1, adds LEPI comparison figures, a mask visualization, and Table 5, and relocates several retained figures. The original standalone optimization illustration and teaser's dragon panels are omitted; the doll failure is reused within a new controlled comparison.

R1.justification: v4 adds references including Prompt-to-Prompt, Segment Anything, DreamGaussian, LucidDreamer, and newer image/video diffusion work. Related work expands to Gaussian-based 3D optimization and additional editing methods, while the main positioning against text-to-3D and single-image-to-3D approaches remains.

T1.justification: v4 substantially extends the mathematical formulation with localization-mask and masked-attention definitions in Equations 10–11 and local/global LEPI supervision in Equations 15–21. Core IPSD and combined Zero-1-to-3 supervision equations are retained. v3's preliminary VSD optimization equations are removed. Neither version provides formal guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v4 materially addresses a demonstrated weakness in the paper's central controllability goal: v3's failed doll edit becomes a controlled LEPI comparison in Figure 3, supported by further ablations and Table 5. The added mechanism explanation and implementation workflow strengthen this evidence. LEPI-specific study details and uncertainty reporting remain limited, and runtime disclosure is weakened, but the demonstrated mitigation of an important failure makes the overall improvement substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe IPDreamer. Their complete main texts and appendices, including figures, tables, and equations, support reliable comparison despite changes in title, organization, and layout.

after.justification: v4 retains these empirical results and adds qualitative comparisons, CLIP scores, and user preferences evaluating LEPI.

before.justification: v3 reports original 3D-generation experiments, FID and CLIP scores, an 80-person preference study, and geometry and texture ablations.

title: IPDreamer: Appearance-Controllable 3D Object Generation with Complex Image Prompts

C1.justification: The appearance-control claim remains, but v6's introduction, contribution list, and conclusion elevate composition from multiple diverse images into a central capability. The introduction additionally claims successful generation for ambiguous or unclear-subject prompts where existing text-to-3D and image-to-3D methods fail. This substantively broadens the claimed contribution beyond v4's emphasis on complex-reference appearance transfer and reference/NeRF mismatch.

C2.justification: v6 replaces the introduction's explanation based on VSD's LoRA-training randomness with one based on insufficient appearance information in text. It interprets the new localization-label experiment as evidence of compositional diversity. It also removes v4 Appendix G's specific qualifications about imperfect appearance/color matching and deployment speed, while retaining the main explanations of image guidance and alignment.

D1.justification: v6 no longer documents the explicit Zero-1-to-3 initialization, DMTet mesh extraction, and DPT normal-estimation recipe given in v4's method section. It also drops the blanket LEPI-off-unless-indicated statement and the user study's text-only image-generation clarification. Hardware, optimization steps, timestep schedules, memory, batch size, rendering resolution, and code-link disclosure remain. GPT-4v, SAM, and ControlNet preprocessing details largely move from Appendix F.3 into Section 3.3.

E1.justification: v6 retains the original 20 textual prompts and adds ten challenging prompts, including leaves flying in the wind, ripples, and splashing waves, targeting generation without a clear principal subject. Figure 6(b) adds composition from multiple separate reference images. Conversely, the dedicated single-image reconstruction experiments in v4 Appendix D are absent. These change the evaluated input conditions and task coverage.

E2.justification: v6 Tables 1–2 add LRM and LGM to DreamFusion, Magic3D, Fantasia3D, and ProlificDreamer in the quantitative comparison and user study. Meanwhile, the evaluated Zero-1-to-3 and SyncDreamer comparisons in v4 Appendices D–E disappear, although their citations remain. ProlificDreamer/VSD in the new challenging-prompt illustrations is an existing comparator.

E3.justification: The quantitative evaluation expands from 20 to 30 prompts. The user study now samples 16 prompts from the larger pool and compares six baselines, retaining 80 volunteers and 1,280 comparisons. v6 Figure 6(b) introduces a control that holds the coarse model and reference images fixed while swapping localization labels. Metrics and optimization budgets remain unchanged; the delta_geo ablation references the revised prompt pool without establishing whether it was rerun.

E4.justification: The geometry-guidance, delta_geo, and qualitative LEPI ablations are retained under new numbering and terminology. v6 adds the localization-label swapping case in Figure 6(b), but removes the quantitative LEPI validation in v4 Table 5 and the Zero-1-to-3-only versus combined-loss artifact analysis in Figure 13. This substantially changes the evidence testing alignment and integration effectiveness.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-generation run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Both report user-preference percentages without uncertainty estimates; adding comparator rows does not change that practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 reports replacement results on the expanded prompt set: IPDreamer's FID/CLIP scores change from 257.17/0.2859 to 253.32/0.2716, which is not a same-setting performance comparison. v6 adds LRM/LGM results, including 70.27%/65.48% preference for IPDreamer, and new challenging-prompt and composition outputs. v4 Table 5 and Figures 13–15 disappear. The four original user-preference rows and delta_geo scores of 0.8228/0.8389 remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The core geometry, texture, masked-attention, and local/global optimization procedures survive the IPSD-to-IPSDS and LEPI-to-Mask-guided Compositional Alignment renaming. Much of v6 Section 3.3 already appears in v4 Appendix F.3. The substantive adaptation accepts multiple separate reference images through this alignment procedure; v6 also omits the auxiliary joint IPSD/Zero-1-to-3 optimization variant from v4 Appendix D.

P1.justification: v6 substantially rewrites the introduction and conclusion, reorganizes the method around IPSDS and compositional alignment instead of explicit NeRF/mesh stages, and brings detailed LEPI training into the main text. Experiments are reorganized around single and multiple complex images, terminology shifts from texture editing toward object generation, and the appendix hierarchy is extensively restructured.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is comprehensively redrawn around mesh optimization and masked attention. Figures 1 and 6 gain panels, and the main qualitative comparison is rebuilt using material from v4 Figure 12 alongside revised and new outputs. Table 1 is transposed; user-study results and localization-mask visualization move into the main text. Several supplementary displays are removed, and the document adopts a different title, header, and citation layout.

R1.justification: v6 adds Hong et al.'s LRM and Tang et al.'s LGM references and incorporates them into its comparisons. References to InstantID, DPT, and DMTet are removed. The diffusion-model, controllable-generation, and 3D-generation related-work discussions otherwise remain substantially similar; citation-style and author-name formatting changes are not new research positioning.

T1.justification: The core mathematical definitions and optimization gradients remain equivalent after renaming and relocation; v4 Appendix F.3 Equations 15–21 correspond to v6 Equations 11–17. v6 removes the coarse Zero-1-to-3 gradient in v4 Equation 2 and the combined-loss definitions in Appendix D, Equations 12–14. These are limited removals of auxiliary formulations; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v6 more directly tests its broadened claims through challenging prompts, LRM/LGM comparisons, and multiple-image composition, while making the alignment procedure easier to find. However, it removes quantitative validation of that central component in v4 Table 5, explicit appearance and speed limitations, and useful initialization and normal-estimation details. Broader evidence and clearer focus coexist with weaker reproducibility and qualification of claims, leaving the net effect on overall quality uncertain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe IPDreamer. Their complete main texts and appendices, including figures, tables, and equations, support reliable comparison. Renamed and relocated material can be matched across versions.

after.justification: v6 reports original generation results, quantitative comparisons, user preferences, and ablations, including retained experiments and new challenging-prompt and multiple-image examples.

before.justification: v4 reports original 3D-generation experiments, quantitative comparisons, component ablations, and an 80-participant user study, including supplementary results.

title: IPDreamer: Appearance-Controllable 3D Object Generation with Complex Image Prompts

C1.justification: The principal empirical claim shifts from accurate SR predictions and faster TD learning in Pinball to online SF-based navigation and adaptation relative to LSTM and CSCG. V2 drops the advertised HMM-version-of-RNN contribution and adds claims about long-horizon belief propagation and neuromorphic implementation. The core contribution of local Hebbian temporal memory remains.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantial discussion of fast learning versus weak trajectory generalization, correlated-buffer overfitting, and encoder non-stationarity as a possible explanation for AnimalAI baseline failures. It qualifies that LSTM/CSCG are not inherently incapable of solving the tasks and proposes a future fast/slow hierarchy. These interpretations and limitations extend well beyond v1's encoder caveats.

D1.justification: V1 mainly documents the encoder and a brief experimental setup. V2 adds explicit Hebbian update formulas, baseline architectures and training regimes, buffer sizes, validation rules, DHTM dimensions, initialization, learning rates, pruning and planning thresholds (Appendix D). It also details preprocessing and environment interaction and supplies a source-code access link; the link's availability was not independently verified.

E1.justification: The Pinball environment and its force-field scenarios are removed. V2 evaluates fully observable coordinate-based Gridworld, partially observable colour-based Gridworld, and first-person visual navigation in AnimalAI. These change the observation conditions, dynamics and navigation requirements.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates LSTM, RWKV and factorial CHMM against DHTM. V2 removes RWKV from experimental comparisons and introduces Q-table and SR-table agents in fully observable Gridworld (Figure 3). LSTM remains in partially observable Gridworld (Figure 4), and the clone-HMM comparison lineage continues through CSCG, with a differently described implementation.

E3.justification: V1 measures prediction surprise and reward using short Pinball episodes and one-/five-step TD predictions. V2 measures steps to the goal and introduces trajectory-buffer refresh and change-oracle protocols. Planning uses ten steps in fully observable Gridworld and adaptive horizons up to 50 elsewhere, with respective discounts of 0.99 and 0.8 (Appendix D). These are replacement experimental protocols.

E4.justification: V1's explicit one-versus-five prediction-step ablation is removed. V2 instead compares CSCG with and without an environmental-change oracle in both Gridworld settings, testing whether renewed random-policy data collection restores adaptation (Figures 3–4). This changes the central diagnostic question from prediction horizon to training-data refresh.

E5.justification: V1 reports averaging three trials and displays shaded bands without identifying their statistical meaning. V2 explicitly reports at least five differently seeded runs per setup and identifies the displayed variation as standard deviation. This describes the new evaluations, not additional runs of the earlier Pinball experiments.

E6.justification: The Pinball surprise and adaptation results are replaced by navigation results. V2 reports faster Gridworld adaptation than CSCG, approximately 13 steps versus a nine-step optimum after the partially observable maze changes, and stable AnimalAI goal reaching after about 150 episodes. AnimalAI baseline training failures are also reported. These findings cannot establish same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: V1's agent explicitly learns SR through n-step TD and uses log reward priors for valuation. V2 specifies direct SF rollouts under a uniform future policy, adaptive stopping and linear feature-reward Q estimates (Section 3.3). The segment-likelihood computation also changes through an added mean-synaptic-efficacy multiplier (v1 Equation 11; v2 Equation 8), while the underlying Hebbian factor-graph memory remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, agent explanation and conclusion are substantially rewritten around SF-based planning. Methods is reorganized into factor-graph, neural-implementation and agent subsections. The single encoder appendix becomes part of an A–F appendix structure with dedicated explanations and a glossary; the original encoder discussion is largely retained.

P2.justification: V1's compact three-panel method figure is replaced by separate, expanded factor-graph and neural-implementation diagrams, plus a new biological illustration. Pinball screenshots and plots disappear, replaced by larger Gridworld/AnimalAI learning curves and new environment illustrations (v2 Figures 3–9). This substantially revises the visual organization.

R1.justification: V2 adds targeted references and connections concerning successor features, episodic memory, cortical layers, AnimalAI and baseline implementations, including Gershman, Touati et al., and Staiger and Petersen. Godot and several earlier cortical-model references disappear. The principal positioning around Factorial HMMs, world models and local Hebbian learning is retained.

T1.justification: The mathematical revisions are localized: Section 2.3 changes SR from finite-horizon observation occupancy to infinite-horizon future-state occupancy; Appendix B adds a feature-additive reward approximation and value decomposition. V2 Equation 8 also revises the segment-likelihood interpolation. The underlying factor-graph formulation remains, without a new theorem or proof framework.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves assessability and reproducibility through explicit learning rules, baseline training details, uncertainty definitions and implementation information. Its comparative Gridworld navigation tests and oracle controls address adaptability more directly than v1's prediction comparison and DHTM-only horizon ablation, while new limitations constrain interpretation. Losing the predictive-surprise and horizon analyses, and lacking successful AnimalAI baseline curves, narrows some evidence, but the methodological transparency and more direct validation provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DHTM research, despite the title changing from Successor Representations to Successor Features. The complete text, equations, figures and appendices support comparison; the experiments are substantially revised.

after.justification: V2 reports original navigation experiments in fully and partially observable Gridworld and in AnimalAI, with learning curves in Figures 3–5.

before.justification: V1 reports original Pinball experiments measuring prediction surprise and adaptation after environmental changes, including a prediction-horizon comparison (Figures 3–4).

title: Learning Successor Features with Distributed Hebbian Temporal Memory

C1.justification: Although the abstract is essentially unchanged, the introduction and conclusion redefine the contribution around episodic memory that matches table episodic control while supporting distributed representations and their dependencies. v3 also introduces an order-of-magnitude sample-efficiency claim against Dreamer V3. v2 primarily emphasized an online Factorial-HMM-like memory outperforming LSTM and CSCG.

C2.justification: v3 argues that episodic trajectory recall explains much of DHTM's performance and interprets the new ablation as evidence for cross-feature dependencies. It proposes DHTM as an adaptive trajectory buffer for a slower generalizing model, replacing v2's emphasis on a two-layer DHTM hierarchy. New qualifications address uniform-policy nonoptimality, evaluation limited to basic RL setups, and excessive segment growth in noisy environments.

D1.justification: v3 documents encoder datasets, 64x64 image inputs, VAE epochs and batch size, EC pseudocode, softmax temperatures, factor configurations and a segment-count limit. These replace extensive spatial-pooler implementation details in v2. Some earlier disclosures, including synapse initialization and pruning thresholds, are no longer stated. The anonymous source-code resource identifier also changes; its availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: v3 removes the fully observable 5x5 Gridworld scenario reported in v2 Section 4.1 and Figure 3. Partially observable Gridworld with a blocked path and the AnimalAI room-navigation task remain. The new encoders and factor configurations concern retained tasks, rather than additional environments or task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds an episodic-control dictionary comparator in both environments, Dreamer V3 in AnimalAI, and an explicitly plotted LSTM-oracle comparator in Gridworld. Q-table and SR-table comparisons disappear with the fully observable experiment. AnimalAI now includes plotted CSCG and LSTM comparisons using K-Means; v2 described their unsuccessful training with its spatial-pooler encoder.

E3.justification: Appendix D substantially revises training protocols: LSTM's buffer changes from 100 to 1000 trajectories, with a new learning rate and update schedule; CSCG's buffer changes from 2500 to 500 steps and its smoothing coefficient from 0.9 to 0.05. Oracle handling changes to memory reinitialization and buffer clearing. DHTM initialization, learning rates and AnimalAI discounting also change. v3 introduces encoder pretraining, total-step metrics and a Dreamer evaluation without the other agents' frame skipping.

E4.justification: v3 adds a substantive test of distributed prediction: Figure 3B varies context factor size from 1 to 5 and includes the factor 1* control with additional hidden-variable copies to investigate state collisions. The new EC comparison also tests whether simple trajectory storage explains DHTM's performance. v2 lacked these analyses; its changing-maze adaptation test is retained.

E5.justification: Section 4 changes the replication statement from 'at least five' experiments with different seeds to five. Both versions report standard deviations. This makes the reported run count more specific without establishing that the number of runs actually increased or decreased.

E6.justification: v3 replaces the experimental curves, removes the MDP results, and adds EC parity and factor-size findings. Its revised oracle CSCG results show sustained post-change recovery, unlike v2's earlier oracle procedure. Appendix F newly reports Dreamer solving AnimalAI after about 105,000 raw steps, converted by the authors to 35,000 versus DHTM's 3,500. These results involve changed or unequal protocols and do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The core DHTM factor graph, belief propagation and Hebbian updates are retained. The AnimalAI encoder component changes substantially within that retained architecture: v2's event preprocessing and online spatial pooler are replaced by pretrained K-Means or categorical VAE encoding. The VAE adds a linear reward-prediction loss and deterministic latent-state selection (v3 Appendix C).

P1.justification: v3 extensively edits retained introductory and methodological prose, rewrites the experimental narrative and conclusion, and reorganizes the background around SR, HMM and episodic control. Learning receives a separate subsection, and the value-decomposition, biological-interpretation and encoding appendices are reordered. The impact statement is removed and the glossary is revised.

P2.justification: v3 redraws and combines v2 Figures 1–2 into a two-panel Figure 1. Experimental displays become paired learning-curve and total-step plots, while the fully observable Gridworld plot and map are removed. New appendix displays show factor-graph configurations and Dreamer learning. The retained biological illustration and environment images are relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: v3 substantially positions DHTM within episodic memory and control, adding literature on model-free, neural and successor-feature episodic control and integrating it into Sections 2.4 and 3.5. It adds explicit HTM-neuron attribution and encoder-related references while removing spatial-pooler-related works. Dreamer was already cited in v2, but becomes an evaluated comparator and a prominent positioning reference.

T1.justification: v2's explicit bootstrapped SR updates in Equations 3–4 are removed. The relocated value-function decomposition removes an extra feature multiplier from the reward formula and changes successor-feature probability conditioning from an individual hidden component to the full hidden vector (v2 Appendix B; v3 Appendix A). Core DHTM mathematical updates remain, without a new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central distributed-memory contribution: v2's AnimalAI implementation used one encoded feature, whereas v3 tests multiple features, cross-feature factor sizes and a collision control. Shared-encoder baseline comparisons and the EC control also make the mechanism and comparative benefits much clearer (Figures 2–3). Removing fully observable Gridworld narrows coverage, and the tenfold Dreamer claim remains inadequately controlled because encoder pretraining and action protocols differ. Nevertheless, the direct validation and clearer explanation of the central contribution represent a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DHTM research work. All 20 pages of each version, including equations, figures, references and appendices, are readable and support comparison after matching relocated material.

after.justification: v3 reports original Gridworld and AnimalAI experiments, including baseline comparisons, a factor-size ablation and the Dreamer V3 experiment in Appendix F.

before.justification: v2 reports original navigation experiments in fully and partially observable Gridworld and AnimalAI, with learning curves in Figures 3–5.

title: Learning Successor Features with Distributed Hebbian Temporal Memory

C1.justification: The central contributions—online Hebbian episodic memory, successor-feature planning, and distributed representations—remain unchanged. V4 extends the abstract and introduction's comparative claim to RWKV and adds a qualified novelty claim concerning episodic control in partially observable environments. The conclusion's principal claims remain stable.

C2.justification: V4 adds substantive explanations of why factorization tolerates noisy features and why including all variables loses that advantage. Appendix H.2 discusses exploration-dependent memory growth, unstable policies in larger grids, linear computational costs, and planning-horizon limitations requiring pruning or alternative planning approaches. These considerably sharpen v3's broader limitations discussion.

D1.justification: V4 documents segment-creation conditions, KL-based stopping, RWKV implementation and training, EC's VAE mapping, and parameters for the scalability and noise experiments. It replaces the anonymous code reference with a named GitHub repository and iclr25 branch. Conversely, it removes the explicit statement that the oracle-CSCG buffer continuously grows, without specifying a replacement behavior.

E1.justification: The two navigation domains remain Gridworld and AnimalAI. V4 expands their test scenarios with empty 5x5, 7x7, and 10x10 grids with opposite-corner goals, and AnimalAI observations containing an additional noisy feature (Appendices H.2–H.3). This broadens conditions within the existing task coverage.

E2.justification: RWKV becomes an evaluated baseline in both main experiments, having only been discussed in v3. Figure 2 also adds oracle-reset EC, while Figure 3 adds EC using VAE codes mapped through a dictionary. These materially strengthen the comparator set beyond the retained LSTM, CSCG, EC, and Dreamer comparisons.

E3.justification: V4 adds controlled evaluations of grid size, memory use after 300 episodes, episode length under 100 episodes of uniform exploration, and noisy features with varying factor sizes. Appendix E specifies different planning horizons, temperatures, discounts, and reward thresholds for these tests. Figure 3 also replaces the displayed LSTM K-Means condition with VAE, and Figure 2 adds an EC reset control.

E4.justification: Appendices H.2–H.3 introduce substantial analyses of scalability, memory growth with experience, and robustness to an irrelevant noisy variable. Figures 10–12 test these questions directly. The original clean-input factor-size analysis and Dreamer experiment remain; their relocation is not an additional analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five experiments with different seeds. D1.justification: v3 Appendices A.1–A.3 document contrastive-data filtering, 1,024/2,048-token limits, loss weighting, revised batch sizes and learning rates, and eight 40GB A100 GPUs. v1 instead specifies its normalization pipeline, cross-compilation environment, and A5000/A10 infrastructure. E1.justification: v3 adds AnghaBench pretraining and evaluates HumanEval-Decompile plus Binutils, Curl, ImageMagick, SQLite, OpenSSL, and Putty. Generated/Codeflaws and BinaryCorp testing disappear; BinaryCorp remains BCSD fine-tuning data. ARM64 coverage and cross-architecture translation are removed. Binary recovery continues as decompilation, so that terminology change does not itself introduce a new task.

E2.justification: For BCSD, v3 retains jTrans and adds evaluated comparisons with DiEmph and CodeArt. For recovery/decompilation, GPT-3.5 remains, GPT-4 and LLM4Decompile are added, and v1's published-score comparisons with Coda and Neutron disappear (v1 Tables 2–7; v3 Tables 2–8).

E3.justification: BCSD changes from twelve optimization directions at pool sizes 32 and 10,000 to O0-to-O3 retrieval at sizes 50, 100, 200, and 500, with Recall@1 replacing MRR-focused reporting. Decompilation uses executable Pass@1/10 evaluation instead of lexical recovery metrics. Model scales, preprocessing, and fine-tuning budgets also change; v3 specifies one fine-tuning epoch rather than v1's two.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's Nova/Nova+ comparisons and illustrative cases, v3 introduces component ablations removing contrastive learning and hierarchical attention on both retained tasks. E5.justification: v3 newly presents embedding-distance distributions as boxplots (Figure 13) and specifies 20 sampled decompilations per assembly for Nova and LLM4Decompile (Section 3.2). These add distribution and sampling information, but neither version reports training-seed variability, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: v1's BinaryCorp, Generated, and Codeflaws results are replaced by new benchmark and ablation results. For example, v1 reports Nova+ MRR 0.727 at pool size 10,000, whereas v3 reports Nova-6B average decompilation Pass@1 of 29.42% and average Recall@1 of 0.67 at pool size 500. These are different-condition results, not directly comparable performance gains between versions.

M1.justification: v1's StarCoder-based Nova/Nova+ uses language modeling followed by optimization generation and optimization-level prediction. v3 replaces these auxiliary tasks with functionality and optimization contrastive learning, introduces instruction-summary tokens and hierarchical attention, and uses DeepSeek-Coder as its backbone (Sections 2–3). These change the architecture and training procedure substantially.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and explanatory narrative are extensively rewritten around security applications, low information density, and optimization diversity. Related work moves after the results, training details move into an expanded appendix, and the conclusion/limitations order changes. The appendices are reorganized from task examples into implementation details and analyses.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the motivation and overview figures and introduces attention-mask diagrams, contrastive-learning illustrations, embedding projections, boxplots, and attention heatmaps. Tables are redesigned around decompilation optimization levels, individual BCSD projects, and ablations. These substantially replace v1's three-task schematics, architecture-by-metric tables, and large code-example displays.

R1.justification: v3 substantially revises positioning around recent assembly models, discussing CodeArt, SLaDe, and LLM4Decompile and adding DeepSeek-Coder, SimCSE, and attention-analysis literature. It replaces v1's broad first-generative-binary-LLM positioning with distinctions concerning architecture and assembly-specific training, and removes the separate disassembler discussion.

T1.justification: v3 Section 2.3 introduces quantified constraints separating same-function and different-function embeddings, an ordering constraint across optimization levels, and corresponding contrastive losses and a combined objective. Its BCSD loss also differs from v1's cosine-similarity softmax formulation. These are substantive mathematical changes, although neither version contains theorem-and-proof developments.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation through executable decompilation tests, contemporary baselines, component ablations, and appendix representation analyses. This addresses v1's reliance on similarity metrics that can reward incorrect recovery: Figure 8 gives incorrect code 100% token accuracy. Coverage narrows, and reporting defects weaken exact claims: v3 Table 4 repeats a Pass@10 baseline row under Pass@1, while Table 2's Nova-1B scores average 20.695%, not 22.09%. Despite these defects, the improvement in assessing functional correctness and explaining component effects is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the Nova assembly-language-model research by the same authors, despite extensive redesign. The complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original executable decompilation and binary similarity results, component ablations, and embedding and attention analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original binary similarity, cross-architecture translation, and source-code recovery experiments, including model-generated examples and appendix embedding comparisons.

title: Nova: Generative Language Models for Assembly Code with Hierarchical Attention and Contrastive Learning

before.justification: v3 reports original decompilation and binary-similarity experiments, ablations, embedding analyses, and attention analyses.

title: Nova: Generative Language Models for Assembly Code with Hierarchical Attention and Contrastive Learning

C1.justification: V2 makes breaking intrinsic system symmetries and consistently recovering a unique true solution in phase retrieval central claims in the abstract, introduction, and teaser. V1 emphasized text-controlled ambiguity reduction and fast linear reconstruction. The underlying contribution of text regularization through adaptive negation remains.

C2.justification: V2 develops a symmetry-based explanation contrasting image-statistical priors with semantic text guidance. Its new limitations section qualifies uniqueness: complex backgrounds can leave residual symmetry, dataset-category knowledge is assumed, and suitable prompt selection remains unresolved. V1's detailed interpretation linking adaptive negation to quality-related negative prompts is removed.

D1.justification: V2 supplies separate DPS pseudocode, a previously unspecified DPS step-size rule and branch-specific guidance scales, and Adam hyperparameters for phase retrieval. Existing Stable Diffusion 1.5, CLIP backbone, CG settings, and promised code-access information are retained. These disclosures do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: V2 adds Fourier phase retrieval on FFHQ, extending evaluation from linear degradation operators to nonlinear magnitude-only measurements with symmetry ambiguities. Inpainting, AFHQ, FFHQ, LHQ landscapes, Food-101, and ImageNet were already represented in v1, including its supplement.

E2.justification: V2 adds Stable-Inpaint and Repaint, labelled Stable-Repaint in Figure 6(a), to the inpainting comparison. Table S1 additionally compares PSLD with adaptive negation. The SR/deblurring comparator set—PSLD, PnP, PSLD+DDS, and PSLD+PnP—is unchanged.

E3.justification: V2 introduces phase-retrieval settings including 256-pixel padding on each side, a distinct update schedule, and CFG scale 4.0. It also adds runtime comparisons at NFE=200, omitting PSLD's fixed-point constraint for nonlinear measurements. Existing Food-101 sample counts, degradation settings, and reconstruction metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds text-versus-null-text phase-retrieval trials testing symmetry breaking and a runtime analysis examining computational cost and adaptive-negation overhead. Existing ambiguity and DPS ablations remain. The adaptive-negation ablation is condensed from four examples in v1 Figure 7 to two retained examples in v2 Figure 2(b).

E5.justification: Both versions report the same ten-seed ambiguity experiment, pixel-wise standard-deviation maps and profiles, and mean reconstruction scores. V2 introduces no new explicit seed-count reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: V2 adds the phase-retrieval finding of more consistent face reconstruction with text, new inpainting baseline outputs, and comparative runtimes. Table S1 reports TReg versus PSLD at 0.26 versus 1.47 minutes for linear reconstruction and 1.09 versus 1.12 minutes for nonlinear reconstruction. V1 Tables 1–2 are numerically unchanged in v2 Table 1; selected supplementary qualitative results are omitted.

M1.justification: The core adaptive negation and latent optimization procedure remains. V2 adds a nonlinear phase-retrieval adaptation using Adam instead of CG for pixel-space optimization, with lambda=0 and task-specific DPS guidance. Alternating DPS steps for inpainting was already described in v1's supplement.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the introduction around phase retrieval, reorganizes background and sampling subsections, and restructures the experimental narrative. Inpainting and selected supplementary analyses move into the main text, while the supplement is condensed and reorganized around implementation, runtime, additional results, and limitations.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout with extensively recomposed figures. V1 Tables 1–2 become v2 Table 1; SR/deblurring comparisons and FFHQ galleries are merged. However, Equation (5) changes the predicted-noise multiplier from sqrt(1-alpha_bar_t) in v1 to sqrt(alpha_bar_t) in v2, creating an inconsistency with v2's forward diffusion formula and algorithms. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens the paper through nonlinear phase-retrieval evidence, inpainting competitors, measured runtime comparisons, and explicit prompt-dependent failure conditions. The established reconstruction scores remain unchanged, and the new reconstruction evidence is primarily qualitative. Pruned supporting examples and explanations, together with the new Equation (5) inconsistency, limit the net gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same TReg research, with matching core methods and benchmarks. Their complete main texts, supplements, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: V2 retains original quantitative reconstruction results in Table 1 and reports additional phase-retrieval examples, inpainting comparisons, and runtime measurements in Table S1.

title: Regularization by Texts for Latent Diffusion Inverse Solvers

C1.justification: v3 foregrounds computational efficiency in the abstract and replaces v2's introductory applicability claim for 'any inverse problem' with cross-domain zero-shot applicability. C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of early text guidance versus late measurement refinement, the PSNR/FID tradeoff from adaptive negation, empirical convergence and JPEG failure at Q10. It retains the prompt-dependence limitations in Appendix J, but removes v2's discussion of inherited model bias and potential misuse. D1.justification: Most implementation settings and the promised code-access location are retained. v3 documents alternative-label construction, P2L prompt initialization and the JPEG implementation source. before.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction experiments, quantitative Food-101 comparisons in Table 1, repeated-reconstruction analyses and appendix runtime results.

title: Regularization by Texts for Latent Diffusion Inverse Solvers

C1.justification: The central contribution remains efficient, group-wise sparse and explainable attacks. v2 explicitly strengthens the explainability contribution to superiority over both structured and traditional sparse attacks, while dropping the abstract and contribution-list assertion about maintaining lower perturbation magnitudes.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly characterizes first-stage coordinate selection as a heuristic and adds an interpretation of effectiveness against adversarially robust models. It removes v1's discussion of SAIF outperforming GSE at high saliency percentiles, while emphasizing group-wise sparsity's role in explainability. It also adds concrete explanations for excluding SAPF and Homotopy from further comparisons.

D1.justification: v2 supplies ResNet20 training details, pretrained-weight sources, the hyperparameter-search objective, runtime batch size and reported availability of ImageNet indices, target labels and grid-search code. These are substantial documentation additions, not proof that previously undocumented procedures changed. Conversely, v1's explicit Gaussian-kernel size of 5 and d2,0 patch size of 8 are no longer stated.

E1.justification: v1 actually evaluates CIFAR-10 and the NIPS2017 image collection, despite sometimes using the ImageNet label. v2 adds a separate ImageNet validation-set evaluation while retaining NIPS2017 in Appendix E.1. This substantially broadens the evaluated data, although targeted and untargeted image classification remain the tasks.

E2.justification: SAPF joins the Homotopy comparison in Table 1 and appears in additional comparisons. The explainability comparison replaces SAIF with comparisons involving PGD0, Sparse-RS and SAPF, as shown in Figures 2 and 5. StrAttack and FWnucl remain the principal benchmark comparators.

E3.justification: The CIFAR-10 untargeted sample count in Table 2 increases from 1,000 to 10,000, and v2 adds ViT_B_16, WideResNet and adversarially trained ResNet50 configurations. The reported CIFAR-10 step size changes from 0.0025 to 0.005, ACP changes to averaging successful attacks only, and runtime hardware changes from Tesla T4 to A40. These changes prevent treating the revised results as identical-setting comparisons.

E4.justification: Section 3.4.4 and Table 5 introduce a substantive robustness test against an adversarially trained ImageNet classifier, absent from v1. The explainability analysis also expands its comparison of structured and conventional sparse perturbations. The existing qualitative image examples are retained rather than newly added case studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Best, average and worst cases summarize target-label outcomes rather than repeated-run uncertainty.

The broad low-bit performance and 4.3-hour efficiency claims remain, with the latter explicitly scoped to weight-only quantization.

The explicit v3 qualification that window optimization remains local and cannot completely eliminate accumulated errors is removed with the homologous-reconstruction discussion.

title: CBQ: Cross-Block Quantization for Large Language Models

C1.justification: The original claims about joint Gaussian diffusion and adaptive schedules remain. V2 broadens the central contribution to initialization and data-type homogenization, and makes scalability a prominent claim: faster training, improved handling of high-cardinality features and accommodation of arbitrary category counts. These extend the paper's claimed contribution beyond v1's emphasis on sample quality and competitive sampling speed.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations for emphasizing low noise levels, slower convergence with feature-specific schedules, and TabDDPM's apparent preference for categorical fidelity. It discusses mixed effects in the component ablation and explicitly acknowledges ARF's categorical-marginal advantage. New limitations address schedule-selection cost, embedding-initialization sensitivity, privacy-sensitive applications and possible disadvantages on specialized data such as time series.

D1.justification: Appendices F–J substantially expand implementation information with baseline package versions and sources, licenses, RTX 4090 hardware, PyTorch 2.2.2, architecture dimensions, optimizer settings, EMA decay and warmup. Appendix P supplies detailed runtime measurements. However, v1's quantile-transformation and dequantization instructions disappear; this establishes lost documentation, not that preprocessing actually stopped.

This expands evaluation into additional income, forest-cover, hospital-readmission, lending and news settings, including high-cardinality categorical features. V2 also changes diffusion sampling settings, increases detector tuning from 25 to 50 trials, introduces a 50,000-sample evaluation cap, revises downstream learners and metrics, and replaces signed DCR differences with absolute differences. Rank aggregation introduces explicit penalties for unavailable baseline results.

Appendices K–M add learned-schedule fit diagnostics, univariate and bivariate distribution comparisons, and feature-level correlation-error visualizations.

V2's predictive-result captions explicitly incorporate these seeds into the uncertainty description, whereas v1 describes standard deviations across model averages. For example, adult CDTD per-type correlation error changes from 0.094 to 0.125 (v1 Table 9; v2 Table 7), under revised models and settings rather than a controlled performance comparison. V2 also resolves v1 Table 1's apparent JSD/Wasserstein label swap relative to its appendix averages.

It adds learned time-dependent normalization of the joint loss and changes noise-schedule initialization from approximately uniform to emphasizing low noise levels, with mu changing from 0.5 to 0.25. These substantially revise the architecture and training procedure while retaining the joint Gaussian diffusion framework.

The appendices are substantially reorganized while retaining and expanding earlier calibration and timewarping material.

P2.justification: The framework diagram is redrawn, and v2 adds architecture, noise-schedule, runtime, density and correlation-heatmap figures. The main results table changes from mean metric values to ranks, with updated mean results in Appendix N. Detailed tables gain comparator and real-data columns, while new ablation and runtime tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 adds discussion of Diffusion Forest's scalability and cites Karras et al. (2023) and Kingma and Gao (2023) for adaptive loss normalization, alongside additional dataset and software references. References connecting v1 to non-uniform diffusion, Diffusion Transformers and numerical-feature embeddings disappear. The principal positioning around score interpolation and mixed-type diffusion remains intact.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix B adds an analytical derivation showing how output initialization yields expected unit loss across timesteps for both data types, extending v1's terminal-time calibration argument. Appendix A explicitly incorporates EDM weighting and preconditioning. Sections 2.1 and 3.3 correct diffusion coefficients to include the noise-schedule derivative. The existing logistic CDF, inverse and density derivations are retained in Appendix D.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for its design choices through component ablations, broader benchmarks, explicit architecture and training-budget controls, and an initialization derivation. Expanded implementation details improve reproducibility, and the JSD/Wasserstein summary inconsistency is corrected. Fixed baseline configurations replace per-dataset tuning, preprocessing documentation is lost, and learner-count captions remain inconsistent. Nevertheless, the gains in experimental scrutiny, mathematical explanation and transparency are substantial; the judgment does not depend on treating revised scores as performance gains.

title: Continuous Diffusion for Mixed-Type Tabular Data

C1.justification: The abstract and central CDTD contributions remain stable. The introduction narrows the first-use claim for advanced diffusion techniques to mixed-type tabular data directly in data space, and the conclusion explicitly qualifies this as requiring no latent encoding.

C2.justification: New Appendices M-N develop arguments about latent reconstruction errors, rare-category information loss, feature balancing and computational costs. Appendix L explains initialization sensitivity through embedding dimensions and category counts. Limitations now cite sensitivity evidence and discuss imputation requirements; the assertion that type-specific schedules always outperform feature-specific schedules is softened.

D1.justification: v3 supplies implementation sources and settings for SMOTE and TabSyn, including TabSyn's architecture and training allocation. Appendix K newly explains finite-difference sampling updates. Existing CDTD hyperparameters and hardware disclosures are largely retained, while the CTGAN/TVAE embedding specifications are corrected.

E1.justification: The eleven datasets and their generation and downstream prediction tasks are unchanged. New sensitivity and feature-fidelity analyses use the existing acsincome, adult, beijing and churn datasets. Imputation remains future work.

E3.justification: v3 adds controlled sampling and initialization sweeps and featurewise extrema metrics within the retained evaluation framework. Main splits, training budgets and prediction models remain unchanged. Appendix G revises the stated CTGAN/TVAE embedding dimensions from 258 to 256; this does not establish that their experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Tables 6-8 examine sensitivity to sampling steps, embedding initialization and initial noise-level weighting. Table 9 investigates worst-feature fidelity against TabSyn. These substantially extend the questions examined beyond the retained component ablations and learned-schedule visualizations.

E5.justification: Both versions average generation metrics over five sampling seeds and machine-learning evaluations over ten model seeds, retaining the same uncertainty reporting in detailed tables. The added experiments use the existing five-seed averaging practice; no new statistical estimation procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: Original per-dataset and component-ablation values are retained, but v3 adds SMOTE/TabSyn results, timing measurements and Tables 6-9. Table 1 ranks are recomputed for the expanded comparison set. Table 6 newly reports RMSE discrepancies of 0.033 at 200 sampling steps and 0.028 at 500 steps. Some new default-result entries conflict across tables.

M1.justification: Both versions retain the same score matching/interpolation framework, learned embeddings, loss calibration, initialization and adaptive noise schedules. The default Euler sampler also remains unchanged. Appendix K in v3 documents its implementation more explicitly without establishing a procedural revision.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing exposition are retained. v3 edits the introduction, contribution bullets, results discussion and limitations, adds dedicated appendix sections, and updates terminology and cross-references. This is a focused editorial expansion rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 6-10, expands benchmark tables and redraws runtime, distribution and correlation figures to include additional baselines. Figures 9-11 are consolidated onto one page. The document also adopts different title, author, heading and page-header formatting, with denser result displays.

R1.justification: Appendices M-N and Table 10 substantially expand positioning against latent diffusion, particularly TabSyn, and distinguish CDTD through feature balancing and data-space diffusion. New citations include Zhang, Chawla, Kendall, Ma, Lugmayr and Liu on the associated baselines, loss balancing and imputation.

T1.justification: v3 Appendix K adds a featurewise probability-flow ODE derivation, its discretized Euler update and mathematical reasoning for using finite noise increments near the terminal timestep. The original loss-calibration, initialization and timewarping derivations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: The added baselines, targeted sensitivity analyses and explicit sampler derivation improve evaluation coverage and reproducibility beyond v2. However, Table 8 reports a default detection score of 0.651 versus 0.560 in Tables 2, 6 and 7 under apparently matching settings. This unexplained inconsistency weakens the new robustness evidence and limits the overall gain.

improvement.justification: Broader ablations make component effects across the benchmark more assessable, while preprocessing details, sampler pseudocode, and the replication-code link improve reproducibility documentation. Changed settings and aggregation limit what the revised scores establish, so the net improvement is limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CDTD and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Corresponding material can be matched despite appendix renumbering and expanded experiments.

after.justification: v4 retains original benchmark experiments and reports expanded ablations, a categorical-cardinality experiment, and additional sampler findings.

title: Continuous Diffusion for Mixed-Type Tabular Data

C1.justification: The central contribution changes from fixed-point inversion to regularized Newton–Raphson inversion. v2 emphasizes convergence in one or two iterations and claims interactive editing at approximately 0.5 seconds with LCMs, whereas v1 emphasizes approximately five-second FPI editing. The prompt-adjustment claim expands from improving FPI to benefiting iterative inversion methods generally.

C2.justification: The original prompt-misalignment explanation remains, but v2 adds interpretations involving out-of-distribution roots, regularization strength, and amplification of inconsistency by guidance scale. Its new limitations section and Appendix G connect convergence failures to incorrect captions and suggest mismatch detection as a future application. v1's dismissal of Newton–Raphson as impractical is replaced by a proposed workaround for its Jacobian cost.

D1.justification: v2 adds PyTorch automatic differentiation and regularization information, with lambda 0.1 favored by the sensitivity analysis; the numerical stabilizer's value remains unspecified. The 512-by-512 input size and A100 hardware are retained. v1's square-cropping and scheduler-stride specifications, detailed time-capped baseline settings, and promise of public code upon acceptance disappear, without replacement code-access instructions.

E1.justification: Both cover reconstruction, text-guided editing, seed interpolation, centroid finding, and rare-concept generation using COCO and ImageNet1k classes grouped by LAION2B prevalence. The LCM experiments change model configurations, while the larger COCO convergence audit examines additional samples and failures within existing dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's DDIM, Null-text, and EDICT comparisons, v2 evaluates AIDI and ExactDPM in LDM reconstruction and ReNoise in LCM comparisons. AIDI also enters editing, user-study, interpolation, and rare-concept comparisons. DDIM no longer appears in the LDM reconstruction plot, although it remains in other reported comparisons.

E3.justification: The reported backbone changes from Stable Diffusion 1.5 to 2.1, LCM configurations are added, and five FPI iterations become two RNRI iterations per diffusion step. New evaluations include guidance-scale 7.5 controls and the 118,000-pair convergence audit. User-study results now cover four LDM choices and a separate two-method LCM comparison. Reporting remains inconsistent: Section 5 specifies four LCM steps, while Figure 5 specifies two.

E4.justification: v2 expands the iteration analysis into a solver comparison, adds regularization ablation and lambda sensitivity (Figure 3 and Appendices C–D), and tests prompt-aware adjustment across solvers at high guidance scale (Table 1). Appendix G adds a large convergence audit and incorrect-caption failure cases. The original qualitative prompt-adjustment analysis and cake-to-hat editing failure are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and display error bars in Figure 3 without defining their statistical meaning. v2 follows this practice in its lambda plot and introduces no repeated-run counts, random-seed reporting, confidence-interval definitions, or significance tests. The new convergence percentage is an additional outcome rather than a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Rare-concept results change from FPI's 87.3% tail accuracy, 95.0% total accuracy, and 6.4 FID to RNRI's 89.1%, 95.8%, and 6.3 (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 3). User preference changes from 61.7% in the original three-way comparison to 40.4% in the four-way LDM comparison, with a new 89.9% LCM preference against ReNoise. Changed methods, settings, and choice sets prevent interpreting these as controlled gains or losses. v2 adds LCM results, AIDI entries, and 95.4% convergence; the proposed interpolation/centroid numbers remain identical.

M1.justification: v1's fixed-point solver is replaced by a componentwise Newton–Raphson update using derivatives of an L1 residual plus Gaussian negative-log-likelihood regularization (v2 Sections 4–4.1, Equations 7–8). This changes the objective and inversion procedure substantially. The short prompt-aware preprocessing procedure is retained.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, method narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Preliminaries become a separate section, rare-concept background moves into the experimental discussion, and supplementary Sections 6–10 become Appendices A–G. Forward/backward terminology and author information are also revised.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. v2 redesigns the opening figure, expands performance plots and qualitative grids into LDM/LCM comparisons, and adds prior and failure displays. The original user-study table becomes prose, while a new ablation occupies Table 1. Retained material is also rearranged: v1 Figures 13–15 reappear as Figures S5, S6, and S1.

R1.justification: Fixed-point inversion, presented as the main novelty in v1, becomes an approach attributed to prior AIDI work in v2. The revised positioning distinguishes RNRI from AIDI, ExactDPM, and ReNoise, adds consistency/distillation literature, and expands discussion of stochastic DDPM inversion, including LEDITS++, while explicitly excluding that family from the paper's scope.

T1.justification: v1's conditional fixed-point contractivity argument is replaced by scalar residual and regularized-objective definitions, conditional Newton convergence discussion, and a Taylor-based componentwise update derivation in Appendix A. The inversion noise coefficient is also corrected from sqrt(alpha[t-1]) to sqrt(alpha[t]) in v2 Equations 3–4. The added derivation does not establish the asserted equivalence between a root of the regularized objective and its minimizer.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens empirical scrutiny through closer baselines, regularization and guidance ablations, and quantified failure analysis. However, its new central formulation asserts a root/minimizer equivalence that its Gaussian log-density objective and Appendix A do not justify. Conflicting LCM step counts also leave the headline speed evidence ambiguous. These issues affect the mathematical foundation and performance interpretation, so the substantial empirical additions do not establish a reliable net direction in overall quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same diffusion-inversion work despite retitling and a substantial solver revision. The text, equations, figures, tables, and complete supplementary sections are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports RNRI experiments with latent diffusion and consistency models, comparative user studies, regularization ablations, and a convergence audit of 118,000 COCO image-caption pairs.

before.justification: v1 reports original COCO reconstruction and editing experiments, a 60-image user study, and interpolation and rare-concept generation results, including supplementary examples.

title: Lightning-Fast Image Inversion and Editing for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models

The headline runtime changes from 0.5 seconds for the earlier few-step setting to 0.4 seconds for SDXL-Turbo/Flux, under a revised evaluation scope.

It expands the explanation of Newton extrapolation reaching unsuitable latent solutions, acknowledges that the guided objective may lack an exact zero, and interprets trajectory decay as contraction. Incorrect-caption failures remain in Appendix C, while the explicit discussion of particular editing failures in v2's appendix is removed.

It removes the prompt-aware adjustment ablation in v2 Table 1, the 10,000-image latent-consistency analysis, and Figure S6. E5.justification: Both versions report averaged metrics and display error bars in convergence and lambda-sensitivity plots without defining their statistical meaning or specifying independent-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. E6.justification: v4 adds Flux and PIE-Bench results, including GNRI background PSNR 30.22 and inversion time 0.521 seconds in Table 1. These substantially change the presented procedure, although the PDFs do not establish corresponding implementation changes.

P2.justification: The opening comparison becomes a consecutive Flux-editing demonstration; Figure 3 becomes a three-panel diagnostic; and the main reconstruction/editing displays are redesigned.
