R1.justification: v2 explicitly places stochastic DDPM inversion outside its comparison scope; v4 brings such editors into its competitive positioning. Related work also expands to Direct Inversion, both TurboEdit papers, Flux/rectified-flow models, Euler scheduling and underdetermined Newton methods. This broadens the research positioning beyond citation-format or publication-metadata changes.

T1.justification: v4 adds Euler scheduling and inversion equations, revises the formal guidance definition, and introduces Appendix B's fixed-point reformulation and contraction argument. Appendix A now discusses nonunique scalar Newton updates and convergence to nonzero minima. These are substantive mathematical additions; the contraction discussion uses empirical trajectory decay rather than establishing contraction throughout a neighborhood.

improvement.justification: The added Flux and PIE-Bench evaluations and broader baselines provide useful applicability tests that v2 lacked. However, unchanged baseline results receive different method attributions in Tables 2–3 without explanation. New theoretical support also introduces the incorrect claim that Newton root-finding for x²+1 converges to its minimum (Appendix A), while trajectory decay does not establish the contraction claimed in Appendix B. These reliability concerns counterbalance the empirical gains, preventing a reliable judgment of net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Newton-Raphson diffusion-inversion research, with RNRI renamed GNRI. All 17 pages of v2 and 18 pages of v4, including figures, tables, equations and appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: v4 reports original COCO and PIE-Bench evaluations, Flux experiments, a revised human-preference study, interpolation and rare-concept results, and convergence diagnostics.

before.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction and editing experiments, a human-preference study, interpolation and rare-concept generation results, and appendix ablations and convergence analyses.

title: Lightning-Fast Image Inversion and Editing for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The central claims remain efficient, training-free guided inversion, rapid editing, and improved interpolation and rare-concept generation. Explicitly mentioning flow-matching compatibility clarifies coverage already represented by Flux.1 in v4 rather than introducing a new core contribution.

C2.justification: Appendix B explicitly connects the existing non-zero-minimum discussion to GNRI's nonnegative objective. Appendices H and I explain the stochastic-inversion fidelity/speed tradeoff and distinguish distribution-aware guidance from Anderson acceleration, including possible application of guidance to other iterative methods.

D1.justification: Appendix H explains the reported 6 NFEs as four steps averaging 1.5 Newton-Raphson iterations. Appendix J specifies the 40 GB A100 and 24 GB RTX 3090Ti hardware. These extend technical disclosure; the original implementation information and code/data access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The underlying COCO, PIE-Bench, and ImageNet-based coverage remains. v5 adds a deliberately non-typical COCO test population in Appendix I and simultaneous editing of different object categories in Appendix K, extending test scenarios within the existing image-editing domain.

E2.justification: EditFriendly, already present in v4's editing comparisons, is added to PIE-Bench Table 1 and the reconstruction comparison in Table H2. Appendix I adds a dedicated Anderson-acceleration comparison beyond v4's existing AIDI evaluations. The broader comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: The original benchmark and human-study protocols remain unchanged. Added evaluations use Flux.1 for qualitative PIE-Bench comparisons, select 300 COCO images with the lowest reported likelihood, introduce NFE measurements, and compare memory and timing on A100 and RTX 3090Ti GPUs.

E4.justification: v5 retains the guidance ablation, lambda sensitivity, contraction measurements, and caption-mismatch failure analysis. It substantially broadens supplementary analysis through the low-likelihood Anderson comparison, NFE and hardware-memory studies, and simultaneous multi-object editing case studies in Appendices H–K.

E5.justification: The existing averaged results and plot error bars are retained. v5 introduces no new repeated-run counts, experimental seed protocols, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Existing Table 1 rows and Tables 2–3 retain their values, but Tables H1–J1 substantially expand reported findings. Examples include GNRI's 6 NFEs; EditFriendly's 26.1 versus GNRI's 23.9 reconstruction PSNR, with inversion times of 32.3 versus 0.521 seconds; and low-likelihood PSNR of 25.8 versus Anderson's 18.3. New qualitative results appear in Figures F2 and K1. Figure 4 also newly claims a 2× speedup over DDIM, which conflicts with its retained runtime plot.

M1.justification: The residual objective, Gaussian guidance term, scalar Newton-Raphson update, initialization, and scheduler formulations remain unchanged. The expanded guidance explanation and corrected equation references do not introduce a different algorithm.

P1.justification: The main narrative remains intact, with localized explanatory edits and corrected implicit-equation references. The appendices are split and reorganized, including a separate no-zero-crossing discussion. v5 also adds acknowledgments, changes the conference header, and condenses affiliations.

P2.justification: Tables H1, H2, I1, and J1 and Figures F2 and K1 substantially expand the visual presentation of computational comparisons, difficult inputs, and editing examples. Table 1 gains a comparator row; Figure 1 replaces the notebook's Work edit with ICLR; Figures 3–4 receive label and caption edits. Existing appendix figures are largely retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: Section 4.1 newly credits Hong and Garibi for applying norms to inversion residuals, clarifying GNRI's distinction. Appendix I adds substantive positioning against Anderson acceleration. Reference deduplication and author/year corrections concern existing works rather than newly added research.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulations, Appendix A derivation, and contraction argument remain unchanged, with the latter moving from Appendix B to C. New Appendix B expands the existing discussion of objectives without zero crossings but supplies no new proof, derivation, or formal convergence result.

improvement.justification: The added NFE, memory, EditFriendly, and low-likelihood comparisons make computational costs, robustness, and reconstruction tradeoffs more assessable than in v4. These are useful, focused additions to an already extensive evaluation. The new Figure 4 claim of a 2× speedup over DDIM contradicts its plot, introducing a limited accuracy defect that reduces, but does not outweigh, those benefits.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GNRI research work. The text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across appendix renumbering.

after.justification: v5 retains those original results and adds computational measurements, a low-likelihood COCO comparison, and additional qualitative editing experiments.

before.justification: v4 reports original image reconstruction, editing, interpolation, rare-concept generation, and human-evaluation results, together with appendix ablations and failure analyses.

title: Lightning-Fast Image Inversion and Editing for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models

C1.justification: v1's introductory claim of sublinear dependence on superarm size is withdrawn; v2 acknowledges worst-case linear dependence in Section 3.1. The abstract drops the claim of reduced dependence on prior informativeness. Conversely, the introduction adds a claim that BUCB permits less exploration while retaining theoretical guarantees and broadens the novelty wording from the first Bayesian regret bound to the first regret bound for GP-BUCB.

C2.justification: v1's substantive discussion of inducing-point instability, optimization resets, clustering, graph-kernel assumptions, and prior-dependent behavior is removed. v2 adds interpretations of confidence-parameter tuning and theoretical qualifications concerning worst-case eigenvalue dependence and possible logarithmic improvements. The limitations of the retained inducing-point heuristic are no longer discussed.

D1.justification: Experimental documentation is substantially replaced: detailed SUMO initialization, synthetic-network construction, and prior-specific instructions disappear, while GP reward-generation parameters, GPyTorch implementation information, and exact route endpoint identifiers are supplied. The earlier disclosure of a 500-eigenpair graph-kernel approximation is absent. Kernel formulas and vehicle parameters are largely retained in Appendix B rather than newly introduced.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates a synthetic grid and traffic simulations on Luxembourg and Monaco. v2 removes the grid and replaces the traffic environments with GP-generated energy costs on the retained road topologies. Monaco coverage also changes from one evaluation route to two. These changes substantially alter the represented navigation scenarios.

E2.justification: v1's principal algorithm comparison evaluates GP and Bayesian-inference models with BUCB and Thompson sampling. v2 retains these combinations and adds GP-UCB and BI-UCB to the actual comparison in Figure 2. This is a limited expansion of the comparator set; the BUCB name change is not a new method.

E3.justification: The city-network horizon changes from 200 to 500 rounds, and reported random regret based on an estimated best route is replaced by cumulative regret under generated rewards. The prior and reward-generation settings change substantially. The stated GP optimization budget changes from batches of 8000 with five gradient steps to batches of 2500 with one step; v2 also introduces confidence-parameter and lengthscale sweep protocols.

E4.justification: v1's comparisons of five kernel compositions and three levels of prior informativeness disappear. v2 instead tests UCB/BUCB confidence parametrizations and kernel lengthscales from 0.1 to 2.0, with extended results in Appendix C.1. Exploration visualizations are also replaced with comparisons covering all six algorithms on four routes, changing the questions investigated.

E5.justification: v1 specifies ten repetitions for synthetic-network experiments and five for city-network experiments. v2 specifies five repetitions per configuration throughout its replacement experimental suite. Means and standard errors remain the reporting practice; the removed ten-run experiments do not establish a reduction in repetitions for a matched experiment.

E6.justification: The earlier synthetic results, city energy-consumption table, and visited-edge counts are removed. v2 reports replacement 500-round results, including GP-BUCB versus GP-UCB and new parameter-sensitivity findings in Figures 2–6. These are not same-setting performance improvements. The new lengthscale plots generally show decreasing GP regret as lengthscale grows, although the accompanying sentence on page 10 incorrectly states an increase.

M1.justification: The core selection rules, composite graph-feature kernel, and rectified routing procedure remain; Bayes-GP-UCB is renamed GP-BUCB. However, v2 Algorithm 3 removes v1's explicit Adam updates of kernel and likelihood parameters, while Appendix B.3 still specifies an Adam learning rate. It is unclear whether the optimization procedure changed or its description became incomplete.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and contribution narrative are extensively rewritten. Finite-case theory is brought into the main analysis, the separate application and experimental sections are consolidated, and kernel details move to Appendix B. The notation appendix and extended discussion disappear, while a dedicated experimental-results appendix is introduced. This substantially changes the document's organization and emphasis.

P2.justification: v2 adds the related-work comparison table and replaces the earlier experimental displays with compact multi-panel algorithm and sensitivity plots. Numerical result tables and the notation table disappear; exploration maps are redrawn and placed in Appendix C. Separate TS and BUCB pseudocode displays are combined with UCB, while the unchanged vehicle-parameter table moves to the appendix.

R1.justification: New Table 1 systematically positions the work against related GP-bandit theory. Section 3.1 changes the comparison with Nika et al. from v1's claimed advantage in superarm-size dependence to matching its order, and adds comparison with Takeno et al. (2024). References supporting offline navigation and discrete inducing-point discussions are removed, while newer theoretical and implementation references are added.

T1.justification: The regret bounds replace v1's noise-only constant with a factor involving the largest within-superarm posterior covariance eigenvalue. New Lemma A.12 supplies the corresponding variance/information-gain argument, changing the worst-case dependence on superarm size. Lemma 3.1 also adds the logarithmic case where ξ/ω equals one, while the main BUCB theorems specialize to ξ > ω > 1. These are substantive revisions beyond reorganizing existing proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 improves the central analysis by addressing the missing covariance dependence in v1's variance bound and qualifying the superarm-size claim; the added UCB and tuning comparisons are also useful. However, replacing traffic simulations with GP-generated costs and removing kernel/prior studies and substantive limitations weakens application and robustness support. The contradictory lengthscale summary adds a reporting defect. These substantial gains and losses do not establish a reliable net direction in overall quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same combinatorial Gaussian-process bandit work despite the changed title and substantially revised experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments using GP-generated energy costs on Luxembourg and Monaco road networks, including algorithm comparisons and sensitivity studies in Section 4 and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original bandit experiments on a synthetic network and SUMO simulations of Luxembourg and Monaco, including algorithm, kernel, and prior comparisons in Section 5.

title: Bayesian Analysis of Combinatorial Gaussian Process Bandits

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions: Bayesian regret bounds for the three GP algorithms, the claimed first GP-BayesUCB bound, and a contextual combinatorial framework for energy-efficient navigation.

C2.justification: Section 2.1 adds an explanation of the finite per-round arm restriction. Section 3.1 expands discussion of possible gaps in dependence on K and tightness in T, explicitly distinguishing unavailable general Bayesian lower bounds from cited non-Bayesian bounds.

D1.justification: Section 4.1 corrects the documented variance scaling used to specify the GP environment and observation noise. Appendix B's kernel implementation, route endpoints, optimizer rates, batch size and inducing-point count remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate simulated energy-efficient navigation on the same Luxembourg and Monaco networks, with routes A and B in each. Context features and the represented navigation scenarios are unchanged.

E2.justification: The main comparison retains GP-UCB, GP-BUCB and GP-TS alongside BI-UCB, BI-BUCB and BI-TS. The comparator sets in the parametrization and lengthscale experiments also remain unchanged; newly cited methods are not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the stated GP variance from 0.25^2 sigma_det to 0.25^2 sigma_det^2, and noise variance from 0.1^2 sigma_det to 0.1^2 sigma_det^2, where sigma_det denotes standard deviation. This revises the reported simulation settings, but the PDFs do not establish reruns. Other evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The confidence-parameter comparison, lengthscale sensitivity analysis and route-exploration visualizations are retained. Removing v2's standalone Luxembourg A lengthscale figure does not remove an analysis: those results remain in Appendix C.

E5.justification: Both versions report five evaluations per experimental configuration and retain the same mean and standard-error reporting. No repeated-run count, seed information or statistical testing procedure is added or revised.

E6.justification: The reported experimental curves, uncertainty regions and route visualizations are retained across Figures 2–3 and Appendix C. The results displayed in v2 Figure 4 remain in v3 Figure 5. The revised variance description is not accompanied by changed reported outcomes.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–3, the GP-UCB/GP-BUCB/GP-TS selection rules, combined graph and feature kernel, rectification procedure and SVGP optimization remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 adds limited explanatory passages, consolidates author and affiliation information, removes the keyword line and makes small wording edits. The main section sequence and organization of Appendices A–C remain intact.

P2.justification: Document-wide ICLR reformatting changes margins, typography, title and author layout, and figure placement and sizing. Table 1 gains a regret row and expanded caption; Figure 3 uses a more compact arrangement with shared labeling. The redundant main-text lengthscale figure is removed while its appendix counterpart is retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds Wen et al. (2015), Merlis and Mannor (2020), Scarlett (2018), and Cai and Scarlett (2021) to contextualize bound dependence and possible optimality gaps. Table 1 also gains explicit regret-rate comparisons. The broader research positioning is retained.

T1.justification: Theorems 3.2 and 3.6, Assumptions 3.3–3.4, the lemmas and Appendix A proofs are unchanged. The added comparisons with existing bounds provide interpretation rather than a new formal result or revised derivation.

improvement.justification: v3 corrects the dimensionally inconsistent variance specification in Section 4.1 and makes theoretical scope and possible bound gaps clearer through Sections 2.1 and 3.1 and Table 1. These improve clarity and reproducibility without changing the proofs or empirical evidence. The added non-Bayesian lower-bound comparison remains suggestive rather than establishing Bayesian optimality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables and complete Appendices A–C. Their methods, theoretical results and experiments can be reliably matched despite reformatting.

after.justification: Section 4.2 and Appendix C retain original navigation experiments, including five-run algorithm comparisons and lengthscale sensitivity results.

before.justification: Section 4.2 and Appendix C report original navigation simulations on Luxembourg and Monaco road networks, including algorithm comparisons, parameter sensitivity and exploration visualizations.

title: Bayesian Analysis of Combinatorial Gaussian Process Bandits

C1.justification: The contribution changes from DW supported by human judgments and a frequency-guidance training loss to FWD emphasizing domain agnosticism, interpretability and robustness. Claims that the metric aligns with the user study and that wavelet guidance improves a generator disappear. The broader motivation of combining spatial and frequency information remains.

C2.justification: v1's interpretations of user preferences and DDPM background-frequency errors are replaced by explanations involving classifier histograms, domain-specific retraining and limited training data. v2 adds substantive limitations concerning usefulness on ImageNet, semantic information absent from FWD, and possible joint optimization of FID and FWD.

D1.justification: v2 adds specific FID/KID implementation references, pretrained-weight information, training schedules, batch sizes and GPU hardware for domain experiments. Appendices A.5–A.6 disclose computing resources and DNDD processing from 3,600 source images into 57,600 patches. v1's promise to release a reference Python package is absent from v2.

E1.justification: The five original generation benchmarks remain, while v2 adds FFHQ and the agricultural DNDD dataset. CelebA attributes and DNDD labels also support domain-specific backbone training. The human image-realism discrimination task is removed, and corruption coverage changes to include uniform noise and JPEG compression.

E2.justification: v2 adds KID and PSNR to the main metric comparison and introduces FID with domain-retrained backbones. The Fourier power-spectrum KL comparator is removed. Table 1 also drops WaveDiff and Diffusion Transformer result rows and adds BigGAN on ImageNet; Projected FastGAN participates in the new domain-bias comparisons.

E3.justification: ImageNet evaluation changes from 10K images to 50K validation images. FID values previously taken from the literature are replaced by values reported as computed with a common implementation. New protocols include domain-specific backbone training and optimized selection of 50K samples from a 250K pool. The wavelet-guided fine-tuning protocol is removed.

E4.justification: v2 adds backbone-retraining controls, class-histogram analyses, FID-optimized sampling and JPEG-corruption tests. Packet analysis shifts to explaining DDGAN versus StyleGAN2 through per-packet Fréchet distances. Fourier ablation, rotation sensitivity, wavelet-family/degree sensitivity and guidance-loss experiments disappear. Gaussian-blur analysis already existed in v1's appendix and is reworked, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 Figures 8–9 report means and standard deviations over five images, and appendix Figure 15 also displays uncertainty bands. v2's perturbation plots omit these bands, while Table 3 newly reports mean and standard deviation over five runs for the sampling experiment. This does not establish increased replication of retained experiments.

E6.justification: v2 replaces DW results with FWD, adds KID/PSNR scores and reports recomputed FID values; CelebA-HQ StyleSwin FID changes from 3.25 to 23.257 under the revised computation. CIFAR10's best wavelet ranking changes from DDPM under DW to DDGAN under FWD, without implying comparable-metric improvement. Domain-bias and optimization results are added; human-study, Fourier and guidance-loss results are removed.

M1.justification: v1's symmetrized KL divergence between normalized wavelet power spectra is replaced by FWD, which averages Gaussian Fréchet distances computed from per-packet means and covariances. The default wavelet changes from Symlet-5 to Haar. The proposed wavelet guidance loss and associated generator fine-tuning method are removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten around FWD and domain bias. The architecture survey moves to the appendix, loss and user-study sections disappear, and a dedicated limitations section is introduced. The title, author list, terminology and appendix organization also change.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column to a single-column layout. Table 1 gains metric and image-size columns; introductory illustrations are replaced, and a new FWD flowchart and domain-bias displays appear. Many empirical plots are redesigned or removed. The basic transform schematics survive as v1 Figures 10–12 becoming v2 Figures 7–9.

R1.justification: Related work is repositioned around domain-agnostic versus domain-dependent metrics, with substantive additions covering KID, PSNR, Fourier image-quality measures and Projected GANs. The earlier emphasis on higher-order wavelets versus Haar-based prior work is reduced. Much of the generative-architecture survey moves to Appendix A.4 rather than being removed.

T1.justification: The central mathematical definition changes from normalized power distributions and symmetrized KL divergence to per-packet statistical estimates and an average Gaussian Fréchet distance. v1's appendix derivation of perfect-reconstruction and alias-cancellation conditions is removed. Basic wavelet-transform equations survive, including material moved into v2's main method section.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens the domain-bias investigation through retrained-backbone controls and agricultural-data tests, and improves implementation disclosure. However, the replacement metric lacks v1's direct human validation, and Table 3 contains incorrect percentage changes: FWD rising from 0.338 to 0.398 is about 17.8%, not 2.5%. These gains and validation/reporting weaknesses leave the net effect on overall quality unclear.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe successive versions of the same wavelet-based image-generation metric research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison despite the extensive revision.

after.justification: v2 reports original FWD evaluations, generator and InceptionV3 training experiments, domain-bias analyses, and corruption and sampling-optimization tests.

before.justification: v1 reports original metric evaluations, a 41-participant user study, perturbation and wavelet-choice analyses, and a DDPM fine-tuning experiment.

title: Fréchet Wavelet Distance: A Domain-Agnostic Metric for Image Generation

C1.justification: The original domain-agnostic, interpretable FWD contribution remains. v3 adds computational efficiency and FD-DINOv2's residual domain bias and high computational cost as explicit introduction contributions. The abstract and conclusion extend the critique to FD-DINOv2, and the conclusion adds environmental-cost and complementary-use claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations involving DINOv2 training-data overlap, SWD random-projection variability and StableDiffusion-2.1 image artifacts. It removes v2's explicit limitations concerning FWD's limited added utility on ImageNet, its frequency/spatial rather than semantic emphasis, and possible joint optimization of FWD and FID. These qualifications are not relocated to an appendix.

D1.justification: v3 supplies an explicit FWD implementation link and identifies the FD-DINOv2 code source. It documents the Sentinel winter subset, its 31,825 images, format conversion and generator-training settings, and identifies the StableDiffusion versions evaluated. Appendix compute information changes from A40 GPUs to A100 GPUs and ties the resources to sample generation. These materially expand or revise reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v3 adds Sentinel remote-sensing imagery and Conceptual Captions text-to-image evaluation, while removing CIFAR-10 coverage entirely. It also adds human realism judgments. The DNDD description changes from sugar beet to winter wheat and rye, but retained sample counts and scores leave unclear whether this corrects documentation or reflects different underlying data.

E2.justification: FD-DINOv2 becomes a central evaluated comparator. Tables 8–9 add FID-infinity, IS, IS-infinity, Clean-FID and SWD, and introduce KID into the domain-bias comparison. PSNR and SSIM disappear, while FD-DINOv2 replaces KID in the reweighting and corruption comparisons. Some cross-domain retrained-Inception comparisons from v2 Table 2 are removed.

E3.justification: New protocols include real-versus-generated image choices with over 1,000 responses from 50 volunteers, Conceptual Captions evaluation against external user ratings, and feature-extraction GFLOPs and throughput measurements over 50,000 images. The reported Proj. FastGAN learning rate on CelebA-HQ and DNDD changes from 2e-4 to 1e-4; the PDFs do not establish whether those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds human-perception validation, an SWD-versus-FWD reproducibility analysis in Table 9, and a CelebA-HQ class-histogram comparison for DDGAN and Proj. FastGAN in Figure 5a. It extends the existing corruption and FID-optimization analyses to FD-DINOv2. The packet-interpretability analysis is retained, while some cross-domain retrained-backbone checks disappear.

E5.justification: Table 9 newly reports minimum, mean and standard deviation across five independent metric computations. Conversely, the retained reweighting results lose v2 Table 3's explicit five-run caption in v3 Table 6, although their uncertainty values remain. This does not establish a change in the underlying run count.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial numerical evidence for FD-DINOv2, Sentinel, EDM, human perception, efficiency and additional metrics. Existing ImageNet values also change: Improved Diffusion VLB has FID 42.257 and FWD 2.221 in v2 Table 1, versus 33.522 and 2.182 in v3 Table 4. With unchanged reweighting means, the reported FID change is corrected from -47% to -52.53%, and FWD from +2.5% to +17.75%. CIFAR-10 and several comparison entries are removed.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same Haar wavelet-packet decomposition, pixel normalization, per-packet means and covariances, Fréchet distances and averaging procedure. The resolution-dependent transformation-depth rule is also retained. New evaluated generators and comparison metrics do not alter FWD.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: domain bias leads, the broad generator comparison moves later, and a user-study section is introduced. Related-work material moves into Appendix B, appendices are reorganized into A–C, and the limitations section disappears. The introduction, results interpretation and conclusion are extensively revised, alongside language and author-information edits.

P2.justification: v3 restructures the benchmark and retrained-backbone tables, adds efficiency, perception and additional-metric tables, and introduces extensive sample grids in Appendix C. The corruption plot moves to the appendix with a changed comparator legend; the DNDD histogram moves into a combined main-text figure. Sample panels, captions, figure placement and the conference-template layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: The positioning expands beyond Inception-based and traditional pairwise metrics to address FD-DINOv2 and SWD as important alternatives. New discussion cites Stein et al., Oquab et al. and Nguyen et al. to motivate training-domain, computational and reproducibility concerns. Additional generator and dataset references support the expanded evaluation; moving the spectral-method discussion to Appendix B is separately a structural change.

T1.justification: Equations 1–9 retain the same wavelet construction, statistical definitions and Fréchet-distance formulation. The appendix explanation of forward and inverse wavelet transforms is preserved. No substantive mathematical assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs are added or removed.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the empirical grounding of the unchanged metric through relevant FD-DINOv2 and other comparisons, measured computational cost, broader domains and an original human-realism study. These address important gaps in v2's perceptual validation and practical comparison. The implementation link and corrected percentages also help. Removing explicit limitations weakens balance, and Table 7 uses external ratings whose comparability to the evaluated samples is undocumented. Nevertheless, the direct comparisons and original human evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Fréchet Wavelet Distance work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: v3 retains original evaluations and adds computational measurements, Sentinel results and an original 50-volunteer perception study. The externally sourced ratings in Table 7 are distinct from these original results.

before.justification: v2 reports original generator evaluations, retrained-Inception comparisons, sample-reweighting experiments and corruption tests in Tables 1–3 and Figure 6.

title: Fréchet Wavelet Distance: A Domain-Agnostic Metric for Image Generation

C1.justification: v3 explicitly adds MR-Score to the claimed contributions. The headline GPT4-versus-GPT3.5 advantage changes from approximately tenfold diagnostic success to fivefold performance measured by MR-Score. The central claims about meta-reasoning evaluation and weaknesses concealed by conventional benchmarks remain.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes caution about GPT4 grading because of false positives; v3 argues that it can serve as a useful automatic evaluator because aggregate MR-Scores closely match manual scores, while still encouraging manual annotation. v3 also adds an overfitting interpretation of output-format failures and expands the discussion of counterfactual reasoning and grounding. The limitation that diagnostic fine-tuning need not improve GSM8K performance is retained.

D1.justification: v3 specifies GPT4-Turbo-1106 as the automatic grader and documents the new scoring weights and clipping rule. Annotation procedures, evaluation and data-generation prompts, sampling temperatures and fine-tuning details were already supplied in v1; their relocation does not constitute new disclosure.

E1.justification: Table 1 retains the same 1,418 original, 222 Program-of-Thought and 1,360 reversed examples. v3 Section 7 additionally reports trying solutions sampled from different generating models, adding a limited test scenario, although those models and sample sizes are unspecified.

E2.justification: The benchmark comparison retains Claude2, GPT3.5, GPT4, WizardMath-70B, Mammoth-70B, MetaMath-70B and the diagnostic fine-tuned llama2 model. Table 3 also retains the GSM8K-only llama2 control. Renaming llama2-70B-diag to llama2-70B-MR does not introduce another comparator.

E3.justification: v3 Section 3.2 replaces binary accuracy with MCC and introduces MR-Score, combining clipped MCC, error-step accuracy and error-reason accuracy with weights 0.2, 0.3 and 0.5. Automated-grader validation expands from a balanced 100-instance sample to a reported 1,668 judgments. The main zero-shot/three-shot settings and temperature 0.5 remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1's small automated-grading confusion matrix becomes a broader validation of whether automatic grading preserves benchmark scores: v3 Appendix B adds per-model manual-versus-automatic comparisons and a larger confusion matrix. Section 7 also briefly reports checks using different solution generators. Existing prompt observations, fine-tuning analyses and appendix case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The larger grading sample changes the evaluation design, without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Results change beyond percentage formatting: under the same stated main settings, GPT4's correctly located error steps increase from 784/1573 to 823/1573, and complete diagnoses from 644/1573 to 677/1573. Other model counts also change, without an explanation of their origin. v3 additionally reports MCC, MR-Score and automated-grading results, including GPT4 manual/automatic MR-Scores of 0.495/0.512.

M1.justification: The three diagnostic tasks, evaluation prompt, GPT4-based training-data generation and QLoRA fine-tuning procedure are retained. The appendix prompt images are identical. MR-Score changes evaluation aggregation rather than the model or diagnostic procedure.

P1.justification: The title and benchmark terminology change, and the introduction is substantially shortened and reorganized. Evaluation gains separate dataset and metric subsections; discussion and limitations are separated. Annotation procedures, fine-tuning implications and prompt discussions are redistributed into a reorganized appendix with additional subsections.

P2.justification: Tables 2 and 3 are redesigned around MCC and MR-Score, and a manual-versus-automatic comparison table is added. Figure 1 changes its axis and displayed metric; the benchmark schematic moves earlier, the reasoning-tree illustration moves to Discussion, and the confusion matrix moves to the appendix. Existing appendix prompt and example images are reused.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting automated judging, including Zheng et al. and Liu et al., alongside Matthews for MCC and Gudibande et al. for imitation limitations. Some alignment and stochastic-parrot references are removed. The main related-work discussion and positioning of meta-reasoning evaluation remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: v3 introduces the mathematical definition of MR-Score, including zero-clipping MCC and weighting the three component scores, absent from v1. This is a limited addition of formal definitions; no theorem, proof or theoretical guarantee is added.

improvement.justification: The explicit scoring definition and per-model grading comparison make the benchmark easier to apply and provide evidence that automated grading preserves model rankings, improving on v1's preliminary 100-instance check. The gain is limited by unexplained changes in benchmark counts and an unresolved inconsistency: v3 Table 4 totals 1,692 step-correct judgments, whereas Table 5 summarizes 1,668.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same meta-reasoning benchmark study, renamed from DiagGSM8K to MR-GSM8k. The main text, tables, figures, equations and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including the image-based prompts and examples.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark and fine-tuning results, revises several reported values and presents an expanded comparison of manual and automated grading in Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations on 3,000 annotated question-solution pairs, an in-domain fine-tuning experiment and a 100-instance assessment of automated grading.

title: MR-GSM8K: A Meta-Reasoning Benchmark for Large Language Model Evaluation

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the meta-reasoning paradigm, MR-GSM8K, and MR-Score. v4 strengthens benchmark transformation into an explicit contribution claiming robustness against overfitting and contamination, and adds the introductory finding that much smaller models can outperform larger ones. These extend the claims without replacing the paper's central thesis.

C2.justification: v4 adds interpretations concerning model size versus data quality, demonstration-induced prediction bias, and equation-equivalence and unit errors. Appendix A introduces a substantive applicability limitation for holistic or creative subjects. title: Exposure Bracketing Is All You Need For A High-Quality Image

C1.justification: The abstract narrows analysis of 'all possible limits' to 'different limits' and explicitly states empirical applicability to deep nonlinear networks. The central contributions—an exact finite-width solution with arbitrary initialization and three feature-learning mechanisms absent from the kernel phase—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 removes the adaptive-optimizer interpretation and adds explanations involving initialization-dependent GD–SGD differences, hyperparameter transfer, and large initialization entering the kernel regime. The conclusion replaces planned exploration beyond one-dimensional inputs with speculation about impossibility and drops the statement that alignment findings are preliminary. The core alignment, norm, and generalization interpretation remains.

D1.justification: Appendix B.1 newly specifies the regression sampling distribution and noise scale and documents initialization, loss, and training-selection details for the added experiments. These disclosures do not establish changes to the retained regression setup. CIFAR-10 hyperparameters and the ResNet implementation pointer remain unchanged; exact learning rates for the new tests are not supplied.

E1.justification: v2 adds MNIST image classification and classification of samples from two Gaussian distributions, N(0,1) and N(4,1), in Figures 2, 6, and 7. Synthetic regression and CIFAR-10 remain, so coverage expands within the existing supervised-learning scope.

E2.justification: The SGD–Adam comparison under Xavier+ and Kaiming+ initialization in v1 Figure 5 and Appendix B.1 is removed. The corresponding CIFAR-10 comparison still includes NTK, mean field, Kaiming±, and Xavier±. RMSProp was discussed but not experimentally compared.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce substantial evaluation designs: additional activation functions, four- and six-layer networks, a matrix-based alignment measure, and binary cross-entropy classification. The MNIST experiments use full-batch GD with batch size 2000 to control for SGD's alignment bias, selecting learning rates for convergence within 1000 iterations. The retained CIFAR-10 protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 substantially broadens tests of the alignment mechanism across activations, network depth, initialization scale, and regression versus classification losses (Figures 1, 2, 6, and 7). These directly examine generality beyond v1's linear/ReLU toy demonstrations and indirect ResNet evidence. The optimizer-sensitivity analysis in v1 Figure 5 is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports empirical repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty bands. The theoretical distributions of initialization quantities are retained and do not constitute experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds alignment trajectories for sigmoid, swish, and leaky ReLU, depth and initialization results on MNIST, and classification findings including departures from perfect alignment under non-ReLU activations. The SGD–Adam results disappear. Matched CIFAR-10 curves and their reported approximately 5% and 10% accuracy gaps remain unchanged; the expansion does not establish improved performance under those settings.

M1.justification: The analyzed model remains a two-layer linear network trained by gradient flow on squared loss, with separate layer learning rates and arbitrary initialization. The additional nonlinear and deeper networks are empirical tests, not changes to the proposed analytical model or training procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially rewritten, related work becomes a dedicated section, and the solution presentation is reorganized around a proposition and appendix proof. Explanations are condensed or revised throughout, alongside changes to the title and affiliations. This is a substantial narrative reorganization beyond renumbering or local copyediting.

P2.justification: Figure 1 changes from four panels to a ten-panel activation comparison with shared legends and revised axes. New Figures 2, 6, and 7 display depth and classification analyses, while v1's optimizer figure is removed. Retained CIFAR-10 figures and Table 1 are resized or relocated, and the table caption moves above the table.

R1.justification: The new Related Work section substantially expands positioning against finite-width corrections, mean-field analyses, and deep-linear-network theory. Added references include Braun et al. on exact dynamics with prior knowledge, Bordelon and Pehlevan on finite-width fluctuations, and Yang et al. on hyperparameter transfer. It explicitly distinguishes perturbative or special-initialization results from the paper's exact arbitrary-initialization solution.

T1.justification: v2 adds a matrix alignment definition and a derivation bounding final alignment away from zero under stated feature-learning conditions in Section 4. The existing one-dimensional loss reduction becomes Proposition 1 with an expanded Appendix A.1 proof, whose equations omit the averaging factor and squared-loss notation. The main exact-solution theorem, phase theorem, and corollaries are retained.

improvement.justification: Direct layer measurements on MNIST and the activation/loss checks strengthen support beyond v1's shallow demonstrations and indirect ResNet norm evidence. Expanded related work also clarifies the contribution. These gains outweigh the removed optimizer analysis, but the new Appendix A.1 proof introduces averaging and squared-loss inconsistencies, limiting the net improvement.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe the same two-layer linear model, exact solution, phase diagrams, and shared experiments. The complete main texts and Appendices A and B are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulations and CIFAR-10 results and adds experiments with additional activations, deeper networks on MNIST, and synthetic binary classification.

before.justification: v1 reports original alignment simulations, CIFAR-10 experiments with ResNet-18 and two-layer networks, and an appendix comparison of SGD and Adam.

title: Three Mechanisms of Feature Learning in a Linear Network

C1.justification: The central contributions remain an exact finite-width linear-network solution for arbitrary initialization, three feature-learning mechanisms, phase diagrams, and empirical relevance to nonlinear networks. v3 explicitly mentions one-dimensional data in the abstract, but that restriction already appears in v2's problem setting and conclusion.

C2.justification: Section 3.4 qualifies the earlier universal preference for small initialization and distinguishes disalignment at large initialization from entering the kernel regime. Appendix D adds interpretations of generalization trajectories, sample-size effects, and the absence of grokking from a shared learning timescale. The conclusion explicitly discusses the limitations of deterministic dynamics and the potential roles of noise and regularization.

D1.justification: Appendix C.2 and the new figure captions document synthetic data generation, sample and input sizes, network width, output scaling, relative learning rates, and special initialization constructions. Existing benchmark preprocessing, training hyperparameters, and the borrowed-code link are carried over from v2's Appendix B.

E1.justification: Figures 8–9 add synthetic multivariate Gaussian regression with inputs outside a one-dimensional subspace, extending the scalar-input toy regression coverage in v2. The established MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Gaussian-classification tasks remain.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain the same methods: Figure 4 uses NTK, mean-field, Kaiming+, Kaiming−, Xavier+, and Xavier−; the alignment experiments retain kernel/feature-learning and orthogonal/near-orthogonal initialization comparisons. Newly cited work is not introduced as an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: New synthetic protocols compare sample counts of 10 versus 100, use a learning rate 15 times that in Figure 1, and test a three-layer linear network with width 300 and gamma = 1/d^2. Figure 10 compares training and population MSE with 1 versus 10 samples. Table 1 also changes the stated Kaiming exponents (c_u, c_w) from (0, −1) to (−1, 0), without establishing that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix C.2 adds explicit tests of sensitivity to dataset size, input dimension, large learning rates, and linear-network depth. Section 4.1 and Appendix B.4 add quantitative weight-evolution scaling analysis, while Appendix D examines training and generalization trajectories. These substantially extend v2's activation, initialization, and depth checks.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies repeated-run counts, seeds, empirical confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures. The added plots and empirical scaling exponents do not introduce a documented uncertainty-estimation or statistical fitting procedure.

E6.justification: Figure 1 replaces numerical trajectories, including linear-network near-orthogonal alignment ending around 0.90 in v2 versus 0.10 in v3; incompletely specified settings prevent treating this as a matched-setting improvement. v3 adds Figures 8–10 and reports weight-evolution exponents 0.47, 1.08, and 1.93 for NTK, Xavier−, and Kaiming−, respectively. The existing real-data accuracy plots are retained.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 broadens the analyzed model from a linear network to networks with power activations z^beta and introduces a scalar-ODE reduction for this family. The original linear solution becomes the beta = 1 specialization; MSE training and layer-specific gradient flow remain.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and introduction are rewritten, with explicit contribution bullets and a roadmap. The Gaussian-alignment argument moves from Section 4 to Section 3.2, and the corollaries move before Section 4.1. The appendix organization expands to separate related work, theory, experiments, and generalization dynamics.

P2.justification: The ICLR format changes typography, headers, text width, and figure/table placement. v3 adds Figures 8–10 and the notation-summary Table 2, redraws Figure 1, and changes Figure 4's width axis from linear to logarithmic. Several retained figures are regrouped or relocated.

R1.justification: New Appendix A substantially expands positioning against few-step feature learning, large-learning-rate catapult dynamics, alternative meanings of alignment, and asymptotic convergence analyses. The main text adds comparisons with Kunin et al. (2024), Beneventano and Woodworth (2025), Everett et al. (2024), and the Tensor Programs framework.

T1.justification: Proposition 1, Theorem 1, and their proofs are extended to power activations and a scalar-ODE reduction. Appendices B.4 and D add weight-scaling and empirical/population-loss derivations, and the phase-condition statements are revised. The revision also introduces an inconsistency: Equation (7) drops the initial-coordinate subtraction terms present in v2's weight reconstruction, generally violating the stated initial condition.

improvement.justification: The added robustness experiments, quantitative weight-scaling analysis, and clearer research positioning strengthen the paper. However, the expanded analytical presentation introduces problems: Equation (7) loses initialization terms retained in v2, and Proposition 1 retains beta-independent effective-data formulas despite the beta-dependent moments in Appendix B.1. These compromise the reliability of the expanded theoretical result. The empirical and explanatory gains coexist with unresolved mathematical defects, preventing a reliable net-quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work despite changes to the title and format. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds robustness experiments and training/generalization-loss simulations in Figures 8–10 and Appendices C–D.

before.justification: v2 reports original synthetic regression and classification experiments, MNIST alignment experiments, and CIFAR-10 experiments in Figures 1–7, including Appendix B.

title: Three Mechanisms of Feature Learning in a Linear Network

C1.justification: The central SPN-in-MIO and LiCE contributions remain. The abstract and introduction change the comparative framing from distance-focused explanations being implausible to plausibility-focused methods sacrificing proximity, and explicitly claim simultaneous likelihood, closeness and sparsity. This refines the claimed advantage within the existing contribution.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes leading KDE plausibility and discusses FACE outliers and LiCE's sparsity shortcomings. v2 recasts the empirical message around similarity and sparsity with comparable likelihood, and emphasizes the strength of two-stage MIO selection. It adds substantive explanations and qualifications concerning threshold-dependent failures, small-dataset difficulties, possible VAE misconfiguration, questionable GMSC timings and rejection of KDE for categorical data.

D1.justification: Appendices A.3–A.4 add extensive preprocessing rules, dataset-specific constraints, training and SPN hyperparameters, numerical margins, solving limits, hardware and compute information. v2 reports using OMLT/Pyomo and supplies a repository link where v1 promised future release. Appendix A.4 nevertheless retains inconsistent future-release wording; actual repository availability is not established by the PDFs.

The earlier closest-versus-likeliest MIO analysis is removed, and Figure 1 replaces the Adult case study with a German Credit example.

E6.justification: Benchmark results are extensively replaced and expanded. Adult LiCE's reported valid/actionable rates change from 51.6%/51.6% in v1 Table 1 to 92.4%/62.6% for LiCE(median) in v2 Table 2 under revised settings. P2.justification: v2 adds a capability matrix and redraws Figure 1 with different data, axes, markers and legend placement. Results are reorganized into separate success-rate, multi-dataset quality, variant and timing tables, replacing the earlier table organization. The five notation tables largely carry over with revised caption placement.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted positioning around PROPLACE and counterfactual disagreement, plus implementation and piecewise-modeling references. Explanations for excluding PlaCE and DACE are revised, while the broader relationship to MIO and tractable probabilistic models remains.

improvement.justification: v2 makes the work more reproducible and informative through detailed experimental documentation and comparisons that expose threshold sensitivity beyond Adult. However, it replaces v1's separate KDE plausibility check with the SPN already guiding generation and selection, reducing independent validation. The documentation and diagnostic gains support a net improvement, but these unresolved evaluation weaknesses limit its overall magnitude.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on Adult, Give Me Some Credit and German Credit, including benchmark comparisons, LiCE variants and timing results in Tables 2–3 and 9–11.

title: Generating Likely Counterfactuals Using Sum-Product Networks

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: encoding SPNs in MIO and generating plausible, close, sparse counterfactuals satisfying common constraints. The changed experimental discussion does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: Section 5 changes the likelihood interpretation from comparable performance to best performance for the proposed methods. Appendix A.5 changes the runtime interpretation from a broad LiCE disadvantage to comparability on Adult and Credit, and attributes optimizing LiCE's delay mainly to proving optimality. The explanation based on common-factual comparisons is removed.

D1.justification: V3 removes the documented recipe for the omitted sample-threshold configuration: bounding likelihood by the smaller of the factual's likelihood and the training median. Retained implementation libraries, hyperparameters, hardware, preprocessing, and code/data-access information are unchanged. Alpha = 0.1 was already disclosed in v2.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate counterfactual explanations for the same neural-network classification tasks on GMSC, Adult, and German Credit. No dataset, domain, or distinct test scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: The baseline suite remains DiCE, VAE, C-CHVAE, FACE with epsilon and knn variants, PROPLACE, and MIO. No baseline is selectively added or removed from a retained comparison. Changes to LiCE variants and deletion of the entire common-factual analysis concern ablation coverage.

E3.justification: V3 removes the auxiliary evaluation restricted to common successful factuals: 12 GMSC, 64 Adult, and 54 Credit instances in v2 Table 9. Success-rate and timing comparisons also replace quartile LiCE with optimizing LiCE. The core five-fold evaluation, 500 factuals per dataset, preprocessing, classifier, metrics, and 120-second solver budget remain as stated.

E4.justification: V2 Appendix A.5.1 and Table 9 analyze all methods on shared factuals to address differences in their successful evaluation subsets; this entire control analysis disappears. The LiCE variant study also drops the sample-dependent threshold ablation. V3 Table 9 corresponds to v2 Table 10, retaining optimize, quartile, and median variants rather than introducing a new ablation.

E5.justification: Both versions describe five-fold cross-validation and report means with standard deviations for counterfactual quality. Neither adds seeds, repeated-run information, confidence intervals, significance tests, or a different uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: MIO/LiCE results are extensively revised while external baseline scores remain unchanged. Table 2 changes GMSC median-LiCE validity from 3.2% to 53.6%; Table 3 changes its Credit NLL from 47.4 ± 18.3 to 30.5 ± 3.2. Median-LiCE GMSC runtime changes from 1851.30 to 122.27 seconds. Shared-factual and sample-variant results disappear. These are reported revisions, not established same-sample performance gains, since successful subsets change and the underlying revisions are unexplained.

M1.justification: The SPN encoding, classifier encoding, and counterfactual-generation procedures remain unchanged. The likelihood term incorporated into v3 Eq. 13 was already defined in v2 Appendix A.2.1, Eq. 14, and tested with alpha = 0.1 in Appendix A.5.2. Its promotion to the main text is not a new method.

P1.justification: V3 brings the existing likelihood-optimization explanation into Section 4, locally rewrites experimental interpretations, and reorganizes Appendix A.5. Most prose and section structure remain intact. The revised appendix introduces an unfinished sentence and explicit editorial placeholders.

P2.justification: The common-factual results table is removed, while the variant and runtime tables are relocated, renumbered, and have their rows revised. Table 3 adds downward arrows and explains that lower values are better. Figure 1 and the overall visual format remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Table 1 changes the attribution of sparsity from FACE to DiCE, a limited revision to the characterization of prior methods. The bibliography, related-work discussion, and principal novelty positioning otherwise remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The SPN approximation bound, assumptions, and mathematical constraint formulations remain unchanged. Integrating v2's existing weighted objective into v3 Eq. 13 and renumbering appendix equations introduce no new derivation, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: V3 makes the two existing LiCE objectives clearer in the main text, but removes the shared-factual comparison that addressed the acknowledged difficulty of comparing methods on different successful subsets. It also leaves unfinished editorial notes in Appendix A.5 and a timing caption referring to the Credit time limit despite newly reported subsecond results. These losses in evidential support and editorial consistency outweigh the limited clarity gains; more favorable reported numbers alone do not establish improved paper quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LiCE research. All 31 pages of each version, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains original experiments on the same datasets and reports revised success rates, counterfactual quality, variant comparisons, and runtimes.

before.justification: V2 reports original counterfactual-generation experiments on GMSC, Adult, and German Credit, including success rates, quality measurements, variant comparisons, and runtimes.

title: Generating Likely Counterfactuals Using Sum-Product Networks

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution lists retain the same principal claims: an MIO formulation of SPNs, SPN likelihood as a plausibility measure, and LiCE for producing plausible, close and sparse counterfactuals satisfying common desiderata. Causality receives less main-text emphasis but its formulation and claimed support remain in the appendices.

C2.justification: v4 substantially qualifies reliance on SPN likelihood. F.4 discusses lost statistical superiority under successful-factual comparisons and poor win95pts rankings; G.4 suggests insufficient training coverage as an explanation for weaker andes density estimates. It also expands explanations of threshold tradeoffs and infeasible Credit cases, beyond v3's emphasis on computational overhead and possible numerical failures.

D1.justification: v4 specifies the sum-node big-M constant as 100 and documents the bnlearn software, target variables and sampling procedures for the new synthetic experiments. The rough total compute estimate rises from 15,000 to 20,000 CPU hours. Most original hyperparameters and hardware details remain; the repository was already linked in v3.

E1.justification: The three real-world datasets are retained. v4 adds synthetic distributions from eight Bayesian networks for density-estimation evaluation (G.4), including counterfactual-generation tasks on asia, alarm and win95pts (F.4). These introduce substantial coverage of scenarios with known generating probabilities.

E2.justification: The external baseline roster remains DiCE, VAE, C-CHVAE, both FACE variants and PROPLACE; PlaCE and DACE remain unevaluated. Within the matched variant comparison, LiCE (sample) is added (v3 Table 9 versus v4 Table 10). The runtime comparison also gains quartile and sample variants (v3 Table 10 versus v4 Table 12).

E3.justification: The original preprocessing, neural-network architecture and five-fold design are retained. v4 adds comparisons on common successful factuals, synthetic CE experiments using 10,000 training samples and 100 fresh factuals, and density evaluation using 1,000 test samples. New metrics include true generating probabilities and density-fit measures. Synthetic optimizing LiCE uses alpha = 1, whereas the real-data experiments retain 0.1.

E4.justification: Beyond v3's variant and runtime comparisons, v4 tests MIO approximation accuracy against the actual SPN output (Table 2), compares methods on common factuals (F.2), evaluates CEs against known probabilities (F.4), and assesses SPN distribution fidelity (G.4). The sample-threshold variant also extends the sensitivity analysis.

E5.justification: v3 already reports standard deviations and five-fold experiments. v4 adds five-seed synthetic experiments, Friedman and Nemenyi significance tests with critical-difference diagrams, and significance tests for density correlations. F.4 aggregates synthetic runs, while G.4 explicitly selects the best-performing SPN from five fits.

E6.justification: Many retained benchmark and runtime values are revised. For example, LiCE (optimize) Credit NLL changes from 30.3 ± 3.8 to 28.8 ± 3.3, and LiCE (median) GMSC success changes from 53.6% to 60.0%. v4 also adds approximation, synthetic-probability, ranking and correlation results. These are revised and additional reports, rather than demonstrated controlled performance gains between versions.

M1.justification: Appendix F.1 introduces LiCE (sample), which sets the likelihood threshold to the minimum of the factual's likelihood and the training median. This adds an adaptive threshold rule to the retained SPN/MIO method; its main architecture, distance-likelihood objective and desiderata constraints remain.

P1.justification: The introduction, method exposition and results discussion are extensively revised. Prerequisites become separate from related work, and v3's single nested Appendix A becomes thematic Appendices A–G. Existing causality, diversity and encoding material is redistributed, and unfinished editorial notes in v3's supplementary discussion are removed.

P2.justification: v4 adopts a substantially different conference layout, transposes and revises Table 1, and redraws Figure 1 with a different example and explicit likelihood clipping. It adds approximation and common-factual tables, synthetic evaluation tables, critical-difference diagrams and an eight-panel density-fit figure. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates or renumbering.

R1.justification: v4 substantially expands research positioning through comparisons with adversarial-random-forest and GAN approaches, CeFlow, PPCEF and diffeomorphic counterfactuals. Section 3 and G.3 develop the distinctions between SPNs, GMMs, flows, autoregressive models and autoencoders, particularly categorical-data support and compatibility with linear MIO formulations.

T1.justification: v4 supplies explicit binary/big-M inequalities for sum-node maximization and an argument for tightness under likelihood maximization (Section 4), replacing v3's solver-level max expression. It removes the assertion that hard-EM training makes the approximation exact and adds formulation-size reasoning in F.3. The existing log-sum-exp bound and most other mathematics remain.

improvement.justification: v3 evaluates plausibility primarily through the same SPN used by LiCE and acknowledges that methods succeed on different factuals. v4 substantially addresses these weaknesses through known-probability synthetic evaluations, common-factual comparisons, direct approximation checks and statistical analyses. It also reports unfavorable findings that clarify dependence on SPN quality. Best-of-five selection in the density study and weak win95pts results limit generality, but the added validation and more explicit limitations substantially improve the paper's evidential quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LiCE research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: v4 retains original real-data experiments and adds SPN approximation measurements, synthetic counterfactual experiments and distribution-estimation evaluations.

before.justification: v3 reports original counterfactual-generation experiments on GMSC, Adult and German Credit, including validity, plausibility, similarity, sparsity and runtime results.

title: Generating Likely Counterfactuals Using Sum-Product Networks
