E5.justification: Standard-deviation reporting, five-seed synthetic procedures, Friedman tests, Nemenyi comparisons at alpha = 0.05, and correlation significance reporting are retained without changes.

E6.justification: Corresponding numerical entries and findings are unchanged throughout the main text and appendices. For example, Table 4 retains Adult LiCE (median) NLL of 12.9 ± 1.0. All four figures retain the same graphical results.

M1.justification: The SPN-to-MIO formulation, input encoding, classifier constraints, counterfactual objectives, and LiCE variants are unchanged. Mentioning newer SPN-learning methods does not change the implemented procedure.

P1.justification: v5 makes brief wording additions in Sections 6–7 and Appendix B.2, adds citations, and edits the acknowledgment grant number. The section hierarchy and substantive narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: Existing displays are repositioned: Table 2 moves from page 8 to 9, Table 12 from 25 to 26, Tables 17–18 from 32 to 31, and Figure 4 from 31 to 32. Display designs, captions, and graphical content are retained.

R1.justification: v5 adds Laugel et al. (2023) on counterfactual diversity, Trapp et al. (2019) on Bayesian SPN learning, and Trapp et al. (2020) on structured Gaussian-process mixtures. These provide limited additional context without revising the central novelty positioning.

T1.justification: Equations 1–24, the log-sum-exp approximation bound, and the desiderata and histogram formulations in Appendices B and C are unchanged. No mathematical definition, derivation, or proof is added or revised.

improvement.justification: The added diversity survey and SPN references modestly improve scholarly context, particularly around the retained learning algorithm and future-work options. The method, empirical evidence, mathematical arguments, reproducibility information, and limitations remain unchanged, so the quality gain is limited to literature coverage and contextual clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LiCE study. Their complete main text, equations, four figures, eighteen tables, and Appendices A–G support reliable comparison without material reading gaps.

after.justification: v5 retains the original real-data experiments and appendix simulations, including counterfactual quality, runtime, statistical comparisons, and distribution-fit results.

before.justification: v4 reports original counterfactual-generation experiments on GMSC, Adult, and German Credit, plus Bayesian-network simulations and SPN-fit evaluations in Appendices F and G.

title: Generating Likely Counterfactuals Using Sum-Product Networks

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion shift the central contribution from the interpretability ladder toward prediction, intervention simulation, and counterfactual generation. Beyond terminology, v2 foregrounds a claim that joint training increases the causal effect of concept interventions and changes decision-making, and broadens predictive-comparability claims to black-box models and more expressive CBMs.

C2.justification: v2 extends v1's explanation that sparsity encourages decisive features: increased influence among top-ranked concepts and reduced influence among weaker concepts are interpreted as simpler explanations and greater robustness across datasets. Most limitations remain, although the suggested use of concept embedding reasoners to mitigate bottlenecks is removed.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents uniform training-target sampling, PyTorch Lightning 2.1.2, dataset licenses, M3 Max hardware with 36 GB RAM without GPU use, and reported computation requirements of 80 hours overall and 10 hours for reproduction. Existing hyperparameters, loss weights, and code URL remain. v1's explicit statement about removing color-label correlation on test images is omitted, without establishing an actual protocol change.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same dSprites, MNIST addition, and CUB tasks, including color-confounded dSprites and concept-noise interventions. The added CaCE analyses use retained datasets. The new knee X-ray example is illustrative, without a reported medical benchmark evaluation.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated Black Box and Concept Embedding Model predictors to the generalization comparison (v1 Table 5 versus v2 Table 7). This is a limited expansion of predictive comparators; BayCon, C-CHVAE, VAE-CF, and VCNet remain the counterfactual-generation baselines.

E3.justification: The central explanation evaluation is substantially reworked from predictor-weight inspection and a color-intervention summary to CaCE measurements, including comparisons of the top 10% and bottom 50% of concepts and their score distributions. Existing training budgets, hyperparameters, and counterfactual metrics remain unchanged. These are reported evaluation changes, without establishing reruns of retained experiments.

E4.justification: v2 replaces the global and local feature-importance illustrations in v1 Figures 3 and 9 with systematic concept-intervention analyses: dSprites concept effects, MNIST/CUB percentile comparisons, and CaCE distributions (Tables 1–2 and Figure 8). These examine how joint training concentrates concept influence. The existing noise-sensitivity analysis is retained.

E5.justification: v2 adds Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests for CaCE distributions and Mann-Whitney U tests for concept-percentile comparisons, with reported p-values. This extends statistical reporting for the intervention analysis. Both versions already report means and standard errors over five initializations; no increase in run count is stated.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial CaCE results and Black Box/CEM predictive scores. Its dSprites color effects are 0.17±0.03 for post-hoc CBMs and 0.02±0.01 for CF-CBMs, replacing v1's approximately 15% versus unaffected description. Local explanation examples are removed. Existing validity results, counterfactual plots, and predictive scores remain unchanged; v1's ACBM row is renamed CF-CBM without numerical changes.

M1.justification: The latent-variable architecture, shared predictors, counterfactual generation, and loss components are retained. v2's explicit loss coefficients correspond to weights already documented in v1 Table 4. Its expanded intervention procedure describes functionality already supported in v1 Section 3.4.

P1.justification: The title is shortened, and the ladder narrative is extensively rewritten around What, How, and Why not. The abstract, introduction, background, and intervention-results discussion change substantially. Motivation is absorbed into the introduction, the fruit example becomes a knee X-ray example, and the best-bet/multiverse discussion moves to Appendix B.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to predominantly single-column text with wrapped figures and tables. The ladder illustration is replaced, the architecture diagram is redrawn, attribution plots are removed, CaCE tables and histograms are added, and the predictive table gains comparator rows. Retained counterfactual and noise plots are relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds the CounterGAN citation by Nemirovsky et al. and removes Poeta et al. and Rudin references. It expands introductory discussion of why input-level counterfactual methods lack interpretable interventions. The broader relationships to concept-based models and structured generative models are largely retained.

T1.justification: The graphical-model factorization, variational approximation, and Appendix A ELBO derivation are substantively retained. Explicit loss coefficients, probabilistic background notation, and intervention equations elaborate the existing setup rather than introduce new theoretical results or corrected proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 provides stronger empirical support for its interpretability argument through quantitative intervention effects and statistical comparisons across datasets, while additional predictive baselines and computation details improve assessment and reproducibility. The gain is limited by incomplete methodological updating: Appendix C.2 still describes weight inspection rather than fully documenting the new CaCE analysis.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CF-CBM research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite the changed title and layout.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds concept-intervention analyses and predictive baseline results in Section 5 and Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original predictive, counterfactual-generation, intervention, and robustness results on dSprites, MNIST addition, and CUB in Section 5 and Appendix C.

title: Counterfactual Concept Bottleneck Models

C1.justification: V3's introduction explicitly frames the contribution as explaining the model's decision-making rather than discovering true causal relationships in the data. This qualifies the contribution's scope while retaining the central claims about answering three query types, comparable prediction, and benefits of joint training.

C2.justification: V3 explains why omitting input reconstruction simplifies optimization and why added latent components preserve concept-level interpretability. Appendix C.3 interprets competing loss-weight effects, while Appendix E attributes some implausible baseline outputs to soft concept values. The existing limitations largely remain.

D1.justification: V3 documents the new encoders, 143 CIFAR10 and 19 SIIM concepts, and benchmark-specific hyperparameters. It newly describes validation on a training subset and optional staged or warm-up training. The repository link, software versions, hardware, and original hyperparameter entries remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V3 adds ten-class object classification on CIFAR10 and binary pneumothorax classification on chest X-rays from SIIM, retaining the original three datasets. These substantially broaden domain coverage and evaluate settings without supplied concept annotations.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain Black Box, CBM, and CEM for predictive performance and BayCon, C-CHVAE, VAE-CF, and VCNet for counterfactual generation. V3 extends these comparator sets to new datasets without adding or removing comparison methods.

E3.justification: The added benchmarks introduce automatic concept extraction, CLIP ViT-B/16 and CXR-CLIP encoders, and training budgets of 30 and 100 epochs, respectively. Table 7 adds controlled loss-weight variations on MNIST addition. Previously stated settings for the original datasets remain unchanged; the newly described validation-based selection is additional disclosure.

E4.justification: New Table 7 tests how loss-weight emphasis affects validity, sparsity, and proximity. New Appendix E examines generated examples across all five datasets, exposing infeasible concept combinations and unnecessary changes. These add sensitivity and qualitative failure analyses beyond the retained confounder and concept-noise experiments.

E5.justification: Both versions specify means and standard errors over five runs with different initializations and retain the Kolmogorov–Smirnov and Mann–Whitney tests in Section 5.2. Additional results follow the existing uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: V3 adds predictive, counterfactual, timing, sensitivity, and qualitative results. Table 3 reports CF-CBM validity of 100.0% on CIFAR10 and 99.9% on SIIM; its revised averages cover five datasets. Original tabulated benchmark scores are retained, but Figure 5 roughly doubles intervention-proximity values for retained datasets, such as VCNet on dSprites from about 24% to 48%, without explaining the revision.

M1.justification: The two-latent-variable architecture, shared predictors, training objectives, and inference procedures remain unchanged in Section 3 and Appendices A–B. V3's benchmark-specific encoders and discussion of optional training schedules do not establish a revision to the core CF-CBM procedure.

P1.justification: V3 makes localized abstract and introduction revisions, replaces the arthritis illustration with pneumothorax throughout the explanatory examples, and expands architectural and hyperparameter explanations. It adds acknowledgments and Appendix E and moves the efficiency discussion to Appendix D, while retaining the main section structure.

P2.justification: V3 redraws the introductory medical illustrations and expands the main trade-off figures from three wrapped panels to full-width five-panel displays. Benchmark and hyperparameter tables gain columns, new ablation and counterfactual-example tables are added, and the expanded timing figure moves to Appendix D.

R1.justification: V3 adds positioning against concept discovery and causal inference through Stammer, Louizos, and Xia, and expands discussion of concept interactions and memory reasoning. It also cites the new datasets and encoders. These extend the existing positioning without replacing its central comparison with CBMs and counterfactual generators.

T1.justification: The graphical-model factorization, objectives, Appendix A ELBO derivation, and Appendix C.2 metric definitions are retained. V3 adds explanatory prose but no new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens empirical support for applicability beyond supplied concept annotations through object and chest-X-ray evaluations. Table 7 exposes tuning trade-offs, and Appendix E makes feasibility claims inspectable through actual outputs, addressing important gaps in v2. These gains outweigh reporting problems: unexplained Figure 5 rescaling, inconsistent loss-weight numbering, and the overstated SIIM highest-validity claim despite 99.9% versus 100.0% for several baselines.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Counterfactual Concept Bottleneck Models. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V3 retains those original experiments and adds CIFAR10 and SIIM Pneumothorax results, loss-weight sensitivity experiments, and generated counterfactual examples.

before.justification: V2 reports original classification, counterfactual-generation, intervention, and robustness experiments on dSprites, MNIST addition, and CUB.

title: Counterfactual Concept Bottleneck Models

C1.justification: The two central contributions and headline effectiveness/efficiency claims remain. V2 makes initialization-free operation and reliable attack success explicit introductory advantages, removes the characterization of the approximation as unbiased, and softens the conclusion from consistently discovering minimum-norm perturbations to finding more effective and reliable perturbations.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the new component ablations as showing that all nontrivial components are essential, adds applicability guidance concerning t ≤ 0.1, and acknowledges the fixed-budget advantage of sPGDu on C4. D1.justification: V1 provides a direct public code link; v2 replaces it with a statement that code accompanies supplementary material and will become public upon acceptance. E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same image-classification tasks on MNIST, CIFAR10, and ImageNet. V2's mention of nine additional models concerns cited AttackBench work, not new evaluations reported here.

title: $\sigma$-zero: Gradient-based Optimization of $\ell_0$-norm Adversarial Examples

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same methodological contributions and claims about effectiveness, efficiency, reliability, and avoiding costly tuning. Updating the introduction's model count from 18 to 22 expands supporting evidence without redefining the contribution.

E2.justification: Corresponding existing experiments retain their comparator membership. The added experiments reuse established comparators, including FMN, BBadv, Sparse-RS, and the two Sparse-PGD variants. σ-zero* is a configuration of the proposed attack.

E3.justification: v3 adds two ℓ0-robust CIFAR-10 targets, C11/C12, and two larger ImageNet targets, I7/I8. Table 15 extends white-box iteration budgets from the previous maximum of 5,000 to 10,000 on C3/I2. Tables 6 and 10 additionally evaluate σ=1 and τ0=0.1, alongside the retained defaults. The Matérn performance headline remains, while the separate ten-dataset surrogate-learning contribution is dropped.

C2.justification: v3 Appendix B.3 emphasizes rapid covariance decay and potentially inadequate SE modeling capacity. v4 instead attributes failure primarily to initialization-induced vanishing gradients and explains why Matérn kernels and larger initial length-scales help. It also connects concentrated priors to this mechanism. New Appendix D explicitly acknowledges that the maximum workable input dimensionality remains unknown.

D1.justification: v4 explicitly discloses the default initialization of approximately 0.693, additional NUTS prior choices and the BoTorch log-EI implementation. It removes v3's experiment-code link and explicit 400/300-step budget sentence, although those budgets remain visible in plots. Hardware information and most baseline implementation sources are retained.

E1.justification: The eleven main BO benchmarks remain, but v3's separate ten-dataset surrogate-prediction evaluation is removed rather than relocated. v4 retains narrower prediction checks on Hartmann6/Rosenbrock and Mopta08/DNA, substantially reducing prediction-task coverage. The briefly reported polynomial-optimization experiment in v3 Appendix B.1 also disappears.

E2.justification: VBO is newly evaluated in the main BO comparisons, and log-EI joins the acquisition-function comparison. Removing the regression study also removes its ProjGP, AddGP and SaasBO surrogate comparisons. BNN Laplace/HMC remain in v4 Appendix C.1, so their absence from the main figures is not an overall removal.

E3.justification: v3 Appendix B.3's kernel-learning experiment becomes a crossed dimension/initialization study in v4 Section 4, extending the dimension range from 50–300 to 50–600 and measuring gradients and parameter changes alongside MSE instead of reporting test log likelihood. The SE BO comparison is now specified with L-BFGS MAP training in v4 Section 6.1, whereas v3 Appendix B.3 specified MLE.

E4.justification: v4 adds initialization sensitivity experiments and direct gradient/update measurements during training and SVM/Rosenbrock BO runs, linking failure to the proposed remedy in Figures 1–2. It also tests log-EI rather than merely suggesting it. v3's quantitative prior-sensitivity prediction Tables 8–9 disappear; MAP/MLE/NUTS and UCB exploration analyses largely remain.

E5.justification: The redesigned Hartmann6/Rosenbrock experiment reports twenty repetitions per dimension and initialization, versus five repetitions for v3 Appendix B.3's experiment. This does not establish additional runs of unchanged experiments. BO comparisons retain ten-run reporting and variability displays.

E6.justification: v4 adds initialization-dependent failure thresholds, RI/VBO optimization results and log-EI scores, while removing v3's regression Tables 4, 5, 8 and 9. The main SVM Matérn outcome changes from approximately -0.14 in v3 Figure 2 to -0.05 in v4 Figure 4, but v4 Figure 7 retains the older MAP range; this is not a verified same-setting gain. Timing values in v3 Tables 6–7 are unchanged in v4 Tables 4–5.

M1.justification: v4 Section 5 introduces dimension-dependent length-scale initialization, ℓ0 = c√d, with c = 1 in experiments, producing SBO-SE(RI). This adds an explicit procedure for preventing SE-kernel training failure that v3 did not propose. Existing Matérn MAP/MLE and single-length-scale variants largely remain under revised names or appendix placement.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, result discussion and conclusion are substantially rewritten around initialization and gradient failure. GP background is compressed, related-work subsections are flattened, and training/BNN analyses are reorganized into the appendices. New proof and limitations sections change the narrative structure; the author list also expands.

P2.justification: v4 adds gradient-diagnostic plots and threshold tables, redraws main comparison panels for RI/VBO, and consolidates trajectory displays using best/median/worst baseline summaries. BNN/training displays and timing tables move, while regression tables and several standalone endpoint plots disappear. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: The structural-BO related-work discussion largely remains. v4 adds Bengio/Hanin gradient-vanishing citations, removes the Batlle operator-learning connection and Li BNN-study discussion, and expands the already-cited Hvarfner/VBO work into a focused comparison between dimension-dependent prior regularization and initialization.

T1.justification: v3 provides standard GP/BO formulas and a heuristic explanation of SE-kernel decay. v4 adds gradient derivations, threshold Propositions 4.1 and 4.3, probability-bound Lemma 4.2 and initialization Lemma 5.1. New Appendix A supplies proofs, with the probability bounds assuming independently sampled uniform inputs.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially advances v3's tentative explanation of SE failure by connecting initialization to gradient diagnostics, formal bounds and an experimentally tested remedy in Sections 4–5 and Figures 1–5. This improves both explanatory and practical value. The bounds remain limited by their sampling assumptions, and removing regression comparisons and the code link reduces breadth and reproducibility. The unexplained main/appendix SVM discrepancy limits confidence in exact scores, but the broader mechanism-and-remedy evidence supports a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study and retain matching optimization benchmarks. All 26 pages of v3 and 24 pages of v4, including appendices, figures, tables and equations, are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v4 reports original optimization results, initialization experiments and gradient diagnostics in Sections 4–6 and Appendix C, including synthetic experiments repeated twenty times.

before.justification: v3 reports original repeated optimization experiments, surrogate-prediction results, ablations and computational timings in Section 4 and the appendices.

title: Standard Gaussian Process is All You Need for High-Dimensional Bayesian Optimization

C1.justification: The introduction expands the empirical contribution from eleven benchmarks spanning 30–388 variables to twelve spanning 30–1,003. Matérn's best-or-near-best claim changes from covering all tasks to nearly always. The central gradient-vanishing explanation and robust-initialization contribution remain.

C2.justification: The practical interpretation of training reliability is substantially revised. v5 emphasizes that default Matérn also needs initialization protection at extreme dimensions and adds optimizer-dependent stability limitations. It removes v4's substantive explanations of concentrated-prior-induced failure and the marginal optimization benefit versus large computational cost of fully Bayesian GP fitting.

D1.justification: v5 adds a code-release link, Humanoid construction details, Adam/RMSProp settings, SoftPlus parameterization, explicit sharing of initial datasets across methods, and a survey of GP-library initialization defaults. Existing L-BFGS priors and tolerances move to Appendix B.3. Detailed standard-GP NUTS settings and measured timing information are removed with their analyses.

E1.justification: v5 adds Humanoid-Standup: direct optimization of 59 steps of 17 motor actions in a MuJoCo environment, totaling 1,003 variables (Appendix B.2). This extends BO testing into a new simulated-control environment and the over-1,000-variable regime. The eleven earlier benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: The external baseline families remain, including VBO and both BNN methods. Main comparisons add SBO-Matérn(RI). The retained acquisition-function comparison replaces separate UCB(MAP) and UCB(MLE) arms with one UCB arm, while retaining EI, log-EI and both TS variants (v4 Figures 14–15; v5 Figures 9–10).

E3.justification: v4 specifies L-BFGS MAP fitting for the main comparison; v5 reports selecting among L-BFGS, Adam and RMSProp, with marginal-likelihood training and 1,500 epochs for Adam/RMSProp. Humanoid-Standup introduces 50 initial evaluations, versus 20 elsewhere. These materially revise the reported fitting protocol, although v5 does not identify the optimizer used for each experiment.

E4.justification: v4 Appendix C.2's standard-GP MLE/MAP/NUTS comparisons, prior-sensitivity tests, prediction-versus-ground-truth diagnostics and computational-cost analysis are removed, not relocated. v5 adds explicit Matérn initialization comparisons. Single-length-scale, UCB exploration and acquisition-function analyses remain, with revised plots.

E5.justification: v4 reports ten BO runs per method. v5 explicitly adds ten extra runs for all standard-BO variants and VBO, while retaining ten for other methods. Mean/standard-deviation and violin-summary reporting continue; the separate GP-training diagnostics still use twenty repetitions.

E6.justification: v5 adds Humanoid-Standup and SBO-Matérn(RI) results and revises numerous retained outcomes. For example, SBO-SE is competitive on DNA in v4 Figure 4 but performs poorly in v5 Figure 4; Ackley(150,150) also shows substantially different SBO-SE behavior. Default Matérn fails on the new Humanoid task, while robust initialization succeeds. Training/prior results and wall-clock timing tables disappear. Changed fitting protocols and run sets preclude interpreting these as uniform same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The GP kernels, BO procedure and robust initialization rule l0 = c sqrt(d) remain unchanged. v5 explicitly evaluates Matérn with robust initialization, but v4 already formulated the rule for both kernels. Revised optimizer configurations concern experimental settings rather than a new proposed component.

P1.justification: The title, author/header presentation and citation style change, with localized prose revisions. Appendices gain Humanoid and library-initialization sections, lose the alternative-training section, and move limitations from D to E. The seven-section main narrative and most theoretical exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: Most empirical plots are redrawn with revised legends, colors and panel arrangements. The combined runtime Figure 5 becomes separate synthetic and real-world Figures 5–6; Humanoid panels are added. v4 Figures 7–12 and timing Tables 4–5 are removed, while the synthetic-benchmark table moves into the appendix. Conference formatting substantially reorganizes figure placement.

R1.justification: v5 adds the MuJoCo citation and distinguishes its trajectory-optimization benchmark from Hvarfner et al.'s linear-policy Humanoid benchmark. References to the NUTS and Adam papers are removed. The broader positioning against structural high-dimensional BO methods and VBO remains.

T1.justification: Propositions 4.1 and 4.3, Lemmas 4.2 and 5.1, their assumptions and all four Appendix A proofs are retained. Equation 6 changes a length-scale subscript equivalently under the stated common initialization; it introduces no substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: v5 adds useful evidence about default Matérn's limits at 1,003 dimensions, additional repeated runs and code-release information. However, it removes extensive controlled training/prior analyses and computational-cost evidence while introducing optimizer choices without identifying their use per experiment. That missing context matters for interpreting the revised failure patterns, so the benefits and losses do not establish a reliable net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GP-based Bayesian optimization study despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v5 reports original results on twelve optimization benchmarks, including Humanoid-Standup, together with GP-training diagnostics and supplementary comparisons.

before.justification: v4 reports original GP-training diagnostics, optimization experiments on eleven benchmarks, and supplementary training, prior and acquisition-function studies.

title: Standard Gaussian Process is All You Need for High-Dimensional Bayesian Optimization

C1.justification: v1 primarily claims interpretable architectures with competitive predictive performance. v2 adds headline claims of outperforming interpretable baselines and receiving better human assessments, makes the user study a separate contribution, and incorporates synthetic evaluation into its stated scope. The original sparse, user-defined interpretability claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive discussion of explanation-presentation confounds, limited user-study generalizability, appropriate uses of each architecture, tuning sensitivity, and validation before production use. Conversely, it removes v1 Appendix E's warning that route weights can reflect majority-class prediction rather than feature importance and depend on initialization. These materially change the qualifications attached to interpretability claims.

D1.justification: New Appendices A, D, and E document dataset statistics, access/licensing and EDU privacy restrictions, survey materials and compensation, hardware and training times, hyperparameter grids, and epoch budgets. These substantially expand reproducibility information. Some earlier details disappear, including the padding instruction and explicit feature-set provenance of the 97-feature DSP case study retained in Table 11.

E1.justification: v2 adds OpenXAI synthetic data with ground-truth explanations and a teacher evaluation, introducing explanation-recovery and human-assessment tasks. The main EDU comparison narrows from six courses to four, but Structures and Ventures remain represented in Appendix G.2.3. AG News, SST, and Breast Cancer remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds NAM and SENN feature/concept baselines to non-text predictive and synthetic explanation comparisons, and compares NAM/SENN explanations in the user study. Top-k routing is newly included in EDU comparisons; its renamed text/health counterpart already existed in v1. The fixed-feature BiLSTM comparison disappears with the earlier DSP ablations.

E3.justification: New protocols include synthetic explanation accuracy and Pairwise Rank Agreement, plus a user study using four randomly selected DSP students, randomized explanation order, and five Likert-scale criteria. Appendix D reports excluding five of 56 recruited participants. Retained EDU splits and prediction horizons are unchanged; newly disclosed tuning grids and epoch budgets do not establish changes to earlier training settings.

E4.justification: v2 removes much of v1 Appendix E: dynamic versus fixed feature selection, easy-hard and pretrained-expert comparisons, unweighted versus weighted routing, threshold sensitivity, and route-behavior diagnostics. The 40%/60% sparsity comparison survives as Table 11, and six-course grouping plots survive in Appendix G. This substantially reduces architectural ablation evidence without deleting all earlier analyses.

E5.justification: v1 labels main results as means with 99% confidence intervals and gives EDU routing point estimates. v2 newly specifies three random seeds, reports means and standard deviations, uses 95% intervals for comparisons, and supplies EDU routing uncertainty. It also adds Friedman, ANOVA, and Tukey HSD analyses. The newly disclosed seed count does not demonstrate an increase in runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds baseline, synthetic-faithfulness, and teacher-rating results while removing many DSP appendix results and main Structures/Ventures performance rows. Retained numbers also change: Breast Cancer Feature Gating is 74.67 in v1 versus 78.19 in v2. Group Routing means 94.85, 90.35, and 91.75 belong to AG News, SST, and Breast Cancer in v1 Table 5, but Breast Cancer, AG News, and SST in v2 Table 2. Corresponding top-k values are similarly reassigned without explanation; these cannot establish performance gains.

M1.justification: The core discriminator, Gumbel gating, feature masking, and weighted expert aggregation remain unchanged. v2 adds a specific grouping procedure for synthetic data: assigning each feature to the cluster with the greatest mean absolute feature value (Section 4). This is a limited grouping adaptation within the existing architecture.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the title, introduction, background, and conclusion, moves related work before methodology, and reorganizes results around performance, faithfulness, and human preference. Dataset/grouping explanations move into expanded appendices, the DSP case study is abridged, and a conference checklist is inserted. The narrative structure changes substantially.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. Separate architecture diagrams merge into Figure 1; performance tables are consolidated and expanded with color-coded comparisons. v2 adds conceptual and user-study displays, relocates grouping tables and activation figures to appendices, and removes several DSP diagnostic tables and plots. Many retained graphics are redisplayed rather than new results.

R1.justification: v2 expands positioning through Background and Table 1, contrasting faithfulness, sparsity, coverage, granularity, and user-defined concepts. SENN and NAM become central related methods, with new references supporting synthetic evaluation and study design. Several sources associated with the removed DSP case study disappear. This exceeds citation renumbering or relocation.

T1.justification: The Gumbel sampling, sigmoid reduction, and straight-through estimator derivations are retained from v1 Appendix C in v2 Appendix F. Main masking equations use revised masked-input notation without substantive mathematical change. No theorems, proofs, or formal metric derivations are added.

improvement.justification: The synthetic evaluation, interpretable baselines, teacher study, and reproducibility details address important gaps in v1. However, v2 removes substantial ablation evidence and a consequential warning about interpreting route weights. Routing score pairs are reassigned across datasets without explanation between v1 Table 5 and v2 Table 2. Section 5.3 also claims significant superiority over SENN on trustworthiness, whereas Figure 11 does not mark that comparison significant. These unresolved issues affect central performance and interpretability evidence, preventing a reliable net quality judgment despite the substantial additions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe InterpretCC and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained architectures and experiments can be matched despite substantial restructuring and additions in v2.

after.justification: v2 reports original predictive experiments, synthetic explanation evaluations, and a teacher user study, including additional appendix analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original predictive experiments on education, text, and healthcare datasets, plus sparsity and routing analyses in its appendices.

title: Intrinsic User-Centric Interpretability through Global Mixture of Experts

C1.justification: The architecture contributions and principal performance and teacher-preference claims are retained. v4 softens the abstract's guarantee of human-centric interpretability into an objective of optimizing human understanding, and more explicitly limits the claimed explanation to local feature/concept use.

C2.justification: v4 explicitly explains that the black-box discriminator's selection rationale is outside the explanation's scope. It adds warnings about misleading correlations and discussion of auditing, interpretable-input requirements, specialization, noise reduction and overfitting. Sections 6 and Appendix I also substantially expand architectural tradeoffs and applicability boundaries; the earlier user-study presentation caveat is retained.

D1.justification: The core reproducibility appendix retains its hardware, training-time, epoch and tuning details. v4 adds sensitivity-grid settings, FRESH's BERT backbone and rationale fractions, RF tree counts/depths, and guidance on specifying feature groups. The explicit MIT-license statement for the authors' code/models disappears with v2's checklist; the public code link remains.

E1.justification: Both versions cover the same eight primary benchmarks, the supplementary Structures and Venture MOOCs, and the same teacher study. The added experiments reuse existing datasets. Raw speech, video and graph-based time-series applications are prospective discussions, not evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: v4 adds FRESH to the AG News/SST comparison in Table 2, Integrated Gradients, LIME and SHAP to the synthetic explanation comparison in Table 4 and Appendix I.2, and Random Forest to the tabular comparison in Figure 19. These substantially expand the evaluated comparator families beyond v2's original baselines.

E3.justification: v4 adds top-5 Rank Agreement and Feature Agreement to the synthetic evaluation; PRA is retained in Appendix I.2. New experiments introduce temperature/threshold sweeps, cross-routing controls for specialization, and FRESH evaluations using BERT with specified rationale fractions. Existing benchmark splits, core training budgets and teacher-study procedures are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix D.2 tests Gumbel parameter sensitivity and sparsity on DSP and Breast Cancer. D.3 tests whether experts predict better on their assigned data across DSP, SST and Breast Cancer. Appendix I.1 adds an RF-versus-ICC feature-importance comparison. Earlier regularization, prediction-horizon and grouping analyses remain present.

E5.justification: Appendix I.4 newly specifies five random seeds for FRESH, while the general three-seed setup remains; this does not establish increased runs for existing results. The new sensitivity analysis selectively omits confidence intervals from performance plots and lists high-variance configurations. Existing mean/std reporting and teacher-study significance tests are retained.

E6.justification: v4 adds extensive comparator, explanation-metric, sensitivity and specialization results. For example, FRESH scores 88.73 ± 0.69 on AG News and 82.05 ± 0.56 on SST. Existing Table 2 entries and teacher-study scores remain unchanged. However, new Figure 19 reverses the synthetic scores 89.51 ± 0.51 and 84.67 ± 4.04 between ICC FG and SENN Concepts relative to Table 2 in both versions.

M1.justification: The principal feature-gating and group-routing methods remain unchanged. Appendices I.3 and I.5 newly propose optional tree/SVM discriminators and graph-based components. These extend the proposed architectural options, but are explicitly unevaluated alternatives, not changes to the models producing the reported benchmarks.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting and terminology refinement. v4 removes the NeurIPS checklist, adds acknowledgements, introduces a taxonomy appendix, and reorganizes and expands the appendix narrative. These changes extend beyond inserting new scientific results.

P2.justification: v4 expands Tables 2 and 4, adds sensitivity plots, specialization heatmaps, the RF comparison and an extractive-rationale comparison table. It relocates the existing Tukey plot into the main text and AG News examples into the appendix, changes Table 1's layout, and corrects Figure 1's feature-gating caption to match the existing method.

R1.justification: v4 substantially expands positioning against extractive-rationale methods, including FRESH, Bastings et al. and Yu et al., with a dedicated discussion and comparison table. It adds XAI taxonomies, expert-informed concept approaches and classical MoE foundations. It also revises the characterization of post-hoc sparsity and replaces Table 1's coverage axis with predictive stage.

T1.justification: The routing equation and Gumbel derivation remain unchanged. Appendix I.2 adds quantitative definitions separating Ground Truth Alignment from Ground Truth Faithfulness, with asserted faithfulness bounds in Table 4. This extends metric definitions and formal properties without adding a proof of the guarantees.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens validation where v2 lacked an external interpretable text baseline, direct post-hoc explanation comparisons, and Gumbel-parameter and expert-specialization checks. These additions test central performance and interpretability claims more thoroughly, while the discriminator-scope discussion improves their interpretation. Figure 19's swapped synthetic scores and stale user-study cross-references introduce reporting defects, but the broader comparative and diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same InterpretCC research, with matching architectures, datasets and teacher study. Their complete main texts and appendices, including tables, figures and equations, support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds baseline comparisons, parameter-sensitivity experiments and expert-specialization analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original predictive benchmarks, synthetic explanation evaluations, routing analyses and teacher-study outcomes.

title: Intrinsic User-Centric Interpretability through Global Mixture of Experts

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions now claim sample-complexity guarantees, improvements over naive history summarization, and exponentially sharper GOLF guarantees through HABE. This substantially extends v1's recursive-structure contribution, which relied on a specialized reward-machine learner. The framework and dueling-reduction claims remain.

C2.justification: Section 3.2 newly explains why separately learning rewards across timesteps misses recursive structure and motivates joint Q-function classes. It qualifies the improvement as requiring dense intermediate feedback and notes that HABE and BE dimensions are not universally ordered. Section 2.2 also expands the deployment-based rationale for regret versus sample complexity.

D1.justification: Appendix F adds GOLF's confidence-set update, auxiliary function-class information and a prescribed beta parameter, absent from v1. Neither version supplies an experimental implementation or code/data release.

E1.justification: Neither version evaluates datasets or conducts sampled task evaluations. The revised combination-lock scenarios are mathematical constructions.

E2.justification: Neither version reports empirical baseline comparisons. Expanded comparisons with GOLF and P-OMLE concern theoretical guarantees.

E3.justification: Neither version reports experimental splits, training budgets or testing protocols. The added PAC objective and policy-selection argument are theoretical developments.

E4.justification: No empirical ablations, robustness tests or error analyses are added. The dense-versus-sparse combination-lock comparison establishes mathematical dimension separations, assessed under T1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated experimental runs, seeds, error bars or significance tests. Changes to theoretical confidence bounds belong to the algorithm and theory.

E6.justification: Neither version contains empirical result entries. Changes concern regret bounds, sample-complexity guarantees and analytical examples rather than measured performance.

M1.justification: v2 adds a model-free PORRL approach using GOLF and joint, model-realizable Q-function classes, alongside the retained model-based algorithms. Assumption 1 broadens known reward functions to known reward-function classes, and the least-squares confidence radius is revised.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and model exposition are extensively rewritten. Generic optimism templates move from the main text into Appendix C; the separate recursive-dynamics section becomes a model-free subsection within Section 3. The title, contribution framing and appendix organization also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds algorithm displays for generic model-free optimism, GOLF and standalone POR-UCRL/POR-UCBVI instantiations, and compacts Algorithm 1. Equations and paragraphs are reformatted, while the overall single-column presentation remains similar. Neither version contains figures or result tables.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against history summarization and existing Bellman-eluder guarantees. Remark 3 changes the emphasis from recovering Chatterji et al.'s guarantees to improving them and adds a cardinal-versus-dueling query-complexity comparison with Wang et al.'s P-OMLE. PAC and reward-machine references are added, while the DPO discussion is removed.

T1.justification: v2 adds regret-to-PAC lemmas and sample-complexity corollaries, the HABE dimension, and a new GOLF regret analysis. Proposition 1 and Appendix F replace v1's specialized reward-machine argument with dense/sparse-feedback dimension comparisons. Confidence-radius formulas and the stated POR-UCBVI dimension dependence also change.

improvement.justification: The GOLF/HABE analysis develops v1's limited treatment of recursive structure, and the reorganization improves accessibility. However, Appendix B Lemma 5 claims a high-probability guarantee for one uniformly sampled policy while its proof substitutes an average over policies. This does not establish the claim as written, and several new sample-complexity corollaries depend on it. The substantive additions and this reliability concern prevent a confident net quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PORRL framework. Their complete main texts, equations, algorithm displays and appendices support comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: v2 remains theoretical, including its combination-lock analysis. References to experiments in a process-supervision preprint do not report original experiments in this paper.

before.justification: v1 presents algorithms, theoretical guarantees and analytical examples, including the reward-machine construction in Appendix A.5, but no original empirical results.

title: A Theoretical Framework for Partially-Observed Reward States in RLHF

C1.justification: The abstract's main contribution claims remain unchanged. v3 adds practical implications as an explicit contribution and advertises general transition-function approximation in the introduction, modestly broadening the stated contribution scope.

C2.justification: v3 adds practical guidance concerning actor-critic methods and strengthens the sparse-feedback interpretation to an algorithm-independent hardness claim. Appendix F adds substantive qualifications: strong-SAIL bounds exclude exploratory-policy regret, and the corresponding dueling extension requires a single exploratory policy. The shared-Q-network recommendation already appeared in v2.

D1.justification: Appendix F specifies technical setup for the new variants, including storing policy–trajectory pairs, recursive likelihood confidence-set updates, and a threshold beta defined using bracketing numbers and confidence level delta. Existing algorithms' technical descriptions are largely retained.

E1.justification: Neither version actually trains or evaluates on datasets or benchmarks. The additional function-approximation settings in v3 are theoretical model classes, not newly evaluated tasks.

E2.justification: Neither version contains empirical baseline comparisons. KTO and DPO are added as motivating citations in v3, while OMLE supplies theoretical building blocks; these are not evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: Neither PDF reports experimental splits, preprocessing, evaluation budgets, or testing protocols. Appendix F's exploratory-policy rules belong to proposed algorithms rather than conducted experiments.

E4.justification: Both retain analytic combination-lock and memoryless-policy examples. No empirical ablations, robustness tests, sensitivity studies, or error analyses are added; the new hardness argument is theoretical.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated experimental runs, seeds, error bars, or significance tests. Their confidence sets and high-probability bounds concern theoretical algorithms, not empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Neither version contains measured performance values, experimental rankings, or empirical result entries. The newly reported quantities are mathematical regret bounds.

M1.justification: Appendix F adds general-transition variants of POR-UCRL and POR-UCBVI beyond v2's concrete tabular constructions. These introduce likelihood-based transition confidence sets and bonuses, with strong-SAIL variants executing additional exploratory policies. The original tabular procedures and GOLF remain.

P1.justification: The introduction and selected explanations receive targeted edits, and Section 5 gains practical-implication bullets. Inserting Appendix F shifts the former F/G appendices to G/H; most existing proof prose and the main narrative structure remain. Affiliation and senior-authorship text also change.

P2.justification: v3 adds the two-panel Figure 1 illustrating cardinal and dueling feedback. It also widens the text area, adjusts spacing and page breaks, and relocates Algorithm 1 relative to the reduction theorem. Existing algorithm displays are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to KTO, DPO, and Xiong et al. (2024), removes several broad alignment and LLM references, and develops its relationship to the already-cited Liu et al. (2022b) for transition approximation. The central RLHF and POMDP positioning remains.

T1.justification: New Appendix F introduces transition-complexity definitions, derivations, Theorems 10–12, and Corollary 6 for general function approximation. Proposition 1 and Appendix G.2.2 also add a claimed Omega(sqrt(A^H T)) sparse-feedback lower bound using a bandit argument. Assumption 1 changes the feedback mean from 'known' to 'unknown' and explicitly describes the Lipschitz constants as unknown.

improvement.justification: v3 improves exposition and supplies explicit general-transition extensions absent from v2. However, Theorems 11–12 explicitly omit exploratory-policy regret, and the new sparse-feedback lower bound invokes generic bandit bounds without clearly establishing their applicability to the restricted Bernoulli(q)/zero combination-lock construction in Appendix G.2.2. These unresolved scope and proof issues coexist with useful additions, preventing a reliable net judgment of overall quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PORRL framework and retain matching algorithms and proofs. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, including v3's added figure and theoretical appendix.

after.justification: v3 remains theoretical throughout its main text and appendices. The new transition-model extensions and illustrative diagram do not report original empirical outcomes.

before.justification: v2 reports mathematical guarantees, proofs, and analytic toy examples, but no original experimental, simulation, user-study, or data-analysis results.

title: A Theoretical Framework for Partially-Observed Reward States in RLHF

C1.justification: V2 broadens its central theoretical contribution from strongly convex and PL-conditioned results to general non-convex convergence guarantees under both learning-rate policies. The abstract and introduction also make heterogeneous, time-varying resource availability a central contribution, while retaining the claim that DSpodFL unifies existing decentralized methods.

C2.justification: V2 revises the learning-rate and participation interpretation of the optimality gap, replacing v1's simple proportionality claims with participation-dependent residuals. Appendix O explains the tradeoff between accuracy per iteration and delay, and decomposes the resource savings. Section 6 acknowledges limited dataset/task validation, although O.5's new assertion that all methods converge to the same global model exceeds the general non-convex stationarity guarantee.

D1.justification: Section 5 newly identifies a cluster of three NVIDIA A100 GPUs with 40 GB memory. This adds reproducibility information absent from v1; it does not establish a hardware change between experiments.

E1.justification: Fashion-MNIST/SVM and CIFAR10/VGG11 image classification, including IID and non-IID cases, are retained. Appendix O.4 adds a distinct environment with computation and communication availability changing during training; v1's empirical participation probabilities remain fixed.

E2.justification: Corresponding empirical comparisons retain DGD, DFedAvg, Randomized Gossip, and Sporadic SGDs. The additional experiments reuse these comparators; changes to the related-work comparison in Table 1 do not introduce evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The main experimental settings remain stable. New protocols resample participation probabilities every 1000 iterations, sweep CIFAR10 client counts, and evaluate accuracy by iteration and delay components at specified accuracy targets. Figure 6b changes its stated measurement delay from 5000 to 500, without establishing that the experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained heterogeneity and connectivity sweeps, Appendices O.4-O.6 add temporal-resource robustness tests, accuracy-by-iteration comparisons, and processing-versus-transmission delay decomposition. These analyses substantially extend the examination of whether DSpodFL's advantage comes from iteration efficiency or reduced resource costs. Figure 6c also extends the client-count sensitivity analysis to CIFAR10.

E5.justification: V1 does not describe repeated-run uncertainty reporting. V2 explicitly reports means and one-standard-deviation uncertainty across multiple runs, adding bands and error bars to the main experimental figures. title: PQMass: Probabilistic Assessment of the Quality of Generative Models using Probability Mass Estimation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same claims about likelihood-free distribution comparison, assessing generative models, computational efficiency, and operation without feature extraction.

C2.justification: Interpretations and qualifications are unchanged, including Section 4's limitations concerning sample size, tessellation choice, independent samples, and distance metrics, and Appendix I's discussion of reused samples.

D1.justification: Implementation information, Appendix D model hyperparameters, preprocessing, hardware and runtime disclosures, and code/data access information are unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions retain identical coverage of synthetic distributions, image datasets, time series, Adult Census tabular data, astrophysical data, and protein sequences. No dataset or test scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged throughout, including Wasserstein, MMD, JSD, FID, FLD, novelty metrics, and the weighted and unweighted nearest-neighbor tests in Appendix H.

E3.justification: Sample sizes, splits, metrics, model configurations, training budgets, and evaluation procedures are identical. For example, both retain the 100-epoch MNIST experiment comparing 2,000 generated and 2,000 test samples.

E4.justification: The reference-count and distance-metric ablations, mode-dropping and small-mode tests, noise sensitivity, memorization analysis, sample visualizations, and permutation-test analyses are all retained unchanged.

E5.justification: Repeated-run information and uncertainty reporting are identical, including the 20 reference-point repetitions and standard deviations in Section 3.2, repeated MNIST training experiments, and appendix significance reporting.

E6.justification: All numerical results, plotted findings, rankings, and qualitative observations are unchanged. Tables 1–6 and the result figures, including those in the appendices, are identical.

M1.justification: The Voronoi partitioning, reference-point selection, multinomial comparison, Pearson chi-squared statistic, and permutation-test procedure are unchanged.

P1.justification: Page 1 changes the displayed author name from Nikolay Malkin to Esmeralda S. Whitammer, and page 11 changes the acknowledgment initials from N.M. to E.S.W. The arXiv version/date stamp also changes; scientific prose and section organization remain identical.

P2.justification: All 23 figures and six tables retain their content, captions, axes, legends, structure, and placement. There is no restructuring of the page layout beyond the text substitutions recorded under P1.

R1.justification: The cited works, bibliography, and positioning relative to earlier methods are identical. The author-name update does not change the paper's relationship to prior research.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, assumptions, equations, Propositions 2.1 and 2.2 and their proofs, and Appendix I permutation-test reasoning are unchanged.

improvement.justification: v4 updates author identification, acknowledgment initials, and the arXiv stamp while preserving the scientific content and all appendix evidence. These administrative edits leave the paper's scientific support, reproducibility information, and explanatory quality unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable 27-page versions of the same PQMass paper, including Appendices A–I. Full-text and rendered-page comparisons support reliable assessment.

after.justification: v4 retains the same original experimental results in Section 3 and the appendices, including sampling comparisons and generative-model evaluations.

before.justification: v3 reports original null tests, sampling-method evaluations, image-generation experiments, and additional empirical studies in the appendices.

title: PQMass: Probabilistic Assessment of the Quality of Generative Models using Probability Mass Estimation

C1.justification: The main contribution shifts from introducing MUDG and a three-stage dataset-construction pipeline to explaining modality-gap retrieval failures and proposing improved indexing, adaptive augmentation and diversity-preserving finetuning. The abstract and contribution list additionally claim stronger retrieval and zero-shot performance and comparisons with name-only transfer methods.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations linking query–centroid distance to retrieval failures, label-feature variance to descriptor quality, and initial-prediction regularization to preserved diversity. It acknowledges restrictive theoretical assumptions and an unproved geometric implication. Existing hubness explanations and limitations concerning source coverage, semantic alignment and saturated zero-shot accuracy remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B and Table 9 add index and augmentation hyperparameters, descriptor-bank provenance, the loss weight, GPU resources, storage requirements, and timings for indexing, retrieval, labeling, clustering and downloading. v1 documented basic finetuning and dataset-specific settings but lacked this infrastructure and runtime information. The code-access link remains unchanged.

E1.justification: All 20 classification benchmarks and the LAION-2B source remain. v2 substantially extends task coverage to approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval, including image-to-image, text-to-text and text-to-image evaluation, and adds a synthetic Gaussian retrieval scenario (Figures 2–4 and 8). Other source datasets mentioned in the introduction are not demonstrated experimentally.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds CuPL for both backbones and author-reported SuS-X results for ViT-B/16, introducing a directly relevant MUDG comparator. New comparisons also include standard versus paired k-means, alternative training losses, and random sample selection. v1's GPT Descriptors is retained under the name Visual Descriptors.

E3.justification: v2 introduces retrieval protocols measuring R@1 against probe count and query latency at 4-, 8- and 16-bit quantization levels. It also documents a 20M-LAION analysis and a 10,000-point, 20-cluster Gaussian demonstration. Existing classification backbones, training budgets and dataset-specific retrieval settings remain largely unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds component ablations for indexing, adaptive augmentation and the training loss; alternative-loss and random-selection controls; convergence analyses; descriptor-quality examples; and probe-count sensitivity (Figures 3–5 and 10; Tables 4–6 and 11). Earlier hubness and sample-selection analyses largely survive in Appendix C, although the ViT-L/14 skip-clustering results are no longer reported.

E5.justification: Both versions report classification averages over three experiments or trials. Neither introduces experimental error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests or seed reporting; the expanded results do not establish a changed uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Many MUDG entries are replaced with results for the revised pipeline: ViT-B/16 ImageNet changes from 69.9 to 70.4, Aircraft from 33.7 to 32.8, and Terra Incognita mean from 37.2 to 38.7. The eleven-dataset mean remains 71.1. New retrieval, augmentation and ablation outcomes substantially expand the results, while PACS/VLCS scores are retained.

M1.justification: v2 adds paired k-means indexing, replaces random query augmentation with adaptive descriptor selection, and replaces plain cross-entropy finetuning with a diversity-preserving objective using initial predictions (Sections 3.1–3.3). Rank pseudo-labeling and clustering-based sample selection remain core components.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, gains an author, and extensively rewrites its abstract, introduction, method narrative and conclusion around cross-modal retrieval. Much of the original method exposition moves into Appendix C, while proofs become Appendix A and experimental details become Appendix B.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text from two columns to one, combines the earlier pipeline diagrams with new components in Figure 1, and adds retrieval, theory, ablation and radar graphics. Results tables are reorganized, and many existing qualitative figures and domain results move to the appendices. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly positions MUDG alongside SuS-X's name-only transfer setting and develops a new relationship to modality-gap and retrieval-adaptation research. It adds citations supporting these connections, the adopted diversity-preserving loss, and the mathematical analysis. This substantially revises positioning beyond the earlier emphasis on data-centric dataset construction.

T1.justification: v2 adds spherical and Gaussian assumptions, two theorems, a corollary, probability-density derivations, and proofs and geometric arguments in Appendix A. This is a substantial theoretical addition to v1's algorithmic formulation. Theorem 1 and its proof contain inconsistent definitions and interpretations of rho.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens empirical support through SuS-X comparisons, component and loss ablations, retrieval diagnostics, and computational-cost documentation. However, its new headline theory has correctness concerns: Theorem 1 describes rho(s') as close to 1, while Appendix A.1 defines rho below 0.5 and equates that single-sample quantity with an n-sample nearest-neighbor probability. These inconsistencies undermine the theoretical contribution. The empirical and reproducibility gains are clear, but their net effect against these new reliability problems cannot be assessed confidently.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable and describe the same MUDG research. Despite the changed title and substantial expansion, methods, experiments, figures and appendix material can be matched reliably. No material reading gaps prevent comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original classification, nearest-neighbor retrieval, adaptive augmentation and component-ablation results, alongside retained experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments across 20 benchmarks, retrieval and clustering ablations, hyperparameter studies, and a Terra Incognita pseudo-labeling case study.

title: Multimodal Unsupervised Domain Generalization by Retrieving Across the Modality Gap

C1.justification: v3 removes the abstract's explicit assertion of no source–target relationship and qualifies the introduction by requiring source coverage of target visual concepts and their CLIP alignment. These boundaries already appeared in v2's limitations, making this a refinement of the main claim. The central retrieval and accuracy claims remain.

C2.justification: Figure 10 makes the existing alignment limitation concrete: it attributes failures for 'paddle' and 'clean room' to concept mismatch, and failures for 'playing Daf', 'lacelike', and 'silverbush' to inadequate alignment. The previous discussions of saturation, hubness, diversity, and overfitting remain.

D1.justification: v3 identifies Guo et al.'s DeepCore implementations as the source for the new coreset baselines and documents the setup of the added diagnostics. Existing implementation details, hardware costs, hyperparameter tables, and the code-access URL are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use LAION-2B-en and the same 20 target benchmarks, including the appendix datasets. The added comparisons and diagnostics reuse existing coverage; the new e-commerce example is motivational, not an evaluated task.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds five ViT-B/16 coreset comparators: Margin, Least Confident, Entropy, Herding, and K-Ctr Greedy. It also adds a 16-shot supervised reference. This substantially expands the comparison methods while retaining the previous comparators in their corresponding experiments.

E3.justification: v3 adds a separate protocol that finetunes ViT-B/16 on 16-shot target training data. Figure 18 additionally samples 100 ImageNet class names for a text-feature comparison using augmentations with losses 0 and 16. Existing benchmark protocols and Tables 9–10 settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Figures 9–10 compare retrieval examples against SuS-X and examine retrieval failures. Appendix Figure 18 adds a t-SNE diagnostic of augmentation-induced feature contraction. These extend the existing qualitative analyses; the numerical component ablations and sensitivity studies are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages of three experiments or trials in Tables 2, 3, and 8. No changed run counts, seed reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are documented.

E6.justification: All matching numerical rows in Tables 2–8 are retained, but Table 2 adds a substantial comparison block across 11 datasets. Herding and K-Ctr Greedy report means of 70.9 and 70.5, versus the unchanged MUDG mean of 71.1. The new supervised reference averages 83.9 under different training conditions. Figures 9, 10, and 18 add qualitative findings.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2, adaptive augmentation, rank pseudo-labeling, clustering-based sample selection, and the diversity-preserving loss are unchanged. The new figures explain or evaluate the existing procedure rather than introduce method components.

P1.justification: The introduction gains an e-commerce example and revised problem framing, and its six-item contribution list becomes two core retrieval contributions. Citation style and conference headings change throughout, but most prose and the main section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: v3 adds Figures 1, 9, 10, and 18, separates v2's combined overview into Figures 2–4, redraws several plots, expands Table 2, and places Tables 2–3 together. These substantially alter presentation. Figure 8 also introduces misleading accuracy axes: bars labeled 85.7 and 61.2 appear within an axis spanning 68–73.

R1.justification: v3 adds Coleman et al. (2019), Guo et al. (2022), and Welling (2009), connecting the evaluation more directly to coreset selection. Sener and Savarese was already cited. The broader positioning against DG, SuS-X, retrieval augmentation, and modality-gap research remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Formal Assumptions 1–2, Theorems 1–2, Corollary 2, and the derivations and proofs in Appendix A are retained. The added conceptual and empirical illustrations do not introduce new mathematical results.

improvement.justification: The added coreset comparisons and supervised reference strengthen the comparative context, while explicit source requirements and concrete failure cases clarify applicability. These provide a limited overall improvement. Figure 8's inconsistent accuracy axes are a presentation regression, but its numerical labels and the retained appendix tables preserve the underlying results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MUDG work. The complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–C are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial visual reformatting.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds coreset comparisons, a supervised reference, and qualitative retrieval and text-feature analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original retrieval experiments, MUDG classification results, ablations, simulations, and qualitative analyses in the main text and appendices.

title: Multimodal Unsupervised Domain Generalization by Retrieving Across the Modality Gap

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same claims about clustering-based robust dataset distillation, theoretical justification, and improved generalization across subgroups.

C2.justification: The explanations of subgroup coverage, robustness, synthesized-sample distributions, and CVaR sensitivity are unchanged. Section 3.1 also retains the same exclusion of training-procedure convergence guarantees from the analysis.

D1.justification: v2 adds a clickable 'Source Code' link to a GitHub repository at the end of the abstract; v1 lacks this access pointer. Implementation descriptions and hyperparameters are otherwise unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same SVHN, CIFAR-10, ImageNet-10, and additional ImageNet subsets, with identical subgroup, image-corruption, and cross-architecture scenarios.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in every corresponding experiment, including Random, DSA, DM, KIP, IDC, and GLaD in Table 1 and the retained comparator subsets in Tables 2–5.

E3.justification: Sections 4.1–4.8 retain the same preprocessing, IPC settings, model architectures, batch size, clustering settings, CVaR ratio, metrics, and evaluation procedures.

E4.justification: The robustness tests, cross-architecture analysis, CVaR-component ablation, parameter sensitivity analysis, and synthesized-sample visualizations are identical, including Appendix B.

E5.justification: Table 1 retains the same five-run averaging statement and uncertainty reporting. Neither version adds or removes seed information, statistical tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in Tables 1–5, plotted results, qualitative visualizations, and reported findings are unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Algorithms 1–2 retain identical clustering, CVaR objectives, and synthetic-dataset optimization procedures.

P1.justification: The abstract gains the words 'Source Code.' and the arXiv version/date stamp is updated. The remaining prose, terminology, and section organization are unchanged.

P2.justification: Figures 1–8, Tables 1–5, captions, and their placement are unchanged. The new abstract link fits on the existing line without altering the page layout.

R1.justification: Section 2, the bibliography, and the paper's novelty positioning relative to dataset distillation and distributionally robust optimization are identical.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, Assumptions 3.1–3.2, Proposition 3.3, DRO arguments, and theoretical details and proof in Appendix A are identical.

improvement.justification: The new source-code pointer makes implementation resources easier to locate, providing a limited improvement in reproducibility documentation. Methods, evidence, theory, and appendices are unchanged. The supplied PDFs alone do not establish the linked repository's completeness or usability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same research work, with readable text, equations, tables, figures, and complete Appendices A and B. Pages 2–14 have identical extracted text and rendered appearance; differences are confined to page 1.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experimental results in Section 4, Tables 1–5, and the main-text and appendix visualizations.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original dataset-distillation experiments on SVHN, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet subsets, including robustness evaluations, ablations, and parameter analysis.

title: Group Distributionally Robust Dataset Distillation with Risk Minimization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contribution: clustering and risk minimization improve distilled-data generalization and subgroup robustness, with theoretical and empirical support. The emphasized Double-DRO terminology describes nesting already present in v2's analysis. The first-work positioning is also retained.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations connecting excessive clustering and small batches to insufficient samples for CVaR optimization, discusses initialization insensitivity, and acknowledges additional computation. It also interprets transfer and domain-generalization results as broader applicability evidence. These refine practical boundaries and interpretations while retaining the original account of group coverage and robustness.

D1.justification: Appendices G–H newly disclose dataset statistics, RGB-space KMeans evaluation with ten groups, hardware, baseline-specific details, and distillation schedules, including network-training sample budgets and image-update counts. Earlier architectural and default hyperparameter information is retained after relocation. v2's direct code link disappears; v3 instead states that code accompanies supplementary material, whose availability cannot be verified from the supplied PDFs.

E1.justification: v3 adds MetaShift, ImageNetBG, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet-50-to-CUB-200 transfer. It also introduces unseen-class retrieval from ImageNet-10 to the existing ImageNet-A/B subsets, changing task requirements beyond their original within-subset classification evaluations. The original SVHN, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet-subset coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v3 newly evaluates IDM in Table 5 and DREAM and PDD in Table 8, each with and without the proposed robust optimization. Table 12 additionally compares MMD, RSC, and HYPO as training pipelines combined with GLaD and its robust variant. The original Random, DSA, DM, KIP, IDC, and GLaD comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include 50-IPC subpopulation-shift evaluations, downstream fine-tuning, and nearest-neighbor retrieval on unseen classes with the query excluded from candidates. Appendix D adds controlled cluster-count, batch-size, and initialization comparisons. Original settings such as alpha=0.8 and batch size 256 are retained; the additional implementation disclosure does not establish changes to those experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained CVaR-component ablation, alpha sensitivity, cross-architecture tests, and visualizations, v3 tests sensitivity to cluster count, mini-batch size, and initialization in Tables 9–11. It adds transfer and subpopulation robustness tests, compatibility with domain-generalization pipelines, and an efficiency analysis reporting the additional optimization cost.

E5.justification: Uncertainty reporting expands substantially. v2 provides ± values mainly for robust-method results in its standard-accuracy table; v3 also supplies them for baseline results and the retained robustness, cross-architecture, ablation, and ImageNet-subset comparisons. Five-run averaging was already stated in v2 and is specified for several new v3 tables. The PDFs do not establish increased run counts for retained results.

E6.justification: The matched original tables retain their central accuracy values, while v3 adds substantial new results. Table 3 reports GLaD/GLaD-robust worst-group accuracies of 51.3/57.0 on MetaShift and 32.2/38.6 on ImageNetBG; Table 6 reports 49.2/54.6 on CUB-200 transfer. Additional method, sensitivity, and timing outcomes also appear. These are newly reported comparisons, not performance gains over v2 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The proposed formulation is substantively generalized. v2 Algorithms 1–2 define L(S) through the optimized cluster-CVaR objective and update synthetic data using Gaussian zero-order estimates. v3 Algorithm 1 alternates robust network optimization with synthetic-data optimization under a plug-in matching objective. The clustering/CVaR criterion remains, and the original zero-order update survives as an optional procedure in Appendix B. This does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: The introduction and algorithm exposition are extensively rewritten. Analysis becomes a separate main section; related work and implementation details move to appendices; robustness results precede standard accuracy; and the existing additional ImageNet results move to Appendix D. New appendix organization and a reproducibility statement substantially reshape the narrative.

P2.justification: The main document changes from two columns to one, with extensive table and figure rearrangement. Original Tables 3 and 4 become paired panels in v3 Table 4, and the ImageNet-subset table moves to Table 13. Numerous new tables are added. Existing sample visualizations are retained and relocated, while the alpha plot is reformatted without changing its reported trend.

R1.justification: v3 broadens the cited research context to subpopulation shift, transferability, and domain generalization through works supporting the new evaluations. It also adds dataset-parameterization and recent adversarial-distillation literature, plus Nash and Morse-Saard references for the convergence argument. The original DD/DRO positioning and first-subgroup-DRO claim remain, but the supporting literature coverage expands substantially.
