T1.justification: v3 strengthens Assumption 3.1 with a positive lower bound on subgroup probability and adds Theorem 3.3 asserting fixed-point convergence under Morse-Saard and compact-solution-set conditions, supported by a brief cooperative-game argument. v2 explicitly excluded training convergence guarantees. The existing large-deviation proposition and its appendix proof remain substantially unchanged after renumbering.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central robustness claim by adding subpopulation-shift benchmarks beyond v2's clustered and corrupted test sets. Sensitivity, initialization, transfer, and timing analyses address important validation gaps, while expanded uncertainty reporting and implementation details improve assessability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the less explicit code access and weaknesses in the newly asserted convergence theorem, which lacks a developed proof and refers to Algorithm 2 despite the surrounding discussion of Algorithm 1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same dataset-distillation work and contain readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Relocated material, including the zero-order algorithm and ImageNet-subset results, can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds subpopulation-shift evaluations, transfer experiments, additional method comparisons, and sensitivity analyses in Section 4 and Appendix D.

before.justification: v2 Section 4 reports original distillation experiments, robustness evaluations, cross-architecture comparisons, ablations, and parameter analyses.

title: Group Distributionally Robust Dataset Distillation with Risk Minimization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand the contribution from GeoNGNN and three established invariant models to a general family of complete geometric subgraph GNNs under stated conditions. v2 also strengthens the restricted-unidentifiable-space claim to an explicit measure-zero claim and presents expansion of the geometric model design space as a central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds a low-dimensional-distance-graph explanation for the collapse of traditional expressiveness hierarchies. Its 3BPA discussion identifies weaker generalization than MACE, especially under larger temperature shifts, and proposes equivariant representations as a possible remedy. It explicitly cautions that empirical separation does not prove PaiNN/MACE completeness. Interpretations concerning sampling failures disappear with those analyses.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies ModelNet40 downsampling to 256 points, documents 3BPA settings, and adds dataset-specific training times. Hardware reporting changes from RTX 3090/A100 to RTX 4090/A100 with 80GB specified. These improve implementation and resource documentation; the PDFs do not establish whether the newly disclosed downsampling itself changed.

E1.justification: v2 adds 3BPA energy and force prediction, including evaluation at higher temperatures than the training data. This is a targeted extension into temperature-shift scenarios within molecular prediction. Existing synthetic, rMD17, MD22, QM9, ModelNet40, and chirality coverage remains; v1's ModelNet already denotes the same 40-class dataset.

E2.justification: Allegro is removed from the rMD17 comparison in Table 1, although it remains in MD22 and participates in the new 3BPA comparison. The other retained benchmark comparator sets are unchanged. Newly discussed geometric subgraph GNNs are theoretical constructions, not newly evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: For rMD17, reported DisGNN depth changes from 6 to 7 layers and GeoNGNN from (5,1) to (5,2) inner/outer layers; the polynomial envelope changes from p=5 to p=6. The QM9 symmetry assessment now explicitly discards initial labels. The added 3BPA protocol uses a 450/50 training/validation split, 300K training, and RMSE evaluation at 300K, 600K, and 1200K.

E4.justification: v2 removes the extensive node-type and METIS/BRICS partition-sampling analyses, including their negative findings (v1 Appendix E, Tables 6–7). It adds temperature-shift generalization analysis on 3BPA and revises the real-data symmetry assessment. The subgraph-radius sensitivity experiment is retained as v2 Figure 6, rather than newly added.

E5.justification: The new 3BPA table explicitly reports standard deviations over three runs. v1 already includes uncertainty values for chirality results, which remain unchanged, but does not specify this three-run reporting protocol. Neither PDF establishes an increase in repeated runs for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces DisGNN and GeoNGNN scores: for example, GeoNGNN aspirin energy MAE changes from 0.0490 to 0.0502 and ethanol force MAE from 0.0616 to 0.0482. These accompany changed configurations, and ranks also reflect Allegro's removal. v2 adds 3BPA results, revises symmetry proportions, and removes sampling results. Synthetic separation, MD22, efficiency, and chirality results are retained.

M1.justification: v2 introduces a general geometric subgraph-GNN family with distance-aware local operations, inter-subgraph aggregation, and alternative pooling schemes (Section 4.2 and Appendix D). It removes v1's node-type sampling and GeoNGNN-P designs. The base DisGNN schematic also replaces paired dense layers with residual blocks. The central GeoNGNN nesting and GeoNGNN-C directed-distance mechanisms remain.

P1.justification: The introduction, preliminaries, and symmetry exposition are extensively rewritten around unlabeled point clouds and C/D-symmetry. Detailed anchor derivations move to the proofs, related work moves to an expanded appendix, and MD22 and subgraph-size discussions move out of the main experimental narrative. Vanilla DisGNN is generally renamed DisGNN, and the appendices are substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with extensive display reflow. v2 redraws and combines symmetry illustrations, adds a prior-work set-containment diagram, revises the symmetry plots and architecture schematic, and adds the 3BPA table. The partition schematic and two sampling tables disappear. Several retained figures and tables are relocated or resized.

R1.justification: The introduction and expanded Appendix A substantially reposition the work against complete point-cloud invariants, Hordan's near-completeness characterization, 2FWL-based models, and continuous-frame approaches. New references include Widdowson/Kurlin, injective-network theory, and recent frame methods. The relationship to traditional subgraph-GNN hierarchies becomes central, while partition-method references disappear with the sampling appendix.

T1.justification: Beyond reformulating existing anchor arguments as C/D-symmetry, v2 adds general subgraph-GNN completeness theorems and proofs, a measure-zero argument, and an O(n^5) complexity derivation including injective-function costs. The earlier O(n^3) accounting excluding those costs remains. The new Proposition B.3 contains an unjustified implication from distinct distance multisets to distinct squared-distance sums, affecting its support for Theorem B.4.

improvement.justification: v2 adds broader completeness analysis, informative temperature-shift evaluation, and useful computational documentation. However, it removes sampling evidence, and its newly emphasized measure-zero argument relies on Proposition B.3's unjustified inference that distinct distance multisets imply distinct squared-distance sums. These gains coexist with a substantive gap in a new theoretical contribution, preventing a reliable judgment of net overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, core GeoNGNN constructions, and overlapping experiments. All 30 pages of v1 and 39 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable. Text extraction and visual inspection support matching equations, figures, and tables across the substantial revision.

after.justification: v2 retains original GeoNGNN and GeoNGNN-C evaluations, revises molecular prediction and symmetry results, and adds original 3BPA generalization results in Appendix F.2.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic separation experiments, molecular prediction results, symmetry assessments, chirality evaluations, and sampling-policy experiments in the main text and appendices.

title: On the Completeness of Invariant Geometric Deep Learning Models

C1.justification: The central near-completeness and completeness contributions remain. The claimed improvement over Hordan is narrowed from two larger asymmetric sets to one, following the revised set-inclusion result. The abstract and conclusion explicitly emphasize full connectivity and cease presenting downstream competitiveness as a headline contribution, although those evaluations remain in Appendix F.

C2.justification: New Section 5.4 explains why invariant message passing loses local information and why extending completeness to sparse graphs requires stronger conditions than connectivity alone. It also explains the relevance of theoretical completeness when practical implementations use finite cutoffs. Earlier observations about generalization differences and equivariant models' advantages remain.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies farthest-point sampling for the existing 256-point ModelNet40 preprocessing. Appendix G adds QM9 splits, batch size, subgraph radius, layer counts, and approximately 36–100 training hours on an RTX 4090. Existing implementation details largely remain, although the conflicting MD22 cutoffs reduce reproducibility clarity.

E1.justification: v3 Appendix F.4 adds supervised prediction of 12 QM9 properties, including dipole moment, polarizability, orbital energies, and thermodynamic quantities. QM9 previously appeared only in the symmetry survey. This substantially broadens predictive task coverage; the earlier molecular dynamics, synthetic, ModelNet40, and chirality evaluations remain.

E2.justification: Comparator changes are localized: v3 adds SphereNet and GemNet to the synthetic separation comparison and VisNet-LSRM to MD22, while removing 2F-DisGNN from the efficiency table. The new QM9 comparison includes PhysNet and ComENet, which were not evaluated as baselines in v2.

E3.justification: v3 introduces a QM9 protocol with 110K/10K training/validation examples, batch size 32, and four inner plus one outer layer. The ModelNet40 deviation-error sweep also changes. Appendix F.2 now states a 5 Å MD22 message-passing cutoff, whereas v2 specified 7 Å; however, v3 G.2 still states 7 Å, leaving the actual setting unresolved.

E4.justification: The noise-tolerance analysis is revised: v3 Figure 2 samples additional intermediate ModelNet40 tolerances and changes the plotted symmetry evidence relative to v2 Figure 4. The synthetic separation diagnostic also covers two additional invariant models. The subgraph-radius sensitivity analysis and 3BPA distribution-shift tests are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same three-run standard-deviation practice for 3BPA and retain the chirality tables' uncertainty values. No new seed reporting, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures are introduced.

E6.justification: v3 adds the complete QM9 results table and 100% synthetic separation results for SphereNet and GemNet. MD22 DisGNN and GeoNGNN values are revised; for example, GeoNGNN's Ac-Ala3-NHMe energy/force errors change from 0.106/4.9 to 0.093/3.6. These are revised results, not established same-setting gains given the cutoff ambiguity. Symmetry curves also change, while rMD17, 3BPA, chirality, and subgraph-size results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: GeoNGNN retains its marked subgraphs, inner and outer DisGNNs, distance encoding, and pooling. GeoNGNN-C also retains its orientation-sensitive distances. The explicit GeoNGNN equations in v3 Section 5.1 describe procedures already documented in v2, including Appendix G.

P1.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes and rewrites the narrative: related work becomes Section 2, definitions and GeoNGNN exposition are expanded, a dedicated discussion section is added, and the symmetry survey moves into the main experiments. Molecular prediction evaluations move into Appendix F, proofs are reordered, and Appendix G gains an extended NGNN explanation.

P2.justification: v3 adds the QM9 table, a larger counterexample gallery, and an NGNN schematic. It redraws the prior-work set-inclusion diagram, revises the symmetry plots' axes and legends, and restructures comparator columns and highlighting in several tables. Existing displays are also relocated within the reorganized ICLR layout.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion substantively revises its treatment of GWL's neural realizability and adds positioning against recent equivariant and sparse-graph work, including Cen et al., Wang et al., and Sverdlov and Dym. The comparison with Hordan is narrowed mathematically. v2's discussion of weighted continuous frames and its associated citations is removed; these changes extend beyond relocating related work or updating bibliographic metadata.

T1.justification: v2 Proposition B.3 asserts inclusion of the distinct-geometric-degree set in the C-asymmetric set; v3 Proposition C.2 replaces this with inclusion in the D-asymmetric set and rewrites the proof. v3 Appendix B.1 independently derives the zero-measure result using polynomial constraints instead of relying on the earlier inclusion argument. Definition 4.1 also excludes zero total mass from barycenter construction.

improvement.justification: v3 improves theoretical precision by replacing the overstrong C-asymmetry comparison with a D-asymmetry result and a separate zero-measure argument. Its fuller explanation of connectivity assumptions and additional QM9 and separation evidence also help readers assess applicability. These benefits are partly offset by inconsistent MD22 cutoff documentation and removal of the 2F-DisGNN efficiency comparison, supporting a limited net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research on invariant geometric models. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–H are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical evaluations and adds QM9 property-prediction results, alongside revised MD22 and symmetry-assessment results.

before.justification: v2 reports original symmetry assessments, synthetic separation experiments, molecular energy/force predictions, and chirality-related evaluations, including results in the appendices.

title: On the Completeness of Invariant Geometric Deep Learning Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same DisGNN near-completeness claim and completeness contributions for GeoNGNN, geometric subgraph GNNs, DimeNet, GemNet, and SphereNet. The depth-assumption correction does not alter these headline contributions.

C2.justification: Interpretations concerning expressiveness versus generalization, full-connectivity limitations, and sparse-graph open questions in Sections 5.4 and 7 and Appendix F are unchanged. No explanatory or limitations discussion accompanies the theorem correction.

D1.justification: Appendices G and H retain the same architectural details, hyperparameters, training procedures, hardware, training times, and evaluation instructions. No implementation or reproducibility information is added or removed.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same QM9 and ModelNet40 symmetry assessments, synthetic separation cases, rMD17/MD22/3BPA/QM9 benchmarks, and chirality classification, enantiomer ranking, and binding-affinity tasks.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged within every comparison in Tables 1–7. Table 1 retains SchNet, DisGNN, DimeNet, SphereNet, GemNet, PaiNN, and MACE alongside GeoNGNN; Appendix H retains the same chirality baselines.

E3.justification: Experimental splits, preprocessing, metrics, cutoffs, and model configurations in Appendices C.3, G, and H.2 are unchanged. Theorem 5.3 revises a theoretical sufficient-depth assumption, not a reported experimental setting.

E4.justification: The noise-tolerance assessment in Section 6.1, subgraph-size sensitivity in Figure 6, efficiency analysis in Table 4, and temperature-shift evaluation in Table 5 are retained without modification.

E5.justification: Table 5 retains its standard deviations computed over three runs, and Table 7 retains the same uncertainty entries. No run-count, seed, uncertainty-estimation, or significance-testing information changes.

E6.justification: All numerical results and reported findings are identical. For example, Table 1 retains 0% separation for SchNet and DisGNN and 100% for the other six models in both case groups; Tables 2–7 and Figures 2 and 6 are unchanged.

M1.justification: GeoNGNN's procedures, Definition 5.2's general geometric subgraph architecture, and Appendix H's GeoNGNN-C remain unchanged. The revised theorem assumption does not change the proposed algorithms or their implementations.

P1.justification: Theorem 5.3 receives a short rewrite making its depth condition explicit, and the first-page arXiv version/date stamp changes. The remaining prose, terminology, section order, and appendix structure are unchanged.

P2.justification: The expanded theorem statement causes slight local spacing and text reflow on page 7, and the marginal arXiv stamp changes. All figures, tables, captions, and other page layouts remain identical.

R1.justification: Section 2, Appendix A, and the bibliography retain the same cited works and research positioning. The theorem revision introduces no new attribution or novelty claim.

T1.justification: v3's Theorem 5.3 imports all Theorem 5.1 conditions, including GeoNGNN's Nin >= 5 and Nout >= 0. v4 instead requires general geometric subgraph depth greater than a node-count-independent constant C, retaining only the full-connectivity and whole-graph-subgraph conditions. This is a limited correction to the sufficient assumptions; the proof is unchanged.

improvement.justification: The revised Theorem 5.3 better matches Appendix B.5's existing proof, which allows an additional layer for SV pooling, improving the precision of the sufficient-depth condition. The benefit is limited: Appendix B.5 still repeats the old theorem statement, and nearby prose still claims exactly the same conditions as GeoNGNN.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same research work, including complete Appendices A–H. Text and rendered-page comparisons establish that all pages except the first-page arXiv stamp and page 7 are identical; the substantive revision concerns Theorem 5.3.

after.justification: v4 retains these original empirical results, including Section 6, Tables 1–7, and the evaluations in Appendices F and H.

before.justification: v3 reports original symmetry assessments on QM9 and ModelNet40, synthetic point-cloud separation experiments, and GeoNGNN benchmark and chirality results in Appendices F and H.

title: On the Completeness of Invariant Geometric Deep Learning Models

C1.justification: The central contribution expands from learning effective neural-policy AMPO mirror maps to investigating both tabular and non-tabular PMD. v2 adds headline claims that estimation error poorly predicts performance and that small policy updates accompany fewer performance dips. Its abstract also strengthens potential transferability into a claim of good generalization.

C2.justification: v2 introduces interpretations linking policy-update size to stability and explaining why estimation-error bounds do not rank empirical performance well. It removes v1's effective-horizon explanation for learned-map behavior and its discussion of Breakout's weak transfer. The warning about insufficient exploration remains, and v2 explicitly limits direct theoretical diagnostics to the tabular setting.

D1.justification: v2 adds tabular implementation details, four-A40/12-hour resource reporting, and ES population, generation, and noise settings in Appendix C. It drops several earlier hyperparameters, explicit parameter-normalization instructions, and the future code-release statement. The main-text positive-orthant parameter domain also conflicts with the simplex domain retained in Appendix A.2, reducing reproducibility clarity.

E1.justification: v2 adds training over a distribution of Grid-World tasks and evaluation on five held-out configurations and 256 randomly sampled configurations. It removes Breakout from the non-tabular benchmark and transfer comparisons, retaining Acrobot, CartPole, Asterix, Freeway, and SpaceInvaders.

E2.justification: The non-tabular comparison replaces greedy-exp, the doubled-step-size negative-entropy baseline in v1 Figure 2, with the ℓ2 mirror map in v2 Figure 3. Negative entropy is retained and also becomes an explicit comparator in the transfer table, where v1 compared only learned maps.

E3.justification: Non-tabular hyperparameter tuning changes from per-environment to per-suite settings. For example, BCS parallel environments change from 10/16 to 4, and all discount factors become 0.99. v2 also introduces a Grid-World protocol using grid search, 128 PMD iterations, and 2^18 environment steps. These are reported setting changes, not merely additional disclosure.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial diagnostics connecting value trajectories to exact Q-estimation errors and distances between successive policies in Grid-World. Transfer analysis now assesses performance against negative entropy. The earlier greedy-exp comparison testing whether increased greediness or step size explains performance is removed.

E5.justification: Non-tabular figure captions report 100 realizations in v2 instead of 20 in v1. v2 additionally specifies 256 runs for Grid-World plots and 100 runs for transfer results. Learning curves retain mean and standard-error reporting; no new significance-testing or confidence-interval procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: v2 adds Grid-World results and replaces the non-tabular curves and transfer scores. Acrobot changes from favoring negative entropy over the learned map in v1 to a higher final value for the learned map in v2. The Asterix self-transfer entry changes from 14.43 in v1 Table 2 to 30.22 in v2 Table 1. Revised objectives, settings, and final-policy reporting prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains.

M1.justification: The learning objective changes from average return throughout training in v1 Section 4.2 to final-policy value in v2 Equation (7). v2 also introduces tabular PMD with a monotone neural parameterization of the inverse potential and multitask, rank-based OpenAI-ES, alongside the retained piecewise-potential and sep-CMA approach for AMPO.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution narrative, experimental discussion, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Preliminaries, methodology, and experiments are reorganized around tabular and non-tabular settings, and the appendices are rebuilt around different proofs and training details. The title changes from 'Meta-learning the mirror map in policy mirror descent' to 'Learning mirror maps in policy mirror descent.'

P2.justification: v2 retains only the parameterization panel from v1 Figure 1, adds the Grid-World diagnostic figure, and redraws the non-tabular comparison. The transfer heatmap and appendix raw/normalized tables become a colored main-text table with a negative-entropy row. The three-action illustration and algorithm box disappear, and the document adopts substantially different typography and layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting Grid-World, GAE, and future evaluation directions, including Oh et al., Chevalier-Boisvert et al., Schulman et al. (2016), and Osband et al.; it removes Laidlaw et al. The established PMD positioning largely remains, with increased emphasis on Xiao's tabular analysis. Jackson's venue/year update concerns the same cited work.

T1.justification: v1's AMPO convergence theorem and approximation, concentrability, and distribution-mismatch assumptions are replaced by tabular inexact-PMD bounds and new proofs in v2 Theorem 2.2 and Appendix B. The invariance and policy-derivative results and proofs are removed, while the parameter-validity argument is retained. As printed, the new convergence formulas omit the averaging factor on the value sum.

improvement.justification: The held-out Grid-World diagnostics, ℓ2 comparisons, and explicit transfer baseline strengthen evidence for claims that v1 supported mainly through benchmark curves. However, v2 removes Breakout and useful reproducibility details while introducing mathematical inconsistencies: Equation (4) and Theorem B.4 lack the value-sum averaging factor, and the main-text parameter domain conflicts with Appendix A.2. These problems affect the theoretical and implementation basis of the expanded claims. The substantial empirical benefits and losses in correctness and clarity leave the net quality change uncertain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same mirror-map learning research, with common authors, methods, and experiments despite substantial revision. All 17 pages of v1 and 16 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original Grid-World experiments and diagnostics, revised non-tabular learning curves, and transfer evaluations in Section 4, Figures 2–3, and Table 1.

before.justification: v1 reports original AMPO experiments on Basic Control and MinAtar environments, learned mirror maps, and cross-environment transfer results in Section 5 and Appendix B.3.

title: Learning mirror maps in policy mirror descent

C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion extend the learned-map superiority and transfer claims to continuous control, including transfer from Hopper to other MuJoCo tasks. The central claims about mirror-map choice, evolutionary discovery, and the mismatch between theoretical bounds and empirical performance remain.

C2.justification: Appendix F newly explains the computational tradeoff favoring ES over differentiation through long training trajectories, emphasizing memory constraints and JAX parallelism. Appendix C adds geometric interpretation of Bregman divergence. Existing explanations of estimation error, small policy updates, and possible exploration failures are retained.

D1.justification: v3 adds an implementation-repository location, previously unspecified tuning details such as Optuna's CmaEsSampler and the 256-task Grid-World selection objective, and MuJoCo hyperparameters, software, hardware, and runtime. This substantially expands reproducibility information; the PDFs alone do not verify repository contents or accessibility.

E1.justification: Section 4.3 adds Brax-simulated Hopper, Halfcheetah, and Ant. This substantially extends coverage from discrete-action environments to continuous-action control, while retaining all earlier environments.

E2.justification: The existing comparisons retain negative entropy and the ℓ2 mirror map. MuJoCo uses the already evaluated negative-entropy comparator. Newly discussed Mirror Learning and algorithm-discovery methods are not added as experimental baselines.

E3.justification: v3 adds a complete continuous-control protocol: 256 OpenAI-ES generations on Hopper, followed by evaluation across three environments using 10 million environment steps and 488 PMD updates. Tables 2 and 4 specify the additional training configuration. Existing experimental settings are retained; expanded descriptions of their tuning are disclosures rather than demonstrated protocol changes.

E4.justification: Figure 4 adds a transfer test: the mirror map learned on Hopper is reused on Halfcheetah and Ant. This extends the existing generalization analysis to continuous control. Earlier error-tracking, policy-distribution, and cross-environment analyses remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Figure 4 introduces an eight-realization reporting setting for MuJoCo. The existing 256-run Grid-World and 100-run discrete-suite reporting remains unchanged. Means and standard-error shading are retained; no new significance-testing procedure or increase in existing run counts is reported.

E6.justification: Figure 4 adds learning curves showing higher final mean returns for the Hopper-learned mirror map than negative entropy on all three continuous-control tasks. These are new results under new conditions, not improvements to previously reported scores. Figures 2–3 and every numerical entry in Table 1 are unchanged.

M1.justification: v3 adds parameterized-policy PMD for continuous actions in Equation (5), implemented using a deep policy network, Adam, and GAE. This is a limited procedural extension; the existing tabular PMD, discrete-action AMPO, mirror-map parameterizations, and evolutionary search mechanisms remain.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section order are retained. Method subsections are renamed around PMD and AMPO, limited explanations are expanded, and related-work, geometric, computational-cost, reproducibility, and acknowledgment sections are added. Existing appendices are renumbered rather than replaced.

P2.justification: v3 adds Figure 4, splits the original combined hyperparameter table into PMD and AMPO tables, incorporates MuJoCo settings, and renumbers the ES table. Figure 1 is resized and wrapped by text, and ICLR styling replaces the preprint layout. Figures 1–3 retain identical artwork.

R1.justification: New Appendix A explicitly positions the work against automatic RL algorithm discovery, particularly Lu et al. and Jackson et al., contrasting drift penalties with Bregman regularization and discussing differences in theoretical guarantees. Added literature includes Houthooft et al., Kirsch et al., Belousov and Peters, and Jackson et al. (2023), substantially expanding the closest-work comparison.

T1.justification: Equation (4) gains the missing division by T, and the appendix's summed bound gains a factor T before the optimal value. Appendix C adds a Taylor/Hessian characterization of Bregman divergence. These are local mathematical additions and corrections; Theorem D.4 still lacks averaging, and Appendix A's new drift formula omits the function f introduced in its prose.

improvement.justification: Section 4.3 provides useful evidence that learned mirror maps transfer beyond discrete-action tasks, while the repository pointer, fuller tuning disclosure, and closest-work comparison improve reproducibility and contextual understanding. These gains are bounded by mathematical inconsistencies: the averaging correction is not propagated to Theorem D.4, and the new related-work formula omits f. The original empirical evidence is preserved.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across additions, relocation, and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds MuJoCo continuous-control experiments in Section 4.3 and Figure 4.

before.justification: v2 reports original Grid-World, Basic Control, and MinAtar experiments, including learning curves and cross-environment transfer results in Figures 2–3 and Table 1.

title: Learning mirror maps in policy mirror descent

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion shift from adapted-score consistency and easy/diverse selection to DLC and FlexRand as the central contributions. V2 adds explicit claims about adapting sampling preferences across data regimes and achieving 35× pruning acceleration. V1's claim of stable LLM tuning outperforming full-data training with 10% of instructions is replaced by superiority over random selection across several LLMs.

C2.justification: The mechanism explanation shifts from representation gaps, early-layer generalization and dense-region redundancy to capacity-based hardness, regime-dependent preferences and sampling-induced distribution shift. V2 interprets missing-label pretraining experiments as evidence of robustness and presents score transfer as an accuracy–efficiency tradeoff; v1 emphasized that transfer could improve performance. V2 also explicitly identifies storage and memory costs from retaining masked models.

D1.justification: V2 Appendix B adds dataset sizes and class counts, learning-path stopping information, the interval-splitting search range, and HuggingFace, PEFT and LM-Eval implementation information. Hardware reporting changes from RTX 4090 to L40, alongside revised training recipes. Dataset counts are newly documented rather than established changes to previously stated sample sizes; the FGVCAircraft counts are internally inconsistent. DeepCore/PyTorch usage and the supplementary-code availability statement remain.

E1.justification: CXRB10, DTD/Texture and Sketch are retained, while DeepWeeds and FGVCAircraft add visual domains. UltraChat is replaced by Alpaca Cleaned and Dolly & HH-RLHF; MMLU introduces subject-wise question-answer classification evaluation in place of the earlier response-quality evaluation. V1's ImageNet-21K pretraining coverage is also absent from v2's stated ImageNet-1K setup.

E2.justification: V2 adds SSP to the main image comparison while retaining the other named vision baselines. Its LLM comparison retains Random/Ours but drops v1 Table 3's full-data and Small-score controls. CCS and BoundarySet are related-work additions without reported comparison results. The LC bar in v2 Figure 1 matches Least Conf in Table 1, rather than retaining v1's proposed LC as a baseline.

E3.justification: Image validation changes from 25% to 20%, batch size from 64 to 128, weight decay from zero to 1e-5, and a tuned learning rate to fixed 1e-3; the BatchNorm head component is removed. Model and pretraining configurations change, including adding ViTs and larger LLMs. Geometric baselines now undergo full-data fine-tuning. LLM experiments change from one epoch with 10% data to three epochs with 50% data, LoRA and five-shot MMLU. Nine image budget fractions remain, although v2 inconsistently describes ratios as removed versus retained data.

E4.justification: V1's layer-count and cluster-count sensitivity studies are replaced by learning-path-size, L1-versus-random-masking and interval-splitting studies (v2 Figure 6). V2 adds MMD measurements of sampling-induced distribution shifts, masking-versus-optimization loss analyses and qualitative easy/hard image examples (Figures 2–4 and 7). Architecture transfer is retained with revised experiments; v1's LLM convergence analysis is removed.

E5.justification: V1 presents point estimates without explicit repetition counts or uncertainty displays. V2 Table 1 adds ± quantities for accuracy and timing, Figure 5 adds shaded bands, and Figure 6b examines masking variability across ten seeds. Appendix B.1 newly specifies three seeds for EL2N scoring. The main table's uncertainty statistic and repetition count remain undefined; these disclosures do not establish an increase in runs over v1.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and expanded under changed conditions. V1 Table 1 reports RN18 LC accuracy of 56.86% across three datasets; v2 Table 1 reports 57.31% across five and adds ViT results. V1's LLM perplexity/direct-score results are replaced by MMLU results, including Mistral/Alpaca STEM accuracy of 51.74% for Random versus 52.74% for Ours. V2 also reports 29.5 seconds total pruning time against approximately 1,033 seconds for one-shot baselines. These are revised experiments, not controlled cross-version performance gains.

M1.justification: V1 uses layerwise weighted-KNN confidence for images, reciprocal perplexity across dropout subnets for language, and easy-image selection within K-means clusters. V2 replaces these with L1-based weight masking, prototype-based loss integration approximated by Monte Carlo, and FlexRand sampling from adjustable easy/hard intervals (Sections 3.1–3.3). Scoring, subnet construction and selection procedures change substantially.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, method explanation and discussion are extensively rewritten. The separate motivation subsection disappears, instruction pruning becomes a method subsection and a dedicated experimental branch, and detailed settings move into an expanded experimental appendix. Appendix B changes from a proof appendix to experimental documentation, with detailed results organized under B.2 rather than Appendix C.

P2.justification: The main document changes from two-column to single-column layout. V2 adds an opening efficiency/accuracy chart, qualitative image pairs, loss-trajectory grids and MMD displays. Main tables separate architecture columns and scoring/total timing, replacing v1's slash-separated model entries; appendix results become separate architecture-specific tables. Accuracy-gap plots are reorganized by dataset and gain uncertainty bands.

R1.justification: The scientific positioning shifts from early-exit and multilevel-confidence ideas toward weight pruning, model-capacity generalization, optimization trajectories and Monte Carlo estimation. Corresponding references such as Han et al., Neyshabur et al. and Caflisch are added. Appendix A retains its taxonomy but adds SSP, CCS and BoundarySet and expands discussion of the already-cited Moderate Coreset. Its changed publication year does not constitute a new cited work.

T1.justification: V1 Proposition 3.1 and Appendix B's Gaussian-mixture proof connecting weighted-KNN confidence to density are removed, together with the formal diversity criterion. V2 instead defines Learning Path through limiting risk and Learning Complexity as a loss integral, then develops mathematical arguments for optimization and masking paths and their Monte Carlo approximation. This replaces the formal framework rather than relocating the earlier proof.

improvement.justification: V2 improves empirical assessability through five visual domains, CNN/ViT coverage, three LLMs with a specified five-shot MMLU protocol, and targeted masking and sampling analyses. Uncertainty displays and an explicit memory limitation also strengthen reporting. These gains are tempered by the loss of v1's training-free geometric comparison setting and full-data LLM control, plus undefined uncertainty statistics and inconsistent pruning-ratio descriptions. The evidence supports a limited net quality improvement despite the extensive revision.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe successive versions of the same downstream dataset-pruning work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial methodological and experimental revision.

after.justification: V2 reports original DLC/FlexRand classification and timing experiments, MMLU evaluations, masking and sampling ablations, and transfer results, with additional experiments in Appendix B.

before.justification: V1 reports original image-classification accuracy and timing results, ablations, architecture-transfer experiments and QWen instruction-tuning results, including additional results in Appendix C.

title: Exploring Learning Complexity for Efficient Downstream Dataset Pruning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions: training-free DLC scoring, adaptive FlexRand sampling, effectiveness for image and instruction pruning, and the reported 35-fold image-pruning speedup.

C2.justification: The limitations paragraph replaces possible storage/memory overhead with dependence on meaningful pretrained representations. Section 5 reframes model-quality discussion around pretraining-data quality, while C.2.4 adds an explanation distinguishing FlexRand's unequal easy/hard bins from DQ sampling.

D1.justification: New Appendix B specifies the masking threshold, binary mask and elementwise weight operation. Figure 2's caption newly discloses min-max normalization of the existing loss plots. Existing hyperparameters, hardware, software and supplementary-code information are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use CXRB10, DeepWeeds, DTD, FGVCAircraft and Sketch, plus Alpaca Cleaned and Dolly & HH-RLHF instruction tuning evaluated on MMLU. The added analyses reuse existing datasets and classification tasks.

E2.justification: Table 14 adds Dataset Quantization's under-sampling strategy as a comparator to FlexRand using the same DLC scores. This comparison is absent from v2; the existing benchmark comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix C.2.5 adds full-dataset linear-probing evaluation of the existing weakly and fully supervised encoders. C.2.4 adds a sampling-strategy comparison holding DLC scores and fine-tuning settings fixed. Previously reported image and instruction evaluation protocols are retained.

E4.justification: The added sampling comparison tests FlexRand against DQ while controlling the scoring function, and the linear-probing analysis characterizes pretrained representation quality. Existing learning-path, masking, interval-splitting, weak-pretraining and score-transfer analyses remain.

E5.justification: Existing uncertainty displays and seed information are retained, including three fine-tuning runs for EL2N scoring and ten seeds in the masking comparison. The added tables introduce no new run-count disclosure, uncertainty estimation or significance testing.

E6.justification: Table 14 adds DQ results, reporting 55.98% average accuracy versus FlexRand's 57.08%, and Table 15 adds linear-probing accuracies. Tables 1–13 retain their values. Figure 4a also slightly revises the plotted MMD values while preserving their ordering.

M1.justification: DLC's weight masking and Monte Carlo scoring, FlexRand's sampling procedure, and the instruction-scoring adaptation remain unchanged. New Appendix B explicitly formulates the previously described masking operation without establishing a procedural change.

P1.justification: There are localized terminology corrections, paragraph reordering and rewrites in Sections 4–5, plus acknowledgments and a conference-publication header. A method-details Appendix B is inserted and the experimental appendix becomes C; the main narrative structure remains intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 14–15 and expands the captions of Figures 2 and 6. Figure 4a lowers its MMD-axis minimum from 0.03 to 0.01, exposing the random baseline. Other displays are retained with limited layout changes.

R1.justification: v3 adds Zhou et al.'s Dataset Quantization and explicitly positions FlexRand against its sampling strategy. It removes the Radford et al. visual-representation citation and reference. The broader related-work treatment remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The learning-path and learning-complexity definitions, optimization argument, Monte Carlo approximation and sampling probabilities are retained. Appendix B expresses the existing masking rule mathematically as implementation clarification; it adds no distinct theoretical result or substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: The controlled DQ comparison strengthens evidence for FlexRand, while linear-probing results and explicit masking details improve transparency. Clearer captions and the representation-quality limitation also help readers assess the method. These are bounded gains over an otherwise stable paper; removing the earlier storage/memory caveat loses a useful practical qualification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DLC/FlexRand research and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. The experimental appendix moves from Appendix B to Appendix C, with its existing material retained.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds a Dataset Quantization sampling comparison and linear-probing results in Tables 14–15.

before.justification: v2 reports original image-pruning accuracy and timing, instruction-tuning results on MMLU, ablations and detailed appendix experiments.

title: Exploring Learning Complexity for Efficient Downstream Dataset Pruning

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from showing that a GNN on a weighted clique expansion can approximate HyperGNNs for node classification to introducing a training-free feature generator for multiple downstream tasks. The abstract replaces the emphasis on superior classification accuracy and memory/runtime efficiency with competitive performance, reduced training complexity, information utilization and oversmoothing resistance.

C2.justification: v2 newly explains smaller hyperlink-prediction speedups through the greater cost of its prediction head and interprets alpha sensitivity as showing particular benefits from preserving individual features on heterophilic datasets. The stated limitation changes from lacking hyperlink-prediction evaluation to lacking hypergraph-level evaluation. v1's concluding questions about whether node classification needs higher-order interactions are no longer presented.

D1.justification: v1 states that WCE-GNN code and data are available through GitHub; v2 announces a prospective anonymous SHNN code release with running commands. v2 also identifies the DeepSets implementation used for hyperlink prediction and clarifies which baseline accuracies are reused or newly measured. PyTorch and RTX 3090 remain unchanged. Additional hyperparameter disclosures cannot be checked because the referenced appendix is absent.

E1.justification: Node-classification coverage contracts from nine datasets to six: Cora, Pubmed and Walmart are omitted, while the other six remain. v2 adds hyperlink prediction on Cora-CA, Citeseer and House, introducing a distinct task beyond the node classification evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: The node-classification comparison adds HNHN and Deep-HGNN and removes SheafHyperGNN. UniGCNII matches the earlier UniGNN implementation described in v1 Appendix B and is not a new comparator. The ablation comparisons also change substantially: v1 evaluates GAT, SGC and GCN alternatives, whereas v2 uses a pure MLP and SHNN component controls.

E3.justification: The node-classification split remains 50%/25%/25%. The new hyperlink protocol specifies the same split proportions, five fake hyperedges per real hyperedge, message passing using real training and validation hyperedges, and AUC evaluation. Efficiency measurement changes from seconds per epoch averaged over 100 training-and-validation epochs to relative training time required to reach optimal performance; these timings are not directly comparable.

E4.justification: v1 studies cross-model depth sensitivity and memory/runtime scaling, and crosses four GNN architectures with weighted or unweighted clique expansion. v2 instead studies SHNN depth jointly with alpha and compares a pure MLP, unweighted SHNN and weighted SHNN. The weighting question persists, but the architecture, propagation and oversmoothing controls are substantially redesigned.

E5.justification: Both versions specify ten node-classification runs and display results with ± quantities and depth-study error bars. v1 explicitly identifies standard deviations; v2 does not define the dispersion quantities or state repetition counts for hyperlink prediction. With the referenced v2 appendix unavailable, changes to the full uncertainty-reporting procedure cannot be established reliably.

E6.justification: v2 replaces the proposed-model results and adds hyperlink AUC, relative training-time and new ablation findings. For example, Cora-CA accuracy is 86.25 ± 1.25 for WCE-GNN in v1 and 86.54 ± 1.32 for SHNN in v2; these concern different models. AllSetTransformer's House/Senate scores change from 69.33/51.83 to 51.83/69.33 without explanation. The dataset tables also interchange their House/Senate homophily values.

M1.justification: v1 trains GCNII-based WCE-GNN propagation layers jointly with an MLP classifier. v2 replaces this with fixed polynomial propagation, SX_V, computed before training, and trains only the downstream prediction model. Learnable propagation matrices and nonlinearities are eliminated. The hyperedge-size weights and normalization are retained, but the actual learning procedure changes substantially.

P1.justification: The title changes from Hypergraph Node Classification With Graph Neural Networks to Simplifying Hypergraph Neural Networks. The abstract, introduction, related work and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The organization changes from preliminary material followed by theory and the practical framework to notation, methodology and subsequent analysis, with substantially revised terminology and narrative.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn as a two-pipeline training comparison. The earlier depth, memory and per-epoch runtime displays are replaced by relative-time bars, hyperlink AUC/time plots and alpha-depth plots. Tables gain a model-formulation overview, dataset semantics, average-accuracy columns and ranking marks; the ablation table becomes a component-presence comparison. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: Research positioning changes from bridging graph and hypergraph learning, particularly relative to Agarwal et al., to reducing training costs through ideas from SIGN and SGC. v2 adds substantive comparisons with LightHGNN and Hypergraph-MLP, distinguishing their inference-efficiency objectives from its training-efficiency objective. This substantially revises the related-work argument.

T1.justification: The main theoretical program changes from input-space equivalence, shared inductive bias and spectral expressivity to HNN simplification, L-hop propagation support, entropy equality and SHNN convergence. Some polynomial and regularized-smoothing arguments already appear in v1 Appendix E and are adapted rather than entirely new. Nevertheless, v2's Lemma 3.2 and Proposition 4.1 introduce materially different formal statements. Its referenced full proofs are unavailable.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's stated lack of hyperlink-prediction evidence and adds useful propagation and alpha controls for the revised model. However, node-classification coverage narrows, unexplained table-value swaps weaken reporting reliability, and important new proofs and settings depend on an appendix absent from the supplied PDF, whereas v1 supplies extensive proofs. These benefits and limitations do not support a reliable net judgment of overall quality improvement.

A1.justification: The PDFs describe the same substantially revised work, with identifiable continuity in weighted clique expansion, mathematical arguments and benchmarks. v1 includes Appendices A–I. v2 ends at the references despite repeatedly referring to an appendix for proofs and experimental details, limiting comparison of that supporting material.

after.justification: v2 reports original SHNN classification results, component ablations and hyperlink-prediction experiments. Section 6.1 explicitly identifies the hyperlink-prediction results as experiments conducted by the authors.

before.justification: v1 reports original WCE-GNN classification results on nine datasets, alongside architecture ablations, depth studies and computational-efficiency experiments in Section 6.

title: Training-Free Message Passing for Learning on Hypergraphs

C1.justification: The central efficiency, information-utilisation and oversmoothing claims remain. v4 additionally presents the unified aggregation framework as a distinct contribution, explicitly claims the first decoupling of structural processing from model learning, and replaces the Cora-CA headline example with a large-scale Trivago claim.

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations attributing performance to fewer trainable parameters and reduced overfitting, and attributes SIGN's disadvantage to its classifier's feature-merging burden. It adds explicit hyperedge-node importance learning as future work. Existing oversmoothing and heterophily interpretations, and the lack of hypergraph-level evaluation, remain.

D1.justification: Appendices I, K and L supply dataset descriptions, negative-sampling construction and per-dataset model depths, widths, learning rates, alpha and regularisation settings missing from the supplied v2. The text changes promised code release to claimed code/data availability at the TF-HNN address. These improve documentation without establishing changed implementation; settings for Trivago and several added comparisons remain incomplete.

E1.justification: v4 adds Trivago, an accommodation/browsing-session hypergraph with 172,738 nodes, for classification and hyperlink prediction. Appendix J also extends hyperlink prediction from Cora-CA, Citeseer and House to DBLP-CA, Congress and Senate. The original classification datasets remain.

E2.justification: v4 evaluates SGC and SIGN with clique expansion in Table 6 and adds HyperGCL and HDSode classification comparisons in Appendix J. The MLP-only comparator from v2 Table 5 disappears. The original nine classification HNNs and four hyperlink-prediction HNNs remain; the EDGNN figure label becomes ED-HNN.

E3.justification: v4 adds controlled experiments replacing only the message-passing module with SGC or SIGN while keeping other components fixed. Its new Trivago evaluation reports 64-layer Deep-HGNN for classification and two layers for hyperlink prediction. Existing splits, accuracy/AUC metrics and the 5:1 negative-to-positive ratio remain unchanged; appendix settings are disclosures rather than established revisions.

E4.justification: The new module-replacement study tests the proposed propagation against training-free graph alternatives across four datasets. Conversely, v2's MLP-only ablation testing the benefit of structural propagation is removed. The depth/alpha sensitivity analysis and weighted-versus-unweighted comparison remain, although v4 reverses the latter's row labels.

E5.justification: v4 newly specifies five runs for hyperlink prediction and reports numerical uncertainty for absolute training times in Tables 4–5, 10 and 12. Ten classification runs and existing score uncertainty are retained. The five-run statement is new disclosure, not evidence of increased repetitions; neither PDF clearly defines the meaning of all ± values.

E6.justification: The original six-dataset classification scores are identical, but v4 adds substantial results for new benchmarks and comparators. Trivago classification reports 94.03% for TF-HNN versus 84.06% for Deep-HGNN, with training times of 38.09 versus 3352.35 seconds. Appendix J adds hyperlink results, including ED-HNN outperforming TF-HNN on Senate. MLP-only and CE-homophily entries disappear. Table 7 assigns retained ablation scores to opposite weighted/unweighted labels, contradicting its discussion.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure remains parameter removal and linearisation followed by precomputed propagation using the same hyperedge-size weighting, symmetric normalisation, self-loops and residual mixture. v2's SHNN becomes the TF-MP-Module within TF-HNN; the task-specific training pipeline is unchanged.

P1.justification: The title changes from Simplifying Hypergraph Neural Networks to Training-Free Message Passing for Learning on Hypergraphs. Abstract, introduction and methodological framing are extensively rewritten around MP-Modules and TF-HNN. A method overview is added, discussions are reorganised, and named appendix sections replace unsupported generic appendix references.

P2.justification: v4 changes the document from two columns to one, redraws Figure 1, merges method formulas and complexity comparisons into Table 1, and transposes the dataset table while dropping homophily/task fields. It adds experimental and hyperparameter tables and restructures the component ablations. Figures 2–4 largely retain their plotted content with revised sizing and labels.

R1.justification: v4 expands positioning through a four-mechanism HNN taxonomy, graph-filter applicability restrictions and optimisation connections, adding references such as Kim et al. (2024), Ortega et al. (2018) and Yang et al. (2021). It strengthens the first-decoupling novelty claim and develops comparisons with training-free graph methods. The earlier SIGN/SGC inspiration and distinction from inference-focused hypergraph methods remain.

T1.justification: Relative to v2's available statements and proof sketches, v4 supplies extensive formal material in Appendices B–H and M: mechanism-specific derivations, propagation-support proofs, explicit weighting assumptions, entropy arguments and the limiting optimisation derivation. Most main mathematical results are retained or reformulated; Proposition 3.3 adds an explicit i != j restriction. This establishes expanded documented support, not that every argument was newly developed.

improvement.justification: The direct SGC/SIGN comparisons and large-scale Trivago experiments address important gaps in evidence for the method's distinctiveness and efficiency. Supplied proofs and reproduction settings substantially improve inspectability over the available v2. These gains outweigh the removed MLP control, incomplete settings for new experiments and Table 7's reversed labels, although those defects weaken reproducibility and the component analysis.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching core equations and experiments despite renaming. The supplied pages are readable, but v2 refers to appendices absent from its PDF, whereas v4 includes Appendices A–M. Earlier supplementary proofs and settings therefore cannot be compared directly.

after.justification: v4 retains original experiments and reports additional Trivago results, training-free module comparisons and supplementary benchmark results in Tables 4–6 and Appendix J.

before.justification: v2 reports original SHNN classification results, hyperlink-prediction experiments and ablations in Table 4, Figures 3–4 and Table 5, even though some baseline classification scores are borrowed.

title: Training-Free Message Passing for Learning on Hypergraphs

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: training-free hypergraph message passing, a unifying framework, training efficiency, information utilisation, and resistance to oversmoothing. The headline Trivago claim is unchanged. Added supporting experiments do not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: v5 explicitly qualifies Proposition 4.1's entropy as conceptual in Section 4 and Appendix U. Appendices N and R add explanations involving information loss during learned feature projection and memory-constrained latent dimensions. Appendix Q explains zero-degree applicability, and Appendix S interprets hyperparameter interactions. The future-work discussion replaces explicit hyperedge-node importance learning with automated hyperparameter search.

D1.justification: v4 provides selected final hyperparameters but little tuning documentation. v5 adds Trivago configurations to Tables 13–14, extensive model-specific search ranges, validation-based checkpoint and hyperparameter selection, memory restrictions, and the eight-RTX-3090 setup for search timing. It also documents zero-degree handling and changes the code-access disclosure from an anonymous address to a GitHub link.

E1.justification: Appendix P and Table 18 add node classification on the Yelp hypergraph. The seven original hypergraphs and both existing tasks remain. This extends the evaluated data by one benchmark without introducing a new task; the added sensitivity and timing experiments use retained datasets.

E2.justification: Tables 15–16 newly compare against APPNP with the clique expansion from Equation (5) on Cora-CA and Citeseer. Table 17 also evaluates parameter-free variants of four existing baselines. The original HNN, SGC/SIGN, and appendix HyperGCL/HDSode comparisons are retained; those appendix baselines are not new additions.

E3.justification: v5 adds procedures measuring complete grid-search runtime and preprocessing separately, plus paired validation/test evaluations across hyperparameter combinations. The retained experiments keep their 50%/25%/25% splits, accuracy/AUC metrics, and negative-sampling settings. Newly documented search ranges and final configurations do not establish changes to the earlier experiments.

E4.justification: Appendix O tests removing only learnable parameters from four baselines on Cora-CA and Citeseer, isolating a design step not separately tested in v4. Appendix S adds extensive pairwise hyperparameter sensitivity analysis on DBLP-CA, beyond the retained depth/alpha analysis. Appendices S and V additionally investigate tuning cost and preprocessing overhead, substantially broadening the diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions specify ten node-classification runs and five hyperlink-prediction runs and retain the same plus/minus uncertainty reporting. The additional results introduce no explicit changes to run counts, seeds, uncertainty estimation, confidence intervals, or significance testing.

E6.justification: Tables 15–21 and Figure 5 add substantial comparison, ablation, sensitivity, and timing results. For example, TF-HNN achieves 36.06 ± 0.32% accuracy on Yelp with 6.54 ± 0.96 seconds training time. Original benchmark scores are retained. Table 7 swaps the condition labels: v5 assigns average accuracy 77.02 to weighted S and 76.02 to unweighted S, reversing v4's attribution and aligning the table with the discussion.

M1.justification: The TF-HNN procedure remains unchanged: fixed linear message passing with the weighted clique-expansion operator is precomputed before training the task-specific module. Equations (1) and (4)–(6) retain the same operations. New explanations and baseline ablations do not establish a modification to TF-HNN.

P1.justification: The main seven-section narrative and existing appendices remain recognizable. v5 makes local paragraph edits, replaces 'model learning' with 'model training,' expands introductory explanations and cross-references, and adds acknowledgements and equal-contribution information. The substantial appendix additions mainly document new evidence and discussion rather than extensively reorganizing existing prose.

P2.justification: v5 adds seven tables and Figure 5, which presents 15 pairs of validation/test heatmaps. Tables 13–14 gain Trivago rows, and Table 7's condition labels are corrected. Existing figures and tables are retained with caption shortening, resizing, and reflow. The new comparative and diagnostic displays substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Section 3.1 and the new Appendix N substantially expand positioning against APPNP, explaining its relationship to GCN/PageRank and distinguishing training-time propagation from TF-HNN preprocessing. Additional references support the new discussions of entropy, tuning, datasets, and hypergraph applications; Eswaran et al. (2020) is removed. The principal change is the detailed treatment of closely related methodology.

T1.justification: Appendix T adds Lemmas T.1–T.2 and proofs connecting the clique-expansion operators, including their dependence on hyperedge size. Section 2 drops the prohibition on duplicate hyperedges, and Appendix V adds an O(m) preprocessing-complexity statement. The central propositions and earlier derivations remain largely unchanged, with several proof cross-references corrected.

improvement.justification: v5 substantially strengthens reproducibility and support for the efficiency claim by documenting search spaces and selection rules and measuring previously unreported tuning and preprocessing costs. The APPNP comparison, parameter-removal controls, sensitivity analyses, and Table 7 correction also address important evidential gaps. These gains outweigh remaining theoretical problems: the conceptual entropy qualification does not fully reconcile the formal equality claim, and the new UniGNN derivation in Lemma T.2 contains a normalization inconsistency with Appendix D.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TF-HNN research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across pagination changes.

after.justification: v5 retains those original experiments and adds APPNP comparisons, Yelp evaluation, parameter-removal experiments, sensitivity analyses, and computational-cost measurements.

before.justification: v4 reports original TF-HNN node-classification and hyperlink-prediction results, training times, and ablations in Section 6 and Appendix J.

title: Training-Free Message Passing for Learning on Hypergraphs

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain their principal claims. However, v2 explicitly restricts the introduction's claim that escape neurons prevent local minimality to scalar-output networks; v1 states that introductory claim without this qualification.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies the proposed rarity of type-2 local minima and adds discussion of unresolved third-order behavior in Appendix F.2.1. Remark D.2 also corrects v1 Remark 4.7's interpretation that local maxima require weights orthogonal to every input: the revised statement requires that no inputs are activated.

D1.justification: New Appendix M supplies a URL for the numerical-experiment code, whereas v1 provides no such access information. Existing data values, training hyperparameters and perturbation details are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same five-sample scalar regression example and illustrative two-dimensional gradient-descent cases. The multilayer extension in v2 is analytical and introduces no additional evaluated dataset or task.

E2.justification: The same initialization-scale comparison is retained, and neither version reports additional competing-method evaluations. Comparisons with prior network-embedding research are theoretical rather than empirical baselines.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 retains 50 hidden neurons, 500,000 training epochs and a gradient-descent step size of 0.001. The two initialization scales and the uniform-noise perturbation procedure also remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The initialization-scale analysis, local-minimum perturbation check, illustrative stationary-point cases and learned-function trajectories are retained. In particular, v1 Appendices E and J correspond to v2 Appendices G and L; their relocation adds no new empirical analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same 5,000 random perturbations. There are no added or revised training-seed disclosures, repeated-run uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: The empirical figure images and reported outcomes are retained: saddle escapes near epochs 42k and 152k, two versus four learned kinks, and positive loss changes for all 5,000 perturbations. v1 Figures 11–12 become v2 Figures 13–14 without changed results.

M1.justification: New Appendix B adapts the directional-derivative computation to multiple hidden layers using layerwise recursion and perturbation-dependent back-propagation. This extends the analytical procedure; the principal shallow model, squared loss, training procedure and network-embedding operations remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most prose remain intact. Targeted restructuring concentrates Section 4.3 on unit replication, consolidates local-maxima material in Appendix D, and moves inactive-unit discussions into Appendices I–J. v2 also adds an intuitive explanation in Appendix E and makes local wording and terminology edits.

P2.justification: The two-column main text becomes a single-column layout with resized and wrapped figures. v1's three-panel Figure 6 is split into v2 Figures 6, 11 and 12, with two panels relocated to appendices. Figure placement and several captions change substantially, although the underlying figure images are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Boursier and Flammarion's work on early alignment and Liu Ziyin et al.'s work on SGD convergence to local maxima. It also makes the contrast with stationarity preservation in smooth networks more explicit. The principal research positioning remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds a substantive mathematical extension of Lemma 3.2 to multiple hidden layers, including recursive derivative formulas and treatment of downstream activation signs. Fact 4.8 becomes Fact 4.6 and corrects the invariant from ||w_i||^2 - h to ||w_i||^2 - h^2, with the corresponding absolute-value balance relation. The central stationary-point and embedding theorems are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 improves precision through the corrected training invariant, scalar-output qualification and corrected local-maxima interpretation. The code pointer, intuitive explanation and multilayer derivative extension improve accessibility and completeness. These are useful but limited gains: the central theorems and empirical evidence remain largely unchanged, and the multi-output local-minimum question remains unresolved.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures and appendices support comparison despite substantial reformatting and appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments in Sections 4.1–4.2 and Appendices G and L, including training trajectories, learned functions and perturbation outcomes.

before.justification: v1 reports original gradient-descent experiments on five regression samples, comparisons between initialization scales, and a 5,000-perturbation experiment in Appendix E.

title: Loss Landscape of Shallow ReLU-like Neural Networks: Stationary Points, Saddle Escape, and Network Embedding

C1.justification: V2 presents proposed stationarity conditions; v5 explicitly identifies the established directional-stationarity notion and emphasizes its suitability for characterizing GD stagnation. The escape-neuron and embedding contributions remain stable. Excluding alternative scalar-output saddle-escape mechanisms was already claimed in v2 Section 4.2.

C2.justification: V5 substantially expands the rationale and boundaries of its stationarity notion, including exceptional GD-stalling points it can miss (Appendix C). It explains the higher-order proof difficulty behind restricting the main theorem to shallow networks and interprets vector-output escape through nonzero output-weight cancellation and neuron splitting (Section 4.1 and Appendix I.2).

D1.justification: V5 documents the exact input and target arrays, network widths and initialization distributions for the added experiments. Its reproducibility statement replaces v2's anonymous repository pointer with a GitHub code pointer. The implementation information for the retained main experiment is essentially unchanged.

E1.justification: V2's neural-network experiments use five two-dimensional inputs with scalar targets. V5 retains this coverage and adds seven-sample three-dimensional-input/scalar-output and four-sample two-dimensional-input/vector-output regression problems (Appendix I), substantially extending the represented input and output settings.

E2.justification: Neither version reports empirical comparisons against competing algorithms. V5's added comparisons with Clarke and canonical-axis stationarity concern mathematical definitions, rather than experimentally evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The retained main experiment keeps 50 hidden neurons, 500k epochs, step size 0.001 and initialization standard deviation 5e-6. The added Appendix I experiments retain 50 neurons but use standard deviation 9.51e-11 and trajectories extending to approximately 600k and 300k epochs (Figures 11–12). These are additional settings, not revisions of the original runs.

E4.justification: Appendix I.2 adds a substantial analysis of successive vector-output saddles, using component residuals and approximate derivative calculations to identify escape neurons and investigate neuron splitting. It also adds a separate 5,000-perturbation local-minimum check. The original initialization-sensitivity study and scalar-output perturbation analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-seed replication, confidence intervals or significance tests. V5 applies the existing 5,000-random-perturbation and histogram practice to another experiment; this adds results without changing the statistical reporting practice.

E6.justification: V5 adds a three-dimensional-input trajectory with four saddle escapes and reported zero final loss, plus a vector-output trajectory with three escapes, neuron splitting and a final underfitting local minimum (Appendix I, Figures 11–14). The original experimental plots and findings are retained unchanged. These additions are results under new settings, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The studied architecture, ReLU-like activations, squared loss, GD procedure and network-embedding operations remain unchanged. V5 explicitly identifies its directional-stationarity formulation as equivalent to the existing conditions; the additional theory and experiments do not introduce a new algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, stationarity discussion and training-dynamics narrative are extensively rewritten. V5 adds Section 3.2.1 and an appendix contents list, moves the larger-initialization discussion into Appendices J–K, and relocates embedding applications to Appendix Q. This substantially reorganizes retained material as well as accommodating additions.

P2.justification: V5 adds the aligned-coordinate illustration in Figure 9 and the training, perturbation and residual displays in Figures 11–14. It revises the flowchart labels, relocates the larger-initialization plots from v2 Figure 5 to v5 Figure 15, and adopts a substantially different conference layout. The retained experimental plot contents are unchanged.

R1.justification: V5 substantially expands its positioning within nonsmooth optimization through comparisons involving directional, Clarke and canonical-axis stationarity, citing works including Li et al. (2020), Clarke (1975), Davis et al. (2020) and Yun et al. (2019). Kumar and Haupt (2024) also becomes central to the saddle-dynamics positioning. These changes exceed citation-format updates.

T1.justification: The central Theorem 4.2 and embedding Proposition 4.8 remain intact. V5 adds Proposition C.1 and its GD escape-time proof, Proposition C.6 and Fact C.7 connecting directional and Clarke stationarity, and a counterexample to canonical-axis stationarity. Corollary 4.6 also formalizes the restriction on saddles approached from vanishing initialization.

improvement.justification: V5 improves conceptual grounding and research positioning through Section 3.2.1 and Appendix C, while Appendix I illustrates important multidimensional behavior absent from v2. These are useful gains in explanation and support for the retained central results. However, the new worked validation contains numerical inconsistencies: Appendix I.2 states e12 = +0.12 near epoch 100k, whereas Figure 14b shows it as negative. This limits the reliability of the added quantitative explanation and qualifies the overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same shallow ReLU-like loss-landscape study, with matching central theorems, experiments and embedding analysis. Their text, equations, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V5 retains these empirical results and adds original higher-dimensional input and vector-output experiments, including parameter trajectories, residual analysis and another perturbation check (Appendix I).

before.justification: V2 reports original GD training trajectories, experiments with two initialization scales, and a 5,000-perturbation local-minimum check (Section 4 and Appendices G and L).

title: Loss Landscape of Shallow ReLU-like Neural Networks: Stationary Points, Saddle Escape, and Network Embedding

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion elevate modality-sequential training and adaptive stopping into central contributions alongside fusion. Claimed empirical scope expands to seven tasks, including touch and thermal reasoning. The efficiency claim changes from approximately 96% fewer trainable parameters to over 90%, with the stated per-modality requirement changing from under 5M to 4–10M.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 adds substantive explanations involving incompatible modality representations, dominant-modality convergence, and the benefits of sequential optimization. It also attributes weak alternative fusion results to architectural changes and limited downstream data. Appendix C newly identifies limited temporal modeling from image-only pre-training and overhead from computing additional modalities as specific limitations.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds dataset-construction descriptions, split sizes, and additional modality settings; Table 11 extends prompts to four new tasks, and the license section adds their sources. Most encoder, hardware, and pre-training details remain unchanged. v2 drops the explicit cross-entropy-loss statement and OneLLM reimplementation description, and does not specify a numerical early-exit threshold.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from three benchmarks to seven. v2 adds TouchQA material recognition from Touch&Go, ThermalQA past-action recognition from Thermal-IM, PerceptionTest multiple-choice QA, and VGGSound classification reformulated as QA. These extend the represented sensory domains and task requirements. Existing benchmarks and appendix-documented pre-training sources remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds Mirasol3B to the NExT-QA comparison, CMC to TouchQA/ThermalQA, and CAV-MAE plus Mirasol3B variants to VGGSound. It removes the 13B and 33B LLaMA-VQA entries from NExT-QA while retaining the 7B variant. OneLLM and X-BLIP zero-shot comparisons already existed in v1.

E3.justification: v2 evaluates expanded modality configurations, including V/P/D/N on SQA3D and V/A/F/D/N on MUSIC-AVQA. New protocols include reduced-epoch controls for adaptive stopping, a fixed-batch single-GPU memory comparison, and VGGSound accuracy both before and after excluding out-of-vocabulary predictions. These substantially extend evaluation design; retained benchmarks keep their stated evaluation splits.

E4.justification: v2 adds adaptive-exit convergence and training-budget analyses (Table 6 and Figure 2), joint-versus-sequential training ablations (Table 16), and a training-memory comparison (Table 14). Fusion and easy/hard analyses are revised. Pre-training and LoRA-rank ablations remain, and the qualitative examples are retained and regrouped rather than newly added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests for its experimental results. Both primarily report point estimates; parenthesized improvements are score differences rather than uncertainty estimates.
