E6.justification: Many results are added or replaced. For NExT-QA, the original fused variant reports 73.0 accuracy and 1.46K GFLOPs, whereas the revised method reports 73.9 and 2.47K. New SQA3D and MUSIC-AVQA configurations report 54.6 and 81.7, respectively, under expanded modality inputs. Four added benchmarks and new training analyses supply further results. Baseline parameter counts also change, including BLIP-2 from 188M to 108M for one modality; zero-shot and rank/pre-training results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Equation 3 changes fusion from element-wise addition of video and gated supporting features to concatenation. Section 3.3 introduces modality-sequential updates within each minibatch and gradient-based adaptive early exit. These substantially change fusion and optimization, while retaining the frozen backbone and modality-specific adapters.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, integrates the separately named Espresso variant into the CREMA narrative, rewrites Section 3.3 around modular training, and reorganizes quantitative analysis around research questions. Qualitative analysis and broader impacts move into the appendix, while experimental discussions and appendix organization are substantially revised.

P2.justification: The document changes from a predominantly two-column to a single-column layout. The introductory comparison schematic is removed, the architecture diagram is redrawn with additional modalities and training information, and an early-exit plot is added. Tables are added and reorganized, while the same eight qualitative examples are regrouped into appendix figures.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the new datasets and comparators, alongside works such as VAST, ViT-Lens, and SOK-Bench. Sections 3.3 and B.4 newly acknowledge alternating adaptation and distinguish CREMA from MLA's shared classifier and gradient projection. The broader positioning against existing multimodal LLMs remains largely intact.

T1.justification: Equation 3 revises the mathematical definition of fused queries. Sections 3.3 and 4.3 introduce a gradient-threshold stopping rule and an early-stop indicator. Existing LoRA equations remain, and neither version provides theoretical guarantees or proofs; the mathematical changes are limited algorithmic definitions.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for CREMA's central generality and practical-efficiency claims through touch/thermal evaluations, controlled sequential-training and early-exit analyses, and a matched-batch memory comparison (Tables 4, 6, 14, and 16). Specific temporal-modeling and preprocessing-cost limitations also improve qualification of those claims. Removed larger LLaMA-VQA comparisons, an unspecified stopping threshold, and unclear SQA3D configuration matching in Table 7 weaken parts of the presentation, but the added controlled evidence provides a substantial net improvement beyond higher headline scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CREMA by the same authors, with substantial shared methods and experiments. Their main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support a reliable comparison despite extensive revision.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and reports additional task evaluations, sequential-training and early-exit ablations, and training-memory measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning and zero-shot experiments on SQA3D, MUSIC-AVQA, and NExT-QA, together with fusion, modality, pre-training, and LoRA-rank analyses.

title: CREMA: Generalizable and Efficient Video-Language Reasoning via Multimodal Modular Fusion

C1.justification: The abstract narrows the extensibility wording from incorporating 'any new modality' to 'many new modalities'. The principal claims about efficient modular fusion, seven-task performance, and reduced trainable parameters remain, as does the conclusion's broader extensibility claim.

C2.justification: Appendix B.8 adds interpretations concerning video prioritization, learnable feature alignment, and the accuracy–cost trade-off supporting 32 query tokens. A new Ethics Statement claims modality augmentation mitigates hallucinations without a dedicated evaluation. Appendix C's temporal-modeling and modality-extraction-overhead limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A.4 newly states that comparisons share modality encoders and estimators. Appendix A.5 explains that existing two-modality zero-shot evaluations bypass fusion and concatenate tokens directly. These clarify retained experiments; the original hardware, hyperparameters, prompts, and code-access statements remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use SQA3D, MUSIC-AVQA, NExT-QA, TouchQA, ThermalQA, PerceptionTest, and VGGSound, with the same auxiliary pre-training sources. The new backbone experiment and design analyses reuse existing datasets, tasks, and modality coverage.

E2.justification: New Table 6 substantially expands the NExT-QA comparison with Video-LLaMA, Video-LLaVA, VideoChat2, MotionEpic-VoT, and LLaVA-NeXT, including a reproduced Mistral-7B VideoChat2 baseline. Earlier comparator sets remain; X-BLIP's appearance as X-InstructBLIP is only a naming change.

E3.justification: The new backbone evaluation introduces Mistral-7B with 16 frames alongside the retained Flan-T5XL 3B, four-frame experiments. Appendix B.8 also introduces controlled modality-prioritization and connector comparisons and 16/32/64-query-token settings. Existing splits, metrics, and original hyperparameter tables remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds backbone-portability validation and Appendix B.8 tests video versus depth prioritization, an FC connector versus interpolation, and query-length sensitivity. Figure 5 adds attention maps to an existing qualitative example. These extend the design evidence beyond the retained fusion, early-exit, sequential-training, pre-training, and LoRA-rank analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for its experimental results. The additional tables retain the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Existing result entries are retained. New Table 6 reports 78.9% and 79.4% for Mistral-based CREMA versus 78.4% for reproduced VideoChat2. These use different conditions from the retained 73.9% Flan-T5XL result. Tables 20–22 add depth-priority accuracy of 62.1%, interpolation accuracy of 78.9%, and query-length results, while reusing some earlier results as reference rows.

M1.justification: Section 4.2 adds an implemented VideoChat2/Mistral-7B variant alongside the original BLIP-2/Flan-T5XL model. The MMQA adapters, self-gated fusion, sequential updates, and adaptive early-exit procedure remain unchanged. Appendix A.5's zero-shot fusion bypass is newly disclosed implementation information.

P1.justification: The introduction and sequential-training explanation receive localized revisions, with added backbone discussion, an Ethics Statement, and Appendix B.8. Citations switch to author–year format. Most prose and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 redraws Figure 1 with explicit token/fusion graphics, adds comparison Table 6, ablation Tables 20–22, and attention-map Figure 5. Existing qualitative figures are redistributed across pages, and the document adopts different headers, heading styles, table sizing, and spacing. Earlier result displays remain identifiable.

R1.justification: v3 adds brief positioning against MultiPLY and X-VILA and references for VideoChat2, BLIP-3, and Qwen2-VL. References to Brown et al., Kiela et al., and Tian et al. disappear. The central positioning against separate Q-Formers and universal multimodal encoders remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–3, the low-rank parameterization, fusion definition, and gradient-based early-exit criterion are unchanged. The expanded training explanation introduces no new mathematical assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

improvement.justification: Table 6 provides empirical support for backbone portability, Tables 20–22 test previously unexamined design choices, and Appendix A.5 clarifies zero-shot inference. These strengthen an otherwise largely retained paper. The gain is limited by sparse training details for the new backbone experiment and the Ethics Statement's unevaluated hallucination-mitigation claim.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CREMA research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v2 reports original CREMA fine-tuning and zero-shot results across seven video-language benchmarks, together with ablations, efficiency measurements, and qualitative analyses.

improvement.justification: v4 updates publication metadata and acknowledgements, including NIH support, with minor layout adjustments. title: CREMA: Generalizable and Efficient Video-Language Reasoning via Multimodal Modular Fusion

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list expand the formal claims beyond linear separable feature selection to loss bounds for general nonlinear, multiclass models. They also elevate failure under class-correlated background shifts across practical hyperparameters to a main contribution. The central warning that label augmentation can favor low-variance spurious features remains.

C2.justification: v2 explains why weak background intensities are needed for weight decay to succeed and explicitly limits its general-model theory to loss bounds without optimization-dynamics guarantees. It adds a small-scale-experiment limitation, while removing v1's discussion of noise-induced weight-decay failure and its possible dependence on experimental settings.

D1.justification: The documented experimental recipes substantially change: synthetic sampling, Gaussian channel concatenation, and uniform/Gaussian noise instructions are removed. v2 specifies shaded-MNIST background intensities, train/test color permutation, network width, and training duration. The PyTorch/P100 disclosure and retained binary-CIFAR implementation details remain unchanged; no code-access information is added.

E1.justification: v2 retains the binary CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 class pairs but removes the synthetic classification task and full multiclass CIFAR experiments with appended class-specific channels. It adds ten-class shaded MNIST, with class-correlated background colors permuted between training and testing.

E2.justification: The comparisons continue to evaluate weight decay, label smoothing, and Mixup, with ordinary ERM represented by zero hyperparameter settings. Invariant risk minimization is newly cited to motivate the MNIST setup but is not evaluated as a comparator.

E3.justification: The multiclass evaluation changes from 100-epoch ResNet-18 training with fixed hyperparameters and epoch-wise error curves to a two-layer ReLU network with 2048 hidden units, 20 epochs, and full hyperparameter sweeps on shaded MNIST. These are replacement experiments under different conditions. The retained binary-CIFAR splits, preprocessing, optimizer settings, and sweeps remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1's Appendix B tests whether conclusions survive nonzero variance in spurious features, including a reported sensitivity of ResNet weight decay to Gaussian noise; these analyses disappear. v2 adds background-permutation robustness testing and nonlinear-model hyperparameter sensitivity on shaded MNIST. The binary-CIFAR weight-ratio diagnostic is retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report means over five training runs and shaded one-standard-deviation bands. No change in repeated-run counts, seed reporting, confidence intervals, or significance-testing practices is documented.

E6.justification: The binary-CIFAR plots are identical: v1 Figures 2 and 3 become v2 Figures 1 and 2. Synthetic, ResNet, and noisy-feature results are removed. New shaded-MNIST results show roughly 10–15% test error with positive weight decay versus approximately 50–70% for label smoothing and Mixup (v2 Figure 3). These are new-condition results, not comparable-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Both versions analyze the same ERM/weight-decay, label-smoothing, and Mixup training procedures and objectives. Architecture changes concern experimental testbeds; no new training method or modification to these procedures is proposed.

P1.justification: The contribution roadmap becomes a three-part contribution list, preliminaries are reorganized, and the data model moves into a split binary/multiclass theory section. Experimental explanations and appendix organization are substantially rewritten, and explicit Limitations and Broader Impacts paragraphs are added. The conclusion also corrects v1's reversal of which variance features are learned.

P2.justification: The synthetic plots, ResNet learning curves, channel-concatenation illustration, and appendix noise panels are removed. v2 adds a paired shaded-MNIST sample/performance figure. The retained binary-CIFAR figures are resized and repositioned with unchanged plotted content, substantially altering the presentation of the empirical evidence.

R1.justification: Most related-work discussion is retained. v2 adds Arjovsky et al. (2020) to position the background-shift experiment and removes He et al. (2015) with the ResNet study. Its comparison with earlier Mixup feature-learning work now qualifies the mixing distributions as symmetric.

T1.justification: v2 substantially revises the binary data assumptions and proofs, replacing exact zero-weight conclusions under zero conditional variance with variance-dependent bounds. The binary Mixup theorem adds a symmetry requirement on the mixing distribution. New multiclass Propositions 3.9 and 3.10 assert output-variance loss bounds, supported by a new Jensen-gap lemma and additional Appendix A proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 adds a useful background-shift sweep and clearer limitations, but removes the ResNet and nonzero-variance robustness evidence. Its central theoretical expansion is also not securely established: Appendix A.3 does not justify replacing conditional Jensen benchmarks with the global loss optima used in the new general-distribution bounds. Because this gap affects the main claimed gain, alongside mixed changes in empirical support, a reliable net-quality direction cannot be established.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with the same title, authors, and central research question. Their main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original binary-CIFAR experiments and a shaded-MNIST background-shift experiment in Section 4, with results averaged over five training runs.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-data, binary-CIFAR, and ResNet experiments in Section 4, plus noisy-feature experiments in Appendix B.

title: For Better or For Worse? Learning Minimum Variance Features With Label Augmentation

C1.justification: v2 emphasizes the negative consequence of learning low-variance spurious correlations. v3 adds a central positive claim that lower-variance hidden representations correlate with better standard-benchmark performance, framing the phenomenon as both beneficial and harmful. This substantially broadens the abstract, contribution statement, and conclusion while retaining the original theoretical separation and failure claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds a useful-latent-feature hypothesis, an explicit correlation-versus-causation caveat, an Adam/nonconvergence explanation for ERM failures, compact-support applicability qualifications, and discussion of unexplained activation-variance oscillations. Appendix C.4 interprets output variance beyond target-class variability. The standalone limitations paragraph disappears, but the lack of nonlinear optimization-dynamics analysis remains acknowledged in the theoretical discussion and Appendix B.

D1.justification: v3 supplies substantial new implementation information for synthetic data generation and ResNet training, including sample sizes, augmentations, optimizers, and depth-specific batch sizes. Reported hardware changes from P100 to A5000. A new reproducibility statement says supplementary code includes figure-generation instructions, although availability cannot be verified from the PDFs. Some explicit binary-subset counts and training details from v2 are omitted or replaced by cross-references.

E1.justification: v3 adds full multiclass CIFAR-10/100 classification without injected spurious correlations, beyond v2's modified two-class subsets. Appendices C.1-C.2 add two-dimensional and ten-dimensional synthetic datasets. The original binary CIFAR and background-permuted MNIST tasks remain; shaded MNIST becoming colored MNIST is a rename.

E2.justification: ERM with optional weight decay remains the comparator for label smoothing and Mixup. The retained experiments preserve their comparator membership. New ResNet experiments compare the same training families with shared weight decay; no additional competing algorithm is evaluated.

E3.justification: v3 introduces ResNet-18/50/101 protocols, 200-epoch AdamW training, crop/flip augmentation, activation/output-variance metrics, and separate synthetic protocols. For retained binary CIFAR, v2 specifies 100 epochs, Adam, and batch size 500; v3 instead references Section 4.1's settings but subsequently still says Adam. This ambiguously revises the documented protocol without establishing that the retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses examine activation/output-variance trajectories, target-only versus total output variance, synthetic decision boundaries, and high-variance feature weights. v3 also reports sensitivity checks involving feature scales, added noise, and adding weight decay to label smoothing/Mixup. The original weight-norm-ratio and MNIST background-shift analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report means over five training runs with one-standard-deviation uncertainty. v3 extends that convention to additional tables and plots, without changing the stated replication count or introducing seed specifications, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive numerical and qualitative results. Table 1 reports ResNet-18 CIFAR-10 test errors of 8.40, 7.96, and 5.90 for ERM+WD, ERM+WD+LS, and ERM+WD+Mixup. Appendix C adds synthetic and deeper-ResNet findings, including higher final activation variances for augmented ResNet-101 models in Table 5. v2 Figures 1-3 remain unchanged as v3 Figures 2-4; the additions are not same-setting improvements over v2.

M1.justification: The ERM/weight-decay, label-smoothing, and Mixup objectives and augmentation procedures in Section 2 remain substantively unchanged. ResNets and synthetic experiments extend the evaluation of these existing methods; no new algorithm or augmentation rule is introduced.

P1.justification: The contribution list is rewritten around a central message, the abstract and conclusion are reframed, and the experimental narrative now presents standard-benchmark benefits before spurious-correlation failures. Existing experimental descriptions are condensed and reorganized, theoretical motivation is expanded, and separate ethics and reproducibility statements are introduced.

P2.justification: v3 adds multi-panel error/variance trajectories, synthetic decision-boundary and weight-norm plots, and nine numerical tables. The original three figures are retained, resized, and renumbered within a larger set of eight figures. Conversion to the ICLR template also changes typography, title/author formatting, headers, text width, and figure placement.

R1.justification: v3 adds substantive positioning around neural collapse, citing Papyan, Kornblith, Zhou, and Guo, and discusses selective-classification findings from Zhu and Xia. Appendix B substantially expands comparisons with Chidambaram et al. (2023) and Zou et al. (2023), distinguishing population linear minimizers from patch-based neural-network training dynamics.

T1.justification: Propositions 3.9-3.10 and Appendix A.3 replace conditional variances with variances of conditional expectations: for example, Var(g(X) | Y=y) becomes Var(E[g(X) | Y=y]). For fixed conditioning values, the new terms vanish, materially weakening the written bounds. v3 also expands Corollary 3.4's proof, adds a class-balance qualification, and introduces synthetic-data Definition C.2.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially broadens v2's restricted empirical support through standard CIFAR/ResNet experiments, synthetic checks, and useful diagnostic and implementation detail. However, the revised Propositions 3.9-3.10 make their variance penalties vanish as written, and unchanged experimental plots accompany ambiguous revised training descriptions. Table 5 also qualifies the broader low-activation-variance claim. These material theoretical and reproducibility problems prevent a reliable net quality judgment despite the empirical gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work by Chidambaram and Ge. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained experiments across renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds standard CIFAR experiments with ResNets, synthetic classification experiments, and activation/output-variance analyses in Appendix C.

before.justification: v2 reports original trained-model test errors and weight-norm analyses on modified binary CIFAR tasks and background-shifted MNIST, averaged over five training runs.

title: For Better or For Worse? Learning Minimum Variance Features With Label Augmentation

C1.justification: V1 centers its contribution on running uncompressed Mixtral on 24GB GPUs with large single-batch gains over offloading systems. V2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion broaden the central claim to adaptive heterogeneous execution outperforming specialized competitors across ordinary generation, long prefills, and beam search.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of the complementary strengths of CPU-based and offloading baselines, and interprets Appendix D/E results as evidence of distribution robustness and applicability beyond Mixtral. The underlying communication/computation explanation, compression compatibility, and assumption that non-expert weights fit on the GPU remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds baseline version numbers, llama.cpp ngl settings, specific CPU models, initialization-time latency profiling, and disclosure of an AVX512_BF16 expert kernel. V1's explicit non-persistent DeepSpeed pipeline statement disappears. These are bounded changes in implementation and reproducibility documentation; the PyTorch basis and code-access URL remain.

Its exact main length grid is inconsistent: Section 4.1 specifies four input and four output lengths, while Figure 4 plots five input and three output lengths.

These substantially broaden the diagnostic evidence. The sparsity and expert-popularity analyses are retained, while microbenchmarks and hardware-dependent popularity calculations are revised.

Both retain 32 microbenchmark executions with means and standard deviations. This is a limited loss of statistical reporting, without evidence that the actual repetition counts decreased.

E6.justification: V1 reports 8.2x/10.1x speedups over Mixtral-Offloading in its two environments. V2 reports 1.26x over llama.cpp across revised environments, 11.57x for beam search, and 6.5x over DeepSpeed-MII for Phi-3.5-MoE, alongside new sensitivity and latency-breakdown results. These are new or replaced comparisons, not matched-setting performance changes. Microbenchmark and Environment 2 hit-rate results also change; Table 2's sparsity values remain identical.

M1.justification: The reported scheduling rule changes substantially. V1 Section 3.2 jointly partitions experts to minimize the maximum aggregate CPU/GPU latency; v2 Algorithm 1 independently assigns each uncached expert by comparing CPU latency against GPU computation plus weight-transfer latency. Popularity-based initial placement already existed in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, design explanation, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Design is reorganized into overview, execution strategies, algorithm, and optimizations, with explicit contribution bullets. The original sparsity and microbenchmark appendices exchange order, and new appendices D-F are added.

P2.justification: V2 adds high-level and initialization/execution diagrams, redraws v1 Figure 1 as a three-case execution diagram, and introduces an algorithm display plus multiple benchmark and diagnostic panels. Existing plots are also redesigned. The sparsity table and popularity heatmap are retained. Several v2 plot legends inconsistently call the proposed system Twiddler while captions use Fiddler.

R1.justification: V2 substantially revises positioning by acknowledging CPU-based hybrid inference, particularly llama.cpp, and distinguishing Fiddler through adaptive execution rather than CPU computation alone. Related work and motivation expand to newer MoE models, heterogeneous deployment, long-context applications, and additional inference systems.

T1.justification: V1's central min-max optimization over disjoint CPU/GPU expert sets, justified by parallel completion time, is removed. V2 substitutes an expert-wise latency inequality with separate GPU computation and transfer costs. This substantively changes the formal scheduling model, while retaining the linear-CPU and constant-GPU latency assumptions. Neither version provides an optimality proof.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's evaluation: it adds the stronger CPU-based llama.cpp comparator and tests workloads that expose different execution tradeoffs. Dataset sensitivity, a second MoE model, and latency breakdowns substantially strengthen evidence for applicability and performance. Omitted end-to-end run counts and setup/plot inconsistencies weaken reproducibility and clarity, but the broader, more relevant comparative evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Fiddler and provide readable main text, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across renumbering and reorganization, supporting comparison despite the substantial revision.

E5.justification: Appendix A retains 32 workload executions, one per Mixtral layer, with averages and standard deviations. Figure 7's uncertainty display and the other statistical reporting remain unchanged.

E6.justification: The numerical tables and plotted results are retained, including the reported 1.26-fold single-batch and 11.57-fold beam-search speedups. Changes to figure legends and rendering do not change result entries or trends.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Algorithm 1 retain the same CPU/GPU execution selection, expert placement and specialized CPU kernel. The changed plot labels identify the same proposed system.

P1.justification: Plot legends change the system name from Twiddler to Fiddler, matching the existing text. The arXiv version/date stamp changes; prose, headings and document organization remain identical.

P2.justification: Figures 4-6 and 9-12 receive corrected system-name legends. Appendix plots also show small typography, spacing and styling adjustments, including a different green shade in Figure 9. No figures or tables are added, removed or relocated.

R1.justification: Section 2, the citations and the bibliography are unchanged, as is the positioning against offloading, CPU-based inference and model-compression approaches.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 retains the same constant GPU-latency and linear CPU-latency assumptions and execution comparison. No mathematical definitions, derivations or proofs are added or revised.

improvement.justification: Replacing Twiddler with Fiddler in Figures 4-6 and 9-12 resolves a repeated inconsistency between the plots and text, making result attribution clearer. This is a limited presentation improvement; the scientific methods, evidence and conclusions remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Fiddler and contain complete, readable main text and Appendices A-F. Their text, algorithms, tables and figures support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experimental results in Section 4 and Appendices A-F.

before.justification: v2 reports original inference benchmarks in Section 4, plus microbenchmarks, sparsity analysis, dataset sensitivity and additional model evaluations in the appendices.

title: Fiddler: CPU-GPU Orchestration for Fast Inference of Mixture-of-Experts Models

C1.justification: v1 presents a general program for zero-shot ODE-system inference, with imputation as an application. v2 makes zero-shot imputation of hidden ODE solutions the central contribution, explicitly separating point-wise and temporal missingness, and adds phase-portrait reconstruction from one observed coordinate as a headline capability. Arbitrary-dimensional application without downstream fine-tuning remains a core claim.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the explanation of applicability and failure. It distinguishes local interpolation from global information needed across temporal gaps, explains normalization problems for nearly constant noisy signals, and identifies sparse-coordinate failures of channel independence using PhysioNet. It also discusses window-resolution tradeoffs, rapid-derivative failures and errors introduced by PCA. v1's limitations mainly concerned high-frequency dynamics and its approximately 32-point context requirement.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents normalization and output rescaling, detailed temporal-module architecture and optimization, dataset masks and preprocessing, and LatentODE search grids, training schedules and runtimes. It also reports high-dimensional inference costs and describes a reproduction script. The availability statement changes from pretrained models being online in v1 to forthcoming online availability in v2, although supplementary code and weights are still asserted.

E1.justification: v2 adds air-quality, traffic, solar-power, electricity and healthcare evaluations, including PhysioNet2012 and PhysioNet2019 in Appendix F. It also adds single-coordinate phase-portrait reconstruction and four synthetic regression tasks. ODEBench, Lorenz, motion capture and Navier-Stokes remain; the separate ETTh2, ETTm1 and ETTm2 interpolation demonstrations from v1 disappear.

E2.justification: Reported comparisons expand substantially to include Neural ODE Processes, BRITS, SAITS, GP-VAE, CSDI, BayOTIDE and numerous additional imputation methods. Cubic splines join the retained Lorenz comparison, while motion-capture comparisons include LatentODE, npODE, GPDM and VGPLVM. ODEFormer, ODEFormer-opt and PySR remain in v2 Table 9; their move out of the main comparison is not removal.

E3.justification: The default local-model training dataset changes from 8M to 2M trajectories, with revised sampling distributions and a separate temporal-gap training dataset. Evaluation adds window sweeps and derivative scoring. Lorenz corruption is described as additive rather than v1's multiplicative noise. Motion capture and Navier-Stokes expand from single examples to 43 and 61 trajectories, with PCA and direct-space evaluation. v2 inconsistently states minimum contexts of four and eight observations.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled studies of parameter count, training-set size, BiLSTM versus transformer encoding, context limits, temporal-gap sizes and training trends (Tables 4-8). It also studies window-count sensitivity, including the Lorenz sweep in Figure 8, and PCA versus direct-space imputation. v1's explicit FIM denoising comparison with and without Savitzky-Golay filtering is not retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report ODEBench variation across ten corruption realizations and trajectory-level standard deviations. v2 additionally displays predictive derivative uncertainty in Figure 3 and identifies imported TSI-Bench baseline deviations as coming from five training rounds (Tables 21-22). These extend uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in repeated FIM training runs.

E6.justification: Existing scores are replaced and substantial new results appear. At 50% subsampling and noise 0.05, v1 Table 1 reports R2 accuracy of 80.2 ± 1.7 for FIM and 79.6 ± 1.5 for FIM-N; v2 Table 9 reports 83.7 ± 0.7 for four-window FIM-ℓ and 91.6 ± 1.9 for sixteen windows. These involve revised configurations, not controlled version-to-version gains. New results include derivative errors, quantitative imputation comparisons and clinical-data failures.

M1.justification: v2 adds a learned temporal-gap imputation module above the frozen local estimator FIM-ℓ: a transformer processes local embeddings and scale statistics to predict the missing interval's representation, followed by boundary-conditioned integration (Section 3.2.2; Appendix C). This substantially extends v1's upsampling and window-composition approach. The stated local reconstruction objective also changes from squared to absolute error.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and method narrative are extensively rewritten around imputation. Experiments are reorganized into phase-portrait reconstruction and two missingness categories; limitations are integrated into the conclusion, and a reproducibility statement is added. The appendices are substantially reorganized into model-specific documentation and task-specific evaluations, beyond simply appending new experiments.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. v2 introduces a graphical-model/architecture schematic, phase portraits, derivative-uncertainty panels and a window-sensitivity plot. Lorenz plots are redesigned to include derivatives, and tables become extensive window/dimension breakdowns and benchmark matrices, including landscape appendix tables. v1's ETT panels and Navier-Stokes image demonstration are removed.

R1.justification: The positioning shifts from ODE identification and analogies with language models toward amortized inference and time-series imputation. v2 adds discussion and citations for Stuhlmüller, Paige and Wood, zero-shot learning, channel-independent modeling, and major imputation families and benchmarks. Much of v1's neural-ODE training and transfer-learning discussion is removed. ODEFormer's preprint-to-publication update represents the same cited work.

T1.justification: The path-wise ODE reduction and overlapping-window interpolation are retained. v2 adds derivations for rescaling derivatives and variances (Appendix B.1) and constructing continuous solutions across a missing interval (Appendix C.6), while removing v1's alternative kernel-operator formulation. These are localized mathematical developments rather than a new theoretical guarantee.

improvement.justification: v1's imputation evidence was largely illustrative. v2 supplies an explicit temporal-gap method, broad quantitative comparisons, controlled ablations, detailed implementation information and concrete failure analyses, substantially strengthening validation and reproducibility. Reporting problems remain: minimum-context specifications conflict, Table 23's Navier-Stokes RMSE contradicts the claimed benefit of avoiding PCA, and Table 22 shows linear interpolation outperforming FIM on some datasets highlighted favorably in Table 2. These qualifications limit particular claims but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in evidential support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FIM research, retaining the synthetic-training framework, local ODE estimator and several benchmarks. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison despite substantial changes in title, scope and organization.

after.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction, derivative-estimation and imputation results, including extensive benchmark comparisons and architecture, training-data and windowing ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original FIM experiments on ODEBench and Lorenz trajectories, alongside motion-capture and Navier-Stokes imputation demonstrations and ETT interpolation.

title: Zero-shot Imputation with Foundation Inference Models for Dynamical Systems

C1.justification: The introduction narrows contribution (ii) by removing the assertion that FIM outperforms target-trained state-of-the-art models on the 63 ODE series. The central claims of zero-shot reconstruction and imputation across diverse, high-dimensional datasets remain.

C2.justification: Appendix I adds interpretations concerning fine-tuning feasibility, cross-scale retention and noise robustness, alongside a warning about fitting noise and motivation for a future emission model. Section 4.1 also softens the attribution of rapid Rössler acceleration changes to being outside the training distribution from definite to likely.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a public access link and states that pretrained models, the repository and tutorials are available, replacing the earlier release promise and supplementary-access description. Appendix C.5 newly specifies architectures for existing size and encoder ablations; Appendix I documents fine-tuning hyperparameters.

E1.justification: The training and evaluation domains and tasks are retained. Appendix I reuses the existing Lorenz-system data; its fine-tuning procedures do not introduce different dataset or task coverage. Newly discussed meta-learning applications are cited examples, not additional experiments.

E2.justification: The established benchmark comparator rosters remain unchanged. Table 25 adds a limited within-FIM comparison between pretrained, noisy-target fine-tuned and clean-target fine-tuned models. The meta-learning methods newly discussed in Appendix A are not empirically evaluated.

E3.justification: Appendix I introduces a two-epoch fine-tuning protocol with learning rate 1e-6, four training windows and all Lorenz coordinates. It compares noisy and clean reconstruction targets and evaluates multiple window counts. Existing benchmark protocols are retained.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendices E–J report original deep-ensemble experiments for out-of-distribution and misclassification detection, including numerical results in Tables 2–9.

before.justification: V1 contains theoretical derivations and conceptual illustrations, including Appendix A, but no original experimental or data-analysis results.

title: From Risk to Uncertainty: Generating Predictive Uncertainty Measures via Bayesian Estimation

V3 adds the conclusion that energy-based measures fit the framework, while its introduction more explicitly credits earlier work for the underlying risk decomposition. These refine and extend the retained central contribution.

T1.justification: V3 adds central-prediction derivations and the zero-one degeneracy discussion (Appendix L), additional decomposition identities (Appendix F), energy and logit-covariance identities (Section 4.2; Appendix G), and closed-form Beta-Bernoulli uncertainty expressions (Appendix M). improvement.justification: V3 better substantiates the framework through central-prediction and energy derivations, closer engagement with prior work, per-configuration variability reporting and explicit sensitivity analyses. E3.justification: The single illustrative evaluation protocol is removed: synthetic problems with n = 100 and d = 5, varying robustness radius, and population-risk estimation using 100,000 samples. No replacement experimental protocol is introduced.

Section 3.2 strengthens comparison with the already-cited Regularization via Mass Transportation. The main positioning relative to Azizian, Iutzeler and Malick remains.

However, new Proposition F.1 applies Theorem E.1's robust-risk comparison at rho >= rho_crit + alpha/sqrt(n), outside its stated range rho <= rho_crit/4 - beta/sqrt(n). This unresolved gap in a newly added proof prevents a reliable net quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Wasserstein generalization work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures and Appendices A–F are readable, allowing additions, removals and relocated material to be distinguished.

before.justification: v1 Figure 1 reports original results from 500 synthetic logistic-regression instances. Section 3 describes the experiment and estimates how frequently the generalization bound holds.

title: Universal generalization guarantees for Wasserstein distributionally robust models

E2.justification: Neither version reports evaluated baseline comparisons. Expanded discussion of earlier theoretical work does not introduce experimental comparators.

E3.justification: Neither version specifies an empirical evaluation protocol. Sample-size conditions and radius choices concern mathematical guarantees, not experimental settings.

E4.justification: Neither version contains empirical ablations, robustness tests, or case studies. The analytical counterexample in v2 Proposition F.3 is retained as v3 Proposition F.4.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, empirical uncertainty estimates, or significance tests. The probability bounds are theoretical statements, not experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: No empirical result entries are added, removed, or revised. The existing main bounds and linear-model constants are retained; the new formal characterization belongs to the theoretical changes.

M1.justification: The standard and doubly regularized WDRO objectives, loss formulations, and dual representations are retained. No algorithm, model component, or training or inference procedure changes.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work by the same authors. The complete main texts, equations, two figures, and Appendices A–F are readable and support reliable matching across versions.

before.justification: v2 reports theoretical guarantees, proofs, and analytical examples. Its two figures are proof schematics; no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes appear in the appendices.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's four contributions, and discussion retain the same central claims: FedDistill's resilience, the LMA/CPA attacks, ExpGuard's defence, and HIPS obfuscation. Additional experiments support these contributions without redefining them.

E1.justification: Both versions use synthetic NetLogo forest-fire evolution and the Next Day Wildfire Spread dataset, retaining the forecasting tasks, observational variables and stochasticity levels. Appendix F also introduces quantitative comparisons involving AR-NCA and multilayer/bottleneck convLSTMs; v1's bottleneck comparison was qualitative.

E3.justification: v2 adds all 25 combinations of five training and five testing S-Levels, extends this design across architectures, and varies evaluation sample counts at timestep 59 (Figure 6; Appendices F and H). Table 3 additionally evaluates ECE within Dice-overlap strata. The original 700/300 simulation split and 10-frame observation/50-frame prediction setup remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 expands v1's limited stochasticity-mismatch demonstration into systematic cross-level and cross-architecture tests of ECE's discrimination. It adds sample-size sensitivity analysis and a real-data model-selection case study. The original mismatch experiment and macro-variance analyses are retained in Appendices G and E.

E5.justification: v2 removes the 95% confidence intervals accompanying Dice-stratified results in v1 Table 3, while retaining the bin supports and existing Monte Carlo/standard-deviation reporting. E6.justification: v2 adds cross-level heatmap results, architecture comparisons, convergence results and stratified ECE scores. These unexplained revisions do not establish performance improvements.

M1.justification: The simulator, micro/macro framework, convLSTM-CA architecture, BCE training and ECE formula remain unchanged. v2 introduces the limited Conv-CA architectural adaptation, which removes Conv-AE's spatial bottleneck (Section 5.1; Appendix D.1).

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are substantially rewritten around two explicit research questions and the new process-fidelity terminology. P2.justification: v2 adds cross-level and architecture heatmaps, convergence plots and a model-ranking table. Table 3 becomes a compact single-column table with ECE. These are substantial display and layout changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted references for AR-NCA, U-Net, SegFormer, model-ranking conflicts and broader physical-system applications. However, v2 removes Table 3's confidence intervals and strengthens process-identification claims while calling the per-pixel Statistic-GT a joint distribution, without resolving the marginal/joint distinction acknowledged in v1. These central validity and uncertainty-reporting concerns coexist with better testing, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same wildfire-evaluation study, with matching authors, framework, datasets and retained experiments. All main-text and appendix pages were readable, including figures, tables and equations, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds cross-stochasticity evaluations, architecture comparisons, model rankings and sample-size analyses in Figure 6, Table 4 and Appendices F and H.

before.justification: v1 reports original forest-fire simulations, convLSTM evaluations, calibration analyses and Next Day Wildfire Spread results in Sections 4–5 and Appendices C–D.

title: Has the Deep Neural Network learned the Stochastic Process? An Evaluation Viewpoint

C1.justification: The central proposal to evaluate stochastic-process fidelity using ECE remains. However, v3's abstract and introduction newly claim a formal necessary-condition result and explicitly state that low calibration error is not sufficient, qualifying v2's broader characterization of ECE. Statistic-GT itself already appears in v2.

C2.justification: Beyond v2's sample-size and discrimination caveats, v3 explicitly acknowledges that calibration ignores dependencies and cannot establish full process fidelity. It explains limited discrimination through the excluded refinement term, discusses heterogeneous agents and unobservable mixed stochasticity levels in real wildfire data, and identifies validation beyond wildfire as future work. These substantially qualify interpretation and applicability.

D1.justification: v3 Section 4.1 explicitly assigns 1,000 simulations and 700 training simulations to each S-Level and identifies the main ConvLSTM as single-layer. This clarifies existing experimental documentation rather than demonstrating larger datasets or changed architecture. Kernel sizes, temporal windows and loss remain documented as before.

E1.justification: Both evaluate synthetic forest-fire evolution and Next Day Wildfire Spread, retaining the stochasticity levels and forecasting tasks. Added calibration and convergence checks reuse existing data settings. Epidemic and rumor propagation remain discussion or future-work topics.

E2.justification: Recall is removed from the reported cross-S-Level, long-horizon and architecture-comparison plots: v2 Figures 6, 7 and 14 become v3 Figures 5, 6 and 13. MSE is also dropped from the sample-size convergence comparison. Some captions still mention removed panels. The five NDWS model comparators remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v3 adds fixed training at S-Level 10 to the sample-size convergence evaluation and evaluates a perfect Statistic-GT predictor. Its written calibration definition also permits a representative bin probability, often the midpoint, whereas v2 specifies the mean forecast within each bin. Whether the implemented calculation changed is unstated; retained training splits and prediction windows are unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds checks of perfect-predictor calibration and convergence under mismatched stochasticity levels in Appendices E.6 and E.4. It removes v2's cross-S-Level macrovariance boxplots and steady-state histogram, and reduces NDWS qualitative examples from five to two. The main architecture, long-horizon and overlap-stratified analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both use 1,000-realization Monte Carlo characterization, metric standard deviations and shaded convergence curves. No changed repeated-training scheme, seed reporting, confidence-interval definition or significance-testing procedure is specified. Additional curves do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: The NDWS tables are numerically identical: v2 Tables 3–4 become v3 Tables 1–2, retaining U-Net's AUC-PR of 0.3302 and AR-NCA's ECE of 0.0012. Retained main cross-S-Level heatmap values also match. New results include near-zero perfect-predictor ECE and mismatched-training convergence curves; several metric panels, supplementary distributions and qualitative examples are removed.

M1.justification: The NetLogo interaction rules, ConvLSTM-CA and Conv-CA architectures, BCE training, autoregressive forecasting and use of ECE remain. The revised theoretical treatment and additional controls do not establish a changed prediction algorithm or model.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and substantial main-text passages are rewritten. Evaluation theory becomes Section 3.4, wildfire literature moves into Appendix B, the macrovariance experiment moves to Appendix E.1, and discussion and conclusion are consolidated. Earlier supplementary sections E–H are reorganized under a unified Additional Results section.

P2.justification: v3 replaces the two-column main layout with a single-column format, introduces the conceptual Figure 1, redraws and condenses multiple plots, relocates existing figures to appendices and adds perfect-predictor plots. Several panels and case-study rows disappear. Captions for Figures 5 and 13 still reference absent Recall panels, creating presentation inconsistencies.

R1.justification: v3 adds Blattenberger and Lad's calibration/refinement reference and Shi et al.'s ConvLSTM reference. It removes Stephenson et al., Jin et al. and Wainwright and Ellis, alongside shortening the corresponding decomposition, video-prediction and cosmology discussion. The broader wildfire and stochastic-evaluation positioning remains.

T1.justification: v3 Section 3.4.1 adds a central necessary-condition argument based on estimating conditional positive frequencies and explains why ignored dependencies prevent calibration from being sufficient for process fidelity. v2 primarily motivates ECE through Brier decomposition without this argument. v3 also presents a binned calibration/refinement decomposition and corrects the written S-Level formula for the stated percentage convention.

improvement.justification: v3 makes the evaluation target clearer and adds an important necessary-versus-sufficient qualification, supported by perfect-predictor and convergence checks. These provide a modest interpretive improvement over v2. The gain is limited because broad claims that ECE exclusively evaluates process fidelity remain, some comparative evidence is removed, and stale captions reduce consistency; the principal benchmark results are unchanged.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title and format, both PDFs describe the same wildfire-evaluation study. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocations and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains the original synthetic and real-world experimental results and adds perfect-predictor calibration and mismatched-training convergence results in Appendix E.

before.justification: v2 reports original NetLogo simulations, trained-DNN experiments, metric sensitivity analyses and comparisons on the Next Day Wildfire Spread dataset, including supplementary results.

title: Has the Deep Neural Network learned the Stochastic Process? An Evaluation Viewpoint

C1.justification: The central scientific claims remain: Statistic-GT motivates F2SP, conventional metrics do not exclusively measure it, and ECE provides a necessary but insufficient test. The additional domains support applicability beyond wildfire already proposed in v3, rather than replacing the core contribution.

C2.justification: v3 makes metric prioritization application-dependent; v4 Section 5, Appendix G.4 and Appendix H recommend checking ECE first and rejecting models with high ECE. MSE is reframed from separate Fidelity to Statistic to balancing F2R and F2SP. v4 also adds substantive qualifications concerning simulation realism, regression and univariate extensions, and NDWS's next-day-only horizon.

D1.justification: v4 adds a code-repository pointer, generation details and parameters for the two new simulators, and Appendix H's instructions for batching predictions, computing per-time-step metrics and averaging scores across time. It also identifies metric-library implementations. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to the retained training implementation.

E1.justification: v4 adds evaluated synthetic host-pathogen and stock-market systems alongside the retained forest-fire and NDWS tasks. These introduce competing-state dynamics and different prediction targets, substantially extending coverage beyond wildfire (Table 1 and Figure 3).

The NDWS model set and architectural variants are retained.

E3.justification: The added domains introduce ten-frame observation and twenty-frame prediction protocols, with three S-Levels per domain. The existing forest-fire protocol retains ten observed and fifty predicted frames, five S-Levels, and the 700/300 training/testing split. These are adaptations for new experiments rather than documented revisions to the retained experiments.

E4.justification: v4 Figure 16 adds ECE to the macro-variance sensitivity analysis, and Figure 17 adds MSE convergence alongside the existing ECE sample-size analysis. The architectural comparisons, stochastic-mismatch experiments, long-horizon tests and perfect-predictor calibration analyses already appeared in v3 and remain present.

E5.justification: The existing 1,000-simulation Monte Carlo analyses, standard-deviation reporting and shaded convergence plots are retained. Additional curves extend these reporting practices; neither PDF establishes a change in training-run counts, seed reporting, confidence-interval procedures or significance testing.

E6.justification: v4 adds numerical matrices for two synthetic domains and additional evaluation metrics, plus ECE sensitivity and MSE convergence results. These substantially expand the reported evidence. Retained wildfire heatmaps and NDWS tables preserve their results, including U-Net AUC-PR 0.3302 and AR-NCA ECE 0.0012 in v3 Table 2 and v4 Table 7.

M1.justification: The ConvLSTM-CA and Conv-CA architectures, BCE training, autoregressive forecasting, and binned ECE calculation are retained. Applications to additional target states and expanded evaluation guidance do not establish a changed prediction or metric-computation algorithm.

P1.justification: The title changes from 'A Wildfire Perspective' to 'An Evaluation Viewpoint', and the introduction, contributions and explanations are extensively rewritten around complex systems. Related work is reorganized, macro-variable analysis and NDWS rankings move into appendices, and notation and practical-guide sections reshape the document's narrative.

P2.justification: v4 redraws the framework diagram, expands the main heatmap into a three-domain comparison, adds simulation, metric-comparison and convergence displays, and introduces notation and guidance tables. The NDWS stratification table gains color encoding. Numerous retained figures and tables are relocated, including the long-horizon plots and model-ranking table.

R1.justification: Related work expands from predominantly wildfire and video prediction to agent-based complex systems, calibration methods, segmentation forecasting and metric-sensitivity research. New Section 6 and Appendix C explicitly position the work against calibration studies and low-dimensional scoring-rule analyses, with additions such as Guo et al. and Pinson and Tastu.

T1.justification: Section 3.4.1 replaces the brief unbiased/consistent-estimator argument with a displayed expectation derivation for a perfect predictor. The formal setup also generalizes binary fire indicators to target-state indicators in discrete-state systems. The necessary-but-not-sufficient conclusion and Brier decomposition remain; this is a limited mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: The additional competing-state benchmarks and broader metric comparisons strengthen empirical support beyond v3's wildfire study, while simulation and aggregation details improve reproducibility. However, the new practical guide sometimes treats low ECE as establishing that the stochastic process was learned (Table 8), despite the retained necessary-but-insufficient result in Section 3.4.1. The evidence and usability improve, but this stronger interpretation limits the overall gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Statistic-GT/F2SP evaluation research. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, including equations, tables and figures, and retained material can be matched across substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v4 retains the original wildfire experiments and reports additional synthetic host-pathogen and stock-market experiments, metric comparisons, and convergence results.

before.justification: v3 reports original neural-network experiments on simulated forest fires, NDWS model evaluations, and supplementary sensitivity and convergence analyses.

title: Has the Deep Neural Network learned the Stochastic Process? An Evaluation Viewpoint

C1.justification: The contribution set expands to include HiZOO-L and preservation of predictive performance with memory close to MeZO. The highlighted SST-2 claim changes from up to 30-fold step reduction to an eightfold forward-pass speedup and reported 1.55% accuracy improvement averaged across models. The original novelty claim about Hessian-informed zeroth-order LLM fine-tuning remains.

C2.justification: v2 interprets HiZOO-L's similar performance as suggesting noise in the Hessian estimates and motivates further compression (Appendix D.2). It also uses measured per-step costs to justify forward-pass counts as a runtime proxy. The memory limitation receives more explicit treatment, while v1's general recommendation of smoothing scale 1e-6 is removed.

D1.justification: The code-access URL and existing hyperparameter grids remain unchanged. v2 adds low-rank implementation pseudocode and timing details covering 80GB A100 hardware, lack of NV-Link, batch sizes and measurement length. Some earlier disclosures disappear, including Table 4's explicit classification sample count and task-specific tuning configurations.

E1.justification: The NLP datasets, task requirements and three synthetic test functions are retained. Phi-2 and Llama3 introduce model configurations on existing tasks. The missing many-shot RoBERTa table changes result reporting, rather than establishing different dataset or task coverage.

E3.justification: v2 adds Phi-2 (2.7B), Llama3 (8B), controlled A100 timing measurements and forward-pass-based efficiency comparisons. Toy convergence comparisons explicitly use a loss threshold of 0.1. Table 4 now labels objectives as F1, whereas v1's caption specified classification accuracy; unchanged scores do not establish reruns. Existing RoBERTa/OPT hyperparameter grids and training budgets remain.

E4.justification: New comparisons test whether curvature compression preserves accuracy and convergence, using HiZOO-L versus HiZOO on OPT-13B and Llama3 (Table 5, Figures 12–14), alongside additional efficiency analysis. The SNLI smoothing-scale sweep expands to include 1, 1e-2 and 1e-4. Existing multisampling and Hessian-term-omission ablations are retained.

E5.justification: The retained RoBERTa accuracy table still reports means and standard deviations across five runs. No additional training-run counts, seed studies, confidence intervals or significance tests are introduced. The new timing average over 100 steps specifies measurement sampling, rather than independent training repetitions or uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds model, HiZOO-L and timing results, while removing v1's many-shot RoBERTa Table 7 and separate few-shot PEFT rows. Retained OPT scores also change: HiZOO's OPT-13B MultiRC result changes from 55.5 to 61.3 (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 8). OPT-30B MeZO-prefix RTE changes from 72.6 to 66.1, reversing its ranking against HiZOO's unchanged 68.6 (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 9).

M1.justification: v2 introduces HiZOO-L, which stores row/column factors of curvature information and reconstructs preconditioners for perturbations and updates (Appendix D.2, Algorithm 3). This substantially extends v1's diagonal-state method. HiZOO-multi largely corresponds to v1's existing multisample variant, although its pseudocode now includes the preconditioning factor in projected gradients.

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution list are rewritten, the update procedure precedes the Hessian estimator, convergence analysis moves into Methods, and toy visualization moves before the LLM experiments. Appendices are reorganized around test functions, variants, consolidated model experiments and timing. The generic impact statement is removed.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. v2 adds an optimizer schematic, benchmark bars, compression plots and a timing table; existing tables gain averages or combine PEFT rows. Numerous loss plots use forward-pass axes, toy results are redistributed between main text and appendix, and the many-shot and hardware-capacity tables disappear.

R1.justification: v2 adds Adafactor as motivation for HiZOO-L, plus citations concerning QLoRA, GaLore, LISA, FlashAttention and Phi models. The optimizer literature review and central positioning relative to MeZO remain largely unchanged. These citations do not establish additional evaluated baselines.

Smoothness and convergence statements are also rewritten using minibatch losses. The principal proof structure, Gaussian-moment lemma and O(epsilon^-4) convergence rate remain.

improvement.justification: HiZOO-L addresses a concrete weakness: v2 Table 10 reports 29GB versus 53GB for standard HiZOO on OPT-13B, with similar accuracy in Table 5. Measured timings and additional model evaluations strengthen the practical evidence. These gains are tempered by missing many-shot and separate PEFT results and new reporting errors: for example, Table 1 lists an FT average of 74.9 although its entries average 73.05. The net improvement is therefore limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HiZOO research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds Phi-2/Llama3 evaluations, HiZOO-L comparisons and measured per-step timings.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-model fine-tuning results, synthetic optimization experiments, ablations and memory measurements.

title: Second-Order Fine-Tuning without Pain for LLMs: A Hessian Informed Zeroth-Order Optimizer

C1.justification: The abstract and introductory contributions retain the same claims: formalizing informed meta-learning, introducing INP as a proof of concept, and demonstrating potential data-efficiency and robustness benefits. The added failure studies qualify applicability without redefining these core contributions.

C2.justification: Section 5 expands the general expressiveness caveat into specific, empirically examined limitations involving insufficient training tasks, increasing knowledge complexity, and spurious correlations. F.2–F.4 explain failures through overfitting the relationship between knowledge and data. Section 3.4 also removes the general expectation that predictions without knowledge should perform no worse than NP.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies a 0.3 knowledge-masking rate for sinusoidal regression, identifies 1000 training tasks for the original illustrative experiment, and discloses 60 evaluation tasks per classification setting. Hardware and optimizer details are relocated but unchanged, as are the code and generated-text availability statements.

E1.justification: All original datasets and application domains remain. Appendix F.4 adds a distinct synthetic scenario with correlated training parameters and independent test parameters, extending the earlier frequency-distribution shift experiment. F.2–F.3 otherwise retain the existing regression task.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain the same NP and informed/uninformed INP comparisons. The added experiments also compare INP with NP; the knowledge-complexity variants are controlled configurations of INP, not newly introduced competing methods.

title: Towards Automated Knowledge Integration From Human-Interpretable Representations

title: Signature Kernel Conditional Independence Tests in Causal Discovery for Stochastic Processes

title: RNNs are not Transformers (Yet):  The Key Bottleneck on In-Context Retrieval

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central claims: CoT improves RNN expressiveness but leaves a retrieval bottleneck, while retrieval augmentation or one Transformer layer closes the representation gap. Hotpot-QA supplies additional empirical support for these retained claims.

C2.justification: v4 explicitly qualifies Theorem 4.6: RNNs can retrieve within short contexts, with supported context length limited by state size. Section 6.2 also discusses instruction-following differences and context length as alternative explanations for observed performance.

D1.justification: New Appendix B discloses a server with eight A100 GPUs and an estimated reproduction time within two days. Its IsTree embeddings, optimizer, sample budgets, and learning rates were already documented in v3's Section 6; the code-access link is unchanged.

E1.justification: v4 adds natural-language, multi-document reasoning on Hotpot-QA to the retained synthetic IsTree coverage. It evaluates both randomly ordered paragraphs and a scenario placing supporting paragraphs last.

E2.justification: Section 6.2 adds a distinct pretrained comparison suite: Phi-1.5 1.3B and its distilled Mamba and Transformer-Mamba hybrid counterparts from Bick et al. (2024). The existing LLaMA, Mamba, and single-layer-hybrid IsTree comparison remains.

E3.justification: The new Hotpot-QA protocol uses four-shot CoT, 350 validation examples selected for joint correctness with two supporting paragraphs, and paragraph counts of 2, 4, 6, and 8. It also controls paragraph ordering. The reported IsTree settings are retained.

E4.justification: Section 6.2 adds retrieval-difficulty sensitivity analysis and a control for context length: the same paragraph sets are evaluated with supporting paragraphs placed last. This supplies a new test of whether degradation reflects retrieval demands rather than length alone.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests. Figure 6 continues the existing practice of reporting point estimates without uncertainty.

E6.justification: The IsTree results in Figures 2 and 5 are unchanged. New Figure 6 reports Hotpot-QA accuracy of approximately 0.75 for Transformer, 0.67 for hybrid, and 0.53 for RNN with eight randomly ordered paragraphs; placing supporting paragraphs last substantially reduces the losses.

M1.justification: The regular-expression retrieval procedure, proposed single-Transformer-layer hybrid, and Algorithms 1 and 2 remain unchanged. The additional pretrained models are evaluation choices, rather than revisions to the proposed methods.

P1.justification: The introduction, theory explanations, and several theorem statements receive targeted rewrites. Section 6 gains synthetic and natural-language subsections, training details move to Appendix B, and proofs become Appendix C. The overall narrative and most proof prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v4 adds the two-panel Hotpot-QA plot in Figure 6, changes Figure 4's hybrid label to 'Attention + MLP,' and clarifies Figure 5's caption. Existing IsTree plots are retained, with ordinary pagination and layout reflow elsewhere.

R1.justification: v4 adds references to xLSTM, Jamba, Samba, and recent Mamba-hybrid research, plus sources for Phi-1.5, distilled models, and Hotpot-QA. These update architectural relevance and experiment provenance while preserving the existing positioning against retrieval, CoT, and streaming-complexity research.

T1.justification: Section 3 replaces the formal regular-RNN conditions with a constant-size characterization, and Theorem 4.1 narrows its stated class accordingly while retaining the term 'regular.' Appendix proofs largely remain unchanged; other theorem revisions mainly regroup existing guarantees or reformulate parameter-bit counts.

improvement.justification: The Hotpot-QA experiment and paragraph-order control strengthen the retrieval-bottleneck argument beyond v3's synthetic validation. The applicability qualification and hardware disclosure also help. The overall gain is limited by the selected 350-example evaluation, absent uncertainty estimates, and reduced formal clarity from removing the regular-RNN definition while retaining its use.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, figures, equations, and complete appendices support comparison; v3's proof Appendix B maps to Appendix C in v4.

after.justification: v4 retains the original IsTree experiments and adds original Hotpot-QA evaluations in Section 6.2 and Figure 6.

before.justification: Section 6 and Figures 2 and 5 report original IsTree experiments comparing Transformer, Mamba, and hybrid models with and without CoT and retrieval.

title: A Theoretical Analysis of Self-Supervised Learning for Vision Transformers

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand from explaining masked reconstruction to claiming convergence guarantees and contrasting learned attention patterns for both MAE and CL. The central contribution now includes CL's global attention collapse even under mild feature imbalance.

C2.justification: v3 extends the existing MAE interpretation with a mechanism for CL collapse: global features receive larger initial gradients, and learning them suffices for the contrastive objective without position-specific local reconstruction. It also explains the CL-specific embedding simplification and introduction of noisy data.

D1.justification: For the newly analyzed CL procedure, v3 supplies parameter prescriptions including noise variance σ0²=1/d, temperature τ=O(1/log d), and regularization conditions in Appendix B. These add theoretical setup details; the retained empirical implementation and code/data-access disclosures are unchanged.

E1.justification: Empirical coverage remains the attention analysis of ImageNet-1K-pretrained vision transformers on the same 152 example images. The new noisy contrastive-learning distribution is a theoretical assumption, not an experimentally evaluated dataset or scenario.

E2.justification: The attention-diversity comparison retains MAE, MoCo v3, DINO, and DeiT. Figure 1 retains the same MAE, MoCo, and DINO attention maps. The newly formulated theoretical CL model is not added as an empirical comparator.

E3.justification: v2 Section 6 and v3 Section 7 retain ViT-B/16, its 12 final-layer attention heads, 152 images, top-10 attended patches, and the same coordinate-distance metric. Changing the patch-grid notation from P to N does not change the protocol.

E4.justification: The illustrative attention maps and per-head diversity analysis are retained. Neither version adds or removes empirical ablations, robustness tests, or sensitivity studies; the new contrastive-learning analyses are mathematical derivations.

E5.justification: Both versions use the same boxplots to describe variation across images. There are no changes to repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance testing. The new theoretical probability bounds are not uncertainty estimates for empirical results.

E6.justification: Figure 1's attention maps and the attention-diversity plot in v2 Figure 2/v3 Figure 3 are unchanged. The displayed distributions and finding that MAE has greater attention diversity are retained, with no added or revised empirical result entries.

M1.justification: v3 adds an analyzed contrastive-learning transformer with position-to-content attention, average-pooled outputs, masked positive pairs, stop-gradient handling, and a regularized contrastive objective (Section 2.4). v2 specifies only the masked-reconstruction model and objective, which v3 retains.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around the two SSL objectives. v2 Appendix A becomes the main-text proof overview in v3 Section 5; v2 Appendices B–G are consolidated into Appendix A. Related work and experiments exchange order.

These directly affect support for the added convergence claim, preventing a reliable net quality judgment from the supplied PDFs.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title and expanded theoretical scope, the authors, retained MAE framework, proofs, and experiments establish that these are versions of the same work. Both PDFs, including their figures, equations, and complete appendices, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 7 retains the original attention-diversity analysis and its results, now displayed in Figure 3. Retained empirical results still qualify.

before.justification: Section 6 reports an original attention-diversity analysis of four pretrained ViT-B/16 models across 152 images, with results in Figure 2.

title: A Theoretical Analysis of Self-Supervised Learning for Vision Transformers

C2.justification: v2 develops a decision-boundary interpretation of reliable and unreliable regions, distinguishes low ECE from effective failure rejection, and explains gradient stopping and conflicting single-head losses. title: Towards Calibrated Deep Clustering Network

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction narrow the headline calibration advantage from approximately 10× to 5× on average; the conclusion similarly reduces its stated factor. The central contributions concerning dual-head calibration, confidence-aware selection, initialization, and improved clustering remain.

C2.justification: New discussion explains mini-cluster penalty strength, SSL thresholding failures, initialization-related stability, computational tradeoffs, and applicability to other clustering models and OOD rejection. The explicit v2 limitation that cluster count must be known is removed, although v3 still assumes predefined clusters.

D1.justification: v3 adds a CDC code-access link, identifies the solo-learn library, describes K-means++ initialization and a PyTorch implementation, and reports parameter counts, runtime, and memory in Table 7.
