E2.justification: Appendix C.1 adds evaluations of FlexMatch and FreeMatch thresholding both directly and integrated into CDC, plus CDC augmented with Gradient Synchronization Filter and Prototype Proximity Filter. These introduce substantive alternatives to CDC's sample-selection strategy. Comparator membership in the original benchmark tables is retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include transferring ImageNet-10 hyperparameters to larger ImageNet subsets with ResNet-50, evaluating OOD detection through maximum-softmax scores, and applying CDC for 100 epochs after SCAN or SeCu. The original six-benchmark splits, main training budgets, and metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds batch-size/mini-cluster sensitivity, hidden-width and expanded entropy-weight ablations, a label-smoothing sweep, alternative sample-selection analyses, hyperparameter transfer, and OOD robustness tests. Conversely, v2's all-versus-selected-samples head-training ablation and MLP-depth sweep disappear. The principal component ablations in Table 2 remain.

E5.justification: Appendix C.2 newly specifies eight runs and reports mean and standard deviation for CDC and several baselines across all six benchmarks in Tables 10–11. v2 lacks explicit run counts and corresponding uncertainty tables. Table 5 additionally reports variability across hyperparameter settings, distinct from repeated-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: Numerical entries in the original Tables 1, 2, and 4 are unchanged, but substantial new results are added. For example, Table 12 reports ImageNet50 ACC/ECE of 77.8%/7.5% for CDC versus 76.8%/14.2% for SCAN-3 under the added setting. The CIFAR-20 calibration comparison in prose is corrected from 52.3%→40.6% to 52.3%→4.9%, matching both versions' Table 1.

M1.justification: The reported pseudo-label selection rule changes: v2 multiplies average confidence over all samples assigned to a class by floor(B/C), whereas v3 sums confidence over its top floor(B/C) samples and rounds down. This refines sample selection while retaining the dual-head architecture, losses, initialization, and inference procedure.

P1.justification: Contributions, related work, and several method explanations are extensively rewritten. Initialization moves from Section 3.1 to 3.3, Algorithm 1 moves from the appendix into the main method section, and experiments and appendices are reorganized. Citation style, affiliations, and conference headers also change.

P2.justification: v3 adopts the ICLR layout, revises framework labels, restructures tables, and adds sensitivity, sample-selection, and OOD displays. Existing appendix Figures 5–7 become Figures 6, 7, and 9 with retained content; Figures 5, 8, 10, and 11 provide new displays. Figure 3 also corrects ARPC to AURC.

R1.justification: Positioning expands beyond the original deep-clustering and supervised-calibration survey. v3 discusses CLIP-based SIC/TAC, distinguishes domain-adaptation calibration using labeled source data, and substantially relates CDC to moderately confident sample selection and FlexMatch/FreeMatch thresholding in Appendix C.1.

T1.justification: v3 corrects Theorem 1's reversed region indices: confidence is penalized in unreliable region F and preserved in reliable region T, consistent with the existing proof. Appendix A.1 also adds an explicit feature-normalization assumption. The principal propositions, theorems, and derivations otherwise remain.

improvement.justification: The eight-run uncertainty tables, relevant SSL comparisons, and transfer/OOD evaluations substantially strengthen evidence for CDC's stability and applicability beyond v2's original evaluations. Resource reporting and code-access information further improve reproducibility. Removed ablations and the explicit cluster-count limitation are drawbacks, as is overstated robustness prose: Table 5's CIFAR-20 ACC spans 58.1–62.6%, exceeding the claimed ±1.4-point variation. These issues temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial empirical strengthening.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same calibrated deep clustering (CDC) work. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds original sensitivity studies, repeated-run results, transfer evaluations, and out-of-distribution detection experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original CDC experiments on six image benchmarks, including clustering, calibration, failure rejection, and component ablations.

title: Towards Calibrated Deep Clustering Network

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes OM superiority for preventing reward drops and regularizing away from hacking policies. v2 makes a new formal definition and a proxy-quality-dependent improvement guarantee central contributions, adds claims about χ² versus KL including RLHF, and recommends replacing current KL regularization. The regularizing-away contribution is dropped.

C2.justification: v2 explains hacking through breakdown of reward correlation under distribution shift and motivates χ² through its stronger penalty on unlikely behavior. It newly acknowledges that the RLHF evaluation reward model can itself be hacked and discusses limits of OM/AD equivalence for future multi-turn or tool-using agents. Earlier AUROC-based explanations and the λdrop recommendation disappear.

D1.justification: v2 adds ORPO pseudocode, a 1%-per-tail trimmed divergence estimator, proxy-reward scale values, pandemic network details, and RLHF model, dataset and software specifications. Appendix D explains previously tabulated clipping behavior but removes discriminator-training epoch counts and earlier glucose history/feature-selection guidance. These are substantive changes to implementation documentation.

E1.justification: The tomato gridworld, Flow traffic, SimGlucose and pandemic environments remain, sometimes under renamed headings. v2 adds language-generation/RLHF experiments using AlpacaFarm preference and SFT data, substantially extending domain and task coverage (Appendix C.4).

E2.justification: The main comparison expands from KL-based AD and OM regularization to comparisons across both divergence families, including a new AD χ² comparator against χ² ORPO. The best-case early-stopping baseline in v1 Table 1 disappears. Base-policy, unregularized and true-reward-training comparisons remain for the original environments.

E3.justification: v2 introduces held-out-prompt RLHF evaluation with separate proxy and evaluation reward models, plus new χ² coefficient sweeps. Appendix D also revises the reported traffic/tomato discriminator depth from four 256-unit layers to two and specifies this architecture across non-LLM environments. Original PPO budgets remain unchanged; the revised documentation does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds proxy/true-reward correlation analyses across environments and controlled ablations of discriminator update order and reward clipping (Figure 2 and Appendix E.2). It removes v1's AUROC detection analysis and the λdrop coefficient-selection experiment. These changes substantially replace the questions investigated by the supplementary analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report five random seeds and median rewards with standard deviations in tables. The main coefficient-sweep plot changes from standard-deviation error bars in v1 Figure 3 to shading showing the range across seeds in v2 Figure 5. No increased repeated-run count is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds χ², RLHF, correlation and ablation results, while removing detection, early-stopping, λdrop and regularization-away results. New RLHF best-coefficient scores are 16.94 ± 0.07 for χ² and 16.81 ± 0.27 for KL. Some changed summaries reuse earlier results: gridworld AD KL changes from 6.19 to 6.33, but 6.33 already appears in v1 Table 4. Several retained appendix standard deviations also change.

M1.justification: v1 primarily optimizes proxy reward minus an occupancy KL penalty. v2 introduces a square-root χ² occupancy penalty, changing the discriminator-based reward adjustment from a linear score to an exponential score normalized by estimated divergence (Section 6 and Appendix B). It also implements direct χ² regularization for RLHF and omits v1's regularizing-away variant.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The narrative is reorganized into preliminaries, definitions, mitigation and experiments; much ORPO derivation moves to Appendix B and environment descriptions to Appendix C. Terminology changes from safe policy to base policy, and the appendices are substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. New correlation, glucose-distribution and RLHF graphics replace earlier toy, ROC and regularization-away displays. The coefficient-sweep figure becomes separate χ²/KL rows across five environments; result tables are redesigned, and algorithm and ablation displays are added. Existing training-board and traffic illustrations remain in Appendix C.

R1.justification: v2 repositions the contribution around formalizing reward hacking, explicitly contrasting correlated proxies with prior unhackability and bounded-error robust-MDP formulations. It expands the distinction from offline RL and adds relevant robust-RL, RLHF and multi-turn-agent references, including Derman, Gadot and Coste. Earlier early-stopping and TV-bound supporting references are removed.

T1.justification: v1's AD counterexample, TV return bound and tightness argument are replaced by correlated-proxy/reward-hacking definitions and Theorem 5.1's correlation-dependent χ² improvement bound with occupancy-support assumptions. Appendix A introduces contextual-bandit equivalence for general f-divergences, and Appendix B derives the new optimization gradient. Definition 4.1 does contain a normalization inconsistency: its stated standard deviations are printed as variances.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the connection between proxy quality, a theoretical improvement bound and the implemented regularizer, addressing a limitation of v1's generic return-distance argument. New RLHF comparisons and controlled ORPO ablations add relevant empirical support and identify implementation failures. These gains outweigh losing earlier diagnostic and alternative-strategy studies, although removing the λdrop experiment weakens practical coefficient-selection evidence. Definition 4.1's normalization error and remaining discrepancies between main and appendix result summaries still require correction.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same reward-hacking and ORPO research, despite the changed title and substantial revision. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments in the retained environments and an added RLHF setting, including reward correlations, regularization comparisons and implementation ablations (Figure 2, Table 1 and Appendix E).

before.justification: v1 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments in four environments, including regularization comparisons, reward-hacking detection and regularization-away results (Tables 1–3 and Appendix B).

title: Correlated Proxies: A New Definition and Improved Mitigation for Reward Hacking

C1.justification: The headline contributions and empirical scope remain essentially unchanged. The conclusion narrows its unconditional prediction that AD and OM regularization will cease to be equivalent for multi-turn or tool-using agents to saying they will 'likely diverge'.

C2.justification: Section 5 and Appendix A.1.3 explicitly explain that preventing reward hacking does not guarantee positive improvement, even when a policy improving both rewards exists. New discussions address near-optimality and the conditions for AD/OM equivalence in sequential LLM generation. Appendix B interprets the discriminator diagnostic as supporting the approximation. Conversely, v2's explicit warning about selecting coefficients without access to true reward is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix C.4 corrects the SFT base-model name from 'Python-1.4B' to 'Pythia-1.4B', without establishing a model replacement. The new win-rate evaluation identifies its evaluator, tool, and coefficients. Existing architecture descriptions, hyperparameter tables, stabilization details, and code-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate traffic control, pandemic mitigation, glucose monitoring, AlpacaFarm-based RLHF, and the tomato-watering gridworld. AlpacaEval is introduced for win-rate scoring, without identifying a new prompt population or distinct task; the discriminator diagnostic also uses an existing environment.

E2.justification: The AD, state-OM, and state-action-OM regularization comparisons retain their KL and chi-squared variants and existing reference policies. The new RLHF win-rate comparison evaluates the already studied KL- and chi-squared-trained policies against the existing SFT policy.

E3.justification: Appendix E.1 adds AlpacaEval/GPT4o-mini win-rate evaluation at the selected regularization coefficients. v3 Table 10 also specifies state-only OM regularization for pandemic ablations, whereas v2 Table 9 specifies state-action OM. This is a reported setting revision, although the surrounding ablation introduction was not updated consistently.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds Figure 6, comparing the glucose discriminator's output with the occupancy-measure log ratio to assess approximation accuracy. The existing update-order and reward-clipping ablations remain, with revised pandemic results under the newly captioned configuration.

E5.justification: Both versions already report five-seed medians, standard deviations, and ranges in their tables and Figure 5. The new win-rate table uses medians and ranges across five seeds, without introducing a different uncertainty procedure or establishing an increase in runs.

E6.justification: New Table 4 reports median RLHF win rates of 52.83 for chi-squared and 51.50 for KL, with ranges 51.98–53.98 and 11.93–53.75. Pandemic ablation entries are replaced, including the default result changing from -12.18 ± 0.46 to -10.68 ± 0.15 under the changed configuration; this is not a same-setting gain. Figure 6 adds qualitative discriminator-agreement evidence. Existing main benchmark results and coefficient-sweep values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The regularized objective, discriminator-based reward adjustment, alternating discriminator/PPO updates, and KL variant remain unchanged in Section 6 and Algorithm 1. The added theory and diagnostics do not introduce a new algorithm component.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and substantial portions of Sections 2–6 undergo extensive paragraph rewriting and explanatory restructuring. Appendix A gains a more detailed subsection hierarchy, and the related-work and experimental appendices gain new subsections. This exceeds routine copyediting despite retaining the broad main-section order.

P2.justification: v3 adds Figure 6, the win-rate table, and an MDP schematic for the new proof. Figure 2 replaces its pandemic and glucose illustrations, and several captions are rewritten. Existing principal plots and table structures remain largely intact, with appendix tables renumbered and material reflowed.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantive positioning against alternative RLHF divergences and DPO, including Go, Wang, and Huang. It distinguishes Huang's chi-squared preference optimization from this work's online, general reward-hacking approach, and contrasts Nika's deterministic-MDP setting with its stochastic setting. These additions materially expand discussion of closely related approaches beyond isolated citation updates.

T1.justification: Appendix A adds results on near-optimal base policies, counterexamples and positive examples for optimizing the lower bound, failure of AD regularization, autoregressive KL equivalence, and correlation implied by low reward-prediction error. Definition 4.1 corrects the variance formula, and Definition 4.2 distinguishes policy-level reward hacking from a hackable proxy. The original main bound and ORPO derivation are retained.

improvement.justification: v3 better explains the guarantee's limitations, addresses closely related methods, and adds useful discriminator and GPT4o-mini-based RLHF checks. However, the new Lemma A.4 reward assignments conflict with its subsequent zero-mean calculation on PDF pages 23–24, and the introduction retains an unqualified 'provable improvement' claim despite the new limitations. These unresolved reliability issues limit the net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Correlated Proxies work and ORPO algorithm. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–E are readable and support comparison, including the substantially expanded theoretical appendix in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds discriminator-validation results and GPT4o-mini-based RLHF win rates.

before.justification: v2 reports original reinforcement-learning results across five environments, regularization-coefficient sweeps, and ORPO ablations in Section 6 and Appendix E.

title: Correlated Proxies: A New Definition and Improved Mitigation for Reward Hacking

C1.justification: The principal definition, guarantee, and empirical advantage claims remain. However, v4 removes Section 2's explicit claim to be the first application of occupancy-measure regularization to reward hacking and instead emphasizes specific distinctions from prior definitions in Section 4.

C2.justification: The mechanism explanations for OM versus AD and chi-squared versus KL, qualifications concerning guaranteed improvement, and limitations of the RLHF true-reward model remain unchanged. Appendix interpretations of discriminator accuracy and ablation robustness are also retained.

D1.justification: Appendices B–D retain the same implementation details, architectures, hyperparameters, clipping procedure, trimmed-mean estimator, and RLHF implementation information. The abstract provides the same code-access link.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same traffic, pandemic, glucose, RLHF, and tomato-watering environments. The AlpacaFarm-based RLHF setup and Appendix E's AlpacaEval evaluation are also retained.

E2.justification: Table 1 and Appendix E retain the same AD, state-OM, and state-action-OM comparisons using chi-squared and KL divergences, together with the same reference-policy, unregularized, and true-reward baselines. RLHF-specific exclusions are unchanged.

E3.justification: Section 6 and Appendices C–E preserve the coefficient sweeps, architectures, training budgets, held-out-prompt evaluation, reward metrics, and win-rate procedures. No experimental setting is substantively revised.

E4.justification: The coefficient-sensitivity analysis in Figure 5, discriminator-accuracy analysis in Figure 6, and training-order and reward-clipping ablations in Appendix E.3 are unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions report five random seeds, medians and standard deviations in result tables, and seed ranges in Figure 5 and Table 4. No run-count or uncertainty-reporting practice changes.

E6.justification: The numerical entries in Table 1 and Appendix E's Tables 4–10, plotted results, and qualitative findings match. For example, Table 4 retains median RLHF win rates of 52.83 for chi-squared regularization and 51.50 for KL.

M1.justification: ORPO's discriminator objective, reward adjustment, and alternating discriminator/PPO updates remain unchanged in Section 6 and Appendix B. Renaming the base policy to the reference policy does not change the procedure.

P1.justification: v4 renames the base policy to the reference policy, streamlines passages in Sections 1–4, explicitly lists the two existing desiderata, and reorganizes discussion of prior definitions. It also retitles Definition 4.2, relocates an equation to Appendix A, and adds an equal-contribution note.

P2.justification: Figures and tables retain their substantive displays, with updated policy labels and limited caption edits. ICLR publication headers and page reflow change presentation, including moving Table 5 onto Appendix E's opening page.

R1.justification: v4 adds Fluri et al. (2024), Kwa et al. (2024), and Skalse et al. (2024). Sections 2–4 revise the comparison with earlier reward-hacking definitions and replace the broad priority claim with more specific positioning.

T1.justification: Definitions 4.1–4.2, Theorem 5.1, and the appendix results and proofs are mathematically unchanged. The return–occupancy identity moves from v3 Equation (3) to v4 Equation (8) in Appendix A.1; this is relocation, not new theory.

improvement.justification: v4 improves clarity and scholarly context by explicitly organizing the definition's desiderata and comparing it with additional related formulations, while moderating the broad priority claim. Some introductory explanations are shortened, but the technical material and experimental evidence remain available. The overall gain is limited to exposition and positioning.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–E. Content can be reliably matched despite terminology changes and page reflow.

after.justification: v4 retains original experimental results in Table 1, Figures 2–6, and Appendix E, including RLHF evaluations and ORPO ablations.

before.justification: v3 reports original policy-training experiments across five environments, RLHF win-rate evaluations, discriminator analyses, and ORPO ablations.

title: Correlated Proxies: A New Definition and Improved Mitigation for Reward Hacking

C1.justification: The central contribution remains off-policy learning using only state-value critics. The revised abstract and introduction explicitly claim a nontrivial transfer of full-loss importance weighting to deep networks and promote the variance analysis and stabilizing design choices as contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix B newly interprets tuning behavior through the method's combination of on-policy and off-policy characteristics. The abstract also attributes twin critics to avoiding optimization bias, while the body retains the earlier regularization explanation. The substantive sample-efficiency and HalfCheetah limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds hyperparameter-search grids, best-configuration selection information, Nvidia V100 hardware, approximately 1–3 days of training, and software-source/license information. It also revises MPO table entries. Conversely, v1's reproducibility statement promising a camera-ready code release disappears; v2 supplies no Vlearn code-access replacement.

E1.justification: Both evaluate Hopper-v4, Walker2D-v4, HalfCheetah-v4, Ant-v4, Humanoid-v4, and DMC dog-walk, dog-trot, and dog-run. The additional appendix discussion introduces no new evaluated task or environment.

E2.justification: The benchmark comparisons retain SAC, MPO, PPO, on-policy TRPL, and the one-step V-trace variant. The Humanoid component comparisons also retain the same alternatives; no evaluated comparator is added or removed.

E3.justification: Table 2 revises reported DMC MPO settings, including buffer size from 256 to 1e6, policy-update interval from 10000 to 1, and Polyak weight from 1 to 5e-3. These appear to correct misplaced entries; the PDFs do not establish reruns. Other benchmark protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The replay-buffer and component ablations are retained, moving from v1 Figure 2 to v2 Figure 4. Appendix B adds qualitative sensitivity observations about learning-rate/trust-region compatibility, batch size, and warm starts, without new quantitative ablation plots.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten seeds and means with 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals, including ten seeds for the buffer-size ablation. The new theoretical effective-sample-size discussion does not change empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The benchmark and ablation curves are retained, as is the reported 25% Humanoid improvement over SAC. Appendix B newly reports that smaller batches worked better for Vlearn and off-policy V-trace and that warm-start samples provided no observed benefit.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same importance-weighted Bellman loss, TRPL policy updates, twin value critics, delayed updates, and importance-weight clipping. Algorithm 1 reformulates the loop and update conditions without establishing a different learning procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial introductory, related-work, and explanatory passages are rewritten. Section 3 gains a separate estimator subsection and descriptive subheadings; appendices are reorganized, the reproducibility statement is removed, and the brief impact statement becomes an expanded Broader Impacts appendix.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column to a predominantly single-column layout, with redesigned title, author, equation, and algorithm placement. Figure 2's seven panels become five benchmark panels plus separate Figure 4 ablations. Plots are resized and relabeled, and both hyperparameter tables drop the redundant 'use critic' row.

R1.justification: v2 more explicitly positions Vlearn as transferring established linear importance-weighting ideas to deep RL, adding discussion of TD(0) and LSTD. Added references include Bradtke and Barto, Graves and Ghiassian, Owen, and DMC/MuJoCo sources. The principal relationships to existing methods remain intact.

T1.justification: v1 derives the bandit estimators but only expects squared importance weighting to have higher variance. v2 Appendix A.3 adds effective-sample-size definitions and an ordering argument, then asserts an unconditional variance ordering. This substantially strengthens the theoretical assertion, although its justification is incomplete. The original upper-bound and consistency proofs are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 improves reproducibility through search details, hardware/runtime disclosure, and corrected MPO entries, while clarifying prior-work attribution. However, Appendix A.3 strengthens v1's tentative variance intuition into a universal claim without establishing why an ordering based only on weights guarantees the reward-dependent estimator-variance ordering. The code-release commitment also disappears. These benefits and substantive qualification concerns leave the net quality change uncertain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Vlearn research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments in Section 4 and Figures 2–4 and additionally reports qualitative hyperparameter-tuning findings in Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gymnasium and DMC continuous-control experiments, baseline comparisons, and Humanoid ablations in Section 4 and Figures 2–3.

title: Efficient Off-Policy Learning for High-Dimensional Action Spaces

C1.justification: The abstract changes from introducing a novel importance-sampling loss to using an existing weighted loss, and removes the exploration/exploitation claim. The introduction emphasizes feasibility and practical design insights while retaining the central state-value-only learning and high-dimensional-control claims.

C2.justification: v3 extends the twin-critic regularization interpretation by suggesting greater benefits in higher-dimensional problems, and discusses overactuated systems and categorical critics as future directions. The HalfCheetah weakness remains in Section 4.3, although the conclusion no longer repeats it.

D1.justification: Table 2 now explicitly documents the hyperparameters for MyoHand by sharing the dog-task configuration. Existing algorithm details, hyperparameter values, hardware and training-time disclosures remain; the new reproducibility statement mainly directs readers to this material.

E1.justification: v3 adds ten 39-dimensional MyoHand tasks from MyoSuite, covering pose, reaching and object manipulation with standard and hard variants (Figure 3). This substantially extends coverage beyond locomotion; all five Gymnasium and three DMC dog tasks remain.

E2.justification: The retained benchmark comparisons still evaluate SAC, MPO, PPO, on-policy TRPL and one-step V-trace, and the component variants remain the same. The new MyoHand comparison uses existing comparators SAC, PPO, TRPL and V-trace; Figure 3 does not report MPO results.

E3.justification: v3 introduces success-based MyoHand evaluation and cross-task IQM aggregation (Figure 3), supplementing the existing per-task return evaluations. Settings for the retained tasks in Tables 1–2 and the controlled one-step V-trace comparison remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Component ablations expand from Humanoid-v4 alone to Ant-v4 and, in Appendix C Figure 6, Hopper-v4, Walker2D-v4 and HalfCheetah-v4. These substantially broaden the investigation of whether importance sampling, TRPL, twin critics and clipping are beneficial across tasks.

E5.justification: v3 adds an interquartile-mean estimate with a 95% bootstrapped confidence interval across MyoHand tasks (Figure 3). Per-task reporting continues to use ten seeds, means and 95% bootstrapped intervals; no increase in runs for retained results is stated.

E6.justification: v3 adds MyoHand success curves showing Vlearn's highest aggregate performance with task-specific exceptions, plus results from the expanded component ablations. Figure 6 also shows that removing twin critics improves HalfCheetah performance. The retained benchmark curves and the reported 25% Humanoid improvement over SAC are unchanged.

M1.justification: The weighted Bellman-error objective, TRPL policy update, twin critics, importance-weight clipping and replay-buffer procedure remain unchanged. Renaming the loss to LWIS and moving the unchanged Algorithm 1 to Appendix B do not change the method.

P1.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the narrative around high-dimensional control, expands the WIS explanation and restructures experiments into high-dimensional tasks, design choices and low-dimensional tasks. It also retitles the paper, moves pseudocode into the appendix, adds a reproducibility section and removes the broader-impacts appendix.

P2.justification: Existing Gymnasium and dog plots are regrouped into Figures 2 and 5; a new MyoHand Figure 3 and appendix ablation Figure 6 are added. Figure 4 becomes a wider three-panel comparison, and the algorithm moves from a wrapped main-text display to a full-width appendix display.

R1.justification: v3 expands the connection to prior linear WIS and TD(0) work and clarifies attribution. It adds references for MyoSuite, double sampling, Sutton and Barto's textbook, and recent critic/stabilization approaches, while retaining the overall positioning against Q-function methods and V-trace.

T1.justification: Theorem 1, the upper-bound and consistency proofs, and the bandit variance/effective-sample-size analysis in Appendix A remain mathematically unchanged. Loss renaming, notation corrections and expanded explanations introduce no new formal result.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for the central generality claim: v2 evaluated locomotion and examined components only on Humanoid, whereas v3 adds musculoskeletal hand control and checks component effects across all five Gymnasium tasks. The new results expose task-dependent exceptions, while clearer attribution distinguishes the existing WIS foundation from the practical algorithm contribution. These changes materially improve validation and scientific clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Vlearn research despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds original MyoHand evaluations and component ablations on additional Gymnasium tasks.

before.justification: v2 reports original experiments on five Gymnasium tasks and three DMC dog tasks, plus Humanoid component and replay-buffer ablations.

title: Efficient Off-Policy Learning for High-Dimensional Action Spaces

C1.justification: v2 broadens the abstract's reconstruction claim from Mel-spectrograms to Mel-spectrograms or discrete tokens. The contributions now emphasize three enhanced losses and reduced GPU memory use, and the introduction newly claims the fastest diffusion-based waveform reconstruction to the authors' knowledge. The headline speed changes from approximately 90 to 97 times real-time.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations for stronger guidance effects with tokens, the STFT loss's magnitude-versus-phase tradeoff, and ViSQOL's apparent preference for GAN outputs despite audible artifacts. It also discusses bandwidth saturation and MBD's sound-effect performance. v1's disclosure that preliminary direct text-to-complex-spectrogram TTS underperformed a cascade is removed, although the proposed future direction remains.

D1.justification: v2 adds auxiliary-loss weights and their gradient-norm rationale, overlap size, codec feature-extraction settings, training hardware and durations, baseline repository links, and detailed external-test construction instructions. Existing optimizer, crop, batch-size, and backbone details largely move to Appendix A.1. Conversely, v1's direct RFWave repository link and explicit TTS-checkpoint availability statement are omitted; this does not establish that the resources became unavailable.

E1.justification: v2 retains the principal Mel-reconstruction datasets but removes the Universal-dataset experiment. It adds actual EnCodec-token reconstruction experiments, training with Common Voice, DNS Challenge speech, Jamendo, FSD50K, and AudioSet. The external evaluation suite in Table A.4 substantially broadens coverage across speech, vocals, and sound effects.

Vocos also becomes a comparator in the Jamendo experiment, where v1 reports only RFWave. The speed comparison expands accordingly.

Appendix A.3 expands spectrogram case studies to additional methods and music artifacts. Conversely, v1's 100-step sampling comparison and 80-versus-100-dimensional Mel-input comparison disappear.

This is a new reporting practice, but training-seed replication, listener counts, and interval-construction procedures are not specified.

E6.justification: v2 substantially replaces and expands the reported results, adding MOS, codec-bandwidth results, and new ablation outcomes. For example, Table 1 reports average MOS of 3.95 for RFWave, 3.47 for Vocos, and 3.75 for PriorGrad. Reported RFWave GPU throughput changes from 91.46 to 97.01 times real-time. Universal, CPU, and preliminary direct-TTS results disappear. Many quality scores use revised configurations or test subsets and therefore do not establish controlled performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: v2 introduces overlapping subbands with a consistency loss, an STFT loss applied to the estimated clean signal, and classifier-free guidance, including its use for EnCodec reconstruction. These change training and inference. The shared ConvNeXtV2 backbone remains, and v1's time-balanced loss is renamed energy-balanced with the same Equation 5. EnCodec conditioning was already described in v1.

P1.justification: The introduction is extensively rewritten, the method is reorganized into model structure and loss functions, and the results place application comparisons before ablations. Implementation details move into a structured appendix with separate resources, examples, and tables sections. Terminology and the author block also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds an overlap schematic, restructures results into aggregate and detailed tables, and expands the compact spectrogram comparison into three appendix figures with ground truth and additional methods. The weighting plot is redrawn, the model schematic is restyled, and resource and dataset-construction tables are added. Page geometry and headers also change substantially.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around neural codecs and diffusion competitors through discussions of PriorGrad, FreGrad, SoundStream, VALL-E, and UniAudio, and adds flow-matching TTS context. The earlier Parallel WaveNet, ClariNet, and WaveGrad discussion disappears. Together with the new fastest-diffusion claim, this changes the research positioning beyond bibliographic maintenance.

These are limited mathematical additions; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's central quality and efficiency claims relied largely on automatic metrics and comparison with Vocos. v2 adds human listening evidence with uncertainty, direct diffusion competitors, codec reconstruction tests, and ablations addressing the new losses and guidance. These substantially strengthen support for the paper's central claims, while the appendix improves reproducibility. Listener counts and confidence-interval procedures remain unspecified, and removal of the negative preliminary TTS result and direct code/checkpoint disclosures weakens transparency. Those losses do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RFWave and retain identifiable corresponding architecture, equations, and experiments. Their main text, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison despite substantial expansion in v2.

after.justification: v2 reports original Mel-spectrogram and EnCodec-token reconstruction experiments, human listening evaluations, ablations, and efficiency measurements, including detailed appendix results.

before.justification: v1 reports original waveform-reconstruction scores, domain and loss ablations, spectrogram comparisons, and inference-speed measurements in Tables 1–3 and Appendix A.

title: RFWave: Multi-band Rectified Flow for Audio Waveform Reconstruction

C1.justification: The central claims about efficient, high-quality, frame-level multi-band reconstruction remain. v3 adds sampling-time selection as a fourth stated contribution, updates the headline speed from 97 to 160 times real-time, and explicitly claims speed comparable to GAN-based methods in the introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations connecting time-domain performance to periodic signals introduced by ISTFT, relating this mechanism to Snake activation, and attributing cross-domain advantages to better preserved harmonics. It also discusses the necessity of Rectified Flow, backbone efficiency, and scaling tradeoffs. Earlier discussion of MBD's sound-effect strengths and CFG's approximately 50% latency overhead is removed.

D1.justification: New details include sampling-grid calibration using one batch of 96 examples and 100 integration steps, half/double-size backbone configurations, explicit STFT-loss formulas, and the BigVGAN repository. Most optimizer, preprocessing, hardware, and training-duration information is retained. v3 omits v2's explicit Mel-test subset sizes of 20, 300, and 50; this establishes reduced documentation, not changed sample selection.

E1.justification: The existing training corpora and broad speech, singing, music, and codec coverage remain. v3 adds a focused scenario: Mel-spectrogram reconstruction on MUSDB18 using LibriTTS-trained models, covering vocals, drums, bass, other instruments, and mixtures. MUSDB18 already contributed codec-test samples in v2; its speech-to-music transfer role is new.

E2.justification: BigVGAN becomes an evaluated comparator in quality and speed benchmarks, and Table 6 adds DDPM and ResNet alternatives. Vocos is removed from the original multi-dataset comparison in Tables 1 and A.5 and its corresponding spectrogram panels, while participating in separate GAN comparisons. The Vocos, PriorGrad, and FreGrad rows from v2's LJSpeech ablation table also disappear.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include a separate GAN listening study, a 50-step DDPM control, a similarly sized ResNet backbone, and half/double-size model configurations. The speed benchmark adds GPU-memory measurement and explicit 44.1-kHz comparisons. These extend the experimental protocol substantially; the retained default training configuration and ten-step RFWave budget remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds tests of equal-straightness sampling, Rectified Flow versus DDPM, backbone choice, model scaling, and speech-to-music generalization. Figures A.8–A.9 newly illustrate artifacts from omitting STFT and overlap losses. Conversely, the frequency-domain energy-balanced variant and two CFG ablation rows reported in v2 are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report MOS with confidence intervals, explicitly identified as 95% intervals in Table 1. Additional interval-bearing results in v3 use the existing reporting practice. Neither version supplies training-seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial results: MUSDB18 average MOS is 3.67 for RFWave, 3.51 for BigVGAN, and 3.10 for Vocos; the equal-straightness ablation reports PESQ 4.275 versus 4.211 without it. Reported RFWave speed changes from 97.01 to 162.59 times real-time, without explaining the cause. Original diffusion and EnCodec scores are largely retained, while some Vocos/CFG entries disappear. The new LibriTTS MOS comparison is explicitly a separate listening study.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 adds equal-straightness selection of nonuniform Euler sampling times, with implementation in Appendix A.5. This refines inference while retaining the multi-band architecture, ConvNeXtV2 backbone, normalization procedures, and three training losses. Appendix A.4 documents existing STFT losses rather than introducing another objective.

P1.justification: The introduction is extensively condensed and rewritten. Previously separate experiment and results sections become a structured experiments-and-analysis section separating diffusion, GAN, codec, ablation, and speed evaluations. Subband details move to the appendix, appendix explanations are reorganized, and the conclusion loses the future-TTS and ethical-concerns discussion.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn as an integrated architecture diagram. Existing spectrogram comparisons change from five to four panels, while new sampling, GAN-comparison, and loss-effect figures are added. Tables are reorganized around separate comparison groups, and the speed table gains memory and high-sample-rate entries. The document also adopts different headers, typography, and table formatting.

R1.justification: v3 expands context through references to flow matching, stochastic interpolants, additional diffusion vocoders, and BigVGAN/Snake, and explicitly distinguishes energy-balanced loss from PriorGrad's adaptive prior. Some codec and future-TTS references are removed. These refine the existing research positioning; citation-style and bibliography-format changes do not themselves constitute substantive changes.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 introduces the straightness functional S(v) and uses equal accumulated deviation to define sampling intervals. The original Rectified Flow and loss equations remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added. Appendix A.4 mainly supplies formulas for previously specified STFT-loss components.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation through speech-to-music transfer tests, BigVGAN comparisons, controls isolating Rectified Flow and backbone choices, and diagnostic loss examples (Tables 2–6; Figures A.6–A.9). These address important gaps in evidence for generalization and design decisions in v2. Some earlier Vocos/CFG results and explicit test-subset counts are lost, and the speed revision is unexplained, but the added diagnostic and comparative evidence provides a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RFWave work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds GAN comparisons, cross-domain evaluation, sampling and backbone analyses, and resource measurements.

before.justification: v2 reports original listening tests, objective reconstruction measurements, ablations, and inference-speed benchmarks in Tables 1–4 and A.5–A.6.

title: RFWave: Multi-band Rectified Flow for Audio Waveform Reconstruction

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds simple diffusion-backbone initialization and transfer using limited target data. v3 makes systematic identification of effective adaptation choices a principal contribution, with headline findings about annotation quality, stochasticity and image-level supervision. It emphasizes dense perception while retaining GenPercept's transfer claim and moving pose evidence to the appendix.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations for LoRA's limitations, annotation quality and supervision effects on detail, and depth-versus-disparity tradeoffs. It explicitly qualifies semantic generalization with failures on unseen cats and cars (Figure 4). Meanwhile, v1's MAE/CLIP/CoCa representation-learning discussion and interpretations of the removed data-volume and PixArt experiments disappear.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-repository pointer and documents sampling ratios, noise/ensemble defaults, prompt strings, LoRA ranks and MMPose rendering. It omits v1's explicit learning-rate decay, DIS/matting normalization and clipping instructions, and runtime/memory measurements. These change reproducibility documentation within an otherwise retained implementation framework; the link alone does not establish external code availability.

E1.justification: v3 adds ScanNet depth evaluation, Sintel normal evaluation, and Taskonomy/Cityscapes training for the data-quality comparison (Tables 5–7). Appendix E.6 additionally reports MHP pose experiments. The original COCO pose coverage is retained in Appendix C, rather than removed.

E2.justification: The depth benchmark gains DepthAnything, DepthAnything v2, Metric3D v2, Marigold, GeoWizard and DepthFM. Normal comparisons replace FrameNet, VPLNet, TiltedSN and Bae et al. (2021) with Omnidata variants, Metric3D v2, DSINE and GeoWizard. Matting adds HATT, SHM and MODNet. Conversely, v1's DINOv2 depth and semantic-segmentation comparisons disappear. P3M becomes P3M-Net with the same comparator scores.

E3.justification: Default ablations change from Hypersim-only training at resolution 768 and batch size 16 (v1 Section 3.5) to 90:10 Hypersim/Virtual KITTI sampling at 480×640 and batch size 32 (v3 Appendix D). Normal evaluation drops RMSE and adds 5° and 7.5° thresholds. v3 also introduces average ranks across depth metrics. These are substantive reported protocol changes.

E4.justification: v3 expands the noise/component studies to test both noise forms, multi-resolution noise, image-level losses, prompts, timesteps, LoRA ranks and synthetic versus real training data (Tables 1–5). It adds qualitative ablation and semantic failure examples. Conversely, v1's training-data-volume sweep, PixArt and VAE-encoder tests, and explicit ensemble/runtime analysis are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Inference ensembles and discussion of diffusion stochasticity do not establish statistical uncertainty reporting; both versions principally report point estimates.

E6.justification: v3 substantially replaces and extends geometry and ablation results under revised settings. DIS overall maxFβ changes from 0.840 to 0.863 (v1 Table 4; v3 Table 8); matting SAD/MSE change from 12.44/0.0037 to 12.77/0.0027 (v1 Table 5; v3 Table 10). These are revised reported outcomes under changed training, not controlled same-setting improvements. GenPercept's semantic mIoU and COCO pose scores are retained.

M1.justification: The one-step backbone and optional decoder mechanism remain, but task-specific learning changes substantially. v3 adds disparity prediction, uses MSE/scale-shift-invariant/gradient depth losses instead of v1's VNL/HDN/MSE/L1 combination, and adds image-angular supervision for normals. Colormap segmentation changes from latent-space supervision to pixel-wise MSE. These revise outputs and objectives beyond merely documenting the existing architecture.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten. The method-first narrative becomes a preliminary overview followed by question-driven analyses and explicit findings before task experiments. Detailed formulations move to Appendix A, human pose moves to Appendix C, and implementation and supplementary results receive separate appendices. This is substantial narrative reorganization.

P2.justification: Figure 2 becomes a multi-panel visualization of noise forms, schedules and predictions; Figure 4 gains generalization and failure examples. Geometry tables expand to additional datasets, methods and training-sample columns, while the semantic table loses baseline and architecture columns. Boxed findings and extensive appendix comparison grids are added, alongside relocation of the pose table and figure.

R1.justification: Research positioning shifts from broad foundation-model transfer and NLP/pretraining analogies toward identifying unresolved diffusion-adaptation choices. Marigold and DMP remain but become central reference points. GeoWizard, DepthFM, DepthAnything, Metric3D v2 and newer inverse-rendering work substantially expand the contemporary context, while much of the earlier NLP, DINOv2 and representation-learning discussion is removed.

T1.justification: The diffusion formulations and beta-equals-one derivation in v1 Section 2, Equations 1–8, are retained in v3 Appendix A. No new theorem, proof or substantive formal derivation is introduced. The expanded empirical explanations do not change this mathematical content.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the justification for adaptation choices: Table 1 investigates both stochastic and deterministic noise schedules, and Tables 2–5 isolate supervision, conditioning and fine-tuning choices that v1 examined less fully. Broader geometry comparisons and explicit semantic failure cases improve the assessment of applicability. Removing DINOv2 comparisons, data-scaling evidence and measured runtime/memory results loses useful support, but the stronger investigation of the central design questions provides a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs clearly describe the same GenPercept work, and their supplied text, equations, tables and figures are readable. However, v1 refers to supplementary DIS comparisons that are absent from its supplied PDF, limiting comparison of that material. The principal method, experiments and revisions remain assessable.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark results and extensive adaptation ablations, with additional empirical comparisons and qualitative results in its appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original GenPercept experiments on depth, surface normals, segmentation, matting and human pose, together with component and training-data ablations.

title: What Matters When Repurposing Diffusion Models for General Dense Perception Tasks?

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction replace the explicit finding that stochasticity harms perception with the scheduler-special-case claim that multi-step generation can become one-step without performance loss. The principal contributions—GenPercept, data-quality analysis and task-specific supervision—remain.

C2.justification: Section 3.1 replaces the earlier Gaussian-versus-RGB difficulty explanation with ground-truth shortcuts and training/inference mismatch; new Appendix B develops this interpretation. V4 acknowledges weaker benchmark performance against MVANet and ViTAE-S while emphasizing generalization, recommends depth versus disparity by scene type, and identifies LAION data scale versus diffusion pretraining as an unresolved source of benefits.

D1.justification: V4 specifies scheduler interpolation and UperNet class-channel outputs, identifies geometry results evaluated using released weights and Marigold/DSINE protocols, and documents runtime hardware and measurement settings. Existing training hyperparameters largely persist. The GenPercept code URL in v3's abstract is removed without replacement, reducing documented access information.

E1.justification: Matting coverage expands substantially beyond portraits: v4 adds zero-shot AIM500 evaluation and Composition-1K training, including semi-transparent and hollow objects (Table 10; Appendix H.4; Figures 16–17). It also adds ADE20K training, whereas v3 used ADE20K only for zero-shot evaluation on overlapping semantic classes.

E2.justification: V4 adds MVANet to DIS comparisons, Mask2Former with ResNet50/Swin-T/Swin-L to semantic segmentation, and ViTAE-S to matting comparisons. Table 6 also adds DMP Official to the final depth comparison, although DMP already participated in v3's ablations. These additions substantially strengthen comparator coverage across tasks.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include 1024-pixel DIS inference, training subsets ranging from 90K to 5.6K images, and runtime/memory measurements averaging 100 images at 768×768 on an RTX 4090 (Tables 8, 11–12). Supervised ADE20K and matting-transfer evaluations also introduce additional settings. The newly identified Marigold/DSINE protocols for retained geometry scores are documentation, not evidence that those experiments changed.

E4.justification: V4 adds training-volume sensitivity, runtime/ensemble/decoder comparisons, and synthetic-versus-real training comparisons under challenging visual conditions (Tables 11–12; Figure 9). Expanded cross-dataset DIS comparisons and portrait-to-general-object matting tests provide additional robustness evidence. The original architecture, timestep, prompt and training-strategy ablations remain.

E5.justification: Section 3.1 newly reports varying random seeds during training and inference when investigating scheduler performance. V3 does not report these checks. V4 provides no run counts, seed identifiers, error bars or confidence intervals, so this is a limited reporting addition rather than a documented increase in repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include supervised ADE20K mIoU of 50.2, AIM500 SAD of 75.5 versus ViTAE-S's 112.52, 1024-pixel DIS results, runtime measurements and data-volume results (Tables 8–12, 14). Tables 6–7 add baseline entries distinguished from authors' evaluations. Retained GenPercept geometry and pose scores are unchanged; the added training and inference settings should not be read as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The deterministic one-step GenPercept procedure, U-Net fine-tuning, optional decoders and task-specific losses are retained. The clarified UperNet output format and applications to additional datasets do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, preliminaries and Section 3.1 undergo substantial rewriting, including an equation-led explanation and a different mechanism narrative. Findings and conclusions are revised, the appendix is reorganized into additional thematic sections before the references, and matting implementation details move into the appendix.

P2.justification: V4 expands comparison tables and adds provenance markers, training/test-dataset columns, and runtime/data-volume tables. Figures 5–6 gain comparator columns; the cross-dataset segmentation display expands considerably; new synthetic-versus-real and general-matting figures appear. Figure 2's plot styling and several captions change. Numerous older qualitative panels are retained despite relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: V4 replaces the DINO object-detection citation with Caron et al.'s self-supervised vision-transformer work, adds DINOv2 discussion, and cites the newly included comparators and Composition-1K source. Most of the related-work narrative and the positioning around repurposing diffusion priors remain.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 newly gives an explicit mathematical definition of the variance schedule using interpolation between square-root endpoints (v4 Equation 5). The diffusion objectives and one-step reduction otherwise retain v3's mathematics; equations brought into the main text largely restate material already in v3 Appendix A.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially strengthens previously under-supported practical claims through measured runtime and data-volume analyses, stronger baselines, and broader generalization tests. Tables 8–10 also expose task-specific weaknesses and produce more balanced conclusions, while baseline-provenance disclosures improve interpretability. These gains outweigh removal of the code link and reporting weaknesses: seed variation remains unquantified, and Appendix C's claimed 27% GPU-memory reduction conflicts with Table 11's 6.95-to-6.32 GB change, approximately 9%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GenPercept study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V4 retains these original results and adds runtime measurements, training-data-volume experiments, stronger benchmark comparisons and general-object matting results.

before.justification: V3 reports original experiments on depth, surface normals, segmentation and matting, plus component ablations and appendix results on human pose estimation.

title: What Matters When Repurposing Diffusion Models for General Dense Perception Tasks?

C1.justification: v1's central empirical claim concerns inadequate separation in unmodified models. v2 expands the stated contributions to mitigation evaluation and claims that the tested prompting and fine-tuning approaches do not reliably provide both separation and high utility (abstract, introduction, and Section 7). This substantially broadens the scientific claim.

C2.justification: v2 interprets separation alongside instruction-following utility and adds substantive qualifications: system/user roles are imperfect instruction/data proxies, GPT-4 may benefit from generating SEP, and unsuccessful mitigation experiments cannot establish impossibility. It discusses alternative optimization choices and residual failures despite high aggregate scores, substantially expanding the applicability and limitations analysis.

D1.justification: Where v1 Appendix B mainly identifies evaluated models, v2 Appendices B.1–B.4 document mitigation-data construction, prompt templates, optimization settings, TRL/PEFT implementation, and NVIDIA A6000 hardware. Table 10 supplies LoRA and training hyperparameters. These are substantial reproducibility details for the new experiments; the code and SEP access statement is retained.

E1.justification: The 9,160-element SEP evaluation dataset and Appendix A task inventory are retained. v2 additionally uses SQuAD-based inputs and Alpaca-derived probes for mitigation training and validation, including open-ended probes without witnesses. This substantially expands the represented training data and task requirements beyond the original synthetic evaluation setup.

E2.justification: The model comparison removes Llama-2-13B, OpenHermes 2.5, and Dolphin 2.2.1, while adding Gemma-2B/7B, Phi-3-mini-4k, Llama-3-8B, and Starling. Tables 3–4 also introduce comparisons between original models and prompt engineering, prompt optimization, and fine-tuning.

E3.justification: v2 adds utility evaluation, separate 10,000-example training and 1,000-example validation datasets, validation-based selection, and optimization/fine-tuning budgets. It introduces textual system/user delimiters for Gemma and Starling. GPT-3.5 changes from the reported 0613 endpoint to 0125, and GPT-4 from 0125 to 2024-04-09, preventing direct same-checkpoint comparisons.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial analysis of mitigation effectiveness versus utility, including Figure 2 and failure cases despite engineered prompts in Tables 8–9. The insistence, probe-position, and task-domain analyses are retained in Appendix D with updated results. v1 Appendix C.1's separate diagnostic of GPT-4's witness agreement across prompt locations is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report standard errors without specifying benchmark replication counts or seeds. v2 adds a fitted linear regression summarizing the utility–separation relationship in Figure 2. This is a limited statistical addition; the expanded result tables otherwise retain the existing uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Reported SEP scores change for retained models: Llama-2-7B changes from 44.7% to 44.3%, and Zephyr from 29.1% to 30.0%. GPT results are replaced under newer endpoints. New mitigation results show, for example, average open-model separation rising from 37.5% to 81.8% after fine-tuning while utility falls from 67.8% to 19.2%. Appendix subgroup results also change.

M1.justification: v1 introduces measurement and benchmarking without implementing mitigations. v2 adds template-based prompt selection, adapted gradient/coordinate prompt optimization targeting task-specific outputs rather than fixed refusals, and LoRA fine-tuning (Section 6 and Appendix B). These are substantial new procedures; the original separation computation remains equivalent.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution statement, and formal exposition undergo substantial rewriting. A dedicated mitigation section reorganizes the narrative, and the appendices are restructured around experimental details, failure cases, and dataset-factor results. Terminology shifts from instruction prompt to task prompt; authorship, affiliation, and document-header text also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds a ChatGPT screenshot, a utility–separation scatter plot, model-output and failure-case tables, and parameter tables. It replaces v1's dataset-example figure with a different example table and expands the main results into separate separation and utility tables. Retained appendix result tables are transposed and reformatted, alongside a changed document template.

R1.justification: v2 positions the work as both a measurement study and a mitigation investigation, adding substantive discussion of StruQ, spotlighting, and robust prompt optimization. It newly emphasizes dataset diversity and adaptations of prior defenses, with corresponding method and dataset references. This extends the earlier positioning around defining and benchmarking instruction-data separation.

T1.justification: Definition 4 adds a formal empirical utility score, while the KL-based separation definition and empirical separation ratio remain equivalent to v1. No theorem or proof is added. The revised witness reasoning introduces an internal inconsistency by associating small empirical separation with many surprise witnesses despite linking witnesses to large divergence.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses an important limitation of v1's separation-only evaluation: apparent separation may accompany poor instruction following. Utility measurements and three concrete mitigation experiments, selected using separate data, make this distinction empirically assessable. Detailed implementation information, residual failure cases, and explicit caveats strengthen reproducibility and interpretation. Utility remains a narrow proxy and the witness discussion contains inconsistent reasoning, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial empirical gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SEP study and retain matching core definitions and dataset documentation. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of nine models, mitigation experiments, utility measurements, and qualitative failure cases in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original SEP evaluations of seven language models in Table 1, with further experimental breakdowns in Appendix C.

title: Can LLMs Separate Instructions From Data? And What Do We Even Mean By That?

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statement narrow the formal contribution to single-turn models. Section 6.1 softens the conjecture that separation will require fundamentally new approaches to saying it will benefit from them. The central contributions—formal characterization, SEP, and empirical evidence of inadequate separation—remain.

C2.justification: v3 introduces task superposition as a hypothesis for why larger models execute both instructions and probes. It interprets revised fine-tuning results as reducing usefulness for some tasks, replacing v2's stronger statement that many resulting models are no longer useful. Training data and scale are added as possible explanations for GPT performance.

D1.justification: Appendix B.4 newly documents DPOTrainer, disabling LoRA adapters for reference-model passes, the 50:50 Guanaco mixture, and equal-step learning-rate searches. Table 13 adds 40 warm-up steps and DPO beta 0.1. Hardware, most existing hyperparameters, and code/data access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds Guanaco instruction-tuning data for mixed training and replaces the introductory translation demonstration with an email/API simulation. SEP's 9,160 examples and task inventory remain unchanged. Appendix B.4 names SEP as a training-mixture component, conflicting with Section 4's evaluation-only restriction; actual overlap cannot be established.

E2.justification: v3 adds DPO and balanced SFT to the fine-tuning comparison and compares SFT/DPO combined with prompt engineering on three models (Tables 11–12 and 17–18). The nine-model main comparison is retained. Appendix E evaluates a StruQ-inspired combination, rather than documenting a separate reproduction of StruQ itself.

E3.justification: The reported fine-tuning schedule changes from constant learning rate with warm-up to cosine with warm-up (v2 Table 10; v3 Table 13), and embedding adaptation is excluded. Added experiments specify a 50:50 data mixture and combined-template training on three models. SEP size, empirical metrics, and the stated three-epoch budget remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Balanced SFT tests whether adding ordinary instruction-tuning data preserves utility, while new Appendix E tests whether combining the best prompt template with SFT or DPO improves separation. These substantially extend the mitigation analysis. Existing insistence, position, domain, and GPT failure-case analyses are retained; Figure 1 replaces the translation case with an email/API failure.

E5.justification: Uncertainty reporting becomes less uniform: v2 Table 4 reports standard errors for SFT utility, whereas v3 Table 12 presents revised SFT and balanced-SFT utilities as point estimates; Table 18 also omits utility uncertainty. Main tables retain standard errors. Neither version reports repeated-run counts or seeds.

E6.justification: Original/Naive and prompt-based results remain unchanged, but fine-tuning results are replaced and expanded. For example, Phi-3 separation/utility changes from 27.7%/1.5% under v2 SFT to 97.0%/69.2% under v3 DPO; this is not a same-setting improvement. New training and combination results appear in Tables 11–12 and 17–18. v3 inconsistently reports average DPO separation as 95.5% in Table 4 and 96.0% in Table 11.

M1.justification: The mitigation procedures expand from supervised LoRA fine-tuning to include mixed-data SFT targeting separation and utility, DPO using probe/no-probe response pairs, and fine-tuning with the strongest prompt template. Appendix B.4 also changes LoRA targets from including embeddings to excluding them. The empirical witness-based scoring procedure remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction and related-work narrative are substantially rewritten around email/API and RAG applications. Metric exposition and the fine-tuning discussion are revised, Original is renamed Naive, and Appendix E is added. The main section sequence and much of the dataset and appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adopts ICLR formatting, changing headers, typography, text widths, and table placement throughout. Figure 1 becomes a full-width colored email/API example, and Figure 2 is rescaled and updated. New Tables 11–12 and 17–18 display expanded experiments; Table 2 redisplays an existing prompt template. Existing failure-case and dataset-breakdown tables are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: The introduction and related work substantially expand coverage of RAG and agentic prompt injection, instruction hierarchy, activation-based detection, and data-minimization defenses. Added works include AgentDojo, ConfusedPilot, Wallace et al., Abdelnabi et al., and Bagdasarian et al. The earlier five-part differentiation is replaced by positioning centered on isolating instruction-data separation from attacks and harmful-query safety.

T1.justification: Definition 1 explicitly limits the abstraction to single-turn models. Definition 2 replaces the fixed KL divergence with a general distributional dissimilarity, mentioning KL and Wasserstein, and reverses the displayed argument order. Surprise-witness and empirical separation/utility definitions remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: The additional training-objective and combined-mitigation comparisons strengthen evidence beyond v2's single fine-tuning approach, while explicit single-turn scope and a softer architectural-necessity claim improve calibration. These gains are limited by conflicting descriptions of SEP's role in training and inconsistent DPO summaries across Tables 4 and 11, which weaken confidence in parts of the expanded evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SEP study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching v2 Appendices A–D to v3 and inspecting the new Appendix E.

after.justification: v3 retains original model evaluations and reports additional SFT, DPO, mixed-data training, and combined prompt-engineering/fine-tuning results.

before.justification: v2 reports original separation and utility measurements for nine language models, mitigation experiments, failure cases, and analyses by dataset attributes.

title: Can LLMs Separate Instructions From Data? And What Do We Even Mean By That?

C1.justification: The two principal methodological contributions and high-compression superiority claim remain. V4 adds GPU/CPU inference acceleration to the introduction's contributions and updates the stated evaluation scope from 11 datasets and seven models to 10 datasets and eight models. The KV-cache benefit remains claimed despite its relocation.

C2.justification: V4 interprets the new calibration tests as showing limited sensitivity and the generation examples as demonstrating useful generation at high compression, including 80% with LoRA in some cases. The adaptation-loss-based motivation in v1 is replaced by a qualitative activation-drift explanation. No substantive discussion of the proposed method's limitations is added.

D1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds three algorithms detailing per-weight whitening, factor storage, and sequential layer updates beyond v1's prose and equations. V4 also identifies LM-Evaluation-Harness, 2048-token calibration units, and the AMD EPYC 7643 CPU used for throughput testing. The code address and reliance on LLM-Pruner's LoRA configuration remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V4 retains WikiText-2, PTB, C4, ARC-e, and ARC-c, but replaces SST-5, MNLI, MRPC, COLA, SNLI, and ARC-b with OpenbookQA, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, PIQA, and MathQA. Coverage consequently shifts from sentiment, inference, paraphrase, and acceptability tasks toward commonsense and mathematical reasoning. Appendices A.3-A.4 also add open-ended generation cases.

E2.justification: Matched experiments retain vanilla SVD, FWSVD, and ASVD, the same ASVD comparisons for LoRA and component ablations, and the same GPTQ and LLM-Pruner integration comparisons. Added throughput and generation experiments reuse original-model and ASVD controls; no new competing compression method is introduced.

E3.justification: Downstream accuracy evaluation expands from 20% compression in v1 to 20%-60% in v4 Table 1, with LM-Evaluation-Harness explicitly identified. OPT-6.7B is added while Vicuna remains. New protocols vary calibration sample counts and source corpus, and measure throughput across compression ratios, batch sizes, and sequence lengths on GPU and CPU.

E4.justification: V4 adds calibration sensitivity analyses covering sample count, sampling seed, and source corpus (Figure 4 and Table 6), plus generation case studies with and without LoRA (Tables 10-11). V1 Table 1's adaptation-loss analysis is removed. The component ablation and KV-cache analysis remain; the latter moves to Appendix A.5.

E5.justification: V1 reports no sampling seeds or repeated-run analysis. V4 Figure 4(b) compares seeds 3, 10, 42, 57, and 100, and Table 6 identifies seed 3. This adds limited evidence about seed variability, while primary results still lack confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run summaries.

E6.justification: V4 adds or replaces substantial reasoning, OPT, calibration, throughput, and generation results. Under the same stated LLaMA-7B/60% setting, WikiText-2/PTB/C4 perplexities change from 53.74/438.58/345.49 to 42.30/312.28/246.89 (v1 Table 3; v4 Table 1). High-compression LoRA values also change between v1 Figure 4 and v4 Table 4. Accuracy averages across the replaced task suites are not directly comparable.

M1.justification: The whitening, SVD truncation, and sequential closed-form update remain, including the 40% update threshold. However, v4 explicitly includes S^-1 in weight reconstruction and the least-squares update in Equation 7, where v1's update formula omitted it. This is a limited correction to the reported computational specification; the PDFs do not establish an implementation change.

P1.justification: V4 rewrites and condenses the method exposition, merges the separate dataset and high-compression performance discussions, reorganizes experimental subsections, moves KV-cache discussion into the appendix, and removes Broader Impacts. It also changes author-year citations to numerical citations and simplifies mathematical terminology and notation throughout.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. Figures 2-3 are redrawn, v1 Tables 2-3 become an expanded combined table, and the LoRA plot becomes a numerical table. Calibration and throughput plots, generation tables, and algorithm displays are added. The unchanged KV-cache plot moves to Appendix A.5.

R1.justification: V4 adds references for the replacement benchmarks, OPT, LM-Evaluation-Harness, and an efficient-inference survey, while removing references associated with discarded tasks and the GPT-3 example. The substantive positioning against FWSVD, ASVD, pruning, and quantization remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The whitening lemma, theorem, corollary, and Appendix A.1 derivation remain. V4 specializes the theorem and corollary conditions from any S satisfying SST = XXT to the Cholesky factor, and revises the closed-form update mathematics to include inverse-whitening factors. These are limited mathematical revisions rather than a new theoretical framework.

improvement.justification: Calibration sensitivity tests and measured GPU/CPU throughput strengthen practical validation that v1 lacked, while the expanded procedural documentation helps readers understand implementation. Gains are tempered by removal of adaptation-loss evidence and errors in the new pseudocode, including intersection with an initially empty factor set in Algorithm 1. The retained all-dataset superiority claim also conflicts with v4 Table 1, such as OpenbookQA at 20% compression (0.22 versus ASVD's 0.25). Overall, the additional evidence provides a limited net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SVD-LLM by the same authors. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, allowing reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V4 retains original experimental results and adds calibration sensitivity tests, GPU/CPU throughput measurements, and generation examples in Section 4 and Appendix A.

before.justification: V1 reports original compression benchmarks, component ablations, compression timing, LoRA experiments, and KV-cache memory measurements in Section 4.

title: SVD-LLM: Truncation-aware Singular Value Decomposition for Large Language Model Compression
