The introduction expands its superiority claims to structured pruning and one-bit quantization, including a QuIP# hybrid claimed to outperform OneBit. Claimed scale coverage narrows from four scales through 65B to three scales through 30B.

C2.justification: v5 introduces an optimization-interference explanation for sequential updates and interprets DRONE differences through memory use and numerical stability. Appendix A.11 adds specific limitations concerning high-compression accuracy loss, KV-cache reconstruction latency, and poor generation despite low perplexity. These substantive qualifications were absent from v4.

D1.justification: v5 newly specifies Alpaca with 50K samples for parameter updates, explains incremental accumulation of XX^T, and documents the 40% SVD compression followed by two-bit QuIP# procedure. These are concrete implementation disclosures; naming Alpaca does not establish that v4's optional LoRA experiment used different data. The repository URL and A100/AMD hardware information are retained, while detailed LoRA hyperparameters remain unspecified.

E1.justification: The stated ten-dataset evaluation changes composition: PTB and ARC-c disappear, while TruthfulQA and GSM8K introduce explicit generation evaluations. Appendix A.5 also adds experiments on randomly generated weight and activation matrices. These changes broaden task requirements beyond the earlier benchmark coverage.

E2.justification: v5 adds reported comparisons with SliceGPT, BlockPruner, FLAP, PB-LLM, BiLLM, OneBit, StableLM-3B, and DRONE. The original SVD, FWSVD, and ASVD comparators remain. v4's GPTQ and LLM-Pruner hybrid comparisons are removed; LLM-Pruner remains in a direct comparison, and the quantization hybrid now uses QuIP#.

E3.justification: Main comparisons now include sequentially fine-tuned SVD-LLM and whitening-only controls. Table 1 changes its compression grid from 20–60% in ten-point increments to 20/40/60/80%; the scale study drops LLaMA-65B. New protocols include BLEU and exact-match generation evaluation, comparisons under specified memory budgets, and synthetic-matrix compression tests. v5 no longer explicitly states the earlier zero-shot setting, so unchanged prompting cannot be assumed.

E4.justification: The component ablation is revised for the replacement update method. v5 adds update-order sensitivity, normal versus sequential LoRA comparisons, singular-value spectrum analysis, and DRONE numerical-stability experiments. Calibration sensitivity studies remain. v4's non-fine-tuned generation case study is removed; v5 Table 14 retains a subset of the earlier fine-tuned examples.

E5.justification: v5 Table 10 newly states that compression timing covers five compressions, without specifying aggregation or variability. The seed-sensitivity sweep remains, but Table 6 drops v4's explicit seed=3 labels. Neither version reports confidence intervals or significance tests for the main benchmark results.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and expanded. At 40% compression, Table 1's LLaMA-7B WikiText-2 perplexity changes from 13.11 to 9.27 under the revised method and training, not a controlled same-setting improvement. FWSVD's 13B/30B entries change from OOM to 15.98/20.54. Reported compression time changes from 15 minutes in v4 Table 5 to 3.5 hours in v5 Table 13. New task and comparator results appear, although v5 Tables 1 and 4 conflict on whitening-only results.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 replaces the layer-wise closed-form update of U with sequential LoRA fine-tuning of the two compressed factors, freezing one while updating the other across the model. v4 already tested LoRA as an optional extension, but this sequential global update becomes a core method component in v5. Truncation-aware whitening is retained.

P1.justification: The introduction's six findings become three contribution bullets, Section 3.2 is rewritten, and the experimental narrative is reorganized around comparison groups and inference efficiency. Compression-speed discussion moves to Appendix A.8, while KV-cache analysis moves into the main text. Appendix ordering, terminology, and substantial explanatory prose also change.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn for sequential fine-tuning, the closed-form-update diagram is removed, and a spectrum figure is added. Main tables gain different task columns, memory annotations, controls, and accuracy results; several comparison and ablation tables are added. The throughput figure is largely retained and relocated, while the KV-cache figure is redrawn with fewer compression ratios and an original-model baseline.

R1.justification: v5 substantially expands positioning beyond FWSVD/ASVD and compression-method compatibility. It acknowledges DRONE's earlier data-aware optimum and argues practical memory, runtime, and numerical advantages, while adding recent structured-pruning and extreme-quantization literature. GPTQ, AWQ, and knowledge-distillation references disappear. This exceeds the accompanying citation-style and bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The whitening theorem and corollary remain, with a corrected summation endpoint and an expanded derivation in Appendix A.3. Substantial additions include the claimed optimal-loss equivalence with DRONE in Appendix A.5 and inference computation/memory derivations in Section 4.2. The earlier closed-form least-squares update expression is removed with the method replacement.

improvement.justification: v5 adds useful generation tests, broader comparisons, sequential-update controls, and explicit limitations. However, central reporting becomes inconsistent: whitening-only perplexities are 13.73/66.62 in Table 1 but 13.11/42.30 in Table 4, and Section 3.2/Algorithm 3 specify the opposite update order to the Table 5 row reproducing the main scores. Appendix A.7 also claims superiority on every dataset although Table 12 shows lower PIQA and MathQA scores. These unresolved issues affect interpretation and reproducibility, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SVD-LLM, with matching authors, the same whitening foundation, and identifiable corresponding experiments. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: v5 reports original compression benchmarks, generation evaluations, ablations, hardware measurements, and synthetic-matrix experiments, including results in Appendices A.4–A.10.

before.justification: v4 reports original compression benchmarks, component and calibration ablations, hardware measurements, and generated examples in Section 4 and the appendices.

title: SVD-LLM: Truncation-aware Singular Value Decomposition for Large Language Model Compression

These adjust contribution scope while preserving the main research claims.

It adds application-specific interpretations of MMS and Wav2Vec weaknesses, a learned-front-end hypothesis for adversarial robustness, and explicit language/scenario generalization limitations. Earlier stability interpretations and attack-specific model-selection recommendations disappear.

D1.justification: v2 adds a dataset repository address, dataset licenses, Bridges-2/V100 hardware information, additional effect parameters, and detailed selection rules for accented and conversational speech. Appendix B newly discloses punctuation removal and lowercasing before WER computation; this does not establish that preprocessing changed. v1 already supplied code access and substantial perturbation implementation details.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's LibriSpeech and Spanish Multilingual LibriSpeech evaluations, v2 adds TEDLIUM, selected Common Voice accents, and CHiME-6/AMI conversations with near- and far-field recordings. Evaluated conditions also expand to music, crosstalk, real room responses, and additional audio effects. These introduce substantive speech-domain and input-environment coverage.

Additional Whisper, Wav2Vec, HuBERT, and MMS participants enter these comparisons; some were already represented elsewhere in v1. Spanish comparisons add Canary and Whisper-base. Simulated-RIR severity changes from SNR-based grouping to RT60, while real RIRs use SRMR.

E4.justification: v1's prediction-stability analysis under repeated Gaussian and environmental noise is removed. v2 adds a focused Canary-versus-Whisper failure analysis for acoustics and effects (Figure 4), Spanish adversarial diagnostics, and gender-disparity analysis across additional corpora. Existing severity and within-family model-size analyses remain, with revised evidence.

These are localized statistical changes; neither version reports confidence intervals or training-seed replication. WERV measured prediction variability, not confidence in estimated mean performance.

E6.justification: Result sets and rankings change substantially. v1 Figure 5a ranks Spanish Wav2Vec-large ahead of Whisper-large, with NWER 0.335 versus 0.379; v2 Figure 3e ranks Whisper-large first, followed by Canary and MMS under NWERD. Different metrics and perturbation settings prevent interpreting this as a same-setting performance gain. Numerous model, natural-speech, Spanish-attack, and speech-quality results are added, while WERV results disappear.

M1.justification: The benchmark pipeline changes substantially. v1 requires target and baseline ASR transcriptions and includes repeated perturbations for prediction stability. v2 replaces the baseline-ASR branch with DNSMOS/PESQ speech-quality estimation, processes inherently noisy recordings directly, and removes the stability component (Section 3 and Figure 1).

P1.justification: The introduction and benchmark-positioning discussion are extensively rewritten. Evaluation is reorganized into separate model, clean-accuracy, non-adversarial, and adversarial sections. Definitions and model documentation move into expanded appendices; a limitations section is added, the conclusion is shortened, and v1's impact statement and acknowledgments are removed.

P2.justification: The main text switches from two columns to one, diagrams are redrawn, and result plots become reorganized panels and per-perturbation small multiples. Speech-quality and license tables are added, and the model table moves to the appendix. v1 Figure 12 is reused unchanged as v2 Figure 10. v2's taxonomy figure partly extends beyond the page boundary.

R1.justification: The introduction and Section 2.3 substantially reposition SRB as integrating existing speech benchmarks and complementing the Open ASR Leaderboard. This replaces much of v1's emphasis on limited benchmarking beyond digit recognition. New discussion and references cover conversational/noisy datasets, additional models, speech-quality estimation, and fairness through robustness.

T1.justification: Mathematical revisions concern metric definitions: baseline-ratio NWER is replaced by speech-quality normalization, WERV's definition is removed, and WERD is explicitly defined. WER degradation already appeared in v1's language comparison. WER, LWERR, and the SNR/PGD derivations are retained or relocated; no theorem or proof development is added.

improvement.justification: The added accented and conversational speech evaluations substantially strengthen the basis for real-world robustness conclusions: they expose additional model weaknesses and show that gender-disparity direction depends on the corpus. Separating clean accuracy from degradation and adding curation, access, licensing, and hardware information improve interpretation and reuse. Losing prediction-stability testing and retaining prose/chart ranking inconsistencies, such as Section 4.4 versus Figure 3c, are drawbacks, but the broader diagnostic evidence and better-qualified conclusions provide a substantial overall gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Speech Robust Bench. All 15 pages of v1 and 20 pages of v2, including their appendices, support matching the methods, equations, experiments, and displays. Minor clipping of v2's taxonomy figure does not prevent comparison because its embedded image and accompanying descriptions are available.

after.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original experiments across expanded speech datasets and model comparisons, including robustness, gender disparities, and estimated speech-quality results.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix B report original ASR experiments on perturbed English and Spanish speech, including accuracy, prediction stability, adversarial robustness, and gender disparities.

title: Speech Robust Bench: A Robustness Benchmark For Speech Recognition

C1.justification: The conclusion removes v2's explicit claim to be the first ASR robustness benchmark containing long-form speech. The central contributions—comprehensive standardized evaluation, model robustness analysis and subgroup disparities—remain. Recasting 114 perturbations as 114 challenging scenarios mostly changes framing.

C2.justification: v3 adds the hypothesis that Whisper's robustness reflects diverse digital-media and acoustic training conditions, motivating broader data curation. It removes v2's learned-front-end explanation for adversarial robustness and explains why model-specific attacks should use WERD rather than quality-normalized NWERD. The general limitations paragraph remains essentially unchanged.

D1.justification: Table 4 newly documents dataset splits, hours, utterance counts and speaker composition; Appendix A specifies attack development samples and provides pseudocode. Access instructions also change: the dataset URL is omitted, the code link becomes anonymous, and the release description explicitly excludes perturbed TEDLIUM and adversarial recordings. Existing hardware and basic augmentation settings are retained.

E1.justification: Table 7 extends evaluation beyond English/Spanish to MLS-DU and MLS-FR clean and corrupted speech. Spanish evaluation also adds Common Voice 17 accented speech and synthetic speech, which are absent from v2's Spanish results. These additions substantially broaden the languages and speech conditions tested.

The focused corruption comparison also changes from Canary, Whisper-medium and Whisper-small in v2 Figure 4 to Canary, Whisper-medium, Whisper-large and Parakeet in v3 Figure 3.

These are reported-setting differences; the PDFs do not establish reruns or resolve the actual noise regime.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 adds architecture-based robustness comparisons and analyses relating robustness to clean accuracy, including Pareto-optimal points (Figure 5c–e). The within-family size analysis now includes Parakeet. Existing perturbation, severity and subgroup analyses are largely retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new architecture boxplots summarize variation across evaluated models rather than introducing uncertainty estimates for benchmark results.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 7 add substantial numerical results for new models, language subsets and speech conditions. For example, v3 reports Canary's Spanish-accent NWERD as 699.9, exposing a failure condition absent from v2's Spanish evaluation. These expanded-setting results should not be interpreted as same-setting performance changes; several older appendix plots remain identical.

M1.justification: Scenario generation gains a language-specific component: v3 uses Bark and its speaker library for Spanish synthetic speech alongside the existing English YourTTS/VCTK route (Section 3.1). The core perturbation, transcription and scoring pipeline remains; expanded attack descriptions alone do not establish a changed attack algorithm.

P1.justification: Related work is rewritten around three shortcomings, dataset and perturbation descriptions are consolidated into Scenario Simulation, and evaluation is reorganized around adversarial/non-adversarial comparisons, correlates and subgroup disparities. This constitutes substantial main-text rewriting and restructuring beyond the citation-style and header changes.

P2.justification: v2 Figure 3 moves unchanged to appendix Figure 8 while a new numerical Table 1 becomes the main summary. Pipeline and taxonomy diagrams are redrawn, comparison and gender figures are revised, and dataset-statistics and extensive result tables are added. The former Figure 5 is redistributed and expanded across several figures.

R1.justification: v3 adds focused citations supporting the expansion, including SpeechBrain, CTC, SpecAugment, Bark and the PESQ implementation, while dropping SpokenWOZ and replacing the accented-language-identification citation with CSLU. Section 2.3 sharpens criticism of older benchmark coverage, but the overall research positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: Appendix A adds a formal utterance-agnostic attack specification with an infinity-norm constraint, CER-based success criterion and Algorithm 1, beyond v2's brief description and generic constrained expression. The existing SNR derivation and WER/LWERR definitions remain; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: Broader evaluated coverage, explicit numerical comparisons and new architecture/accuracy analyses make v3 more informative, particularly by exposing Canary's Spanish-accent weakness. The gain is limited by documentation regressions: the dataset link is omitted, noise SNRs conflict between Section 3.1 and Table 2, and Table 7 labels the Spanish-accent value 205.0 as NWERD although Section 4.2.1 identifies it as WERD.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Speech Robust Bench with the same authors and underlying benchmark. Their main texts, appendices, equations, tables and embedded figures support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark experiments and adds model comparisons, language coverage and robustness analyses, reported in Tables 1 and 7 and Section 4.

before.justification: v2 reports original ASR evaluations under clean, corrupted and adversarial conditions, including model-size and demographic analyses in Section 4 and the appendices.

title: Speech Robust Bench: A Robustness Benchmark For Speech Recognition

C1.justification: Both claim that lower-timestep denoising is harder and that an easy-to-hard curriculum improves generation and convergence while remaining compatible with existing techniques. SiT adds evidence for the retained model-agnostic claim. Correcting 'descending' to 'ascending' difficulty aligns wording with the already-described method.

C2.justification: The curriculum-design discussion removes v1's explicit attribution of anti-curriculum gains to SNR clustering. Appendix I adds a limited qualification concerning hyperparameter choices and model-adaptive curricula, refining the existing future-work discussion. D1.justification: v2 newly discloses eight A100 GPUs, optimizer/learning-rate reuse for observation experiments, and that the retained qualitative comparisons use final DiT-B checkpoints. Conversely, v1's dataset-size summaries are omitted. These are documentation changes, not evidence of changed hardware or regenerated comparison images.

Appendix B changes the reported DiT observation sampler from 250-step DDIM to DDPM and specifies EDM quantile intervals instead of v1's uniform-interval description. These reporting revisions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

SiT convergence curves and 2M-iteration DiT-L samples are also new. Existing tabulated numbers and qualitative comparison images are retained; these additions are not improvements over v1 under identical settings.

Section 5 clarifies the same procedure; applying it to SiT does not introduce a new curriculum component. The algorithms are relocated and renumbered.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites clarify cluster accumulation and pacing and correct the difficulty-order wording. KL estimators, algorithms and metric descriptions move into appendices, an appendix contents page is added, and orthogonality becomes part of Section 6.3. The overall narrative and main-section order remain.

P2.justification: v2 substantially revises typography and page layout, adds the curriculum overview diagram in Figure 3, expands Figure 1 from four to six panels, and reorganizes Table 1 around prediction parameterizations. It also adds five large sample collages in Figures E–I and rearranges retained figures, tables and algorithms.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to SiT, Karras et al.'s diffusion training-dynamics work and Switch Diffusion Transformer, while removing DiffWave and Weinshall–Amir's curriculum-theory reference. The positioning around denoising difficulty and curriculum learning remains substantially unchanged.

improvement.justification: The SiT experiments strengthen support for applicability across prediction parameterizations, while Figure 3 and clearer curriculum explanations improve comprehension. before.justification: v1 reports original DiT and EDM generation experiments, convergence measurements and curriculum ablations in Sections 4 and 6 and Appendix E.

title: Denoising Task Difficulty-based Curriculum for Training Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The abstract is identical, and the introduction and conclusion retain the same principal claims: smaller-timestep denoising is harder, and difficulty-based curriculum training improves generation and convergence while remaining compatible with existing techniques. The new experiments support these retained claims.

E1.justification: Both versions cover unconditional FFHQ generation, class-conditional CIFAR-10 and ImageNet generation, and MS-COCO text-to-image generation. The new ImageNet convergence analysis reuses existing dataset and task coverage; longer training and larger models add settings.

P1.justification: v3 adopts author-year citations, updates publication and author-affiliation information, subdivides Appendix A, and adds focused experimental and discussion paragraphs. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v3 adds Table 2 and Appendix Figures A-B, expands the model-size table with XL rows, and adopts ICLR headers and typography. Existing displays are repositioned and renumbered, including regrouping qualitative panels. The original plots and sample images are retained.

improvement.justification: The matched 2M-iteration comparison adds quantitative support beyond v2's qualitative samples, while DiT-XL results and the ImageNet convergence analysis strengthen validation of scalability and the central observation. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same curriculum-learning work. Text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds longer-training comparisons, DiT-XL results, and convergence analyses in Appendix B.

before.justification: v2 reports original convergence experiments, image-generation benchmarks, ablations, and qualitative results in Sections 4 and 6 and Appendices F-G.

title: Denoising Task Difficulty-based Curriculum for Training Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The central contributions remain literature synthesis, a curated benchmark, architectural baselines, and reusable code. v3 refines the earlier multi-class/multi-label framing toward standardized multi-label PAM evaluation and explicitly includes standardized training protocols and released trainable model parameters among its contributions. The new empirical evidence principally supports already stated goals.

C2.justification: v3 develops substantive explanations of covariate shift, label uncertainty, task shift, and adaptability beyond v1's brief challenge list. It adds interpretations of architecture and training-regime differences, validation-leakage concerns, and limitations concerning restricted test environments and the absence of detailed rare-species or location-specific failure analyses (Sections 2, 4.2, and 5; Appendices B.2 and C.6).

D1.justification: v3 adds model and optimizer settings, preprocessing and augmentation parameters, sampling limits, hardware descriptions, metadata schemas, licensing, and dataset-maintenance information (Table 8; Appendices B–D). It also provides trained-checkpoint and detailed-results access information beyond v1's high-level dataset/code links and tracking statement.

E1.justification: v1 presents generic XC training and soundscape testing without dataset-specific experiments. v3 reports training on XCL/XCM and dedicated subsets, testing on PER, NES, UHH, HSN, NBP, SSW, and SNE, and using POW for validation and VOX for augmentation. This establishes substantial empirical coverage across American and European environments (Table 4; Appendix B.5).

E2.justification: v1 promises unspecified architectural baselines but reports no comparisons. v3 evaluates EfficientNet, ConvNext, AST, EAT, and W2V2 across three training regimes, with inference-only Perch included in the LT comparison (Tables 5 and 9–11). BirdNET is explicitly excluded for leakage; it was not an evaluated comparator in v1.

E3.justification: v3 adds operational protocols for newly reported large, medium, and dedicated training experiments. These specify five-second evaluation segments, the 0.5-second label-overlap rule, cmAP/AUROC/T1-Acc metrics, POW validation for LT/MT, a 20% validation split for DT, checkpoint selection, and model-specific training budgets (Sections 3–4; Appendix C). v1 provides only a schematic protocol.

E4.justification: v3 adds illustrative validation-loss curves examining early overfitting in AST and ConvNext versus continued improvement in EAT (Appendix C.6, Figure 10). Appendix B.6 also adds descriptive species-composition, vocalization-overlap, and geographic analyses. These are limited diagnostic additions; v1 contains no corresponding analyses.

E5.justification: v1 reports neither repetitions nor uncertainty. v3 introduces repeated-seed means and standard deviations throughout Tables 9–11. Section 4.1 and Table 8 specify three seeds for LT/MT and five for DT, but Table 11's caption says five for LT. The reporting addition is clear, although the actual LT run count is unresolved.

C2.justification: V2 explains how greedy acceptance can impair later iterations through target-distribution modifications and why that procedure cannot simply replace verification in the unchanged loop. It explicitly qualifies the new optimality guarantee by this algorithmic scope and adds an interpretation connecting drafter quality to verification gains.

The additional methods discussed in related work are not experimental baselines.

Figures 3–4 and Appendix C, Table 3 address whether better drafters amplify gains and whether maximizing acceptance within one block improves iterative decoding.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging across three random seeds. V2 newly reports standard deviations for efficiencies, speedups, and relative improvements in Table 1 and Tables 4–8. This improves uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in run count.

Some baseline values change, while detailed greedy timing and shorter-block results disappear. Changed procedures and unmapped model names limit direct cross-version score comparisons.

V2 introduces a different main verifier with recursively clipped acceptance probabilities and a revised residual distribution, allowing subsequent iterations to use the unchanged target model.

The title and author list also change.

The two Luo 2024 entries correspond to the previously cited Energy-calibrated VAE work. The main related-work discussion and research positioning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, objectives, Proposition 1, and Appendix C proof are retained. Removing the explicit multiplication symbol in Equation 3 is mathematically equivalent typesetting, not a theoretical revision.

improvement.justification: The added ImageNet-64 and FFHQ-1024 experiments broaden empirical support beyond v5's CIFAR-10 training-from-scratch evidence, while COCO reporting and the feature-layer analysis provide useful additional checks. The gain is limited by sparse documentation of the new protocols and an overbroad ImageNet interpretation: Table 5 reports YOSO FID 2.65, behind StyleGAN-XL at 1.52, ADM at 2.07, and EDM at 1.36. Overall, the evidence strengthens the paper, but does not fully support the breadth of the added performance language.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same YOSO research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison. v6 retains Appendices A–G and adds Appendices H–I.

after.justification: v6 retains those original results and adds ImageNet-64, FFHQ-1024, and zero-shot COCO experiments in Tables 5–7, plus additional qualitative comparisons.

before.justification: v5 reports original CIFAR-10 generation experiments, text-to-image evaluations, component ablations, and qualitative application results in Tables 1–4 and Figures 1–8.

title: You Only Sample Once: Taming One-Step Text-to-Image Synthesis by Self-Cooperative Diffusion GANs

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and closing section retain the same central contributions: exposing limitations of VQA/captioning-based ICL evaluation, introducing a broad multimodal benchmark, and identifying VLLM strengths and weaknesses. The expanded experiments support this existing agenda.

C2.justification: v1 primarily attributes poor shot scaling to context and image-token limitations. v2 qualifies this explanation by arguing that context extension alone is insufficient, interprets model-size comparisons as evidence of an emergent ICL threshold, and discusses progress over release dates. Its Discussion also explicitly acknowledges limited text-to-image model coverage.

D1.justification: Appendix Table 6 expands configuration documentation with connection modules, image-token representations and context windows for newer models. Conversely, v2 removes v1's code/dataset access link and A100-80GB hardware disclosure. These are documentation changes; the PDFs do not establish that the resources became unavailable.

E1.justification: The main suite expands from eight to ten tasks, adding Fast Counting and Fast Attribute Matching, which require generating images using newly learned count or attribute names. v2 also evaluates an artificial-label Fast Matching MiniImageNet variant; conventional Matching MiniImageNet results remain in Appendix Table 23.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated models including IDEFICS2, VILA, Mantis, Phi3-Vision, LongVA, LLaVA-OneVision and InternLM-XComposer2.5. Appendix Table 27 additionally evaluates Anole-7B on text-to-image MiniImageNet. LongVA and Mantis also join the retained many-shot comparisons in Tables 42–45.

E3.justification: v2 introduces peak accuracy, normalized ICL efficiency and average-rank summaries, plus controlled 4K-to-16K SelfExtend evaluations and LLaVA-OneVision comparisons at 0.5B, 7B and 72B parameters. The COCO judging protocol is inconsistently described: Section 2.2 now names GPT-3.5, while Table 12 retains v1's LLaVA-Next attribution, so an actual judge replacement is unresolved.

E4.justification: v2 adds context-extension and model-size studies, efficiency-versus-zero-shot analysis, and performance trends by model release date. It expands the existing 64-shot study to additional models. Earlier prompting, repetition and instruction-tuning analyses remain, while v1's aggregate per-shot accuracy-increment analysis is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three random seeds and retain the same average and plus/minus reporting practices in detailed result tables. Additional rows extend these practices without introducing new uncertainty procedures, significance tests or an increased run count.

E6.justification: New tasks, models, metrics and controls add substantial results, and the expanded comparison identifies LLaVA-OneVision-72B instead of GPT4V as the overall image-to-text leader. LLaVA-Next-7B's 4-/5-shot Fast Open-Ended MiniImageNet entries change from 0.00/0.33 to 37.24/36.95 (v1 Table 12; v2 Table 16). However, v2 Table 54 retains the old values, preventing a clean performance-gain interpretation.

M1.justification: The work remains a benchmark using pretrained models and support/query prompting, without proposing a revised learning algorithm, architecture or objective. SelfExtend appears as an additional controlled evaluation of an existing technique.

P1.justification: v2 shortens the title and several task descriptions, folds Text Variation into a paragraph, renames Conclusion to Discussion, and relocates qualitative discussion to Appendix C. Most introductory prose, motivation and the main section sequence remain recognizable.

P2.justification: The main results presentation shifts to summary Tables 2–5 and selected curves. The updated radar plot moves earlier, while full benchmark curves and qualitative images move to the appendices. Figure 1 gains two task illustrations, and new model-size, efficiency, context-extension and temporal plots substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds recent model and SelfExtend references, cites additional multimodal ICL studies, and explicitly distinguishes its scope from Jiang et al. (2024b)'s recognition-focused many-shot evaluation. The existing related-work organization and principal novelty positioning remain intact.

T1.justification: v2 defines ICL efficiency through normalized area above zero-shot performance and states the bound that zero-shot accuracy plus efficiency cannot exceed 100% (Section 4.1 and Appendix B.7). The original probabilistic ICL formulation remains unchanged; no substantial theorem or proof development is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves the benchmark's diagnostic value by experimentally probing context length and model size, addressing v1's largely conjectural explanation of shot-scaling failures. Added generation tasks and artificial-label matching broaden the learning abilities tested, while efficiency summaries distinguish adaptation from zero-shot competence. These gains outweigh the reduced reproducibility documentation and reporting inconsistencies, particularly conflicting LLaVA baseline entries and caption-judge attribution, which still require clarification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VL-ICL Bench work. Their complete text, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable, allowing retained, revised and added material to be matched.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations of further tasks and models, context extension and model-size scaling.

before.justification: v1 reports original VLLM benchmark evaluations, image-generation results and analyses of shot scaling, prompting and instruction tuning in Section 4 and the appendices.

title: VL-ICL Bench: The Devil in the Details of Multimodal In-Context Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and discussion retain the same central contributions: limitations of conventional VQA/captioning evaluations, a diverse multimodal ICL benchmark, and evidence of uneven model capabilities. The added analyses do not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: B.10 newly presents demonstration selection as a promising route to improving ICL and claims consistent benefits, although its tables contain exceptions. B.11 concludes that the strongest models are LLaVA-like but finds no general separation between architecture families. Existing limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands benchmark-construction documentation across all ten tasks, including source-split sampling, TextOCR filtering and largest-text selection, CoBSAT partitioning, and synthetic counting-image construction. B.10 specifies retrieval modalities and ordering, and the abstract adds a project-page link. These are disclosures, not evidence that the original datasets changed.

E1.justification: The ten-task suite and auxiliary VQA, captioning, and text-only evaluations remain. The new selection experiments reuse CLEVR, TextOCR, and CoBSAT. Although v2's separate Matching MiniImageNet Table 23 disappears, that task remains in Figure 10 and v3 Table 53.

E2.justification: v3 adds comparisons between three CLIP-based selection/order variants and random selection in Tables 7–10. The main VLLM roster is unchanged, but the full multi-model Matching MiniImageNet comparison in v2 Table 23 is removed; its two-model chain-of-thought comparison remains.

E3.justification: The added selection study compares most-similar-first, least-similar-first, and shuffled retrieved demonstrations against random selection at 1, 2, 4, and 8 shots. Existing benchmark metrics and settings remain unchanged. Appendix A's new sampling descriptions disclose construction details rather than establish revised experiments.

E4.justification: Appendix B.10 adds a systematic sensitivity study of demonstration selection and ordering across both output modalities, addressing a previously untested factor in ICL performance. B.11 additionally examines architecture families alongside release dates. Existing prompting, context-extension, model-size, and qualitative analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions state that experiments use three random seeds and report averages. Retained detailed tables preserve their uncertainty entries. The new retrieval tables provide point estimates without introducing a different run-count policy, uncertainty estimator, or significance test.

E6.justification: Tables 7–10 add retrieval-condition results: for example, Phi3-Vision's CLEVR peak is 42.0% with retrieval versus 34.5% with random selection. These are new protocol comparisons, not revised same-setting scores. v2 Table 23's separate Matching results are removed; matched retained numerical tables are unchanged.

M1.justification: Appendix B.10 adds an optional context-construction procedure using CLIP embeddings to retrieve top-k demonstrations and arrange them in three orders. This supplements the existing random-selection procedure; the evaluated model architectures, training objectives, and default benchmark remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section organization are retained. v3 adds acknowledgements and appendix subsections, updates the contents list and citation presentation, and makes limited wording corrections, including the Figure 3 caption.

P2.justification: v3 adds four retrieval tables and an architecture-comparison figure, removes v2 Table 23, and relocates the unchanged qualitative Figure 17 as Figure 18. Conference formatting changes headings, headers, and float placement, while existing plots and table designs largely remain.

R1.justification: B.10 adds positioning around demonstration selection, citing new works by Yuanhan Zhang et al. (2023b), Li et al. (2024c), and Yang et al. (2023), alongside previously cited Chen et al. Most other reference changes update publication metadata, including the attribution of the same GPT-4 technical report.

T1.justification: The conditional-probability formulation of ICL, task definitions, ICL-efficiency definition, and zero-shot/efficiency constraint remain unchanged. Neither version adds a theoretical proof or derivation.

improvement.justification: The dataset-construction disclosures and new selection controls make the benchmark easier to reproduce and interpret. Benefits are tempered by removal of the full Matching comparison and an overstated retrieval conclusion: Table 10 gives Mantis a CLEVR peak of 40.2% with random selection versus 36.0–36.5% with retrieval. The retained main evidence is unchanged, supporting a limited net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VL-ICL Bench study. The main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–D support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v3 retains those original evaluations and adds demonstration-selection experiments and an analysis by model architecture in Appendices B.10–B.11.

before.justification: v2 reports original multimodal ICL evaluations, controlled analyses, and qualitative findings, with detailed numerical results in Appendix D.

title: VL-ICL Bench: The Devil in the Details of Multimodal In-Context Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and discussion retain the same benchmark contributions and claims about existing ICL evaluations and VLLM capabilities.

C2.justification: Interpretations of model size, context length and instruction tuning are unchanged, as are the qualitative error discussions and limitation concerning limited text-to-image model coverage.

D1.justification: Model configurations, decoding instructions, prompts, dataset sampling/filtering details and project access information remain unchanged in Section 4.1 and Appendix A.

E1.justification: The same ten benchmark tasks, VQA/captioning evaluations, text-only comparisons and supplementary test scenarios are retained.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged throughout, including the three LLaVA-OneVision sizes in Figure 7 and the base/instruction-tuned models in Table 40.

E3.justification: The Fast Open-Ended MiniImageNet panel in Figure 7 changes its final shot count from 8 to 5, and Table 40 changes its final column from 8-Shot to 5-Shot. E4.justification: The model-size, instruction-tuning, context-extension, prompting and other supplementary analyses are retained. The shot-label corrections do not introduce new analyses or additional evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions state three random seeds in Section 4.1 and retain the same averaging and uncertainty reporting in the appendix tables.

E6.justification: Accuracy values, model rankings and qualitative findings are unchanged. Figure 7 and Table 40 revise shot-count labels rather than performance values; these reporting corrections are covered under E3 and P2.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction, model components and in-context inference procedures are unchanged.

P1.justification: Only the first-page arXiv version/date stamp changes, from v3 dated 2 February 2025 to v4 dated 31 March 2025. Prose, terminology and section organization are unchanged.

P2.justification: Figure 7's Fast Open-Ended MiniImageNet panel is redrawn with a five-shot endpoint and corresponding horizontal spacing. Table 40's final column heading changes to 5-Shot. The remaining figures, tables and document layout are retained.

R1.justification: The cited works, bibliography and research positioning in Section 5 are unchanged.

T1.justification: The ICL formulation in Equation 1, task definitions and ICL-efficiency reasoning are unchanged. No formal assumptions, proofs or derivations are added or revised.

improvement.justification: The revised shot labels improve consistency with five-shot reporting already present in Table 20 and Figures 8 and 12, reducing misleading descriptions of experimental conditions. The benefit is limited: scores and conclusions are unchanged, and Table 63 still retains a conflicting 8-Shot heading.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same VL-ICL Bench study, with complete main text and Appendices A-D. Their text, equations, tables and rendered figures support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains these original benchmark results, model comparisons, ablations and qualitative analyses.

before.justification: v3 reports original VLLM benchmark experiments, including image-to-text and text-to-image results in Tables 2-3 and supplementary experiments in Appendices B-D.

title: VL-ICL Bench: The Devil in the Details of Multimodal In-Context Learning

C1.justification: The central claims about training-time physical constraints, residual reduction, unchanged inference, and regularization remain. However, the contribution statement replaces the explicit '1–2 orders of magnitude' claim with 'significantly reduces,' drops the claim of minimal additional training cost, and explicitly extends applicability to differentiable surrogate constraints or objectives.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes ideal sample-based consistency from the conflicting objective introduced by mean estimation and uses this to explain convergence differences. It adds qualifications about discretization bias, excessive residual weighting causing collapse, and reduced accuracy with an uninformative prior. The topology discussion acknowledges that compliance comparisons are affected by differing volume errors, adding an important interpretation boundary.

D1.justification: v2 adds DDIM implementation details, topology conditioning and finite-element assembly/interpolation instructions, and expanded hyperparameter tables. Appendix G discloses GPU hardware and training times, including 13/16/22 hours for standard/mean-estimation/sample-estimation Darcy models. v1 promised code upon publication; v2 states that code is available and supplies a repository link. Availability is reported by the PDF, not independently verified.

E1.justification: v2 adds conditional structural topology optimization using 30,000 optimized structures, with both seen and unseen boundary-condition test scenarios (Section 4.2). This extends coverage from unit-circle sampling and unconditional Darcy fields to constrained mechanical design. The original toy and Darcy tasks remain, partly relocated to Appendix F.

E2.justification: The Darcy comparison retains standard diffusion, PG-Diffusion, and CoCoGen. v2 adds evaluated topology-optimization comparisons against TopoDiff-G and DOM in Table 1, alongside standard diffusion. TopoDiff's earlier citation in v1 did not constitute an experimental comparison.

E3.justification: Toy training changes from 200 to 400 epochs and from learning rate 0.001 to 0.0005. v2 introduces batch size 16 for Darcy sample estimation versus 64 for mean estimation, and a larger topology model trained for 600k iterations with batch size 4. The new topology protocol reports residual, compliance, and volume-fraction metrics and explicitly evaluates DOM without SIMP post-processing (Appendices F–G).

E4.justification: v2 compares mean and sample estimation on Darcy residuals and convergence, and extends the four toy loss/data ablations to both estimators (Figures 2, 5–6). The topology study additionally tests generalization to unseen boundary conditions. These introduce substantive questions about estimator behavior and robustness beyond v1's retained toy ablations.

E5.justification: The toy results newly report averages over ten training runs with different seeds and 25th/75th-percentile bands (Figures 5–6). v1 Figure 2 reports averaging over generated samples without training-run uncertainty. This is a meaningful but localized reporting improvement; comparable repeated-run uncertainty is not added to the main PDE benchmarks.

E6.justification: v2 adds sample-estimation results, replaces toy curves under revised training settings, and adds the topology results in Table 1. For example, PIDM's in-/out-of-distribution residuals are 1.24e−3/1.29e−3 versus standard diffusion's 1.86e−3/1.97e−3, while standard diffusion has lower compliance error. The new results establish additional tradeoffs; revised toy and Darcy curves should not be interpreted as same-setting gains between versions.

M1.justification: v2 adds a two-step DDIM sample-estimation alternative to evaluating constraints on the predicted conditional mean (Section 3.3, Algorithm 1, Appendix D). The written loss also changes residual aggregation and variance weighting relative to v1 Eq. (19). The topology-optimization adaptation introduces conditioning inputs, joint density/displacement outputs, and finite-element residual evaluation.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: the toy study moves to Appendix F.1, detailed Darcy setup to F.2, loss simplification to C, and inequality/optimization objectives to E. Section 3.3 is rewritten around two estimators, while related work and the conclusion are condensed. The appendices gain a thematic A–H structure.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is revised to show both estimators, the Darcy learning-curve display gains another method, and the toy display becomes two appendix figures with uncertainty bands. v2 adds the topology comparison table and design/residual figures, expands the architecture/training tables, and reorganizes Darcy sample displays with an additional appendix gallery. These are substantive display changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands its theoretical context through DDIM, score-based SDEs, Jensen-gap analysis, consistency models, and score-matching literature. Section 5 additionally positions PIDM against topology-specific TopoDiff and newly cited DOM, emphasizing the absence of auxiliary datasets or surrogate models. The original comparison with inference-time physics corrections remains.

T1.justification: v2 adds an idealized continuous-time score-model consistency proposition and proof in Appendix A, replacing v1's brief consistency argument with a formal treatment. Section 3.3 identifies the Jensen-gap inconsistency of mean-based residual evaluation. The residual becomes a concatenated constraint vector, with MAE separately defined for evaluation. Much of v1's likelihood-ratio and auxiliary-objective mathematics is retained in Appendices C and E.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important weakness in v1's consistency rationale by identifying the mean-estimation approximation, providing an explicitly idealized proof, and testing a sample-based alternative. Conditional topology optimization substantially broadens validation, while seeded toy results, implementation details, timing disclosures, and reported code access improve transparency and reproducibility. The topology comparisons remain limited by differing volume errors and training budgets, and the proof does not guarantee practical discretized behavior, but the overall gains in scientific support are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Physics-Informed Diffusion Models work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including material moved between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on unit-circle sampling, Darcy flow, and topology optimization, including estimator comparisons, generated samples, and quantitative benchmark results in Table 1.

before.justification: v1 reports original unit-circle and Darcy-flow experiments, including generated samples, residual errors, and training/test-loss curves in Figures 2–4.

title: Physics-Informed Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The abstract makes the outperformance claim benchmark-specific, including up to two orders of magnitude lower flow residuals. The introduction explicitly positions PIDM as filling a missing first-principles framework unifying diffusion models and PINNs, extending v2's presentation of constraint-informed training and synergies. The principal regularization, inference-speed, and constraint-generality claims remain.

C2.justification: Section 3.1 adds an interpretation of the residual objective as sampling from an unnormalized target and distinguishes this from data-free sampling. Section 3.3 adds a temperature/annealing analogy. The sensitivity discussion also gives more specific guidance on balancing diversity and residual minimization; the existing fixed-grid limitation remains unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix A.6.3 documents the added baselines' residual components and explains that CoCoGen's full Jacobian exceeds available GPU memory, motivating constant scaling and a parameter search. v3 also explicitly supplies the toy residual formula and Darcy residual assembly. The architecture and training tables, hardware, runtimes, and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the unit-circle toy problem, Darcy permeability/pressure fields, and topology optimization with in- and out-of-distribution boundary conditions. The Gaussian-prior toy variant already appears in v2. The added weight sweep uses the existing task and does not introduce new data or environmental conditions.

E2.justification: v3 Table 1 adds PG-Diffusion and CoCoGen to the topology-optimization comparison, alongside the retained Diffusion, TopoDiff-G, and DOM baselines. These two methods previously participated only in the Darcy comparison. This is a limited extension of comparator membership within an existing benchmark.

E3.justification: v3 Figure 7 introduces evaluation of 400 generated samples at each of six residual weights: 0, 0.005, 0.02, 0.04, 1, and 5. Appendix A.6.3 specifies equilibrium and volume residuals for the added topology baselines and a constant CoCoGen scaling selected by median residual on the in-distribution test set. Existing splits, metrics, and training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix A.6.1 and new Figure 7 systematically test how residual weighting affects constraint error and sample diversity. v2 already compared four loss/prior configurations and discussed collapse under excessive residual weighting, but lacked this six-setting sensitivity analysis. The existing ablations and out-of-distribution evaluations are retained.

E5.justification: Figures 5–6 retain the same reporting of 10 training runs with different seeds and 25th/75th-percentile bands. Figure 2 retains averages and individual residuals for 16 samples every 10,000 iterations. No new repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or statistical estimation procedures are specified for the added results.

E6.justification: Retained benchmark scores and sample figures are unchanged. New Table 1 rows report in-/out-of-distribution residuals of 1.82e-3/1.92e-3 for PG-Diffusion and 1.51e-3/1.56e-3 for CoCoGen, plus compliance and volume errors. Figure 7 adds residual values from 0.080 at c=0 to 0.0024 at c=5, accompanied by lost diversity. These are additional results, not improvements to previously reported PIDM scores.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the PIDM loss, equation 13 in v2 and equation 14 in v3, retain the same training procedure, residual weighting, and mean or two-pass DDIM estimation. The architectures and extensions for inequality constraints and optimization objectives are unchanged. New baseline adaptations do not change PIDM itself.

P1.justification: The abstract, portions of the introduction, and Darcy-results discussion are rewritten, with added explanations of coordinates, residuals, and clean-signal estimates. Citations become author–year references, and Appendices A–H become subsections A.1–A.8. The main section sequence and most technical prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds the six-panel sensitivity Figure 7, expands and resizes Table 1, and reformats the hyperparameter tables. Retained figures are relocated or regrouped, and the document adopts ICLR title, heading, and running-header styling. Earlier Figures 7–8 remain as Figures 8–9 with the same sample content.

R1.justification: v3 adds connections to data-free sampling through Zhang and Chen's Path Integral Sampler, Vargas et al., and Berner et al., and to annealed combinatorial optimization through Sanokowski et al. The first-principles novelty positioning becomes more explicit, while most related-work discussion remains. Publication and title updates for retained references are bibliographic changes.

T1.justification: The consistency proposition and proof, score-based estimation, likelihood-ratio approximation, DDIM derivation, and auxiliary-objective mathematics are retained. The newly displayed residual-vector equation in Section 2.2 restates v2's concatenation of PDE and boundary-condition residuals rather than introducing a new mathematical construction.

improvement.justification: The added topology baselines broaden the comparative evidence, while Figure 7 directly demonstrates the residual–diversity tradeoff that v2 discussed largely qualitatively. Clearer residual definitions and baseline implementation details also improve interpretability. These are limited gains: the core method, proof, and retained results are unchanged, and the new CoCoGen comparison applies to the disclosed constant-scaling adaptation rather than an exact reproduction.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Physics-Informed Diffusion Models by the same authors. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison; v2 Appendices A–H correspond to v3 Sections A.1–A.8.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds topology-optimization baseline results and a unit-circle loss-weight sensitivity study.

before.justification: v2 reports original Darcy-flow and topology-optimization experiments, plus unit-circle experiments comparing training objectives and residual-estimation methods.

title: Physics-Informed Diffusion Models

C1.justification: v1 presents LS-induced degradation as something this work reveals; v2 explicitly credits earlier observations and frames the empirical contribution as broader validation, emphasizing dependence on LS strength. The central claims about imbalanced regularization and recovery through logit normalization remain.

C2.justification: v2 expands the distinction between marginal calibration and per-sample uncertainty ranking. Appendix F adds interpretations of boundary errors and explicitly identifies cases where normalization leaves confident errors unresolved. The central mechanism remains the same, with much epistemic-uncertainty language recast in terms of model fit.

D1.justification: New Appendix B.3 specifies the normalization search grid p=1 through 8 and its AURC objective; Section 5 and Appendix E.5 clarify that centralization is omitted. v1's statement that an accompanying CIFAR-10/ResNet-20 demo is provided disappears. Full project code and checkpoints remain promised future releases in both.

E1.justification: Both evaluate ImageNet classification, the ImageNet-plus-Sketch mixture, Cityscapes segmentation, and CIFAR-100 classification. Additional score comparisons and illustrative images use existing coverage; they introduce no distinct task or input environment.

E2.justification: v2 Appendix E.1 adds DOCTOR and entropy across LS levels, and Energy for CE and LS with alpha=0.2, to the ResNet-50/ImageNet comparisons. These supplement the retained MSP and logit-normalization comparisons, with the expansion confined to this setting.

E3.justification: The original splits, training budgets, architectures, preprocessing, and quantitative evaluation protocols are retained. The added qualitative Cityscapes case studies explicitly use p=5 for both CE and LS (Appendix F), supplementing the retained quantitative normalization evaluations with validation-selected p=4 and p=8.

E4.justification: v2 adds targeted checks of dependence on uncertainty-score choice (Appendix E.1), another ImageNet error example, and segmentation boundary-error and normalization-failure case studies (Appendix F). The Sketch robustness tests and logit-distribution analyses already appear in v1.

E5.justification: Both use descriptive mean-plus-or-minus-standard-deviation bands over samples, including the same sliding-window procedures. The new relative-distribution panels redisplay this information. Neither version reports repeated training seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Principal benchmark results are retained. v2 adds alternative-score results, including Energy %AURC of 11.27 for CE and 12.57 for LS alpha=0.2 (Figure 18), exact coverage at 1% risk (Figure 1), and qualitative cases. v2 Figure 13 also replaces v1 Figure 12's mIoU-labeled 72.4/72.0 with 5.1/5.2, conflicting with v2 Figure 3; this does not establish a comparable performance decline.

M1.justification: LS training and post-hoc scoring by the maximum p-normalized logit remain unchanged. v2 corrects the explicit norm formula and explains the omission of centralization, without establishing a changed algorithm or implementation.

P1.justification: The introduction and explanatory narrative are extensively rewritten. Experimental findings and gradient analysis become separate main sections, experimental details move, and the aleatoric/epistemic exposition is replaced by simpler model-fit language with an appendix note. v2 also adds an appendix contents page and separate reproducibility and ethics statements.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document template and redesigns many plots with risk-difference or relative-logit panels. Figures are split, combined, and relocated; the segmentation example moves to Figure 1 with a coverage table. New score-comparison and failure-case figures accompany substantial redisplay of existing results.

New Appendix E.5 develops a detailed comparison with Cattelan and Silva's explanation of normalization. This extends well beyond the latter citation's publication update or citation-style changes.

T1.justification: New Appendix C derives the empirical one-hot-loss gradients and separate maximum-logit regularization for correct and incorrect predictions (Equations 19–21). v2 Equation 16 also corrects the p-norm expansion to include absolute values. The population-loss analysis and positive-logit theorem and proof are otherwise retained.

improvement.justification: v2 more carefully positions its contribution, checks dependence on uncertainty-score choice, adds the one-hot-loss derivation, and documents failures of normalization (Appendices C, E.1, and F). These strengthen and qualify largely unchanged findings. The gains outweigh the localized reporting regression in Figure 13's inconsistent mIoU entries, but do not establish a substantial overall advance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same label-smoothing and selective-classification study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, segmentation, distribution-shift, and logit-normalization experiments in the main text and Appendix A.

title: Towards Understanding Why Label Smoothing Degrades Selective Classification and How to Fix It

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: LS harms selective classification through imbalanced max-logit suppression, and post-hoc logit normalisation can counteract this effect. Added experiments support these retained claims; replacing 'regularisation' with 'suppression' does not redefine them.

C2.justification: v3 adds localized qualifications about weaker tabular effects and unreliable risk-curve estimation with few errors, a fuller rationale for centering potentially negative logits, and possible instability of negative LS. Appendix H expands practical implications and future directions. The limitations illustrated by segmentation failures were already present in v2.

D1.justification: v2 promises future code and model releases; v3 reports their release and supplies explicit GitHub and Hugging Face access links, a CIFAR-10 demo and plotting notebooks. Appendix C adds TorchUncertainty and binary-loss implementation information, tabular/text architectures and preprocessing, double-precision logit calculations, and updated hardware specifications. Resource availability is assessed as reported in the PDFs.

E1.justification: Appendices B.4–B.5 add evaluated tabular binary classification on Bank Marketing and Online Shoppers, and sentiment classification on IMDB. This substantially extends coverage beyond the retained vision tasks. CIFAR-10 is mentioned as a reproducibility demo, without a new reported benchmark result.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the retained experiments is unchanged, including CE versus LS and comparisons involving MSP, DOCTOR, entropy and Energy. title: Do LLM Agents  Have Regret? A Case Study in Online Learning and Games

improvement.justification: New application studies and explicit statistical assumptions improve coverage and transparency. title: Do LLM Agents  Have Regret? A Case Study in Online Learning and Games

improvement.justification: v5 corrects the invalid clipping formula, removes a broken Introduction reference, and improves prose, captions and bibliographic accuracy. after.justification: v5 retains these original experiments, including online learning, repeated games, recommendation and negotiation case studies, and trained-Transformer analyses.

title: Do LLM Agents  Have Regret? A Case Study in Online Learning and Games

(2023), and controlled frame-description experiments using eight, 16 and 180 frames. Existing principal dataset splits and zero-shot training conditions remain. M1.justification: V1 describes likelihood-ranking 16 frames to select eight and supplying the highest-ranked frame to MVU. V2 instead describes uniformly sampled frames, a center-frame input, and detection/tracking over 16 rather than eight frames. Appendix G also introduces free-form answer generation. These substantially revise input processing and inference, although Figure 3 and Appendix B retain inconsistent frame-selection references.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and contribution narrative are extensively rewritten. These refine the retained contributions.

D1.justification: V3 supplies an MVU repository address in the abstract and an LVNet code source in the reproducibility statement. title: AgentStudio: A Toolkit for Building General Virtual Agents

title: Efficient Learning with Sine-Activated Low-Rank Matrices

C1.justification: The headline contribution broadens from tree-search reasoning to general tree-structured inference, explicitly encompassing few-shot prompting and speculative decoding. v2 promotes both Node and Flatten implementations and replaces the two-task 1.7–2.4× claim with separate end-to-end and attention claims of up to 2.52× and 3.82× across three workload families.

C2.justification: v2 explains how KV materialization dominates unpaged execution and how paging shifts the bottleneck toward attention (Section 4.2). It attributes modest reasoning gains to narrow trees and limited attention overhead, and explicitly limits substantial gains to sufficiently large shared contexts or numerous queries (Sections 4.3 and 5). Appendix A.6 additionally explains declining benefits as suffixes grow.

D1.justification: v2 supplements the retained pseudocode with a backend/paging matrix, an explicit depth-first layout description, and workload specifications covering stopping criteria, tree shapes, and recorded speculative acceptance lengths (Tables 5–6 and 10; Appendix A.5). However, v1's explicit 100-tree workload count is no longer reported.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates sorting 128 numbers and document merging. v2 retains these and adds keyword counting, set intersection, and APPS-based few-shot prompting and speculative-decoding workloads (Tables 6–7 and 10), substantially broadening the tasks and tree-structured inference scenarios evaluated.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the stated model from Llama2-7B-HF to Llama3-8B, although v2's citation still identifies Llama 2. v2 introduces explicit paged/unpaged configurations, separate attention timing, and expanded partial-result IO accounting. New protocols include approximately 4,000-token prompts with 400 decoding iterations and speculative token trees of 32–256 queries.

E4.justification: v2 adds a Node-versus-Flatten split ablation linked to node-length dispersion (Figure 5), memory-management latency decompositions (Figures 4 and 13), and tree-width sensitivity analysis (Figure 14). v1's thought-length distributions and task-averaged reasoning iteration plots (Figures 7–8) are not retained. E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed timing experiments, confidence intervals, significance tests, or defined uncertainty estimates for performance. v2 Figure 5's standard deviation describes tree-node lengths, not uncertainty in measured speedups; v1's 100 trees are workload samples rather than reported repeated runs.

M1.justification: The core attention algorithms persist: Algorithms 1–4 match across versions after the DEFT-Subtree-to-DEFT-Flatten rename. v2 reports adapting DEFT kernels to paged as well as unpaged KV storage (Table 5 and Appendix A.1), a limited system extension. P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and contribution narrative are substantially rewritten around general tree-structured inference. System, kernel, and workload explanations are reorganized between the main text and appendices; experiments gain dedicated bottleneck and ablation sections, and the appendix gains a contents list and expanded organization.

P2.justification: The interaction and QKV-grouping diagrams are substantially redrawn, and results are reorganized into separate attention, end-to-end, and IO tables. Existing diagrams are also relocated, including v1 Figures 2 and 5 becoming v2 Figures 6 and 11, while the document template changes.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix A.3 substantially expand positioning against ChunkAttention, Hydragen, and Bifurcated Attention. title: DeFT: Decoding with Flash Tree-attention for Efficient Tree-structured LLM Inference

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds efficient online unlearning under less restrictive assumptions. v3 explicitly claims applicability to non-convex, non-smooth objectives and the first non-convex theoretical analysis of certified unlearning. Its abstract and conclusion also elevate superiority in generalization and deletion capacity to central contributions, while retaining the original efficiency claims.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's existing step-size discussion, v3 adds explicit limitations concerning O(nTd) precomputation, O(nd) storage and unstable non-convex training. It interprets the new LFW performance loss as an applicability limitation and discusses potentially loose bounds near rho = q. Appendix E.2 proposes grouped storage and sharpness-aware training as future remedies, not evaluated components.

D1.justification: v3 removes v1 Appendix B.1's detailed CNN architecture, numerical clipping thresholds and explicit experimental noise scale of 0.1. It adds settings for LFW and the revised large-model comparisons, and adds RTX 3090 to the hardware disclosure. The code URL, PyTorch/CUDA versions and CPU information remain, but important reproduction details are lost.

E1.justification: v3 adds LFWPeople face recognition across 29 identities. MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CelebA remain represented; Fashion-MNIST results move to the appendix. This is a limited extension within the existing vision evaluation.

CIFAR-10 NegGrad changes from two epochs at 0.0001 with batch size 1 to one epoch at 0.00005 with batch size 2. v3 also specifies the new LFW protocol and adds distance measurements to application comparisons.

E4.justification: v3 removes the sequential deletion-and-repair validation from v1 Appendix C.2/Figure 7 while retaining the repair method. It also removes accuracy trajectories from the small-step-size and epoch studies and drops the step-size-1 results. These remove evidence about repair effectiveness and the utility consequences of hyperparameter choices, although the four principal distance-based sensitivity studies remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report seven random seeds and minimum/maximum error bars for the principal verification experiments, and identify seed 42 for the sensitivity studies. v3 introduces no new confidence intervals, significance tests or repeated-run reporting practice.

E6.justification: CIFAR-10 Table 3 replaces several reported values, including the proposed method's distance of 0.09 with 0.06. v3 Tables 4–7 add LFW, expanded CelebA and resource/distance results; LFW accuracy is 71.92% versus 80.89% for retraining. Changed CelebA and NegGrad settings prevent interpreting their replacements as same-setting improvements. Figure 1(b)'s revised inset also shows about 0.68 at 30% deletion while the text retains 0.96.

M1.justification: The affine-recursion approximator, HVP computation, vector-addition unlearning and optional repair strategy remain. However, Algorithms 1 and 2 change the stated gradient-rescaling operation from rescaling the batch-averaged gradient to rescaling individual gradients before averaging.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution list and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Section 4 places generalization analysis before algorithm design, the research-question framing is removed, and appendices are reorganized into separate related-work, proof, experiment, ablation and discussion sections. These are substantial narrative and structural changes.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, and figures are redrawn or relocated. v1 Table 2 is redistributed across v3 Tables 2 and 6, with an added distance column in the latter. New large-model tables replace or expand earlier displays, while accuracy panels and the repair figure are removed.

R1.justification: The new Appendix A substantially expands discussion of SISA, federated unlearning, influence functions, distillation and Fisher-based alternatives, with additional citations. Research positioning shifts toward theoretical certified unlearning and an explicit first-non-convex-analysis claim; new sharpness-aware minimization references support future directions.

T1.justification: v3 substantively revises existing guarantees rather than introducing generalization and deletion capacity for the first time. It revises the approximation-error normalization, changes the generalization term from rho^T 2ML/lambda to rho^T 2L^2/lambda, and changes the supporting contraction argument from SGD to GD. Appendix E.1 replaces Hessian-Lipschitz/asymptotic conditions with smoothness and empirical optimality, while Appendix B.6 adds a bound-tightness analysis.

improvement.justification: Broader evaluation, especially the LFW failure case, and explicit scalability limitations make v3 more informative. However, it removes important reproduction settings and repair validation, introduces a figure/text inconsistency, and strengthens nonsmooth-certification claims without clearly resolving their dependence on Hessians and Taylor expansions. These substantive benefits and unresolved reliability losses prevent a confident net quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Hessian-free recollection method. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables and figures support comparison despite the changed title and organization.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and reports additional LFW and expanded CelebA evaluations, including accuracy, model distance and computational costs.

before.justification: v1 reports original unlearning experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CelebA, including runtime measurements, sensitivity studies and repair validation.

title: Hessian-Free Online Certified Unlearning

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction foreground online deletion without requiring an empirical-risk minimizer, while removing v3's prominent claims about non-smooth objectives and near-identical retraining. The headline precomputation claim changes from O(nd) to O(n^2 d) in Table 1 and the conclusion. These materially revise the advertised applicability and efficiency contributions.

The repair strategy is qualified as heuristic without certified guarantees. Section 6 and Appendix D.4 explain why matching retraining can preserve vulnerability to deletion-membership attacks and discuss the limits of noise-based mitigation.

D1.justification: v4 adds explicit HVP pseudocode, documents storage of intermediate training models, and supplies previously unspecified privacy parameters, clipping threshold 10, and large-model noise standard deviation 0.01. It also updates the anonymous code-access link to a named repository. Figure 9's exact settings remain ambiguous because its labels disagree with Appendix E.1.

P1.justification: v4 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, theoretical narrative, and limitations, and adopts a new title. It separates developer and adversary evaluations, moves discussions ahead of proofs in the appendices, and adds an appendix contents page. P2.justification: v4 adds attack, repair, learning/unlearning tradeoff, and clipping figures, and redraws several retained sensitivity plots. (2024) on certified deep-model unlearning, replacing the earlier broad first-non-convex framing. Appendix C.1 also supplies a new reweighting and chain-rule derivation.

improvement.justification: The direct privacy audits and more candid applicability limits make v4's forgetting claims easier to assess than v3's reliance on distance, correlation, and accuracy evidence. A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe the same Hessian-free unlearning work, with matching authors, core methodology, and experiments. The main text, mathematical material, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains original benchmark experiments and reports additional membership-inference, repair, and gradient-clipping results in Section 6 and the appendices.

before.justification: v3 reports original unlearning experiments, runtime measurements, and sensitivity analyses in Section 5 and Appendices C-D.

title: DRoP: Distributionally Robust Data Pruning

It also discusses effectiveness with a stronger full-data model and competitiveness with additional robustness methods. The stated limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly supplies a code-repository link and the added Wide-ResNet configuration. Appendices A/D describe its expansion factor and removal of early downsampling layers. Existing splits, preprocessing and model configurations are retained.
