The existing pre-training-length ablation and class-wise analyses are retained and relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report three-seed averages with min/max bands for pruning comparisons, five-seed averaging for EL2N/GraNd scores and ten datasets for the Gaussian simulation. The added Wide-ResNet experiment follows the existing reporting practice; no increased run count or new statistical estimation procedure is reported.

E6.justification: v4 adds results showing continued DRoP robustness benefits with Wide-ResNet-101, lower-density Waterbirds results, imported baseline scores and alternative-accuracy/group breakdowns. Most existing curves remain unchanged, and Table 2 largely tabulates existing comparisons. That table reports 45.3% worst-class accuracy for Random+DRoP on half of CIFAR-100, while both versions' main text gives 45.4%; this is an unresolved reporting discrepancy, not an established performance change.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains validation-error-based class quotas, saturation handling and random sampling within classes. The added Wide-ResNet architecture is an evaluation configuration, not a revision to the proposed pruning procedure.

P1.justification: v4 separates Related Work from a numbered Data Pruning Is Not Robust section, reorganizes the final appendices and adds localized explanatory passages. The title gains 'Data', the publication header changes and acknowledgements are added; most existing prose remains intact.

R1.justification: v4 adds targeted references for Waterbirds robustness competitors and their reported scores, model-size robustness and Wide-ResNet. These extend the empirical positioning, while the broader related-work discussion and novelty claims remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The Gaussian-mixture definitions, optimal-prior derivations, Theorem B.1, Lemma B.2, SSP analysis and multivariate isotropic extension are unchanged. Section renumbering and equation reflow do not alter the mathematical arguments.

improvement.justification: v4 modestly strengthens validation through the larger-model check and broader Waterbirds comparison. Imported comparator scores provide less assurance than controlled reruns, and Table 2 introduces the small 45.3% versus 45.4% inconsistency, but these limitations do not outweigh the incremental gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DRoP research. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching renamed sections and relocated analyses.

after.justification: v4 retains these original experiments and adds Wide-ResNet-101 results and Waterbirds analyses. Its empirical evidence is not limited to the newly quoted results from other work.

before.justification: v2 reports original Gaussian-mixture simulations and image-classification experiments, including pruning, class robustness, imbalanced-data and Waterbirds evaluations.

title: DRoP: Distributionally Robust Data Pruning

P1.justification: The title drops the BinaryDM prefix, and the abstract and portions of the introduction and method receive targeted rewrites. P2.justification: v2 converts the main text to a single-column layout, redraws the overview, adds an accuracy-efficiency plot, and splits or relocates major tables. improvement.justification: EBB addresses v2's persistent extra-basis inference cost, supported by new transition ablations. The methodological gains coexist with reduced comparative evidence and weaker claim accuracy, preventing a reliable net-quality judgment.

E1.justification: v1's controlled caption-information interventions use synthetic MAD. v2 adds natural-caption truncation experiments on CC12M and image-image matching with selectively cropped views on MS COCO (Appendices F.1 and F.4). E2.justification: v2 Table 5 adds a real-words baseline within the ideal-word and shifted-ideal-word comparison; v1 Section 4.3 reports only their alignment similarities. Appendix F.1 also evaluates L2I alongside RMG as an alternative gap measure. The established CLIP/SigLIP and RMG/L2M comparisons remain.

Dimension-ablation plots use RMG instead of L2M, and Table 5 revises the stated centering treatment for shifted ideal words. New caption-length, temperature-freezing, and image-image experiments introduce additional controlled evaluation designs.

E4.justification: v2 adds caption-truncation and temperature ablations, CommonPool filtering analysis, CLIP/CLIP-A stratification, controlled word-prior experiments, and image-image/direct-embedding tests distinguishing information imbalance from loss or initialization effects. The ideal-word analysis now tests downstream accuracy. Existing MAD and dimension-ablation analyses remain, but v1 Figure 7b's caption-presence classification-accuracy panel is removed.

E5.justification: v1 reports three-seed MAD averages without correlation significance tests. v2 adds significance indicators in Table 1 and numerical p-values in Table 3 and Appendix D.2, materially expanding uncertainty assessment for central evidence. MAD's three-seed practice remains; five seeds are reported for the new image-image experiment, rather than an increase for retained experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial caption, entropy, filtering, word-prior, and image-image results; Table 8 reports RMG 0.006 without versus 0.149 with information imbalance. Table 5 replaces v1's CLIP/MIT-States ideal-word cosine values 0.19/0.56 with 0.388/0.858 and adds accuracies. Revised correlations and shifting procedures preclude interpreting these replacements as same-setting gains. Table 2's neighborhood distances remain identical.

M1.justification: The core CLIP objective, MAD construction, and intended RMG/MOAD procedures are retained. New temperature and encoder configurations serve as experimental controls. Formula corrections and additional evaluation measures do not establish a revised proposed learning algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and explanatory prose; reorders the modality-gap analyses; absorbs the former Section 4.3; and reorganizes Section 6 into two subsections. Detailed definitions and examples move into reorganized appendices, while the standalone Discussion section disappears.

P2.justification: v2 changes page format and typography, redraws the information-imbalance and MAD diagrams, reorganizes v1 Figures 3–4 into Figures 4/11, and redistributes Figure 8 across Figures 7/12. New experimental plots and Tables 3–9 substantially expand the displays. Figure 7a's new subtitle incorrectly reverses the bias trend shown by its curves and main caption.

R1.justification: v2 engages Fahim et al. (2024)'s contrastive-gap explanation through replication and discussion, and adds references to language rewrites and UMAP. It removes v1's discussion connecting the work to multimodal identifiability and captioning-based representation learning. The broader positioning around information imbalance versus existing gap explanations remains.

T1.justification: v2 corrects RMG's matching-pair and exclusion indices, corrects the second mismatch pair in the retained toy construction, and defines L2I. The expanded MOAD and loss expressions largely restate existing mathematics. Appendix F.3 also introduces an inconsistent nonnegative coordinate restriction despite retaining solutions with negative coordinates.

improvement.justification: v1 Section 7 acknowledges that controlled validation relies on synthetic MAD. v2's CC12M interventions provide direct real-data evidence for the modality-gap hypothesis, while temperature and alternative-cause controls substantially strengthen its empirical explanation. Correlation p-values also improve transparency. These substantive gains outweigh the local inconsistencies introduced in Figure 7a and Appendix F.3.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study of modality gap, object bias, and information imbalance. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical analyses and adds CC12M training, temperature interventions, word-frequency controls, and image-image experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of pretrained models, controlled MAD training experiments, embedding ablations, and a numerical toy experiment.

title: Two Effects, One Trigger: On the Modality Gap, Object Bias, and Information Imbalance in Contrastive Vision-Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's seven findings and conclusion retain the same substantive contributions concerning information imbalance, modality separation, object bias and logit entropy. The added experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: Section 4.1 narrows its interpretation to weak indications of negative correlation for some pretraining datasets. New Appendix G discusses limits from training scale and caption-removal variability, extending existing statistical caveats. Appendix F.6 tentatively attributes reduced transfer accuracy to distribution shift.

D1.justification: V3 adds an explicit project-code availability link and documents DCI fine-tuning hardware, optimizer settings, learning-rate schedule, warm-up and temperature cap. Existing implementation recipes are retained; these are additional reproducibility disclosures.

E1.justification: V3 adds CC3M training and fine-tuning on the Densely Captioned Images (DCI) dataset in Appendix F. These extend image-text data coverage, including dense captions, while retaining the existing downstream datasets and tasks.

E2.justification: The evaluated VLM collection and comparator membership in the filtering and real/ideal/shifted-word comparisons are retained. The added experiments vary training conditions and model configurations without introducing another competing method.

E3.justification: Added protocols include ViT-S and sentence-wise caption removal in Figure 15, alternative dimension selection in Figure 12, and ten-epoch DCI fine-tuning with batch size 256 and learning rate 1e-5. These supplement existing protocols; the original settings and metrics are retained.

E4.justification: V3 substantially broadens robustness testing of the modality-gap explanation across backbone choice, caption-removal scheme and independent training data (Figure 15). Appendix F.6 additionally tests gap reduction in pretrained CLIP and SigLIP through dense-caption fine-tuning. Figure 12 checks separability under alternative dimension selection.

E5.justification: The three-seed MAD reporting, five-seed Appendix F.4 experiments and correlation significance reporting are unchanged. The added experiments introduce no new stated repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or statistical testing procedures.

E6.justification: Tables 1-9 retain their results, while new robustness and fine-tuning outcomes materially expand the empirical evidence. In v3 Table 10, DCI fine-tuning reduces COCO RMG from 0.572 to 0.499 for CLIP and 0.623 to 0.562 for SigLIP. Their R@1 changes from 52.84 to 59.24 and 67.68 to 67.58, respectively; ImageNet accuracy falls from 66.75 to 65.13 and 75.61 to 73.87. These are newly reported experimental comparisons, not revisions to v2 scores.

M1.justification: The proposed measurements and underlying model procedures are retained. BRACE names the generic MOAD calculation already described in v2; the additional backbone and fine-tuning experiments do not introduce a new proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: V3 makes localized wording corrections, adds the conference header and BRACE terminology, and appends subsections on fine-tuning, limitations and partial multi-label learning. The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact.

P2.justification: V3 adds Figures 12 and 15 and Table 10, clarifies Figure 4's caption, and relocates several existing displays, including Figures 5 and Table 9. Existing plots largely retain their designs; v2 Figures 12-14 correspond to v3 Figures 13, 14 and 16.

R1.justification: Appendix H adds a connection to partial multi-label learning, citing Xie and Huang, Struski et al., and Hang and Zhang. Urbanek et al. is added for DCI. The main positioning relative to prior modality-gap and object-bias research remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The loss equations, modality-gap definitions and toy-optimum reasoning are retained. BRACE's equation in Appendix E.2 substitutes generic concept groups for MOAD's objects and attributes; v2 already explicitly allowed this use, so it restates existing mathematics.

improvement.justification: V3 strengthens v2's real-data validation through targeted robustness checks and pretrained-model fine-tuning, while adding code-access information and clearer limitations. Table 10 usefully documents that shrinking the gap does not consistently improve downstream performance. These additions improve evidential coverage and qualification, but the limited statistical support for the gap-performance relationship and lack of large-scale intervention experiments remain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains these original results and adds robustness experiments and fine-tuning results on densely captioned images.

before.justification: V2 reports original evaluations of 98 VLMs, controlled MAD and CC12M experiments, embedding analyses and numerical simulations.

title: Two Effects, One Trigger: On the Modality Gap, Object Bias, and Information Imbalance in Contrastive Vision-Language Models

C1.justification: v1 claims the first global-convergence guarantees for federated policy-based RL. v3 narrows that novelty claim to asynchronous federated policy-based RL and adds first-order stationary convergence as an explicit contribution in the introduction and conclusion. The main sample-speedup and asynchronous timing claims remain.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive limitations concerning malicious agents, compatibility with communication-saving techniques, second-order optimization, and experimental scale. It also discusses opposite agent-count effects in its two timing scenarios and explicitly explains policy-induced data heterogeneity even with identical environments in Appendix C.

D1.justification: v3 documents Walker2D's action/state dimensions and revises its network and training hyperparameters in Tables 2–3. The new reproducibility statement mainly points to existing pseudocode and experimental documentation; it adds no code-access resource. Software, GAE, and GPU specifications remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds reported Walker2D-v4 evaluation to the three existing MuJoCo tasks; v1 only listed Walker2D hyperparameters. Appendix A.3 also covers both one-fast-agent and one-slow-agent timing scenarios, whereas v1 covered only the latter. The scenario names in v3 are inconsistently assigned.

E2.justification: v3 Figure 4 adds A3C and Vanilla, defined as AFedPG without delay-adaptive lookahead, at N=4 and N=8. The corresponding v1 Figure 5 compared only AFedPG and synchronous FedPG. These additions substantially broaden the empirical comparison methods.

E3.justification: Table 3 changes the listed Walker2D network from 256×256×256 to 512×512, timesteps from 512 to 1024, and iterations from 3000 to 5000. The reported Humanoid timing budget at N=8 changes from 80,000 to 120,000 trajectories, and heterogeneity sweeps add N=16. These reported setting changes do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 introduces a direct ablation of the central delay-adaptive lookahead component in Figure 4. Appendix A.3 also expands the existing heterogeneity analysis to two contrasting timing scenarios and additional agent counts, substantially extending the questions tested.

E5.justification: Both versions report convergence experiments over 10 runs using seeds 0–9, smoothed mean curves, and 95% confidence intervals. Repeating these details in v3 captions and extending the same reporting practice to additional curves does not change the statistical procedure.

E6.justification: v3 adds Walker2D outcomes and A3C/Vanilla comparison curves, and substantially revises the heterogeneity results. At heterogeneity ratio 9, v1 Figure 6 shows speedups of 5–8, while v3 Figure 6 reports values in the hundreds. The three original reward-versus-sample plots are unchanged. Changed budgets and inconsistent scenario descriptions prevent interpreting all differences as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 retain the same normalized server update, delay-dependent lookahead, trajectory sampling, and update-direction averaging. Expanded explanations and additional theoretical guarantees do not introduce a new AFedPG component.

P1.justification: v3 makes Related Work a standalone section, moves assumptions and key lemmas into Appendix B, and reorganizes experimental supplements into Appendix A. It replaces the standalone conclusion with Discussions, adds limitations and a reproducibility statement, and expands explanations of the asynchronous challenges and lookahead mechanism.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column ACM layout to a single-column format. Table 1 is restructured around FOSP and global complexity, task figures expand from three to four panels, timing plots gain additional comparator curves, and Figure 6 becomes two panels. Settings tables and the timing schematic move to the appendix.

R1.justification: The FedRL discussion substantially expands its treatment of closely related work, including Chen et al. on federated PG, Ganesh et al. on global convergence with adversaries, and additional heterogeneous, multi-task, and communication-complexity research. This supports the narrower asynchronous novelty positioning. Table 1 also distinguishes vanilla from normalized PG.

T1.justification: v3 adds the FOSP criterion, Theorem 5.1 claiming O(epsilon^-3.5) sample complexity, and an Appendix B.5 derivation with different step-size schedules. The original global theorem and supporting assumptions and lemmas are largely retained and relocated. The new theorem states a final-iterate guarantee, while its proof bounds a weighted average of gradient norms.

improvement.justification: The added A3C comparisons, lookahead ablation, and explicit limitations strengthen empirical assessment and scope disclosure. However, the new FOSP theorem and appendix proof concern different convergence outputs, while the revised heterogeneity results introduce unexplained speedups in the hundreds and conflicting scenario descriptions. These unresolved issues affect important additions to the theory and scaling evidence, preventing a reliable judgment of net overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AFedPG, with matching algorithms and the same core global-convergence analysis. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix A report original experiments on four MuJoCo tasks, including additional baseline comparisons, a lookahead ablation, and expanded computing-heterogeneity results.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original MuJoCo reward and timing experiments on Swimmer, Hopper, and Humanoid, including comparisons across agent counts and computing heterogeneity.

title: Asynchronous Federated Reinforcement Learning with Policy Gradient Updates: Algorithm Design and Convergence Analysis

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: asynchronous policy-gradient learning with delay-adaptive lookahead, convergence guarantees, linear per-agent sample-complexity improvement, and reduced training time. The revised theorem details do not change these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations of communication-load redistribution and interprets longer training as achieving similar rewards faster. It acknowledges suboptimal PG hyperparameters on Humanoid and explicitly discusses noncommunicating stragglers. Section 7.1 removes the limited-agent-scale caveat without adding a larger-agent experiment.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 newly specifies float32 parameter representation for communication accounting and describes the agent/server measurement setup. The existing MLP architectures, learning rates, GAE setting, PyTorch implementation, and A100 hardware information remain unchanged; no new code-access information is supplied.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Swimmer-v4, Hopper-v4, Walker2D-v4, and Humanoid-v4 and retain the same computing-heterogeneity scenarios. Communication measurements and longer training use this existing coverage; the newly discussed noncommunicating-agent case is not a new experiment.

E2.justification: The original comparisons retain single-agent PG, synchronous FedPG, A3C, and the vanilla variant without delay-adaptive lookahead. Figures 7–8 reuse FedPG and PG. Newly discussed related methods are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix A.3 adds supplementary protocols: Figure 8 uses five times Figure 3's sample budgets, and Figure 7 measures transmitted bytes with eight agents on Swimmer-v4, including a server window corresponding to one synchronous round. The original experimental settings and Table 3 remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v4 adds two substantive analyses: communication-load distribution across agents and server time steps, and longer training to examine eventual rewards versus convergence speed. These extend the retained lookahead ablation and computation-heterogeneity analysis.

E5.justification: The added Figure 8 reports five independent runs with seeds 0–4 and 95% confidence intervals. The original results retain ten runs with seeds 0–9 and 95% intervals. This adds a different repetition count for the supplementary experiment, without reducing repetitions for the original comparisons.

E6.justification: Figures 3, 4, and 6 retain their results. New Figure 7 reports similar cumulative communication volumes but different agent allocation and smoother server traffic. Figure 8 adds longer-training curves showing broadly similar eventual rewards across AFedPG agent counts, with faster attainment using more agents and a remaining Humanoid PG deficit. These are additional results under extended settings.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 revise the distributed update procedure. In v3, agents compute lookahead parameters and momentum directions and transmit directions. In v4, agents transmit gradient estimates; the server maintains the direction recursion using its previous update direction and computes and transmits lookahead parameters. The basic normalized-update and lookahead ingredients remain.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence largely remain. v4 reverses the presentation order of the global and FOSP theorems, retitles appendix sections, adds roadmap and proof-explanation prose, and moves the existing C.1 discussion to C.2. These are localized structural and language changes.

P2.justification: v4 adds the two-panel communication Figure 7 and four-panel longer-training Figure 8, reformats the algorithm boxes, and relocates existing figures and tables through page reflow. The original result plots and Tables 1–3 retain their content and visual design.

R1.justification: v4 adds references including Fu, Gaur, Wang (2024a), Xiong, Zheng, and Zhu. New Appendix C.1 substantially expands positioning against Shen et al. (2023), contrasting algorithm class, function parameterization, convergence complexity, and delay assumptions. The original FL/FedRL discussion is retained as C.2.

T1.justification: v4 adds the explicit Fisher-matrix lower-bound assumption B.3 and substantially revises and expands the error-recursion and delay-bound derivations. It also introduces fixed-runtime reasoning and uses a delay condition in Equation 38. The FOSP theorem changes from a last-iterate bound with a bias floor to a weighted-average, bias-free statement, aligning it with the result already targeted in v3 Appendix B.5.

improvement.justification: v4 improves empirical interpretation through communication measurements and longer-training evidence, and aligns the FOSP statement with its appendix proof while making the Fisher assumption explicit. The gain is limited by remaining inconsistencies: global Theorem 5.1 still omits the new B.3 assumption used by its supporting lemma, and the scale limitation is removed without a larger-agent experiment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AFedPG research. Their main text, algorithms, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–C are readable and support comparison, including relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v4 retains those experiments and adds communication-overhead results in Figure 7 and longer-training results in Figure 8.

before.justification: v3 reports original MuJoCo reward and training-time experiments in Figures 3–4 and computation-heterogeneity results in Figure 6.

title: Asynchronous Federated Reinforcement Learning with Policy Gradient Updates: Algorithm Design and Convergence Analysis

C1.justification: Section 1 narrows the asserted literature gap from insufficient study of global convergence and time complexity to time complexity. The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same AFedPG novelty, convergence, and speedup claims.

C2.justification: Section 7 newly identifies extension from discounted rewards to average rewards as an open direction. It also elaborates the existing adversarial-worker and second-order-method limitations by connecting them to synchronous robustness and centralized optimal-sample-complexity results.

D1.justification: The implementation descriptions, Table 3 hyperparameters, Appendix A.2 settings, and reproducibility statement remain unchanged, including PyTorch, GAE, policy-network configurations, and A100 hardware. No code or data access information is added.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Swimmer-v4, Hopper-v4, Walker2D-v4, and Humanoid-v4 under the same scenarios. Newly mentioned application areas, including diffusion models, cloud computing, and finance, are background examples rather than additional evaluations.

E2.justification: The corresponding experiments retain single-agent PG, synchronous FedPG, the vanilla variant without delay-adaptive lookahead, and A3C. Added literature citations do not introduce evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: Sections 6.1–6.2 and Appendix A retain the same metrics, agent counts, sample budgets, heterogeneity settings, communication measurements, and Table 3 model and training configurations.

E4.justification: The lookahead ablation and Appendix A.3 analyses of computation heterogeneity, communication overhead, and extended training are retained without substantive changes.

E5.justification: Both versions report 10 runs with seeds 0–9 for the main convergence results and five runs with seeds 0–4 for Figure 8. Averaging, smoothing, and 95% confidence-interval reporting remain unchanged.

E6.justification: The experimental plot images in Figures 3–4 and 6–8 are identical between versions, and the accompanying numerical statements and findings are retained. Figure 8 is enlarged without changing its results.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 retain the same policy-gradient estimation, normalized server update, and delay-adaptive lookahead procedure. No algorithmic component or objective changes.

P1.justification: The revision makes localized language edits, updates the publication header, adds acknowledgments, and places conclusions before the expanded limitations in Section 7 using inline headings. The overall narrative and section organization remain largely intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is slightly reduced and Figure 8's panels are enlarged while preserving their content. The author block is reformatted, and expanded references cause repagination. All figures and tables are retained.

R1.justification: The cited literature substantially expands across FL fairness, asynchronous multi-model FL, multi-agent learning, diffusion alignment, average-reward RL, and application domains. Several earlier application references are removed or replaced, and Section 1 narrows the literature gap to time complexity. Section 2 and Appendix C retain their central technical comparisons.

T1.justification: Definitions 4.1–4.2, Theorems 5.1–5.2, the complexity comparison, and Appendix B's assumptions, lemmas, derivations, and proofs are unchanged after matching corresponding pages.

improvement.justification: V5 clarifies limitations and narrows an overly broad literature-gap statement while retaining the technical and empirical evidence. However, some new citation connections are unclear: Chen et al. (2024a), titled as electricity-price forecasting, supports data-center allocation, while Chen et al. (2024b), titled as agricultural aquifer-recharge control, supports cloud computing. The PDFs do not explain these connections. Clearer scope and these attribution concerns coexist, leaving the net quality effect uncertain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AFedPG study and provide readable main text, algorithms, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–C. Matching content across pagination changes supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix A retain the original MuJoCo experiments and their empirical reward, timing, ablation, and communication results.

before.justification: Section 6 and Appendix A report original MuJoCo experiments, including reward curves, timing comparisons, a lookahead ablation, and communication-overhead analysis.

title: Asynchronous Federated Reinforcement Learning with Policy Gradient Updates: Algorithm Design and Convergence Analysis

C1.justification: The central contribution expands from TR-DPO to a class covering DPO, IPO and KTO, with an explicit claim that reference updates offer benefits beyond lowering beta. v2 withdraws level-of-detail improvement from the headline HC claims and changes the conclusion from consistently improved performance to improvement in the majority of scenarios.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new sweeps as evidence for benefits beyond weakened KL regularization and explains its preference for HC scoring through possible reward-model distribution shift. It connects the lack of detail improvement to shorter responses and discusses a repetition-related length anomaly. The discussion adds specific qualifications concerning GPT-4 evaluation, untested generalization and the unexplained length mechanism.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents eight 80GB A100 GPUs, 3–12 hours of training per model, DeepSpeed, maximum gradient norm 2, KTO loss weights and dataset/model licenses. These are additional disclosures, not evidence that previously unspecified implementation choices changed. Conversely, v1's explicit five-generations-per-sample detail for diversity evaluation is no longer stated.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Anthropic-HH dialogue alignment and Reddit TL;DR summarization using the same described datasets. The 150-example provocative HH subset for human-centric evaluation is already present in v1. No new dataset, domain or task is introduced.

E2.justification: The DPO-only comparisons expand to include IPO and KTO as evaluated baselines for their respective TR variants in Table 1 and supplementary analyses. v2 Figure 1 also introduces explicit comparisons against SFT, which served as an initialization/reference policy without this reported comparison in v1.

E3.justification: The reported DPO beta changes from 0.1 to 0.05, and maximum generated tokens increase from 256 to 512. v2 removes the 410M configuration and concentrates cross-size comparisons on alpha = 0.6 and tau = 512. It adds beta-sweep controls, removes reward-model scoring, and revises the HC judge prompt with six scored examples in Appendix H.3. These are documented protocol changes, without independently establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds beta sweeps testing whether reducing regularization substitutes for reference updates, relating HC quality to KL divergence and Self-BLEU. It extends update-rate sensitivity and gradient analyses to IPO/KTO and adds a beta-dependent length analysis. The earlier reward-based diversity/KL analyses disappear, and the illustrative generation cases are replaced.

E5.justification: Both versions report bootstrapped Probability of Improvement confidence intervals and Fisher's exact tests. v2 extends these existing practices to additional results without introducing a new uncertainty-estimation procedure. Neither version specifies training seed counts or repeated-training-run counts.

E6.justification: Numerous results are replaced, added or removed. For Pythia 2.8B with alpha = 0.6 on HH, Table 1 changes from 49.4% wins and 30.4% losses to 42.4% and 32.4%. Because beta and evaluation settings also change, this is not a same-setting performance decline. v2 adds IPO/KTO, SFT-comparison and beta-sweep results, removes reward-model and 410M results, and reports no improvement in level of detail.

M1.justification: v1 proposes TR-DPO and leaves IPO/KTO extensions for future work. v2 introduces TR-IPO and TR-KTO, applying reference updates within their different training objectives. The soft and hard update rules remain unchanged, but the proposed algorithm family substantially broadens.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and closing discussion are substantially rewritten around the broader TR family. The separate update-rate, diversity and gradient narrative is reorganized around the new Section 4.4 question about lowering beta. The appendices are restructured, and the conclusion becomes a discussion with explicit limitations and societal impacts.

P2.justification: v2 adds the SFT comparison chart, redesigns Table 1 around three methods, introduces multiple IPO/KTO and beta-analysis panels, and removes the reward-based displays. Generation examples change from prose sections to comparison tables. The original method schematic is retained as Figure 2, so that particular change is relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: The literature coverage remains largely intact. v2 develops IPO's stability positioning, adds Kahneman and Tversky and DeepSpeed citations, and removes Tang et al. and the accompanying rationale for concentrating solely on DPO. The Anonymous-to-Liu citation update concerns the same rejection-sampling paper, rather than a newly added work.

T1.justification: v2 adds IPO/KTO loss definitions and their gradient expressions, including separate chosen/rejected KTO terms, in Equations 3–4 and 9–10. These extend the existing gradient explanation; the reference-update equations, DPO gradient and trust-region argument remain substantively unchanged. No new theorem or formal trust-region guarantee is introduced.

improvement.justification: Section 4.4 and Appendices D–E directly address an important weakness in v1: whether the reported benefits merely reflect weaker KL regularization. Together with actual IPO/KTO experiments and more qualified claims, these controls substantially strengthen the paper's evidential foundation. Removing reward-model cross-checks and unexplained numerical discrepancies remain drawbacks: for example, v2 Table 1 gives a 39.8% HH win rate for 2.8B TR-DPO at tau = 512, while Table 3 gives 209/500, or 41.8%. These limit confidence in exact figures but do not outweigh the substantial analytical improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same reference-policy updating study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison despite the substantial expansion in v2.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices C–G report original experiments with DPO, IPO, KTO and their TR variants, including benchmark results, parameter sweeps and gradient analyses.

before.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original Pythia experiments comparing TR-DPO with DPO, including GPT-4 evaluations, reward-model scores and training-dynamics analyses.

title: Learn Your Reference Model for Real Good Alignment

C1.justification: v2 centers its contribution on overcoming an unnecessarily restrictive static reference policy. v3 makes mitigation of offline reward overoptimization a central claim and explicitly extends claimed effectiveness to general-purpose Llama3 assistants. This changes the principal scientific framing and claimed application scope while retaining the reference-update contribution.

C2.justification: v3 introduces a vanishing-curvature/reset hypothesis and interprets preserved sequence probabilities as reduced leakage into OOD outputs. It replaces broad near-optimality claims for α = 0.6 and τ = 512 with task-dependent guidance, acknowledges mixed KTO results and absent KTO toy overoptimization, and adds limitations concerning large update intervals on small datasets.

D1.justification: v3 documents toy-RNN dimensions and training trajectories, Llama3 training and generation settings, new dataset access information, and additional licensing details (Appendices B, D, and F). Pythia settings, hardware, training-time information, and judging prompts are retained. The explicit KTO setting λw = λl = 1 from v2 Appendix D.2 is omitted.

E1.justification: v3 retains Anthropic-HH and Reddit TL;DR and adds general instruction-following coverage through UltraChat-200k, UltraFeedback, AlpacaEval 2, and Arena-Hard. E2.justification: DPO, IPO, and KTO remain the principal comparison methods. However, v2 Figure 1's Pythia comparison against SFT on Anthropic-HH disappears; SFT instead appears in the new Llama3 benchmark comparison. Newly cited methods such as SimPO and Nash-based approaches are not evaluated as additional comparators.

E3.justification: v3 adds Llama3-Base/Instruct protocols, including PairRM selection among eight generated responses, length-controlled win rates, and GPT-4-1106-preview benchmark judging. It also introduces toy-RNN and matched-KL probability-analysis protocols. The reported Reddit preference-validation size changes from 26,198 to 21,198 (v2 Section 4.1; v3 Table 4), without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test ID/OOD probability dynamics in toy MDPs, chosen/rejected sequence probabilities on Anthropic-HH, and hyperparameter sensitivity through expanded Pythia and Llama3 sweeps (v3 Appendices B, C, and E). Existing HC, KL, and diversity analyses largely remain, but v2's IPO/KTO gradient-time-course analyses are removed.

E5.justification: Beyond v2's Fisher tests and bootstrap PoI intervals, v3 reports 100 different seeds with means and standard deviations for toy simulations, plus benchmark standard deviations and 95% confidence intervals. Existing Fisher and PoI results remain, although the explicit bootstrap-description sentence disappears. The new reporting does not establish repeated LLM training runs.

E6.justification: Main Table 1 and the Fisher-test results are unchanged. v3 adds extensive benchmark, simulation, and ablation results; for example, Table 2 reports Llama3-Base Arena-Hard scores of 21.3 for TR-DPOα versus 10.5 for DPO. v2's SFT-relative scores and IPO/KTO gradient traces disappear. New Table 6 also reports a 22.8% tie rate for TR-DPO at α = 0.5, conflicting with the retained 21.8% result.

M1.justification: The soft parameter-averaging and periodic hard-copy rules remain unchanged, as do the underlying DPO, IPO, and KTO objectives (v2 Equations 5–6; v3 Equations 8–9). Explicit stop-gradient notation and clarified parameter replacement document the existing procedure rather than establish a new method.

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions, related work, motivation, and discussion are substantially rewritten around overoptimization. Methods gain separate motivation and implementation subsections; experimental setup is subdivided; HC discussion moves into the appendix; and appendix organization is extensively revised. These changes exceed routine renumbering or added scientific paragraphs.

P2.justification: The opening SFT comparison is replaced by two benchmark panels, and v3 adds MDP/probability figures and benchmark/ablation tables. Existing KL panels are combined into Figure 5, HC plots are relocated, DPO gradient axes are rescaled, and IPO/KTO gradient panels disappear. The title, headers, typography, and overall page layout also change.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially repositioned around overoptimization, adding Gao, Coste, and Rafailov studies and contrasting offline TR methods with online Nash approaches by Rosset and Munos. The earlier target-network/EMA motivation and TRPO citation disappear, while new alignment, dataset, and benchmark references expand the research context.

T1.justification: v3 introduces the DPO Hessian and its derivation (Equation 7 and Appendix A), substantially changing the mathematical analysis. Conversely, v2's explicit KL-constrained trust-region objective and IPO/KTO gradient derivations are removed. The rearranged DPO gradient itself is algebraically equivalent to the earlier expression.

improvement.justification: The Llama3 evaluations and probability-dynamics experiments substantially address v2's narrow empirical coverage and largely speculative mechanism explanation. Hyperparameter sweeps also replace overbroad default-setting claims with better-supported guidance. These gains outweigh removed gradient analyses and reporting inconsistencies, including TR-KTOα's Arena-Hard score of 15.3 in v3 Figure 1 versus 14.9 in Table 2. The proposed mechanism remains a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated guarantee.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TR-DPO/TR-IPO/TR-KTO research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds original Llama3 benchmark evaluations, toy-MDP simulations, probability analyses, and hyperparameter experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original Pythia experiments on Anthropic-HH and Reddit TL;DR, including preference comparisons, human-centric scores, and training-dynamics analyses.

title: Learn Your Reference Model for Real Good Alignment

C1.justification: The introduction revises headline DPO/IPO/KTO gains from 10.8/10.5/5.6 to 9.5/15.1/2.3 points. The new numbers match AlpacaEval length-controlled gaps, although the text still references Figure 1b, which shows Arena-Hard. The central claims about reference updates and reduced overoptimization remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix F adds interpretations of task-dependent capability gains and losses. Appendix G explicitly limits applicability: reduced overoptimization does not confer jailbreak robustness. Section 3.1 and Appendix A extend the curvature explanation to IPO while newly acknowledging that KTO support remains empirical.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly specifies 50 SFT epochs, 200 preference-training epochs, and the toy ID/OOD partition; these are disclosures, not established experimental changes. v4 also documents reference-model memory requirements, relative runtime overhead, jailbreak tooling and settings, and Table 2 baseline provenance. Existing hardware and hyperparameter tables are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix F adds MixEval coverage of knowledge, comprehension, commonsense, and mathematical tasks, including MMLU, GPQA, HellaSwag, MATH, and GSM8K. Appendix G adds adversarial scenarios using GPTFuzz questions and AdvBench prompts. Existing training datasets and preference benchmarks are retained.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the retained experiments is unchanged: SFT and the relevant DPO, IPO, and KTO baselines remain. The new evaluations extend these comparisons; GPTFuzz and ReNeLLM are attack procedures, not additional alignment baselines. Replacing baseline scores does not change method membership.

E3.justification: v4 introduces downstream evaluation and a detailed jailbreak protocol with specified attack/evaluator models, search limits, and top-one, top-five, and overall attack-success metrics. Appendix D.3 adds a one-epoch UltraFeedback runtime comparison. Previously reported training settings, splits, and preference-evaluation procedures remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix G adds explicit adversarial robustness tests asking whether alignment gains confer jailbreak resistance. Appendix D.3 adds an analysis of reference-update computational overhead. Existing hyperparameter, probability-mass, human-centric, diversity, response-length, and generation-example analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report 100-seed toy experiments, standard deviations, benchmark confidence intervals, Fisher tests, and probability-of-improvement analyses. v4 introduces no new uncertainty-estimation procedure or increased run count; changed uncertainty values accompany revised results.

E6.justification: Tables 2 and 7 replace baseline values: for example, Llama3-Base Arena-Hard DPO changes from 10.5 to 15.9 and IPO from 8.9 to 17.8, with v4 attributing baselines to Meng et al. TR table scores remain unchanged. Figure 1 corrects soft TR-KTO's Arena-Hard value from 15.3 to 14.9, already reported in v3's Table 2. Added results include MixEval scores, uniformly 100% ReNeLLM attack success, and 2.87–7.44% training-time overhead.

M1.justification: The DPO, IPO, and KTO objectives and their soft and periodic hard reference-update procedures remain unchanged. The additional derivation and implementation explanations do not introduce a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: v4 condenses introductory exposition and part of Section 4.2, subdivides Appendix A, and adds efficiency and evaluation sections with corresponding appendix renumbering. Headers and affiliation change to ICLR 2025 and T-Tech. Most existing prose and the main narrative order are retained.

P2.justification: v4 adds two MixEval tables and a jailbreak table, redraws Figure 1 with revised bars, labels, and Arena-Hard axis range, and reflows existing material. Figures 2–19 retain their graphics. The new knowledge-results table inadvertently carries both Table 8 and Table 9 captions.

R1.justification: v4 adds references for MixEval and its constituent benchmarks, EasyJailbreak, GPTFuzz, ReNeLLM, and AdvBench. These support the expanded evaluation; Section 2's positioning relative to RLHF, offline alignment, and Nash-based methods remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds the IPO gradient and Hessian derivation, including the residual definition and Hessian decomposition in Equations 12–15. This extends the existing curvature analysis; the DPO derivation and alignment objectives are retained.

improvement.justification: The added capability and jailbreak evaluations better delimit the unchanged method's benefits, while runtime and toy-training disclosures improve practical assessment. Reporting problems limit these gains: Section 4.3 retains a KTO interpretation contradicted by revised Table 2, and Table 11 reports 99% top-one but 98% top-five attack success for soft TR-DPO. The new IPO derivation also does not establish its asserted overall curvature decrease. The useful expansion therefore provides a modest overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Trust Region alignment work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocations and renumbering.

after.justification: v4 retains original experiments and adds downstream-task, jailbreak, and computational-overhead results. Its attribution of certain baseline scores to Meng et al. does not change the presence of original results.

before.justification: v3 reports original toy-MDP simulations and Pythia/Llama3 experiments, including preference comparisons, hyperparameter ablations, and overoptimization analyses.

title: Learn Your Reference Model for Real Good Alignment

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion expand the empirical scope from two custom benchmarks to evaluation on three benchmarks. The central claims about compositional world modeling, cooperative tree-search planning, and generalization across agent counts remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix C adds explanations of intent adaptation through observation history, attributes VLM advantages to pretrained knowledge and multimodal integration, and proposes causes of generation failures involving guidance conflicts and action misunderstanding. It also discusses limits from restricted cooperator diversity and hidden physical variables. Appendix B adds possible alternatives when reachability information is unavailable; the existing slow-inference limitation remains.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2 newly documents 4,000 training environments, 40,000 intent-tracker rollouts, 138,000 evaluator examples, shared submodule models, and one-epoch LoRA fine-tuning with batch size, GPUs, and runtime. Appendix C.2 supplies the supervised comparator's architecture and training details, and Appendix D describes real-world fine-tuning. Existing diffusion-model sizes and budgets are retained. The project-video access link also changes.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained TDW tasks, v2 adds visual 2D-FetchQ cooperation with replayed human trajectories and a physical human–XArm puzzle task using collected real-world training data. It also extends TDW-Game transfer evaluation to two agents. These substantially broaden task requirements and interaction environments.

E2.justification: v2 adds reported comparisons against BC-single, BC-GAIL, and Co-GAIL on 2D-FetchQ, plus a CLIP/BERT-based supervised model against the three VLM planning modules in Table 7. Existing TDW comparators and AVDC remain; Oracle Cooperator is renamed Shared Belief Cooperator, rather than removed.

E3.justification: v1 specifies a 60-step maximum and 10 episodes for the main TDW evaluation; v2 Table 1 reports success over a 30-step horizon and 20 episodes. New protocols include 60-episode human-trajectory replay, five physical trials, and component prediction-accuracy evaluation. Some v2 successful-episode averages exceed 30 steps, leaving their relationship to the stated horizon unclear.

E4.justification: v2 adds intent-tracker adaptation cases and prediction-error analysis, supervised-versus-VLM component comparisons, and a classification of world-model failures with visual examples in Appendix C. Agent-count generalization also extends to two agents. The existing loss-scaling and search-budget analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed-based variability, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. Changed evaluation-episode counts and the new physical-trial count describe sample sizes, without introducing a different statistical uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Main-table values change under revised reported settings: COMBO with TDW-Cook Cooperator 1 changes from 1.0 success/21.3 steps to 0.90/22.8, which is not a same-setting performance comparison. New results include 81.3% on 2D-FetchQ versus Co-GAIL's 53.3%, 100%/10.5 steps for two-agent TDW-Game, component accuracies in Table 7, and 4/5 physical successes with 8.4 average successful-trial steps. v1 Tables 2–3 retain their values as v2 Tables 3–4.

M1.justification: The proposed COMBO procedure retains two-stage compositional diffusion training, agent-dependent loss scaling, state inpainting, three VLM planning modules, and the same tree-search algorithm. Explicit initial-frame conditioning clarifies the existing state-conditioned procedure. Appendix C.2 introduces a supervised comparison model without replacing the main COMBO method.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the explanation: Problem Statement becomes part of expanded Preliminaries, Section 4 is rewritten around current-state and future-frame conditioning, and task and implementation descriptions move into separate appendices. The original appendix is reorganized into task and implementation sections alongside new analysis and real-world sections. Introduction wording, terminology, authorship, and citation style also change.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 1, clarifies state and prediction labels in Figures 2 and 4, and adds Figures 8–13 for the new environment, intent tracking, failures, and physical experiments. It adds Tables 2, 7, and 8, combines success/steps within Table 1 cells, and expands the agent-count table. The conference template also changes typography, margins, headers, and figure placement throughout.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 sharpens the comparison with VLP and newly discusses RoboDreamer's compositional robot planning. New citations support Co-GAIL evaluation, implementation details, and proposed extensions, while generic references such as Genie and NOPA disappear. These refine the existing multi-agent research positioning without replacing it.

T1.justification: The DEC-POMDP formulation, score composition, diffusion losses, and sampling relationships retain their substance. New preliminary subsections reorganize and explain the existing diffusion mathematics, while explicit initial-frame conditioning clarifies notation. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's evidence was confined to two custom simulated tasks and left planning-module training substantially underspecified. v2 addresses these weaknesses through an additional cooperation benchmark, a physical pilot, component comparisons, intent and failure analyses, and concrete fine-tuning documentation. These materially improve empirical support and reproducibility. The physical study remains preliminary at five trials, and the stated 30-step horizon is difficult to reconcile with some reported averages, but these reporting limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe COMBO and retain matching core methods and experiments. All 23 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, references, and appendices, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports retained and revised TDW experiments, plus original COMBO results on 2D-FetchQ, component-level analyses, and a five-trial human–robot experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original TDW-Game and TDW-Cook experiments, generated-video evaluations, component ablations, and planning-budget and agent-count comparisons.

title: COMBO: Compositional World Models for Embodied Multi-Agent Cooperation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements, and conclusion retain identical claims about compositional world modeling, cooperative planning, and generalization across tasks, cooperators, and agent counts.

C2.justification: The explanations of cooperation performance, intent adaptation, VLM advantages, and generation failures are unchanged, as are the limitations concerning inference speed, diverse cooperators, and hidden physical variables.

D1.justification: Appendices A–B and C.2 retain identical architecture, data collection, hyperparameter, hardware, and training-time details. Resource links and their destinations are also unchanged.

E1.justification: Both evaluate TDW-Game, TDW-Cook, adapted 2D-FetchQ, and the real-world human–robot puzzle task. Cooperator policies and agent-count scenarios are unchanged.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is identical in Tables 1–3, 5, and 7, including the planning baselines, BC-single/BC-GAIL/Co-GAIL, AVDC, and the simpler supervised submodule model.

E3.justification: Evaluation metrics, observations, training settings, and sample counts are unchanged. Both retain the 20-episode main TDW evaluation, 60-episode 2D-FetchQ replay evaluation, and five real-world trials.

E4.justification: The Intent Tracker and loss-scaling ablations, search-budget and agent-count studies, alternative-submodule comparison, and Appendix C prediction and failure-case analyses are identical.

E5.justification: Both use the same point estimates and episode/trial aggregation. Seed information, repeated-run uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, error bars, and significance tests are absent from both.

E6.justification: All numerical entries and qualitative findings match. Examples include COMBO's 81.3% success rate in Table 2 and the 4/5 successful real-world trials with 8.4 average successful-trial steps in Table 8.

M1.justification: Sections 4–5 and Algorithm 1 are identical, retaining the compositional video diffusion model, agent-dependent loss scaling, world-state estimation, VLM submodules, and tree-search planning.

P1.justification: On page 1, Zheyuan Zhang's affiliation changes from the University of Michigan to the University of Massachusetts Amherst; remaining affiliation numbers are adjusted and Massachusetts Institute of Technology becomes MIT. The arXiv stamp is updated. Scientific prose and document structure are unchanged.

P2.justification: The shortened first-page affiliation block no longer extends beyond the main text's right margin. Figures 1–13, Tables 1–8, their captions, and all layouts on pages 2–24 remain identical.

R1.justification: Section 2, the reference list, and comparisons with prior research are identical. The affiliation edits do not change research positioning.

T1.justification: The DEC-POMDP formulation, diffusion definitions, compositional reasoning, and Equations 1–8 are identical. No formal assumptions, derivations, or proofs are added or revised.

improvement.justification: v3 updates affiliations and the version stamp, with a small improvement in first-page text fit. The scientific content, empirical evidence, analyses, reproducibility information, and appendices are identical, establishing no meaningful overall quality change.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same COMBO paper, with 24 readable pages including Appendices A–D. Text and rendered pages 2–24 are identical; first-page differences are confined to affiliations and the arXiv version/date stamp.

after.justification: v3 retains those original empirical results, including the benchmark evaluations and five real-world human–robot trials.

before.justification: v2 reports original benchmark experiments and ablations in Section 6, additional analyses in Appendix C, and human–robot experiments in Appendix D.

title: COMBO: Compositional World Models for Embodied Multi-Agent Cooperation

C1.justification: The central contribution remains interpretable, controllable probability estimation through BIRD. The headline advantage changes from 35% over GPT-4, with over 65% human alignment, to approximately 30% over LLM baselines. The introduction and conclusion strengthen the decision-making claim from performance comparable to CoT to outperforming CoT, supported particularly by the added Llama-3.1 experiments.

C2.justification: v2 explains why rankings alone can be insufficient for constrained planning and why relative human judgments are used instead of absolute probabilities, citing its inconclusive annotation pilot. It attributes Llama-3.1's stronger decisions partly to more comprehensive factors. The unrestricted applicability discussion, including hierarchical handling of multiple outcomes, is omitted. Unknown predictions and the proposed CoT fallback remain acknowledged.

D1.justification: v2 supplies previously undocumented prompts for Vanilla, probability CoT, EC, and decision-making CoT baselines (Figures 11–14), plus the self-correction prompt. It specifies greedy decoding at temperature 0 for the logit baseline and provides additional dataset-construction and verification details. Core optimization hyperparameters and the training pseudocode were already present; no code-release information is added.

E1.justification: The benchmark suite remains COMMON2SENSE, TODAY, PLASMA, MATRES, and TRACIE. Within PLASMA, v2 introduces generated conditions supporting manually identified less-common outcomes, revising the represented planning situations (A.4). Figure 1 also replaces restaurant and flight examples with a constrained charging-station planning case. Coverage changes within the existing broad domains.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds logit-based probability baselines and Llama-3.1 Vanilla, CoT, and EC comparisons. Its BIRD ablation rows switch from Llama-2 to Llama-3.1, although Llama-2 ablations remain in Table 2. Figure 1 replaces the illustrative GPT-4 comparison with OpenAI o1. The principal existing comparison approaches are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds Llama-3.1-70B as an experimental backbone. The probability-evaluation annotation pool changes from 400 to 450 examples; v2 obtains 366 agreement-qualified examples and filters these to 350 on which every evaluated method makes correct binary decisions, unlike v1's stated selection process. PLASMA is reconstructed as 1,395 instances across 279 scenarios rather than 1,357 instances. Follow-up evaluation instructions also shift toward informing the choice between outcomes (Figure 4). These materially revise the reported evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses addressing several previously untested questions: failure attribution for BIRD-wrong/CoT-correct cases (Table 4), comparative factor quality across backbones (Table 5), human verification of generated datasets (A.4), and the feasibility of absolute-probability annotation (A.5). It also extends factor-generation ablations to Llama-3.1 in Table 7. The earlier pepper example is retained as Table 6, rather than newly added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed replication, across-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Both use point estimates and vote-based aggregation. The added annotation-quality outcomes do not introduce uncertainty estimates for the reported model comparisons.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces Llama-2 BIRD's reported F1 of 0.651 with 0.592 and adds Llama-3.1 results, including 0.588 for optimized BIRD. Table 2 reports PLASMA BIRD/CoT accuracies of 74.0/76.8 instead of 92.0/99.6; Table 3 revises its PLASMA scores and averages. Follow-up preferences change from 126 wins, 40 ties, and 84 losses to 132, 36, and 82. New diagnostic results are also reported. Changed procedures and data prevent treating these as same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The Bayesian aggregation, training losses, and Algorithm 1 remain substantially unchanged. However, v1's hierarchical/direct entailment ensemble is replaced by direct entailment with self-correction in v2 Section 3.4. Follow-up generation also changes from randomly selecting an unobserved factor to selecting the most important one and its highest-probability outcome-aligned value (v1 A.10; v2 A.9). These are localized procedural refinements.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around incomplete information and constrained planning. Modeling is reorganized to introduce marginalization earlier and present Bayesian parameter optimization before entailment. Experimental explanations and related work are substantially rewritten, and appendix sections are reorganized. These changes reshape the narrative beyond merely inserting new experiments.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 2 are substantially redesigned around charging-station planning. Main comparison tables and the factor-generation ablation table gain structures for two backbones, and new error-analysis and factor-comparison tables appear. Appendix prompt screenshots become consistently styled text boxes, with additional prompt figures. Typography, headings, and page composition also change throughout.

R1.justification: Related work is substantively broadened with a probabilistic-inference subsection discussing uncertain NLI, ThinkSum, and probabilistic language-of-thought approaches. v2 explicitly positions BIRD against these methods through incomplete-information handling and interpretability, and identifies Hou et al. (2024) as a close uncertainty-decomposition comparison. Decomposition and uncertainty-sampling coverage also expands beyond v1.

T1.justification: Equation 4 replaces v1's equality identifying the conditional probability with the opinion-pool estimate with estimated-probability notation and an approximation sign, qualifying its mathematical status. The marginalization derivation in A.1, weak-ordering and noninteraction assumptions in A.2, and optimization equations otherwise remain unchanged; no new proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 improves empirical support and auditability through a second backbone, logit comparisons, dataset checks, diagnostic analyses, and fuller prompt documentation. The clearer organization also helps explain the existing framework. However, the central evaluation still measures filtered relative judgments rather than validating the absolute probabilities motivating the planning example. v2 also introduces a reproducibility inconsistency: Section 4.2 assigns the 1/2 ablation a fallback probability of 0, while Appendix A.6 retains 1/2. The additions support a net improvement, but these limitations constrain its significance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BIRD framework and share identifiable methods, experiments, and appendix material. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are sufficiently readable for reliable comparison, including the image-based prompts in v1.

after.justification: v2 reports original results for both Llama-2 and Llama-3.1, alongside transfer-training and human evaluations. Its appendices also report dataset quality checks, error analysis, and an annotation pilot.

before.justification: v1 reports original probability-estimation evaluations, decision-making experiments, transfer-training results, component ablations, and human preferences for generated follow-up questions.

title: BIRD: A Trustworthy Bayesian Inference Framework for Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central claims about reliable probability estimation, interpretable and controllable Bayesian inference, decision making, soft supervision, and follow-up questions. The additional ablation supports the existing framework without redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix A.3 newly characterizes 128 samples as a training minimum, suggests more samples improve alignment, and provides an expert-informed Likert-scale rationale for probability mappings, including claimed insensitivity to small adjustments. A.9 adds the interpretation that both losses are crucial. Existing failure analyses remain.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-availability link, discloses grid-search tuning using a PLASMA validation set, clarifies scenario-specific parameters and training samples, and explains the temporal training underlying Table 3 in new A.10. Prompt templates are revised. Conversely, Section 4.1 removes the general temperature-0.7 statement.

E1.justification: Both versions use COMMON2SENSE, TODAY, and PLASMA, with MATRES and TRACIE retained for supervision-transfer evaluation. The new loss ablation uses existing tasks; the revised scenario count does not establish new task or domain coverage.

E2.justification: The established Vanilla, Logit, CoT, EC, and existing ablation comparators are retained. New Table 8 adds two evaluated comparison variants, BIRD without MR loss and BIRD without MSE loss.

E3.justification: Sections 4.1 and A.4 change the reported COMMON2SENSE scenario count from 213 to 216, retaining 3,822 instances. Sections 4.2 and A.5 remove the stated filter requiring every method to make correct binary decisions, retaining 350 evaluation examples. This revises the reported selection protocol without establishing a rerun. Table 8 also introduces loss-removal controls.

E4.justification: New Appendix A.9 tests whether each component of the existing two-loss objective contributes to decision accuracy. Table 8 reports separate MR-loss and MSE-loss removals across three datasets using Llama-3.1-70b. Earlier factor-generation ablations, probability-assignment ablations, and error analyses remain.

E5.justification: The versions retain point-estimate reporting and the human-annotation replication procedures. The added ablation introduces no experimental seed reporting, run-to-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes Llama-3.1 CoT average F1 from 0.346 to 0.309, with all three class scores also revised, and changes fixed-initial-probability Different1 F1 from 0.616 to 0.614. New Table 8 adds six loss-ablation scores. Other benchmark and follow-up results are retained. The revised selection description prevents assuming strict same-setting comparability for Table 1.

M1.justification: The Bayesian model, objectives, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged, but the supplied inference prompts change operationally. Figure 8 replaces single-statement entailment with factor-value selection, an explicit None option, and tie-breaking; Figure 9 replaces strict removal of unsupported values with a more lenient deletion rule.

P1.justification: v3 makes targeted language and terminology corrections, rewrites several prompt examples, adds acknowledgements and two appendix subsections, and updates the publication header. The main narrative and section organization remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds the loss-ablation Table 8, relocates Figure 2 before Related Work, and revises its caption and several prompt boxes. The existing follow-up-question table becomes Table 9, with unchanged results. These are localized display and layout changes.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive research positioning remain unchanged. DeLLMa's reference changes from its 2024 preprint to its 2025 ICLR publication, which is a bibliographic update to the same work.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, Equations (1)-(13), Appendix A.1 derivation, and A.2 assumptions are substantively unchanged. The parameter-count expression added in A.3 makes the existing parameterization explicit rather than introducing new theory.

improvement.justification: v3 supplies separate loss-component evidence absent from v2 and adds useful code-access, tuning, and training explanations. These provide limited gains in evidential support and reproducibility while the central results and theory remain stable. The unexplained evaluation-selection revision and removed general temperature statement temper the improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BIRD framework and research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison across relocations and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical studies and adds a loss-component ablation in Appendix A.9, Table 8.

before.justification: v2 reports original benchmark experiments, human evaluations of probabilities and follow-up questions, supervision-transfer results, ablations, and error analyses.

title: BIRD: A Trustworthy Bayesian Inference Framework for Large Language Models

C1.justification: Both versions retain the central findings that stochasticity drives DBP robustness and ADDT improves purification. v2 adds an explicit recommendation to decouple and combine stochasticity-based and purification-based robustness, while removing precise-gradient reevaluation from the headline contribution list. This refines the contribution emphasis without replacing the main findings.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations involving gradient variance, EoT effectiveness, and the distinction from randomized smoothing. It changes DW-box from an explicitly hypothetical diagnostic in v1 to a potentially realistic scenario when random seeds are known. Sections 6.4-6.5 also discuss limited scaling gains, model/data requirements, attack computation costs, and the clean-accuracy tradeoff from increased stochasticity.

D1.justification: v2 supplies explicit Tiny-ImageNet and ImageNet training schedules and reports the high-resolution evaluation cost: approximately seven days on eight RTX 4090 GPUs. It drops v1's explicit statement that RBGM processes each image channel independently. The fixed-AutoAttack access link and general code-release promise remain equivalent.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual ImageNet-1k training and evaluation at 224 × 224 resolution, substantially extending the earlier CIFAR and Tiny-ImageNet coverage. It also adds the DWRev scenario, where the attacker knows reverse-process noise while forward-process noise remains unknown.

E2.justification: The principal CIFAR-10 comparator set remains unchanged, including GDMP variants, COUP, DiffPure, and the diffusion-model baselines. However, v2 Table 8 adds vanilla DPEDM and its ADDT counterpart to the retained Tiny-ImageNet comparison, which contained only DPDDPM and DPDDIM in v1 Table 6.

E3.justification: v2 adds PGD200+EoT20 evaluations alongside the existing PGD20+EoT10 protocol. Its new ImageNet experiment uses ResNet-101, an l-infinity bound of 4/255, and 12 training epochs followed by eight ADDT epochs. These substantially extend the evaluation settings; the stronger-attack scores are newly reported results under different conditions.

E4.justification: v2 adds stronger-attack validation, reverse-noise-only analysis, and a lambda_unit sensitivity study across five NFEs. Conversely, v1's rank-distribution histogram analysis in Appendix D disappears, and its clean/MSE-guided fine-tuning ablation across five NFEs is reduced to the default NFE for each model in v2 Table 5. The earlier Corrector and fixed-AutoAttack analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without adding confidence intervals, error bars, significance tests, or quantified repeated-run variability. The statement about independent implementation and training cross-checks is retained. Increased EoT iterations change attack construction rather than uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: Most matched legacy scores, including Table 2, are unchanged. v2 adds stronger-attack results, ImageNet results, Tiny-ImageNet DPEDM scores, and lambda_unit results, while removing nondefault CGPO-control results and the rank histogram. For example, Table 7 newly reports 41.02% vanilla versus 46.19% ADDT accuracy for DPDDPM under PGD200+EoT20. The new DWRev result is inconsistent: Figure 2 gives 38.00% for DPDDPM, whereas Table 11 gives 35.25%.

M1.justification: The core CGPO, RBGM, noise-mixture, and diffusion-training objectives are retained. However, Algorithm 1 changes RBGM(delta) to RBGM(delta, epsilon), potentially reusing the Gaussian sample also mixed into the input. Section 5.2 still describes sampling a Gaussian tensor separately. The PDFs do not resolve whether this changes noise coupling or merely clarifies the function interface.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around a stochastic perspective. Section 4 is reorganized, the method subsections reverse order, evaluation-method discussion moves into Appendix E, and experimental and appendix sections are substantially restructured. These changes extend well beyond inserting new experiments.

P2.justification: The main text switches from a two-column layout to a single-column layout with wrapped figures and tables. Figure 4 is rearranged, Figure 2 gains DWRev bars, the rank histogram is removed, and several tables are added or reformatted. The DDIM NFE table moves into the appendix, and captions and labels are widely revised.

R1.justification: v2 adds a focused comparison with Cohen et al.'s randomized smoothing and acknowledges similar evaluation protocols in Chen et al. (2023) and Kang et al. (2024). Dataset and FID references are added, while the Li et al. and Kim et al. loss-landscape references disappear. The broader adversarial-training and purification positioning remains recognizable.

T1.justification: The principal diffusion equations and ADDT objectives are retained. v2 removes v1's explicit conditional-Gaussian and uniform-rank justification for RBGM. Appendix D introduces formal mappings distinguishing noise-conditioned DBP predictions from distribution-valued predictions and randomized-smoothing aggregation. These are limited changes to mathematical assumptions and definitions; no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: The stronger-attack tests address v1's limited attack-strength validation, and ImageNet evaluation reveals the modest gains at larger scale.
