title: Neural Context Flows for Meta-Learning of Dynamical Systems

C1.justification: v2 principally claims competitive generalization on three main benchmarks. v3 claims state-of-the-art OoD performance on five of six, convergence guarantees, interpretable representations and uncertainty estimation. It also elevates the benchmark collection to an explicit core contribution.

C2.justification: v3 develops contextual self-modulation, physical-parameter identifiability and explanations involving nonlinear adaptation and spurious associations. It adds substantive limitations concerning discontinuous dynamics, initialization sensitivity and hyperparameter tuning, while revising v2’s quadratic-cost discussion around context pooling and its accuracy–cost tradeoff.

D1.justification: v3 substantially expands per-method architectures, optimizer and budget tables, hardware, frameworks, solver tolerances and regularization settings. It documents dataset parameters and a common split/tensor interface, and updates implementation examples for second-order expansion and pooling. Code and dataset links already existed in v2. Conflicting SP variant and LV pool-size descriptions still limit reproducibility.

E1.justification: v3 retains SP, LV, GO and GS, adding Sel’kov Model, Brusselator and Navier-Stokes evaluations. It also expands LV adaptation to a wider parameter range on a 25-by-25 grid and evaluates physical-parameter recovery. SP was already evaluated in v2’s appendix.

E2.justification: CAVIA and CoDA-l1 remain the main external baselines, and OFA remains the SP comparator. v3 additionally compares the earlier first-order NCF against NCF-t2 and includes a dedicated CoDA-versus-NCF parameter-recovery comparison in Figure 5 and Appendix A.2. The external baseline families are unchanged.

E3.justification: Reported settings change substantially: v2 specifies 120,000 LV training epochs and GO context dimension 1024; v3 specifies 10,000 epochs for LV NCF-t1 and GO dimension 256. Optimizers, architectures and learning-rate schedules also change. New analyses introduce MAPE and matched-architecture parameter-recovery protocols. These changes do not establish that every retained result was rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds context-pool and Taylor-removal ablations, runtime analysis, grid-wide adaptation, attractor-specific errors, parameter recovery and GO context clustering. It replaces the SP context-size sweep with a broader LV sweep. The three-network ablation is retained, including v2 Table 4 as v3 Table 8.

E5.justification: Beyond v2’s existing uncertainty displays, v3 introduces predictive uncertainty from candidate trajectories: Figure 6 reports means and standard deviations across 9 LV and 21 SM forecasts, with deviations magnified tenfold for display. Figure 14 explicitly identifies seed-averaged results and standard-deviation bars, without specifying the seed count or establishing increased runs for retained results.

E6.justification: v3 Table 1 adds NCF-t2 and three benchmark result sets, with NCF-t2 achieving the lowest OoD MSE on five of six tasks. SP and architecture-ablation tables retain their values.

M1.justification: v3 introduces NCF-t2 with second-order Taylor expansion and proximal alternating minimization, configurable context pools and L2 weight regularization. Unlike v2’s cross-context adaptation, v3 disables Taylor expansion during adaptation. These substantially change training and adaptation procedures.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and discussion are substantially rewritten around meta-learning and contextual self-modulation. Extended related work moves into the main text; methods receive separate training, adaptation, pooling and testing subsections; results separate interpolation from extrapolation; and the appendices are extensively reorganized.

P2.justification: v3 merges and expands the main benchmark tables, revises the NCF diagram and adds parameter-grid heatmaps, uncertainty plots, identification panels, runtime plots and trajectory displays. Existing SP and architecture-ablation figures are relocated, while the GS visualization is retained with a revised caption. Algorithms and page layout are also substantially reformatted.

R1.justification: Beyond relocating related work, v3 explicitly positions NCF relative to CAMEL/Blanke and Lelarge’s interpretable, linearly parameterized systems and claims an extension to nonlinear settings. It adds substantial positioning around proximal optimization, uncertainty estimation and scientific foundation models, supported by new references.

T1.justification: v2 explicitly leaves theoretical guarantees for future work. v3 adds Proposition 3.1 and its second-order JVP proof in Appendix A.1, plus a conditional convergence theorem under KL, smoothness and boundedness assumptions. The applicability of its smooth-loss assumptions to the stated L1-regularized objective is not reconciled.

improvement.justification: v3 implements the scalability remedy deferred in v2 and supports it with accuracy/runtime ablations. Broader nonlinear adaptation tests, parameter-recovery analyses and substantially fuller experimental documentation strengthen the paper’s practical evidence. These gains outweigh added tuning complexity, although conflicting settings and the unresolved applicability of the convergence theorem to the nonsmooth objective temper the stronger claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Neural Context Flows, with matching authors, methods and retained experiments. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark results, including additional Sel’kov, Brusselator and Navier-Stokes experiments, alongside adaptation, interpretability and ablation analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original NCF experiments on Lotka-Volterra, Glycolytic Oscillator, Gray-Scott and Simple Pendulum, including benchmark comparisons and appendix ablations.

title: Neural Context Flows for Meta-Learning of Dynamical Systems

C1.justification: v5 explicitly adds an affine-system identifiability proof to the introduction's contributions. The central claims about contextual self-modulation, interpretability, uncertainty estimation, benchmark provision and best OoD performance on five of six comparison problems remain.

C2.justification: v5 adds substantive applicability qualifications: OPE can become preferable with sufficient data and time, noisy identification deteriorates outside the training convex hull, and uncertainty coverage requires problem-specific interpretation. It explains pooling-strategy convergence differences and removes proximal optimization from the SM performance explanation, retaining the higher-order Taylor interpretation.

D1.justification: v5 adds a PyTorch implementation link, OFA/OPE architecture and budget details, SP generation/testing details, and instructions for the new analyses. E2.justification: v5 adds One-Per-Environment (OPE) to the SP comparison, which previously evaluated OFA and NCF. It also evaluates OFA and OPE against NCF in the new BT sample-efficiency study. CAVIA and CoDA remain the comparators in the unchanged six-system comparison.

The SP training description changes from NCF-t2 with 500 outer and 20 inner iterations to NCF-t1 with 12000 epochs. Since v3 elsewhere already labels SP as NCF-t1, this establishes revised documentation, not an unambiguous history of rerunning the experiment.

E4.justification: v5 adds noisy LV parameter-identification tests, quantitative uncertainty/error diagnostics, SP and BT sample-efficiency studies, environment-scaling measurements and a controlled comparison of pooling strategies. These test robustness, data requirements, computational scaling and design choices beyond v3's retained pool-size, context-size and architecture ablations.

E5.justification: v3 already includes error bars and candidate-trajectory mean/standard-deviation plots. v5 adds empirical three-sigma intervals and coverage reporting, specifies ten Gaussian-noise seeds and three repeats for pooling and SP validation studies, and reports across-epoch timing variability. These additions do not establish increased run counts for the retained benchmark results.

E6.justification: The six-system comparison is numerically unchanged between v3 Table 1 and v5 Table 2. SP scores and architecture-ablation values are revised: the LV full-NCF ablation row changes from 1.28/0.80 to 6.73/7.92 for InD/adaptation MSE, all times 10^-5. v5 also adds uncertainty, noise, timing, sample-efficiency and pooling outcomes. Revised SP settings prevent a same-setting performance interpretation, and v5 Tables 1 and 7 contain unreconciled SP values.

M1.justification: The NCF-t1/t2 procedures, three-network architecture, objectives, Algorithms 1–4 and adaptation rule remain unchanged. The three pooling strategies already existed in v3; v5 relocates and evaluates them. Revised experimental configurations do not introduce a new method.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially rewritten and reordered. Pooling-strategy explanations move from the main text to Appendix A.6, the datasets/ablations/implementation appendices are reordered, an appendix contents page is added, and Broader Impact becomes an Ethics Statement. Extensive prose editing accompanies this reorganization.

P2.justification: v5 adds figures and tables for noise, uncertainty, sample efficiency, scaling and pooling. The SP table gains OPE and revised column scaling; its training plot gains normalized progress and validation curves. Figure 25 combines retained LV plots with new SM examples, while conference formatting substantially reflows the displays.

R1.justification: v5 expands positioning around parametric PDEs and foundation models, adding works such as Herde and Takamoto, and cites Duan for affine identification and Serrano for uncertainty evaluation. Arjovsky, He and Portwood references are removed. The central positioning relative to CoDA, CAVIA and CAMEL remains.

T1.justification: v3 invokes the prior CAMEL identifiability result and illustrates parameter recovery empirically. v5 adds Proposition 2, explicit affine-system assumptions, an extended proof and parameter-recovery derivations in Appendix A.2. The existing Taylor/JVP proof and optimization convergence theorem are retained.

improvement.justification: v5 improves assessment of NCF through OPE controls, sample-efficiency and timing studies, noise tests and pooling ablations, making its useful operating conditions clearer. However, Appendix A.2 does not justify inferring Taylor equality on open neighborhoods from zero sampled loss; Eq. (26) normalizes candidate dispersion by trajectory length N rather than candidate count p; and SP values in Tables 1 and 7 remain unreconciled. These issues temper the empirical gains and limit confidence in the added theoretical and uncertainty claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Neural Context Flow work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–F are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v5 retains those original experiments and reports additional noise, uncertainty, sample-efficiency, timing and pooling-strategy results.

before.justification: v3 reports original dynamical-system forecasting and adaptation experiments, benchmark comparisons, interpretability results and ablations.

title: Neural Context Flows for Meta-Learning of Dynamical Systems

C2.justification: Appendix B.3 corrects the misleading condition 'neither data nor training time are not a concern' to 'neither data nor training time is a concern.' This clarifies when OPE should be preferred; other interpretations and limitations are retained.

D1.justification: The architecture specifications, hyperparameters, hardware, solver details, code listings, and code/data access information remain unchanged. Appendices D-E receive copyedits without new reproducibility information.

title: Neural Context Flows for Meta-Learning of Dynamical Systems

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from inertial acceleration, INP convergence, KL limit-point convergence and stochastic oracle optimality to coupled smoothing/penalization and conventional approximate criticality. V3 newly emphasizes its claimed complexity advantage over RADMM and bijective-operator coverage, while narrowing the permitted last-block regularizer to convex functions.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive explanations for smoothing only the last block, recovering criticality through an auxiliary proximal point, and rescaling multipliers. It interprets its comparisons as favoring primal-dual methods and attributes RADMM's limitations to conservative fixed parameters. V1's INP-strength and stochastic-acceleration interpretations disappear; caution about conservative surjective-case steps remains.

D1.justification: Implementation guidance is substantially reworked: v3 supplies the smoothed-block proximal computation, a stopping criterion and IPDS/RADMM parameter values. V1's SPIDER sampling/batch recipe, noisy-signal generation instructions, l1/2 and DC proximal recipes, and common random-initialization disclosure disappear. MATLAB, hardware specifications, basic data normalization and the supplemental-code statement remain.

E1.justification: V3 restricts evaluation to sparse PCA, removing noisy sparse recovery and its Gaussian/DCT sensing cases. Its PCA plots cover Gaussian, MNIST, TDT2 and sector data, versus TDT2/sector in v1's visible PCA plots; Gaussian and MNIST were already listed in v1's dataset appendix. V3's additional motivating applications are not evaluated tasks.

E2.justification: The sparse PCA comparator set changes from SubGrad, PDM and non-inertial standard ADMM to SubGrad, SPGM and RADMM. Thus two principal comparators are replaced in the corresponding experiment. V1's recovery comparison and appendix comparison involving IRPL-ADMM-SPIDER also disappear.

E3.justification: The reported sparse PCA formulation changes from DC l1-largest-k regularization to l1 regularization, and the component count changes from 30 or 50 to 20. Experimental penalty settings change from beta0=10 with adaptive p=2 updates to beta0=50*rho with p=1/3. V3 also evaluates rho=1 and 100 alongside 10 and revises some dataset sample counts.

E4.justification: V1's comparison against ADMM with alpha=0 provides a limited check of inertial acceleration; that comparison disappears. V3 Appendix E.3 instead adds limited sensitivity evidence across regularization strengths rho=1, 10 and 100. It does not isolate the individual IPDS components.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. V1's stochastic-gradient variance analysis is theoretical and does not constitute empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The experimental curves are substantially replaced. V1 reports faster sparse PCA convergence for IRPL-ADMM but no speed advantage over PDM on noisy recovery; v3 reports generally lowest sparse PCA objectives for IPDS-ADMM across its revised comparisons and regularization strengths. These are results under changed objectives, ranks, algorithms and comparators, not same-setting performance gains. V1's qualitative SPIDER advantage claim is removed.

M1.justification: IRPL-ADMM's inertial extrapolation and flexible regular penalty rules are replaced by IPDS-ADMM's non-inertial updates, last-block Moreau smoothing and coupled increasing-penalty/decreasing-smoothing schedule. V1's SPIDER extension is also removed. These are substantive procedural changes, not merely a renamed algorithm.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution narrative and much of the algorithm exposition are rewritten. V3 introduces a dedicated motivating-applications section, separates relaxation-related discussion, integrates complexity into the convergence section and reorganizes the appendices. These changes substantially alter the narrative beyond terminology and numbering.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. Table 1 loses its stochastic-complexity column and changes its comparison structure; algorithm displays are consolidated and redesigned. Four-panel experimental figures are replaced by eight-panel PCA displays, the recovery figure disappears, and two additional eight-panel figures appear in the appendix.

R1.justification: V3 substantially repositions the contribution around Moreau smoothing and RADMM, adding Li et al. (2022) to Table 1 and explicitly comparing complexity and operator restrictions. It adds smoothing and application references while removing substantial KL and stochastic-estimator literature associated with deleted contributions. Publication updates to retained works are not treated as new citations.

T1.justification: V1's INP hierarchy, O(epsilon^-1) surrogate guarantee, KL finite-length analysis and stochastic complexity proofs are replaced by Moreau-envelope lemmas and an O(epsilon^-3) critical-residual analysis. V3 requires convex hn, adds boundedness assumptions and extends the identity case to bijective matrices with kappa<2. The rates concern different criteria. The new parameter rule also permits a negative coefficient in Lemma 4.3's norm bound, an unresolved inconsistency in Appendix D.3.

improvement.justification: V3 addresses v1's acknowledged difficulty connecting positive-tolerance INP points to criticality and adds inspectable supplementary curves and relevant smoothing baselines. However, its central theoretical gain is not established securely as written: permitted parameters kappa=1, xi=0.9, delta=0.25 and sigma=1.5 in Equation (5) yield q approximately -0.246 in Lemma 4.3, making the stated norm upper bound impossible. Alongside narrowed assumptions and reduced task coverage, this unresolved proof issue prevents a reliable net-quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs concern the same multi-block nonconvex ADMM research, and their main text, equations, proofs and displayed experiments support comparison. However, v1 Appendix H.1-H.2 contains unresolved 'Figure ??' references, with no corresponding stochastic-results plot, limiting verification of those supplementary claims.

after.justification: V3 Section 5 and Appendix E report original sparse PCA experiments across eight data configurations and three regularization strengths in Figures 1-3.

before.justification: V1 Section 6 and Figures 1-2 report original objective-versus-time experiments for sparse PCA and noisy sparse recovery.

title: ADMM for Nonconvex Optimization under Minimal Continuity Assumption

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same headline claims: IPDS-ADMM under one-block continuity, convergence for bijective and surjective operator cases, O(ε^-3) critical-point complexity, and empirical effectiveness on sparse PCA.

C2.justification: Remark 4.16 newly explains p=1/3 as balancing the two rate terms. Appendix E.3 singles out beta0=50ρ and 100ρ as favorable settings, but its broad 'consistently outperforms' interpretation does not explain the failures visible at smaller penalties.

D1.justification: Code-access directions change from supplemental material to the author's research webpage, without a direct URL. v4 explicitly reports theta1=1.01 and theta2=0.60 where v3 reports only theta=1.01. MATLAB, hardware, data preparation and orthogonality-projection details remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate sparse PCA using Gaussian random matrices, MNIST, TDT2 and sector data. The additional parameter combinations and changed MNIST feature counts retain the same data sources and task.

The plots now report common 20-second windows instead of dataset-dependent windows.

E4.justification: Appendix E.3 expands comparisons at three regularization values and one initial-penalty multiplier into a joint four-by-four parameter study. This directly examines sensitivity to the initial penalty and reveals poor behavior at small penalties and slower convergence in some large-penalty settings.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The additional curves retain the same uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v4 reports replacement convergence curves and sixteen parameter combinations versus three in v3. Changed parameters and MNIST dimensions prevent interpreting the replacement curves as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same penalty and smoothing schedules, proximal block updates and relaxed multiplier update. The parameter-selection formulas are unchanged apart from notation; revised experimental parameter choices do not introduce a new method.

P1.justification: The main section and appendix organization remains intact. v4 consolidates related-work discussion and several lemma/proof pairs, renames Section 3 subsections, edits explanatory prose, and adds acknowledgments and a conference header. Most narrative is retained.

P2.justification: Experimental presentation expands from three figures to seventeen, including sixteen appendix parameter combinations and a new mapping table. Figure 1 repeats Figure 8's setting. Curves, time axes, MNIST labels and captions are revised; Table 1 is relocated and highlights nonsmoothness assumptions in color.

R1.justification: v4 adds references including Franca et al. (2018), Lin et al. (2022b) and Yuan (2024, 2025), removes several inertial-method citations, and revises RADMM's stated scope and Table 1's assumption descriptions. Remark 3.7 replaces the assertion that Lemmas 3.4–3.5 are novel with their derivation through standard convex analysis.

T1.justification: v3 Definition 4.17 and Theorem 4.18 use summed squared residuals and p in (0,1/2); v4 Definition 4.14 and Theorem 4.15 use unsquared residuals and state bounds for p in (0,1). Appendix D.13 substantially reworks the complexity derivation while retaining O(ε^-3) at p=1/3. title: Transformers Can Learn Temporal Difference Methods for In-Context Reinforcement Learning

CartPole pretraining uses context length 250 and 10,000 MRPs. These supplement the retained experimental settings rather than revise their reported performance under matched conditions.

Appendix G adds RNN training diagnostics and context-length tests probing architectural dependence. The earlier depth, parameter-sharing, and nonlinear-attention analyses are retained.

New context-length plots also use standard errors; their 300- and 500-task sample sizes concern new evaluation designs, without changing replication counts or uncertainty procedures for retained experiments.

E6.justification: The original experimental plots are retained unchanged. New results show transformer MSVE decreasing with context (Figure 1), TD-like parameter patterns after CartPole pretraining (Figure 10), and reduced RNN training error without sustained improvement from longer context (Figures 11–12).

after.justification: v4 retains those original experiments and adds context-length evaluations, CartPole pretraining results, and RNN experiments in Figure 1 and Appendices F–G.

before.justification: v3 reports original transformer-training experiments on randomized Boyan’s-chain tasks, architecture analyses, and numerical verification of its constructions in Section 4 and Appendices C–E.

improvement.justification: v6 adds useful comparator coverage, backbone tests, and procedural documentation, but removes data-abundant evidence and explicit limitations. title: Node-Time Conditional Prompt Learning in Dynamic Graphs

D1.justification: Appendix E consolidates and revises dataset-specific model dimensions, while Appendices F–G disclose runtimes, the full-test-set timing scope and parameter counts. P2.justification: Tables 5–9 add displays for the new dataset evaluations, runtimes, alternative splits and component comparison. Figure 2 is redrawn with class prototypes and explicit loss references. The original result plots and tables are retained, with some layout and placement adjustments.

R1.justification: Appendix G and Table 9 substantially expand positioning against GraphPrompt, ProG and TIGPrompt through component-level distinctions and a parameterization comparison. improvement.justification: The added datasets and TIGPrompt-split evaluation strengthen validation beyond the original experimental coverage, while runtime measurements provide practical evidence absent from v6. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DYGPROMPT research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v8 retains those empirical results and adds DGraph and ML-Rating evaluations, runtime measurements and experiments using TIGPrompt's splits in Appendix F.

before.justification: v6 reports original node-classification and link-prediction experiments, ablations, backbone comparisons and embedding visualizations in Tables 1–3 and Figures 3–4.

title: Node-Time Conditional Prompt Learning in Dynamic Graphs

D1.justification: v4 supplies the complete GPT-4o mini judging prompt, access information and metadata for the added preference datasets, and scoring and perturbation instructions for the new comparisons. E6.justification: The original Table 2 and matched ablation/capability results are unchanged. v4 adds DExperts and Toxification Reversal toxicity scores of 13.87% and 27.94%, HH-Golden win rates of 78.2% for ProFS versus 74.1% for DPO, and PKU-SafeRLHF win rates ranging from 0.56 to 0.88. M1.justification: Section 4 and Algorithm 1 retain the same embedding differences, corpus-mean projection, top-k singular-vector selection and MLP-weight projection. DeTox becomes ProFS; applying the procedure to broader preferences does not introduce a documented algorithmic adaptation.

P1.justification: Beyond renaming the paper and method, v4 rewrites and reorganizes related work and preliminaries, revises rank-selection and layer-attribution explanations, restructures the appendices around robustness, mechanisms and broader preferences, and removes the NeurIPS checklist. P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn with colored subspaces and a clearer weight-editing diagram. Figure 3 reverses its curve colors while retaining the old color description in its caption.

The earlier extended task-vector discussion and some associated citations are removed.

improvement.justification: v4 makes the evaluation more informative by adding relevant detoxification competitors and their fluency tradeoffs, plus initial evidence beyond toxicity with a disclosed judging prompt. The revision broadens the evidence without substantially resolving its reliability limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same projection-based model-editing work, renamed from DeTox to ProFS. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, and their methods, equations, figures and tables can be matched despite reorganization.

after.justification: v4 retains these original experiments and adds detoxification-baseline comparisons, broader preference-alignment results and qualitative case studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original toxicity and capability evaluations across five models, comparisons with DPO, ablations, robustness experiments and layer-attribution analyses.

title: Model Editing as a Robust and Denoised variant of DPO: A Case Study on Toxicity

C1.justification: The central claims remain sample-efficient, noise-robust, tuning-free editing and a connection to a denoised DPO step. Section 9 now says 'unwanted behaviors' rather than 'model toxicity', but broader preference alignment was already claimed and evaluated in v4 Sections 7 and H.

C2.justification: New Appendix F.1 interprets the examples as showing recognition of malicious intent, refusal without explicit refusal alignment, and retained knowledge for benign discussion. These interpretations were previously absent. The existing limitations concerning singular-vector selection and restriction to MLP layers remain unchanged.

D1.justification: The implementation recipes, rank and layer settings, DPO/LoRA hyperparameters, hardware, compute accounting and code/data access information are retained. The new KTO result is not accompanied by KTO-specific implementation or training details.

E1.justification: v5 adds benign-use scenarios involving toxic vocabulary, including etymological and educational requests (Table 16). All named datasets remain unchanged. The malicious Wi-Fi and phishing examples in new Table 15 already appeared in v4 Tables 16 and 15.

E4.justification: The new 'Robustness to Toxic Prompts' analysis examines whether editing merely suppresses words or prevents benign discussion of related concepts. E5.justification: Both versions retain the same three-run mean and standard-deviation reporting and existing uncertainty displays. The added KTO row follows Table 3's existing point-estimate format; no new seed, repeated-run or statistical-testing procedure is reported.

E6.justification: v5 adds KTO's 41.13% toxicity result and qualitative comparison indicators in Table 3, plus two benign-prompt continuations in Table 16. Previously reported numerical results remain unchanged, including Table 4's 74.1% DPO and 78.2% ProFS win rates. Redisplayed malicious examples are not new outcomes.

M1.justification: The three-step ProFS procedure remains unchanged: remove the corpus-mean direction, identify a toxic subspace using SVD, and project MLP weights away from it. Equations (1)–(3) and Algorithm 1 retain the same operations.

P1.justification: v5 copyedits several passages, trims introductory repetition, condenses and rearranges Section 9, adds acknowledgments and the robustness paragraph, and changes the publication header. The overall section structure and narrative remain substantially the same.

P2.justification: v5 restyles Figure 1, adds metric-direction arrows and a KTO row, and introduces Tables 15–16, with Table 15 redisplaying existing examples. Several retained figures and tables move, and subsequent tables are renumbered. Existing plotted results are unchanged.

R1.justification: v5 adds Ethayarajh et al. on KTO, Bajaj et al., Syamkumar et al., and two Uppaal et al. references, while removing Hammarling's SVD reference. These are limited citation additions and a removal; the main positioning relative to editing and tuning remains intact.

improvement.justification: The added KTO comparison and benign-vocabulary examples modestly broaden the evidence, while copyediting improves clarity. These gains are limited: KTO lacks supporting setup details, and the new refusal interpretation overstates an ambiguous phishing response. The additions improve coverage without resolving a major deficiency; the core method and established results remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ProFS research, with readable text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–H. Content can be matched reliably across pagination changes and table renumbering.

after.justification: v5 retains these original experiments and additionally reports a KTO comparison and benign-prompt generation examples.

before.justification: v4 reports original toxicity-reduction, model-capability, sample-efficiency, robustness and alignment experiments in the main text and appendices.

title: Model Editing as a Robust and Denoised variant of DPO: A Case Study on Toxicity

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds a unifying connection between neural operators and conditioned neural fields. v2 makes CViT and coordinate-embedding theory the central contributions, explicitly claiming spectral-bias mitigation and extending its performance claims to reaction-diffusion and larger pretrained models. The unifying perspective remains, but becomes supporting material rather than the leading contribution.

C2.justification: v2 introduces a substantial Lipschitz-based explanation of embedding performance and spectral bias, connects retained ablations to that explanation, and hypothesizes that Fourier features explain OFormer's advantage over GNOT. It also discusses DPOT's rollout-loss advantage and qualifies exact grid-matching guidance using the new robustness test. The original computational, data-scarcity, and geometry limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds diffusion-reaction equations, coefficients, data-generation details, and task-specific training information while retaining most implementation and timing details. It omits v1's explicit JAX vmap and grid-feature initialization descriptions. Its Reproducibility Statement replaces v1's direct public-code link with supplementary ablation code and a planned full release upon acceptance; the PDFs do not establish actual repository availability.

E1.justification: v2 adds PDEBench's coupled two-dimensional diffusion-reaction task, predicting activator and inhibitor fields. This materially extends evaluation beyond the retained advection, shallow-water, and Navier-Stokes tasks to reaction-diffusion dynamics (Section 4.1 and Appendix F.6). The additional latent-grid tests do not change dataset coverage.

Comparator membership in the original three benchmarks is retained. Extending the existing FNO, FFNO, transformer, and DPOT comparators to diffusion-reaction is separate from this limited baseline-family addition.

Appendix F.6 specifies diffusion-reaction data downsampled to 128 x 128 spatial points and 101 time points, a 900/100 training/test split, and a learning rate of 5e-4. Appendix F.4 adds three latent-grid configurations. The original benchmarks' stated splits, budgets, and metrics remain unchanged.

It compares 95 x 191, 97 x 193, and 128 x 200 grids against 96 x 192. Existing patch-size, embedding-type, grid-scale, interpolation-parameter, latent-width, and attention-head ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or experimental uncertainty estimates. Advection's mean, median, and worst-case summaries are retained; the new experiments do not introduce a different statistical reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds a full diffusion-reaction results column: CViT-S/B/L achieve 1.13%, 1.11%, and 0.68% relative L2 error, respectively, versus 0.73% for fine-tuned DPOT-L (Table 3). Table 6 adds grid-robustness results ranging from 0.01562 to 0.01572. These are additional results, not improvements over v1 under the same settings. Original benchmark tables retain their values apart from equivalent rounding.

Patchification, Perceiver temporal aggregation, normalized grid interpolation, and query-wise cross-attention otherwise remain. Renaming the interpolation parameter from epsilon to beta is not a method change.

Previously appendixed rollout figures replace compact main-text snapshots. It expands the Navier-Stokes table with diffusion-reaction comparisons and adds a grid-resolution table and two diffusion-reaction rollout figures.

R1.justification: v2 adds substantial background and architecture-level comparisons with OFormer, GNOT, DPOT, and MPP, replacing v1's brief query-dependence contrast. New citations support spectral-bias theory, neural-field conditioning, and physics pretraining, including Rahaman, Rebain, and McCabe and colleagues. Several grid/interpolation antecedent references disappear, while the earlier neural-field survey is retained in the appendices.

T1.justification: v2 adds Appendix E's Lipschitz definitions, initialization assumptions, coordinate-embedding theorem, and proofs comparing linear, Fourier, and Gaussian-grid embeddings. v1's FNO derivation is retained as Appendix D. The new analysis contains a substantive mismatch: Equation 21 studies an unnormalized Gaussian sum, whereas the architecture's Equation 1 uses normalized interpolation weights.

improvement.justification: The diffusion-reaction benchmark and grid-resolution test broaden empirical support, and the reorganized architecture description improves accessibility. However, the new central theoretical justification analyzes an unnormalized embedding rather than the normalized embedding actually specified in Equation 1. Documented code access also weakens from a direct link to an acceptance-contingent full release. These empirical benefits and theoretical/reproducibility concerns prevent a reliable net quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CViT research, despite the changed title and emphasis. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across the reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds CViT diffusion-reaction results and a latent-grid resolution study, reported in Tables 3 and 6 and Appendix F.

before.justification: v1 reports original CViT experiments on advection, shallow-water, and Navier-Stokes problems, including benchmark results and architectural ablations in the main text and Appendix C.

D1.justification: v2 describes supplementary ablation code and a planned full release; v3 states that all code and data are public and supplies a concrete repository address. v3 also identifies CViT-B as the backbone for existing appendix ablations and documents settings for the new compressible-flow and timing experiments. E6.justification: Existing benchmark scores and training-time entries are retained. New results include CNS error of 1.29% for CViT-L versus 1.31% for fine-tuned DPOT-L, Fourier-frequency results, and CViT-L/16 errors decreasing from 6.56% to 3.18% when queries increase from one to six. P1.justification: Section 2 gains Background, Transformer-Based Operator Learning, and Open Challenges subheadings, and the temporal-aggregation explanation is expanded. Publication headers, acknowledgments, terminology, and cross-references receive targeted edits; most existing prose and the overall organization remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 expands Table 3 with a CNS column and adds ablation and timing tables, compressible-flow figures, and attention visualizations. Existing rollout figures gain time-step labels, and the architecture diagram's tensor labels change. v2's diffusion-reaction Figures 6 and 13 become appendix Figures 18–19. Together these additions and display revisions substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: The reference lists contain the same works, and the detailed positioning against OFormer, GNOT, DPOT, and MPP is retained. Section 2 reorganizes the existing background and challenges without substantively changing the novelty positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix F.6 adds the formal compressible Navier–Stokes system and associated physical definitions, including Equations 59–61. The conditioned-field analysis, FNO proposition, and Lipschitz theorems and proofs remain unchanged apart from numbering. The relative-L2 denominator's j-to-k correction is notational.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens an already substantial evaluation through compressible-flow testing, controlled ablations, attention analyses, and transparent inference timings, while improving code/data access information. The gains are limited by incomplete timing configuration details and the erroneous 'activator and inhibitor' wording in the new compressible-flow setup. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CViT research work. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds compressible-flow evaluation, further ablations, attention analyses, and inference timings.

before.justification: v2 reports original CViT benchmark results and ablations, including Tables 2–3 and 5–6 and Figures 4 and 9.

The new coupling proof leaves the accepted-token count undefined when all sampled indicators succeed and ends with a particular success-run example rather than a complete general expected-runtime derivation. With empirical evidence unchanged, the net quality benefit of the theoretical expansion remains uncertain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Distributed Speculative Inference and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–D. The retained and revised material can be reliably matched.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix D retain the original measurements and simulation results in Table 1 and Figures 1 and 6.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original model-latency and acceptance-rate measurements, plus inference simulations reported in Table 1 and Figures 1 and 6.

title: Distributed Speculative Inference (DSI): Speculation Parallelism for Provably Faster Lossless Language Model Inference

C1.justification: The losslessness, acceleration, and 1.29–1.92x speedup claims remain. V3 promotes Speculation Parallelism as a distinct contribution and explicitly claims simulation speedups across configurations within a single node of up to eight GPUs. Its contribution statement also distinguishes expected superiority to SI from the guarantee of being no slower than non-SI.

C2.justification: V3 substantially expands the mechanism interpretation through hidden verification latency, Amdahl-law arguments, and compatibility with tensor/pipeline parallelism. The limitations discussion replaces v2's explicit warning about omitted communication overhead with stronger assurances of simulation realism, while retaining the admission that an eight-GPU node was simulated. Appendix E.1 additionally characterizes the overhead-omitting SI latency estimate as an upper bound.

D1.justification: V3 documents server-to-GPU assignments, thread-pool operation, TTFT/TPOT wait handling, and exclusion of tokenization from end-to-end latency. Code availability changes from a future-release promise to a stated Apache-2.0 release, although no project repository URL is supplied. Much of Appendix A relocates the existing 50-prompt, 20-token profiling procedure rather than introducing new settings.

E1.justification: Both versions use CNN-DM for summarization, Alpaca for instruction following, and HumanEval and MBPP for code generation. Dataset prompts and model families are retained. The added latency ratios concern existing model/dataset combinations, not new task coverage.

E2.justification: The corresponding evaluations retain SI, non-SI, and the faster-of-SI-and-non-SI comparison. Newly discussed methods such as MagicDec and model-parallel approaches are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The heatmap study's reported resource constraints change substantially. V2 fixes DSI lookahead at 1 and allows the required target-server count to grow with the target/drafter latency ratio. V3 instead states that simulations use feasible lookaheads satisfying ceil(target_latency/(lookahead*drafter_latency)) <= 7, limiting deployment to eight GPUs including the drafter. This is a reported protocol revision; the unchanged plots do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix E.2 adds a diagnostic comparison of prefilling versus decoding costs through per-model/dataset TTFT/TPOT ratios. The drafter-latency/acceptance-rate sweep and fixed-lookahead analysis already existed in v2; renaming the former 'Ablation' does not constitute a new analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions average five SI repetitions per synthetic configuration. Neither introduces seed reporting, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added latency-ratio rows do not change uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: All ten benchmark rows in v2 Table 1 and v3 Table 2 retain their numerical values, including the 1.29–1.92x speedup range. Both sets of retained heatmaps are also unchanged. V3 Table 3 adds 18 TTFT/TPOT entries, including 5.36 for Vicuna-13B on CNN-DM and 1.35 for Starcoder-15B on HumanEval; these are additional latency results, not improved speedups.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, verifier selection, thread termination, and optional rejection sampling remain unchanged. Speculation Parallelism names the existing concurrency mechanism; the expanded lookahead discussion documents the batching approach already described as preemption in v2 rather than establishing a new algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction, contributions, implementation narrative, and limitations are extensively rewritten. Section 3 gains substantial explanations of SP, lookahead, and model parallelism; profiling details move into a new Appendix A. The title also adds 'is Provably Faster.' These are substantial narrative changes beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: V3 adds a scheduling timeline in Figure 1, its illustrative token-count Table 1, and latency-ratio Table 3. Existing benchmark and heatmap displays are retained and renumbered, with revised captions and placement. The overall visual format and existing prompt figures remain stable.

R1.justification: The introduction substantially reframes prior work around conserving existing resources versus using additional computing resources, positioning SP relative to data, tensor, pipeline, and context parallelism. Added references include MagicDec, FlashAttention-2, Mamba, and NeMo. This expands the research positioning beyond citation maintenance; publication updates to existing references are not new works.

T1.justification: The assumptions, Theorems 1–2, and Proposition 1 remain. V3 removes Proposition 2 and its separate proof while retaining the overlapping SI-comparison theorem, whose proof gains an explicit coupling statement. It also corrects the softmax input dimension in Equation 1 and adds calculations relating acceptance, lookahead, and hidden verification latency. The central theoretical framework is preserved.

improvement.justification: V3 improves the mechanism explanation and adds useful latency-calibration results. However, stronger realism assurances replace an explicit communication-overhead caveat, and unchanged heatmaps are described under materially different resource constraints without establishing how they were reconciled. Appendix E.1 also incorrectly justifies an upper latency bound by omitting overhead. These explanatory gains and evidential concerns prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same distributed speculative inference work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial rewriting and renumbering.

after.justification: V3 retains the original measurements and simulations and additionally reports TTFT/TPOT ratios in Appendix E.2, Table 3.

before.justification: V2 reports original GPU latency and acceptance-rate measurements, model-based speedup simulations in Table 1, and simulation sweeps in Figures 1 and 6.

title: Distributed Speculative Inference (DSI): Speculation Parallelism for Provably Faster Lossless Language Model Inference

C1.justification: The central contributions remain lossless DSI, overlapping drafting and verification through speculation parallelism, acceleration beyond SI's useful drafter regime, and adaptation to available hardware. The rewritten abstract and contribution bullets retain the same scientific scope and 1.29–1.92x simulation claim.

C2.justification: v4 adds practical arguments about staggered requests reducing contention and using per-server KV caches with SpecInfer-style management. It also adds future-work discussion of models requiring multiple GPUs and realistic multi-node communication. The simulation-only limitation remains, while v3's separate broader-impact statement about increased resource consumption is removed.

D1.justification: v4 supplies an explicit code-repository URL, clarifies OS-thread orchestration, and newly states that latency measurements used MP degree one with models fully resident in GPU memory and no offloading. It adds KV-cache implementation guidance; model sources and prompts are retained. The earlier explicit Apache-2.0 code-license statement is omitted.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate CNN-DM summarization, Alpaca instruction following, and MBPP/HumanEval code generation, alongside the same simulated drafter configurations. Evaluation with models requiring multiple GPUs and realistic multi-node deployment remains future work.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparators remain SI, non-SI, and the faster of SI/non-SI in Figure 2(d). PEARL is newly discussed in related work but is not added to the reported experiments.

E3.justification: The retained settings include 50-token main simulations, lookahead values {1, 5, 10}, at most seven target servers, and latency calibration using 50 prompts with 20 generated tokens each. v4 makes the existing hardware-feasibility restriction explicit; it does not establish a changed evaluation protocol.

E4.justification: The drafter-latency/acceptance-rate sweep and fixed-lookahead-5 analysis already appear in v3. They are reorganized into v4 Section 4.1 and Appendices F.3/F.7 without new ablations, robustness experiments, or implementation-overhead measurements.

E5.justification: v3 specifies five repeats for SI in the offline sweep; v4 Appendix F.3 explicitly specifies five repeats for both SI and DSI. This newly discloses DSI's repetition count without establishing an increase in runs. Neither version reports confidence intervals or error bars.

E6.justification: All ten Table 2 configurations and numerical values, all eighteen Table 3 ratios, and the plotted heatmaps are unchanged. However, Figure 2's caption qualifies the earlier 'always faster' finding: v4 states strict speedup for nonzero acceptance rates and non-slowdown for all configurations. This is a limited correction to the reported qualitative finding.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same thread spawning, verification, rejection, pruning, and verifier-relabeling procedure. The lookahead extension already appears in v3; v4's additional resource-allocation and KV-cache discussion does not establish a new implemented method component.

P1.justification: The introduction and empirical narrative are extensively rewritten, with explicit contribution bullets and online/offline simulation terminology. Background, formal preliminaries, the algorithm walkthrough, and lookahead details move into dedicated appendices; experimental documentation is consolidated under Appendix F. The title and section structure also change.

P2.justification: v4 adopts ICLR headers and a redesigned title/author block, places Figure 1 beside Table 1, groups Table 1 into best/worst cases and removes its redundant initial-time column, and reorders Table 2. Captions and display placement change, but the existing diagrams and heatmaps retain their plotted content.

R1.justification: v4 substantially expands research positioning through a dedicated related-work section and a detailed PEARL comparison covering scheduling depth, hardware scalability, and guarantees. It adds test-time-scaling motivation and several newer speculative-decoding and parallelism references. SpecInfer and MagicDec publication updates are retained works, not new comparators.

T1.justification: The two main theorems, Proposition 1, and their proofs are retained. v4 corrects Assumption 2's model indices, revises the SP/lookahead capacity statement and processor accounting, and adds consistency reasoning for geometric acceptance-rate estimation in Appendix F.2.1. Appendix F.4 also corrects the overhead-free SI latency estimate from an upper bound to a lower bound.

improvement.justification: v4 improves navigation and reproducibility through reorganized appendices, an explicit repository URL, clearer experimental assumptions, and corrections to mathematical and latency-bound statements. The expanded positioning against PEARL is useful. These gains are limited by new practical assurances about contention and KV-cache overhead that receive no additional validation; the underlying empirical evidence and main proofs remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DSI research work. Their main text, algorithms, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v4 retains these original measurements and simulation results in Tables 2–3 and Figures 2 and 7. Their retention from v3 does not change their empirical status.

before.justification: v3 reports original model-latency and acceptance-rate measurements, simulated DSI speedups in Table 2, and sensitivity results in Figures 2 and 7.

title: Distributed Speculative Inference (DSI): Speculation Parallelism for Provably Faster Lossless Language Model Inference

C1.justification: The title, abstract, and formal setup recast the contribution from sparse top-K MoE to MoE analyzed without top-K selection. This materially changes the scope of the advertised guarantees. The central claim of slow cosine-router estimation and polynomial improvement through perturbation remains.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly connects expert-estimation rates to expert specialization, contrasts its first-derivative parameter interaction with earlier second-derivative interactions, and interprets Appendix F as support under misspecification. The existing limitations concerning well-specified data and pointwise rather than uniform rates remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix E.2 newly specifies 16 experts, top-2 gating, and an eight-dimensional routing embedding for language modeling. It also corrects the medium-model description from 36 parameters to 36 million. These clarify existing experiments; hardware, training budgets, and reported training times are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix F adds synthetic coverage using linear-router-generated data, creating misspecified settings for cosine models with ReLU or quadratic experts. This is a limited expansion within synthetic regression. All three language corpora and five DomainBed datasets were already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds the conventional linear router to the domain-generalization comparisons in Tables 3-5 and evaluates it against the perturbed router in Appendix F.2. This introduces an important comparison family absent from v1's empirical evaluations. Language-modeling comparators remain unchanged despite replacing the XMoE row labels.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 replaces the stated top-2 data generator and top-4 over-specified fitting with dense mixtures, specifies ReLU instead of ReLU or identity, and uses revised Voronoi losses. Appendix F additionally introduces shared-data comparisons and quadratic experts. These are reported protocol changes; the identical Figure 1 plots do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix F.1 tests cosine and perturbed routers on the same linear-router-generated data, directly examining misspecification. Appendix F.2 tests the predicted advantage over linear routing with quadratic experts. These add substantive controlled analyses beyond v1's well-specified simulations; the existing domain-generalization analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report 20 experiments per synthetic sample size, means with two-standard-deviation error bars, and three-run averages for language modeling and domain generalization. Appendix F follows the existing reporting practice. No new seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: New Figure 2 reports convergence rates n^-0.45 versus n^-0.10 for perturbed versus cosine routing, and n^-0.47 versus n^-0.13 for perturbed versus linear routing. Tables 3-5 add linear-router scores, and Table 3 adds cross-dataset averages. Existing language and cosine-router domain scores remain unchanged. v2 also removes v1's erroneous 0.15-0.20 BPC reduction statement.

M1.justification: The main regression models replace sparse TopK selection with dense softmax weighting over all experts: compare v1 Equations 2 and 9 with v2 Equations 2 and 8. This changes the model output procedure. The norm perturbation and least-squares objective remain, while real-data implementations still use sparse routing.

P1.justification: Exact-specified cosine analysis moves from Section 2.1 to Appendix A.1, domain generalization moves from Appendix F to Section 5.3, and Appendix F becomes additional synthetic experiments. The introduction, practical implications, language-modeling explanations, and proof background are also substantially reorganized or expanded.

P2.justification: v2 adds the theoretical-rate summary Table 1 and two-panel Figure 2, moves three domain-generalization tables into the main text, and restructures tables with linear-router rows and an average column. The language table is reformatted. Figure 1 retains its plots but revises its caption, leaving the loss labels inconsistent with the axes.

R1.justification: v2 adds language-modeling and expert-specialization references, including Bengio, Graves, Jelinek, and Krishnamurthy, while removing works on temperature, Gaussian gating, and top-K sparse gating. Related discussion places greater emphasis on specialization and linear-versus-cosine sample efficiency without replacing the central research positioning.

T1.justification: Voronoi losses change from maxima over selected expert subsets to sums across the full mixture. v1's Proposition 1 on required activated-expert counts and its routing-region stability lemma are removed, with corresponding proof revisions. Appendix B.1 revises the covering argument, and C.1 replaces a detailed proof with an analogy. Exact-specified results are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: New linear baselines, shared-data experiments, and routing details strengthen evaluation and reproducibility. However, v2 replaces sparse analysis with dense analysis while retaining top-2 applications, and changes Figure 1's stated generator and losses without changing its plots; the revised caption also conflicts with its axes. These unresolved connections between theory, settings, and evidence prevent a reliable net quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, figures, and tables are readable and support comparison despite substantial changes in theoretical scope.

after.justification: Section 5 retains original synthetic and real-data results and adds linear-router comparisons. Appendix F reports additional synthetic experiments.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original synthetic convergence and language-modeling results. Appendix F reports original domain-generalization experiments.

title: Statistical Advantages of Perturbing Cosine Router in Mixture of Experts

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: potentially non-polynomial estimation under cosine routing and polynomial rates for identifiable experts under perturbed routing. The proposed contribution and headline scope remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 2 qualifies the parameter-rate interpretation to 'at least one' slow rate and makes expert slowdown conditional on the expert parameter's rate. It adds possible effects of slow routing on joint training and asserts Top-K applicability. Section 4 newly identifies unresolved approximation theory as an obstacle to misspecified-model analysis.

D1.justification: Appendices E.2–E.3 newly describe two-layer experts, ReLU/GELU activations, dropout of 0.1, and the domain-generalization hidden width of four times the input dimension. A new reproducibility statement promises code release upon acceptance; it does not supply released code.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same synthetic settings, Enwik8, Text8, Wikitext-103, and five DomainBed datasets: PACS, VLCS, OfficeHome, TerraIncognita and DomainNet. Appendix F retains the same misspecified data-generating scenarios.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged within corresponding experiments: vanilla cosine routing in the language-modeling and synthetic comparisons, and linear routing in domain generalization and Appendix F.2.

E3.justification: The stated synthetic settings, model sizes, routing configurations, metrics, training budgets and validation procedures are retained. Newly specified expert-layer and dropout details supplement documentation rather than revise previously stated settings.

E4.justification: Appendix F retains the same comparisons on linear-router-generated data using ReLU or quadratic experts. The domain-shift evaluations are also unchanged; no new ablation, sensitivity analysis or robustness experiment appears.

E5.justification: Both versions report 20 experiments per synthetic sample size, two-standard-deviation error bars, and averages over three runs for language modeling and domain generalization. No additional uncertainty-reporting procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: Tables 2–5 and Figures 1–2 retain their numerical results and trends. For example, average domain-generalization accuracies remain 65.40, 66.70 and 68.37 for linear, cosine and perturbed cosine routing, respectively; Appendix F's fitted convergence exponents also match.

M1.justification: The cosine and perturbed cosine routing formulas, norm perturbations and least-squares objectives remain unchanged. The added expert-network descriptions document existing experiments without establishing an architectural or procedural change.

P1.justification: Localized theoretical discussion and implementation explanations are expanded. Acknowledgements and a reproducibility statement are added, references move before the appendices, citations switch to author–year style, and author/affiliation text changes. The scientific section sequence and most prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The document is extensively reset in the ICLR template, changing typography, margins, spacing and running headers. Tables become more compact, Tables 3–5 are grouped together, and Figure 2 occupies a separate final page. Existing displays are retained; Table 1's caption newly specifies 'worst possible' rates.

R1.justification: v3 adds selected references concerning softmax properties, polynomial experts, Top-K routing, continual learning and minimax estimation, while removing GLaM and GShard references. These extend supporting context without substantially changing the paper's positioning relative to linear and cosine routing.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1 replaces L2-norm approximation and covering estimates with supremum-norm bounds in the proof of Theorem 1. Section 2 adds router-rate reasoning and a quadratic-expert calculation. The numbered theorem statements and identifiability assumptions remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: The supremum-norm revision in Appendix B.1, more qualified Theorem 2 discussion and added expert-network details provide a limited gain in mathematical precision and reproducibility. These benefits outweigh a localized algebraic slip in the new quadratic-expert example, which prints |x| instead of |x|^2. The broader headline claims remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same perturbed-cosine-router MoE study. Their text, equations, five tables, two figures and Appendices A–F support reliable comparison despite reformatting and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and their outcomes in Section 5 and Appendix F.

before.justification: v2 reports original synthetic experiments, language-modeling results and domain-generalization evaluations in Section 5, plus misspecified-model experiments in Appendix F.

title: Statistical Advantages of Perturbing Cosine Router in Mixture of Experts

P1.justification: v2 makes localized explanatory additions, expands the efficiency discussion, retitles Section 4.5 and updates author/affiliation text. The overall argument, section sequence and most prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds six tables and Figures 7 and 23, revises Figure 4 with activation annotations and a top-two-ranking panel, combines existing plots in Figure 1, and substantially rearranges figure placement.
