title: Dynamic Mixture of Experts: An Auto-Tuning Approach for Efficient Transformer Models

C1.justification: The central claims of preserving robustness and improving learning under bounded initial gradients remain. v3 adds explicit novelty claims about requiring no additional gradient-distribution knowledge or tuning, and emphasizes that classical aggregators lack ARC's bounded-output property.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the initialization sweep as evidence that ARC exploits favorable initialization, expands discussion of heterogeneity and initialization effects, and adds a theory-versus-practice discussion. v1's explicit qualification as B approaches zero and its proposed differential-privacy extension are omitted.

D1.justification: v3 Section 5.2 identifies PyTorch's default initialization as the starting point and documents the multiplicative scaling procedure. Existing architecture, preprocessing, hyperparameter, and supplementary-material disclosures in Appendix D are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 under the same heterogeneity and Byzantine-attack coverage. The new initialization sweep changes model settings within the existing MNIST task.

E2.justification: Matched experiments retain CWTM, GM, CWMed, and MK with NNM, static-clipping comparisons, and Byzantine-free DSGD controls. The initialization study uses existing comparison methods; newly cited adaptive-clipping methods are not evaluated.

E3.justification: v3 Section 5.2 introduces a controlled sweep multiplying initial parameters by factors 1-5, using CWTM with NNM, ten honest workers, one adversarial worker, and two retained MNIST heterogeneity settings. Existing benchmark protocols and Table 2 settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figures 2b and 6 add sensitivity analysis testing whether ARC's benefits depend on good initialization and when those benefits disappear. Earlier heterogeneity, attack, clipping-threshold, and gradient-norm analyses remain, including those in Appendices E-F.

E5.justification: Appendix D.4 in both versions specifies seeds 1-5 and standard deviations across those five seeds. The additional plots continue this reporting practice without a stated change in repetitions or uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: New initialization results show ARC accuracy falling from approximately 90% at scaling factor 1 to approximately 10% at factor 5 under extreme heterogeneity (Figure 2b). Table 1's CIFAR-10 values and all earlier plotted results are retained; these are additional findings, not improved scores for the existing benchmarks.

M1.justification: ARC retains the same clipping threshold based on the (k+1)-th largest norm, with k=floor(2(f/n)(n-f)). Algorithms 1-3 and the composition with robust aggregation and NNM retain their procedures.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Problem formulation and background are merged, empirical evaluation precedes the improved-guarantee discussion, related work becomes a separate late section, and several theoretical statements and qualifications move into Appendix C.

P2.justification: The visual organization changes substantially: v1 Figure 15 becomes v3 Figure 1, earlier main-text panels are regrouped, and two initialization plots are added. Table 1 shortens method labels and bolds ARC scores. The template and appendix layout change throughout; Figure 5's caption partly overflows the bottom of v3 page 7.

R1.justification: v3 adds comparisons with Diakonikolas et al. (2020) and Abdalla and Zhivotovskiy (2024), distinguishing required distribution knowledge and probabilistic guarantees. It also adds heavy-tailed-noise clipping references and removes the dedicated privacy-and-Byzantine-robustness discussion and associated citations.

T1.justification: v3 adds the counterexample argument in Lemma C.1 and expands the proof of the previously used output bound into Lemma 5.1. Lemma C.2 replaces v1 Theorem 5.1's maximum-form finite-time bound with a looser additive bound. The principal convergence and breakdown-point results are retained and reorganized.

improvement.justification: The new initialization sweep provides direct sensitivity evidence for a condition central to v1's theory, while the revised narrative and adaptive-clipping comparisons clarify the contribution. These constitute a focused improvement. Some presentation setbacks remain: the output-norm assumption underlying Lemma 5.1 is less visible in the main text, and Figure 5's caption is partly clipped.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ARC research, despite the changed title and organization. Their algorithms, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A-F support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds experiments varying model initialization in Section 5.2 and Figures 2b and 6.

before.justification: v1 Section 6 and Appendices E-F report original image-classification experiments comparing ARC, unclipped robust aggregation, and static clipping under Byzantine attacks.

title: Adaptive Gradient Clipping for Robust Federated Learning

C1.justification: Both versions claim that ARC preserves robustness guarantees, improves convergence under suitable initialization, and strengthens empirical robustness particularly under heterogeneity and adversarial pressure. The revised title and abstract preserve these contributions; added experiments support existing claims.

C2.justification: v5 newly explains that Theorem 5.2's improvement interval can contain at most one integer adversarial-worker count in small systems, and removes the blanket statement that ARC has no downside. Appendix A.1 adds design rationale, while Section 6 identifies privacy-preserving use as requiring further analysis.

D1.justification: v5 Tables 3–4 newly specify CIFAR-10 static thresholds of 0.05, 0.5, 5, and 50; the associated ResNet-18 training details already appeared in v3. v5 also removes Appendix D.4's direction to supplementary per-dataset plot folders. Neither change establishes that resources became unavailable.

E1.justification: Both versions cover the same three classification datasets, heterogeneity regimes, and five attack families. v3 Appendix F.1 already describes Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 static-clipping experiments. Newly displayed results and larger worker counts extend evidence and settings within this coverage.

E2.justification: v5 Figure 26 introduces a direct runtime comparison between ARC and standalone NNM, previously used as a pipeline component. The accuracy-comparison families remain CWTM, GM, CWMed, MK, static clipping, no clipping, and Byzantine-free DSGD. Relocating CWMed/MK results does not remove those comparators.

E3.justification: v5 adds MNIST experiments with 30 honest workers and f = 3, 6, 9; CIFAR-10 experiments with 33 honest workers; and additional adversarial-worker counts with 16 honest workers. Figure 26 introduces controlled runtime sweeps over model dimension and worker count. These substantially extend evaluation settings while retaining the existing training budgets and preprocessing.

E4.justification: v5 adds reported static-threshold sensitivity comparisons on Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10, tests robustness in larger systems, and measures computational scaling. Conversely, v3 Figure 18's honest-gradient norm histogram is removed. The initialization-sensitivity study and most earlier attack analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix D.4 in both versions specifies seeds 1–5 and standard deviations across those seeds. The added accuracy tables follow the existing reporting practice; no increased run count, significance testing, or new uncertainty-estimation procedure is documented.

E6.justification: v5 adds substantial results in Tables 3–4 and 6–7 and the larger-system and runtime figures. Original Table 1 values remain unchanged across v5 Tables 1 and 5. Added results are not uniformly favorable: Table 6 reports GM accuracy of 49.6 ± 1.4 with ARC versus 50.9 ± 2.5 without clipping for f = 3 and alpha = 0.5. These are new results, not deterioration under a matched v3 setting.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–3 retain the same procedures. ARC still clips the largest floor(2(f/n)(n−f)) gradients at the next-largest norm. Appendix A.1 explains this choice without changing the implemented algorithm; the ResNet-18 configuration was already described in v3.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, the abstract and substantial empirical prose are rewritten, and Section 4 is reorganized into static-clipping and no-clipping comparisons. Appendices E and F exchange roles and are reorganized by dataset and system size. Together these materially restructure the presentation despite stable core scientific content.

P2.justification: v3 Figure 17 becomes main-text Figure 2, Figure 1 moves to Appendix E, and Figure 5 is incorporated into v5 Figure 23. Table 1 is split between the main text and appendix, several panel arrangements change, and new tables and plots are added. The gradient-norm histogram is removed; retained plot content otherwise matches.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds positioning relative to privacy and Byzantine robustness, citing works including Abadi et al., Guerraoui et al., Zhu and Ling, and Choffrut et al. The introduction also adds El-Mhamdi et al. The central distinctions from prior adaptive-clipping methods remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix C corrects the norm-ordering inequalities in the proof of Lemma 5.1 from ascending to descending. Section 5.1 adds a derivation of the admissible adversarial-worker interval and its integer-count implications. The principal theorem statements, assumptions, and proof strategies remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v5 strengthens empirical support through previously unreported static-clipping results, larger-system tests, and runtime measurements. The practical-scope discussion and proof correction improve precision. These are incremental gains over an already developed paper: the method and principal results remain stable, one explanatory histogram is lost, and exceptions in Table 6 limit the retained language of consistent superiority.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Adaptive Robust Clipping (ARC) work despite the changed title. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v5 retains original classification results and reports additional static-clipping comparisons, larger-system experiments, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v3 reports original image-classification experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10, including attack, heterogeneity, clipping, and initialization comparisons.

title: Adaptive Gradient Clipping for Robust Federated Learning

C1.justification: V1 broadly suggests amplification when insertion is intermittent, even under adversarially chosen loss landscapes. V2 instead claims no amplification for sufficiently large batches relative to noise and restricts the amplification possibility to smaller batches. This substantially revises the abstract, contribution summary, and implications while retaining the every-step no-amplification claim.

C2.justification: V2 explains competing effects of noise and batch size on propagation of the initial private signal, materially narrowing applicability. It adds initialization and pretrained-model interpretations and refines the difficulty of realizing worst-case landscapes in ordinary networks. The federated-learning application discussion is removed. Its prose describing the amplification-ratio trend conflicts with Figure 4b's direction.

D1.justification: V2 documents A_CotS gradient generation and cosine scoring in Algorithms 6–7, identifies ImageNet as public pretraining data, specifies last-layer AlexNet fine-tuning, and describes bisection for privacy-parameter conversion. Existing implementation libraries, hyperparameter table, and approximately 3,500 GPU-hour disclosure are retained.

E1.justification: CIFAR10 and Housing remain the evaluation datasets. V2 adds auditing with unknown initialization, changing the adversary's information-access scenario (Appendix G, Figure 12). ImageNet supplies pretrained AlexNet weights for a CIFAR10 experiment; it is not an additional evaluated benchmark.

E2.justification: Appendix G newly evaluates A_CotS, adapted from Andrew et al. (2024), against the proposed and loss-based adversaries on Housing. Figure 8's caption names A_GC-R while its legend names A_GC-S, but A_CotS participation is clear. The ConvNet/ResNet comparator curves from v1 Figure 5 are absent from the replacement landscape experiments.

E3.justification: The landscape evaluation expands to B in {1,2,4,8,16}, noise parameter σ in {1,...,8}, and trajectories through T=25, introducing the ε25/ε1 ratio. V2 also adds unknown-initialization testing, last-layer fine-tuning of pretrained AlexNet, and full privacy-profile evaluation. The original real-data training settings and Table 2 remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figures 4 and 14 add systematic batch-size/noise sensitivity analysis central to identifying amplification regimes. Appendix G tests robustness to unknown initialization and examines tightness across privacy profiles. Existing dimension-selection ablations, GDP approximation checks, and threshold-search validation are retained, despite relocation and renumbering.

E5.justification: The 5,000 auditing runs, 95% Clopper-Pearson procedure, Figure 1's 30-run reporting, and Housing repetitions remain unchanged. However, the replacement landscape plots in v2 Figures 4 and 14 omit the explicit five-run averaging statement and variability band accompanying v1 Figure 5. This establishes a reporting change, not fewer actual runs.

E6.justification: New landscape results reveal strong batch-size dependence: v2 Figure 4b reports ε25/ε1 of 0.25 at B=1, σ=8, versus 0.99 at B=16, σ=8. Appendix G adds comparator, initialization, pretrained-model, and privacy-profile findings. These are results under expanded conditions; Figures 1–3 and the retained appendix analyses preserve their earlier plotted data.

M1.justification: Section 6 substantially generalizes the loss-landscape adversary: its gradient function changes from values bounded by C to batch-gradient sums bounded by BC, and updates explicitly divide the gradient sum and noise by B. This changes the modeled dynamics and adversary capabilities. The real-data A_GC-R and A_GC-S procedures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Rewriting concentrates on the abstract, contribution summary, landscape analysis, and discussion, with new remarks and Appendix G. The main section sequence, background, core gradient-crafting descriptions, and much experimental prose remain intact. Citation and heading styles also change.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the main landscape displays with trajectory panels and a numerical heatmap, adds several appendix plots and an algorithm display, and regroups/resizes retained appendix figures. The document template, title block, headings, and figure placement also change substantially. Relocated existing analyses are distinguishable from genuinely new displays.

R1.justification: V2 substantially revises positioning through comparison with Annamalai's concurrent no-amplification result, discussion of Asoodeh and Diaz's constrained nonconvex guarantees, and Feng and Tramèr's privacy-backdoor constructions. These qualify novelty and practical realizability beyond merely adding citations. It also adds black-box auditing literature and removes the federated-learning reference associated with the deleted discussion.

T1.justification: Section 6 revises the formal stochastic model through explicit batch averaging and the admissible range g in [-BC,BC], replacing the earlier [-C,C] formulation. Its optimality discussion shifts from a T=2 worst-case conjecture to batch-dependent tightness claims. Appendix A's definitions, lemma, and corollary remain substantively unchanged; no new formal proof establishes the new regime claims.

improvement.justification: The batch-dependent formulation and Figures 4/14 address an important omission in v1's landscape analysis, replacing a broad amplification suggestion with substantially better-supported regime boundaries. New comparator and robustness checks strengthen the empirical assessment. Caption inconsistencies, contradictory ratio wording, and reduced uncertainty reporting for the replacement landscape plots are drawbacks, but do not outweigh this central scientific improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same privacy-auditing work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds batch-size/noise experiments, a comparator evaluation, unknown-initialization tests, pretrained-model auditing, and privacy-profile results.

before.justification: V1 reports original auditing experiments on CIFAR10 and Housing, synthetic loss-landscape experiments, and appendix analyses of adversary variants and auditing approximations.

title: Tighter Privacy Auditing of DP-SGD in the Hidden State Threat Model

C1.justification: The introduction attributes the remaining auditing gap to the inability of 'our adversaries', replacing v2's broader 'known adversaries'. This modestly narrows that attribution; the central claims about every-step insertion and the batch-size/noise regimes remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Remark 3 newly qualifies Gaussian approximation by identifying potential problems for subsampled or shuffled mechanisms. Section 6 also expands the explanation of how larger batches preserve canary information through bounded gradient updates.

D1.justification: New Algorithm 4 explicitly documents gradient insertion, coordinate scoring, midpoint threshold enumeration, and GDP conversion. Algorithms 2–3 now return the selected coordinate as well as the gradient. These are documentation additions; software and resource disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions retain CIFAR10, Housing, ImageNet-pretrained AlexNet fine-tuning, unknown-initialization experiments, and the same synthetic loss-landscape scenarios.

E2.justification: The loss-based adversary AL and the Andrew et al.-inspired ACotS comparator remain in their corresponding comparisons. The four simulated dimension-selection variants also remain; corrected legend labels do not introduce new comparators.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 and Table 2 retain the architectures, batch sizes, insertion periodicities, training horizons, and privacy parameters. Algorithm 4 adds documentation of the existing auditing pipeline without reporting a new experimental protocol.

E4.justification: The Housing ablation comparing noisy/noiseless and per-step/final-model dimension selection has a slightly revised AGC-R reference curve in v3 Figure 4, corresponding to v2 Figure 5. Its question and conclusions remain unchanged, as do the other robustness, approximation-error, and threshold-optimality analyses.

E5.justification: Section 5.2 changes 'five independent runs' to 'five runs', removing the explicit independence qualification. Run counts, 95% Clopper–Pearson intervals, and the canary-norm plot's 30-run mean and two-standard-deviation reporting otherwise remain unchanged.

E6.justification: The AGC-R curve in the Housing ablation changes slightly: its rightmost plotted lower bound is approximately 20.49 in v2 Figure 5 and 20.52 in v3 Figure 4. The other curves in that comparison, main experimental results, and batch-size/noise heatmap remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Algorithm 3 replaces signed parameter differences with squared differences followed by a square root for per-step ranking, and absolute differences for final-model ranking. This corrects the written dimension-selection procedure; the PDFs do not establish whether executed code changed or experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized prose revisions, updates affiliations and conference headers, and adjusts cross-references. The main narrative, section sequence, and appendix organization remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: The canary-norm plot moves from v2 Figure 1 to v3 Figure 8. The Housing ablation is redrawn with corrected variant labels and larger text; Algorithm 4 is added, and appendix figures and the Table 2 caption are rearranged.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to Homer et al., Bok et al., Wang et al., and unlearning work by Guo, Neel, and Gupta and colleagues. These support background and qualifications without substantially changing the paper's positioning against prior auditing methods.

T1.justification: The DP and GDP definitions, Lemma 1, Corollary 1, stochastic-process construction, and threshold argument are retained. The algorithmic ranking correction does not introduce a new theoretical result or proof.

improvement.justification: The corrected ranking rule and Housing legend resolve concrete specification and interpretation problems in v2. Additional auditing detail and the Gaussian-approximation caveat provide limited gains, although new Algorithm 4 contains inconsistent insertion-bit and threshold-label conventions. The empirical support and central conclusions remain essentially unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–G support comparison, including matching material relocated between versions.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and simulations, including their appendix results.

before.justification: v2 reports original privacy-auditing experiments on CIFAR10 and Housing, synthetic loss-landscape simulations, and additional appendix analyses.

title: Tighter Privacy Auditing of DP-SGD in the Hidden State Threat Model

C1.justification: The introduction replaces the broad claim that multimodal perception significantly improves performance with a qualified statement that it helps in some cases but generally does not outperform text-only input. It also narrows the robustness summary toward intent-parameter variation. The benchmark contribution and headline 30.6% success rate remain.

C2.justification: Appendix C.4 newly explains imperfect human performance through task misunderstandings, minor input errors and unfamiliar interfaces under a single-attempt procedure. v3 omits v1's explicit explanation that longer workflows accumulate more mistakes. The main open-source-app limitations and agent failure interpretations remain.

D1.justification: v3 substantially expands reproducibility documentation: the full adapted SeeAct prompt in Appendix D.5, six annotators and two human evaluators with procedural details in C.4, initialization and validation descriptions for five existing robustness tasks in Table 5, and explicit SMS teardown pseudocode. These additions document existing work rather than demonstrate changed experiments.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 116 AndroidWorld tasks across 20 apps and evaluate the same 62-task MobileMiniWoB++ subset. The five tasks newly detailed in Table 5 already appear in v1's robustness experiment; additional related-work benchmarks are not evaluated.

E2.justification: Table 3 retains the same human comparator, four M3A input/model configurations and Android-adapted SeeAct baseline. Appendix D.5 supplies SeeAct implementation details without establishing a changed comparator. Expanded Table 1 entries concern research positioning.

E3.justification: The evaluation retains seed 30, task-specific step budgets, GPT-4 Turbo and Gemini 1.5 Pro, and the same benchmark subsets. Appendix C.4 newly documents the existing human evaluation, including one attempt per participant per task, without reporting a protocol revision.

E4.justification: Appendix C.4 adds a brief human-error analysis covering misunderstandings, input mistakes and unfamiliar interfaces. The five-task seed robustness analysis and four illustrated M3A error categories remain unchanged; the error figures are reordered.

E5.justification: v1 already displays error bars and p < 0.05 markers in Figure 3. v3 explicitly identifies the intervals as 95% Wilson binomial proportion confidence intervals. This clarifies uncertainty reporting without establishing additional runs or a new significance test.

E6.justification: All Table 3 scores and Figure 3 success rates are retained. v3 newly reports over 30 development bugs found and resolved, plus human failure patterns, in Appendix C.4. It omits v1's qualitative statement that agents perform better on data-editing than data-entry tasks.

M1.justification: The M3A action/reflection procedure, text and SoM inputs, Android action interface, parameterized tasks and system-state rewards remain unchanged. The added SeeAct prompt and SMS teardown pseudocode document components already described in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten, and the conclusion is substantially compressed. Experimental interpretation receives a separate Analysis subsection, error discussions are reordered, and the appendices gain ethical considerations, human-evaluation documentation and SeeAct details.

P2.justification: Tables 1 and 5 expand, with Table 5 growing from two examples to seven. Figure 3 extends its vertical axis to 100% and revises its caption. Figures 6 and 7 exchange order, and several displays change size or placement; the overall visual format and remaining figure content are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands benchmark positioning with WorkArena, WindowsAgentArena, Mobile-Env, AndroidControl, AndroidArena and LlamaTouch, among other additions. It adds an explicit distinction from AndroidEnv's instrumented rewards. The B-MoCA comparison changes from 31 tasks across 12 apps to its reported experimental coverage of six tasks across four apps.

T1.justification: Neither version presents theorems, proofs or substantive formal derivations. Expanded task pseudocode and identification of the confidence-interval method introduce no new mathematical definition or theoretical argument.

improvement.justification: v3 improves clarity and auditability by correcting the introduction's overgeneralized multimodality claim, identifying Figure 3's confidence intervals, and documenting human evaluation and the SeeAct prompt. Expanded related work clarifies the benchmark's contribution. A new Table 5 inconsistency describes deletion during initialization of ExpenseAddSingle despite its addition goal. Overall, the documentation gains outweigh this limited defect, while experimental coverage and principal results remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AndroidWorld and M3A. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, code listings and appendices support comparison; relocated and renumbered material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results and additionally reports development bug findings and human failure observations in Appendix C.4.

before.justification: v1 reports original agent and human success rates in Table 3, human task characterizations in Figure 2, and task-parameter robustness results in Figure 3.

title: AndroidWorld: A Dynamic Benchmarking Environment for Autonomous Agents

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statement and conclusion retain the dynamic 116-task, 20-app benchmark, M3A baseline, 30.6% headline success rate and importance of task-parameter robustness. Added experiments support these existing central claims.

C2.justification: V4 adds interpretations of the prompting ablation, a qualified model-size explanation for Gemma's performance, and mechanisms linking seed sensitivity to hidden expense categories and note-edit complexity. The alternate-OS interpretation is explicitly limited to the tested case. The earlier limitations remain, condensed in Appendix A.

D1.justification: Appendix F substantially extends v3's selected examples with task templates, validation methods, associated apps and explicit per-task step limits with a human-derived rationale. V4 also specifies inference temperature, the 15:34 UTC clock reset and the supplementary API code location. Listing 1 omits the previously listed DOUBLE_TAP and SWIPE entries while scrolling remains documented. These documentation changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: Both retain 116 AndroidWorld tasks across 20 apps and the same 62-task MobileMiniWoB++ evaluation subset. V4 adds a Pixel 5/Android 12 test scenario alongside Pixel 6/Android 13. Appendix F documents existing tasks rather than establishing additional task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds M3A-Simple as an evaluated comparison agent using GPT-4 Turbo, Gemini 1.5 Pro and Gemma 2. The human and SeeAct comparators remain; the additional Gemma-backed full M3A is a model configuration of the existing method.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce Gemma 2 27B, a control removing guidelines and reflection, and an alternate device/OS configuration. The existing seed-30 success-rate evaluation is retained. Temperature zero and explicit step-budget rules are newly disclosed, without evidence that settings of retained experiments changed.

E4.justification: V4 substantially extends analysis with the M3A-Simple prompting ablation, benchmark-level seed variation and an alternate device/OS robustness test. Appendix E.5 and Figure 8 add parameter-specific failure cases involving hidden expense categories and note-edit variants. The original five-task seed analysis and earlier error cases remain.

E5.justification: Section 5 newly reports results across three seeds and their mean, and discloses 20 trials per task for the retained five-task analysis. Figure 3 already provided 95% Wilson confidence intervals and significance annotations in v3 and is unchanged; no increase in its trial count is established.

E6.justification: All retained Table 3 scores are unchanged, but substantial new results are added. AndroidWorld/MobileMiniWoB++ percentages are 3.4/35.5, 14.7/55.2 and 19.8/67.7 for M3A-Simple with Gemma, Gemini and GPT-4 respectively, and 9.5/45.6 for full M3A with Gemma. Section 5 adds seed results of 27.6%, 26.3% and 33.2% (mean 29.0%), plus 28.4% on the alternate device/OS. These are additional conditions, not improvements to the retained scores.

M1.justification: Section 4.1.1 introduces M3A-Simple, a variant using minimal prompting without guidelines or reflection. The full M3A action-generation/reflection loop and the SeeAct adaptation remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. Robustness moves from Section 4.4 into an expanded Section 5, limitations move to Appendix A, and the action-space explanation is reorganized. Headings, citation style and selected paragraphs are edited, without a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: V4 adds a substantial task-catalog table in Appendix F and the expense-interface Figure 8. Table 3 is expanded and regrouped into comparison-agent, simplified-agent and full-agent blocks, while Table 1 gains AgentStudio. Existing Figures 1–7 are retained within a restyled and reflowed document.

R1.justification: V4 adds AgentStudio to Section 2.1 and Table 1, adds Ferret-UI and Gemma 2 citations, and removes the AgentGPT and WebLlama references. The central positioning relative to AndroidEnv, OSWorld and MiniWoB++ remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Neither version presents a theorem or proof contribution. No substantive mathematical definitions, assumptions, derivations or proofs are added or revised; the new material is experimental or documentary.

improvement.justification: The new prompting control, open-model evaluation, seed results and device/OS check strengthen empirical support, while explicit task budgets improve reproducibility. These usefully refine an already supported benchmark. Benefits are tempered by the retained single-seed main comparisons and inconsistencies in the new catalog, such as minimum-brightness tasks instructing maximum brightness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AndroidWorld benchmark and M3A study. Their complete text, figures, tables, code listings and appendices support reliable comparison despite reorganization and additions.

after.justification: V4 reports original agent evaluations and robustness results, including additional M3A-Simple and Gemma 2 experiments, three-seed results and an alternate device/OS test.

before.justification: V3 reports original M3A and SeeAct evaluations, human performance, error analyses and task-parameter robustness experiments in Section 4 and Appendix D.

title: AndroidWorld: A Dynamic Benchmarking Environment for Autonomous Agents

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: a reproducible dynamic Android benchmark, initial agent performance, and evidence that task parameterization affects robustness. Condensed wording does not change these claims.

C2.justification: Section 5 drops confusion before reaching the step limit from its failure explanation and removes 'in this specific case' from the OS-variation interpretation. This slightly reduces explanatory detail and explicit qualification; the experiment remains clearly identified, and Appendix A limitations are unchanged.

D1.justification: Section 3.6 removes the explanation that is_successful retrieves the WebView reward through an Android intent. The WebView architecture remains documented, including its restatement in Appendix C.3. Appendix code, prompts, and repository access information are otherwise retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 116 AndroidWorld tasks across 20 apps and the same 62-task MobileMiniWoB++ subset. The alternative Pixel 5/Android 12 scenario is retained. Appendix C.3 clarifies benchmark naming without changing coverage.

E2.justification: Table 3 retains identical comparator membership: humans, SeeAct, M3A-Simple, and the same M3A input/base-model variants. No comparison method is added or removed.

E3.justification: The success-rate metric, base models, temperature, task subsets, human evaluation procedure, and task-specific step limits remain unchanged. Appendix F preserves the complete task list and its numerical step budgets.

E4.justification: Both retain the simplified-agent and input-modality comparisons, fixed-versus-varied parameter experiments, alternative-OS test, and Appendix E error cases. Relocated screenshots do not introduce new analyses.

E5.justification: Section 4.2 retains seed 30 but removes the explicit qualifier 'for model inference', slightly reducing specificity about its scope. The three-seed evaluation, 20 trials per task, Wilson 95% confidence intervals, and p < 0.05 criterion remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Table 3 values and rankings and Figure 3 results match. Both report 30.6% for text-only GPT-4 Turbo M3A on AndroidWorld, a 29.0% mean across three seeds, and 28.4% on Pixel 5/Android 12. Appendix findings are retained.

M1.justification: The parameterized task framework, state-based rewards, M3A action-and-reflection procedure, and SeeAct adaptation remain unchanged. Removing an implementation explanation does not establish a change to the underlying procedure.

P1.justification: v5 condenses several introductory, environment, and robustness paragraphs, changes Section 4.1 terminology from 'computer control' to 'computer use', and adds the ICLR publication header. The overall section and appendix organization remains intact.

P2.justification: The figures and tables retain their content and design, but several move: Figure 2 shifts from page 6 to 5, and Tables 2 and 3 each move one page earlier. Appendix figures, listings, and table page breaks also shift.

R1.justification: The cited works and research positioning remain the same. Gemini and GPT-4 report citations change from Team-based author labels to Gemini and OpenAI; these are bibliographic corrections rather than added references.

T1.justification: Neither version introduces new formal theory or proofs. The task-validation logic and reward calculations in Tables 2 and 5 and Appendix D remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v5 preserves the scientific contribution, experimental evidence, and substantive limitations. Modest gains in concision and citation attribution accompany small losses of implementation detail and reporting qualification in Sections 3.6, 4.2, and 5. These limited editorial tradeoffs leave the paper's overall evidential strength and usefulness essentially unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AndroidWorld and M3A. Their main text, figures, tables, and appendices A–F are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching content across changed page breaks.

after.justification: v5 retains these original benchmark results, robustness experiments, and appendix error analyses.

before.justification: v4 reports original agent and human benchmark results in Table 3, robustness experiments in Section 5 and Figure 3, and error analyses in Appendix E.

title: AndroidWorld: A Dynamic Benchmarking Environment for Autonomous Agents

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion refine the explanatory claim toward 'systematic hallucinations,' explicitly described as structured deviations from factual accuracy. The central CogMir contribution, novelty assertions and claims of prosocial human–agent alignment remain.

C2.justification: New clarifications in Sections 3.2, 4 and 6 explicitly identify simulated human interactions and literature-based human comparisons, qualifying how the alignment claims should be understood. Appendix C.1 explains filtering as a way to exclude pre-existing incorrect beliefs. Existing Appendix B limitations are retained.

D1.justification: v2 documents evaluator expertise, assessment instructions and evaluator temperature zero in Appendix D.1. It also makes the all-50-responses-correct inclusion rule explicit in Appendix C.1 and describes randomly combining synthetic persona attributes in Section 6. These are additional disclosures, without evidence that the existing experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same seven cognitive-bias tasks and Known MCQ, Unknown MCQ, Inform, CogScene, CogAction and CogIdentity collections. The new case studies remain within the existing Known/Unknown MCQ Herd Effect coverage.

E2.justification: The seven-model comparison set in Tables 1–2 and the GPT-3.5/GPT-4.0 comparison in Table 3 are unchanged. Newly cited PersonaGym and RoleEval are not evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: New Appendix D.2 cases record an initial answer and then a response to unanimous-A feedback, including correct consensus for the Known MCQ. This adds a limited procedure/control variation alongside the retained Herd templates using B feedback. The main quantitative experiments retain their sample sizes and metrics.

E4.justification: Appendix D.2 adds two qualitative Herd Effect cases contrasting responses to known and uncertain questions. However, the known-question example has peers agreeing with the correct answer, so it does not demonstrate resistance to conflicting group pressure. Existing supplementary model comparisons are retained.

E5.justification: The reported repetition counts, including 50 queries for Known MCQ validation and ten repetitions in the relevant experiments, are retained. v2 adds no new seed information, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and Figures 3–8 retain their quantitative results. Appendix D.2 adds response-level outcomes: Claude-3 retains answer A on the banana question, while GPT-4 switches from B to A on the future-weather question after unanimous-A feedback.

before.justification: v3 reports original DEEM benchmark results, controlled ablations, and generated examples in Section 3 and Appendices C–F.

title: DEEM: Diffusion models serve as the eyes of large language models for image perception

It also removes Appendix F, including the explicit limitations concerning unmodeled cross-variable correlations and unexplored alternative backbones.

M1.justification: The architecture, complementary masking, adaptive routing, adversarial losses and inference procedure are retained. Although v3 emphasizes synthetic anomalies more strongly, anomaly injection was already used in v1; Appendix A and Table 7 retain the same labeled-data and injected-anomaly sources.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites expand the generalization rationale, gradient-reversal explanation and evaluation description. Appendices C and E gain subsections, while Appendix F is removed. P2.justification: v3 adds fine-tuning, UCR and anomaly-case figures plus a label-free-results table, substantially redesigns Table 8, and expands Tables 1 and 4. Figure 1 is redrawn; the earlier bottleneck-selection and pre-training-source plots are combined into Figure 11, with an updated bottleneck legend. Title, heading, citation and page-layout styling also change.

improvement.justification: The UCR comparison with Timer, additional evaluation metrics and targeted label-reliance and runtime analyses strengthen evidence for generalization and practical usability. before.justification: v1 reports original anomaly-detection experiments on nine evaluation datasets, component ablations, parameter sensitivity and pre-training analyses.

title: Towards a General Time Series Anomaly Detector with Adaptive Bottlenecks and Dual Adversarial Decoders

C2.justification: v4 explains how directly maximizing abnormal reconstruction loss can produce arbitrary decoder outputs and undermine normal-pattern learning. It expands the MoE interpretation around dataset-specific bottleneck preferences and adds interpretations concerning balanced masking, contamination tolerance, and adversarial training stability. The runtime discussion acknowledges ModernTCN's faster inference while distinguishing its downstream training requirement.

D1.justification: v4 adds a code repository link, explains the existing anomaly transformations and random non-overlapping injection procedure, cites injection defaults, and first states that testing retains the final partial batch. Table 4 corrects MSL/SMAP dimensionality to match existing prose. Conversely, replacing Appendix E.4 removes the explicit description of bottlenecks as lightweight MLPs. These documentation changes do not establish corresponding implementation changes.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The additional tables and loss curves do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Substantial new results cover masking, contamination, runtime, expanded MoE comparisons, and qualitative behavior. Table 1 revises A.T.'s SMD F1 from 66.42 to 69.46, D3R's SMD/SWaT values from 78.02/74.39 to 78.04/74.41, and GPT4TS's SMD value from 83.13 to 83.14. M1.justification: The complementary masking, adaptive bottleneck routing, dual adversarial decoders, training objectives, and variance-based anomaly scoring are retained. Section 3.2 clarifies patch embeddings, mask dimensions, and the reconstruction pipeline; the expanded anomaly-injection description documents existing components rather than establishing a changed method.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and the overall section sequence are retained. Local revisions clarify Section 3.2, expand anomaly-injection explanations, rewrite parts of the MoE and timing discussions, and append E.7-E.9. Conference publication text and acknowledgments are also added.

P2.justification: The appendix displays substantially expand through four new tables (11-14), a comparative PSM visualization (Figure 11), and loss curves (Figure 13). Table 10 gains two dataset columns and Table 9 gains a metric row. The original Figure 11 is retained as Figure 12. R1.justification: v4 adds references including MultiRC, CATCH, AutoTSAD, sparsely gated MoE, and TFB, while removing some earlier citations such as LoOP and the Tang outlier-detection works. The central positioning around general, zero-shot time-series anomaly detection remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The substantive mathematics in Equations (1)-(7) is retained. Dimension-symbol edits, patch-mask notation, and the explicit composition defining Recon clarify the existing formulation. Neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs that are added, removed, or revised.

improvement.justification: v4 provides useful evidence about complementary masking and contaminated normal training data, and makes the existing injection and testing procedures clearer. The gains are limited by removal of the isolated bottleneck-overhead check, inconsistent baseline scores between Table 1 and Tables 8/11, and an apparent MSL/SMAP heading reversal in Table 13. The added validation and reproducibility information nevertheless support a modest overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DADA research work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds masking experiments, training-contamination tests, runtime comparisons, and additional visual analyses.

before.justification: v3 reports original benchmark evaluations, component ablations, fine-tuning experiments, parameter sensitivity studies, and appendix results including UCR evaluation.

title: Towards a General Time Series Anomaly Detector with Adaptive Bottlenecks and Dual Adversarial Decoders

C1.justification: Both versions claim an unstructured editing benchmark, a method extending local and term-based editing, superior structured/unstructured editing performance, and robust batch/sequential editing. The new title, terminology, and abstract emphasis do not materially change these central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 reinterprets the middle loss as preserving context rather than promoting paraphrase generalization, and develops an early-decoding explanation for the shallow/deep layer split. It adds interpretations of component ablations, deeper-layer failure, general-ability preservation, and metric correlations. Removing the temperature study also removes its argument that UnKE learns semantics rather than memorizing.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies that human annotators were uninvolved in the project's training and documents the MMLU scoring implementation and aggregation. The detailed optimizer settings, learning rates, optimization steps, Alpaca sampling, hardware, runtimes, and repository access information are retained from v1, largely through relocation to Appendix H.

E1.justification: v2 expands evaluation beyond targeted editing to general-ability preservation using MMLU and unrelated subject/object knowledge in KEBench. These introduce substantive coverage of collateral effects. The underlying 1,000-example UnKEBench collection, structured editing datasets, and original/paraphrased question tasks remain.

Human and structured evaluations retain their existing comparator subsets. Newly discussed methods such as PMET, KEP, and EVEDIT are not added as evaluated competitors.

New experiments vary optimized modules, loss components, and layers L=5–12. The temperature sweep is removed. Main model sizes, single-edit decoding temperature, and human-evaluation sample and rater counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds module and loss ablations, UnKE layer sensitivity, human–automatic metric correlations, and an UnKEBench extension of MEMIT's layer analysis. These test component necessity, layer choice, and evaluation validity. v1's decoding-temperature robustness analysis is removed; batch/sequential analyses and the generation case study are retained, with several moved to appendices.

E5.justification: v2 adds Pearson correlation estimation and associated p-values in Appendix G, including explicit significance interpretation. This statistical addition is confined to metric validation. Human-rating averaging and Fleiss' kappa of 0.57 remain unchanged; neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty for the main performance results.

E6.justification: Reported UnKE FactScore on LLaMA changes from 38.82 to 42.49, and KEBench Ori-Acc/Para-Acc changes from 87.60/70.40 to 94.30/86.40. Batch-editing values are extensively replaced, and MMLU, locality, ablation, layer-sensitivity, and correlation results are added. Temperature results disappear. Metric assignments conflict across v2 Tables 2, 4, 7, and 8, so not every apparent score change supports a reliable performance comparison.

M1.justification: The two-stage key optimization, edited Transformer layer, and three loss terms remain equivalent. Key Paraphrase Loss is renamed Key Causal Loss and reinterpreted without changing its objective. Although v2 calls preservation examples 'pre-training samples' in the main text, both implementation appendices specify the same 20 Alpaca instruction examples.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, motivation, and method exposition are extensively rewritten. Method subsections are reorganized around block key-value storage and causal optimization; explicit contribution bullets disappear. Experiments are regrouped, while baseline descriptions and batch/sequential analysis move into an expanded appendix structure.

P2.justification: v2 revises Figure 1's annotations and redraws Figure 2 with structured/unstructured curves and dual axes. It adds ablation, layer-selection, and correlation tables, expands existing tables with preservation metrics, removes the temperature table, and relocates robustness displays. Typography, headers, spacing, and table-column arrangements also change substantially.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around localization critiques, attention-layer knowledge, and early decoding, citing Hase, Li, Wei, Wang, and Yao. Appendix A adds substantive distinctions from KEP and EVEDIT and expands the Eva-KELLM comparison. These additions strengthen discussion of both the method's motivation and the benchmark's relationship to prior work.

T1.justification: v2's explicit key/value equations restate definitions already present in v1, and the optimization objectives remain mathematically equivalent after notation changes. The labeled hypotheses are empirical motivations, not new formal assumptions or proofs. No substantive theoretical result is added or removed.

improvement.justification: v2 supplies useful evidence missing from v1 about component necessity, layer selection, and collateral effects, while clarifying the method and quantifying human–automatic agreement. These improve empirical scrutiny. However, inconsistent metric assignments across Tables 2, 4, 7, and 8, unexplained replacements of main scores, and removal of temperature-robustness evidence limit the gain. The net improvement is modest.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UnKE method and UnKEBench benchmark despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison. after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and reports additional MMLU results, component ablations, layer-selection experiments, and human–automatic evaluation correlations.

before.justification: v1 reports original UnKEBench and KEBench experiments, human evaluations, and batch, sequential, and decoding-temperature analyses.

title: Everything is Editable: Extend Knowledge Editing to Unstructured Data in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: UnKEBench, non-local block key-value storage, cause-driven optimization, and effectiveness on structured and unstructured editing with batch and sequential capabilities. Additional experiments support these existing claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 materially revises the comparative interpretation. Where v2 emphasizes UnKE's leading FactScore and little general-capability impact, v3 acknowledges IKE's much higher FactScore, attributes it to reading comprehension with supplied answers, and characterizes this as 'cheating'. It also introduces a locality tradeoff attributed to UnKE modifying more parameters. Appendix F qualifies KnowEdit advantages by dataset.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly documents benchmark checks, including matching thresholds of 0.8 and 0.9, entity consistency, regeneration rules, and a 15-token sub-answer limit. Appendix J adds LoRA/AdaLoRA settings, RECT tuning information, and IKE templates, retrieval, and inference details. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation; they do not establish that the previously used benchmark was regenerated. UnKE's own settings and code link remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds actual KnowEdit evaluation on WikiData_recent, ZsRE, WikiBio, WikiData_counterfact, ConvSent, and Sanitation (Appendix F, Table 8), substantially extending evaluated coverage. E2.justification: Table 2 adds LoRA, AdaLoRA, RECT, and IKE with and without ICL to the retained FT-A, FT-L, ROME, MEMIT, and MEND comparisons. The new KnowEdit comparison additionally includes SERAC, ICE, and FT-M as labeled in Table 8. This substantially broadens the evaluated comparator set.

New baseline protocols include IKE answer-containing prompts with or without five retrieved examples and LoRA/AdaLoRA tuning. The retained UnKEBench batch size, decoding temperature, editing layer, and human-evaluation design are unchanged.

The original module/loss ablations, layer sweep, batch and sequential editing analyses, human-correlation analysis, and generation case study remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same three-annotator evaluation of 36 samples per method, Fleiss' kappa of 0.57, and Pearson correlations with p-values. v3 adds no repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or other uncertainty-reporting procedures.

E6.justification: v3 adds baseline, locality, and KnowEdit results. IKE obtains FactScores of 94.60 without ICL and 93.08 with ICL, exceeding UnKE's retained 42.49. Existing metric assignments also change: Table 4's UnKE Bert-Score changes from 98.63/76.85 to 99.61/93.09. The layer-7 MMLU entry changes from 29.72 to 29.68, and reported FT-L/FT-A runtimes change from 24/31 to 14/21 hours. These are added or revised reported results, not demonstrated improvements to UnKE itself.

M1.justification: Section 4 retains the same non-local block key-value representation, last-token optimization, and three-loss objective. Equations 1–7 and UnKE's two-stage editing procedure are unchanged.

P1.justification: Most core prose remains unchanged. Benchmark construction moves from Section 5.1 to Appendix A, Section 5.1 becomes Evaluation Metrics, and the experimental discussion and appendix documentation expand. There are localized wording, cross-reference, author-header, and acknowledgement edits rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The principal comparison in Table 2 is substantially expanded with baseline rows and a locality column, while v3 adds the extensive KnowEdit table and two IKE prompt tables. Figure 1 moves earlier and its caption is shortened; appendix tables and prompt examples are relocated or reformatted. The original four figures are retained.

R1.justification: Appendix B adds AKEW and LEME and distinguishes their entity-concept editing from UnKEBench's direct unstructured-text editing. Additional references address parameter memory and downstream applications. These are localized additions; the existing related-work taxonomy and principal research positioning remain.

T1.justification: The knowledge-localization hypotheses, mathematical representation, and optimization derivations are retained. Equations 1–7 are unchanged, and v3 introduces no new theorem, proof, or substantive formal assumption.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens weaknesses in v2's empirical support: Table 2 introduces competitive parameter-efficient and in-context baselines and directly tests unrelated-knowledge retention, exposing meaningful tradeoffs. KnowEdit broadens the test of applicability, while benchmark-validation and implementation details improve reproducibility. Corrected metric assignments also improve consistency across tables. The dismissive treatment of IKE's advantage and the unfinished RECT configuration sentence are weaknesses, but the gains in evidential coverage and transparency clearly outweigh them.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UnKE method and UnKEBench benchmark. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and reports additional baseline comparisons, locality measurements, and UnKE results on KnowEdit.

before.justification: v2 reports original automatic and human evaluations, structured knowledge editing experiments, ablations, and batch and sequential editing results.

title: Everything is Editable: Extend Knowledge Editing to Unstructured Data in Large Language Models

C1.justification: v2 makes inexpensive online likelihood evaluation an explicit central contribution, whereas v1 emphasized pretraining, PTT sampling, and PTT-based likelihood estimation. Its conclusion also qualifies pretraining's benefits for tightly clustered datasets and acknowledges limited benefits during long training, narrowing v1's broadly positive generative-quality claims.

C2.justification: v2 explains why pretraining offers limited benefits on less clustered data and why long training can again lose equilibrium, recommending combination with optimized MCMC methods (Section 6). It also connects train/test likelihood divergence with increasing privacy loss and analyzes exchange-acceptance versus computational-cost tradeoffs (Appendices H and B.1). These substantially extend v1's interpretations and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 supplies RCM dimensionalities, hidden-unit counts, and pretraining times (Table 5), total training times (Table 4), and implementation details for persistent online-AIS chains (Appendix D.2). The printed code/data pointer changes from nbereux/fast-RBM to anonymousrbm/iclr-2025. These are additional reproducibility disclosures; repository accessibility itself cannot be established from the PDFs.

E1.justification: v2 adds generative-model evaluation on 2D Ising configurations, 32-by-32 black-and-white CelebA images, and full MNIST, while retaining MNIST01, Mickey, and human genome data (Table 2, Figures 2 and 16). This materially broadens coverage to physical configurations, faces, and the remaining digit classes.

E2.justification: v2 directly evaluates Parallel Tempering, reference-distribution Parallel Tempering, and Stacked Tempering against PTT on retained datasets (Figure 4); v1 directly compared PTT with Gibbs sampling and discussed Stacked Tempering through published speedups. v2 also adds reference-distribution AIS comparisons. JarRBM disappears from the plotted training comparisons, although its implementation and failure discussion remain.

E3.justification: Table 3 changes HGD hidden units from 185 to 200 and Mickey from 100 to 200. v2 introduces small-RBM exact-enumeration validation and varying AIS schedules. Sampling comparisons count Gibbs steps across all replicas instead of v1's per-replica steps, and the main PTT acceptance target changes from approximately 0.30 to 0.25. Figure 10 additionally selects models at comparable privacy loss.

E4.justification: New Appendices B.1 and F examine equilibration, exchange-acceptance sensitivity, and learning-rate/hidden-width sensitivity using autocorrelation curves, cost curves, and likelihood grids. Appendix H adds longitudinal privacy and overfitting analyses beyond v1's endpoint comparison. Conversely, v1's supplementary sampling case studies for PCD- and JarRBM-trained machines are removed.

E5.justification: v1 reports jump-count averages over 100 chains without corresponding uncertainty reporting or a stated training-replication count. v2 Figure 2 newly reports 10 trainings and standard-deviation bands conditional on a common low-rank initialization. Figure 4 increases the sampling ensemble to 1000 chains and reports errors of the mean; Appendix B.1 also specifies uncertainty estimation for autocorrelation times.

E6.justification: v2 adds exact-likelihood error curves, broader training results, runtimes, sensitivity scores, and equilibration estimates, while removing JarRBM curves and v1's acceleration-factor table. For example, its new MNIST01 grid reports test likelihoods of -73.99 ± 2.71 for PCD and -66.37 ± 1.10 for pretraining plus PCD at 1000 hidden units and learning rate 0.01 (Figure 7). Results involving changed widths, estimators, or cost accounting are not same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: v2 adds online Tr-AIS using persistent evaluation chains and per-update importance weights, and separates standalone offline Tr-AIS from PTT-based estimation (Section 5.1, Appendix D). It extends the existing bias treatment with a separate dataset-mean direction entering only the visible bias (Appendix A.3). The underlying RCM pretraining framework and PTT swap rule are retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Section 5 is reorganized around trajectory annealing with separate likelihood-estimation and sampling subsections, and the main-text privacy section moves into Appendix H within a substantially reorganized supplement. The title, citation style, and headers also change.

P2.justification: Figure 2 changes from three-method density maps to scatter plots, marginal histograms, and likelihood curves; Figure 4 expands the sampler comparison and changes its cost axis. v2 adds accuracy, sensitivity, and equilibration plots plus timing tables. Low-rank generation panels move from Figure 1 to Figure 15, while the existing PTT schematic is retained as Figure 5.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly positions its approach as a practical extension of earlier RCM work, identifying bias and sampling developments needed for real datasets. It substantially expands AIS/PT, equilibration, phase-transition, and neural/biomedical references, including Neal, Hukushima and Nemoto, Sokal, and Bravi. Several quantum and AdS application references from v1 are removed.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds AIS path-weight identities, and Appendix E derives forward/backward transition corrections before applying the symmetric-update assumption already stated in v1. Appendix G introduces substantial Curie-Weiss and phase-transition mathematics, while Appendix A.3 formalizes the additional bias direction. The new Appendix G nevertheless contains an internal inconsistency: its positive Hm term favors negative magnetization for positive H, contrary to the accompanying interpretation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through exact-likelihood checks on small RBMs, direct comparisons with stronger samplers that account for replica count, replicated trainings, and equilibration diagnostics. These address important weaknesses in v1's evidence, while the new applicability limits make the conclusions better qualified. Removing explicit JarRBM results and introducing the Appendix G sign inconsistency are drawbacks, but they are outweighed by the stronger validation of the central methods.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same low-rank RBM pretraining and Parallel Trajectory Tempering (PTT) work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on the retained and additional datasets, including exact-likelihood validation, sampler comparisons, sensitivity studies, and equilibration measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original training, generation, likelihood, sampling, and privacy results on MNIST01, Mickey, and human genome data.

title: Fast training and sampling of Restricted Boltzmann Machines

However, v3 removes the conclusion's extrapolation about low-rank initialization for deeper architectures and its broad applicability claim for both trajectory methods. PTT's applicability to other EBMs remains stated in Section 4.2.

C2.justification: v2 chiefly links thermal-sampling failure to first-order transitions and poor exchange acceptance. v3 adds the distinct explanation that warming can suppress minority modes, preventing their recovery even with high swap acceptance. This materially refines the interpretation of PT failure and the rationale for following training trajectories.

D1.justification: The advertised code/data repository changes from anonymousrbm/iclr-2025 to DsysDML/fastrbm. Appendix B.1 replaces the specialized PTT listing with separate generic PT and PTT listings. The new diagnostics reuse existing sampling comparators; tethered Monte Carlo reconstructs reference densities rather than becoming a competing performance baseline.

These are additional experiments; the retained benchmark settings and dataset splits in Tables 2–3 are unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.2 and Appendix H.2 add substantial failure analysis: temperature-dependent density reconstruction and AGS continuation of PT/PTT samples test whether apparently successful tempering misses minority clusters. These diagnostics go beyond v2's retained jump-count, autocorrelation, acceptance-sensitivity, hyperparameter, and overfitting analyses.

E5.justification: v3 Figure 2 newly specifies ten independent runs and one-standard-deviation shading for the likelihood-error comparison retained from v2 Figure 3. This documents existing uncertainty bands without establishing additional runs. The pretraining caption also drops v2's explicit qualification that the ten trainings share the same low-rank initializer.

E6.justification: The retained benchmark curves and numerical tables are unchanged, but v3 adds substantive findings about temperature-driven mode redistribution and PT missing an HGD cluster despite high swap acceptance. title: Achieving Dimension-Free Communication in Federated Learning via Zeroth-Order Optimization

The central claims about training-free DBIM sampling, non-Markovian bridges, up to 25× acceleration and latent-space operations remain.

C2.justification: V2 qualifies higher-order gains as relatively modest and attributes improved textures to information from past network outputs. Appendix C.4 adds a Langevin-based explanation for stochastic sampling benefits. Conversely, v1's limitations paragraph, including its explicit one-step-generation and real-time efficiency limitations, is removed.

D1.justification: V2 adds a DBIM code-repository link and Algorithm 1 specifying higher-order sampling. M1.justification: V2 adds second- and third-order DBIM inference procedures in Section 4.3 and Appendices D–E. P1.justification: V2 revises the abstract and selected explanatory passages, moves the loss-weighting discussion to Appendix C.2, and reorganizes the appendices around additional theory and algorithms.
