P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: small-scale generalization moves from Appendix 7.6 to Section 4.5, multi-dataset training moves from Section 4.5 to Appendix A.3, and limitations move to Appendix A.9. Appendix analyses are reordered, with embedding analysis brought forward, and several experimental explanations are rewritten.

P2.justification: Main comparison tables are redesigned with Meta-iNat columns and means only, while full uncertainty tables are redisplayed in Appendix A.10. A new task-generation ablation table is added. The embedding figure is substantially redrawn with shaded clusters, centroids, and distances; learning-curve displays are revised and several figures and tables are relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds BECLR and distinguishes its contrastive few-shot framework from meta-learning. It also adds citations for deep residual learning and the Meta-iNat source. The broader positioning relative to UML, image mixing, and in-context learning remains intact.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 restores the missing '1 minus' in the simplified class-collision probability, correcting its inconsistency with the preceding expression. Appendix A.7 adds a computational-cost argument of O(Q(NK+1)^2 d). The existing training formulation and logistic-phase mathematics remain, without new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the main comparison by replacing v1's mismatched default backbones and leakage-affected PsCo evaluation with common ResNet-50/ImageNet-964 settings. Additional task-generation controls and the BECLR comparison better test the method's contribution beyond its feature extractor. New reporting defects, including reversed CLIP dimensions in A.1 and inconsistent multi-dataset values between Tables 5 and 6(b), limit reproducibility, but the improved experimental controls provide a substantial net gain in evidential quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CAMeLU research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, are readable and support comparison despite substantial experimental revisions and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original classification results and ablations, including additional Meta-iNat evaluations, BECLR comparisons, clustering-based task generation, and a one-query experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original few-shot classification experiments, learning curves, feature-extractor ablations, and task-generation analyses in the main text and appendix.

title: Unsupervised Meta-Learning via In-Context Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: unsupervised task generation combined with in-context learning, strong cross-domain classification without fine-tuning, and efficient inference. Additional appendix evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: Appendix A.4 newly cautions that CLIP training-data overlap cannot be verified. A.5 adds interpretations about task-generation benefits beyond CAMeLU, their combination with in-context learning, and CACTUs-MAML's alleged leakage advantage. A.7 newly interprets measured resource advantages. The existing A.9 limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 promises code upon acceptance; v3 supplies a repository address and reports available code, instructions, models, and pretrained weights. It also revises the CLIP dimensionality description and adds concrete runtime and memory measurements. These are documented disclosures; external resource availability was not checked.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same training data, including ImageNet-964, miniImageNet, and the ImageNet-964/MSCOCO/Fungi combination, and evaluate on miniImageNet, CIFAR-fs, CUB, Aircraft, and Meta-iNat. The added analyses do not introduce new datasets or task requirements.

E2.justification: v3 adds the Proposed + MAML comparison with CACTUs-MAML and UMTRA in Table 8 and introduces PsCo into the resource comparison in Table 11. These extend comparisons using existing baseline names; comparator membership in the original benchmark tables remains unchanged.

E3.justification: The additions introduce a MAML control and measurements of task-construction time, training time per epoch, inference time per task, and CPU/GPU memory. Appendix A.1 also revises the reported CLIP dimensionality specification. Existing splits and training/evaluation budgets are retained, without evidence that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix A.5 newly tests whether the task generator benefits MAML, and A.7 adds empirical resource profiling beyond the existing complexity discussion. Earlier ablations remain. The CUB embedding visualization in v3 Figure 2 repeats v2 Figure 4(c–d), so it is not an additional analysis.

E5.justification: v3 adds a general statement about random-seed initialization, without specifying seed values. Three complete runs and mean/standard-deviation reporting were already documented in v2 and remain unchanged. New Tables 8 and 11 provide point estimates without accompanying uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Matched pre-existing results retain their values. New Table 8 reports Proposed + MAML accuracies, including 31.22 and 41.54 on CUB for one and five shots. New Table 11 reports resource results, including 57 versus 605 ms/task inference time for CAMeLU versus PsCo. These are added results, not improvements over v2 measurements.

M1.justification: Appendix A.5 adds an adaptation that uses the proposed task generator with MAML instead of CAMeLU's in-context learner. The main CAMeLU architecture, mixing strategy, objective, and inference procedure remain unchanged; the new non-causal terminology clarifies the existing approach.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized prose revisions, clarifies non-causal sequence modeling, expands the in-context related-work discussion, and adds a main-text analysis paragraph plus ethics/reproducibility and acknowledgments sections. The overall section order and most explanatory text remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 8 and 11 and redisplays the existing CUB embedding panels as main-text Figure 2 while retaining them in the appendix. ICLR formatting changes headers, typography, and placement, with minor diagram-label edits. Existing plots and table structures are largely preserved.

R1.justification: v3 adds Chan et al. (2022) and Singh et al. (2024), expanding the discussion of data-distribution effects on in-context learning and distinguishing CAMeLU's UML focus. The CAML year update and conversion to author–year citations do not represent additional works.

T1.justification: The task-collision calculation, task and objective equations, SSIM expressions, transformer complexity bound, and logistic-curve analysis are retained. The non-causal sequence explanation introduces no new formal result, assumption, or proof.

improvement.justification: The MAML experiment, resource measurements, specific CLIP leakage caveat, and concrete code/weight access information modestly improve evidence and transparency beyond v2's already extensive evaluation. The gains are limited by sparse protocol details for the new measurements and overbroad interpretation: Table 11 reports higher GPU inference memory for CAMeLU than PsCo, 3224 versus 1630 MiB, despite the general memory-efficiency claim.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CAMeLU and provide readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A.1–A.10. Corresponding material can be matched despite reformatting, renumbering, and additions.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds results for the task-generation strategy combined with MAML and resource measurements comparing CAMeLU with PsCo.

before.justification: v2 reports original classification experiments across five evaluation datasets, feature-extractor and task-generation ablations, and analyses of representations and learning dynamics.

title: Unsupervised Meta-Learning via In-Context Learning

C1.justification: v1's introduction and conclusion emphasize performance against individual fixed hyperparameter configurations. v2 explicitly claims superiority over competitive AutoRL baselines and extends the abstract's empirical scope to Atari. This broadens the central comparative contribution while retaining the shared-target selection idea.

C2.justification: The fixed-population and discount-factor limitations in v1 are replaced by implemented extensions in v2, while the reward-related restriction remains. v2 explicitly connects the theorem's ideal condition to infinite data and drops v1's interpretation that greedy selection necessarily yields the smallest achievable cumulative approximation error. Appendix C adds a concrete tradeoff: the 16-network configuration is sample-efficient but slower than random search.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds Atari preprocessing, search-space tables, tournament and mutation rules, weight preservation, optimizer resets, and Meta-gradient DQN settings. It also newly discloses horizons for the existing LunarLander and MuJoCo experiments, without establishing changed settings. The explicit GPU model and detailed overhead percentages in v1 are omitted. The promise of supplementary code and release upon acceptance remains unchanged.

E1.justification: LunarLander and the six MuJoCo environments are retained. v2 adds vision-based Atari control: three games for finite hyperparameter selection and six for population search, comprising eight distinct games across Figures 20 and 21. Discount-factor experiments additionally evaluate BattleZone and Freeway, both within that Atari coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds random-search references computed from individual runs to the existing MuJoCo comparisons, and evaluates SEARL, DEHB, and random search in the population-search experiment. Figure 8 adds Meta-gradient DQN. These extend v1's individual configurations, grid search, and random-target variants. Figure 7 plots DEHB, although its caption incorrectly mentions grid search.

E3.justification: New Atari protocols introduce stacked grayscale observations, sticky actions, human-normalized scores, and extensive hyperparameter search spaces. Section 5.4 specifies a 40M-frame population-search budget, six random-search trials of 30M frames, and DEHB budgets of 20M–40M frames. It reports running maximum returns for random search/DEHB and population extrema for SEARL. These are added evaluation designs; the stated parameters of the retained LunarLander and MuJoCo experiments largely match.

E4.justification: v2 adds Atari hyperparameter sensitivity studies, robustness tests varying target-update and population-update intervals, and a Pong hyperparameter-evolution case study. Appendix B.1 reports comparisons involving truncation selection and weight resets, while Appendix C adds performance-versus-time analyses. LunarLander Figure 3 gains behavioral-selection distributions. Conversely, the MuJoCo actor-selection distributions shown in v1 are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions use IQM with pointwise 95% stratified bootstrap confidence intervals and retain 20 LunarLander seeds and nine MuJoCo seeds. v2 additionally specifies five seeds for Atari. This adds run-count information without establishing any increase in repetitions for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial Atari results, including aggregate advantages over SEARL with a BattleZone exception in Figure 21, and similar performance to Meta-gradient DQN in Figure 8. The MuJoCo finding of outperforming 13 of 16 configurations in final performance remains. Figure 2 revises the AdaDQN-max curve from negative to positive late-training returns. v1's detailed win-count and resource-overhead tables disappear; Appendix C adds clock-time results and Atari memory measurements.

M1.justification: The original AdaDQN/AdaSAC procedures remain, but Section 5.4 and Appendix B.1 implement a population-based extension with selection and mutation, inverse-loss behavioral selection, and L2 ranking across networks trained with different losses. v2 also introduces training with different discount factors and a common cross-validated discount for network selection. v1 described population evolution as future work and excluded discount-factor tuning.

P1.justification: Related work moves from Section 5 to Section 3, the performance bound moves from the preliminaries to Appendix A, and the method's theoretical motivation is substantially rewritten and integrated into Section 4. The experimental narrative is reorganized around finite and infinite hyperparameter spaces, with an expanded setup appendix. These changes substantially alter the paper's structure and exposition.

P2.justification: v2 adds Atari plots, robustness radar charts, a population-workflow diagram, clock-time plots, and two Atari configuration tables. It merges v1's MuJoCo Figures 5 and 6, removes actor-selection panels, adds a behavioral-selection row to LunarLander Figure 3, and restructures legends and appendix plots. The original resource and win-count tables are removed, alongside a document-wide transition to the ICLR layout.

R1.justification: The AutoRL taxonomy and most related-work discussion are retained. v2 adds relevant references for Atari protocols, hyperparameter landscapes, evolutionary selection, and evaluation, including Mohan et al., Eimer et al., and Obando-Ceron et al. It expands the comparison with meta-gradient methods to discuss target tuning, first-order optimization, and non-stationarity, citing Xu et al.

T1.justification: The formal performance-loss bound, empirical-error selection theorem, and bias-variance proof are retained. v2 moves the cited bound to Appendix A and states the empirical conditional-expectation assumption explicitly in Theorem 4.1, but that assumption already appears in v1's Appendix A proof. The mathematical changes otherwise concern notation and presentation.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly avoided direct AutoRL comparisons despite making AutoRL its central motivation. v2 substantially addresses that gap through comparisons with SEARL, DEHB, random search, and Meta-gradient DQN, alongside Atari validation and tested population and discount-factor extensions. Expanded implementation details and runtime analyses strengthen assessability. Some reporting quality is lost through omitted hardware and overhead details and inconsistencies involving Figures 2 and 7, but the gains in comparative evidence and demonstrated applicability outweigh these limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AdaQN and contain readable text, equations, algorithms, figures, tables, and appendices. The retained content can be matched across the reorganization, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original LunarLander and MuJoCo results and adds Atari experiments, AutoRL comparisons, robustness analyses, and discount-factor selection results.

before.justification: v1 reports original LunarLander and six-environment MuJoCo experiments, including learning curves, ablations, hyperparameter-selection analyses, and resource measurements.

title: Adaptive $Q$-Network: On-the-fly Target Selection for Deep Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims about adaptive shared targets, sample efficiency, performance, robustness, and theoretical soundness. The introduction clarifies the existing focus on online hyperparameter adaptation.

C2.justification: The carbon analysis explicitly limits its estimates to computations producing the reported figures, excluding preliminary studies, and contextualizes them against an annual per-person carbon budget. Existing explanations of performance and Section 6’s limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: V3 supplies a code-repository URL, identifies the Atari codebase’s provenance, and adds Appendix B.2’s baseline aggregation and replay-reuse details. These improve documentation without establishing corresponding implementation changes. The earlier acceptance-contingent code footnote remains.

E1.justification: Both versions use LunarLander, the same six MuJoCo environments, and the same Atari game sets for finite-space, infinite-space, and discount-factor experiments. The extended random-search curve remains within existing task coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain the same individual DQN/SAC configurations, random and grid search, RandDQN/RandSAC, SEARL, DEHB, and Meta-gradient DQN. Newly cited theoretical works are not added experimental baselines.

E3.justification: Figure 4 extends the reported finite-space random-search comparison from approximately 0.5 million to 8 million cumulative environment steps; Appendix B.2 describes sequential-trial postprocessing. Tables 1–4 retain their settings. Newly disclosed replay-data reuse for infinite-space baselines does not establish a change in their implementation.

E4.justification: The new Carbon Impact section adds an environmental-cost analysis using two estimation tools. Existing behavioral-policy and hyperparameter ablations, case studies, and Appendix C’s time and memory analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix B.2 newly discloses Monte Carlo sampling of hyperparameter sequences to estimate random-search performance. The 20/9/5 seed counts and 95% stratified-bootstrap confidence-interval practice remain unchanged; revised band values in Figure 4 are result changes.

E6.justification: Figure 4 revises the grid-search aggregate, extends random-search trajectories, and updates confidence bands. These are revised baseline summaries, not an AdaSAC performance gain. V3 also reports 1.30–1.53 tonnes of CO2 equivalent; the other experimental figures retain their results.

M1.justification: AdaDQN, AdaSAC, target selection, behavioral policies, and the infinite-space evolutionary extension are retained. The new mathematical formulation and tabular analysis do not change the implemented algorithms.

P1.justification: Localized rewrites clarify the introduction, preliminaries, and experimental reporting. New convergence and evaluation-protocol subsections, acknowledgments, and carbon-impact text extend the document while preserving its main narrative and section order.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is reduced in size, Figure 9 moves relative to the experimental-setup text, and citation colors, spacing, and a table caption change. The existing figure and table inventory and overall display structures are retained.

R1.justification: V3 adds Lan et al. (2020) for the convergence framework, Vincent et al. (2025) for implementation provenance, and three carbon-accounting references. The principal AutoRL positioning and related-work comparisons remain stable.

T1.justification: V3 adds the bilevel hyperparameter formulation in Equation (2) and Appendix A.1’s argument for almost-sure tabular convergence, extending Generalized Q-learning to history-dependent target selection. This substantially expands the theory beyond the retained approximation-error result and proof.

improvement.justification: Appendix B.2, the code link, and extended baseline reporting improve transparency. However, Appendix A.1’s new convergence argument asserts an inequality bounding differences between independently selected ensemble members by the distance between ensembles. With identical ensembles but unequal selected members, that distance is zero while the selected values can differ. This substantive proof gap accompanies the documentation gains, leaving their net effect on overall quality uncertain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AdaQN work. Text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–D are readable and can be matched across the added subsections and repagination.

after.justification: V3 retains these original experiments, revises Figure 4 results, and adds estimates of the experiments’ carbon emissions.

before.justification: V2 reports original LunarLander, MuJoCo, and Atari experiments, including baseline comparisons, ablations, and computational-cost measurements.

title: Adaptive $Q$-Network: On-the-fly Target Selection for Deep Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The central refinement claim remains, but its scope and success criterion change. V1 explicitly excludes objective-task transfer from its model; v2 promotes mathematical reasoning as a main application. V2 Section 6 additionally argues that genuine weak-to-strong generalization requires outperforming the unchanged strong model, rather than merely the weak teacher.

C2.justification: V1 explains ICL failures through distribution shift and dependence between content and style; v2 removes that discussion and reframes infer-and-respond around improving style transfer. Ask-to-improve's rationale changes from handling individual examples and context constraints to avoiding harmful concept inference. V2 also discusses misspecified ICL likelihoods and qualifies the limited mathematical-reasoning gains for GPT-4o-mini.

D1.justification: V2 Appendix F.3 adds math-specific context sizes—three examples for GSM8K and two for MATH—along with the grading prompt and weak-label provenance. Reported API expenditure rises from about $60 to $160. Most existing implementation details remain, although some appendix model descriptions conflict with the updated experimental setup.

E1.justification: V2 adds mathematical-reasoning training and evaluation on GSM8K and MATH, while removing the tinyMMLU persona evaluation. Dolly-based persona training, tinyAlpacaEval, tinyTruthfulQA, science-explanation questions and the gender-representation task remain.

E2.justification: V1 primarily compares refinement with the unchanged strong model and direct weak-label fine-tuning. V2 Section 5.1 and Table 1 additionally evaluate bootstrapping and a data-doubling proxy for auxiliary confidence loss. The latter is explicitly a substitute for the original custom-loss method, which the authors could not implement.

E3.justification: V2 adds GPT-4o-mini targets and Mistral/Gemma weak-label configurations. Persona evaluation changes from GPT-4 to GPT-4o, and the new math evaluations require both correct reasoning and a correct final answer for binary credit. Gemma's precise size remains unclear: Section 5 says 1.2B, whereas Table 1 says 2B.

E4.justification: V1's tinyMMLU evaluation supplies a specific distribution-shift failure case contrasting ICL with infer-and-respond; v2 removes that diagnostic evidence. Most illustrative pirate, analogy and incomplete-biography-repair cases remain. The additional infer-and-respond benchmark curves largely extend existing comparisons rather than introduce new controlled ablations.

E5.justification: Repeated persona-grader calls decrease from 20 to 10 per answer, retaining temperature 1 and averaging. V1 Table 3 includes plus/minus uncertainty values for gender results; v2 Table 2 reports only point estimates. These changes concern grading and uncertainty reporting, not documented replication of model training.

E6.justification: V2 adds math, alternative-baseline and GPT-4o-mini results and replaces numerous retained-task scores. For example, GPT-3.5 gender accuracy scores for unchanged, weak-label-trained and refined-label-trained models change from 9.47/8.73/9.48 in v1 Table 3 to 8.97/7.80/9.03 in v2 Table 2. Figure 3 newly reports refinement gains for GPT-3.5 but limited gains for GPT-4o-mini. Revised evaluation settings prevent interpreting the replacement scores as same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 changes from selecting context examples separately for each query and refining all queries to reserving one shared context set and refining the remaining queries. The practical ICL, infer-and-respond and ask-to-improve procedures otherwise retain their core operations; the extensive changes to analytical models and estimators are covered under T1.

P1.justification: The title changes from a statistical framework to a transfer learning framework. Substantial setup, theory and discussion prose is rewritten; general related work moves to Appendix G, guided-refinement discussion shifts into the appendices, and the appendices are reorganized around background, proofs, refinement and experimental details.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the main persona/explanation score tables with multi-panel curves and adds math plots, producing seven numbered figures. It introduces a baseline-comparison table, expands the gender table and removes v1's concept-mapping schematic. The document template, headings and boxed examples are also extensively reformatted.

R1.justification: The earlier general related-work discussion largely survives in Appendix G. V2 adds substantive positioning against concurrent theories by Charikar et al., Lang et al. and Wu and Sahai, and connects its refinement experiments to Yang et al. (2024b). New discussions of Wang et al. and Pathak et al. support the revised statistical formulation.

T1.justification: V1 analyzes fixed prompts, two Gaussian concepts, additive corruption and Wasserstein error using KL-regularized distribution estimators. V2 replaces this with orthonormal linear components, random covariates, biased or noisy weak models, regression estimators and excess-risk bounds. It adds convex-hull feasibility and hidden-Markov convergence results with substantially reworked proofs. The revised Definition 3.1 also uses a regularizer sign inconsistent with Appendix C.1.

improvement.justification: The math experiments and additional baseline comparisons address v1's narrow empirical validation. However, the replacement theory contains unresolved internal contradictions: Definition 3.1 and Appendix C.1 use opposite regularizer signs, and Appendix C.2 assigns a variable mean 2/nICL while bounding it above by 1/nICL. V2 also removes gender uncertainty values and the tinyMMLU failure evidence. These empirical benefits and unresolved correctness and transparency issues prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same weak-to-strong generalization study. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: V2 reports original refinement and fine-tuning evaluations across persona, explanation, mathematical reasoning and gender representation. Its use of externally supplied math weak labels does not change the attribution of its reported model comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original persona, explanation-technique and gender-representation experiments, including refinement and fine-tuning comparisons in Tables 1–3.

title: A transfer learning framework for weak to strong generalization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: a transfer-learning formulation, limitations of naive weak-label fine-tuning, and refinement that elicits latent knowledge, supported by alignment experiments.

C2.justification: The interpretations of experimental results, limited GPT-4o-mini gains, and harmful-concept inference remain unchanged. Appendix B's added sentence about corrupted emissions and correct transitions restates the distinction already present in v2's description and equations.

D1.justification: Section 5 makes the mathematical-reasoning weak-model name more specific, changing LLama-7B-Chat to LLama2-7B-Chat. This is a limited documentation clarification; Appendix F's prompts, hardware, costs, and implementation details remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same Dolly questions, tinyAlpacaEval, tinyTruthfulQA, GSM8K, MATH, generated science questions, and gender-representation scenarios involving 52 occupations. Appendix coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The corresponding experiments retain the same comparators: unchanged strong models, naive fine-tuning, bootstrapping, and the auxiliary-loss proxy. Table 1 and the appendix comparisons have unchanged comparator membership.

E3.justification: The reported datasets, sample counts, grading criteria, training procedures, and ICL example counts remain unchanged. The more specific Llama2 name does not establish a changed experimental configuration.

E4.justification: The supplementary refinement comparisons, harmful-concept examples, gender-bias analysis, and refinement-failure example in Appendices D–F are retained. No ablation, robustness test, or case study is added or removed.

E5.justification: Both versions describe averaging repeated GPT-4o judgments, including ten samples at temperature 1 for persona evaluation. There is no change in seed information, repeated-run reporting, confidence intervals, or significance testing.

E6.justification: Figures 1–7, Tables 1–2, and the reported qualitative outcomes match. For example, Table 2 retains accuracy 9.03 and women representation 0.96 for GPT-3.5-Turbo fine-tuned with ask-to-improve labels.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–3 retain the same ICL refinement, infer-and-respond, and ask-to-improve procedures. Notation and theoretical-formulation edits do not introduce an algorithmic or architectural change.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized spelling, grammar, punctuation, and notation edits, organizes conditions into Assumption 2.1, and retitles Section 5.1 as Comparisons with Augmented Weak Training. The overall narrative and section organization remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds the ICLR 2025 publication header and reformats several mathematical displays, causing localized reflow across pages 2–3 and 18–20. The seven figures and two tables retain their displays, captions, and organization.

R1.justification: The cited works, concurrent-work discussion, Appendix G, and substantive comparisons with earlier research are unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation (2.1) adds the query x to the concept-posterior conditioning. Assumption 2.1 collects existing conditions but changes the target/weak inner product from strictly between 0 and 1 to [0,1]. Appendix B.1 rewrites both HMM likelihoods with explicit hidden-state sums, first-token factors, and changed conditioning. These are localized formal revisions; the theorem bounds and proofs are otherwise retained.

improvement.justification: Clearer assumption organization and minor documentation corrections improve readability, but v3 introduces a mathematical qualification problem. Unlike v2's strictly positive inner-product condition, Assumption 2.1 permits zero, where Theorem 4.3's exponential decay rate vanishes. The following explanation still asserts eventual correct-concept inference without excluding that case. This limited loss of theoretical precision outweighs the modest editorial benefits; the empirical evidence remains unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–G. Textual and visual comparison supports reliable matching throughout.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and their reported outcomes in Figures 1–7 and Tables 1–2.

before.justification: v2 reports original experiments on persona learning, mathematical reasoning, explanation techniques, and gender representation, including appendix results.

title: A transfer learning framework for weak to strong generalization

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central contributions: a second-order account of nonlinear model compositionality, the importance of preserving pre-training knowledge, dual ITA/IEL algorithms, and compositional specialization and unlearning capabilities. The additional evidence and qualifications do not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: v1 interprets ITA's unlearning behavior as suggesting greater knowledge entanglement than TMC; v2 instead argues for more effective disentanglement. v2 also adds substantive discussion of Taylor-approximation validity under parameter drift, Gaussian and diagonal-Fisher approximations, and the absence of a guaranteed improvement over pre-training in Sections 5–6.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies the exact timm checkpoint, initialization for FFT/LoRA/IA3, local cross-entropy and its application to competitors, and validation-based grid search using 10% of training data. Appendix I adds linear-probing learning rates, InfLoRA settings and CLS-prior coefficients. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's existing optimizer, Fisher-estimation and regularization details.

E1.justification: The seven class-incremental datasets remain unchanged. Specialization and unlearning coverage expands from ImageNet-R, CIFAR-100 and RESISC in v1 Table 2 to all seven datasets in v2 Table 7, extending these editing tasks to CUB-200, Caltech-256, MIT-67 and CropDiseases.

E2.justification: v2 adds InfLoRA as an evaluated comparator across all seven datasets, with accuracy, forgetting and standard-deviation entries in Tables 1, 4 and 5. The existing comparator set is otherwise retained, including TMC in the specialization and unlearning comparisons.

E3.justification: Appendix I substantially revises reported settings relative to v1 Appendix G. Examples include ITA-LoRA's CropDisease pre-consolidation budget changing from 15 to 8 epochs, IEL-FFT's CIFAR-100 learning rate changing from 0.00001 to 0.0001, and IEL-LoRA's Caltech classifier regularization coefficient changing from 0.05 to 5. These establish changed reported configurations, without independently establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 Figure 1 adds a targeted diagnostic comparing the composed model's empirical risk, weighted individual-model risk and linear-probed pre-training risk, with and without regularization. v1 provides accuracy ablations but no corresponding risk-bound analysis. The existing regularization-removal and classifier-only ablation designs are retained.

E5.justification: v2 Table 5 first supplies standard deviations for the FFT and IA3 variants whose accuracy results already appeared in v1 Tables 3 and 6. Both versions retain three-repetition averaging; v2 describes 'three runs' instead of explicitly specifying 'three class orders.' No increase in repetitions or new significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: Accuracy, forgetting, ablation and editing results are extensively revised. For example, ITA-LoRA's reported ImageNet-R accuracy changes from 78.43 to 77.79 and CUB-200 accuracy from 81.48 to 85.55; its CIFAR-100 unlearning target accuracy changes from 62.79 to 28.67. InfLoRA results, additional editing results and Figure 1's risk findings are added. Revised settings prevent treating these numerical changes as controlled performance gains or losses.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains task pre-consolidation, accumulated diagonal Fisher information, individual versus composed-model training, and the regularization objectives in Equations 11–19. v2 explicitly documents initialization and local cross-entropy, but does not establish that these disclosures represent changes to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: v2 extensively revises the framework and algorithm explanations, places regularization analysis before compositional tests, and replaces the short conclusion with a developed limitations and future-directions section. The appendices are reorganized into separate implementation, related-work, dataset, results and hyperparameter sections. These changes substantially reshape the narrative beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 changes document-wide title, heading and header styling, boxes the research questions, and adds Figure 1. Table 1 consolidates all six ITA/IEL fine-tuning variants; ablation rows are redistributed between main text and appendix. The compositional tables replace the overall-accuracy column with gain/loss annotations and add an expanded appendix display covering all datasets.

R1.justification: v2 adds InfLoRA positioning and a substantial Appendix F comparing initialization, regularization, composition and inference costs with existing methods. New literature supports the discussions of local cross-entropy, lazy training, loss geometry and curvature approximations. Some earlier continual-learning references are removed; the existing model-merging discussion is relocated rather than newly introduced.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 2 defines all-task empirical risk and transfers the central local-minimum, positive-semidefinite-Hessian and Jensen-bound argument to that risk. v1 assumes local optimality of the per-example loss before averaging its bound. This materially weakens a foundational assumption, although Theorem 1 and the appendix proofs and gradient derivations remain essentially unchanged.

improvement.justification: Explicit checkpoint, initialization, loss and tuning details improve reproducibility; InfLoRA and Figure 1 strengthen empirical assessment, and Section 6 better qualifies the approximations. These support a modest overall improvement. However, the revised empirical-risk assumption does not establish the per-example Hessian positivity still invoked in Section 2.3, and newly listed CLS-prior coefficients remain undefined.

title: On Conformal Isometry of Grid Cells: Learning Distance-Preserving Position Embedding

C1.justification: The introduction newly claims detailed theoretical justification as a contribution. The title and abstract emphasize entity representation learning, while the central claims about relation-guided experts, disentanglement, and strong MMKGC performance remain. No additional downstream task capability is demonstrated or established.

C2.justification: The robustness interpretation expands from noisy modalities to missing information and sparse links. Section 5.6 adds claims of manageable, linear computational overhead and favorable efficiency. The limitations concerning task specificity, lack of LLM integration, and medium-sized datasets are substantively unchanged, moving from Appendix A to C.

D1.justification: Appendix B and Table 6 newly disclose dataset-specific learning rates and embedding dimensions, plus 2000 training epochs and other selected hyperparameters. v1 primarily supplied tuning ranges. Hardware, software, and code/data access information remain unchanged; these additions improve documentation without establishing an implementation change.

E1.justification: The four datasets and link-prediction task remain, but Section 5.4 expands DB15K evaluation from modality noise to missing modalities and sparse training links. These introduce two distinct information-availability scenarios, materially broadening robustness coverage.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds TuckER as an evaluated baseline on all four datasets, increasing the comparison set from 19 to 20. TuckER was already cited and used as MOMOK's scoring function in v1. The robustness comparator set remains AdaMF, TBKGC, and QEB, also spelled QBE.

E3.justification: v2 adds random modality removal at plotted rates of 10–50%, training-triple removal at plotted sparse rates of 5–25%, and time/memory measurements. The original benchmark splits and named link-prediction metrics remain. Appendix B documents existing settings; it does not establish a changed training regime or rerun.

E4.justification: Figure 3 adds substantial tests of robustness to missing modality information and sparse links. New Section 5.6 and Table 4 examine computational cost against MMKRL, OTKGE, and MMRNS. Existing component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity analyses, and modality case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. The newly explained averaging over head and tail predictions is not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds TuckER scores, missing-modality and sparse-link result curves, and resource measurements, including MOMOK's 9.8 seconds and 5900 MB in Table 4. All existing Table 2 scores and Table 3 ablations remain unchanged. TuckER becomes the strongest baseline on several metrics, but the improvement percentages are not updated: KVC16K Hit@1 values of 10.53 versus 9.79 imply about 7.6%, rather than the retained 23.0%.

M1.justification: ReMoKE, MuJoD, ExID, their training losses, alternating optimization, and inference score aggregation remain unchanged. Explicit relation subscripts and expanded CLUB explanations clarify the existing method rather than introduce a new procedure.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, rewrites the opening motivation and parts of the abstract, expands the CLUB explanation, and adds an efficiency research question and section. New analytical and experimental-detail appendices precede the retained limitations and impacts. Most existing methodological and results prose remains closely matched.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is redesigned from two plots into a six-panel comparison with a shared legend. New efficiency and hyperparameter tables are added, while existing figures and tables are resized or relocated. The document also adopts substantially different title, heading, header, citation, and table formatting.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion is shortened, and references to Wang et al.'s 2017 embedding survey, Pezeshkpour et al. (2018), and Liang et al. (2023) are removed. The opening positions the work more explicitly within entity representation learning. Most cited foundations remain; author-year citation formatting is a presentation change.

T1.justification: v1 cites CLUB and states the implemented losses; v2 adds its general definition and Appendix A's two theorems and proofs concerning the upper bound and a KL-based condition for its variational approximation. This is substantial new mathematical content, although Equation 14 uses q-distribution expectations while Proof 2 proceeds with p-distribution expectations.

improvement.justification: The additional robustness scenarios, relevant TuckER comparison, and exact hyperparameters provide a limited net improvement in validation and reproducibility. Reporting defects constrain that gain: Table 2 and Section 5.3 retain outdated improvement margins, Appendix B.2's metric formulas omit the factor of two needed for head/tail averaging, and Appendix A's variational definition conflicts with its proof. The unchanged core results remain useful, but the additions require correction before supporting a substantial quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MOMOK framework despite the changed title. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds missing-modality and sparse-link experiments, TuckER comparisons, and resource measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original link-prediction experiments on four benchmarks, noise robustness tests, ablations, sensitivity analyses, and case studies.

title: Multiple Heads are Better than One: Mixture of Modality Knowledge Experts for Entity Representation Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims about relation-guided experts, mutual-information disentanglement, performance, robustness and interpretability. Additional appendix evidence does not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix C.3 expands discussion of fine versus coarse ranking performance, acknowledges MoSE-BI's stronger FB15K-237 Hit scores alongside different embedding sizes, and explains dataset-dependent ablation effects through the strong TuckER foundation. The existing limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 removes v2 Table 6 and Appendix B.3, losing the exact per-dataset learning rates, selected embedding dimensions and 2000-epoch training budget. These replication settings are not relocated elsewhere. General implementation details and the code/data URL remain, while Appendix C.3.2 newly discloses embedding sizes for the FB15K-237 comparison.

E1.justification: Appendix C.3.2 adds FB15K-237 link prediction to the four existing MMKG benchmarks. The task remains MMKG completion, and the original noisy-modality, missing-modality and sparse-link scenarios are retained.

E2.justification: The original main comparison retains the same 20 baselines. The new FB15K-237 comparison in v3 Table 7 separately reports MoSE-AI, MoSE-BI and MoSE-MI, extending the explicitly compared ensemble variants beyond v2's single MoSE row.

E3.justification: Section 5.2 expands the stated embedding-dimension search from {200, 250, 300} to {200, 250, 300, 400, 500}. Existing splits, metrics and evaluation procedures remain unchanged. This establishes a revised reported tuning protocol, without establishing that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 Table 8 extends the complete modality-contribution and component-removal ablations to MKG-Y and KVC16K. Consequently, all four original benchmarks now have these checks, substantially broadening evidence about the components' contributions across datasets. The existing robustness tests and case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies repeated-run counts or random seeds, or reports confidence intervals, standard deviations or significance tests. The added results retain the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: The main-table scores and original ablation scores are unchanged. v3 Tables 6–8 add Hit@3/Hit@10 results for MKG-W/MKG-Y, FB15K-237 results including MOMOK MRR 36.08, and additional ablation outcomes. Figure 4 also reverses the loss-weight labels while retaining the plotted values, moving the displayed peak from 0.0001 to 0.001 and conflicting with unchanged Section 5.5.

M1.justification: ReMoKE, MuJoD, ExID, their objectives and the training/inference procedures remain unchanged. Equation 3 adds relation subscripts to embeddings already described as relation-guided in v2; this clarifies notation without establishing a procedural change.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact. Changes include conference headers, expanded affiliations, acknowledgments, limited wording corrections, aligned mathematical notation and appendix reorganization around new related-work and supplementary-results sections.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the appendix's results presentation with separate tables for complete benchmark metrics, FB15K-237 comparisons and additional ablations. It moves dataset statistics from the main text, removes the hyperparameter table, shortens Figure 2's caption, and relocates and reformats Figure 4, including reversed loss-weight labels.

R1.justification: New Appendix A organizes existing MMKGC approaches into fusion, ensemble and negative-sampling methods, explicitly positioning MOMOK between fusion and ensemble approaches. v3 also adds several Liang and Zhao citations and removes Chen et al. (2022), while retaining the central research positioning.

T1.justification: The CLUB theorems, KL-divergence condition and proofs move from Appendix A to Appendix B without substantive mathematical changes. Replacing x and y with embedding variables Vi and Vj connects the existing derivation to the model but does not introduce new assumptions or results.

improvement.justification: Tables 6–8 improve empirical completeness through additional metrics, another benchmark and broader component checks. However, removing the exact training configurations weakens reproducibility, and Figure 4 introduces a contradiction about the best loss weight. These concrete gains and losses leave the overall direction uncertain; the PDFs neither resolve the plotting inconsistency nor replace the removed replication information.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MOMOK framework and overlapping experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds FB15K-237 results, additional benchmark metrics and further ablations in Appendix C.3.

before.justification: v2 reports original link-prediction results on four MMKG benchmarks, alongside robustness experiments, ablations, efficiency measurements and case studies.

title: Multiple Heads are Better than One: Mixture of Modality Knowledge Experts for Entity Representation Learning

C1.justification: Section 1.2 drops the assertion that competing multi-token methods necessarily require sequence-to-sequence models; Remark 1 instead contrasts single-token with all-token prediction. This narrows one claimed distinction. The central reduction, discrete-language-diffusion performance, image-generation, and zero-shot infilling claims remain.

C2.justification: Section 4.1 newly contextualizes GGM’s competitiveness with Plaid through its smaller training corpus, OpenWebText versus OpenWebText2. Appendix H removes the stated convergence benefit of sampling multiple timesteps per example. The explanations involving image tokenizers, remaining state-of-the-art gaps, and FID limitations are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix H adds MDLM implementation and license information and revises training hyperparameters. It replaces the image-batch description of 512 examples times four timesteps with a batch size of 2048, leaving the decomposition unspecified. The rare-token suppression disclosure is removed, without establishing whether the heuristic was abandoned. Appendix J.2 newly specifies top-p 0.9 for its unconditional examples.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate OpenWebText language generation, CelebA-HQ and FFHQ image generation, and text/image infilling. Replacement illustrative examples retain these tasks. The new OpenWebText2 mention explains Plaid’s training background rather than introducing another evaluated dataset.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds MDLM as an evaluated language-generation comparator. The GPT2, BERT/Gibbs, Plaid, and SEDD comparisons remain, and Table 2 retains its image-generation comparator set.

E3.justification: Appendix H retunes existing experiments: language training changes from 1.96M steps with a 10M-step cosine schedule to 2M steps with a 2M-step schedule, and peak/final learning rates change from 5e-5/5e-8 to 1e-4/1e-6. FFHQ training increases from 2.44M to 3M steps, with decay extended from 2M to 3M. MDLM uses 170M parameters and 1000 sampling steps. Metrics, generation lengths, and evaluation sample counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix J.1 replaces the four illustrative text-infilling outputs and three corresponding prompts, revising the qualitative evidence for prefix/suffix consistency. The image-masking demonstrations, nearest-neighbor analysis, and design of the BERT sampling-step comparison are retained; no new systematic ablation or robustness study appears.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without experimental seed information, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars. The evaluation sample counts do not constitute repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces GGM perplexities 22.3/22.7/20.6 with 19.5/19.9/18.0 under GPT2-large/GPT2-xl/GPT-Neo evaluation and adds MDLM values 44.2/45.4/40.9. Table 2 changes FFHQ FID from 14.2 to 12.5 while retaining CelebA-HQ FID 9.8. These accompany revised training settings, not a controlled same-setting gain. Figure 2a is updated, and FFHQ and language samples are replaced; the principal findings remain similar.

M1.justification: Appendix G adapts Algorithm A3 from a constant noise distribution to time-varying retention probabilities, changing its inputs, cumulative probability calculation, and final noise draw. This is a limited extension of the direct forward sampler; the architecture, binary-classification objective, and main reverse and conditional procedures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: There are localized wording changes in the contributions, method comparison, results discussion, and Appendices G/H, plus a sampling-description sentence in Appendix J.2. The section organization and overall narrative remain stable; replacement generated passages are experimental outputs rather than extensive rewriting of the exposition.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains an MDLM row and explicit length/step entries for GPT2. Figure 2a is redrawn with a horizontal GGM reference line, and the FFHQ grids in Figures 2b and 8 contain replacement images. Figures 2–3 and Table 2 move within the results pages. The overall visual design and other figure contents remain stable.

R1.justification: v2 adds Gao et al.’s The Pile reference for the OpenWebText2 discussion and Sahoo et al.’s masked diffusion language model reference for MDLM. The existing references are retained, and the related-work survey is otherwise substantively stable. The sequence-to-sequence comparison is also narrowed.

T1.justification: Appendix G relaxes the constant-distribution assumption to constant token-noise proportions with time-varying retention probabilities and revises the associated derivation. It also corrects the prose’s replacement draw to the distribution conditioned on vocabulary tokens. Lemmas 1–3 and their proofs remain unchanged. The generalized overwrite probability still uses 1-product(1-Pi_s(phi)), inconsistent with Equation 1’s implied 1-product(Pi_s(phi)); the tested retention probability of 0.5 masks this discrepancy.

improvement.justification: The added MDLM comparison and clearer disclosures about Plaid’s training corpus and qualitative sampling modestly improve evidence and transparency. Lower GGM scores accompany revised training and do not establish a controlled version-to-version gain. Some inference detail is lost, and Appendix G’s attempted generalization retains a probability error. These limit the improvement, but the core proofs and experimentally used retention probability of 0.5 are unaffected.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Glauber Generative Model research. All 29 pages of each version, including Appendices A–J, are available and readable; text comparison and visual inspection support reliable matching.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and reports revised GGM scores, an additional MDLM comparison, and replacement language and image generations.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-generation perplexities, image-generation FID scores, and qualitative generation and infilling results in Tables 1–2, figures, and appendices.

title: Glauber Generative Model: Discrete Diffusion Models via Binary Classification

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and discussion retain the same claims about reduction to binary classification, language and image generation performance, and zero-shot infilling capabilities.

C2.justification: The interpretations concerning specialized tokenizers and potential performance improvements are unchanged. Both versions retain the same acknowledged performance gaps and Appendix I.2's caveats about FID and baseline preprocessing comparability.

D1.justification: Implementation, hardware, hyperparameter, tokenizer, training-time, and resource-access information remain unchanged. The deleted Algorithm 1 comment loses no unique implementation information because Appendix H.1 retains the explicit multiple-timestep setting.

E1.justification: Both versions retain OpenWebText language generation, CelebA-HQ and FFHQ image generation, and the same zero-shot text and image infilling scenarios, including Appendices C and J.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the same GPT2, BERT-large Gibbs sampling, Plaid, SEDD-medium, and MDLM comparators. Table 2 also retains the same image-generation comparator membership for each dataset.

E3.justification: Evaluation models, sampling settings, training budgets, and metric procedures remain unchanged, including 1,024 text generations and 50,000 images for FID. Although Algorithm 1 removes a multiple-timestep comment, Appendix H.1 still specifies 32 timesteps per language example.

E4.justification: The sampling-step comparison in Figure 2a, nearest-neighbor analysis in Appendix D, and conditional-generation case studies are unchanged. No ablations, robustness tests, or supplementary analyses are added or removed.

E5.justification: Both versions retain point estimates without reported independent-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Statistical reporting practices are unchanged.

E6.justification: All tabulated results, plotted findings, and generation examples are unchanged. GGM's Table 1 perplexities remain 19.5, 19.9, and 18.0; Table 2 FIDs remain 9.8 on CelebA-HQ and 12.5 on FFHQ.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, line 6 changes both log terms to negative terms, correcting the written loss to match Section 3.3's stated cross-entropy minimization. The architecture and sampling procedures remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish an implementation change or retraining.

P1.justification: v3 makes a few punctuation corrections, removes a redundant Algorithm 1 comment, and updates the arXiv version/date stamp. Section ordering, narrative structure, and appendix organization remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Figures 1-8 and Tables 1-2 retain their content, captions, structure, and placement. The localized textual and equation corrections cause only incidental reflow; there is no figure, table, or page-layout redesign.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion, reference list, and positioning against variational discrete diffusion and ratio-matching approaches are unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 corrects the formal definition of D_t,a to condition on the selected token being a, replacing the erroneous condition equating the remaining-token vector to a. Equation 3 also consistently uses the timestep-specific index. The existing proofs in Appendices A-B are unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 corrects the loss signs in Algorithm 1 and the conditioning event in Section 3.3, making the formal training specification more internally consistent and easier to implement faithfully. These corrections improve technical accuracy while the empirical evidence, claims, limitations, and appendices remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same GGM research work, with complete, readable main text and Appendices A-J. Text and rendered-page comparisons support reliable assessment of equations, tables, figures, and appendix material.

after.justification: v3 retains the original GGM experimental results in Tables 1-2 and the graphical and appendix generation examples.

before.justification: v2 reports original GGM language-generation perplexities, image-generation FID scores, and conditional and unconditional generation examples in the main text and appendices.

title: Glauber Generative Model: Discrete Diffusion Models via Binary Classification

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution section retain the same central reduction, performance and infilling claims. Section 5 modestly broadens its concluding statements about current performance limitations and future improvement from GGM specifically to discrete diffusion models generally.

C2.justification: Remark 2 adds an explanation, attributed to Zheng et al. (2024), connecting FP32 Gumbel-max truncation to effectively lower sampling temperatures in SEDD and MDLM. Appendix K interprets joint scaling as beneficial. v4 also removes v3's argument that planned non-release implies no tangible societal impact.

D1.justification: v4 removes the explicit statement that the authors do not intend to release the model publicly, without providing replacement access information. Detailed hyperparameters, hardware and baseline implementation references remain unchanged in v3 Appendix H and v4 Appendix I. This changes disclosure, without establishing changed availability.

E1.justification: Appendix K adds training on RedPajama for a preliminary language-generation scaling experiment. OpenWebText, CelebA-HQ, FFHQ and the existing infilling tasks remain; no additional application task is demonstrated.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in Tables 1–2 is unchanged. MDLM already appears in v3 Table 1 and Appendix H.3; its expanded discussion in v4 does not introduce a baseline. Appendix K adds no evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: Appendix K introduces an approximately 800M-parameter configuration evaluated using GPT2-xl, alongside the retained 387M-parameter experiment. Existing table protocols, metrics, sample counts and sampling settings remain unchanged. Remark 2 discusses published precision effects without documenting FP64 reruns of these comparisons.

E4.justification: Appendix K adds a preliminary check of improvement with increased model size and training data, reporting one additional configuration without separating the two factors. The existing iteration-count comparison, nearest-neighbor analysis and conditional-generation cases are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests for the experimental results. Existing averaging practices are unchanged, and the scaling result adds no uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Appendix K newly reports GPT2-xl generative perplexity of 16.7 for the approximately 800M-parameter RedPajama model. The original 387M-parameter OpenWebText result remains 19.9 under that evaluator; these are different settings. Tables 1–2, figure results and generation examples otherwise retain their findings.

M1.justification: The noising process, binary-classification loss, reverse sampler, conditional inference and transformer design are retained. The explanation of computing vocabulary predictions in one forward pass and the larger experimental configuration do not establish a changed method.

P1.justification: v4 makes localized explanatory edits, adds convergence and scaling subsections, removes the Societal Impact section, and updates affiliation, publication headers and citation style. Most prose and the overall narrative order are retained.

P2.justification: The ICLR template changes typography, table sizing and float placement. Figures 3–4 are grouped on page 10, and Figure 7 moves to a separate appendix page. Figures 1–8 retain the same artwork, and Tables 1–2 retain their comparison structure.

R1.justification: Section 1.1 adds a focused discussion and references on Glauber/Gibbs mixing and applications, and expands MDLM's relationship to D3PM. Remark 2 adds Zheng et al. (2024) on categorical sampling. The central positioning against previous discrete diffusion approaches remains intact.

T1.justification: Section 3.4 and Appendix C add a finite-step output-distribution convergence theorem under perfect classification, extending the original forward-mixing and exact-reversal lemmas. Appendix A changes the coupling bound from T(1−epsilon)^(T/L) to L(1−epsilon)^floor(T/L), also stated in Lemma 1. However, new Equation 9 prints a negative exponent inconsistent with that decaying bound.

improvement.justification: The revised mixing bound and explicit initialization-error analysis modestly strengthen the theoretical account, while the sampling caveat and preliminary scaling result add useful context. Gains are limited by Equation 9's sign inconsistency, sparse documentation of the scaling experiment and removal of the model-release disclosure. The original empirical evidence remains intact.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Glauber Generative Model work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v4 retains these original experiments and adds a preliminary language-generation scaling result in Appendix K.

before.justification: v3 reports original GGM language-generation perplexities and image-generation FIDs in Tables 1–2, alongside generated examples and nearest-neighbor analysis.

title: Glauber Generative Model: Discrete Diffusion Models via Binary Classification

C1.justification: V1 presents a specific SFNO architecture and limits applicability to non-factorized FNO. V2 claims an adaptation for any FNO variant, explicitly including factorized FNO, and newly promotes convex fine-tuning in the abstract and introduction. It also qualifies advantages over numerical solvers with 'under certain conditions'; the central hybrid-learning and large accuracy-improvement claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 explains padding's role in suppressing nonperiodic endpoint artifacts and reinterprets the McWilliams enstrophy spectrum as a k−3 direct cascade rather than the inverse cascade described in v1. It also acknowledges unsuccessful fine-tuning in the highest-Reynolds-number shifted scenario, adding an empirical applicability limit to the existing conditional-convergence caveats.

D1.justification: Appendix C.3 adds substantial reproduction information: generation grids, time steps, downsampling, warmup, 1024 training trajectories and training/testing snapshot construction. Appendix D.3 supplies the fine-tuning learning rate, and Table 6 specifies timing hardware and power controls. Conversely, Table 5 removes Taylor-Green model-size and mode details. Public code and data access already appeared in v1.

E1.justification: The original flow benchmarks remain, while Appendix D.4 adds evaluations with shifted initial-energy concentrations k0 = 2 and 8 and Reynolds numbers 5000 and 10000, substantially extending tested flow conditions. Appendix C.3 also changes the reported Example II forcing from mid-wavenumber forcing to no external force.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 2 remove their FNO3d baseline rows, and Table 3 removes FNO3d trained with the H−1 loss. New Table 6 evaluates FNO3d rollout and IMEX Runge-Kutta comparators, while Figure 13 introduces FNO(2+1)d rollout. These materially change comparator membership within the reported comparisons.

E3.justification: Added experiments use 15-epoch models, 512×512 or 1024×1024 evaluation grids, prediction-step correlation measurements and controlled timing protocols with specified horizons and sampling intervals. Appendix C.3 newly specifies RK4/implicit-Euler data generation, conflicting with the second-order description retained in Section 4.2. The PDFs do not establish whether retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained loss ablations, v2 adds distribution-shift and high-Reynolds-number robustness tests, a nonperiodic-padding comparison in Figure 7, and a prediction/fine-tuning case study in Figure 12. The earlier spectrum analysis is expanded into comparisons across training epochs, trajectories and time points in Figures 8–9.

E5.justification: V1 already reports fixed-seed training and a ten-seed spectrum experiment. V2 specifies seed 1127825, introduces mean-centered error bars of ±10 standard deviations in Figure 8, and reports runtime averages with ± values over 20 runs in Table 6. The runtime dispersion statistic is unspecified; increased training replication is not established.

E6.justification: Tables 6–7 and the new figures add timing, correlation and shifted-distribution results, including a post-fine-tuning L2 error of 2.355×10^6 in the Re = 10000 case. Table 3 changes reported FNO3d L2 errors from 0.0244 to 0.0432 at 10 epochs and from 0.0432 to 0.0387 at 100 epochs. Corresponding proposed-method numbers in Tables 1–3 are retained; the added evaluations are not same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: Section 2.2 revises the stated lifting operator from pointwise projection after time-depth convolution to a construction using projected positional encodings and learnable layer normalization. The central final-layer spectral fine-tuning procedure, negative-Sobolev loss and solver-derived time derivatives remain intact. Renaming SFNO to ST-FNO is not itself a method change.

P1.justification: The introduction is extensively rewritten and reorganizes motivations and contributions. Architecture and hybrid training become separate Sections 2 and 3, while mathematical and de-aliasing motivation moves to Appendix B. The title and SFNO/ST-FNO terminology change, and the lifting, projection and temporal-super-resolution explanations are substantially expanded.

P2.justification: V2 adds architecture diagrams, padding and shifted-flow visualizations, correlation plots, and runtime and robustness tables. The old spectrum figure is replaced and expanded, while v1 Figures 2–4 largely reappear as v2 Figures 4–6. Tables 1–2 become compact side-by-side displays, and the document adopts a substantially revised conference layout.

R1.justification: Appendix B adds comparisons with Bayesian residual correction, distinguishes the H−1 loss from Du et al.'s L2 spectral loss, and incorporates recent Transformer and state-space operator work. Some design-inspiration references, including ConvNeXt, are removed. These extend the existing research positioning without replacing its central operator-learning and numerical-analysis framework.

T1.justification: The principal residual bounds, norm-equivalence proof and local-convexity results are retained. Appendix B adds a Poisson-operator boundedness/stability argument for H−1 residual measurement, and the final convergence argument now specifies a linearly converging step size. The Pythagorean identity is relocated to Appendix B rather than newly introduced.

improvement.justification: The added generation details, timing evidence and shifted-distribution tests make the study easier to reproduce and its practical limits easier to assess, including a clearly reported failure. These gains are tempered by removed baseline comparisons and broader claims: applicability across FNO variants is not tested across architectures, and the new unqualified convexity claim is supported only by the retained local-convexity theory in Lemma E.8.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Spectral-Refiner research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–E are readable and support reliable matching across renaming, relocation and expansion.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark results and adds runtime measurements, spectral analyses and out-of-distribution turbulence evaluations, including unsuccessful fine-tuning.

before.justification: Sections 3.1–3.2, Tables 1–3 and Appendix D report original neural-operator training and fine-tuning results for Taylor-Green vortex and turbulent-flow simulations.

title: Spectral-Refiner: Accurate Fine-Tuning of Spatiotemporal Fourier Neural Operator for Turbulent Flows

C1.justification: The claims about temporal super-resolution, spectral fine-tuning, negative-Sobolev loss and accuracy remain the same. The revised contribution bullet's 'for the first time' wording repeats novelty already asserted in v2's abstract and Section 3.2.

C2.justification: Both versions retain the functional-norm motivation, sufficient-closeness qualifications, restriction to FNO-based architectures and interpretation of the failed high-Reynolds-number experiment. The solver clarification introduces no substantive new limitation or mechanism explanation.

D1.justification: Section 3.3 now explicitly identifies the fine-tuning solver as implicit-explicit, and Appendix B attributes its selection to Wang & Liu (2002) and Wang (2012). This adds implementation provenance; the hyperparameters, hardware and code/data access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use Taylor-Green vortex, forced turbulence and McWilliams decaying turbulence, including the same shifted initial-energy distributions and Reynolds-number scenarios in Appendix D.4.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in Tables 1, 3 and 6 and Figure 13, including PS+RK2, FNO3d, IMEX Runge-Kutta and FNO(2+1)d rollout. Newly cited neural operators are not added to the evaluated comparisons.

E3.justification: Section 4 and Appendices C–D retain the same data splits, grid resolutions, temporal sampling, training budgets, model configurations and metrics. The added IMEX identification does not document a revised experimental setting or rerun.

E4.justification: The loss-function ablations, residual visualizations, padding illustration, spectral-convergence analyses and distribution-shift tests are retained. Tables 2–3 and 7 and Figures 5–13 introduce no new analytical questions or evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same fixed seed in Appendix D.1, 20 runtime measurements in Table 6, and ten training seeds with error bars showing ten times the standard deviation in Figure 8. No statistical reporting practice changes.

E6.justification: The reported numerical results and plotted findings are unchanged. For example, Table 3 retains the fine-tuned L2 error of 2.88 × 10^-4, and Table 7 retains the Reynolds-number-10,000 failure with fine-tuned error 2.355 × 10^6.

M1.justification: The ST-FNO architecture, spectral fine-tuning objective and Algorithms 1–2 are unchanged. Correcting the single-step/multistep solver description and identifying the solver as IMEX clarify documentation without establishing a changed procedure.

P1.justification: Limited edits revise contribution bullets, correctly distinguish single-step RK4 from multistep solvers, clarify solver terminology and remove wording errors such as duplicated 'dealiasing.' The section organization and overall narrative are retained.

P2.justification: Figure 2 and Table 2 receive citation-year updates, while the expanded bibliography and Appendix B cause local page reflow. All thirteen figures and seven tables retain their graphics, axes, legends and structures.

R1.justification: Appendix B adds eight cited works covering neural operators, fluid modeling and numerical solvers, including Transolver, Prometheus and Wang & Liu (2002), without substantially changing the paper's positioning. The FNO citation's 2020-to-2021 update refers to the same work.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, error bounds and norm equivalence in Sections 2–3, derivations in Appendices B–C, and assumptions and proofs in Appendix E are retained. No mathematical correction or new theoretical result is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 corrects v2's classification of RK4 as a multistep solver, makes the fine-tuning solver's identity and provenance clearer, and modestly expands relevant literature coverage. These improve technical clarity and traceability. The experiments, results, theory and substantive limitations remain unchanged, so the overall gain is limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Spectral-Refiner study and contain the main text and Appendices A–E. Text extraction and visual inspection support reliable comparison of the equations, figures, tables and appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and their numerical and graphical results in Section 4 and Appendix D.

before.justification: v2 reports original Taylor-Green vortex and isotropic-turbulence experiments, including accuracy, runtime, ablation and distribution-shift results in Section 4 and Appendix D.

title: Spectral-Refiner: Accurate Fine-Tuning of Spatiotemporal Fourier Neural Operator for Turbulent Flows

C1.justification: The headline evidence changes from 69 detections and over 80% false-alarm reduction to 55 detections and a 5.21-percentage-point FDR advantage over CodeQL. v2 also claims six previously unknown vulnerabilities beyond existing tools' capabilities. Its novelty positioning is narrowed from being the first approach to being among the first.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly interprets filtering benefits as dependent on reasoning capability and acknowledges negative precision/F1 effects for smaller models. It adds the interpretation that inferred sinks can replace CodeQL sinks and extends v1's precision caveat into an upper-bound interpretation of benchmark FDR. Limitations add developer-report usability concerns while removing the earlier cost-amortization argument and detailed per-CWE ablation explanations.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the CodeQL throw/catch dataflow patch and its reference, describes a web interface for triage, and states that code and data accompany supplementary material with public release planned. Hardware, prompting hyperparameters, model API identifiers for retained configurations, and runtime results are otherwise retained. Actual resource availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: The 120-vulnerability Java benchmark and four CWE classes are retained. v2 additionally screens the latest versions of 30 Java projects for previously unknown vulnerabilities, extending evaluation from recovering known, localized vulnerabilities to discovery in projects without those ground-truth locations.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates CodeQL as the external baseline. v2 Table 2 additionally evaluates Facebook Infer, SpotBugs, and Snyk, reporting 0, 4, and 23 detected vulnerabilities respectively, alongside CodeQL's retained 27.

E3.justification: v2 reports complete-pipeline detection with project-averaged FDR and F1 on the 120-project benchmark; v1 separately evaluates filtering on 40 projects with three LLMs. The main comparison narrows from eight LLM configurations to five. Specification auditing changes from ten samples per source/sink role and CWE/LLM combination to a reported 960 labels. New protocols include inspecting 50 sampled alarms and screening current projects.

E4.justification: v2 replaces the contextual-analysis path-reduction table with precision/F1 effects across five LLMs, adds specification recall against CodeQL, expands manual specification auditing, and adds an alarm audit and an Alluxio case study. The source/sink ablation already existed in v1 Appendix C.5; v2 relocates and revises it in Section 5.5.

E5.justification: v2 adds sample-based estimation of alarm FDR through manual inspection of 50 randomly selected GPT-4 alarms, supplementing the existing sampled specification-precision estimates. Fixed-seed reporting remains unchanged, and neither version reports confidence intervals, repeated-run variability, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1 reports 69 GPT-4 detections before contextual filtering; v2 Table 1 reports 55 for the complete pipeline, with 84.82% FDR and 0.177 F1. These are different evaluation stages, not evidence of a same-setting deterioration. v2 also adds baseline and discovery results and revises specification-precision estimates. Appendix runtime and unique/recurring-specification values are retained.

M1.justification: The four-stage pipeline, candidate selection, prompts, specification conversion, and contextual filtering remain substantively unchanged. Appendix C.1 newly documents a CodeQL exception-flow patch, but the PDFs do not establish that this implementation detail was introduced between versions.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution summary, evaluation narrative, and conclusion are substantially rewritten.
