Section 5 is reorganized from three research questions to four, contextual analysis becomes an ablation topic, and source/sink ablations move into the main text. Appendix material is reorganized, including a separate runtime appendix.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the overview and pipeline diagrams, removes Figure 2's prompt panels, restructures detection reporting into overall and per-CWE tables, and adds recall, filtering-effect, discovery-case, and interface figures. The metric illustration is redrawn. Existing candidate statistics and runtime tables are relocated and renumbered, rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v2 adds the SpotBugs-related reference by Lavazza, Tosi, and Morasca. Section 6 explicitly relates IRIS to the already-cited LLM-integrated static-analysis work by Haonan Li and colleagues and softens the first-of-its-kind positioning. Most related-work coverage is unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3.6 expands the binary detection definition into task-specific vulnerable-path counts, project precision/recall, and aggregate FDR/F1 definitions, including averaging domains and discussion of empty outputs. The underlying taint-analysis formalization remains unchanged; neither version adds theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 makes the central detection/false-alarm tradeoff more assessable through complete-pipeline FDR/F1 results, broader baselines, and ablations exposing smaller-model weaknesses. This improves on v1's reliance on detection totals and path-count reductions. However, precision still uses a fix-location proxy, and the abstract overstates six potential discoveries despite Appendix Table 7 reporting zero developer confirmations. These qualifications limit the net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe IRIS and CWE-Bench-Java. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across revisions and relocations.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark comparisons, specification and filtering analyses, and an additional investigation of potentially unknown vulnerabilities.

before.justification: v1 reports original vulnerability-detection experiments, contextual-filtering results, specification-quality measurements, and appendix ablations and runtime results.

title: IRIS: LLM-Assisted Static Analysis for Detecting Security Vulnerabilities

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction reduce the claimed number of previously unknown vulnerabilities from six to four, and the introduction changes the stated LLM count from eight to seven. The central neuro-symbolic contribution, 120-vulnerability benchmark, and GPT-4 result of 55 detections versus CodeQL's 27 remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendices A.3 and C.7 add context-length cost/accuracy reasoning and more specific explanations of detection failures. Conversely, v3 removes the qualification that newly reported vulnerabilities await developer confirmation, without supplying replacement confirmation evidence. The conclusion's general limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: V3 replaces the supplementary-material/future-release statement with reported public code and dataset access links, adds the two new model IDs, and documents S=10 with segmented path sampling that favors function calls. The five-line context window was already specified in v2. Documentation of the custom triage interface and vulnerability-reporting process is removed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 120 Java vulnerabilities across CWE-22, CWE-78, CWE-79, and CWE-94, plus the investigation of 30 projects for unknown vulnerabilities. Additional model configurations and error discussion do not introduce new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluated static-analysis comparators remain CodeQL, Facebook Infer, SpotBugs, and Snyk, with unchanged membership in the corresponding comparisons. The additional LLMs are configurations of IRIS rather than new competing detection methods.

E3.justification: Table 1 adds IRIS evaluations with Qwen-2.5-Coder 32B and Gemma-2 27B. Appendix C.1 stops listing DeepSeekCoder 33B, Mistral 7B, and Gemma 7B, for which v2 supplied no separate result rows. Dataset size, metrics, CodeQL version, and decoding settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix C.7 adds qualitative error analysis, including CVE-2020-11977 and failures involving missing dataflow connections or specifications. This supplies a concrete missed-vulnerability example without a quantified error breakdown. Existing source/sink ablations, contextual-analysis comparisons, and specification analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the fixed-seed statement for GPT models and the same manual sampling descriptions. Neither introduces additional repeated-run reporting, confidence intervals, or significance testing; the added model rows follow the existing reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds Qwen-2.5-Coder results of 47 detections, 92.38% FDR, and 0.097 F1, and Gemma-2 results of 45 detections, 91.23% FDR, and 0.100 F1. Existing rows remain unchanged. Section 5.3 changes six potential unknown vulnerabilities, four reported, to four vulnerabilities and corrects CWE-94's description to code injection. V2's detailed alert/report/confirmation statistics are removed.

M1.justification: The four-stage IRIS procedure and prompt/query listings are retained. Appendix A.3 explains existing prompting and path truncation choices, including previously unspecified sampling details; it does not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: V3 adds IRIS to the title, acknowledgments, localized prose revisions, and author-year citations. Appendix subsections are added and reorganized, while the unknown-vulnerability appendix subsection is removed. The main section order and most explanatory prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V3 adopts ICLR headers and typography, adjusts figure/table placement and listing layout, expands Tables 1 and 6, and reformats Table 5. V2's Table 7 and interface screenshot, Figure 11, are removed. Figures 1–10 and most existing table structures are retained.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds an explicit comparison with InspectJS and references to Hoppity, general query engines, and LLMDFA, while removing the AutoCodeRover/SWE-Agent discussion. These locally broaden positioning without changing the main whole-project neuro-symbolic contribution. Bibliographic corrections and citation-style changes are not substantive additions.

T1.justification: The graph, taint-specification, unsanitized-path, and evaluation-metric definitions remain substantively identical. Notation corrections and revised explanations introduce no new mathematical assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

improvement.justification: The documented path-sampling procedure, public artifact access information, and concrete failure analysis make IRIS easier to reproduce and assess; Table 1 also extends evidence across model configurations. These are incremental gains to an otherwise stable paper. They are partly offset by removal of v2's pending-confirmation disclosure and status table, which makes the revised four-vulnerability claim less transparent.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IRIS system and CWE-Bench-Java study. All 24 pages of each version, including figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–D, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains these original empirical results and adds results for two further IRIS model configurations.

before.justification: V2 reports original vulnerability-detection experiments, manual specification assessments, component ablations, and runtime measurements.

title: IRIS: LLM-Assisted Static Analysis for Detecting Security Vulnerabilities

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes achieving leading results without synthetic data. V2 makes data curation, including synthetic generation and example-based labeling, an explicit contribution and claims sustained leadership across two model releases. It also adds claims of leading clustering/classification performance and generalization to AIR-Bench, extending the original MTEB-centered contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of reversed-stage training trade-offs and latent specialization for review sentiment. Appendix A argues that MTEB improvements need not transfer to out-of-domain retrieval, illustrating this with the SFR models, while interpreting NV-Embed's AIR-Bench results as generalization evidence. These extend the earlier pooling and attention explanations.

D1.justification: V2 documents the mining teacher and cutoff, synthetic generator and prompt templates, uniform training-data sampling, and optimizer restarts between stages. Training counts and instruction tables are revised and expanded. The abstract changes from promising an NV-Embed-v1 release to reporting an NV-Embed-v2 release with a different model link; actual external availability is not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: V2 retains the 56-task MTEB evaluation but adds AIR-Bench evaluation on eight English QA and fifteen long-document datasets, including law and book domains. Training expands through additional retrieval, classification and clustering datasets and 120,000 synthetic examples spanning 60,000 tasks (Sections 4.1–4.3 and Appendix A).

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Bge-en-icl, Stella-1.5B-v5, SFR-Embedding-2R, Gte-Qwen2-7B-instruct and Bge-multilingual-gemma2, while removing Gte-Qwen1.5, Voyage-lite, Google-gecko and LLM2Vec from that comparison. The detailed per-dataset comparator set also changes, and AIR-Bench comparisons introduce Linq-Embed-Mistral.

E3.justification: Reported warm-up steps change from 500 to 50. Training sample counts change substantially, including NLI from 20k to 270k and PAQ from 100k to 500k, and several training/evaluation instructions change. V2 introduces single-stage/reversed-stage controls and AIR-Bench protocols using nDCG@10 and Recall@10. The reported sequence limit, batch size and stage budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The original attention/pooling ablations survive in v2 Table 2. New analyses test single-stage versus two-stage and reversed-stage training, label-based versus example-based supervision, and incremental effects of negative mining, additional public data and synthetic data (Tables 3–5). Appendix C adds a review-sentiment latent-attention case study, and Appendix A examines out-of-domain generalization.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. The added experiments continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: V2 retains NV-Embed-v1's 69.32 MTEB and 59.36 retrieval scores and adds NV-Embed-v2 scores of 72.31 and 62.65 under revised training and instructions. These are distinct model configurations, not an isolated same-setting architectural gain. New ablation and AIR-Bench results include 52.28 QA and 74.78 long-document averages. Some original per-dataset baseline and ablation entries are replaced in Table 11.

M1.justification: Sections 4.1–4.3 introduce E5-Mistral positive-aware negative mining, replacing the earlier encoder-based/BM25 procedures, and use sampled examples instead of label texts for selected multiclass and clustering tasks. V2 also adds Mixtral synthetic-data generation and STS document-side instructions. The latent-attention architecture and two-stage training framework remain.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the architecture and training exposition remain intact. V2 revises the abstract, contribution list and conclusion, adds data-curation and ablation subsections, expands the appendix organization and adds acknowledgments. These are targeted narrative revisions accompanying the scientific additions.

P2.justification: V1 Tables 2–3 are merged into v2 Table 2. V2 adds several ablation and AIR-Bench tables, synthetic-generation prompt tables and the attention heatmap in Figure 2. The detailed benchmark table moves to the appendix with substantially different columns, and the document adopts ICLR formatting. Figure 1 remains materially unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 expands positioning around data curation and reproducibility, discussing Linq-Embed, explicitly adopting NV-Retriever's mining technique, and contrasting Bge-en-icl's few-shot training with zero-shot evaluation. It also discusses newer competitors' limited disclosure and adds references supporting the expanded datasets and methods.

T1.justification: Section 4.1.1 newly defines the negative-score cutoff as the positive score multiplied by a percentage margin, set to 0.95. This is a limited mathematical selection-rule addition. The latent-attention equation and associated definitions remain unchanged, and neither version contains theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the training recipe: Tables 4–5 directly test training order and data-curation choices that v1 did not isolate, while AIR-Bench adds generalization evidence beyond MTEB. Expanded procedural documentation also improves reproducibility. These gains outweigh reduced per-dataset ablation detail and documentation errors, notably Table 9's Medrxiv instructions for Reddit/StackExchange. Uncertainty reporting remains absent, limiting confidence in small score differences.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NV-Embed and contain matching architecture descriptions and original experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds NV-Embed-v2 results, training and data-curation ablations, AIR-Bench evaluations and an attention visualization.

before.justification: V1 reports original MTEB/BEIR evaluations and experiments comparing attention masks and pooling methods in Tables 1–4.

title: NV-Embed: Improved Techniques for Training LLMs as Generalist Embedding Models

C1.justification: The abstract adds model-compression analysis, and the introduction adds a fifth contribution claiming superior accuracy and quantization robustness relative to embeddings built directly on smaller LLMs. This materially expands the contribution scope beyond the retained architecture, training, data-curation and benchmark claims.

C2.justification: Appendix A adds explanations of N:M sparsity's hardware suitability, INT8 versus FP8 representation tradeoffs, and distillation as compensation for removing latent attention. Existing interpretations of pooling, training order and AIR-Bench generalization are retained.

D1.justification: Compression documentation adds the parameter-reduction target, sparsity patterns, GPTQ selection, INT8/E4M3/E5M2 formats and LoRA recovery approach. Original hyperparameters, sample counts, instruction templates and model-access information are preserved. Moving the original experimental setup into Appendix C does not itself add reproducibility information.

E1.justification: The public and synthetic training-data coverage, 56 MTEB tasks, and AIR-Bench's eight English QA and fifteen long-document datasets are retained. The new compression experiments reuse MTEB without introducing different datasets, domains or task requirements.

E2.justification: The compression study adds evaluated embedding baselines built on Llama3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-3B and Minitron-4B in Table 8. Table 6 also compares magnitude-based, WANDA and SparseGPT pruning. The original MTEB and AIR-Bench comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: Appendix A adds experiments with a reported 8B-to-3.5B compression target, 2:4/4:8/unstructured sparsity, retraining and distillation controls, and 16-bit, INT8 and two FP8 formats. These introduce substantial new experimental configurations. Original training budgets, sample counts, instructions and sequence-length settings are unchanged.

E4.justification: New Tables 6–8 examine pruning-method and sparsity sensitivity, accuracy recovery through retraining, the contribution of distillation, and robustness to reduced numerical precision. This adds a substantial compression-analysis component. Earlier architectural, training and data ablations, including the latent-attention visualization, are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or formal significance tests. The new quantization percentage differences describe changes in scores, not statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: Tables 6–8 add extensive compression results, including MTEB scores of 70.41 with ground-truth retraining versus 71.17 with added distillation for 2:4 pruning. Separately, v2 Table 11 becomes v3 Table 14 and swaps NV-Embed-v2's Touche2020 and TREC-COVID scores: 88.44/31.78 becomes 31.78/88.44. The headline 72.31 MTEB score and AIR-Bench results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Appendix A introduces a compressed NV-Embed procedure absent from v2: pruning decoder weights, removing latent attention, quantizing weights and recovering accuracy through LoRA retraining with teacher–student distillation. This substantially extends the architecture and training procedure; the original uncompressed method remains intact.

P1.justification: The experimental-setup subsection moves from the main text into Appendix C, a compression appendix and fifth contribution are added, and the conclusion is shortened. Most existing prose is retained, with limited wording edits and updated cross-references rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v3 adds compact tables for pruning, distillation and quantization, and relocates existing figures and tables. Both figure images are unchanged, and existing table structures are largely preserved. The changes extend and rearrange the displays without a broad visual redesign.

R1.justification: v3 adds references and discussion for SparseGPT, WANDA and GPTQ to situate the compression experiments. The main related-work section and positioning against existing embedding models are otherwise retained.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 newly defines a distillation loss matching intermediate and output teacher–student states, plus the combined contrastive-and-distillation objective. This is a limited addition of mathematical definitions; the earlier equations are retained and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: Appendix A adds useful evidence about compression choices and distillation-based recovery that v2 lacked, while preserving the original experimental evidence. The gains are limited by incomplete compression-retraining and smaller-baseline details, plus reporting inconsistencies: Table 8 labels the decline from 71.17 to 71.14 as a positive 0.03% change. The revision therefore adds practical analytical value, but its new claims are not documented precisely enough to establish a major overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NV-Embed work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across relocations and renumbering, including the new compression appendix in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds pruning, knowledge-distillation and quantization results in Appendix A, Tables 6–8.

before.justification: v2 reports original NV-Embed results on MTEB and AIR-Bench, alongside experiments on pooling, attention masks, training stages and data curation.

title: NV-Embed: Improved Techniques for Training LLMs as Generalist Embedding Models

C1.justification: The central claims of contrastively aligning images, DNA and taxonomy for seen/unseen species classification remain. The abstract reduces the claimed zero-shot accuracy advantage from over 11% to over 8%. The introduction and conclusion more explicitly foreground DNA as a better alignment target than taxonomic text when labels are scarce.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking DNA's advantage to sparse species labels, attention patterns to successful insect recognition, and encoder prealignment to image-to-text performance. It argues that simple classifiers can make BZSL's complexity unnecessary and discusses accuracy–resource tradeoffs. The conclusion newly makes the two-dataset and CLIP-style-training limitations explicit, alongside the persistent cross-modal performance gap.

D1.justification: Implementation reporting expands substantially: v2 specifies bfloat16 AMP, the learning-rate schedule, alternative encoder checkpoints, attention-rollout blocks 2–6, and measured memory use and training times. Reported hardware changes from two to four 80GB A100 GPUs. Appendix A adds detailed class-overlap and sample statistics, while the earlier LoRA projection and parameter-count details are omitted.

E1.justification: BIOSCAN-1M and INSECT remain the experimental datasets; BIOSCAN-5M is discussed without being evaluated. Retrieval-scenario coverage narrows slightly: v1 Table 9 evaluates DNA queries against image references, whereas v2 reports DNA queries only against DNA references. Image-query classification and the seen/unseen-species tasks remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds explicit majority/chance baselines in Table 7 and OpenCLIP-based image/text encoder comparisons in Table 11. The principal existing comparators—BioCLIP, BZSL, CNN DNA encoder, DNABERT-2 and BarcodeBERT—remain, so this is a targeted extension rather than wholesale replacement.

E3.justification: Main training changes from 15 epochs, batch size 800 and learning rate 0.001 to 50 epochs, batch size 2000, a one-cycle schedule spanning 1e-6 to 5e-5, and AMP. BioCLIP and threshold-based IS+DU evaluations move from validation to test, while thresholds remain tuned on validation; v1 already contained test retrieval results. Figure 2 also revises reported seen test-query/key counts from 6878/6530 to 4878/6350 despite retaining the Appendix A partitioning rule.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's modality, key-type and batch-size studies, v2 adds encoder/prealignment comparisons, temperature, AMP and LoRA-versus-full-fine-tuning ablations (Tables 11 and 14–16). It adds attention success/failure cases and compares UMAP embeddings across alignment configurations. The batch-size study is revised, while the averaged-image/DNA-key analysis is removed.

E5.justification: v1 provides no training-run variability reporting. v2 Appendix B.1 and Figure 9 newly report four random-seed training runs for the full trimodal model, with means and shaded uncertainty across retrieval settings and taxonomic levels. The uncertainty definition remains ambiguous: the text says standard deviation, while the caption says standard error.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and supplemented. For example, reported test-set species image-to-image macro harmonic mean for I+D+T changes from 32.4% in v1 Table 8 to 51.2% in v2 Table 1; the best aligned-encoder INSECT harmonic mean changes from 38.1% to 35.0% (v1 Table 6; v2 Table 4). These concern revised training/settings, not controlled cross-version gains or losses. New ablation results appear, while DNA-to-image and averaged-key entries disappear.

M1.justification: v1 trains the encoders through LoRA and fixes the contrastive temperature at 0.07. v2 uses full fine-tuning and learns the temperature initialized at 0.07 (Section 3.1; Appendix C). This substantially changes the optimized parameters, while retaining the encoder families, symmetric trimodal contrastive loss and nearest-neighbor retrieval framework.

P1.justification: Beyond renaming BIOSCAN-CLIP to CLIBD, v2 substantially rewrites the introduction, related work and experimental narrative. It creates a dedicated analysis subsection, consolidates cross-modal/BZSL discussion, moves classifier details into Appendix B.2, and organizes implementation ablations in a new Appendix C.

P2.justification: v2 switches from two-column to single-column layout and extensively restructures tables around query/key combinations, separating macro and micro results. Retrieval examples become a combined three-mode display, UMAP expands from one plot to four panels, and attention and uncertainty figures are added. The split and class-distribution diagrams are also revised.

R1.justification: Section 2 removes the broad fine-grained multimodal survey, including discussions of methods such as ImageBind, BLIP and CLOOB, and refocuses positioning on biological classification, DNA representations and label scarcity. New cited work includes MycoAI, BIOSCAN-5M and environmental-DNA/remote-sensing research. The BioCLIP publication update refers to the same retained work.

T1.justification: The symmetric contrastive-loss equations and trimodal sum remain mathematically equivalent. However, v2 removes v1 Section 3.1's explicit LoRA weight factorization and parameter-count argument, retaining only an empirical LoRA comparison. This is a limited reduction in mathematical method detail; neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical credibility: threshold-based IS+DU results are evaluated on test data rather than the validation set used for tuning, four-seed reporting addresses previously undocumented variability, and controlled ablations support important training choices. Added failure cases and explicit limitations improve interpretation. Removed retrieval analyses and reporting inconsistencies, particularly Figure 9's standard-deviation/standard-error ambiguity, temper these gains, but the stronger validation and supporting evidence establish a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same image–DNA–taxonomy alignment work, renamed from BIOSCAN-CLIP to CLIBD. All 16 pages of v1 and 25 pages of v2, including their appendices, provide readable text, equations, tables and figures sufficient for comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on both datasets, including revised classification results, additional ablations and four-seed training variability.

before.justification: v1 reports original BIOSCAN-1M retrieval experiments, INSECT zero-shot classification results, and modality and batch-size analyses.

title: CLIBD: Bridging Vision and Genomics for Biodiversity Monitoring at Scale

C1.justification: The abstract narrows the first-use claim from contrastive fusion of DNA and images generally to barcode DNA and images. The conclusion explicitly adds the benefit of scarce text-encoded taxonomic labels. The central multimodal-alignment and zero-shot claims, including the over-8% statement, remain.

C2.justification: Appendix D substantially expands applicability limits: laboratory-to-field transfer, barcode errors and hybridization, limited barcode coverage, and the mismatch between held-out species and truly undiscovered species. It also explains expert verification and deployment boundaries. Elsewhere, v4 interprets the SimCLR controls, emphasizes trimodal attention interpretability, and discusses BZSL tuning sensitivity.

D1.justification: v4 adds the SimCLR augmentation recipe, clarifies barcode-pretraining provenance and non-overlap, and describes BZSL validation tuning using the original search space with roughly four hours of search. Appendix D.4 supplies tokenization, parameter, runtime and storage details. Core implementation settings and the project-access link are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate insect taxonomic classification and retrieval using BIOSCAN-1M and INSECT. New experiments retain this coverage. Field imagery, other biological applications and larger datasets are discussed but are not newly evaluated.

E2.justification: v4 adds a SimCLR-trained image-only baseline to Tables 1 and 8–10, and ImageBind-style alternatives that align DNA with frozen BioCLIP image/text encoders in Table 12. These substantially broaden comparisons with alternative learning strategies. Existing BioCLIP, BZSL and encoder comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: New supplementary experiments introduce SimCLR augmentation/initialization controls and frozen-encoder configurations. Appendix D.4 adds computational profiling with batches of 500 and storage analysis of 84,450 records. Existing benchmark splits, top-1 metrics, main training budget and threshold-selection procedure remain unchanged; the added BZSL tuning description does not establish a protocol revision.

E4.justification: New experiments test whether gains exceed image-only domain adaptation, whether SimCLR initialization helps, and whether DNA-only alignment to frozen encoders suffices. Appendix B.4 adds retrieved-neighbor evidence to existing attention examples, while Appendix D.4 adds resource analyses. The earlier temperature, AMP, LoRA, batch-size and larger-encoder analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions already report four random-seed training runs and the same Figure 9 mean curves with shaded uncertainty. v4 adds no new repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: v4 adds SimCLR, initialization, frozen-alignment, broader BioCLIP and resource results. For retained settings, Table 2 changes trimodal image-to-text harmonic-mean accuracy from 10.2% to 8.9%. Table 4 changes fine-tuned BarcodeBERT/CLIBD-I from 23.8% to 31.2%, and CLIBD-D/RN-101 without fine-tuning from 29.3% to 26.4%. These are revised reported values; the best INSECT harmonic mean remains 35.0%.

M1.justification: The core three-encoder contrastive objective and retrieval/IS+DU inference procedures remain unchanged. Appendix B.1.1 adds an optional CLIBD training variant that performs image-only SimCLR pretraining before joint multimodal alignment, introducing a limited additional training stage.

P1.justification: The main six-section organization and most existing exposition remain recognizable. v4 makes localized terminology and paragraph revisions, rewrites the conclusion, subdivides Appendix B.1, and switches to numerical citations. Appendix D adds a dedicated discussion without extensively reorganizing the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v4 adopts the ICLR page format, redraws the partition diagram and class-size plots, replaces Figure 3 retrieval examples, and expands comparison tables. Existing attention examples are regrouped across Figures 11–13 with added nearest-retrieval images, and Figure 14 introduces a modality overview. These are substantial display and layout revisions.

R1.justification: v4 explicitly acknowledges earlier image/genetics and histology contrastive work, including ContIG and studies by Xie and Min, and distinguishes CLIBD through barcode-based taxonomy. It also adds positioning against SimCLR and ImageBind and substantially expands biological grounding through literature on barcode limitations, repositories and applications.

T1.justification: The symmetric pairwise contrastive losses and their three-modality sum are mathematically unchanged; image-embedding notation changes from X to V. Neither version supplies theoretical results or proofs that are added or revised in v4.

improvement.justification: The added controls strengthen attribution of gains to cross-modal learning, while the narrower novelty claim and Appendix D improve scientific qualification and practical context. The established evaluation remains largely intact. Reporting is still imperfect: new Table 13 lists a genus image-to-text row with 81.9% for both seen and unseen accuracy but a 29.7% harmonic mean. Overall, the evidence supports a useful, limited improvement in rigor and clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CLIBD, with matching authors, core methodology and datasets. Their readable text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v4 retains original experiments and adds SimCLR and frozen-encoder comparisons, further training-strategy experiments, and computational/storage measurements.

before.justification: v2 reports original BIOSCAN-1M retrieval/classification experiments, INSECT zero-shot classification results, ablations and qualitative analyses.

title: CLIBD: Bridging Vision and Genomics for Biodiversity Monitoring at Scale

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions: aligning images, DNA barcodes and taxonomic text, improving classification representations, and enabling cross-modal retrieval. The added pooling analysis does not redefine or strengthen these core claims.

C2.justification: Existing interpretations and Appendix D limitations concerning barcode reliability, laboratory imagery and real-world deployment are retained. Appendix C.5 summarizes measured pooling rankings but adds no separate causal explanation or revised applicability boundary.

D1.justification: Section 3.1 and Appendix C.5 newly specify image CLS-token extraction, text mean pooling and projection, and the DNA prediction-head modification from 1027 to 768 outputs. They explicitly identify FFN+softmax+mean as the main configuration. These additions improve implementation disclosure; access information is unchanged.

E1.justification: BIOSCAN-1M and INSECT coverage, taxonomic classification tasks and retrieval scenarios are retained. The new pooling experiments reuse the BIOSCAN-1M test set and existing query/key combinations, adding no dataset, population or task scenario.

E2.justification: Tables 21–22 add three internal comparison variants against the main FFN+softmax+mean configuration: hidden-state mean pooling, CLS-token pooling and FFN+mean. Existing comparisons with SimCLR, BioCLIP, BZSL and other encoders are unchanged.

E3.justification: Section 5 changes the stated main training duration from 50 to 30 epochs, retaining the batch size, hardware and optimizer settings. Appendix C.5 adds comparisons across DNA output configurations under existing evaluation metrics. The PDFs do not establish whether the epoch revision reflects rerunning experiments or correcting their description.

E4.justification: New Appendix C.5 tests how four DNA embedding constructions affect DNA-to-DNA, image-to-image and image-to-DNA retrieval across taxonomic levels. This adds a focused component ablation; the existing temperature, precision, LoRA, batch-size and supplementary analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix B.1 and Figure 9 retain the four-random-seed analysis and existing uncertainty reporting. The new pooling tables do not introduce additional run-count disclosures, uncertainty estimates or statistical tests.

E6.justification: Tables 21–22 add pooling-specific results. For example, Table 21 reports species image-to-image macro harmonic means of 52.5% for hidden-state mean pooling and 51.2% for the default. Retained tables keep their scores. Some newly reported default micro scores differ from retained Table 8: species DNA-to-DNA harmonic mean is 97.1% versus 97.3%, without an explanation of whether runs differ.

M1.justification: The proposed encoders, contrastive objective and retrieval procedures remain unchanged. Appendix C.5 identifies FFN+softmax+mean as the configuration used for the main experiments and evaluates alternatives; it documents the existing implementation without establishing a replacement of the main method.

P1.justification: v5 adds a short embedding-construction paragraph, Appendix C.5 and an expanded Appendix C overview. It locally reorganizes appendix text around the attention figures, makes small wording edits and removes the conference-publication header. The overall narrative and section hierarchy remain stable.

P2.justification: v5 adds the pooling schematic as Figure 14 and results Tables 21–22. The previous modalities overview becomes Figure 15, with small label edits and relocation beside Appendix D. Existing appendix figures and tables are locally repositioned, and Table 9 gains two missing not-applicable dashes.

R1.justification: The same 81 cited works and research positioning are retained. Changes to the BioCLIP reference concern author-name and bibliographic formatting, not a different cited work or relationship to prior research.

T1.justification: The contrastive-loss equations and inference definitions are unchanged. The new pooling diagrams and tensor-shape descriptions explain implementation rather than introducing formal assumptions, theoretical results or mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: Appendix C.5 clarifies previously unspecified embedding construction and supplies useful evidence about pooling sensitivity, improving reproducibility and empirical understanding. These are limited gains to otherwise stable work. Their value is tempered by the unexplained 50-to-30-epoch revision and discrepancies between the default micro scores in Tables 22 and 8.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CLIBD study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v5 retains these original experiments and adds DNA embedding ablation results in Appendix C.5, Tables 21–22.

before.justification: v4 reports original classification and retrieval experiments on BIOSCAN-1M and INSECT, together with ablations, visual analyses and training-resource measurements.

title: CLIBD: Bridging Vision and Genomics for Biodiversity Monitoring at Scale

C1.justification: The central contribution remains interpretable closed-loop experiment design without task-specific model training or an explicit acquisition function. The abstract and introduction now anchor performance claims to Claude 3.5 Sonnet, reporting 21% and 46% improvements instead of 18% and 29%, and describe gene-pair performance as more than twice random.

C2.justification: v1 presents All-Tools as consistently advantageous. v2 substantially qualifies this interpretation: tools benefit some backbones but hurt others. It introduces the hypothesis that larger models already contain information supplied by tools, using token price as a size proxy and prediction overlap as supporting evidence. Existing cell-type and early-round limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds feature provenance and database-specific retrieval details. Model identities and token prices are documented, and a new reproducibility statement specifies prompt/data distribution and offers anonymized CAR-T data upon request. The code link, prompts, pseudocode, and complete agent trace are retained.

E1.justification: The perturbation benchmarks and biological tasks remain unchanged; Steinhart is renamed CAR-T, and six evaluation columns already existed in v1. v2 adds ARCHS4 expression/tissue data and KEGG/Reactome pathways as information sources in evaluated retrieval variants (Appendix D, Table 5), modestly expanding supporting data coverage.

E2.justification: The same random, GeneDisco, and DiscoBax comparators remain in the single-gene comparisons, and random sampling remains the gene-pair comparator. The additional language models are configurations of BioDiscoveryAgent rather than new external baselines.

E3.justification: Evaluation expands from Claude v1 to nine language-model configurations. The new Sonnet observation ablation measures between-run Jaccard similarity after 30 rounds, while the original 10-round comparison remains in the appendix. Appendix D also changes the stated dissimilar-search retrieval count from 50 to 10. Core benchmark budgets and hit-ratio evaluation remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1's individual-tool Claude v1 ablations are replaced by Haiku/Sonnet analyses, broader comparisons of tool effects across models, and six gene-search variants. New Figure 7 examines overlap between tool-assisted and unaided predictions. A Sonnet observation ablation supplements the original Claude v1 analysis, retained as Figure 8 and Table 9.

E5.justification: Most benchmarks retain ten-run, one-standard-deviation reporting. The new main observation ablation uses eight runs, while the original ten-run analysis remains in the appendix. Standard deviations previously reported for Claude v1 All-Tools in v1 Table 5 are absent from the corresponding v2 Table 8 entries.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive model and tool results. Table 2 replaces the original agent's 32.67 round-five hits with 45.1 for Haiku and 40.0 for Sonnet 3.5; these use different backbones. Tool results now include substantial negative effects. Some overlapping entries conflict: v2 Table 6 reports Claude v1/Sanchez as 0.058, while Table 1 retains v1's 0.053.

M1.justification: The gene-search component expands substantially from feature-based similarity/dissimilarity to expression-, tissue-, and pathway-based retrieval, with Reactome enrichment becoming the principal approach (Section 3.1, Appendix D). The overall prompting, feedback, and critic pipeline remains unchanged, including Algorithm 1.

P1.justification: The seven main sections and appendices A-F remain, with much prose and the complete trace preserved. Changes include focused results rewrites and reordering, expanded tool explanations, updated authorship and terminology, and new ethics and reproducibility statements.

P2.justification: Table 1 combines all-gene and non-essential results and introduces grouped model rows. Tool tables gain model panels and percentage annotations, and new cost and retrieval comparisons are added. The workflow and original observation figure move to the appendix, while new observation and overlap figures appear. Document typography and layout also change.

R1.justification: Related work adds biological benchmarks and explicitly distinguishes BioDiscoveryAgent's iterative hypothesis selection from CRISPR-GPT's individual experiment design. Additional citations document newer models, biological databases, and scientific agents. The original positioning around closed-loop biological experiment design remains.

T1.justification: New Figure 7 defines a set-overlap fraction measuring how many tool-added Haiku predictions appear in unaided Sonnet predictions. The single-gene and gene-pair formulations and hit-ratio definition remain unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: The broader model evaluation strengthens evidence beyond Claude v1 and replaces a broadly positive tool-use conclusion with useful model-dependent findings. The net gain is limited by reporting problems: v2 Tables 1 and 6 disagree on Claude v1/Sanchez, and Figure 3 does not support the text's claimed late-round advantage of Observation Only over Prompt Only. The proposed model-size explanation also remains tentative.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BioDiscoveryAgent. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support comparison; renamed datasets and relocated analyses can be matched.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds evaluations across language models, tool configurations, and prediction-overlap analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrospective closed-loop experiments on single-gene and gene-pair perturbation datasets, including baseline comparisons and ablations.

title: BioDiscoveryAgent: An AI Agent for Designing Genetic Perturbation Experiments

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and discussion retain the same central contributions and claims, including 21% and 46% improvements, combinatorial performance exceeding twice the random baseline, and interpretability. The added evaluations do not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: V3 adds practical tool-use recommendations in Appendix D.1, a prediction-confidence hypothesis for differing tool benefits, and interpretations of hybrid performance. Appendix F attributes modest Haiku tool costs to fewer interaction turns. Existing limitations remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: V3 documents the Human baseline's initialization and enrichment procedure, including pathway identifiers in Table 6, and describes hybrid initialization. Table 11 adds actual input-token counts and per-trial API costs. Existing prompts, implementation descriptions, and code/data access provisions remain.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same six single-gene benchmarks and Horlbeck two-gene task. Changing 'five' to 'six' in Section 4.1 corrects the dataset count; longer runs and different batch sizes remain within existing coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds two targeted comparators: the pathway/enrichment-based 'Human' baseline described in Appendix E and Sonnet+Coreset. Original comparators remain, and the hybrid also participates in the new longer-run comparisons.

E3.justification: V3 supplements the retained five-round comparisons with extensive 30-round evaluations using batches of 32 or 128 and non-essential-gene hit ratios (Tables 12–15). V2's existing 30-round prompt ablations are retained. The new comparisons substantially extend experimental budgets and controls; Scharenberg baselines cannot proceed beyond 24 rounds.

E4.justification: V3 adds substantial tests of persistence across experimental horizons and batch sizes, plus an initialization control testing whether agent predictions improve Coreset. Figure 9 and Tables 12–15 supplement the retained prompt/tool ablations. Appendix F additionally examines tool-use costs.

E5.justification: New Figure 9 specifies five-run averages with one-standard-deviation bands, while Tables 12–15 specify ten-run averages and display uncertainty at the final reported checkpoints. Existing results retain their run counts and uncertainty reporting; these additions do not establish increased replication of retained experiments.

E6.justification: Matched original scores remain unchanged, but v3 adds human/hybrid scores, model rankings, resource measurements, and extensive longer-run results. These are new conditions, not same-setting improvements over v2. Results are mixed: Table 12 reports Schmidt1 round-30 hit ratios of 0.293 for Sonnet, 0.303 for Coreset, and 0.314 for their hybrid at batch size 128.

M1.justification: The core agent, prompts, tools, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Section 5 adds the limited Sonnet+Coreset procedural variant, which initializes Coreset using BioDiscoveryAgent's first-round predictions.

P1.justification: V3 condenses tool descriptions, clarifies cumulative hit ratios and dataset counting, and updates front matter and disclosures. It adds Appendix D.1 and a computational-cost section, shifting the complete trace from F to G. Most prose and the main narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: V3 substantially expands the experimental displays with pathway, ranking, cost, and longer-horizon tables (Tables 6, 8, and 11–15) and Figure 9. Table 1 gains comparator rows and Table 3 gains explanatory labels. Existing displays are retained, with appendix relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: Appendix D adds limited discussion connecting the critic to reinforcement learning from AI feedback and agents' verbal reflection. The bibliography and central research positioning remain unchanged. New citation placeholders render as question marks, preventing identification of all discussed works.

T1.justification: The single-gene and two-gene formulations and hit-ratio equations remain unchanged. Section 2's added explanation of cumulative hits clarifies existing mathematics; no new formal assumptions, theorems, or proofs appear.

improvement.justification: V3 strengthens v2's mainly five-round baseline evaluation through longer-horizon tests and an agent-initialized Coreset control, while actual cost reporting improves practical transparency. Reporting problems limit the gain: the broad hybrid interpretation needs qualification given Table 12's counterexamples, and new citations remain unresolved. The added controls and documentation nevertheless provide a modest net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BioDiscoveryAgent, with matching core methods, datasets, and retained results. The main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including the relocated agent trace.

after.justification: V3 retains these original evaluations and adds comparator results, longer-run experiments, and measurements of token usage and API costs.

before.justification: V2 reports original retrospective experiment-design simulations, including single-gene and two-gene evaluations, baseline comparisons, and tool and prompt ablations.

title: BioDiscoveryAgent: An AI Agent for Designing Genetic Perturbation Experiments

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion add theoretical justification as a principal contribution, including a claim that a single-layer decoder can reproduce multilayer representations. The existing empirical claims about competitive accuracy, 13% parameters, and 6.6x/8.0x acceleration remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds an optimization-based explanation of redundancy: successive layers optimize distinct denoising objectives that can allegedly be replaced by one step, with distillation transferring the resulting feature extraction capability. v1 relies on empirical observations and hypotheses about representation size, initialization, and fine-tuning. The few-shot adaptation and retraining limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a SLMRec source-code/data availability link and identifies RecBole as the implementation framework for Caser, HGN, and LightSANs. Existing hyperparameter tables, mixed-precision information, GPU specifications, and efficiency batch sizes are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate next-item recommendation on the same Amazon 2018 Cloth, Movie, Music, and Sport domains. The motivational experiments still cover Cloth and Movie; moving Movie plots to Appendix B.1 adds no coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 2–3 add evaluated Caser, HGN, and LightSANs comparisons across all four domains, substantially expanding the traditional-recommender comparison set. Existing baselines remain; v2's E4SRec corresponds to v1's modified E4SRec*, rather than a newly introduced comparator.

E3.justification: Figure 4 changes the online-distillation and block-number evaluation from Music to Cloth, replacing HR@10 and NDCG@10 with HR@1 and HR@5 while retaining NDCG@5 and MRR. Main-experiment preprocessing, chronological splits, 999-negative sampling, checkpoint selection, and appendix hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The regularizer ablations are retained and redistributed from v1 Tables 2–3 into v2 Tables 4 and 8. Figure 4 replaces the Music model studies with Cloth studies addressing the same questions. Results for students distilled from 32-layer teachers disappear, reducing evidence about teacher/student depth choices.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. The revised plots do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds three baseline result sets and Cloth model-study outcomes, while removing Music model-study outcomes, the 8←32 and 4←32 result rows, and benchmark-table @10 and average-improvement columns. Shared scores and efficiency measurements remain unchanged. A notable new comparison is Cloth HR@5: LightSANs achieves 20.32 versus SLMRec's retained 19.47.

M1.justification: Equation 5 changes the stated auxiliary-supervision loss from averaging over b blocks to averaging over B-1 blocks, excluding the final block. The architecture and other loss components remain equivalent after notation changes. This establishes a limited revision to the specified objective, without establishing an implementation change.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and narrative order remain. Targeted rewrites clarify block notation and motivation; author information, terminology, and citation style change. Appendices are organized into Proof and Experiments with a contents page. A new unresolved 'Appendix??' reference remains in Related Work.

P2.justification: The combined motivational plots are redrawn as separate metric panels in Figures 2 and 5. Benchmark tables are substantially redesigned, ablations separated, and Figure 4's axes and layout revised. New ranking colors are sometimes misleading: Table 2 marks SLMRec's Cloth HR@5 of 19.47 as best despite LightSANs scoring 20.32.

R1.justification: The introduction now distinguishes the work from three recommendation scaling-law studies by model scale and ranking-versus-loss evaluation. The new theory introduces graph-signal and optimization-based positioning, while related work expands to additional recommendation architectures and the newly evaluated baselines. These are substantive additions beyond the citation-style conversion.

T1.justification: New Section 6 and Appendix A introduce a simplified residual-attention recurrence, quadratic denoising objectives, two propositions, and proofs relating multilayer propagation to a single optimization step. v1 contains no corresponding theoretical analysis.

improvement.justification: Additional baselines, clearer metric plots, and implementation links improve comparison and reproducibility documentation. However, v2 removes teacher-size and metric results, introduces incorrect ranking highlights, and overstates its new theoretical support: Appendix A.1 drops the gradient's factor of two between Equations 12 and 14, while the matrix-collapse argument does not establish the claimed equivalent LLaMa decoder. These substantive gains and weaknesses leave the net quality direction uncertain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SLMRec. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains original recommendation and efficiency results and reports additional baseline comparisons and revised model-study results.

before.justification: v1 reports original recommendation experiments on four Amazon domains, efficiency measurements, ablations, and online-distillation and block-number studies.

title: SLMRec: Distilling Large Language Models into Small for Sequential Recommendation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the claims about layer redundancy, distilling competitive small recommenders, approximately 13% of parameters, and 6.6x/8.0x training/inference speedups. Online distillation and theoretical justification were already claimed in v2.

C2.justification: Appendix B.4 newly interprets the traditional-model timing comparison as supporting practical deployment with comparable computational efficiency and nearly 50% performance improvement over SASRec. The existing limitations concerning few-shot adaptation and retraining remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix B.3 adds implementation provenance and code links for the new self-supervised baselines. SLMRec's hyperparameter table, mixed-precision and GPU information, and code/data access statements are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate sequential recommendation on the same Amazon18 Cloth, Movie, Music, and Sport domains. No additional dataset, task, or distinct input scenario is reported.

E2.justification: Tables 2–3 add a self-supervised comparator category comprising S3-Rec, DuoRec, and MAERec across all four datasets. Appendix B.4 also adds SASRec and MAERec to the inference-efficiency comparisons, substantially broadening the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: Tables 2–3 introduce average-rank summaries, and new Table 8 reports relative performance improvement alongside inference time under a shared A100 GPU and batch-size-512 setting. Existing splits, negative sampling, training settings, and recommendation metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The layer-depth experiments, online-distillation and block-number studies, and loss-component ablations are retained. In particular, v2 Table 8 becomes v3 Table 9 with identical results. Added baseline accuracy and timing comparisons do not introduce an ablation, robustness test, or error analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies experimental seed or repeated-run counts or reports confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new average-rank summaries do not add uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds comparative results for three self-supervised methods across all four datasets and new average ranks, including 1.50 and 1.25 for SLMRec in Tables 2–3. New Table 8 reports inference times of 0.015, 0.061, and 0.052 hours for SASRec, MAERec, and SLMRec, respectively. Retained accuracy scores, original efficiency results, and ablation values are unchanged.

M1.justification: Sections 3–4 retain the same architecture, blockwise feature distillation, cosine and norm losses, multiple supervision, and training objective. Figure 3 clarifies the existing supervision paths without establishing a procedural change.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, publication headers are updated, and three related-work topics move into Appendix C, fixing the previous unresolved appendix reference. Baseline descriptions expand locally, while most methodological and explanatory prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: Tables 2–3 gain baseline rows, rank columns, and revised highlighting; a new efficiency table is added. Figure 3 redraws the supervision adapters and scoring paths, Table 1 is wrapped beside text, and existing figures and tables are resized or relocated.

R1.justification: v3 adds references and descriptions for S3-Rec, DuoRec, and MAERec, plus Jin et al. (2025) on knowledge across model layers. The central novelty positioning remains stable; most of Appendix C reproduces related work already present in v2 Section 7.

T1.justification: Section 6 retains the same attention-propagation formulation and two propositions. Appendix A preserves their proofs and derivations, including Equations 10–26; no substantive mathematical revision is present.

improvement.justification: The added self-supervised baselines and traditional-model timing comparison strengthen the empirical context, while implementation links and the clearer Figure 3 improve usability. The gain is limited: the underlying method and retained findings are unchanged, and the new claim of comparable efficiency needs qualification because Table 8 reports SLMRec taking 0.052 hours versus SASRec's 0.015 hours.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SLMRec study and provide readable text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. The title change and relocated related work do not prevent reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds self-supervised baseline results and an inference-time comparison with SASRec and MAERec.

before.justification: v2 reports original recommendation experiments on four Amazon18 domains, including accuracy, efficiency, layer-depth studies, knowledge-distillation experiments, and ablations.

title: SLMRec: Distilling Large Language Models into Small for Sequential Recommendation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same claims about layer redundancy, knowledge distillation, competitive accuracy with fewer parameters, efficiency gains and theoretical justification.

C2.justification: The explanations of the results and applicability limitations are unchanged, including Section 8's limitation that new scenarios require retraining rather than few-shot adaptation.

D1.justification: Implementation disclosures, Appendix B training details, Table 6 hyperparameters, hardware information and code/data access links are unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same Amazon Cloth, Movie, Music and Sport data for the same sequential recommendation tasks and test scenarios.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged throughout the accuracy, efficiency and model studies, including Open-P5, E4SRec variants and the traditional and self-supervised recommenders.

E3.justification: The reported splits, preprocessing, 999-negative-item sampling, ranking metrics, model sizes, batch sizes and training budgets remain unchanged in Sections 2 and 5 and Appendix B.

E4.justification: The layer-depth experiments, regularizer ablations, online distillation comparison and block-count study are unchanged in Figures 2, 4 and 5 and Tables 4 and 9.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. No uncertainty-reporting practice is added or revised.

E6.justification: All numerical results and reported findings are identical, including Tables 2–5 and 7–9 and Figures 2, 4 and 5. The objective correction is not accompanied by revised experimental outcomes.

M1.justification: Equation (6) replaces +λ1Dcos with +λ1(1 − Dcos). Because Equation (3) defines cosine similarity, this reverses that term's optimization direction to encourage teacher–student alignment. This is a localized correction to the stated training objective; the PDFs do not establish an implementation change or rerun.

P1.justification: The first-page arXiv stamp changes from v3 dated 27 January 2025 to v4 dated 20 April 2025. Prose, terminology, headings and section organization are unchanged.

P2.justification: All figures, tables, captions and their placement are unchanged. The corrected equation occupies the same location without document reflow.

R1.justification: Section 7, Appendix C, the reference list and the positioning relative to earlier research are identical.

T1.justification: Equation (6) changes the mathematical definition of the total objective through the corrected cosine term; this is not equivalent notation. The theoretical propositions in Section 6 and their Appendix A proofs remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v4 corrects Equation (6) so that minimizing its cosine term encourages the representation alignment described in Section 4, resolving a sign inconsistency in the training specification. This improves mathematical correctness and reproducibility of the stated method. Results and proofs are unchanged, and the PDFs do not establish that the implementation or experiments changed.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same SLMRec research work, with 22 complete pages including Appendices A–C. Text extraction and rendered-page comparison establish that only Equation (6) and the arXiv version/date stamp differ.

after.justification: v4 retains the original experimental results in Section 5 and Appendix B, including accuracy comparisons, efficiency measurements and ablations.

before.justification: v3 reports original recommendation experiments on four Amazon categories, including accuracy, efficiency, ablations and model studies in Section 5 and Appendix B.

title: SLMRec: Distilling Large Language Models into Small for Sequential Recommendation

C1.justification: The central claims about 3D scene conditioning, independent modality rendering and beneficial cross-modal learning remain. The abstract and introduction broaden stated validation to RAF. v1's prominent claim of outperforming prior work with half the audio data is no longer retained; v2's replacement few-shot statement requires 75% of the data for superiority across all metrics.

C2.justification: v2 reinterprets grid benefits using the capacity-preserving zero-grid control and explicitly presents loss selection as a T60-versus-C50/EDT tradeoff. It removes the lack-of-real-data limitation and adds distinctions between recorded-audio fitting and reusable RIR prediction, plus a grid-detail explanation for RWAVS House underperformance. v1's explicit single-source and difficult-RIR-acquisition limitations are omitted; scene-specific training and static-scene limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 documents NeRAF++ loss weights and batches of 34 complete STFTs, monaural output configuration, RAF camera selection and preprocessing, and RWAVS-specific settings. It newly specifies pose normalization with a 1 mm margin and the waveform-to-STFT evaluation procedure. Feature-size assignments conflict between Appendices B and F. v1's license-information table is removed, while the project-page reference remains.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates six simulated indoor SoundSpaces scenes. v2 retains these and adds RAF's two real rooms with monaural RIRs and directional sources, plus recorded-audio synthesis on RWAVS Office, House, Apartment and Outdoors scenes. Appendix J also evaluates visual synthesis in real scenes.

E2.justification: SoundSpaces Table 1 adds NACF and NACF w/T to the retained AAC/Opus, NAF, INRAS and AV-NeRF comparators. The new RAF comparison includes energy-decay-trained NAF++ and INRAS++ alongside NACF variants. RWAVS Table A2 additionally evaluates ViGAS. Nerfacto remains the visual comparator.

E3.justification: v2 introduces RAF's 80/20 audio split, 0.32-second recordings, 48-kHz processing and camera subsampling, plus RWAVS MAG/ENV evaluation and sparse-image protocols. Within SoundSpaces, feature dimensions become scene-dependent, time normalization changes from [-1,1] to [0,1], and loss ablations expand from three to six scenes. Grid ablations and runtime measurement move to RAF. The main SoundSpaces 90/10 split and audio preprocessing remain.

E4.justification: v2 Table 3 adds a zero-filled-grid control that preserves the feature extractor, directly testing scene information beyond parameter count. It replaces the SoundSpaces grid study with a RAF study and expands the loss analysis. RAF few-shot curves, loudness-map visualizations and RWAVS cross-modal visual analyses add substantial evidence about data efficiency and model behavior.

E5.justification: v1 does not specify repeated-run counts. v2 Section 4.2 newly reports six repetitions per experiment and averaging; this does not establish an increase over v1's unspecified count. Neither version supplies seed identities, dispersion estimates, confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: SoundSpaces Table 1 revises NeRAF's T60/C50/EDT errors from 2.04%/0.39 dB/0.011 s to 2.14%/0.38 dB/0.010 s alongside configuration changes. Vision scores, few-shot curves and ablation results also change. Extensive RAF and RWAVS results are added. RWAVS Table A2 reports mixed rankings: NeRAF's overall ENV is lower than AV-NeRF's, 0.144 versus 0.145, while MAG is higher, 1.596 versus 1.504.

M1.justification: The core pipeline remains, but v2 replaces positional direction encoding with spherical harmonics and introduces NeRAF++ with an energy-decay loss and full-STFT training. Appendix A adds a monaural, source-direction-conditioned RAF configuration. Appendix J adapts NeRAF to query frequencies, predict STFT masks and use magnitude-STFT MSE for RWAVS. These substantially extend the documented procedures.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction and method explanations, replaces the contribution bullet list with prose, and removes the separate Task section. It reorganizes the appendices and moves societal impact out of the main discussion. These changes substantially revise the narrative independently of the added experiments.

P2.justification: Figures 1-4 are redrawn, and visual comparisons gain larger panels and highlighted artifacts. Table 1 combines SoundSpaces and RAF comparisons; Table 2 expands from averaged deltas to per-scene absolute scores and deltas. New loudness maps, RAF few-shot plots and RWAVS tables accompany extensive rearrangement of appendix displays and a changed document template.

R1.justification: v2 adds NACF discussion, distinguishing NeRAF's scene priors from NACF's assumed surface acoustic coefficients. It also adds RAF and VR-NeRF references and a ViGAS citation for the new evaluations. The broader related-work organization and positioning remain largely intact.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix C adds the formal energy-decay objective through per-window energy, reverse cumulative energy and a log-space L1 discrepancy, following cited prior work (Equations 11-14). This is a limited addition to the mathematical loss formulation. No new theorems, proofs or theoretical guarantees are introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly lacked real-world validation, an important gap for its intended applications. v2 addresses this with RAF RIR experiments and RWAVS audio/vision results, while stronger comparators and the zero-grid control better test its central claims. title: Mitigating Object Hallucination in MLLMs via Data-augmented Phrase-level Alignment

These extend the advertised findings without replacing the central contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations concerning prefix denoising, perturbations weakening jailbreaks, refusal versus helpful neutral responses, and alignment versus model size. D1.justification: V2 newly specifies the previously undocumented DT agreement-based detector, including its handling of multiple demographic groups, and provides four algorithms documenting certification and the retained prefix samplers. E1.justification: The BOLD profession/gender and Decoding Trust stereotype/race tasks remain. The original model-response case studies largely remain, with the DT case moved to Appendix E.

E5.justification: Both versions use 95% Clopper-Pearson intervals, but v2 changes the statistical stopping procedure from repeated threshold checks to estimation at a fixed sample count with explicit IID Bernoulli observations. V2 additionally reports averaging five evaluations per baseline prompt set; v1 does not specify that repetition count, so an increase in repetitions cannot be established.

E6.justification: Categorical certification percentages are removed, several numerical estimates change beyond complementing probabilities, and Claude, three-race, sample-count, and case-specific bound results are added. Given the revised sampling procedure, this is a changed reported estimate, not an established same-setting performance decline.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 replaces adaptive sampling and threshold-based biased/unbiased/inconclusive decisions with fixed-sample estimation of unbiasedness probability bounds. The permissible-bias threshold and stopping decision disappear. P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, formalization, and experimental discussion undergo extensive rewriting. V2 separates general from model-specific observations, expands the appendix organization, relocates the DT case study, and redistributes the former standalone limitations section into the conclusion and detector appendix. Terminology consistently emphasizes counterfactual prompts and unbiasedness.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the overview, removes the prompt-distance illustration, and restructures the main results table around average bounds previously reported in v1's appendix. It adds algorithm boxes, sample-count plots, a three-race table, detector-error examples, and sampled-prefix figures. Existing case-study figures are resized and annotated with numerical bounds, while ablation axes and legends change to display lower and upper bounds.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands its conceptual grounding through Counterfactual Fairness, representational harms, local neural-network specifications, and probabilistic programming, adding references such as Kusner, Blodgett, Suresh and Guttag, and Sankaranarayanan. T1.justification: V1's approximate prompt-similarity condition using a user-defined distance and epsilon is replaced by Definition 1's counterfactual prompt sets, requiring identical non-sensitive components and an invariance condition for an unbiased generator. V2 also bounds prompt length by model context and replaces the earlier binomial justification based on similar prompt-level probabilities with an explicit IID Bernoulli formulation. Neither version supplies a new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central certification account: its fixed-sample IID formulation better matches the stated Clopper-Pearson guarantee than v1's repeated threshold-based stopping. Specifying the DT detector fills an important reproducibility gap, while sample-count analyses and detector-error examples make the evidence easier to assess. Detector inaccuracies remain, and the new claim of no current defenses exceeds what the reported evaluations establish, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains in statistical coherence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe QuaCer-B by the same authors. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material that was relocated or renumbered.

after.justification: V2 reports original certification results, including Claude and a three-race evaluation, alongside sensitivity analyses, case studies, and the retained human evaluation.

before.justification: V1 reports original LLM certification experiments on BOLD and Decoding Trust, hyperparameter ablations, model-response case studies, and a human evaluation of its bias detector.

improvement.justification: v3 improves transparency through detector precision/recall reporting, decoding checks, coverage validation, practical instructions, and clearer positioning against prior guarantees. after.justification: v3 retains those original empirical results and adds decoding-parameter ablations, a synthetic confidence-interval coverage experiment, and additional bias-detector evaluation metrics.

before.justification: v2 reports original LLM certification results on BOLD and Decoding Trust, hyperparameter ablations, case studies, and a human evaluation of its bias detector.

title: Is In-Context Learning Sufficient for Instruction Following in LLMs?

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the same central claims about decoding, limited benefits from scaling ICL, and ICL versus IFT in the low-data regime. The new introductory contribution list consolidates claims already present in v2 rather than redefining them.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive applicability and mechanism interpretations: multi-turn weakness depends on demonstration content and formatting, while demonstrations can harm an already instruction-tuned model.
