title: Black-Box Detection of Language Model Watermarks

C1.justification: v2's introduction and conclusion recommend deprioritizing undetectability and suggest that avoiding practical detection may be inherently difficult. v3 narrows the conclusion to detectability of popular practical schemes and presents improved stealth as a research direction. Parameter estimation, already present in v2 Appendix C, is promoted to a headline contribution alongside robustness to additional schemes and modifications.

C2.justification: Section 5.3 replaces v2's suggestion that tested APIs are unwatermarked with an inconclusive interpretation of non-rejection. v3 explicitly acknowledges the absence of theoretical power guarantees and discusses entropy-conditioned stealth versus watermark strength, unevaluated properties, and potentially stronger adversarial modifications. These materially qualify applicability and the interpretation of successful detection.

D1.justification: v3 supplies code-access information and describes its coverage of core tests, deployed-model tests, and appendix experiments; v2 provides no corresponding project-code disclosure. Algorithms 1–5 expand procedural documentation, Algorithm 6 specifies the new variant, and Appendix G adds query/token accounting and dated pricing assumptions. These are substantial reproducibility additions, although some documentation is internally inconsistent.

E1.justification: v3 adds detection scenarios involving no-cache watermarks, SynthID-Text, query-level and token-level watermark disabling, and entropy-conditioned AAR (Appendices F.3–F.6). It also introduces C4-prompted generation for evaluating watermark strength. These substantially extend the tested conditions and task coverage beyond v2.

E2.justification: Neither version benchmarks the proposed presence tests against an external black-box presence-detection method. The added watermark schemes are detection targets. The private-key AAR detector in Figure 6 measures watermark strength in generated text, rather than serving as a competing method for the same presence-detection task.

E3.justification: The main query budgets are retained, but v3 adds YI1.5-9B and QWEN2-7B configurations, GEMMA-7B SynthID evaluation, controlled power simulations, and rejection-rate metrics at 1% and 5%. The entropy-conditioned study introduces 100 C4-prompted completions of 200 tokens, alongside the existing 1,000-query, 50-token presence test. These are substantial additions to evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2's sampling, diversity, multi-key, and parameter-estimation analyses are retained. v3 adds power-versus-query curves, context-estimation distributions, no-cache and SynthID case studies, query/token disabling tests, and an entropy-versus-watermark-strength investigation (Figures 4–6 and Appendices E–F). These materially broaden robustness and failure-boundary analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions already report 100 repetitions, five Red-Green keys, and bootstrap-based uncertainty. v3 clarifies random key selection, specifies 1,000 repetitions for the new power simulations, and adds rejection-frequency summaries with an explicit statement that multiple testing is unadjusted. This extends statistical reporting without establishing increased repetitions for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Some retained numerical results change: the LLAMA2-7B Fixed-Sampling p-value at key length 2048 changes from 1.0e-8 in v2 Table 3 to 0.003 in v3 Table 4 under the reported retained setup. Extensive new results include SynthID's reported median p-value of 0.000 and a detection failure at 5% token disabling with key length 2048 (p = 0.65, Table 9). Public-API Table 2 and key-length estimates remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The three core detection tests remain substantially unchanged, but v3 extends the methodological scope with an entropy-conditioned AAR generation algorithm that gates watermarking on preceding-token information content (Appendix F.6, Algorithm 6). Its SynthID adaptation also requires H = h and recommends context estimation as preprocessing. Algorithms 1–5 primarily document existing procedures.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions, and conclusion are substantially revised. The appendices are reorganized: parameter estimation moves from C to B, scheme details from B to D, and extended experiments from A to F. Separate practical-implications, algorithm-description, power-analysis, cost-analysis, and ethics/reproducibility sections create a substantially different narrative structure.

P2.justification: v3 adds Figures 4–6, Tables 5–10, and six algorithm blocks, and expands the retained appendix results table. Figure 1 moves into the introduction, while the public-API table changes from a wrapped placement to a centered display. Conference formatting also changes typography and page layout throughout.

R1.justification: v3 substantially develops the relationship to theoretical undetectability through Christ et al. and practical constraints discussed through Fairoze et al. This broadens research positioning beyond bibliographic updates to retained works.

T1.justification: v3 adds explicit within-regime logit-invariance and cross-boundary separation properties for context estimation (Appendix B.1, Equations 13–15), beyond v2's brief distribution-change argument. It also mathematically specifies the new entropy-gating rule. The central permutation-test, rarefaction, and multi-key derivations remain, with no new proof of detection power or undetectability.

improvement.justification: v3 improves the paper through more cautious conclusions, experiments exposing power and robustness limits, and substantial reproducibility documentation. However, new reporting defects limit these gains: for YI1.5-9B with LeftHash (2, 0.25), Tables 5–6 report rejection rates of 0.00 at 5% significance but 1.00 at 1%; Algorithm 3 also thresholds using estimated variance where Section 2 specifies standard deviation. The broader evidence is useful, but these inconsistencies weaken confidence in its reporting and reproduction.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, detection framework, and retained experiments. All 14 pages of v2 and 24 pages of v3, including appendices, support comparison; no material reading gaps were found.

before.justification: v2 reports original detection experiments on open-source models and public APIs, sampling and diversity analyses, multi-key experiments, and watermark-parameter estimates.

title: Once-for-All: Controllable Generative Image Compression with Dynamic Granularity Adaptation

Appendix D.3 acknowledges that AmgX constructs preconditioners faster but fails more often, and explains why comparable solution-time testing is omitted. New discussion also connects GNN matrix products to polynomial approximation.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly discloses GPU use whenever supported and identifies the AmgX driver, configuration file and aggregation-based setup. title: Graph Neural Preconditioners for Iterative Solutions of Sparse Linear Systems

C1.justification: The abstract, four stated contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about algebraic neural preconditioning, convergence analysis, training-data generation, scale-equivariance and broad evaluation. Added evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly limits the convergence analysis to infinite precision, explains the fixed test solution and L1 loss choices, expands memory/scalability considerations, and interprets AIR's mixed results and implementation failures. Existing central interpretations and per-matrix training limitations remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix A provides a GNP implementation repository link. F.5 identifies the SA/AIR solver entry points and smoother changes. The existing architecture hyperparameters, training configuration, hardware and primary baseline settings are retained.

E1.justification: Both evaluate the same 867 non-SPD, real SuiteSparse matrices from 50 application areas. The AIR subset and expanded histories use existing matrix coverage; no new dataset, task or input scenario is introduced.

E2.justification: The main comparator set is unchanged. However, v3 Figure 10 adds Jacobi to the first three appendix convergence comparisons, where v2 Figure 9 showed GNP, AMG, GMRES and no preconditioner. New Appendix F.5 compares AIR with SA separately; it does not establish a direct GNP-versus-AIR comparison.

E3.justification: Appendix F.1 adds final-relative-residual ranking under the two existing stopping rules. F.5 introduces an AIR/SA test with replacement smoothers and 83 completed nonsymmetric systems. The main matrix selection, GNP training budget, AUC metrics and stopping settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Supplementary validation expands substantially: F.1 checks sensitivity to the ranking metric, F.5 tests an alternative AMG solver and diagnoses failures, and F.6 extends selected convergence examples to all evaluated systems in three application areas. The original training-data and scale-equivariance ablations remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added percentages and problem counts do not introduce uncertainty estimation; existing distribution-reporting practices are retained.

E6.justification: Tables 1-3 and the main benchmark figures retain their results, but substantial supplementary results are added. New Figure 7 reports GNP winning 16.0% and 19.8% under final-residual ranking with iteration/time stopping. Table 4 adds AIR/SA win-loss-tie counts of 14/8/61 by iterations and 50/29/4 by residual. Figures 10-18 revise or expand convergence histories, including longer time trajectories; these are not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The nonlinear FGMRES procedure, scale-equivariant GNN architecture, Arnoldi/Gaussian training mixture and L1 residual loss are retained. Additional scalability and implementation discussion does not change GNP's procedure.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order remain largely unchanged. v3 makes localized wording edits, adopts conference-style headings and author-year citations, adds acknowledgments and targeted appendix subsections, and renumbers the retained appendices.

P2.justification: The visual appendix expands substantially with final-residual pie charts, Table 4 and multi-panel Figures 11-18. Figure 9 becomes a revised Figure 10 with additional curves and updated legends/time panels. Conference formatting also relocates existing displays, including Table 2 and Figure 6.

R1.justification: v3 adds Trifonov et al. on learned factor corrections, Arioli and Duff on finite-precision FGMRES stability, and two Manteuffel et al. AIR papers. These locally extend positioning without replacing the principal related-work argument.

T1.justification: Theorem 1, Corollary 2, their proofs and the sampling derivations are retained. New Appendix E adds an asymptotic argument for O(nz(A)) computation and a storage expression nz(A) + cn for the existing architecture.

improvement.justification: The final-residual check and broader convergence histories make the retained empirical claims easier to assess. The implementation link and clearer precision/scalability discussion also improve transparency. These are useful refinements to unchanged core work; the AIR comparison stops after 83 nonsymmetric systems because of a hang, so it only partly addresses baseline adequacy.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GNP research work. The main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds final-residual rankings, an AIR-versus-SA evaluation and further matrix-specific convergence results.

before.justification: v2 reports original evaluations on 867 SuiteSparse matrices, including preconditioner comparisons, timing and failure results, design ablations and convergence histories.

title: Graph Neural Preconditioners for Iterative Solutions of Sparse Linear Systems

C1.justification: Both versions claim a distribution-based explanation of RAG benefit and detriment, token-level prediction through representation similarity, and collaborative generation without training or additional modules. The completion/contradiction terminology and revised contribution list reframe these retained claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds an interpretation of the resource measurements as showing little computational overhead, explaining execution with batch size 2. The existing mechanism interpretation and limitation concerning unevaluated 33B/65B models remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents batch size 2 and identifies LLaMA-2-7B for the layer-selection ablation. However, v1's second-half-token sampling restriction is no longer documented. The retrieval corpus, retriever, software stack, decoding strategy, and baseline implementation details are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use Wikitext103, ASQA, Bio, Natural Questions, TriviaQA, WebQ, and SQuAD, including the same noisy-retrieval scenarios. The added mechanism experiments reuse existing datasets and task coverage.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain Logprobs, Uncertainty, Consistency-Lexical, Consistency-Semantic, Standard RAG, NLI+RAG, CRAG, RetRobust, Self-RAG, and INFO-RAG. The new cost table uses the existing Q&A comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 Section 4.1 explicitly assigns label 0 when the pure LLM is correct and RAG is wrong, replacing v1 Section 4.2's broader 'otherwise' rule for differing predictions. This revises the reported protocol without establishing a rerun. v2 also adds memory/runtime evaluation and further model configurations for mechanism probes.

E4.justification: Appendix H extends the existing LLaMA-2-7B/Natural Questions mechanism analysis to OPT-6.7B and Mistral-7B on TriviaQA, WebQ, and SQuAD. Section 4.2 adds computational-cost analysis. These supplement the retained noise-robustness experiment, layer-selection ablation, and six case studies.

E5.justification: The token-classification table retains the same generation counts and p-value ≤0.05 significance markings. Neither version supplies repeated-experiment seed counts or confidence intervals, and the added tables introduce no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Every numerical entry in v1 Tables 1–2 is retained in v2 Tables 3 and 1. New Table 2 reports resource/performance results, including 23.98 GB, 2.24 seconds, and 56.12 accuracy for Tok-RAG. Appendix Tables 4–5 add layer-wise measurements supporting the previously reported mechanism trends.

M1.justification: X-RAG is renamed Tok-RAG. Dynamic layer selection, retrieved-distribution estimation, embedding similarities, and token selection remain the same in Equations 13–19; the rewritten explanations introduce no procedural change.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and substantial theoretical exposition are rewritten around token-level harmonization and distribution completion/contradiction. Theorem 3 moves into the theory section, experimental presentation is reordered, and the classification setup receives a separate stepwise explanation.

P2.justification: v1's combined overview is redesigned into separate method and theoretical-derivation figures. v2 adds a resource table and two appendix mechanism tables, relocates the benchmark displays, and changes document styling. The existing layer plots and case-study figure are retained with presentation adjustments.

R1.justification: v2 adds Ding et al. (2024) on adaptive retrieval and Bengio et al. (2000) on neural language modeling. Its positioning against application-driven RAG methods and its connection to ICL theory remain substantially unchanged; the Xu et al. year-suffix swaps identify existing works.

T1.justification: The mathematical substance of Theorems 1–3, assumptions, and Appendix A–G derivations is retained, including the unsupervised-ICL argument. Moving Theorem 3 into Section 2.3, restating existing findings as corollaries, and changing r(z) to v(z) do not introduce new theory.

improvement.justification: Clearer theory-to-method organization, broader mechanism checks in Appendix H, and measured resource costs modestly improve readability and empirical support. The gains remain limited: revised classification wording is not reconciled with unchanged scores, and the cost discussion calls overhead small despite memory increasing from 17.50 to 23.98 GB relative to Standard RAG.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research despite the changed title and method name. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds computational-cost measurements and further layer-mechanism experiments in Appendix H.

before.justification: v1 reports original token-classification and question-answering results, layer-mechanism experiments, an ablation, and generation case studies.

title: A Theory for Token-Level Harmonization in Retrieval-Augmented Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims about distribution fusion, predicting token-level benefit versus detriment, and training-free collaborative generation. Condensing the contribution bullets does not remove their substantive claims.

C2.justification: Appendix E newly interprets larger detriment as making the theoretical approximation more robust. v3 removes the explicit limitation that 33B/65B models were not evaluated, although no such evaluations are added, and drops the earlier caveat about objectively evaluating long-form factual correctness.

D1.justification: v3 adds a Tok-RAG code-access link and task-specific retrieval, corpus, and context-count details in Appendix I. Existing hardware, framework, model, and decoding disclosures remain. However, explicit descriptions and source citations for ASQA/Bio/NQ and the ablation's model specification are lost.

E1.justification: v3 adds WoW dialogue, CodeXGLUE Python/Java generation, T-REx slot filling, and ELI5 long-form QA. It also adds sequence-generation evaluation on WikiText-103, previously evaluated through token-level benefit–detriment classification. Earlier benchmark coverage remains in the results.

E2.justification: Practical comparisons retain Standard RAG, NLI+RAG, CRAG, RetRobust, Self-RAG, and INFO-RAG; the added tasks reuse this set. Token-level comparisons retain Logprobs, Uncertainty, Consistency-Lexical, and Consistency-Semantic.

E3.justification: The added evaluations introduce F1, CodeBLEU, accuracy, and ROUGE-L protocols with LLaMA-2-7B. Appendix I specifies top-five retrieval for code, slot filling, and language modeling; SCODE-R over deduplicated CodeSearchNET for code; and supplied distractor contexts for WoW/ELI5. Retained experiments have no reported protocol revision.

E4.justification: The retrieval-noise tests, layerwise mechanism analyses, dynamic-versus-fixed-layer ablation, and six case studies are retained. Figure 4 and its ablation discussion move from the main text to Appendix I.5 without new analysis.

E5.justification: Table 3 retains the same p-value threshold and significance markers. Neither version supplies new seed information, repeated-run uncertainty, or confidence intervals. The added Table 2 reports point estimates without introducing another statistical reporting procedure.

E6.justification: New Table 2 reports six result columns, with Tok-RAG highest throughout. For example, Tok-RAG versus INFO-RAG scores are 68.70 versus 65.91 on T-REx accuracy and 27.44 versus 26.75 on Python CodeBLEU. Earlier QA, classification, cost, mechanism, ablation, and case-study results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Tok-RAG retains parallel LLM/RAG decoding, dynamic layer selection, retrieval-distribution estimation, and cosine-based token selection in Equations 14–19. The added prefix-update explanation describes behavior already shown in v2's Figure 1 and Appendix J.

P1.justification: v3 adds a preliminary definitions-and-assumptions subsection, expands proof explanations, reorganizes experimental details, and relocates the ablation. It also condenses contribution bullets and updates publication, affiliation, and acknowledgment text. Most existing exposition and the overall narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds Table 2, adjusts main-table sizing and caption placement, and relocates Figure 4 to the appendix. Existing cost and mechanism tables are renumbered. The other figures retain their content with modest layout changes.

R1.justification: v3 adds references including Rabiner's HMM tutorial, RegaVAE, and sources for new datasets and metrics, while removing several retained-dataset references and Jin et al. 2024b. The central positioning relative to robust RAG and theoretical ICL research remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Although Theorems 1–3 remain, v3 extends the formal analysis: Assumption 2 adds p(d|h_d,z)=1, Equations 5 and 23 correct equality to proportionality, and Appendix B expands the derivations. Appendix E introduces a claimed maximum-error rate sqrt(Upsilon)/exp(Upsilon), a substantive quantitative guarantee absent from v2.

improvement.justification: Table 2 broadens practical validation, while clearer preliminaries, retrieval details, and a code link improve accessibility. However, Appendix E's new error-rate formula increases for 0<Upsilon<1/2, contradicting its unqualified claim of decreasing error with greater detriment. Removal of the large-model limitation and some experimental descriptions also reduces transparency. These gains and weaknesses, particularly in a theory-centered paper, do not establish a reliable net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Tok-RAG work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds practical generation evaluations across additional tasks in Table 2.

before.justification: v2 reports original QA experiments, token-level classification results, computational-cost measurements, mechanism analyses, and a layer-selection ablation.

title: A Theory for Token-Level Harmonization in Retrieval-Augmented Generation

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion broaden the demonstrated contribution from reward design aligned with human driving standards to reward design reflecting implicit human knowledge across driving, locomotion and manipulation. v1 presented broader applicability as potential; v2 explicitly claims superior performance across three simulation settings.

C2.justification: v2 attributes REvolve Auto's smaller advantage in MuJoCo to less informative automated feedback and emphasizes its interaction with evolutionary search. It explicitly notes the absence of MuJoCo generalization tests and expands resource-efficiency arguments in Appendix D using indirect comparisons. The earlier visual-processing and closed-source-model limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds SAC/SB3 architecture and hyperparameters, MuJoCo training times, task-specific prompts and environment/reward code, storage estimates and a future public-code-release statement. However, v1's three-driver, ten-runs-per-driver description disappears. Added Adroit documentation conflicts internally: Table 1 versus Appendix A.1.3 gives 39 versus 97 observations, and Appendix A.1.3 versus Box 11 gives 30 versus 28 actions.

E1.justification: v2 adds MuJoCo humanoid locomotion and dexterous door opening with an Adroit Hand to v1's autonomous-driving coverage. These introduce substantially different behaviors and continuous-control tasks. The original driving environment and two AirSim generalization scenarios remain.

E2.justification: T2R Auto is removed from the driving fitness comparison, while Expert Designed is added to the driving Elo comparison and Eureka is added to both retained generalization scenarios. These are targeted membership changes; the principal REvolve/Eureka and automatic-feedback comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The added MuJoCo experiments use SAC with 5 million training steps per policy and task-specific velocity or completion-time fitness measures, versus the retained driving protocol using Clipped Double Deep Q-Learning and 500,000 steps. Mutation-only and crossover-only experiments introduce new controls. These substantially expand the evaluation design without establishing changes to the original driving training budget.

E4.justification: v2 Section 5.5 and Figure 4 add a direct comparison of mutation alone, crossover alone and their combination, testing a central explanation for REvolve's performance that v1 did not isolate. The existing generalization analysis gains Eureka comparisons. Conversely, v1 Figure 9's population-average fitness analysis is removed.

E5.justification: v1 Section 5.2 explicitly reports a single random seed; v2 reports two, and Figure 3 adds shaded bands to the evolution curves. The existing generalization mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting remains. No new significance tests or confidence-interval procedure are provided, so the statistical expansion is limited.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for both MuJoCo tasks and the operator ablation. Table 3 adds Eureka fitness scores of 0.73 ± 0.04 and 0.57 ± 0.05 in the two generalization environments, while retaining the earlier rows. Driving REvolve Elo changes from 1534 to 1575 in an expanded comparison pool, preventing interpretation as a direct performance gain. Population-average results are removed.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, island-based evolution and Elo-guided feedback remain unchanged. However, the documented driving crossover prompt in Box 3 drops the instruction giving collision and inactivity penalties precedence over other rewards. This is a limited revision to the specified LLM instructions; the PDFs do not establish its experimental effect.

P1.justification: The title, contribution paragraphs and conclusion are substantially rewritten around broader applicability. Experimental setup, training and baselines are reorganized; retained human-feedback related work and episodic-step discussion move into appendices. The appendices gain task-based organization, and ethics and reproducibility sections are introduced. This substantially changes the narrative structure beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the single-task fitness display with three panels, adds an operator-ablation figure and task-summary table, and separates and expands v1's combined Table 1. It moves the framework-comparison schematic to Appendix D, adds task illustrations and a fitness diagram, removes the population-average plot, and reorganizes convergence plots. Typography and page styling also change throughout.

R1.justification: v2 expands the existing evolutionary-versus-greedy positioning, explicitly arguing that Eureka does not qualify as an evolutionary algorithm. It adds references for SAC, MuJoCo, SB3 and resource comparisons, replaces Bäck and Schwefel with De Jong, and removes Salvador and Saludares. Most earlier literature remains, including the human-feedback discussion relocated to Appendix D.

T1.justification: The RDP objective, assumptions, Elo equations and selection reasoning remain. Appendix B.2 adds mathematical definitions for humanoid fitness, conditional on surviving the episode, and Adroit fitness, conditional on successful completion and elapsed steps (Equations 3–4). These are limited formal additions, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v1 evaluated driving without isolating genetic-operator contributions. v2's operator ablation and two additional continuous-control tasks substantially strengthen evidence for the search mechanism and broader applicability. Adding Eureka to generalization comparisons and reporting two seeds further support the evaluation. These gains outweigh the removed T2R Auto and population-average comparisons, although inconsistent Adroit dimensions, limited replication and indirect resource comparisons weaken reproducibility and some claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe REvolve, with matching formalization, algorithm and driving experiments despite the changed title and broader scope. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original driving, humanoid locomotion and Adroit Hand experiments, human-preference rankings and genetic-operator ablations in Figures 3–4 and Tables 2–3.

before.justification: v1 reports original AirSim experiments, human-preference evaluations and reward generalization results, including Figures 4–5 and Table 1.

title: REvolve: Reward Evolution with Large Language Models using Human Feedback

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: evolutionary reward design using LLMs and human feedback, interpretable rewards without an additional reward model, and superior performance across three simulation tasks.

C2.justification: Section 5.4 newly interprets diminishing improvements as convergence by generation 5, without extending the displayed curves. Existing explanations of generalization failures, computational and GPT-4 limitations, and real-world applicability remain unchanged.

D1.justification: The Reproducibility statement replaces a promised public code release with stated open-source availability and a specific repository link; both versions already mention supplementary code. V3 also newly discloses that final evaluation raters were disjoint from training raters and identifies the computing facility.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate autonomous driving, humanoid locomotion, and Adroit Hand manipulation, including the same two additional AirSim generalization environments. No new task, dataset, or environmental scenario is introduced.

E2.justification: Expert Designed, Eureka, Eureka Auto, REvolve Auto, and Human Driving retain their membership in the corresponding comparisons. The additional introductory citations do not introduce evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Section 5.2 changes the stated search budget from five to seven generations, and Figure 4's caption now specifies seven. Population sizes, per-policy training budgets, and metrics remain unchanged. This establishes a reported setting revision; the unchanged plots ending at generation 5 do not establish that experiments were extended or rerun.

E4.justification: The mutation/crossover ablation, two AirSim generalization tests, feedback example, and Appendix G training analyses retain the same comparisons and displayed evidence. No additional ablation or robustness evidence accompanies the revised generation count.

E5.justification: Both versions report two random seeds and retain the same uncertainty-reporting practices, including Table 3's mean and standard deviation. No additional repeated-run information, confidence intervals, or significance tests appear.

E6.justification: Performance curves and benchmark tables remain unchanged, but Section 5.4 adds a reported stabilization-by-generation-5 finding. Appendix D revises calculated feedback requirements from 1,000 to 1,400 pairs and storage from 12.5 to 17.5 GB under the seven-generation budget; these are revised resource totals, not performance gains.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, the island-based evolutionary procedure, human-feedback mechanism, genetic operators, and appendix prompts remain unchanged. The revised generation count changes the reported experimental budget, not the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: V3 makes localized wording edits in the method, automated-feedback description, and ethics statement, and adds acknowledgments. The section hierarchy and overall narrative remain stable; the DrEureka reference receives a publication-metadata update.

P2.justification: Main-text figures and surrounding text are repositioned, and Figure 4 is resized with a revised seven-generation caption, although its axis still ends at 5. Figure and table membership, plotted evidence, and appendix displays are otherwise retained.

R1.justification: The introduction adds Fawzi et al. (2022), Mankowitz et al. (2023), and DeepMind (2024) as RL-success examples. Section 4 changes the citation supporting its evolutionary-algorithm definition from Lehman et al. to De Jong. The substantive positioning against Eureka and Text2Reward remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The reward-design formalization, optimization objective, Elo equations, fitness definitions, and mathematical assumptions are retained. No theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is added or revised.

improvement.justification: The explicit code-access information and disclosure of separate evaluation raters improve reproducibility documentation. However, the seven-generation descriptions are not reconciled with unchanged plots ending at 5, and the added convergence assertion lacks further supporting evidence. These documentation gains and unresolved reporting inconsistencies prevent a reliable judgment of net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REvolve study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A-G are readable and can be matched despite pagination changes.

after.justification: V3 retains these original experimental results, including fitness curves, human-preference rankings, and AirSim generalization tests.

before.justification: V2 reports original RL experiments, human-preference evaluations, genetic-operator ablations, and generalization results in Section 5 and the appendices.

title: REvolve: Reward Evolution with Large Language Models using Human Feedback

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain identical claims about evolutionary reward search, incorporating human feedback without training an additional reward model, and outperforming the evaluated baselines.

C2.justification: Section 5.4 already states that improvements diminish and converge by generation 5; v4 retains that interpretation. Explanations of feedback benefits, generalization failures, computational costs, and reliance on closed-source GPT-4 are also unchanged.

D1.justification: Training hardware and budgets, RL hyperparameters, fitness calculations, prompts, feedback examples, generated reward code, and code-access statements remain identical in the main text and appendices.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same three tasks and the same two additional AirSim generalization environments. Extending Figure 3 across more generations adds no task or environment coverage.

E2.justification: Figure 3 retains REvolve, REvolve Auto, Eureka, Eureka Auto, and Expert Designed, with Human Driving additionally shown for autonomous driving. Comparator membership in Tables 2–3 and the appendix experiments is unchanged.

E3.justification: Section 5.2 already specifies N = 7 generations and K = 16 individuals in both versions; training steps, metrics, and evaluation procedures are also unchanged. Figure 3's extension through generation 7 does not establish an increased training budget.

E4.justification: The genetic-operator ablation in Figure 4, generalization evaluations in Table 3 and Figure 13, and supplementary training analysis in Figure 12 are identical. The Figure 3 update extends the existing main comparison without introducing a separate supplementary analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report two random seeds in Section 5.2 and Figure 3 and retain the same shaded-band presentation and Table 3 mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting. No run-count or statistical estimation practice changes are documented.

E6.justification: Figure 3 adds fitness points for generations 6 and 7 for the four learned-reward variants across all three tasks. These show largely plateauing performance while retaining the method ordering. The tables and appendix results are unchanged.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, the evolutionary procedure in Section 3, and the appendix prompts and reward code are unchanged. Both versions use the same GPT-4 reward generation, genetic operators, and human-feedback mechanism.

P1.justification: The first-page arXiv stamp changes from v3 dated 6 April 2025 to v4 dated 23 May 2025. Manuscript prose, headings, captions, and section and appendix organization are unchanged.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is redrawn with the generation axis extended from 5 to 7, adjusted tick spacing, and slightly changed panel dimensions and surrounding spacing. Its caption and legends remain unchanged; all other figures and tables retain their presentation.

R1.justification: The citations, bibliography, Section 4, and Appendix D are unchanged, including positioning relative to Eureka, Text2Reward, RLHF, and evolutionary algorithms using LLMs.

T1.justification: The reward-design formalization and Equation 1, the Elo and fitness definitions in Appendix B, and the reward formulas in Appendix C are unchanged. No assumptions, derivations, or proofs are added or revised.

improvement.justification: Figure 3 now displays results through the generation-7 horizon already specified in Section 5.2, making the late plateau supporting Section 5.4's convergence claim visible. This modestly improves evidential completeness; the methods, other analyses, and main conclusions remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same REvolve study, with readable main text, references, and Appendices A–G. Full-document text and rendering comparisons establish that changes are confined to the first-page version stamp and Figure 3 with its surrounding layout.

after.justification: v4 retains these original simulation and human-preference results and displays additional generations in Figure 3.

before.justification: v3 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments on autonomous driving, humanoid locomotion, and Adroit Hand manipulation, human-preference evaluations in Table 2, and supplementary experimental results.

title: REvolve: Reward Evolution with Large Language Models using Human Feedback

C1.justification: The central claims remain vector representations for binary features, polytope representations for categorical concepts, and orthogonal structure for semantic hierarchy. v2 foregrounds polytopes, but v1 already defines them; its conditional simplex claim remains in v2 Appendix C. Additional model evidence supports the retained claims.

C2.justification: v1 interprets the observed geometry directly as evidence of semantic hierarchy. v2 explains how high-dimensional geometry and token-set inclusion can produce similar observations, distinguishes sibling from inclusion relationships, and interprets independent-subsampling controls. It also explains the empirical importance of LDA and the causal inner product, substantially refining the interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix E explicitly identifies displays using representations estimated from unsplit token collections, including retained visualizations. Projection captions also specify the normalized dot-product formula. These clarify implementation and reporting without establishing corresponding changes to previously unspecified settings. Existing preprocessing and code-access information remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds a limited intervention scenario testing target-versus-subordinate logit changes for three parent-child contrast pairs in Table 1; v1 empirically examined representation geometry. English WordNet noun/verb coverage and the curated animal/plant examples remain. Adding LLaMA changes model coverage rather than introducing another dataset.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's random-word projection reference, v2 evaluates shuffled-unembedding controls in the retained WordNet analyses, random parent/grandparent assignments, a mean-vector estimator, and an unwhitened Euclidean alternative. Figures 3–5 and 10–12 substantially expand the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: The reported train/test split changes from 80/20 to 70/30. v2 adds whole-token versus independently subsampled estimation, normalized-vector intervention tests, and LLaMA-3-8B noun evaluations. Hierarchy comparisons use inverse shortest-path distance instead of the earlier adjacency reference. These substantially revise and extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2 tests whether apparent orthogonality arises from high dimensionality or token-set inclusion using random relatives, shuffled embeddings, and independent subsampling. Appendix F additionally tests mean estimation and removal of whitening. Table 1 adds intervention case studies. These analyses address alternative explanations largely untested in v1.

E5.justification: v1 Figures 4 and 9 report error bars of 1.96 times the standard error; the corresponding v2 projection analyses use standard deviation. Table 1 also reports standard deviation across token pairs. This changes statistical reporting, without establishing additional repeated runs or seeds.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for interventions, controls, ablations, and LLaMA. For example, Table 1 reports a plant-to-animal intervention changing parent logit differences by 5.1265 ± 1.1731 and subordinate mammal-to-reptile differences by -0.0600 ± 1.2190. Revised projection plots use different splits, so they do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same whitening transformation and LDA representation estimator with Ledoit-Wolf covariance shrinkage in Equations 5.1–5.2. The added theoretical properties, comparator estimators, and evaluations do not change the proposed estimation procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten. The theoretical exposition is reorganized around binary and categorical vector representations; the simplex discussion and animal example move to appendices. The experimental narrative is restructured around representation existence, intervention, similarity, and controlled orthogonality tests.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the principal heatmap arrangement with shortest-distance, original-embedding, and shuffled-embedding panels, and introduces dedicated orthogonality line plots. Projection figures gain training curves and control panels. A numerical intervention table and additional analysis figures are added; the existing categorical visualization is relocated and its viewing angle revised.

R1.justification: v2 adds the LLaMA-3 reference and removes several citations, including Patchscopes, Representation Engineering, and Ri et al.'s contrastive-loss work. It condenses the embedding-literature discussion while retaining the central positioning as an extension of Park et al.'s formalization.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds Corollary 10 and a proof characterizing token projections onto categorical representation subspaces. Appendix G adds a Gaussian mean-vector derivation explaining inclusion-induced orthogonality. These extend the theoretical analysis. The earlier simplex theorem survives as Proposition 9, and the binary-contrast result is reorganized as Corollary 6 rather than newly introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical support left high-dimensional geometry and token-set overlap as substantial alternative explanations. v2 directly investigates these through shuffled embeddings, random relatives, and independent subsampling, materially strengthening support for the central interpretation. Intervention measurements and LLaMA replication provide complementary validation. Changed splits and error-bar conventions prevent direct numerical improvement claims, but the stronger experimental controls constitute a substantial overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching of retained, relocated, revised, and added content.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix F report original Gemma-2B and LLaMA-3-8B results, including projection measurements, intervention effects, and controlled comparisons of hierarchical geometry.

before.justification: Sections 5.2–5.3 and Appendix C report original Gemma-2B experiments measuring token projections and hierarchical representation geometry.

title: The Geometry of Categorical and Hierarchical Concepts in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and discussion retain the same central contributions: vector representations of binary features, polytope representations of categorical concepts, hierarchical orthogonality, and empirical validation on Gemma and LLaMA-3.

C2.justification: The interpretations of semantic structure versus set-inclusion artifacts remain unchanged. Both retain the qualifications about imperfect representations, implications for sparse autoencoders, and the limitation of the whitening approach to final-layer representations.

D1.justification: The same code access information, model dimensions, token filtering, synset processing, and manually inspected ChatGPT-generated visualization sets remain documented. Moving the abstract's code disclosure into a footnote does not change access.
