C1.justification: The introduction removes the 'fully spiking' qualification from its benchmark claim, modestly revising the contribution's characterization. The abstract and conclusion otherwise retain the same claims about parallel probabilistic spiking, surrogate training, scalable architecture, strong SNN accuracy, and computational efficiency.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly limits energy estimates to arithmetic operations, excluding memory I/O, and clarifies GELU use in the comparison tables. It adds interpretations of the ReLU accuracy tradeoff and the loss of sparsity benefits when passing probabilities. Section 3.1.2 also removes the suggestion that spike sparsity enables Sparse FFT training.

D1.justification: The abstract adds an implementation repository link. Appendix D states that the new sequential CIFAR-10 experiment uses hyperparameters similar to LRA Image, providing limited configuration guidance. Existing hardware, discretization settings, memory figures, and Table S1 hyperparameters are retained; repository availability was not externally verified.

E1.justification: Section 4.1 extends speech evaluation from SC10 to the 35-class Speech Command task. Appendix D adds sequential CIFAR-10 experiments, but CIFAR-10 already underlies LRA Image in both versions; the PDFs do not sufficiently specify a distinct data representation to establish additional coverage beyond that retained dataset.

E2.justification: Appendix D adds numerical comparisons with PSN (88.45%) and Sliding PSN (86.70%), while noting their column-based inputs differ from P-SpikeSSM's pixel sequences. Section 4.1 also adds a qualitative speech-baseline comparison involving Bittar and Garner. Comparator membership in Tables 1–3 is unchanged.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 revises energy evaluation by counting convolution operations across all N neurons. New experiments introduce activation and spike-versus-probability controls. Existing accuracy metrics, stated splits, and training settings in Tables 4 and S1 remain unchanged; the added speech and CIFAR experiments provide limited further protocol detail.

E4.justification: Table 5 adds a GELU-to-ReLU ablation testing the accuracy cost of a hardware-friendly activation. Appendix D adds a spike-versus-real-valued-probability comparison on sequential CIFAR-10. The original surrogate, mixer, normalization, parameterization, neuron-count, and LIF comparisons are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies repeated-run counts or seeds, and v3 introduces no confidence-interval or significance-testing procedure. Accuracy tables retain point estimates, and the appendices add no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: The central energy estimate changes substantially from over 70× to 36× following revised accounting in Section 4.2. Table 2 changes P-SpikeSSM's LRA Image accuracy from 80.60 to 82.40 under unchanged listed settings, reversing its ordering against BinaryS4D's retained 82.00. Newly reported results include 96.23% on 35-class speech, 80.40% for the ReLU ablation, and sequential CIFAR-10 accuracies of 85.6% with spikes and 87.2% with probabilities.

M1.justification: The core neuronal dynamics, SpikeSampler surrogate, SpikeMixer, and ClampFuse architecture remain unchanged. v3 adds tested variants that replace GELU with ReLU and pass real-valued probabilities instead of sampled spikes, making limited changes to the evaluated procedures.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized wording corrections and explanatory additions, updates the author affiliation, and adds acknowledgments and conference-publication headers. The principal section sequence and Appendices A–D remain intact, without extensive narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: Figure 1b changes from a heatmap to a probability curve, and several figures are resized. Table 1 moves into the experimentation section, Table 4 moves alongside the hyperparameter discussion, Table 5 gains a row, and the comparison tables gain spiking-status annotations. The overall visual organization remains recognizable.

R1.justification: v3 adds discussion and citations for efficient alternatives to BPTT, plus references concerning parallel spiking neurons, speech recognition, quantized spiking language models, and hardware-friendly activation. It removes the Sparse FFT citation. The broader positioning against transformers, SSMs, and LIF-based approaches remains intact.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 corrects the analytical convolution-cost terms from L² to NL² for S4 and from IFRin·L² to IFRin·NL² for P-SpikeSSM, revising the resulting energy expressions. The main dynamical equations and convolution/HiPPO derivations in Appendices A–B remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 improves rigor by correcting the missing neuron factor in the energy analysis and explicitly limiting the resulting 36× estimate to arithmetic costs. The added activation and probability controls clarify practical tradeoffs, and the repository link improves reproducibility information. These are useful but bounded gains: new speech/CIFAR protocols remain briefly documented, and the PSN comparisons use different input representations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe P-SpikeSSM by the same authors. Their complete main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–D are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds a 35-class Speech Command result, a ReLU ablation, and sequential CIFAR-10 experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original P-SpikeSSM benchmark accuracies, component ablations, timing measurements, and spiking-activity analyses in Section 4 and the figures.

title: P-SPIKESSM: HARNESSING PROBABILISTIC SPIKING STATE SPACE MODELS FOR LONG-RANGE DEPENDENCY TASKS

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add the claim that PopT provides a computationally lightweight, more interpretable alternative with competitive performance against end-to-end methods. The title, abstract, and conclusion broaden the demonstrated scope from intracranial activity to multiple neural modalities and temporal encoders, while retaining the original decoding and interpretability contributions.

C2.justification: The limitations change substantially: v1 emphasizes unavailable comparable intracranial datasets and computational obstacles to end-to-end comparisons; v2 emphasizes dependence on meaningful spatial coordinates, individual brain variability, and difficulty identifying functional channels with low-SNR recordings. v2 also adds an explanation linking the Brant comparison to spatial aggregation and discusses potential geophysical and climate applications.

D1.justification: v2 adds temporal-embedding dimensions and parameter, hardware, and compute tables in Appendices A–B. It revises pretraining time from four to two days but removes the 80-CPU-core/700-GB memory disclosure, the explicit 500 ms temporal threshold, and subject identities for the pretraining-subset study. Core optimizer, schedule, split, and code-access information remains.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates movie-watching intracranial recordings on four auditory-linguistic tasks. v2 retains this coverage and adds TUEG pretraining and TUAB scalp-EEG pathological-versus-normal classification, which the paper labels seizure detection. This adds a distinct recording modality, population, and task.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds fine-tuned Brant and removes the single-channel BrainBERT comparison row. Table 2 adds comparisons with BIOT and LaBraM using scores explicitly attributed to their original works. Deep NN also joins the sample- and compute-efficiency comparisons in v2 Figures 4–5, where v1 Figures 3–4 showed only Linear and the two PopT variants.

E3.justification: The added EEG evaluation uses 21 channels, excludes task subjects from pretraining, and reports balanced accuracy alongside ROC-AUC. New configurations use TOTEM for intracranial data and Chronos/TS2Vec for EEG. The channel-count sweep expands from 1–30 to 1–50 channels, while the original splits and training-step budgets in Appendix A remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 Table 3 adds a reconstruction-only pretraining control beyond v1's added-reconstruction-loss ablation. The channel-count sensitivity analysis is extended to 50 channels. The existing loss/position ablations, held-out-subject study, pretraining-subject scaling, frozen-model analyses, and interpretability studies are retained.

E5.justification: v2 adds means and standard deviations across five random seeds for the EEG experiments in Table 2 and Figure 2b. Subject-level standard-error reporting remains for the intracranial experiments. No increase in repeated runs for the retained experiments is stated.

E6.justification: The original BrainBERT PopT AUROC means remain 0.69, 0.84, 0.86, and 0.89. v2 adds TOTEM/Brant results, EEG results, reconstruction-only scores, and additional scaling and efficiency entries. Table 2 reports PopT+TS2Vec AUROC of 0.8907 alongside quoted BIOT and LaBraM values of 0.8815 and 0.9162. Reported PopT pretraining time also changes from four to two days.

M1.justification: The transformer backbone, frozen temporal embeddings, two discrimination objectives, channel replacement procedure, and downstream fine-tuning remain. The ensemble encoding explicitly described in v2 was already depicted as sequence position in v1 Figure 1. Additional encoders and EEG inputs exercise the existing modular method without establishing a new algorithm.

P1.justification: Beyond the new experiments, v2 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, existing method explanation, discussion, and conclusion, and condenses interpretability descriptions and captions. It reorganizes the loss explanation, changes the title and terminology, and adds a compute appendix while renumbering retained appendices.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn with separate objective panels and a detailed temporal-encoder pipeline. Table 1 is reorganized by encoder, and new EEG, parameter, and compute tables and a summary bar chart are added. Existing plots receive changed axes, legends, grouping, and placement within a new conference layout; the appendix connectivity and frozen-model graphics are retained.

R1.justification: The related-work structure and novelty argument for modular aggregation across variable channel layouts largely remain. v2 adds references for Chronos, TS2Vec, TUEG, BERT, and aggregation approaches, and removes the Nejedly and Islam references associated with the old limitations. Comparisons with already-cited end-to-end models become explicit empirical positioning.

T1.justification: The mathematical substance remains the two discrimination tasks and their summed binary-cross-entropy objective. v2 replaces explicit BCE expansions with prose and expands position-encoding notation. These are expository changes; neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence for encoder/modality generality and its missing end-to-end comparisons through additional encoders, scalp-EEG evaluation, and the Brant comparison. Five-seed EEG reporting and the reconstruction-only control further strengthen the evidence while preserving the original results. EEG competitors remain partly indirect comparisons, and some reproducibility details are lost, but the gains in empirical support and applicability are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Population Transformer work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and can be matched across the revised organization.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds experiments with alternative temporal encoders, a fine-tuned Brant comparison, scalp-EEG evaluation, and a reconstruction-only ablation. The EEG comparison scores attributed to earlier works are distinguished from these original results.

before.justification: v1 reports original intracranial decoding experiments, efficiency and generalization studies, ablations, and analyses of learned connectivity and attention.

title: Population Transformer: Learning Population-level Representations of Neural Activity

C1.justification: The same four contributions remain: generic pretrained channel aggregation, improved downstream decoding including held-out subjects, interpretation of learned weights, and a released usable model. The revised abstract retains the existing claims of efficient, competitive decoding across modalities and temporal encoders rather than introducing a new central contribution.

C2.justification: The scaling discussion now notes a plateau and suggests benefits from more diverse data, replacing the earlier explanation involving adaptation from one pretraining subject. The random-electrode analysis introduces a qualification about electrode-specific sentence-onset decodability. Appendix B narrows the parameter-efficiency comparison to 'some' end-to-end approaches after including BIOT.

D1.justification: V3 adds tensor-shape explanations, a numerical temporal criterion, connectivity pseudocode and a pointer to non-BrainBERT configuration files. It revises documented hyperparameters and recording-duration/channel-count metadata, and adds BIOT resource information. Much of the architecture, hardware, training-budget and code-access documentation already existed; the repeated repository link does not establish new availability.

E1.justification: Both use the same ten-subject movie-viewing iEEG recordings, TUEG/TUAB, four auditory-linguistic tasks and pathological-versus-normal EEG classification. The new dataset citation and correction from 'seizure detection' to 'abnormal EEG detection' do not establish new coverage. Added analyses vary electrode selection or model configuration within this coverage.

E2.justification: The main decoding comparator sets remain unchanged. V3 adds best-single-channel BrainBERT to the held-out-subject comparison in Figure 6, BIOT to the resource comparisons in Tables 4–5, and fraction of significant electrodes as a functional-map comparator in Figure 12.

E3.justification: Appendix A changes the reported pretraining learning rate from 1e-4 to 5e-4 and split from 98/1/1% to 89/1/10%, and revises downstream batch sizes, learning rates and schedules. Figure 7 replaces subject-count scaling on one held-out subject with data-fraction scaling evaluated across test subjects. Functional maps change from Destrieux to DKT regions. These are reported protocol changes; Figure 5 still conflicts with Appendix A over the fine-tuning batch size.

E4.justification: V3 adds random-electrode controls, TOTEM held-out-subject analysis, coordinate-fuzzing and channel-replacement ablations, and quantitative functional-map/connectivity validation. It replaces subject-count scaling with data-fraction scaling. The combined discriminative-plus-reconstruction ablation and frozen-model component ablations are removed; frozen ensemble scaling is retained as Figure 17.

E5.justification: V3 newly reports Wilcoxon rank-sum testing in Tables 1–2 and Dunnett's testing in Table 3, with significance markers and a 0.05 threshold. It also reports five fine-tuning runs for attention maps and their standard deviation in Figure 12. Cross-subject standard errors and five EEG seeds were already reported in v2; their changed numerical values do not establish increased replication.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces BrainBERT-PopT ROC-AUCs of 0.69/0.84/0.86/0.89 with 0.74/0.87/0.90/0.93. Table 2 changes TS2Vec-PopT EEG ROC-AUC from 0.8907 to 0.8883, alongside other revised scores. These accompany changed methods/settings and are not controlled same-setting gains. New results include functional-map correlation r=0.4 and connectivity correlations of 0.42–0.66, plus additional robustness and ablation results.

M1.justification: V3 removes Gaussian coordinate fuzzing from the default model and replaces corrupted channels with activity from a randomly selected channel/time, rather than the same channel at another time. Table 8 explicitly tests the former choices as variants. Connectivity probing also changes from zero-filling a channel to omitting it. The transformer architecture and two-objective framework remain.

P1.justification: The introduction is reframed around temporal-embedding aggregation, method explanations are expanded, and the TUAB task terminology is corrected. Temporal-encoder descriptions are grouped in the setup, and appendix headings and organization are revised. The main section sequence, contribution list and much of the explanatory narrative remain.

P2.justification: V3 replaces held-out-subject and scaling bar charts with point plots, redraws brain maps and connectivity displays, and adds robustness/comparison plots, a connectivity schematic, electrode-level matrices and new tables. Retained frozen scaling is relocated and reformatted, while the frozen-ablation table disappears. These substantially change the visual presentation beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: V3 adds Bommasani et al., Brain Treebank and different anatomical-atlas references, while removing several earlier references including Parvizi and Kastner, Alexander et al. and Destrieux et al. The introduction adds an argument about downsampling in end-to-end models. The central positioning around modular aggregation of pretrained temporal embeddings remains.

T1.justification: The new Algorithm 1 defines connectivity influence through absolute prediction differences, whereas v2 describes increased channel-wise loss; v3's prose still refers to loss changes. Appendix A also adds explicit loss and label formulas, with apparent BCE sign/complement errors and a '<500 ms' label condition conflicting with Section 3's '=500 ms'. No theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: Random-electrode controls, explicit significance testing and quantitative checks of both interpretability analyses strengthen evidence that was less directly validated in v2 (Figure 12 and Table 7). The gain is limited by removal of frozen-component and mixed-reconstruction ablations and by new documentation inconsistencies, including malformed BCE expressions and conflicting batch sizes in Appendix A and Figure 5. Higher decoding scores under revised settings are not, by themselves, evidence of better paper quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Population Transformer work. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical experiments and reports additional electrode-selection controls, ablations and quantitative interpretability comparisons.

before.justification: V2 reports original PopT decoding experiments, efficiency and generalization studies, ablations, and analyses of learned brain representations.

title: Population Transformer: Learning Population-level Representations of Neural Activity

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: Bayesian aggregation of multiple weak supervisors, extension from classification to generation, token-level soft supervision, and further improvement through cDPO. Expanded experimental support and revised terminology do not redefine those claims.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the explanations of ensemble behavior: Bayesian priors provide fault tolerance, weak-model disagreement supports complementarity, TinyLlama's scoring can undermine Joint Decoding, and larger candidate pools exacerbate that failure. Appendix E additionally interprets dynamic weighting as redundant with token-level reliability information. The two-task applicability limitation remains, with the model-count limitation updated to three and five teachers.

D1.justification: v2 discloses the default beam size M=5, validation-based tuning of ceiling models and reuse of those settings, and checkpoint/license information for the added models. Appendix C updates cDPO hyperparameters while retaining most training and hardware details. Conversely, v1's explicit description of the DPO reference model and its SFT initialization is omitted.

E1.justification: Both versions use SciQ reformulated as binary answer-correctness classification and SLURP transcriptions for generative slot filling. Added weak models and ensemble configurations do not introduce new datasets, tasks, populations, or input environments.

E2.justification: v2 adds BLOOM-1B1 and TinyLlama_v1.1 as evaluated single-model and single-weak-to-strong comparators in Tables 1–4. Naive Multi-Weak and Joint Decoding remain the ensemble baselines. The separate full hard-label comparator panel in v1 Table 4 is no longer reported.

E3.justification: v2 adds five-model ensembles alongside the original three-model configuration, plus four-model controls, generation-versus-scoring controls, weighting comparisons, and beam-size experiments with M=3, 5, and 10. Appendix C changes the stated cDPO learning rate from 2×10^-7 to 5×10^-7 and beta from 10 to 2. These substantially expand the evaluation design; dataset splits and principal metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds model-agreement analysis (Figure 3), staged target-token versus other-token probability ablations (Table 6), weighting-strategy comparisons (Table 7), and Joint Decoding teacher-quality and beam-size analyses (Tables 8–9). The original auxiliary-loss comparisons persist, but v1's complete hard-versus-soft-label comparison is replaced by a narrower component ablation.

E5.justification: v1 mainly reports point estimates and two classification p-value comparisons, without explicit repeated-run counts. v2 states three random seeds and reports means and standard deviations across the principal comparisons and ablations; the earlier p-value comparisons disappear. This is a substantial reporting change, but does not establish how many runs underlay v1.

E6.justification: Numerous retained results change: three-model Bayesian classification accuracy with auxiliary loss changes from 0.855 to 0.850±0.006, and the slot-filling ceiling changes from 0.781 to 0.748. v2 adds five-model results, including 0.866±0.006 classification accuracy and 0.724±0.015 SLU-F1 after cDPO, plus new ablation and agreement findings. Changed aggregation, ceilings, configurations, and cDPO settings preclude interpreting higher cross-version PGR values as comparable performance gains.

M1.justification: The Bayesian EDL objective, auxiliary self-training loss, word-mediated token probabilities, and weak-model-guided cDPO procedure are retained. Joint Decoding moves from Section 4.1 to the baseline description in Section 5.2. Expanded explanations and weighting ablations do not establish a change to the proposed core method.

P1.justification: The generation and experimental sections undergo substantial reorganization: Joint Decoding moves into the baseline section, dataset and model descriptions are separated, and results are rewritten around three-versus-five-model comparisons. Probability-estimation explanations are expanded, terminology is revised, and the existing appendices are reordered around the new analyses.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 receive revised labels, captions, and diagram presentation, while Figure 3 adds agreement heatmaps. Main comparison tables are restructured around ensemble size and uncertainty reporting, cDPO receives a separate table, and four appendix analysis tables are added. Title styling, headings, and page headers also change throughout.

R1.justification: v2 adds boosting and bagging references to the ensemble discussion, along with citations for BLOOM and TinyLlama. The existing positioning around alignment, human-opinion variability, and weak-to-strong generalization remains substantially intact. The switch to author-year citations is a presentation change.

T1.justification: The EDL likelihood and regularizer, word-probability decomposition, cDPO objective, and PGR definition remain mathematically unchanged. The regularizer moves from Appendix B to G. v2's tokenwise teacher-forcing formula makes the existing naive generation baseline explicit; no substantive theoretical result, proof, or mathematical correction is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical basis of the ensemble approach through three-seed uncertainty reporting and targeted tests of component contributions, weighting, and teacher-scoring failures. These address important gaps beyond v1's point estimates and broad hard-versus-soft comparison. The lost full hard-label panel and an inconsistent TinyLlama PGR entry in Table 4 weaken parts of the reporting, but the expanded diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net improvement. Higher PGR under changed ceilings and settings is not itself evidence of improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Bayesian WeakS-to-Strong research. All pages, including figures, equations, tables, and appendices, are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original classification and slot-filling results, repeated-seed comparisons, model-agreement analysis, and additional ablations in Tables 1–9 and Figure 3.

before.justification: v1 reports original SciQ classification and SLURP slot-filling experiments, including ensemble, auxiliary-loss, soft-label, and cDPO results in Tables 1–5.

title: Bayesian WeakS-to-Strong from Text Classification to Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements and conclusion retain the same claims about Bayesian weak-model ensembles, extension from classification to generation, token-level supervision and cDPO. Additional experiments support these claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: The explanations involving complementary weak-model errors, Bayesian fault tolerance, auxiliary supervision and Joint Decoding failures remain. The CosmosQA discussion reiterates the existing interpretation concerning uneven teacher quality. The limitations and broader-impact sections are unchanged.

D1.justification: V3 discloses equal classification ensemble weights and generation weights of (0.1, 0.3, 0.2, 0.3, 0.1), and explains averaging PGR across teachers. It replaces the promised future code release with a repository link and adds dataset access information. These are documentation and access additions, not established changes to retained experimental settings.

E1.justification: V3 Appendix D adds CosmosQA commonsense reading comprehension, reformulated as binary answer-correctness classification. This extends the classification domain while retaining SciQ and SLURP and the same two broad task types.

E2.justification: FlyingSquid is newly evaluated in the three- and five-teacher SciQ comparisons in Table 2 and the three-teacher CosmosQA comparison in Table 7. Existing single-teacher, Naive Multi-Weak and Joint Decoding comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The added CosmosQA evaluation specifies 5,000 examples for weak-model training, another 5,000 for strong-model training, and 1,000 for testing, using three teachers and auxiliary-loss controls. This is an additional evaluation setup; the stated settings of the retained SciQ and SLURP experiments are unchanged.

E4.justification: The probability-estimation ablation, weighting analysis, Joint Decoding teacher-quality and beam-size studies, and model-complementarity analysis are retained. V2 Appendices D–F become v3 Appendices E–G. CosmosQA adds benchmark coverage rather than a distinct ablation or robustness analysis.

E5.justification: Table 5 newly reports individual seed-0, seed-1 and seed-2 outcomes alongside the existing means and standard deviations. Both versions already specify three runs; there is no reported increase in runs or new uncertainty estimator or significance test.

E6.justification: V3 adds FlyingSquid scores, CosmosQA results and individual cDPO seed results while retaining existing benchmark scores. On CosmosQA with auxiliary loss, Bayesian Multi-Weak reports accuracy 0.760, versus 0.731 for the best single-teacher configuration and 0.706 for FlyingSquid. Section 6.1 also replaces the earlier 11%/7% comparison wording with 16%/8% relative PGR differences.

M1.justification: Equation (7) revises the stated token-label calculation from allocating word probability using positive-exponent confidence weights to allocating log-probability using negative-exponent weights. This changes the specified target probabilities within the retained pipeline; the PDFs do not establish whether the implementation changed or experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: V3 makes localized explanatory edits, adds the FlyingSquid description and CosmosQA appendix, and renumbers subsequent appendices. Author affiliations, ordering and publication headers are updated. The main narrative and section organization are largely retained.

P2.justification: Table 2 gains FlyingSquid rows, Table 5 expands to show individual seeds, and new Tables 6–7 present CosmosQA results. The asset table gains access-path information. Existing figures and ablation tables remain, with limited spacing changes and relocation.

R1.justification: V3 adds Fu et al. (2020) for FlyingSquid and Huang et al. (2019) for CosmosQA. FlyingSquid introduces a comparison with probabilistic weak supervision, while the related-work section and broader novelty positioning remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation (4) corrects the teacher-specific probability and class-specific one-hot target in the EDL sum. Equation (7) changes the decomposition to log-probabilities, making the implied token-probability product preserve word probability. These are mathematical corrections; the appendix regularization derivation is retained and no new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: Corrected equations, an additional comparator and classification dataset, and clearer reproducibility information provide a limited net improvement. The original claims and results remain stable. A remaining reporting problem tempers the gain: CosmosQA Tables 6–7 imply GPT2-Large PGR of approximately 0.049 without auxiliary loss, whereas 0.077 is reported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Bayesian WeakS-to-Strong. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: V3 retains these original experiments and adds CosmosQA results and FlyingSquid comparisons.

before.justification: V2 reports original SciQ classification and SLURP slot-filling experiments, including ensemble comparisons, cDPO results and appendix ablations.

title: Bayesian WeakS-to-Strong from Text Classification to Generation

C1.justification: v3 broadens the introduction's claims from rectified-flow priors to applicability across flow-matching and score-matching models. It newly claims RFDS/SDS equivalence and diffusion extensions of iRFDS and RFDS-Rev. The original claims of strong text-to-3D generation and competitive editing remain.

C2.justification: v3 makes Reflow central to its mechanism explanation and interprets the differing benefits on InstaFlow, SD3 and diffusion models. It acknowledges SD3's stronger backbone and training data, adds the unresolved CFG-mismatch limitation, and discusses memory obstacles to RFDS-VSD on SD3. The existing multi-face limitation remains.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly specifies RFDS-Rev noise-update step sizes: 1 for InstaFlow and 1−σ_t for SD3. It adds SD3's approximately one-hour runtime and model-specific weighting conventions. Existing hardware, optimization budgets, inversion regularization and code access remain; the newly stated InstaFlow step size does not establish a changed setting.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate text-guided 2D generation, T3Bench's three text-to-3D categories, and editing of internet images with three edits per image. Added backbones and qualitative examples do not establish a new dataset, domain or task.

E2.justification: The editing comparisons remove Rectified Flow Time Inversion from Table 2 and Figures 5 and 11, while adding SD3 and diffusion iRFDS variants. Figure 3 adds diffusion RFDS-Rev. DDS, Null Inversion, SDS, VSD and the RFDS-VSD ablation comparator remain in their corresponding comparisons.

E3.justification: v3 adds SD3 evaluations and diffusion implementations of the proposed methods. T3Bench reporting changes from quality, alignment and combined averages to quality alone. The editing user study changes from four choices to five, as shown in the screenshots and Table 2, although Appendix J retains four-method wording. Both versions report 15 editing images and the same original 3D optimization budget.

E4.justification: The existing noise-step, CFG and convergence analyses gain SD3 conditions (Figures 6, 8 and 10). The noise-step sweep drops n=4 while retaining n=0,1,2. These extend existing sensitivity questions; the Jacobian and RFDS-VSD ablations were already present in v1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for the results. Revised user-preference percentages remain point estimates without uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 retains the original per-category quality scores but removes alignment results; RFDS-Rev's 49.3 combined average becomes a 48.9 quality-only average. SD3 RFDS-Rev adds quality scores of 59.8, 54.5 and 55.2. Table 2 adds SD3/diffusion CLIP scores of 0.297/0.296, and InstaFlow preference changes from 55.5% to 45.3% under different choices, not a comparable performance decline. Table 3 changes iRFDS's reported forward-pass count from two to one.

M1.justification: v3 extends the rectified-flow-specific objectives to schedule-dependent interpolation objectives and introduces a score-to-velocity adaptation for applying iRFDS and RFDS-Rev to diffusion models (Section 3.4). The alternating reversal/distillation procedure remains. The revised InstaFlow residual and weight signs preserve its original update rather than establishing a separate algorithm change.

P1.justification: The preliminaries and method rationale are substantially rewritten around generalized interpolants. v3 adds a diffusion-application subsection, revises the experimental narrative, expands Section 5 into an observations summary, and reorganizes the appendices from A.1–A.9 into A–J.

P2.justification: Comparison grids are extensively rearranged and expanded, Tables 1–2 gain backbone-specific columns, and Table 1 loses its metric subrows. CFG and convergence figures gain SD3 rows. Two SD3 galleries are added, while v1 Figures 12–13 are retained as v3 Figures 14–15. Algorithm placement and the document template also change.

R1.justification: v3 substantially repositions the method within the general Stochastic Interpolants and diffusion PF-ODE frameworks, adding Albergo et al. (2023) and Song et al.'s SDE work as foundations. It also adds SiT and evaluation-related references. The original diffusion-prior review remains, but the relationship to SDS becomes an explicit equivalence claim.

T1.justification: Sections 2–3 introduce general interpolation schedules, conditional-expectation velocity equations and generalized gradient derivations. Assumption 1 is narrowed to Reflow-finetuned models. New Appendix A derives score-based expressions and claims RFDS/SDS equivalence, although Equation 11 appears to omit the time derivative on the coefficient multiplying x_t.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens applicability evidence beyond v1's InstaFlow evaluations and more carefully scopes the Reflow rationale, limitations and implementation guidance. These gains are partly offset by removing alignment and direct time-inversion evidence, retaining an inconsistent user-study description, and introducing an apparent derivative omission in Equation 11. The resulting quality improvement is positive but qualified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RFDS, iRFDS and RFDS-Rev. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding equations, experiments, tables and figures can be matched despite substantial revision.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds SD3 and diffusion-model evaluations, including generation, editing and sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation, image-editing, T3Bench, user-preference and ablation results in the main text and appendices.

title: Text-to-Image Rectified Flow as Plug-and-Play Priors

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same central claims: rectified-flow models can serve as priors, RFDS/RFDS-Rev outperform SDS/VSD in text-to-3D generation, and iRFDS supports competitive inversion and editing. The additional evidence does not redefine these contributions.

improvement.justification: The method, empirical evidence, explanations, limitations, and appendices are identical. The byline and arXiv-stamp edits leave the paper's scientific support and expository quality unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Tool-Planner and contain 49 readable pages, including Appendices A-K. Pages 2-49 have identical extracted text and rendered content. First-page differences are confined to the author list and arXiv stamp.

after.justification: v4 retains the original benchmark results, ablations, efficiency analyses, and appendix experiments reported in v3.

before.justification: v3 reports original Tool-Planner evaluations on APIBench and ToolBench in Tables 2-3, alongside ablations, efficiency analyses, and additional experiments in the appendices.

title: Tool-Planner: Task Planning with Clusters across Multiple Tools

C1.justification: V1 presents a broad eight-category benchmark, including hallucination detection and obfuscation, and emphasizes general RAC difficulties. V2 reframes the contribution around six diagnostic categories, foundational versus complex questions, and deeper ramifications. Its abstract and conclusion newly foreground complete GPT-4o failure and limited o1-preview success on the revised ramification test.

C2.justification: V2 adds hypotheses connecting static-fluent errors to long-context recall, few-shot degradation to spurious correlations, and ramification failures to memorized domain knowledge. Fine-tuning is interpreted much more positively than v1's mixed findings. Beyond the retained English-only and model-resource limitations, Section 7 adds planning-domain bias, prompt sensitivity, restricted RAC complexity and imperfect evaluator limitations.

D1.justification: V2 adds full PDDL descriptions for retained domains, systematic fluent classifications, named planning tools, evaluator-prompt examples, gradient accumulation and filtered fine-tuning sample counts. Hardware changes from eight A100s to eight H100s. Conversely, most detailed task/prompt examples and v1's code/data access link disappear; this establishes lost access information, not that the resources themselves became unavailable.

E1.justification: Coverage contracts from 13 domains to eight, dropping Goldminer, Logistics, Miconic, NPuzzle and Zenotravel. Hallucination-detection and obfuscated scenarios disappear. Object Tracking loses its separate category, although object-property queries remain within Fluent Tracking. V2 introduces deeper ramification scenarios with newly defined fluents and dependencies up to four levels.

E2.justification: V1's reported comparisons include Gemini Pro, Llama2-7B/13B, Llama3-8B and Gemma-7B alongside GPT-4o. V2 retains GPT-4o but replaces those comparators with Llama-3.1-8B/70B and adds o1-preview specifically for ramifications. The fine-tuned comparator also changes from Llama3-8B to Llama-3.1-8B.

E3.justification: Reported train/test totals change from 104,894/6,216 to 149,237/3,498. V2 centers zero-shot-CoT and three-shot evaluation instead of v1's zero-shot and multiple few-shot settings. Llama-3.1-70B replaces RoBERTa for free-answer scoring, while human evaluation focuses on ramifications. Fine-tuning changes from two epochs to six for binary and eighteen for free answers. Test lengths 1, 10 and 19 remain.

E4.justification: V2 removes obfuscation robustness comparisons, transportation/non-transportation analyses, ROUGE failure tests and the accuracy-versus-state-complexity analysis. It adds paired template/paraphrase naturalness assessment, comparisons between composite-question combinations, and concrete GPT-4o/o1-preview ramification error cases. Length, fluent, prompting and fine-tuning analyses remain but are substantially revised.

E5.justification: Both retain sample-based SEM for accuracy using the same formula, without documented repeated-run or seed practices. However, v2's domain summary in Table 12 drops the instance-level mean and standard-deviation columns reported in v1 Table 18, reducing descriptive statistical reporting.

E6.justification: The performance matrices are extensively replaced for revised coverage, models, prompts and scoring. V2 newly reports GPT-4o's 0% and o1-preview's 18.42% overall accuracy on its ramification test, and paired naturalness ratings of 4.2 versus 4.5 for templated and paraphrased questions. These are results under changed settings, not demonstrated same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The four-stage PDDL-to-ASP-to-questions pipeline remains, but its final stage gains Llama-3.1-70B paraphrasing after template generation. Natural-language variants per object, action and fluent decrease from up to five to three. These are concrete changes to a retained generation procedure (Section 3.4 and Figure 1).

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, benchmark explanations and results narrative are extensively rewritten. Data creation and validation are combined, limitations become a main-text section, and appendices are reorganized around an introductory instance, domain specifications, fluent classifications and model responses. Fluent terminology is also regrouped, including self-derived fluents.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to include paraphrasing, and Figure 2 becomes a three-model plot combining answer formats. Numerous earlier diagnostic and training plots disappear. Result tables change model columns and category structure, naturalness ratings gain paired columns, and new training-distribution tables and consistently styled example/code boxes substantially alter presentation.

R1.justification: The literature coverage is substantially refocused. V1's AutoPlanBench/data-generation connection, multimodal RAC discussion and much broader agent/reasoning literature are removed. V2 adds zero-shot-CoT, newer model and reasoning-benchmark references, prompt-format bias and long-context explanations. The central comparison with PlanBench and TRAC persists, including material previously discussed in v1's appendix.

T1.justification: The eight retained domains' state-space expressions move from v1 Appendix G to v2 Appendix F essentially unchanged. Expressions for the five removed domains disappear, and the explicit planning-instance and nested-transition definition in v1 Appendix F.18 is shortened in v2 Appendix G. No new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: V2 adds deeper ramification tests, updated model comparisons, paired fluency assessment and clearer technical documentation. However, it removes obfuscation controls and the code/data link, while replacing the free-answer evaluator without reporting the human-agreement evidence promised in Section 4 and Appendix E. Appendix C also gives validation sample counts inconsistent with eight domains. These substantive gains and unresolved losses prevent a reliable net quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ACTIONREASONINGBENCH. Their text, figures, tables, equations and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions to benchmark coverage and experiments.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark evaluations, fine-tuning results, paraphrase naturalness ratings and GPT-4o/o1-preview ramification experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original LLM evaluations, fine-tuning experiments, human assessments and diagnostic analyses in Sections 4–5 and the appendices.

title: ActionReasoningBench: Reasoning about Actions with and without Ramification Constraints

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same benchmark contribution, coverage, complex-question performance deficit, and headline ramification claims. The shortened conclusion does not redefine the contribution. Notably, the zero-success claim for GPT-4o remains unqualified despite the newly reported binary successes.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations linking inconsistent state-space complexity trends to different LLM heuristics, PDDL performance to pretraining, and templated-input advantages to reduced verbal reasoning demands. Appendix F discusses semantic-similarity scoring failures. The existing six limitations are largely retained, moving from Section 7 to Appendix A.

D1.justification: Section 4 newly clarifies that model evaluations exclude external tools and formal solvers. Table 4 explains missing responses as resulting from longer prompts. These are limited disclosures; existing hardware, optimizer, epochs, batch settings, context limit, and evaluator prompt remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The same eight domains and six question categories remain. v3 extends evaluated scenarios to PDDL and templated inputs in Appendix K and binary questions with ramification constraints in Table 4; v2 reported ramification results only for free answers.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain GPT-4o, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B, and the GPT-4o/o1-preview ramification pairing. Added experiments reuse these models; newly cited benchmarks are not experimentally evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: v3 adds supplementary protocols: Appendix K samples 10% of the test set for input-format experiments, and Appendix F evaluates free answers with F1-BERTScore. The original splits, sequence lengths, prompting conditions, accuracy evaluation, and fine-tuning budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix K introduces input-format sensitivity tests using PDDL and templated language. Appendix F adds concrete cases where BERTScore undervalues a correct paraphrase or rewards an incorrect answer. Detailed domain and fluent breakdowns also supplement previously discussed analyses, substantially expanding diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions report standard errors of the mean using the same stated formula. New tables extend this reporting practice without introducing repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Existing accuracy tables retain their values after relocation. Substantial new results appear in Tables 8–10, 15, 17, and 18. Table 4 adds GPT-4o binary ramification accuracies of 80.95%, 57.14%, and 57.14% at sequence lengths 1, 10, and 19, alongside unchanged zero free-answer accuracy. These are additional conditions and results, not same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: The four-stage PDDL/ASP question-generation and paraphrasing pipeline, ramification construction, and separate binary/free-answer fine-tuning procedures are retained. The additional evaluations do not introduce a new algorithm or model component.

P1.justification: Related work is locally rewritten, selected explanations are refined, and the conclusion is shortened. Limitations move to Appendix A, the results appendix gains subsections, and acknowledgements and publication headers are added. Most methodological and appendix prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: v3 adds a fluent-category plot, six supplementary result tables, and two scoring-example boxes. The ramification table expands to separate free-answer and binary columns. The original binary accuracy table moves into Appendix C, while the existing question-category plot is retained as Figure 3. These substantially expand and reorganize the evidence displays.

R1.justification: Section 2 expands the RAC-versus-planning comparison and discusses parallel ACPBench, adding Natural Plan and TravelPlanner references. New analyses cite McCoy et al. and BERTScore. Guan et al. (2023) and Valmeekam et al. (2024b) are removed, while PlanBench remains. The central research positioning is retained.

T1.justification: The fluent definitions, transition-function description, PDDL specifications, and state-space complexity expressions (1)–(8) are retained in renumbered appendices. No new formal derivation or proof is introduced; the added complexity discussion interprets empirical behavior.

improvement.justification: v3 makes previously discussed domain and fluent behavior more auditable and adds useful tests of input-format sensitivity and scoring failures. These provide a limited improvement in diagnostic support. Important reporting problems constrain the gain: the abstract and conclusion still imply universal GPT-4o ramification failure despite Table 4's binary successes, and Appendix K does not report a matched natural-language baseline for its sampled subset.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ACTIONREASONINGBENCH. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, equations, and appendices support comparison; relocated and renumbered material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds binary ramification results, input-format experiments, and supplementary scoring analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original model evaluations, fine-tuning results, ramification experiments, and human ratings of question naturalness.

title: ActionReasoningBench: Reasoning about Actions with and without Ramification Constraints

C1.justification: Both versions retain the central claims of dynamic, semantically complete visual tokens and a generalist MLLM covering understanding, generation, segmentation and editing. v3's introduction and conclusion revise the contribution description to emphasize explicit contrastive alignment and unified autoregressive training, while dropping v1's introductory claim of easy integration into established MLLMs with minimal adaptation.

C2.justification: v3 develops new explanations connecting reconstruction-only training to insufficient semantic learning, encoder unfreezing to recovery of low-level detail, and concept tokens to editing operations. v1's explanations of threshold generalization and CNN receptive-field limitations disappear with those analyses. Appendix B also revises applicability limits from 7B/13B and 336 resolution to 7B and 384 resolution.

D1.justification: v3 substantially revises implementation and training documentation: Transformer depths, token dimensions, detokenizer and diffusion-MLP construction, fuller dataset sizes, bfloat16 precision and gradient accumulation are specified. Reported hardware changes from 16 A800 GPUs to 16 H100 GPUs, and training recipes are replaced. Some earlier details, including the one-epoch entries, disappear; the project-page access information remains unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds ImageNet reconstruction/classification evaluation and explicit in-context and multi-image reasoning demonstrations. MA5K replaces Emu-Edit, while NoCaps, VSR, IconQA, VizWiz, TextQA and MMBench evaluations disappear. Training coverage also changes substantially, including ImageNet/OpenImages tokenizer supervision and SlimPajama text training. POPE, MME and MM-Vet are retained from v1's separate benchmark table.

E2.justification: v3 adds NExT-GPT, CM3Leon and Chameleon to understanding comparisons; ReLA and SEEM enter quantitative segmentation comparisons while GLaMM and MiniGPT-v2 leave them. LaVIT and Morph-Token enter generation/editing comparisons. Table 3 introduces a separate tokenizer comparator suite, and Appendix E adds MLP and Q-former connector controls alongside the retained Resampler comparison.

E3.justification: The reported configurations change from Vicuna-v1.5 at 7B/13B with ViT-G/14-336 or ConvNext-XXL to LLaMA-2-7B with SigLIP at 384 resolution. Training tables revise learning rates, weight decay, warmup and per-GPU batch size. New evaluations introduce ImageNet rFID/Top-1 and MA5K LPIPS. These settings prevent treating the revised benchmark scores as matched-setting performance changes.

E4.justification: v1's positional-encoding and merger ablations are retained but expanded in v3 Table 6 to contrastive loss and inner/inter-cluster Transformers across reconstruction, understanding and generation. v3 adds encoder-freezing and controlled connector studies. Conversely, v1's threshold-clustering analysis, CNN-versus-ViT analysis and small-data retrofit experiments on Emu, LLaVA and Yi-VL are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or run-to-run uncertainty. v1's feature-score distribution plot concerns clustering behavior rather than uncertainty in reported model performance; average token counts likewise do not constitute repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and expanded. For example, the reported 7B VQAv2/GQA scores change from 79.6/64.4 in v1 Table 1 to 78.7/65.6 in v3 Table 1, under changed configurations. v3 newly reports ImageNet rFID 2.07 and Top-1 accuracy 76.4, alongside revised segmentation, editing and ablation results. These are revised-system outcomes, not isolated performance gains.

M1.justification: v3 adds inter-cluster Transformers and concept-level contrastive training, replaces v1's Q-former/Stable Diffusion reconstruction pipeline with a Transformer-based detokenizer, and uses a diffusion loss for visual next-token generation instead of embedding MSE. Appendix C also changes cluster assignment through a sigmoid and seed-score penalty. These change the proposed procedure beyond renaming the cluster and merger.

P1.justification: The methodology, introductory contribution narrative and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. v3 introduces a separate Settings section, promotes expanded ablations into the main text and reorganizes the method appendix. Separating tokenizer training from SETOKIM's two stages replaces v1's unified three-stage presentation; that regrouping alone does not establish removal of a training stage.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the introductory tokenizer comparison and provides separate SeTok and SETOKIM architecture diagrams. It consolidates understanding tables, restructures generation/editing tables with representation and decoder columns, and adds tokenizer-quality and expanded ablation displays. Token-mask and reconstruction examples change, and new generation, captioning and multi-image panels appear. Several earlier qualitative panels are retained with renumbering and edits.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands methodological positioning around TiTok, GroupViT and autoregressive generation with diffusion loss, and compares against newer systems including Morph-Token and Chameleon. Its tokenizer-quality discussion explicitly contrasts spatial grids and fixed one-dimensional latents with SeTok. The existing scene-decomposition discussion and first-solution novelty claim largely remain; citation-style changes alone are not counted.

T1.justification: v3 adds the formal concept-level contrastive objective in Appendix C.2, substitutes kernel values for Euclidean distances in the density/distance definitions, and revises Algorithm 1's seed selection and mask updates. These are substantive mathematical changes, although neither version supplies theorems or proofs. The two purported contrastive directions in v3 Equations 5-6 are algebraically identical as printed.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens the empirical argument with direct tokenizer evaluation, broader component ablations and comparisons controlling the encoder and training data. However, its new central contrastive objective is not unambiguously specified: Appendix C.2 prints identical expressions for the two claimed directions. MagicBrush is also newly listed as training data while Table 2 retains a zero-shot editing label. The PDFs do not resolve whether these reflect presentation errors or experimental differences. These methodological and reporting uncertainties prevent reliably weighing the added validation against its limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SeTok and SETOKIM under the same title and authorship. All 20 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v3, including Appendices A-E, support comparison through readable text, equations, tables and rendered figures.

after.justification: v3 reports original tokenizer reconstruction/classification results, SETOKIM benchmark results, component and encoder-freezing ablations, connector comparisons and qualitative demonstrations.

before.justification: v1 reports original SETOKIM benchmark results, clustering comparisons, component ablations, transfer experiments and qualitative outputs in the main text and Appendix E.

title: Towards Semantic Equivalence of Tokenization in Multimodal LLM

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: dynamically producing semantically complete visual tokens and integrating them into an MLLM for understanding, generation, editing, and segmentation. The added appendix evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v4 newly recommends a 7:3 language-to-vision mixture to limit language-performance degradation and interprets the matched-data comparison as support for better alignment. Appendix B expands the resolution limitation to discuss encoder fusion, low-resolution detail, and generalization; the model-scale and hallucination limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds detokenizer implementation details, clarifies reconstruction/alignment dataset roles and overlapping training sources, and documents baseline backbones, encoders, resolutions, and data sizes in Table 8. Reported hardware changes from 16 to 64 H100 80GB GPUs, and the project-page address is updated. Most existing hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v4 adds language-only knowledge evaluation on MMLU across humanities, STEM, social sciences, and other subjects, substantially broadening evaluation beyond the existing vision-language tasks. Table 14 also introduces a VQA benchmark labeled VisWiz. The previous benchmark coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v4 newly includes LLaMA-2-7B as a language-only comparator in Table 10. Existing multimodal, segmentation, and tokenizer comparator sets remain intact; Table 14 reuses LLaVA-1.5 under a new training-data control, while Table 8 documents existing baselines.

E3.justification: v4 introduces substantive evaluation controls: varying text/multimodal training proportions before instruction tuning and retraining SeTokIM on the same dataset as LLaVA-1.5 for visual-understanding comparisons. Table 7 also revises the reported LLaVA-595K sample count from 665K to 595K. These additions and reported corrections do not establish that all retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix E adds analyses of language retention versus training-data mixture and performance under matched training data. Table 11 extends the existing reconstruction-only ablation with a contrastive-only condition. The frozen-encoder and connector analyses are retained as Tables 12–13, and the segmentation examples are relocated rather than newly added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeat counts, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The averages across MMLU subject categories in v4 are performance summaries, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantive language-retention, contrastive-only, and matched-data results in Tables 10, 11, and 14. It also revises reported VQAv2 from 78.7 to 78.5, MS-COCO FID from 8.3 to 8.5, MagicBrush L1 from 6.3 to 6.9, and ImageNet Top-1 from 76.4 to 75.4 in Tables 1–3. The matched-data results, including GQA 63.8 versus LLaVA-1.5's 62.0, concern a newly reported training condition, not a version-to-version performance gain.

M1.justification: The dynamic clustering algorithm, token merger, reconstruction and contrastive objectives, autoregressive modeling, and mask decoder remain unchanged. Appendix D.1 expands the detokenizer description without establishing a revised procedure; the additional loss variants are experimental ablations.

P1.justification: v4 makes localized prose edits, expands implementation and limitations explanations, adds Appendix D.4 on baselines, and moves the segmentation discussion into Appendix E. Publication headers, affiliations, contact information, and acknowledgments are updated, while the overall narrative and section organization remain largely stable.

P2.justification: v4 adds four tables: baseline configurations, language-mixture results, loss ablations, and the matched-data comparison. Existing illustrations are retained and rearranged: v3's segmentation Figure 5 becomes appendix Figure 8, with editing, token-mask, and reconstruction figures renumbered and reflowed. These are localized display changes rather than a visual redesign.

R1.justification: v4 adds the Eagle citation to the resolution discussion and a dedicated SEED-X reference, while removing references including OMG-LLaVA and SEEM; SEEM remains in the experimental comparison. Most other reference changes update publication metadata for existing works. The central novelty positioning is retained.

T1.justification: Equations 1–7 and Algorithm 1 retain the same mathematical definitions, objectives, and clustering operations. No theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive derivation is added or revised.

improvement.justification: The added language-retention and loss analyses, matched-data LLaVA comparison, and clearer training-data and baseline documentation improve evidential support and transparency. The gain is limited by reporting defects: v4 still has conflicting VQAv2 values of 78.5 in Table 1 and 78.7 in Tables 12–13, and the new loss-ablation Table 11 incorrectly carries an encoder-unfreezing caption. The method and central conclusions remain stable.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SeTok/SeTokIM research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–E support reliable comparison, including matching relocated analyses and renumbered displays.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds language-retention experiments, an additional loss ablation, and a comparison using the same training dataset as LLaVA-1.5.

before.justification: v3 reports original reconstruction, visual understanding, generation, editing, and segmentation results, together with component and tokenizer ablations.

title: Towards Semantic Equivalence of Tokenization in Multimodal LLM

C1.justification: The central steerability, locality and weight-sharing claims remain. However, the abstract and contributions expand claimed validation from reconstruction, classification and editing to fine-grained segmentation, forecasting and super-resolution/resolution transfer. The asserted applicability and downstream benefits therefore become substantially broader.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive qualifications about attention cost versus locality, insufficient shape reconstruction through meta-learning, and limited equivariance gains on aligned ShapeNet objects. Its class-only segmentation control supports a new interpretation involving positional shortcuts. It also discusses Functa overfitting on OMBRIA, initialization sensitivity and tentative parameter-efficiency benefits, extending v1's mainly general explanations of geometric representations.

D1.justification: Compared with v1's sparse experimental specifications, v4 Appendices A–C provide initialization guidance, autodecoding pseudocode, optimizer and learning-rate settings, RFF bandwidths, architecture sizes, training budgets, preprocessing and H100 hardware information. Section 6 and embedded links add implementation and data-access information, reporting partial experimental code availability while promising the remaining code.

E1.justification: CIFAR10 and CelebA remain, while STL10 disappears and ImageNet1K is added. The earlier 10-class ShapeNet study becomes 16-class occupancy/classification/part-segmentation and 55-class SDF evaluations. New domains include multimodal OMBRIA flood mapping and ERA5 temperature forecasting, with missing-observation and changed-resolution test scenarios.

E2.justification: v4 adds reported comparisons with PointNet, PointNet++, DGCNN and NF2vec for shape segmentation, OmbriaNet for flood mapping, and an identity forecasting reference. Functa remains. The earlier ENF-abs-rel-pos/norm-rel-pos variant disappears from image comparisons, while translation and PONITA roto-translation variants remain under new names. The non-equivariant control changes from absolute coordinates x to concatenated pose and coordinate inputs.

E3.justification: Reported CIFAR10 latent configurations change from 16 points of dimension 32 to 25 of dimension 64; CelebA changes from 25 of dimension 128 to 36 of dimension 64. The downstream classifier changes from four layers using rotational invariants to three layers using attributes matched to the ENF. Added experiments introduce segmentation-specific evaluation, one-hour forecasting, observation subsampling and zero-shot resolution-transfer protocols.

E4.justification: v4 adds a roughly fixed-parameter latent-count/context-dimension ablation (Appendix D.1), a shape-segmentation control using only object class (D.2), and OMBRIA sparsity and resolution-transfer tests. Conversely, v1's shape stitching and appendix CelebA clustering, latent mixing and interpolation demonstrations are removed. Transformation and car–duck stitching demonstrations remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The additional class/instance averages and random sampling descriptions in v4 do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Image reconstruction values change: translation-equivariant CIFAR10 PSNR is 34.8 in v1 Table 1 and 42.2 in v4 Table 1 under revised model settings, while its classification accuracy remains 82.1%. Shape results are replaced by different class/modality settings. Substantial new results include segmentation, robustness, ablation and forecasting outcomes, such as OMBRIA full-observation IoU of 74.00 and ERA5 forecast MSE of 9.44e-06.

M1.justification: The bi-invariant cross-attention and FiLM backbone remains, but v4 introduces attention restricted to each coordinate's k nearest latents. It also specifies new downstream procedures: a second ENF for segmentation and a latent-update PONITA model for forecasting, including a reconstruction-error-aware forecasting objective (Section 4.2 and Appendix C.1). These substantially extend the implemented procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and background are extensively rewritten. Encoding background and meta-learning pseudocode move into an expanded appendix; the method is reorganized into architecture and latent acquisition, and experiments are reorganized around reconstruction and downstream tasks. A reproducibility section and structured technical appendices replace the earlier brief experimental appendix.

P2.justification: v4 substantially redesigns the introductory and method schematics, adds a locality illustration, combines image reconstruction/classification into one table, and introduces segmentation and forecasting displays. Several earlier editing figures disappear, while retained transformation and stitching examples receive revised panels or annotations. Table arrangements, captions, typography and page layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: The principal lineage through Functa, cross-attention neural fields and PONITA remains. v4 adds Spatial Functa as context for global-latent limitations and neural ideograms/Kendall shape VAEs as inspiration, while dropping the earlier Field2Vec/metanetwork motivation. Additional neural-field and dataset references broaden the context without fundamentally changing the method's positioning.

T1.justification: The steerability/bi-invariance lemma and its proof are retained. The written Gaussian-window definition changes from a positive squared-distance term in v1 Section 3.4 to a negative squared-distance bias using positional pose components in v4 Section 3.1. This is a limited mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: v4 resolves important evidential weaknesses: v1 Table 3 juxtaposes ENF SDF reconstruction with Functa voxel reconstruction, whereas v4 Table 2 compares both methods within each representation. New fine-grained tasks, robustness tests and the ShapeNet shortcut control substantially strengthen evaluation, while detailed appendices improve reproducibility. Some editing evidence is lost and reporting errors remain, including the CIFAR10 sentence using 68.7 where Table 1 gives Functa 68.3. Nevertheless, the stronger comparison design and technical documentation establish a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Equivariant Neural Fields work, with matching core definitions and experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: v4 reports original reconstruction, classification, segmentation and forecasting experiments, with additional robustness tests and appendix ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original image reconstruction, CIFAR10 classification and ShapeNet experiments, plus qualitative latent editing and clustering results in the main text and Appendix A.

title: Grounding Continuous Representations in Geometry: Equivariant Neural Fields

C1.justification: The abstract extends the claimed empirical validation to generative modelling. The introduction also narrows separation of shape/geometry from appearance to separating aspects of geometry, specifically feature poses. The central steerability, weight-sharing and localized-representation contributions remain intact.

C2.justification: v5 substantially expands mechanism and applicability discussion: kNN is interpreted as implicit windowing, pose-free latent instability is linked to globally coupled optimization, and runtime differences are attributed to architectural depth. It also acknowledges stronger specialist generative methods and instability when diffusing poses, while adding benefits of global latent representations to the introduction.

D1.justification: Appendix C.4 provides substantial new diffusion implementation details, including conditioning, noise schedule, optimizer, training budget and sampling. C.1-C.2 clarify classifier training and disclose Functa's downstream residual MLP; D.5 identifies the profiling procedure. The abstract adds a submission-code repository link alongside the retained minimal repository. Conversely, v4's explicit ShapeNet16 train/test counts are omitted.

E1.justification: v5 adds unconditional image generation on CIFAR10 and CelebA64×64, substantially extending task coverage beyond reconstruction, classification, segmentation and forecasting. These datasets were already used in v4; the addition concerns task requirements rather than new datasets. Existing coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Table 7 introduces a generative comparison with GEM, GASP and DPF alongside Functa, adding a distinct family of comparison methods. Table 2 also adds NF2vec to ShapeNet16 classification, reporting 93.3% accuracy; v4 included NF2vec only in segmentation comparisons. Existing comparator sets are otherwise retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include FID evaluation using 50,000 generated samples, 200-epoch diffusion training and 512-step sampling; controlled locality and pose-removal experiments; and FLOP, memory and runtime comparisons using three MAML inner steps and batch size 32. Appendix C.2 also confines the previously broadly stated shallow-Functa setting to shape experiments, revising the reported setting without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices D.2, D.4 and D.5 add substantial tests of Gaussian windowing versus kNN, geometry-free latent sets, and computational costs with and without kNN. The Gaussian-window-only condition remains TBD in Table 9. The original latent-size and shape-information ablations are retained; the transformation visualization is relocated rather than newly added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or formal significance tests. The new generation sample count specifies evaluation size, not repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: v5 adds ENF generation FIDs of 33.8 on CelebA64×64 and 23.5 on CIFAR10, new locality and pose-removal results, and resource measurements, including 207 seconds per epoch for kNN ENF versus 2864 for Functa. Table 10 reports pose-free accuracy of 47.9%, while its prose says 0.47. Retained benchmark scores and relocated ShapeNet results are unchanged.

M1.justification: The core ENF architecture, locality mechanism, kNN approximation and encoding algorithms remain unchanged. Appendix C.4 adds a downstream generative procedure: DiT-B diffuses context vectors while retaining poses, then generates samples using poses drawn from training examples and DDIM denoising. This is a limited procedural extension.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence remain intact. v5 expands introductory motivation and attribution, condenses shape-experiment descriptions, adds acknowledgements and appendix subsections, and changes the publication header. The narrative editing is limited despite the added scientific content.

P2.justification: v5 adds generation samples and four new result tables, and substantially reorganizes experimental displays. improvement.justification: The added physiological checks and recurrent-model comparison provide useful validation and context missing from v2. before.justification: v2 reports original neural-response prediction experiments on M1S1 and M2S1, including model comparisons, incremental-learning experiments, and appendix analyses.

title: MMFakeBench: A Mixed-Source Multimodal Misinformation Detection Benchmark for LVLMs

Section 7 newly explains obstacles to extending the framework to Clebsch–Gordan and polynomial models, and explains why bias-free GNNs receive only separation bounds. These extend v1's more general discussion of assumptions and applicability.

E6.justification: Neither version reports empirical measurements, benchmark scores, or experimental qualitative findings. The added separation-power relations are formal results assessed under T1 and C1.

This is a targeted revision to the analytical procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution summary, motivation, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Separability motivation moves before the preliminaries, 'neural spaces' becomes organizing terminology, and the main results are reorganized by architectural factor. Proofs move into an extensively restructured set of appendices, accompanied by expanded explanations and examples.

The title, author block, heading typography, and running headers change, but the basic single-column layout remains and no result tables or empirical plots are introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 improves checkability through corrected affine-space assumptions, explicit bias partitions, fuller derivations, and concrete theoretical applications. However, its new Proposition 4 and the proof of Proposition 3 in Appendix B.3 rely on H-invariance of the entire output representation R^{G/H}; the paper's coset action does not justify this for an arbitrary subgroup H. The substantive clarifications therefore coexist with a reliability problem in added orbit/separation results, preventing a confident net quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, title, and central separation-power framework. The complete main texts, equations, diagrams, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 remains theoretical throughout, including Appendices A–E. Its IGN and circular-CNN applications are mathematical deductions, not empirical evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports mathematical definitions, theorems, proofs, and conceptual illustrations. Its main text and Appendix A contain no original experimental, simulation, user-study, or data-analysis outcomes.

title: Schur's Positive-Definite Network: Deep Learning in the SPD cone with structure

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same principal claims: a generic SPD-preserving architecture supporting additional structure, joint SPD/sparsity guarantees, and effective sparse precision estimation. Added experiments support these existing claims.

Appendix B.3 discusses why the tested GLAD repairs fail, while the conclusion adds computational cost and eigenvalue dynamics as unresolved research directions.

D1.justification: Sections 5 and 7 replace submission-only code and prospective-release statements with an explicit repository link for the PyTorch implementation. Appendix A's architecture descriptions and hyperparameters remain unchanged.
