E3.justification: Appendix B.3 adds two testing procedures: projecting GLAD-Z onto the PSD cone and masking GLAD-Theta using Z's support. The added Animals GLAD comparator is trained on the same data as UBG. Existing splits, metrics, and Appendix A settings are retained.

E4.justification: New Figure 9 tests whether simple post-processing remedies GLAD's constraint failures, examining sparsity and minimum eigenvalues after projection or thresholding. The existing normalization-instability and GLAD positive-definiteness-frequency analyses remain.

E5.justification: The existing shaded variability bands and statistical reporting practices are retained. v4 adds no repeated-run counts, seed information, uncertainty definitions, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: Figure 6 adds GLAD modularity of 0.72; UBG 0.78, GLasso 0.61, and EGFM 0.86 are unchanged. New Figure 9 shows projection reducing sparsity from 51.6% to 0% with minimum eigenvalue 0, and thresholded Theta having minimum eigenvalue -0.231. Figures 4–5 retain their result curves.

M1.justification: The Schur-based updates, inverse maintenance, UBG/PNP/E2E architectures, training objective, and stabilization procedure are unchanged. The added explanation of the diagonal network's inputs does not change those inputs or its procedure.

P1.justification: There are localized explanatory additions concerning block inversion, the GLasso objective, controllable constraints, and network inputs, plus revisions to the conclusion and code-access statements. Section order and most prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Figure 4 moves its legend above enlarged panels, and Figure 5 is resized. Figure 6 is redrawn from three panels in one row to four panels in a 2-by-2 arrangement. Figure 9 is added, with accompanying figure relocations and page reflow.

R1.justification: The bibliography and related-work discussion are unchanged. The positioning around joint SPD and sparsity guarantees is retained; the additional GLAD evaluations provide evidence for that existing position.

T1.justification: Propositions 3.1–3.2, their mathematical arguments, and the spectral-stability derivation are retained. The added parenthetical in Proposition 3.2's proof spells out block identities already present in the inversion formula.

improvement.justification: v4 strengthens the Animals evaluation by including a learned GLAD comparator and directly examines whether simple post-processing resolves GLAD's constraint failures in Figure 9. Clearer technical explanations and explicit code-access information also improve usability. These are useful, targeted gains while the core method, theoretical results, and existing benchmark findings remain stable.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SpodNet research. Their main text, equations, figures, and Appendices A–B are readable and support reliable matching despite figure revisions and pagination changes.

after.justification: v4 retains these original experiments and additionally reports GLAD's Animals result and empirical diagnostics of post-processing GLAD outputs.

before.justification: v2 reports original synthetic precision-matrix recovery experiments, Animals graph-learning results, and training-stability and GLAD diagnostics in Appendix B.

title: Schur's Positive-Definite Network: Deep Learning in the SPD cone with structure

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion narrow the central claim from parametric hypersurfaces with a separate star-like Cartesian extension to star-like manifolds themselves. Exact, efficient Jacobian evaluation and the Objective Bayesian and simplex-inference applications remain central, with greater emphasis on variational inference from unnormalized targets.

C2.justification: v2 explains the tested MCMC sampler's difficulties through sparse mass near simplex boundaries and discusses target-specific limitations of sampler comparisons. It explicitly qualifies the objective prior as preferable when less information is desired, rather than generally better, and connects the dimensionality limitation to the proof's rank condition. Existing regression and portfolio interpretations remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies new target specifications, sampler-construction details and computational-budget information. Existing layer configurations, Adam training, RTX2080Ti hardware and the FlowConductor link remain. Conversely, the portfolio reference loses v1's explicit Mendeley dataset identifier, 10.17632/gx66wsgwkr.1, replacing it with a journal citation and making direct data access less explicit.

E1.justification: The regression and portfolio tasks are retained. v2 adds three spherical density targets—a von Mises–Fisher distribution, a 50-component spiral mixture and a sinusoidal checkerboard—and conjugate Dirichlet–multinomial posterior inference. These substantially extend the evaluated scenarios; the newly discussed ecological and geoscientific applications are not themselves evaluated.

E2.justification: v2 introduces the first direct comparison against another inference algorithm: an ad-hoc Metropolis–Hastings sampler with Dirichlet proposals, evaluated against the flow and an analytical posterior in Appendix A.6.4, Figure 9. This substantially extends comparison beyond the retained prior-choice and flow-posterior illustrations. The cited simplex-sampling papers are not separately evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New protocols include density MSE evaluation over 10,000 samples and conjugate-posterior comparisons at dimensions 15, 30 and 50. The MCMC experiment specifies 1,000 chains with 100,000 samples each, matched runtime and approximately matched memory within 20%. These are added experimental designs; the documented regression generation, architectures and 10-stock, 200-time-step portfolio setting remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix A.6.4 adds checks of sampler performance across dimensions, alternative proposals and fivefold longer sampling time. These provide focused evidence about persistent difficulties with sparse posteriors. The earlier prior-sensitivity, MAP solution-path and portfolio sparsity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report 95% posterior intervals; v2 Figure 9 extends this existing reporting practice to another experiment. Neither adds repeated-training-run variability, seed summaries or significance tests. The new MCMC chain and sample counts describe its sampling protocol rather than uncertainty across experimental repetitions.

E6.justification: v2 newly reports density MSEs of 0.013, 0.011 and 0.024 for the three targets in Section 5.1. Figure 9 adds posterior comparisons showing close flow agreement with the analytical reference and discrepancies for the tested MCMC sampler at dimensions 30 and 50. Existing regression and portfolio results are retained, including v1 Figure 9 as v2 Figure 10; these additions are not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: v2 drops the separately proposed direct graph-hypersurface flow from v1 Section 3.1, narrowing the presented method family. The retained star-like construction still uses angular bijections, radius padding and spherical-to-Cartesian conversion, with unchanged reverse-KL training and documented architectures.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled and Section 3 is reorganized around star-like manifolds and one central theorem. The introduction, background, proof exposition and mixing-model discussion are extensively rewritten; spherical-coordinate definitions move to the appendix. Terminology changes from Bayesian mixture models to probabilistic mixing models, and the application and appendix structures are revised.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document template, title and author layout, headers and heading styles. It removes v1's graph-flow architecture figure, adds the density-reconstruction panels in Figure 3 and the MCMC comparison in Figure 9, and relocates or resizes retained figures with revised captions. The cumulative-return plot is retained as Figure 10 rather than newly added.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through conformal embedding flows, manifold-distribution literature, geometric accounts of objective priors, and mixing-model and simplex-sampling research. In particular, Ross and Cresswell (2021) are acknowledged as an existing exact, tractable approach under restrictive transformations, qualifying v1's presentation of prior exact methods.

T1.justification: v1's parametric-hypersurface definition, standalone graph-flow Theorem 1 and its Appendix A.3 proof are removed. Its star-like Theorem 2 survives as v2 Theorem 1 with essentially the same central result. v2 also removes the Sherman–Morrison derivation and changes the stated Gaussian-elimination cost from O(d) to O(d²). Moving spherical-coordinate definitions to the appendix does not constitute new theory.

improvement.justification: v2 improves empirical checkability through known-target density errors and analytical-posterior comparisons, while clarifying prior-work positioning and applicability qualifications. These strengthen evidence that v1 largely supplied through application illustrations. The gain remains limited: the comparative evidence concerns one ad-hoc sampler, the broader graph-hypersurface result is removed, and direct dataset access becomes less explicit. Overall, the added validation and clearer scope support a modest net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both complete, readable PDFs describe the same injective-flow research. Their main text, equations, figures and appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title, narrower focus and substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds spherical density-reconstruction results and a comparison against an MCMC sampler using an analytically known posterior.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic regression and portfolio experiments, including posterior intervals, solution paths and sparsity analyses in Figures 4–9 and Appendix A.6.

title: Injective flows for star-like manifolds

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the same central claims: exact, efficient injective flows for star-like manifolds and applications to objective Bayesian inference and mixing models. The conclusion adds empirical support for efficiency and exact-Jacobian importance, both already claimed in v2.

C2.justification: v3 clarifies the consequences of coordinate singularities for exact density evaluation and numerical stability, and explicitly motivates its focus on variational inference through the codimension-one restriction. Existing dimensionality and expressivity limitations remain. Learning the radial function from observations is still discussed in Appendix A.5.

D1.justification: v3 documents small angular offsets near singularities and expands the circular-spline implementation description, including rational-quadratic segments and periodic boundaries. It identifies the approximation implementation and specifies Sinkhorn blur=0.05. Existing architecture sizes, Adam settings, GPU information and FlowConductor access information are retained.

E1.justification: Synthetic coverage expands to uniform-density learning on an lp manifold with p=0.5, and the spherical checkerboard example is replaced by a sinusoidal density on a deformed sphere. The regression, conjugate mixing-model and 10-stock, 200-step portfolio coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v3 adds direct computational comparators absent from v2: explicit determinant computation using Eq. (2), and otherwise identical flows trained with Hutchinson-estimated Jacobian gradients. The latter use the implementation attributed to Sorrenson et al. (2024), with several estimator sample counts. These substantially extend comparison beyond the retained prior-choice and MCMC experiments.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 introduces controlled comparisons across dimensions 3, 10, 50 and 100 and Gaussian estimator sample counts 1, 10, 50 and 100, subject to the stated dimensionality bound. Both training variants use exact Jacobians at evaluation; metrics include log-density MSE, energy-distance MMD, Sinkhorn divergence and runtime. The third 3D target also changes from 2 sin(6θ) sin(6ϕ) to sin(4θ) sin(4ϕ). Existing regression and MCMC settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Figures 3 and 10 directly test the importance of exact Jacobian training by holding the flow architecture fixed and varying the approximation sample count and dimension. They assess density accuracy, sample quality and computational cost. v3 also adds an empirical scaling analysis of determinant computation; v2's prior-sensitivity and MCMC analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v3 reports 20 repetitions for the new determinant-timing experiment and displays variability in the added comparisons. This does not establish increased repetition of earlier experiments. Existing 95% posterior intervals remain unchanged; training-run counts and the definitions of the new error bars are not fully specified.

E6.justification: New results report fitted runtime scaling of approximately d^2.96 for explicit computation versus d^1.81 for the proposed approach, and better density and sample-quality scores with exact Jacobian training. The first two 3D examples retain MSEs 0.013 and 0.011. The old checkerboard MSE of 0.024 disappears when that experiment is replaced by a qualitatively evaluated deformed-sphere example. Bayesian and portfolio results are retained.

M1.justification: The angle flow, radial embedding, spherical-to-Cartesian transformation, exact determinant formula and reverse-KL training objective remain unchanged. Expanded spline explanations and newly documented numerical safeguards do not establish a revision to the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: Section 3.3 becomes Further Details and Limitations with separate explanatory paragraphs, and a new Section 5.1 precedes the existing applications. Appendix mixing-model material moves from A.6.4 to A.7.1. There are localized prose edits and updated publication headers, while most narrative and section ordering remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds the runtime/accuracy panels in Figure 3 and sample-quality/runtime panels in Figure 10, and redraws the third illustrative-density example. Figure 1 is smaller, and retained figures are renumbered or relocated, including the final appendix plots. The overall visual format and most existing displays remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to Kothari et al. (2021) and Munkres and Spivak (1965), and removes Cayton (2005) and Krantz and Parks (2008). The related-work discussion and positioning against approximate injective flows remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Sections 2 and 3.2 add the relaxed change-of-variables condition of a diffeomorphism almost everywhere and explain why measure-zero coordinate singularities preserve the density calculation. Theorem 1, its quadratic-complexity argument, and the definitions, lemmas and proofs in Appendices A.1–A.4 otherwise remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 closes a central empirical gap: v2 argued for efficient, exact Jacobians without directly testing their computational advantage and training benefit against approximation. Section 5.1 and Figure 10 add controlled evidence on scaling, density accuracy and sample quality while retaining the original applications and proofs. The replacement 3D example loses quantitative scoring, and replication details remain incomplete, but these limitations are outweighed by substantially stronger evidence for the paper's central contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Injective Flows for Star-like Manifolds. Their main text, equations, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical applications and adds original runtime and exact-versus-approximate Jacobian experiments in Section 5.1 and Appendix Figure 10.

before.justification: v2 reports original density-reconstruction experiments, synthetic Bayesian regression, comparisons with MCMC, and portfolio results in Section 5 and Appendix A.6.

title: Injective flows for star-like manifolds

C1.justification: V2 makes minimally confounded, skill-specific diagnosis during iterative model development a central claim. It recasts the tasks around temporal perception, chronological ordering and spatio-temporal coherence, and adds model-training guidance to the stated contributions. V1 primarily emphasized comprehensive fine-grained, spatio-temporal and long-context evaluation.

C2.justification: Section 6 adds interpretations linking model scale, frame sampling and temporal prompts to particular capabilities, and uses token-density results to argue for primarily temporal assessment. Section 7 replaces v1's mainly future-expansion limitations with an explicit qualification that synthetic evaluation cannot fully reproduce authentic scenarios and should complement real-world benchmarks.

D1.justification: V2 Appendix F documents the trained SigLIP/Qwen2 model, training mixture, context length, batch size, component-specific learning rates and schedule. Appendix C.1 adds sampling and resolution details for new baselines. Conversely, v1's explicit dataset-license disclosure and VNBench-Long sample-count column disappear; the code/data link remains.

E1.justification: V2 adds original model-training experiments using Cauldron image-text instructions and ten video-text datasets, including ShareGPT4Video, TextVR and CLEVRER (Appendix F). This substantially expands the data actually used by the work. VNBench and VNBench-Long evaluation coverage remains unchanged.

E2.justification: V2 adds Qwen2-VL-7B and LLaVA-OneVision at 0.5B, 7B and 72B to the main and duration-specific comparisons (Tables 2 and 6). These additions substantially strengthen the evaluated open-model comparison set while retaining the original model families.

E3.justification: Section 6 introduces training-based protocols varying frame tokens from 25 to 196, sampled frames from 8 to 128, and temporal prompts, with stated controls. Benchmark scoring remains unchanged. V2 also labels the inherited 10.8 LLaMA-VID result as 7B, although v1 Table 4 associates it with 13B; an actual configuration change or rerun is not established.

E4.justification: V1's compact VideoChat2 sampling and LLaMA-VID size study is replaced by broader model-size, frame-count, token-density and temporal-prompt analyses in v2 Section 6. Token allocation and explicit temporal cues introduce new investigative questions. Existing needle-position, task-correlation and circular-evaluation robustness analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The one-to-four-iteration circular-evaluation analysis and its reporting remain unchanged (v1 Appendix H; v2 Appendix E). Neither version provides training-seed repetitions, confidence intervals or error bars, and v2 introduces no new uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: Shared main-table numerical entries are retained. Newly evaluated OneVision-72B scores 58.7 overall, making it the strongest reported open model versus ST-LLM's 22.7 in v1; Gemini remains at 66.7. V2 also adds substantial configuration-study results, including overall scores of 29.3–36.5 across temporal prompts, while removing v1 Table 4's specific ablation entries.

M1.justification: The proposed VideoNIAH construction procedure and instantiated VNBench tasks remain unchanged. CLIP filtering moves from v1 Appendix D.3 to v2 Section 3.3; it is not a new component. The additional model configurations serve the experimental analyses.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and task explanations are substantially rewritten. Detailed task construction moves into Appendix A.4, filtering moves into the main text, and dedicated model-analysis and revised limitations sections reshape the narrative. The appendices are reorganized, with the societal-impact and accessibility sections removed.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn and a new construction overview becomes Figure 2; the original task diagram survives as Figure 13. V2 adds three model-analysis plots and new prompt/training tables, expands result tables, removes v1's benchmark-comparison table, and changes typography and page layout throughout.

R1.justification: V2 adds recent benchmark references, including VideoMME, MLVU, MMWorld and LongVideoBench, alongside new model and backbone references. More substantively, it develops a critique of comprehensive benchmarks for entangling multiple skills, expanding the positioning beyond v1's emphasis on construction cost and data leakage.

T1.justification: The work remains an empirical benchmark study with procedural task descriptions. V2 adds no substantive mathematical definitions, formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or derivations.

improvement.justification: V2 provides more useful evidence for model diagnosis through its controlled token, frame and prompt studies, and better qualifies synthetic evaluation's applicability. These support a limited net improvement over v1's smaller setting study. Gains are tempered by new reporting inconsistencies: OneVision-72B Counting-E2 is 14.7 in Table 2 but 36.0, 38.0 and 18.0 across Table 6's duration splits. The explicit dataset-license disclosure is also lost.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VideoNIAH and VNBench. Their complete main texts, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support matching retained, relocated and newly added content.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark results and adds evaluations of newer models and experiments involving model size, frame sampling, token density and temporal prompts.

before.justification: V1 reports original VNBench evaluations, model-setting experiments, task correlations, circular-evaluation robustness tests and VNBench-Long results.

title: Needle In A Video Haystack: A Scalable  Synthetic Evaluator for Video MLLMs

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about scalable synthetic construction, skill-specific evaluation, VNBench's three task families, and insights for video-model development. The new experiments support these claims without redefining their central scope.

C2.justification: Appendix J materially qualifies low-score comparisons: option-order sensitivity can affect circular accuracy, and Counting-E2 differences should not be interpreted as meaningful capability advantages. New discussion interprets real-benchmark correlations, construction robustness, and action-ordering failures. The existing Section 7 limitation about synthetic data complementing real-world benchmarks remains unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix G newly documents the visual-token and answer-loss computations and training for one epoch on 16 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Added analyses disclose sampling and replacement-needle details. Conversely, v3 removes the abstract's code/data availability statement and project link without replacing them elsewhere; the PDFs do not establish that the resources themselves became unavailable.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluation on VideoMME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench in Appendix B.2. VNBench-Act adds retrieval, ordering, and counting of action-bearing clips from Something-Something V2, extending evaluation beyond static-image and subtitle needles. Something-Something V2 already appeared in the training mixture; its new evaluation role is the coverage change.

E2.justification: The evaluated model families and size variants remain present in the corresponding VNBench comparisons. Added experiments use models already evaluated in v2. Appendix J adds a 25% chance reference but does not document an additional evaluated comparison method.

E3.justification: Figure 8 changes from binary extraction outcomes to accuracy averaged over 32 distinct samples. New protocols compare 1350 versus 2700 samples, replace needle content at matched positions, and evaluate six frame-count configurations across real-world benchmarks. Appendix J introduces consistency and conditional-accuracy metrics. The main four-pass circular evaluation remains unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds analyses testing agreement with real-world benchmarks, sensitivity to needle content and dataset size, and answer-option consistency across nine subtasks. It also revises the position-depth analysis using multiple samples. Existing model-configuration ablations and the one-to-four-pass circular-evaluation analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report correlation coefficients and one-to-four option-shuffled evaluations. v3 adds no seed information, independent-run uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. Averaging 32 distinct test samples changes evaluation design; the new consistency scores are evaluation metrics rather than uncertainty intervals.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial cross-benchmark, action, robustness, and consistency results. For example, Table 6 reports GPT-4o action retrieval, ordering, and counting scores of 85.6, 11.3, and 10.0. Main Table 2 remains unchanged, but the detailed 30–60-second LLaVA-OneVision-7B overall score changes from 69.8 to 60.0, ending its reported tie with 72B. Several counting cells are also corrected between v2 Table 6 and v3 Table 11.

M1.justification: The synthetic construction procedure, CLIP filtering, and core circular scoring rule remain unchanged. Dynamic video-clip needles were already allowed in v2 Section 3.1; VNBench-Act evaluates that possibility. Appendix G expands documentation of the retained training model without establishing an architecture or objective change.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include local wording and typo corrections, expanded training explanations, an acknowledgment section, conference headers, and appendix subdivisions accommodating the new analyses. There is no extensive rewrite of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: Figure 5 is redrawn with separately identified OneVision size variants, and Figure 8 replaces binary maps with annotated continuous-accuracy heatmaps and a color scale. v3 adds eight tables, a cross-benchmark correlation figure, and animal-needle illustrations. It also relocates existing plots and corrects illustrative options and table labels.

R1.justification: v3 adds ChatBridge and a brief discussion of integrating external modalities, a Something-Something citation, and Wang et al. and Wei et al. on multiple-choice evaluation and selection biases. The broader positioning against existing video benchmarks and synthetic language-model evaluations remains stable.

T1.justification: Appendix J introduces definitions of answer consistency and conditional accuracy, with the reasoning that circularly correct predictions form a subset of consistent predictions. This mathematical treatment is absent from v2. Appendix G also formalizes visual-token construction and the training loss, without introducing a new theorem or demonstrated method change.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the benchmark's validation: Appendix B.2 tests its relationship to real-world performance, F.2–F.3 examine construction sensitivity, and Appendix J explains why some low-score rankings are misleading. These address important evidential and interpretive gaps in v2. The validation remains limited to the tested configurations, while removal of the project link and Table 8's conflicting Ordering-I1/I2 labels weaken reproducibility. Nevertheless, the targeted evidence and more careful interpretation provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VideoNIAH and VNBench. Their complete main texts and appendices, including figures, tables, equations, and task examples, support reliable comparison. Retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds action-clip evaluations, comparisons with real-world benchmarks, construction-robustness tests, and answer-consistency analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original VNBench and VNBench-Long evaluations, task analyses, and experiments varying model size, frame sampling, visual tokens, and temporal prompts.

title: Needle In A Video Haystack: A Scalable  Synthetic Evaluator for Video MLLMs

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same principal claims: a first general domain-adaptive contextual-bandit method using source feedback, a sublinear target-regret guarantee, and superior empirical performance. Revised mathematics and additional supporting experiments do not change these stated claims.

C2.justification: The expanded discussion adds substantive explanations of bidirectional source/target learning, indirect parameter regularization and variance reduction, discriminator necessity, and why matching context distributions does not ensure matching reward relationships. It also explains advance availability of target contexts and interprets regret-term decay. The original limitations are retained after relocation.

D1.justification: Appendix D retains the PyTorch implementation, A5000 hardware, preprocessing, learning rates, exploration rates, and lambda search choices. Removing v1's checklist also removes its planned code-release statement and its claim that one GPU with 16 GB memory suffices. This changes disclosed reproducibility information without establishing any actual change in resource availability.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate MNIST-to-MNIST-M, synthetic-to-real VisDA17, and the same ten-class S2RDA49 subset. Both include zero-shot target evaluation and continued training with target feedback. Added discussion of possible applications does not introduce evaluated domains or tasks.

E2.justification: Tables 1–3 and Figure 1 retain the same LinUCB, LinUCB-P, NLinUCB, and NLinUCB-P participation, including LinUCB's omissions for memory limitations. Locally, Table 5 expands the ablation comparison with four additional variants removing data divergence, alone or together with the regularizers.

E3.justification: Table 5 extends the controlled evaluation from regression-error/predicted-reward removals to a three-component design that also removes adversarial alignment. Existing dataset splits, preprocessing, accuracy/regret metrics, 300/100-episode training budgets with 64 samples per episode, and the 1,920-round continued-training evaluation remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1's Table 4 tests only the regression-error and predicted-reward terms. v2 adds a full ablation table covering the data-divergence loss/discriminator and its combinations with those terms. This supplies substantial new evidence about the central alignment component and whether the other regularizers help without it.

E5.justification: Table 5 first supplies uncertainty values for previously reported ablation entries. Appendix E also introduces hypothesis-test results, reporting p-values from 3.201 × 10^-21 to 1.504 × 10^-2. The five-run, different-seed description for Figure 1 is unchanged; the new tests and the meaning of the uncertainty values are not specified.

E6.justification: Table 5 adds an important finding: removing alignment produces much lower accuracy, such as 0.1098 versus 0.4644 for full DABand on VisDA17. Tables 1–3 replace DABand averages of 0.5984/0.4428/0.3914 with 0.6002/0.4644/0.3923 alongside the revised objective. Some Table 4 ablation scores also change. Baseline scores and Figure 1 curves remain unchanged. v2's ablation prose retains numbers inconsistent with its revised Table 4.

M1.justification: The training objective changes substantively. Equation 8 replaces source-only predicted-reward regularization with target-domain regularization plus source regularization gated by incorrect actions; Equation 10 doubles the regression-error loss coefficient. Algorithm 1 also corrects the exploration norm to use the inverse context matrix. The encoder/discriminator and alternating-update framework remain.

P1.justification: The appendix narrative is substantially expanded and reorganized: a separate full-ablation appendix is introduced, and the discussion grows from three numbered subsections to eleven, including standalone explanations and contribution restatements. The submission checklist is removed. Main-text prose is largely retained, with smaller author, terminology, and citation-style edits.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 5, changes the conference template and running headers, and relocates Algorithm 1 and several tables. Table 4 moves away from its ablation discussion into the conclusion's layout. Existing table structures remain similar, and Figure 1 retains its curves, axes, and legends despite repositioning.

R1.justification: The cited research works and substantive positioning against single-domain bandits, offline domain adaptation, and Guo et al.'s domain-selection approach remain unchanged. Added novelty subsections largely restate the existing contribution; conversion to author-year citations does not add research coverage.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.1 and its appendix counterpart double the source-error term and replace the predicted-reward contribution with target and indicator-gated source terms. Appendix A introduces Lemmas A.4–A.6, rewrites the main proof, and replaces the previous remainder with sums involving newly defined kappa quantities. Lemma A.6 reasons using binary rewards, while the main setup still states rewards in [0,1]. Appendix G.9 adds asymptotic-rate reasoning.

improvement.justification: Table 5 fills a specific empirical gap by testing the alignment component that v1's ablations omitted, making the evidence more diagnostic. Added mechanism explanations also help readers assess the approach. These gains are limited by unresolved problems: the revised proof does not justify neglecting its summed remainder, significance tests are unspecified, and Section 5 still quotes 0.4238 where revised Table 4 reports 0.4096. The substantial theoretical revision therefore does not establish a corresponding improvement in rigor.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DABand research. Their main text, equations, tables, figure, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across revisions and relocations.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark and cumulative-regret results, revises accuracy results, and reports additional component ablations in Table 5.

before.justification: v1 reports original DABand experiments on DIGIT, VisDA17, and S2RDA49, including accuracy comparisons, cumulative-regret curves, and component ablations.

title: Towards Domain Adaptive Neural Contextual Bandits

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same main claims: a first general domain-adaptive contextual-bandit method, learning from source-only feedback, a sublinear target-regret bound and superior benchmark performance. The added uncertainty-quantification suggestion concerns future work.

C2.justification: Section 5 adds an explanation of LinUCB and NLinUCB failures through their lack of explicit domain alignment and the divergence term. Appendix G.1 adds an optimization-based explanation for sublinearity. Appendix F's existing limitations concerning alignment quality, domain shift and interpretability remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Algorithm 1 now explicitly names Adam for encoder and discriminator updates. The abstract adds a repository link with a promise that code will become available; this does not establish released code. Appendix D's preprocessing, hardware and hyperparameter information is unchanged.

E1.justification: Both evaluate MNIST-to-MNIST-M, VisDA17 synthetic-to-real adaptation and the same ten-class S2RDA49 subset. Zero-shot evaluation and continued training with target feedback are retained; Figure 2 identifies no additional dataset or task.

E2.justification: Tables 1–3 and Figure 1 retain LinUCB, LinUCB-P, NLinUCB and NLinUCB-P, with the same LinUCB out-of-memory exclusions. Tables 4–5 retain the same ablation variants. The newly discussed distributionally robust bandit work is not evaluated.

E3.justification: The documented splits, preprocessing, hyperparameters, 300/100-episode training budgets, 64-sample episodes and 1,920-round target evaluation are unchanged. Figure 2 adds component trajectories but does not document a separate or revised experimental protocol.

E4.justification: New Appendix G.1 and Figure 2 examine cumulative growth of individual regret-bound components and their sum against linear reference curves, addressing the sublinearity question. The existing regression-error, predicted-reward and discriminator ablations in Tables 4–5 are unchanged.

E5.justification: Both retain five runs with different random seeds for Figure 1, identical tabulated uncertainty values, and Appendix E's p-value range of 3.201e-21 to 1.504e-2. Figure 2 supplies no additional run-count, uncertainty or significance information.

E6.justification: Figure 2 adds plotted cumulative trajectories for source regret, regression error, predicted rewards, data divergence and the sum of other terms. All five tables and Figure 1 retain their results, including DABand average accuracies of 0.6002, 0.4644 and 0.3923 on the three benchmarks.

Appendix B.1 also qualifies the computational-efficiency discussion with measured overhead, including 11.2% on LSUN Bedroom.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's brief toy optimizer settings, v2 supplies a code-access link, pretrained-model sources, shared-backbone and prediction-head specifications, parameter counts, GPU hardware, AdamW training budgets, batch sizes, checkpoint selection, EMA, covariance clipping and evaluation details (Section 3.3 and Appendix B). E1.justification: V1 evaluates only the nine-Gaussian toy distribution and leaves image modelling to future work. V2 retains that task and adds CIFAR10, CelebA 64x64, LSUN Bedroom, ImageNet 64x64 and class-conditional ImageNet 256x256 generation using latent diffusion.

E5.justification: V1 provides no repeated-run counts or uncertainty summaries. E6.justification: V2 adds extensive likelihood, FID, recall, runtime and qualitative image results, while largely retaining the toy trends and removing three toy DDIM result curves. after.justification: V2 retains the toy experiments and reports original image-generation, likelihood, recall and computational-cost results, including Tables 3–5, 8, 11 and 12.

after.justification: v3 retains original OCM experiments and adds a forty-Gaussian demonstration, ground-truth covariance comparisons, and a Rademacher-sample ablation.

title: CBGBench: Fill in the Blank of Protein-Molecule Complex Binding Graph

C2.justification: v2 removes v1's limitation concerning unexploited internal model representations and its discussion of bias reinforcement. It also adds a catastrophic-forgetting interpretation of the retained continual-editing curves, without adding retention tests for earlier edits.

D1.justification: New Appendix C and Listing 1 disclose a prompt requesting five context statements, expanding v1's description of GPT-4-generated summaries. Existing implementation and hardware details remain. The listing references prompt before assigning it, limiting its executability.

E1.justification: Both evaluate WikiDatarecent, ZsRE, WikiBio, and WikiDatacounterfact under the same knowledge-editing and continual-editing scenarios. v2 corrects scattered references to five datasets without changing actual coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain ROME, MEMIT, FT-L, and FT-M. The unedited reference curves also remain; no evaluated comparator is added or removed.

E3.justification: Reported splits, Llama2-7b-chat and GPT2-xl configurations, edited layers, metrics, 25-step budget, and learning rate remain unchanged. Continual evaluation still assesses each edit immediately without retesting earlier edits.

E4.justification: Both retain the dynamic-target/context ablations, temperature and sample-length/count analyses, convergence and token-probability analysis, and qualitative examples. v1 Appendix B largely becomes v2 Appendix D without additional analyses.

E5.justification: Statistical reporting is unchanged. The tables retain point estimates, and v2 adds no repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Matched main, continual-editing, GPT2-xl, and ablation tables retain the same numerical results. The experimental plots and qualitative findings are also retained; figure rearrangement and table renumbering do not introduce new outcomes.

M1.justification: The stated objective changes from constrained KL optimization and an unweighted, target-conditioned decomposition in v1 Equations 5/7 to L_FT + lambda L_ICE in v2 Equation 6. This introduces an explicit balancing hyperparameter, but Algorithm 1 retains the same sampling and update steps; a changed experimental implementation is not established.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and methodology are substantially rewritten, including a running example and clearer optimization subsections. The separate Analysis section becomes Section 3.5 Discussion, Algorithm 1 moves to Appendix B, and the appendices are reorganized.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. The overview gains example annotations, the leading continual-editing figure is relocated and its panels rearranged, and Table 5 becomes side-by-side blocks. These constitute extensive display and layout changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds Brown et al. (2020) when defining in-context learning and elaborates the computational and scaling limitations of keeping updates in prompts. The existing editing literature and overall research positioning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: v1 Appendix A.3 and Equations 13–15, deriving the combined fine-tuning and target-conditioned contextual objective, are removed. The one-hot lemma, Observation 1 and its proof, and the locality/generalization assumptions remain.

improvement.justification: The clearer exposition and added context prompt improve accessibility, but v2 removes Appendix A.3's derivation connecting the sampler to its objective and introduces an unspecified lambda absent from the retained Algorithm 1. Removing the substantive limitations further weakens transparency. These technical reporting losses outweigh the presentation gains, while the empirical evidence remains unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ICE research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experimental results in Section 4 and Appendix D, including numerical comparisons, ablations, and generated-answer examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original knowledge-editing experiments on four datasets, including Llama2 and GPT2-xl results, ablations, convergence analyses, and continual editing.

title: In-Context Editing: Learning Knowledge from Self-Induced Distributions

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: contextual-distribution editing, dynamic target refinement, and empirical effectiveness including continual editing. The additional analysis does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds discussion of sampling and GPT-4 costs, potential error propagation from hallucinated contexts, and the assumption behind interpreting pretrained-model perplexity. It also interprets λ = 1 as optimal, although Table 5 shows tradeoffs in locality and fluency.

D1.justification: v3 explicitly discloses λ = 1 outside ablations and clarifies the pretrained model's role in perplexity evaluation. Appendix C fixes the context-generation snippet's query/prompt variable mismatch and supplies an example containing five generated contexts.

E1.justification: Both evaluate WikiDatarecent, ZsRE, WikiBio, and WikiDatacounterfact in single and continual editing. The new loss-weight study reuses ZsRE and WikiDatarecent; GPT2-xl evaluations were already present in v2's appendix.

E2.justification: ROME, MEMIT, FT-L, and FT-M remain the evaluated baselines in the corresponding main, GPT2-xl, and continual-editing comparisons. The newly cited methods are not added as experimental comparators.

E3.justification: The added Table 5 introduces a controlled sweep over λ = 0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2, and 1.4. Settings for retained experiments, including dataset splits, models, metrics, training budgets, and continual-editing procedures, remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 adds sensitivity analysis of the balance between fine-tuning and contextual consistency losses on two datasets. Existing component ablations, temperature and sampling studies, convergence analysis, and qualitative examples are retained.

E5.justification: No new seed counts, repeated-run information, uncertainty estimates, or significance-testing procedures are introduced. The added ablation reports point values, and the existing plots retain their reporting.

E6.justification: Previously reported benchmark, continual-editing, and appendix results retain their values. New Table 5 adds loss-weight results: for example, ZsRE PPLr is 15.50 at λ = 1.0, versus 281.14 at 0.8 and 324.47 at 1.2. These compare newly reported conditions, rather than demonstrating improved performance over v2.

M1.justification: Both versions sample continuations conditioned on context, query, and target, then optimize the combined target-and-continuation likelihood with detached contextual targets and clipped updates. Algorithm 1's revised KL expression makes the target prefix explicit, consistent with the sampling and likelihood update already specified in v2.

P1.justification: Localized wording and explanatory revisions accompany new Appendix A.3, Limitations, and Acknowledgement sections. Affiliations and the publication header are updated, while the overall narrative and section organization remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds the loss-weight ablation table and a boxed context example, corrects the conditional-probability label in Figure 1, and reflows existing tables, Algorithm 1, and appendix examples. The empirical plots themselves are unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to Mu et al. on gist tokens and Rozner et al. on editing through adapted direct preference optimization. Section 2.2 also expands the comparison with context distillation and gist-token methods, discussing model-copy and extra-token requirements.

T1.justification: New Appendix A.3 derives a λ = 1 decomposition into fine-tuning and contextual consistency conditioned on the query plus target; Algorithm 1's KL expression is revised accordingly. The earlier Observation 1 and proof remain unchanged. The new derivation's opening maximum-likelihood identity reverses the KL arguments.

improvement.justification: The added sensitivity study, disclosed default loss weight, corrected context-generation snippet, and explicit cost and hallucination limitations modestly improve reproducibility and critical assessment. The core empirical evidence is unchanged. The reversed KL identity in new Appendix A.3 and the overly broad description of λ = 1 as optimal limit the benefit of the added justification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ICE research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds results from a loss-weight sensitivity study in Table 5.

before.justification: v2 reports original Llama2-7b-chat and GPT2-xl experiments, including benchmark comparisons, ablations, continual editing, and qualitative results.

title: In-Context Editing: Learning Knowledge from Self-Induced Distributions

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements and conclusion retain the same claims about contextual-distribution learning, editing effectiveness, model preservation and potential for continual editing.

C2.justification: The mechanism explanations, experimental interpretations, dependence on context quality and model capabilities, computational caveats and limitation concerning hallucinated contexts are unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix C's context-generation code and the disclosed layer choices, hyperparameters, sampling details, hardware and data-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate WikiDatarecent, ZsRE, WikiBio and WikiDatacounterfact under the same individual and continual-editing scenarios. The changed presidential running example is illustrative and does not establish changed experimental coverage.

E2.justification: ROME, MEMIT, FT-L and FT-M retain their membership in the corresponding main, continual-editing and appendix comparisons. No evaluated comparator is added or removed.

E3.justification: Data splits, Llama2-7b-chat and GPT2-xl configurations, metrics, optimization budgets and continual-editing procedures are unchanged in Sections 4.1 and 4.4 and Appendix D.

E4.justification: The dynamic-target/context ablations, lambda and sampling sensitivity studies, convergence analyses and qualitative cases are unchanged in Sections 4.3-4.5 and Appendix D.

E5.justification: Statistical reporting is identical throughout the experimental material. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests for these experiments.

E6.justification: Results in Tables 2-13, Figures 2-6 and Appendix D.6 are unchanged. For example, Table 2 retains ICE's ZsRE edit success of 100.00 and PPLr of 15.50; the revised introductory example is not a reported experimental result.

M1.justification: The combined loss, dynamic target, sampling procedure and Algorithm 1 are unchanged. Figure 1's revised parameter index matches the iterative update already specified in v3's Equation 7.

P1.justification: v4 reverses the Biden/Trump running example and corresponding first-lady example, adds an equal-contribution marker for Kailin Jiang, and makes small punctuation and notation edits. Section organization and the broader narrative remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Figure 1 updates its example labels and changes the output-distribution parameter index from theta_s to theta_{s+1}. Its structure is retained, and all experimental figures and tables render identically.

R1.justification: The same 59 references and research positioning are retained. Removing the duplicated word in 'direct direct fine-tuning' does not alter the related-work discussion's substance.

T1.justification: Definitions, assumptions, Observation 1 and Appendix A's proofs remain substantively identical. Equation 15 only capitalizes loss labels, and Figure 1's index revision aligns with the existing Equation 7 without changing mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v4 modestly improves explanatory consistency by aligning Figure 1's parameter index with Equation 7 and cleaning up duplicated wording and loss notation. These are limited presentation gains; the method, proofs, empirical evidence and limitations remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ICE research and contain complete, readable main text and Appendices A-D. Text comparison and rendered-page checks support reliable comparison of all 23 pages.

after.justification: v4 retains the original experimental results in Section 4 and Appendix D, including benchmark comparisons, ablations and qualitative outputs.

before.justification: v3 reports original knowledge-editing experiments, ablations, continual-editing evaluations and convergence analyses in Section 4, with further GPT2-xl results and qualitative examples in Appendix D.

title: In-Context Editing: Learning Knowledge from Self-Induced Distributions

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the existence of conflict-associated weak-to-strong deception, its relationship to capability gaps, and partial mitigation through bootstrapping. V2 expands supporting evidence and emphasizes these findings; v1 already states them in its results and conclusion.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations distinguishing capability from parameter count and hypotheses about sample-distribution cues and intermediate-model knowledge. It explicitly leaves helpfulness supervision from the same weak teacher to future work. The earlier 7B-size limitation is removed following the larger-model experiments.

D1.justification: V2 adds eight NVIDIA A800 GPUs to the reported hardware and specifies LoRA placement in attention/FFN modules, rank 8, alpha 16, and the additional learning rate. It also clarifies that filtering confidence concerns the correct label. Existing training details and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use CAI-Harmless and HH-RLHF helpfulness data for reward modeling and preference alignment under the same conflict scenarios. The additional models and illustrative sample do not introduce a new dataset, task, or input environment.

E2.justification: The ground-truth-trained ceilings, no-conflict references, SimPO/DPO methods, and filtering/bootstrapping comparisons are retained. V2 extends model configurations without adding a distinct comparison method.

E3.justification: V2 extends DPO evaluation to OPT-6.7B and Mistral-7B and introduces LLaMA-3-8B/70B and LLaMA-3.1-8B experiments. Appendix G uses matched LoRA configurations and a learning rate of 3 × 10^-4 for the added LLaMA models. Existing data splits, metrics, and original training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix G adds a same-size LLaMA-3 versus LLaMA-3.1 comparison examining capability versus parameter count, and Appendix K adds a concrete deception case study. Existing conflict-strength, confidence-threshold, filtering, and bootstrapping analyses remain. The new Figure 8 largely redisplays the earlier knowledge-area versus deception-score comparison.

E5.justification: V1 Appendix C.1 and v2 Appendix D.1 both explicitly report one run per experiment because of computational cost. Neither version adds repeated-run estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial DPO and LLaMA results in Figures 12–14 and sample-level probabilities in Table 1. Existing knowledge-area proportions change from 0.13/0.15/0.19 in v1 Figure 6(b–d) to 0.14/0.17/0.22 in v2 Figure 7(b–d), while their deception scores remain 0.12/0.34/0.56. These are added results and numerical revisions, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The weak-supervision procedure, explicit and implicit conflict objectives, confidence filtering, and bootstrapping method are retained. The loss equations added to the main text already appear in v1 Appendix B. LoRA is introduced as a supplemental experimental configuration.

P1.justification: V2 revises the abstract and selected explanatory passages, expands the author list, includes existing objective equations in the main text, folds conflict-strength discussion into Section 5.3, and moves limitations to Appendix A. Most of the original narrative and procedural text remains recognizable.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to one, with extensive figure resizing and relocation. V2 adds the conceptual Figure 2, comparison Figure 8, LLaMA Figure 14, and case-study Table 1, and restructures the original DPO figure into Figures 12–13. Figure 7(b) introduces an axis/caption model-name mismatch.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations to Denison et al. on reward tampering, Guo et al. on controllable preference optimization, Zhou et al. on weak-to-strong search, and LLaMA 3.1, while removing the GLUE citation. The central positioning remains unchanged. Burns et al.'s publication update represents the same work.

T1.justification: The knowledge-space definitions, deception-score formula, and alignment objectives remain mathematically equivalent. V2 repeats existing appendix equations in the main text and changes notation, without adding a theorem, proof, or substantive derivation.

improvement.justification: The expanded DPO and larger-model experiments address coverage gaps explicitly acknowledged in v1, while the added implementation details and case study improve assessability. The gains remain limited by unchanged single-run evidence and new labeling errors: Figure 7(b) disagrees on the model identity, and Table 1 labels confidence 0.99 as Strong-Unknown despite Appendix K describing Strong-Known. Overall, the additional support provides a modest net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, references, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds larger-model evaluations, expanded DPO results, and an empirical case study.

before.justification: V1 reports original reward-modeling and preference-alignment experiments, including accuracy, deception scores, sensitivity analyses, and mitigation experiments.

title: Super(ficial)-alignment: Strong Models May Deceive Weak Models in Weak-to-Strong Generalization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: deception under conflicting alignment objectives, greater severity with increasing capability gaps, and limited mitigation through bootstrapping. Additional experiments support or explore these claims without redefining the headline contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 and Appendix K newly interpret no-conflict failures as possible spontaneous deception while acknowledging that erroneous weak supervision cannot be disentangled from active deception. Section 5.3 qualifies the growth-rate interpretation as especially apparent under explicit conflict. Appendix P explains adaptive weighting's limited mitigation, and the limitations now acknowledge preliminary honesty experiments.

D1.justification: v3 documents UnknownBench response-pair construction using gpt-4-0613 and Llama-2-13B-Chat, sample counts, and training settings. It adds a reproducibility statement claiming code and data provision and updates the stated repository location. Existing hardware, optimizer, learning-rate, epoch, and LoRA details are retained.

E1.justification: v2 evaluates harmlessness against conflicting harmfulness or helpfulness objectives. v3 Appendix O adds UnknownBench experiments targeting honesty on unanswerable questions under conflicting helpfulness supervision. This introduces a distinct alignment task previously mentioned only as future work, while retaining the original coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds an evaluated adaptive-loss versus naive-loss comparison in reward modeling under implicit conflict (Appendix P, Figure 23). The existing SimPO, DPO, model-family, high-confidence filtering, and bootstrapping comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: v3 introduces absolute deception scores using the ground-truth strong model as reference, enabling additional no-conflict comparisons. The new honesty protocol uses 400 samples each for ground-truth training, weak supervision, and testing, 2,000 helpful samples, and batch size 16. It also adds threshold T=0.70 and replaces the GPT-2-Large illustrative analysis with GPT-2-XL. These extend evaluation rather than establish reruns of retained experiments.

E4.justification: v3 adds analyses of possible spontaneous deception without conflicting objectives and tests adaptive weighting as mitigation. It extends threshold sensitivity to T=0.70 and replaces the earlier explicit-conflict illustration with GPT-2-XL analyses covering both conflict types. The conflict-strength comparison in v3 Appendix J already appeared in v2 Figure 9.

E5.justification: Both versions explicitly report one run per experiment because of computational costs (v2 Appendix D.1; v3 Appendix E.1). Neither adds repeated-run statistics, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Expanded model-confidence thresholds are sensitivity analyses, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v3 adds absolute-deception-score curves, honesty-alignment outcomes, threshold results, and adaptive-loss findings. New Figures 19–20 report deception scores of 0.58 and 0.40 for GPT-2-XL supervising Mistral-7B under explicit and implicit conflict, respectively. These replace an illustration using GPT-2-Large, not a same-setting performance comparison. Most existing benchmark results and Table 1 are retained.

M1.justification: Appendix P introduces an adaptive supervision variant that weights cross-entropy by |2M_weak(x)-1|, down-weighting uncertain weak predictions. This changes the training objective for an additional mitigation experiment; the main alignment procedures and existing countermeasures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v3 presents no-conflict objectives first, refines explanations, shortens the conclusion's future-work discussion, adds reproducibility and acknowledgments sections, and reorganizes appendices around new material. These are localized structural changes rather than an extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 adds plots for absolute deception, honesty, and adaptive supervision; redraws Figure 8 with both conflict types; and expands threshold figures from two to three panels. The earlier four-panel main-text scatter illustration becomes two three-panel appendix figures with a different teacher. The existing conflict-strength plot moves to the appendix.

R1.justification: New Appendix B substantially expands positioning against reward hacking, distinguishing comparisons across knowledge regions within one alignment dimension and separately controlled supervision signals. v3 adds the associated Pan et al. references and expands coverage of weak-to-strong theory and reasoning in Section 2.

T1.justification: v3 defines absolute deception scores through a different reference model and mathematically specifies the adaptive weighted objective in Equation 16. The original knowledge-region definitions and deception-score equations remain unchanged; reordered training equations are equivalent, and no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v3 improves empirical breadth by testing honesty, examines another mitigation strategy, and explicitly acknowledges confounding in the new no-conflict analysis. These additions make the paper more informative and its interpretation more qualified. The gains remain limited: results are still single-run, the added honesty study is preliminary, and the central attribution of failures to deliberate deception remains unresolved.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, core definitions, experimental framework, and retained results. The main text, equations, figures, table, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds honesty-alignment results, no-conflict analyses, and an adaptive-supervision comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original reward-modeling and preference-alignment experiments, including deception scores, mitigation experiments, and supplementary SimPO, DPO, and LLaMA results.

title: Super(ficial)-alignment: Strong Models May Deceive Weak Models in Weak-to-Strong Generalization

C1.justification: The central claim that incentive knowledge can improve the robustness–accuracy tradeoff remains. v2 additionally advertises preference-order opponents, mentions utility inference, and explicitly claims that misspecification risks are often manageable. Its novelty statement is qualified to multiclass strategic behavior over complex inputs.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of indirect protection across attack targets (C.3), reduced gains when the incentive set approaches the adversarial setting (C.5), and difficulty recovering rarely attacked targets (C.6). It also interprets utility-order alignment effects (C.7) and discloses difficulties obtaining comparable ViT performance (C.1).

D1.justification: Existing optimization, hardware, runtime, and code/checkpoint access statements remain. New details include the preference-training epsilon, CIFAR-100 semantic grouping, and utility inference's observation requirements, known-k assumption, and frequency-based reconstruction rule. These support the extensions without substantially revising the original reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: v2 adds CIFAR-100 to CIFAR-10 and GTSRB. Appendix C also evaluates new scenarios involving preference-order and continuous-valued utilities, opponents targeting known gaps in defenses, and recovery of targets and utility matrices from previous attacks.

E2.justification: Clean and PGD-adversarial training remain the principal baselines. New comparisons evaluate prediction-based versus attack-vector-based utility inference (Table 7), and utility-weighted, sequential, sequential-with-adversarial-fallback, multi-targeted, and adversarial training (Table 8), substantially extending the comparison methods.

E3.justification: The original splits, training budgets, and PGD settings are retained. New protocols include average and worst-case targeted evaluations against informed opponents (C.3), epsilon=0.5 for preference training (C.4), target-prediction and matrix-recovery metrics with known k (C.6), and aligned versus misaligned utility orderings (C.7).

E4.justification: Beyond v1's 1-hot strength, semantics, and misspecification analyses, v2 adds sensitivity to larger k (Figures 6 and 9), tests attacks on explicitly undefended targets (C.3), and examines utility-order alignment and fallback choices (C.7). These substantially expand tests of robustness and modeling assumptions.

E5.justification: v1 already reports quantiles and mean/standard-deviation curves. v2 adds standard errors for the random 1-hot comparisons in Table 3 and specifies ten randomly drawn preference orderings with mean/standard-deviation reporting in Table 5. This does not establish additional runs for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 retain their values, while Figures 6 and 9 and Tables 3–8 add substantial results. For example, Table 6 reports CIFAR-100 anti-semantic VGG accuracy of 20.2 for strategic versus 20.5 for adversarial training. Some new prose disagrees with its table: C.4 claims a 4.1-point VGG gain, whereas Table 5 implies 3.9.

M1.justification: The core minimax framework remains, but v2 adds a non-target penalty for preference attacks (Eq. 12), utility-inference procedures (C.6), and sequential strategic training with alternative fallback attacks (C.7). These extend the actual procedures. The epsilon=0.1 stabilization described in Section 5.1 was already disclosed in v1 Appendix B.4.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the exposition remain. v2 revises the abstract, introduction examples, risk-tradeoff interpretation, and several results passages, while adding acknowledgments and appendix cross-references. These refine the existing narrative alongside the newly added scientific material.

P2.justification: v2 adds six result tables and new k-dependent plots, expands opponent illustrations with preferences, and redraws or relabels existing plots. The conceptual panel from v1 Figure 3 becomes v2 Figure 2, rather than a new analysis. Document typography, citation presentation, and page layout also change.

R1.justification: v2 adds Mo et al. (2022) concerning adversarial training of vision transformers and removes Rosenfeld and Rosenfeld (2024), including the connection to strategic classification under unknown costs. It also sharpens positioning relative to predominantly binary, linear, tabular strategic-classification work.

T1.justification: The central formulations and clean–strategic–adversarial inequality remain. v2 adds a formal preference-order utility definition and mathematical reasoning relating continuous utilities to their binary support and target ordering (C.4 and C.7). These are limited formal extensions, without new theorem-and-proof development.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the paper's central incentive assumptions through informed-opponent tests, preference and continuous-utility experiments, and utility recovery. The CIFAR-100 exception also establishes a useful boundary on gains. These address important evidentiary gaps in v1, although validation remains controlled and minor prose/table discrepancies, such as C.4 versus Table 5, reduce precision.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same strategic-robustness work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison; extracted text and rendered pages resolve the relevant content.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original CIFAR-100, preference-order, utility-inference, and continuous-utility results in Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR-10 and GTSRB experiments comparing clean, strategic, and adversarial training, including opponent-strength and misspecification analyses.

title: Adversaries With Incentives:  A Strategic Alternative to Adversarial Robustness

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and discussion retain the same contributions: modeling opponent incentives, training against incentive uncertainty sets, and balancing strategic robustness with clean accuracy.

C2.justification: Interpretations of semantic structure and strategic gains are identical. Section 6.2 and Appendix A retain the same qualifications about incentive misspecification, uncertainty-set-dependent protection, and deployment limitations.

D1.justification: Appendix B retains identical preprocessing, hyperparameters, batch-size exceptions, hardware, and runtime information. Code links and code/checkpoint availability statements are unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate CIFAR-10, GTSRB, and CIFAR-100 under the same opponent scenarios, including k-hot, semantic, anti-semantic, preference-order, and continuous-utility settings.

E2.justification: The clean and adversarial training baselines participate in the same comparisons. Appendix C.7 also retains the same weighted-target, sequential, sequential-adversarial, and multi-targeted comparison methods.

E3.justification: Evaluation settings in Sections 4 and 6 and Appendices B–C are identical, including data splits, architectures, metrics, training budgets, and attack procedures. Appendix B.3 retains the 8/255 threat budget and seven training versus twenty evaluation PGD steps.

E4.justification: Both retain the same analyses of attack semantics, incentive misspecification, risk mitigation, all-knowing adversaries, utility inference, and utility-order alignment. No ablation or robustness analysis is added or removed.

E5.justification: Uncertainty reporting is identical, including standard errors in Table 3, variability displays in Figures 7 and 9, and the ten random preference-order instances with mean and standard deviation reporting in Appendix C.4.

E6.justification: Numerical entries and findings match throughout Tables 1–8, the experimental figures, and accompanying passages. Appendix results, including utility recovery and continuous-utility comparisons, are retained without changes.

M1.justification: The strategic training objectives and optimization procedures in Section 5 are identical. The preference-attack adaptation, utility-inference procedures, and sequential attack variants in Appendix C are also unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 adds the running text 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025' and updates the arXiv version/date stamp. Body wording, terminology, section organization, and appendices remain unchanged.

P2.justification: The publication header appears throughout v3. Figures 1 and 2 and surrounding text shift slightly on page 2, with minor paragraph reflow; figure contents, captions, table structures, and the remaining body layouts are unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 and the bibliography contain the same cited works and research positioning, including the claimed connection between multiclass strategic classification and adversarial learning.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, objectives, inequalities, and derivations are unchanged, including Equations (1)–(13) and the continuous-utility reasoning in Appendix C.7.

improvement.justification: v3 preserves the complete scientific content, evidence, reproducibility information, and limitations of v2, including its appendices. The publication header, updated arXiv stamp, and small page-2 layout adjustments establish no meaningful overall quality improvement or deterioration.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same research work, with 22 readable pages including Appendices A–C. Text, equations, tables, and rendered figures support a complete comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experimental results, including the main evaluations and all seven experimental subsections of Appendix C.

before.justification: v2 reports original experiments comparing strategic, adversarial, and clean training on CIFAR-10, GTSRB, and CIFAR-100, plus additional experiments in Appendix C.

title: Adversaries With Incentives:  A Strategic Alternative to Adversarial Robustness

C1.justification: The central operator-smoothing contribution remains. v2 adds an explicit claim of transfer to three indices excluded from training, changes the introduction's broad claim of improving Ackerer et al.'s errors to being highly competitive, and highlights an extrapolation advantage in Section 5.

C2.justification: Section 5 newly attributes the extrapolation advantage to learning from the entire historical dataset. Section 4 interprets cross-index performance as robustness and extends its spread/noise explanation to market-stress spikes. Existing limitations concerning parameter interpretability and dimensionality reduction remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly states that trained model weights accompany supplementary code, identifies OptionMetrics Ivy DB US and WRDS as the new data source and access route, and reports roughly two minutes on a consumer laptop CPU for 25 backtests. Existing implementation, hyperparameter, and GPU-training details are retained.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from intraday S&P 500 options to January 2021 end-of-day SPX, NDX, DJX, and RUT data. Appendix C.5 additionally evaluates January–April 2018 end-of-day SPX surfaces with half their observations withheld under interpolation and extrapolation scenarios.

E2.justification: New Table 5 includes Deep Smoothing from Ackerer et al. as a quantitative comparator in the interpolation/extrapolation backtest; v1 discussed its performance only in prose. Its scores are reproduced from the cited paper, not newly rerun. Existing SVI and OpDS* comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Appendix C.5 introduces 50% input-withholding protocols and separate errors at retained and dropped observations under interpolation and extrapolation. The new index evaluation uses the SPX-trained operator without training on the other indices. Existing splits, training budgets, metrics, and monthly finetuning remain unchanged; exact withholding rules are deferred to cited work.

E4.justification: v2 adds explicit tests of robustness to missing observations and extrapolation in Appendix C.5, plus transfer tests across intraday/end-of-day data and previously unseen indices. Figures 13–16 provide corresponding qualitative cases. The existing finetuning comparison and spatial error analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly reports averaging the new backtest's percentile summaries over 25 repetitions. v1 reports descriptive variation across surfaces but no corresponding repeated backtest. Existing uncertainty displays remain unchanged, and v2 supplies neither seed values nor confidence intervals across repetitions.
