before.justification: v1 reports original linear-probing accuracies, embedding-quality measurements, feature-distribution analysis and qualitative motion-control experiments in Sections 5–6 and the appendix.

title: Words in Motion: Extracting Interpretable Control Vectors for Motion Transformers

C1.justification: v2's central claims concern probing interpretable motion features and using them for inference-time steering. v3 retains these and adds central claims that sparse autoencoding improves control linearity and that calibrated vectors enable zero-shot compensation for unseen dataset characteristics with negligible computational overhead. These additions reshape the abstract, contributions and conclusion.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations linking sparse representations to more distinct control features, interpreting speed/acceleration/agent-vector alignment, and attributing ConvSAE calibration behavior to feature shrinkage (Section 5.3 and Appendix A.16). It also develops the domain-shift interpretation, justifies the ±50% evaluation window, and identifies sensitivity to the low-speed class definition.

D1.justification: v3 documents SAE losses, the reported sparsity weight, Adam optimization, a 10,000-epoch training budget, intermediate dimensions, JumpReLU threshold and patch/kernel settings. Appendix A.11 specifies A6000 hardware, PyTorch Lightning profiling and eager execution for latency measurement. The repository link and original transformer hyperparameters are retained; moving v2 Appendix A.4 into Section 4.4 is not an implementation change.

E1.justification: Argoverse 2 Forecasting and Waymo remain the datasets. v3 adds one synthetic Waymo scenario with future motion slowed by approximately 50% to test zero-shot compensation (Section 5.4). This extends coverage to a specific simulated distribution shift within the existing forecasting task.

E2.justification: The RedMotion, Wayformer and HPTR comparisons are retained. v3 substantially expands comparisons of control-vector construction, explicitly evaluating plain PCA against fully connected SAE, Sparse MLPMixer and ConvSAE configurations (Tables 1–2). The new shifted-Waymo experiment also compares SAE steering against unsteered RedMotion (Table 3).

E3.justification: v3's comparative linearity evaluation targets relative speed changes within ±50%, with method-dependent temperature ranges, whereas v2 reports a single temperature sweep over [-50,50]. New protocols include interpolating the first half of future waypoints to simulate slowdown, SAE configuration sweeps, and an eight-focal-agent latency benchmark. The original transformer training settings are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds explained-variance analyses, control-vector alignment comparisons, SAE-width ablations, encoder-module and speed-threshold sensitivity tests, and a JumpReLU feature-shrinkage analysis (Figures 12–13 and 15; Tables 1–2 and 5–9). It also tests synthetic distribution-shift robustness. The earlier correlation heatmaps and direction-control example are retained, with the latter moved from Appendix A.1 to A.9.

E5.justification: v3 Table 4 newly specifies latency means over 1,000 iterations per configuration. This adds limited repeated-measurement and aggregation information. Neither version reports training-seed replication, confidence intervals or significance tests for forecasting and controllability results; embedding standard deviations describe representations rather than experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: Extensive vector-geometry, ablation, forecasting and latency results are added. v2 Figure 5 reports PCA R² of 0.821; v3 Table 2 reports 0.969 under the revised calibration range, so this is not a matched-setting gain. Within v3's comparison, ReLU SAE reaches 0.984. On the new slowed-Waymo scenario, Table 3 reports minADE of 3.271 without steering versus 1.174 for SAE-128 at temperature -50.

M1.justification: v2 constructs control vectors by applying PCA directly to differences between opposing-feature hidden states. v3 adds an auxiliary sparse autoencoder: differences are pooled in its sparse representation and decoded back into the motion encoder's hidden space before inference. Fully connected, convolutional and MLPMixer variants substantially extend the method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list and conclusion are substantially rewritten around sparse autoencoding and generalization. Existing training details move into the main text, qualitative and quantitative results receive separate subsections, and the appendix is reorganized, including moving title origin to A.1 and the retained qualitative example to A.9.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to show SAE encoding, decoding and control-vector construction. The single calibration display becomes a comparative figure, and v3 adds architecture, explained-variance and shrinkage figures plus nine numbered tables. Existing trajectory examples and distributions are relocated, while speed and acceleration panels are reordered in the probing figures.

R1.justification: v3 adds substantial positioning around sparse autoencoders, dictionary learning, JumpReLU and zero-shot generalization. Sections 2.1–2.2 introduce a robotics mechanistic-interpretability novelty claim and distinguish offline SAE use and last-module steering from earlier language-model approaches. The MotionLM citation is removed, and motion-threshold motivation is attributed to the already-cited Waymo dataset paper.

T1.justification: v3 adds the standard formula for the already-used CDNV metric in Appendix A.17 and briefly invokes Johnson–Lindenstrauss as motivation for SAE decoding. These additions provide mathematical explanation, but no new proof, formal assumption, derived guarantee or substantive revision of existing mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 provides probing results, one calibration analysis and selected steering examples, with little testing of control-design choices or failure conditions. v3's direct PCA/SAE comparisons and module, width and threshold ablations substantially strengthen validation and expose failures; documented slowdown and latency experiments make practical claims more assessable. These gains substantially improve empirical support and reproducibility. The broader generalization claims remain supported by only one constructed slowdown scenario, and performance uncertainty is still unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Words in Motion by the same authors. Their main text, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds sparse-autoencoder comparisons, sensitivity analyses, simulated domain-shift forecasting results and inference-latency measurements.

before.justification: v2 reports original probing accuracies, representation statistics, control calibration and qualitative steering results on Argoverse 2 Forecasting and Waymo, with additional distribution and correlation analyses in the appendix.

title: Words in Motion: Extracting Interpretable Control Vectors for Motion Transformers

C1.justification: V4's abstract explicitly claims that steering preserves prediction feasibility, and its contribution list foregrounds functionally important directions and comparison with KoopmanAE. The central claims about interpretable probing, SAE-enhanced control linearity, and zero-shot generalization remain.

C2.justification: V4 adds explanations involving tied decoder weights and KoopmanAE's lack of sparsity-induced shrinkage. Appendix A.14 discusses unsuccessful AV2F speed-class choices and distribution differences. The conclusion newly acknowledges assumed latent-space flatness and the restriction of neural-collapse analysis to probing accuracy and CDNV.

D1.justification: V4 discloses SAE batch size 528, best-loss epoch selection, reconstruction-loss averaging versus sparsity-loss summation, and broadcasting the final-time control vector across temporal embeddings. It supplies explicit encoder/decoder equations and KoopmanAE architecture and temporal-training details. Code access and the retained latency-measurement setup are unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate AV2F and Waymo motion forecasting, including the reduced-future-speed Waymo scenario. V4's additional probing–linearity analysis reuses these datasets and tasks; its trajectory-length and speed-class choices change protocols within retained coverage.

E2.justification: V4 Table 3 retains the comparisons in v3 Table 2 and adds distinct evaluated rows for Cunningham et al.'s SAE and Azencot et al.'s consistent KoopmanAE. Cunningham was already cited in v3, but lacked this separate comparison row. Bricken and Rajamanoharan labels identify retained SAE rows.

E3.justification: Section 4.4 changes the reported common four-term forecasting loss to position/confidence losses for Wayformer and RedMotion, with heading/velocity terms reserved for HPTR; rerunning retained experiments is not established. E4.justification: V4 adds a targeted probing–linearity analysis with matched trajectory lengths, including an AV2F calibration curve exposing weak deceleration control, and characterizes KoopmanAE's temperature response. Existing dimension, module, threshold, correlation, and qualitative analyses remain. The dimension ablation moves from v3 Table 7 to v4 Table 2.

E5.justification: Both versions report mean inference latency over 1000 iterations. Neither introduces training-seed counts, repeated-training uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Embedding variance and explained-variance analyses retain their existing reporting practices.

E6.justification: V4 adds Cunningham SAE and KoopmanAE results, including R2 values of 0.971 and -0.057, respectively. New Table 4 reports AV2F probing accuracy 0.753 and control R2 0.275 under its stated configuration. Existing comparator and zero-shot scores remain unchanged. The loss table corrects L1/L2 metric assignments and removes the 'Total reconst loss' entries.

M1.justification: The proposed feature quantization, linear probing, opposing-feature PCA, SAE decoding, and temperature-scaled steering pipeline remains intact. V4's equations and explanation of applying vectors across temporal embeddings expand documentation. KoopmanAE is introduced as a comparator.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Results are reorganized into qualitative, similarity, SAE-linearity, and probing–linearity discussions; appendix material is consolidated or reordered. Terminology, notation, citations, and cross-references are revised throughout, beyond the prose needed for new experiments.

P2.justification: V4 adds Table 4 and calibration Figures 15–16, expands the comparator table, simplifies the loss table, and moves the dimension table into the main text. Existing plots and scene images are largely preserved, with resizing, relabeling, and relocation. The ICLR template changes headers and typography without substantially redesigning most displays.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially broadens positioning through concept-based interpretability, latent-space curvature, manifold flattening, and Koopman methods, citing works including Kim, Chefer, Arvanitidis, Psenka, and Azencot. It adds a distinction from Conmy and Nanda's SAE steering. The language-interface survey is retained and consolidated in Appendix A.2.

T1.justification: V4 equations (1)–(3) explicitly express the existing SAE encoding, PCA pooling, and decoding procedure. The CDNV definition and Johnson–Lindenstrauss justification remain substantively unchanged. No new theorem, proof, or mathematical derivation is developed.

improvement.justification: V4 improves reproducibility through explicit steering details and corrected loss reporting, while broader comparisons and stated limitations improve interpretation. The new AV2F analysis exposes a useful failure case, although differences in datasets, speed-class pairs, and calibration ranges limit its support for a causal probing–linearity claim. These benefits are meaningful but limited, with most established experimental evidence retained.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Words in Motion and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. Content can be matched across the restructuring and renumbering.

after.justification: V4 retains these original experiments and adds autoencoder comparisons and an AV2F–Waymo analysis relating probing accuracy to control linearity.

before.justification: V3 reports original motion-transformer probing, control-vector comparisons, ablations, latency measurements, and simulated domain-shift results on AV2F and Waymo.

title: Words in Motion: Extracting Interpretable Control Vectors for Motion Transformers

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the same claims about interpretable representations, control vectors, SAE-enhanced linearity and zero-shot generalization. The edited third contribution bullet preserves its original scientific scope.

C2.justification: Explanations involving feature separability, sparsity and activation shrinkage remain unchanged, as do the flat-latent-space and limited neural-collapse-analysis qualifications. Figure 15 adds an observed outcome without a new mechanism explanation or substantive limitation.

D1.justification: Implementation information, training hyperparameters, classification thresholds and the code-access link are unchanged. Hardware and profiling details move with the latency experiment from Appendix A.10 to A.11 without substantive revision.

E1.justification: The AV2F and Waymo datasets, agent types, forecasting/control tasks and reduced-speed domain-shift evaluation are retained. New Figure 15 illustrates all-agent steering within this existing coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluated motion models and plain-PCA, SAE, SparseMLPMixer, ConvSAE and KoopmanAE comparisons are unchanged. Cunningham et al. changes from a 2023 preprint citation to its 2024 publication, without changing the comparator.

E3.justification: New Figure 15 adds a qualitative testing setup with a default forecast and all-agent steering at eight temperatures from -100 to 100. Existing quantitative protocols remain unchanged. Replacing 'cosine similarity in degrees' with angular-distance terminology clarifies unchanged degree-valued tables.

E4.justification: Appendix A.8 adds a case study showing simultaneous steering of all agents across temperatures. Existing module and speed-threshold ablations, feature-correlation analyses and calibration comparisons are retained, with some relocated.

E5.justification: Statistical reporting practices are unchanged, including latency means over 1,000 iterations. No new seed information, uncertainty intervals or significance tests accompany the added qualitative example.

E6.justification: Figure 15 adds qualitative trajectory outcomes described as consistent multi-agent behavior. Existing numerical results are unchanged after matching reordered tables, including SAE-128 linearity scores of 0.993 Pearson, 0.984 R2 and 0.988 straightness in Table 2.

M1.justification: Motion-feature quantization, linear probing, PCA pooling, SAE optimization and temperature-scaled activation steering remain unchanged. The all-agent illustration uses the existing method.

P1.justification: v5 corrects angular-distance terminology, lightly rewrites the third contribution bullet and reorders Appendix A.9–A.16 with updated cross-references. The main narrative and section structure remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v5 adds the nine-panel Figure 15, adjusts Figure 14's framing and size, revises comparison-table captions and relocates several appendix displays. Existing figures and tables are retained with corresponding renumbering.

R1.justification: The cited works and research positioning are retained. Cunningham et al. and DriveLM receive preprint-to-conference bibliographic updates; these are the same works, not additions to the literature comparison.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(3), the CDNV definition in Appendix A.19 and the underlying mathematical assumptions remain unchanged. The angular-distance wording corrects terminology without introducing a new definition, derivation or proof.

improvement.justification: Correcting the misleading 'cosine similarity in degrees' terminology improves clarity, while Figure 15 provides useful qualitative support for simultaneous steering. The method and quantitative evidence remain unchanged, so these benefits constitute a limited overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both complete 24-page PDFs describe the same Words in Motion study. Text, figures, tables, equations and Appendices A.1–A.19 support comparison, including matching reordered appendix material.

after.justification: v5 retains these original empirical results and adds a qualitative demonstration of steering all agents in Figure 15.

before.justification: v4 reports original motion-feature probing, control-vector evaluations, ablations and zero-shot forecasting results on AV2F and Waymo.

title: Words in Motion: Extracting Interpretable Control Vectors for Motion Transformers

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on captioner and CLIP attacks demonstrating agent vulnerability. v2 makes ARE and component-level robustness central contributions, extending its main claims to reflexion and tree-search agents and to how additional components can either block or amplify attacks.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving adversarial verification, reflections, and value scores, and qualifies defensive benefits by whether components themselves are compromised. Appendix D newly characterizes attack results as lower bounds on risk and limits conclusions to the evaluated agent algorithms. v1's vision-only limitation is replaced as text attacks enter the study.

D1.justification: v2 adds evaluation-matching rules, safety-prompt excerpts, and configuration details for the new agent studies. It omits v1's explicit PGD initialization and checkpoint-selection descriptions, including GPT-4 scoring of CLIP candidates. Model identifiers, hardware, and the code/data repository remain unchanged; omitted details do not establish changed attack implementations.

E1.justification: Both versions use the 200-task VWA-Adv benchmark covering classifieds, Reddit, and shopping, with retained adversarial-goal templates and synthetic image-selection scenarios. v2 adds an evaluated text-access scenario alongside bounded image perturbations, extending coverage within the existing web domains.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated reflexion and tree-search agents and comparisons involving safety prompting, abstention prompting, paraphrasing, and explicit consistency checking. These substantially expand the comparisons beyond v1's base, captioner-augmented, and self-captioning agents. The four backbone model families remain.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce component-edge evaluations and controls that selectively supply clean or adversarial captions. Reflexion permits two attempts, and tree search uses branching factor 3 and depth 1. v1's stepwise-versus-episode evaluation comparison is removed; v2 explicitly describes terminal-state evaluation. These additions establish new protocols without demonstrating reruns of retained experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled analyses of attacking the policy, evaluator, or value function separately and jointly, plus empirical defense tests. It removes v1's cross-goal repeatability study and stepwise-versus-episode validation. The resolution, negative-text, ensemble, and synthetic-context analyses are retained, partly relocated to Appendix C.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests, and both specify temperature-zero decoding. v1's removed 'Repeated ASR' experiment concerns transfer across user goals, rather than statistical uncertainty across repeated runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds GPT-4o text-injection ASR of 40%, reflexion outcomes of 25% with a clean evaluator and 36% under joint attack, and corresponding tree-search outcomes of 26% and 38%. Paraphrasing reduces ASR from 31% to 27.5%. Earlier goal-specific tables and repeatability results disappear, while synthetic-context and CLIP-ablation values remain unchanged. The differently grouped headline rates are not directly comparable performance changes.

M1.justification: v2 introduces ARE's procedure for representing agents as graphs and evaluating attack propagation through components. It also adds direct text injection and implemented defense pipelines involving paraphrasing and consistency checking. The original captioner PGD and CLIP ensemble optimization objectives remain essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. The setup, method, and experimental narrative are reorganized around ARE and component robustness, replacing v1's attack-centered organization. Several retained explanations move to appendices, while much appendix implementation material remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 replaces much of the main results presentation with agent graphs, weighted attack-propagation diagrams, a robustness-utility scatterplot, and a defense bar chart. Earlier detailed result tables and attack examples are removed. The resolution heatmap moves to the appendix, while several agent illustrations and appendix tables are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions the work around compound-agent robustness and distinguishes it from concurrent AgentDojo and EIA research. Related work expands to indirect prompt injection, Agent Smith, defense methods, and the tree-search agent, supporting the shift beyond v1's emphasis on image attacks and captioner vulnerabilities.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3 introduces formal agent graphs, adversarial influence AdvIn(c), expected edge weights, a deterministic-environment assumption, and conventions for unexecuted branches. This is substantial new mathematical formulation beyond v1's attack objectives, although it does not add theorem proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence for system-level conclusions: Sections 5.2–5.4 isolate how evaluators and value functions block or amplify attacks and empirically test defense ideas that v1 largely proposed. ARE provides a common framework for these comparisons. These gains outweigh the loss of repeatability evidence, detailed result tables, and some optimization documentation. Reporting weaknesses remain, including introductory relative-change percentages that do not consistently match the displayed results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VWA-Adv research and retain identifiable attacks, experiments, and appendix material despite the changed title and substantial extension. The text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original text/image attack results, component-isolation experiments, and defense evaluations, alongside retained synthetic experiments and ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack experiments, cross-goal repeatability tests, synthetic-context experiments, and CLIP ablations in the main text and appendices.

title: Dissecting Adversarial Robustness of Multimodal LM Agents

C1.justification: The abstract recasts the claim that adding components can harm robustness as a claim about inference-time compute. This modestly changes the headline framing while retaining the benchmark, ARE contribution, and up-to-67% attack-success claim.

C2.justification: The new joint summary after Section 5.3 explicitly interprets reflexion and tree search as examples of inference-time scaling decreasing worst-case robustness. v2 used separate component-specific summaries. The mechanism explanations and Appendix D limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix B retains identical model identifiers, decoding settings, hardware, attack-text examples, and safety prompts. Code and data access information is also unchanged.

E1.justification: Both use the same 200 VWA-Adv tasks across classifieds, shopping, and Reddit, the same text/image attack scenarios, and the same synthetic screenshot-selection task in Appendix C.2.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in Figures 4–7, including the four backbone LMs, agent configurations, and safety-prompt, abstention, paraphrase, and consistency defenses.

E3.justification: Task selection and starting states, success metrics, perturbation constraints, and evaluation settings are unchanged. Both specify two reflexion attempts and tree search with branching factor 3 and depth 1.

E4.justification: The component-isolation and defense analyses remain unchanged, as do the resolution, negative-text, and CLIP-ensemble ablations and screenshot-context analysis in Appendix C.

E5.justification: Both report point estimates without repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. No uncertainty-reporting practice is added or revised.

E6.justification: All reported results are retained. For example, Figure 6 still reports 31% ASR for the base configuration, 26% with an unattacked value function, and 38% when both components are attacked; Table 7 retains 71% for the full CLIP attack and 46% without negative text.

M1.justification: Sections 3–5 retain the same ARE framework, attack objectives and procedures, agent configurations, and defenses. The inference-time-compute wording introduces no algorithmic change.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized abstract edits, combines two summaries, adds Cisco funding acknowledgment, and replaces the preprint header with the ICLR 2025 publication header. The section structure and remaining prose are preserved.

P2.justification: Two shaded summary boxes on page 9 become one, moving the unchanged Figure 6 and Section 5.3 upward. The abstract and first reference page undergo local reflow; figure and table contents remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The cited works, Section 2 discussion, novelty statements, and explicit comparisons with prior agent-attack research are unchanged.

T1.justification: The agent-graph, adversarial-influence, and edge-weight definitions in Section 3 and the attack objectives in Equations 1–2 are unchanged. No assumptions, derivations, or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: The revised abstract and combined summary emphasize inference-time compute, but the underlying component-level conclusions were already present in v2. Methods, empirical evidence, reproducibility details, and limitations are unchanged. The localized presentation and acknowledgment edits do not establish a meaningful net change in overall paper quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ARE framework and VWA-Adv study. The complete main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D are readable and reliably matched across versions.

after.justification: v3 retains the original experimental outcomes in Figures 4–7, Table 3, Figure 13, and Table 7, including the appendix analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original agent attack and defense experiments in Section 5, plus CLIP ablations and synthetic screenshot experiments in Appendix C.

title: Dissecting Adversarial Robustness of Multimodal LM Agents

C1.justification: The central claim that limited relearning data lacking direct answers can restore unlearned knowledge remains. v2 adds an explicit abstract/introduction claim that generic public information can recover verbatim copyrighted text, extending the stated contribution while preserving its central message.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation through persistent token associations, model/data-format mismatch, claimed PEFT susceptibility, and the importance of knowing RMU's corrupted layer. Sections 8–9 also explain metric-dependent attack success and identify prompt filtering and guardrails as applicability limits, beyond v1's brief future-work discussion.

D1.justification: v2 Appendices A.1, B.1, C.1, and D.1 add optimizers, schedules, learning rates, batch sizes, weight decay, LoRA parameters, and method-specific settings. Appendix D supplies the new relearning prompt and generated text, and page 2 adds a code-access link. However, v1's explicit eight TOFU relearning QA pairs per author is no longer stated.

E1.justification: The original WMDP and TOFU/WHP keyword tasks remain. v2 adds verbatim Harry Potter passage recovery using generic character information, synthetic name-sequence recovery, and actual multiple-choice evaluation alongside generated answers for RMU. These substantially expand task requirements and test scenarios.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates gradient ascent for WMDP. v2 Figure 4 additionally evaluates gradient difference, KL minimization, NPO, and SCRUB; Section 7 evaluates RMU. Table 3 also adds gradient difference and NPO to the LoRA-unlearning comparison. These methods are evaluated, rather than merely cited.

E3.justification: v2 adds Llama-3-8b evaluation and describes full-weight WMDP relearning in Appendix C.1, whereas v1 specifies LoRA. New protocols include 15 split 80-word passages scored with Rouge-L, 100 synthetic prefixes, and likelihood-based MCQ scoring. The TOFU control changes its reported model from OPT-1.5 to Phi-1.5 while retaining identical scores; this establishes revised reporting without establishing a rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses examine token-pair repetition and relearning depth, full-weight versus LoRA unlearning, RMU's disagreement between MCQ and generation metrics, and zero-initialization. Appendix D adds successful and unsuccessful verbatim-recovery cases. The earlier checkpoint heatmaps, TOFU control, and qualitative failure examples are largely retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars. v2's token-pair repetitions and additional evaluation samples concern experimental design, not repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive WMDP, verbatim-recovery, synthetic, and RMU results. For example, Table 4 reports NPO Rouge-L scores of 0.0332 after unlearning and 0.7221 after relearning. The retained example in v1 Table 9/v2 Appendix C.4.4 changes its relearned score from 8 to 9. v2 Figure 4's retain panels duplicate forget values, making its retention results ambiguous.

M1.justification: The core attack algorithm is retained and moved from v1 Appendix F into the main text. v2 Section 7 adds an RMU-specific zeroinit+relearn variant that zeros the known corrupted layer before finetuning. This is a limited but genuine procedural extension.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the introduction, related work, and threat-model explanation. Experiments are reorganized around partial-data versus public-information access, the algorithm moves into the main text, and qualitative material moves into task-organized appendices with an outline. Discussion and conclusion become separate sections.

P2.justification: v2 adds a front-page recovery illustration, WMDP bar charts, a synthetic-loss plot, and new quantitative tables. Existing keyword examples are condensed into a combined table; many other example tables and boxed question lists become appendix prose or bullets. The retained heatmaps are resized and relocated. Figure 4 introduces duplicated forget/retain panels.

R1.justification: Related work shifts substantially toward contemporary LLM unlearning and robustness, adding work including RWKU, MUSE, Ununlearning, intrinsic knowledge traces, and benign-finetuning safety failures. Several classical unlearning and extraction references disappear. The central distinction from prior relearning work—excluding direct evaluation answers from relearning data—remains.

T1.justification: The substantive threat-model assumptions remain. v2 adds explanatory disjoint-set notation and standard objective formulas in Section 6 and Appendix E. Its correlation study provides empirical intuition, without a new theoretical result, proof, or substantive formal derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for v1's broad vulnerability claim through additional unlearning methods, direct verbatim-recovery evidence, and RMU analyses that expose evaluation limitations. Figure 4's duplicated retain panels are a material regression from v1 Table 2 and weaken retention conclusions, but the distinct new experiments, analyses, and implementation disclosures provide substantial overall gains.

after.justification: Sections 4–7 retain original experiments and add unlearning-method comparisons, verbatim text recovery, synthetic correlation experiments, and RMU evaluations.

title: Unlearning or Obfuscating? Jogging the Memory of Unlearned LLMs via Benign Relearning

C1.justification: v4's abstract and introduction explicitly diagnose current approximate unlearning as output obfuscation, strengthening v2's emphasis on susceptibility to relearning. This is limited strengthening: v2's conclusion already states that many optimization-based heuristics fail to truly remove memorized information, and the central contribution remains unchanged.

C2.justification: v4 adds interpretation of data-relevance experiments and notes that strongly related relearning data may be unavailable. Appendix G extends the argument against learning evaluation answers solely from auxiliary text. It also mentions unverified inference-time applicability; existing model-choice, RMU, metric and guardrail limitations remain.

D1.justification: v4 Section 5 clarifies that the synthetic forget set uses common male names, where v2 Section 6 specifies only a subset of names. This is a small disclosure refinement, not evidence of a changed experiment. Existing hyperparameters, data-generation and filtering prompts, and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: The benchmarks and core tasks remain unchanged. v4 adds limited input scenarios: Japanese text, female-name sequences and gibberish in the synthetic experiment, and German and gibberish relearning text for WMDP (Section 6 and Appendix C.5.5).
