C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about checkpoint synergy, adaptation coverage, and performance, including the 67.3% cross-corruption improvement. The shortened conclusion does not change their scope.

C2.justification: The explanations of checkpoint diversity and knowledge retention, small-object pseudo-label limitations in A.5, and computational limitations remain unchanged. A.8 adds qualitative observations without a new mechanism explanation or applicability boundary.

D1.justification: The abstract replaces the statement that code accompanies supplementary materials with an explicit GitHub repository address. This improves access information, although repository availability cannot be verified from the PDFs. Implementation details in A.4 remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both retain the same KITTI, KITTI-C, Waymo, and nuScenes transfer tasks, eight corruption types, and three object classes. Figure 9 illustrates the existing Waymo-to-KITTI task; its RGB image is reference-only.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the existing experiments is unchanged. The new qualitative comparison uses SAR and CoTTA, already evaluated on Waymo-to-KITTI; newly cited methods such as DPO are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The reported splits, metrics, detector configurations, and adaptation settings remain unchanged. Appendix A.4 still specifies batch size 8, K = 5, and L = 112. The new visualization does not document a different evaluation protocol.

E4.justification: Appendix A.8 adds a qualitative case study comparing localization and erroneous detections by SAR, CoTTA, and MOS in one illustrated scene. Existing ablations, sensitivity tests, and checkpoint analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. Statistical uncertainty reporting is unchanged.

E6.justification: The numerical results in Tables 1–11 and existing performance plots are unchanged. Figure 9 adds qualitative evidence of spurious baseline detections and closer MOS box alignment. Appendix A.8 incorrectly calls background false positives 'false negatives'.

M1.justification: The warm-up, synergy-weighted checkpoint assembly, pseudo-label training, and model-bank replacement procedures remain unchanged. Equations (1)–(12) and Algorithm 1 retain the same method.

P1.justification: v3 adds A.8 and funding acknowledgments, updates author and conference-header information, and lightly condenses the conclusion. Most prose and section organization remain intact. A.6 incorrectly changes its Figure 8 reference to Figure 9.

P2.justification: Figure 9 adds a comparison of predicted and ground-truth boxes for SAR, CoTTA, and MOS, with an RGB reference image. Existing figures and tables retain their content and design, alongside limited repositioning and page reflow.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations including DPO, Tokens on Demand, DiPEx, and other detection/adaptation work, without substantially revising the positioning narrative. The existing TTA survey's preprint-to-journal update is bibliographic rather than a new cited work.

T1.justification: The synergy-weight derivation, generalized Gram matrix, similarity definitions, Hungarian matching formulation, and complexity argument remain unchanged. No new theorem, proof, or mathematical correction is introduced.

improvement.justification: The explicit code pointer and Figure 9 modestly improve reproducibility documentation and make comparative detection behavior inspectable. The quantitative study and method are unchanged. These gains are limited by A.8's false-positive/false-negative confusion and A.6's incorrect figure reference, but the additions remain useful.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MOS research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including the new qualitative study in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results and adds a qualitative comparison of MOS, SAR, and CoTTA in Appendix A.8 and Figure 9.

before.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original detector-adaptation experiments, ablations, sensitivity studies, resource measurements, and results across object classes and detector backbones.

title: MOS: Model Synergy for Test-Time Adaptation on LiDAR-Based 3D Object Detection

C1.justification: The central contribution—joint generation of aligned objects enabling hybridization and structure-preserving editing—remains. v2 adds explicit claims about the necessity of transition plausibility and smoothness and effectiveness across backbones. Its introduction and conclusion qualify editing performance as on par with specialized methods, whereas v1 claims superiority in quality and semantic alignment.

C2.justification: v2 substantially develops the mechanism interpretation, separating plausibility regularization from prompt blending and discussing an alignment-versus-realism tradeoff. It explains why limited geometric editing can obtain favorable DIFT scores and discusses backbone-specific weaknesses. The static-object limitation remains, while v1's explicit warning about substantially different proportions is removed.

D1.justification: New Appendices B and C provide architecture, hash-grid, latent-sampling, regularization-weight, initialization, baseline-adaptation, and evaluation details. Examples include 0.5 probability of individual-object sampling, RichDreamer network specifications, MVEdit denoising strength, and the CLIP ViT-L/14 model. These greatly expand v1's sparse implementation information; newly disclosed settings do not establish changes to earlier experiments.

E1.justification: The three tasks and 15 joint-generation prompt pairs remain, including plants already evaluated in v1. Demonstrated coverage contracts slightly: the plant-decoration editing case in v1 Table 2 and mosquito/wasp hybridization example in Figure 8 are absent from v2. RichDreamer adds a model configuration rather than new data coverage.

E2.justification: v1 primarily compares against MVEdit. v2 adds LucidDreamer and GaussianEditor to aligned generation. Editing adds GaussianEditor quantitatively and LucidDreamer through qualitative comparisons and successful per-case results in Table 6; LucidDreamer's failures prevent an aggregate comparison in Table 2.

E3.justification: v2 replaces Chamfer distance with normalized DIFT correspondence distance and adds six GPT-4o evaluation criteria using 90 comparisons per method pair. The editing table changes from 24 cases to 26, and new backbone and ablation configurations are evaluated. CLIP averaging over 120 views is retained.

E4.justification: v1's ablation qualitatively compares separate networks, a shared network without interpolation, and the full method. v2 adds empty-prompt transition guidance and network-depth controls, with aggregate and per-pair quantitative results in Tables 3 and 7. Appendix A additionally tests generalization to the RichDreamer backbone.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. v2's 90 GPT-based comparisons specify evaluation sample size, without adding uncertainty estimates or establishing repeated training runs.

E6.justification: Reported aligned-generation CLIP averages change from A3D/MVEdit 29.46/27.92 to 27.7/27.1; editing averages change from 29.56/28.76 to 27.8/27.9. Revised methods and evaluation prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance changes. v2 also adds extensive DIFT, GPT-based, ablation, and RichDreamer results, while removing some qualitative examples.

M1.justification: v2 adds a substantive RichDreamer-based implementation using DMTet/SDF geometry, staged geometry and texture optimization, and normal-depth/albedo guidance (Appendices A and B.2). The core simplex interpolation, hybridization, and source-anchored editing procedures remain. Its main method description also emphasizes depth and normal-map regularization instead of v1's explicit spectral normalization, although removal of spectral normalization is not explicitly confirmed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method explanation, and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. Terminology shifts toward structural alignment and latent codes, metrics receive a shared explanation, and the single additional-results appendix becomes four focused appendices. These changes substantially reorganize the narrative.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns comparison figures to include more methods and separate appearance/geometry views, expands the ablation display, and adds a RichDreamer figure. The combined comparison table becomes separate task tables with additional metrics. Existing hybridization examples are condensed and rearranged, while v1's trajectory Figures 3 and 10 are omitted.

R1.justification: v2 removes the broad 2D diffusion survey, expands discussion of 3D editing and amortized generation, and adds a dedicated latent-space regularization subsection. Connections to StyleGAN and adversarial interpolation substantially develop the methodological positioning. RichDreamer was already cited in v1; its new experimental use is a separate change.

T1.justification: v2 defines a normalized, bidirectional DIFT correspondence distance mathematically in Appendix C, adding a formal metric construction absent from v1. The existing NeRF, SDS, and simplex formulations remain substantially unchanged, and neither version develops theorem-and-proof results.

improvement.justification: v1's limited comparator coverage, qualitative-only ablations, and sparse implementation information leave important validation and reproducibility gaps. v2 substantially addresses these through additional baselines, quantitative component controls, a second implementation, and detailed appendices. Some illustrative examples disappear and uncertainty remains unreported, but the stronger experimental support and technical transparency provide a clear overall improvement despite mixed performance results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe A3D and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The shared method and experiments can be matched reliably despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original comparative experiments, quantitative ablations, and RichDreamer-based results in Tables 1–7 and associated figures.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation and transformation measurements in Tables 1–3, alongside hybridization examples and qualitative ablations.

title: A3D: Does Diffusion Dream about 3D Alignment?

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: jointly generating structurally aligned objects through plausible, smooth transitions, enabling hybridization and structure-preserving editing, and improving asset quality over editing-based alternatives.

C2.justification: Appendices D.1–E substantially expand interpretation: they develop the existing alignment–realism tradeoff, explain the limited role of MLP depth through hash-grid capacity, and attribute restricted diversity to strong guidance and backbone training. The ethics statement adds specific inherited-data limitations. The original static-object limitation remains.

D1.justification: New Appendix B.4 discloses A100 hardware, approximately 20k iterations and 1.5 hours per generated pair, scaling budgets for additional objects, and competitor runtimes. These details were absent from v2; the existing architecture, loss weights and baseline implementation instructions largely persist.

E1.justification: The original 15 prompt pairs and 26 transformation cases remain. Appendix E adds limited qualitative coverage of controlled prompt paraphrases and transformations of meshes reconstructed from images using CRM, extending input conditions within the existing 3D asset domains.

E2.justification: MVEdit, LucidDreamer, GaussianEditor and the original A–F ablation configurations remain. Figure 9 adds the weaker-plausibility-regularization comparator G, and Figure 11 includes a MVDream/A3D diversity comparison.

E3.justification: v4 extends ablation evaluation beyond DIFT to CLIP and GPTEval3D in Tables 8–9 and adds controlled prompt variations and a weaker transition-sampling configuration. The original 120-view evaluation, 90 GPTEval3D comparisons and main sampling probability of 0.5 remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 already tests shared representation, transition plausibility and MLP depth. Appendices D.1–E substantially extend the analysis with quality measurements for these ablations, regularization-strength sensitivity, fixed-prompt diversity and paraphrase robustness, addressing tradeoffs and failure behavior beyond structural alignment.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed counts, run-wise uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. Figure 11 adds qualitative examples of generation diversity but does not document a statistical repetition or uncertainty-estimation protocol.

E6.justification: Existing numerical results in Tables 1–7 are retained. New Table 8 reports ablation CLIP scores, including means of 27.7 for A3D and 28.5 for independent MVDream. Table 9 reports A3D overall-quality preference of 33.9% against B and 68.8% against C. New qualitative results show regularization tradeoffs, limited diversity, paraphrase robustness and image-derived transformations.

M1.justification: The latent-conditioned neural field, interpolated text embeddings, SDS and normal regularization, hybridization, and structure-preserving transformation procedures remain unchanged. The CRM examples supply new input meshes to the existing Section 4.3 procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work and preliminaries receive selective tightening. v4 adds a method overview, ethics and reproducibility statements, and further appendix subdivisions. The main section sequence and most method and experimental prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v4 adds the method diagram in Figure 3, five experimental figures numbered 9–13, and Tables 8–9. The original qualitative ablation moves from main-text Figure 6 to appendix Figure 8. Existing tables are regrouped, and Table 7 gains an average row repeating the previously reported aggregate results.

R1.justification: v4 adds references for Instant-NGP, CRM and inherited dataset risks, while removing the Instant3D and ProlificDreamer citations and associated discussion. The central positioning against independent generation and sequential editing is retained.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5, the latent-simplex formulation and the Appendix C DIFT definition are unchanged. Naming the existing sampling probability p clarifies its description; no new theoretical assumptions, propositions, proofs or substantive derivations are introduced.

improvement.justification: Tables 8–9 make the quality costs of stronger alignment more assessable, while computational budgets and new sensitivity and diversity examples improve reproducibility and qualification of the findings. These are useful, targeted gains; the original comparative evidence remains unchanged, and the new robustness and application demonstrations are qualitative without statistical uncertainty reporting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe A3D. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding methods, equations, tables and figures can be matched despite additions and relocation.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds ablation quality measurements, regularization sensitivity, diversity and prompt-robustness examples, and transformations of image-derived models.

before.justification: v2 reports original experiments on 15 prompt pairs and 26 structure-preserving transformations, quantitative ablations, hybridization examples and a RichDreamer implementation.

title: A3D: Does Diffusion Dream about 3D Alignment?

C1.justification: Adaptation without expert labels moves from a future direction in v1's conclusion to an achieved main contribution in v2. The introduction adds the shared codebook and replaces the emphasis on structurally close transfer with broader adaptation claims with or without supervision. The claimed number of tasks with state-of-the-art single-task results also changes from six to seven.

C2.justification: V1 interprets input-adapter instability as restricting successful transfer to compatible instance structures. V2 instead argues that low-rank sharing reduces task-specific representation separation and interprets its new controls as evidence of multi-task synergy. It also discusses the supervised/unsupervised cost tradeoff, explicitly limits applicability to easily enforced constructive feasibility, and sharpens the practical scaling limitation beyond roughly 1,000 nodes.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-repository link, node/edge codebook dimensions of 8/4, the learning-rate decay factor, and expanded per-task feature, action and trajectory specifications. Hardware changes from eight A100s to eight V100s. Some documentation remains inconsistent: Section 4 names HiGHS as the UMSP oracle, whereas Appendix E.15 names ORTools.

E1.justification: Transfer evaluation expands from four to eight tasks, adding Prize-Collecting TSP, Sequential Ordering, Maximum Covering Location and Open Shop Scheduling, including a new location domain. The original eight training task families remain. OVRP/OCVRP and SDVRP/SDCVRP are retained tasks with revised naming, not additional tasks.

E2.justification: V1 compares transfer against training from scratch. V2 Figure 3 additionally compares the multi-task backbone against fine-tuning seven individually pretrained task models on four transfer problems. This substantially expands the controls for assessing multi-task pretraining, while Table 1 retains its external baseline membership.

E3.justification: Reported training settings change from batch size 128 to 256, validation sets of 512 to 128 instances, and approximately 500 to 400 epochs. UMSP changes from 100x10 to 100x20, and supervised transfer from 64 to 128 labeled instances. The appendices revise JSSP processing times from U(1,10) to U(1,100) and OP prizes from random integers to distance-dependent values. Unsupervised transfer adds a time-budget comparison. These are reported protocol changes; the PDFs do not establish which changes reflect reruns versus documentation corrections.

E4.justification: V2 adds codebook ablations across eight transfer tasks and comparisons testing the benefit of multi-task versus single-task pretraining. The original mixed-attention and multi-type ablations are retained in Figure 5. V1's distance-shift experiments, large-instance JSSP analysis, adapter relearning/freezing observations and t-SNE analysis are no longer reported.

E5.justification: V2 first specifies best-of-ten reporting for supervised and unsupervised transfer curves and ten-run means with uncertainty bands for codebook ablations. V1 provides no comparable repeated-run reporting. Appendix C's phrase 'confidence interval of 100' leaves the interval construction unclear. These are new reporting practices, not evidence of an increase from a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 revise numerous gaps and runtimes: multi-task ATSP100 changes from 0.45% to 0.50%, and BQ-NCO's ATSP200 entry from 1.55% to 1.90%. V2 adds extensive transfer results, including best-of-ten unsupervised gaps of 0.11% for SOP and 2.92% for MCLP in Figure 4. Earlier shift and JSSP generalization results disappear. Changed training, data and transfer settings prevent interpreting the revisions as uniform same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: V2 introduces low-dimensional input projections followed by a shared codebook (Section 3.4). Transfer now trains fresh adapters instead of relying on compatible pretrained input adapters. Section 4.2 also adds unsupervised imitation-improvement: an expert samples 128 solutions from the current model and returns selected improvements for imitation. These change the architecture and adaptation procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction, transfer section and conclusion are substantially rewritten, and the attention explanation is reorganized. The appendices are extensively restructured: hyperparameters move forward, supervised transfer and codebook sections are introduced, and task descriptions change from domain-grouped sections to an expanded alphabetical catalogue. The title changes from 'Agent Learner' to 'Agent Learning'.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn to include the codebook. New transfer and uncertainty-band panels replace or supplement earlier displays, while the original attention and multi-type plots are merged into Figure 5. Table 2 moves to the appendix and loses its JSSP block. Grouped task overview tables become per-task specifications with relocated illustrations, and the t-SNE and distance-shift figures disappear.

R1.justification: V2 adds RouteFinder, Expert Iteration, self-labeling and self-improvement references, plus an HGS reference. It situates the new unsupervised procedure relative to these approaches. The broader positioning against specialized neural solvers and routing-focused multi-task approaches remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The tail-recursive BQ-MDP formulation, multi-task disjoint-union construction and mixed-attention mathematics are retained. V2 reorganizes v1's attention equation into equivalent expressions. It adds no substantive theorem, proof or formal guarantee.

improvement.justification: V1 identifies unstable learning of new input adapters as a central transfer bottleneck. V2 addresses it with a concrete codebook mechanism and ablations, demonstrates fresh-adapter transfer with and without labels, and adds single-task pretraining controls that better test the value of multi-task learning. Expanded implementation documentation further strengthens the paper. Removed shift/JSSP evidence, unclear uncertainty definitions and remaining oracle inconsistencies are drawbacks, but the central generalist-transfer contribution is substantially better supported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GOAL by the same authors. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark results, supervised and unsupervised transfer experiments, comparisons with individually pretrained models, and architecture ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark results, transfer experiments, architecture ablations, distribution-shift tests and latent-representation analyses.

title: GOAL: A Generalist Combinatorial Optimization Agent Learner

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central claims: a generalist backbone across CO domains, efficient transfer to new problems and strong single-task performance on seven of eight training tasks.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly qualifies Table 1's gaps as relative to the oracle, rather than necessarily the optimum. Section 4.3 additionally discusses relaxing parameter sharing between type-specific attention blocks during fine-tuning. The existing feasibility and quadratic-scaling limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds the 2.1-million-parameter backbone size, approximate adapter sizes and clearer node/edge dimensions. Appendix D and Figure 8 explain scheduling-specific inputs and attention blocks. Existing hardware, optimizer settings and code access remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same eight training problems and eight transfer problems. The expanded generalization experiments evaluate larger instances of retained problems, without introducing new task requirements or dataset families.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds RouteFinder-TE for CVRP and CVRPTW and Gumbeldore for JSSP. Table 2 adds explicit traditional-solver comparison rows, while retaining the neural comparators in its existing ATSP and CVRP comparisons.

E3.justification: New experimental settings include frozen-backbone fine-tuning, HGS one-second versus one-minute budgets, and additional size grids, including JSSP 10x15, 15x15 and 20x15. The core training budget, architecture sizes and existing evaluation metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figure 6 adds a control testing whether updating the pretrained backbone matters during supervised transfer. Table 2 substantially broadens size-generalization analysis from ATSP and CVRP to include CVRPTW, OP, KP and JSSP. The existing attention, multi-type and codebook ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report best-of-ten fine-tuning results and retain the same ten-run codebook analysis and confidence-interval description. No new seed reporting, uncertainty estimation procedure or significance testing is introduced.

E6.justification: Numerous reported scores and timings change. In Table 1, multi-task ATSP rises from 0.50% to 0.91% and UMSP from 2.01% to 3.84%; Table 2's ATSP1000 gap changes from 2.37% to 1.96%, with runtime changing from 28 to 5 minutes. v3 also adds extensive scaling results and frozen-backbone curves. The PDFs do not explain the numerical revisions.

M1.justification: The shared backbone, adapters, codebook, mixed attention, multi-type architecture and training objectives remain unchanged. Section 3.6 and Appendix D explain the existing procedure; backbone freezing is added as an experimental control.

P1.justification: The title expansion changes from Agent Learning to Agent Learner. v3 adds a dedicated training-procedure subsection and scheduling appendix, and refines explanations of BQ-MDPs, adapters and problem definitions. The overall narrative and section sequence remain largely stable.

P2.justification: Figure 2's multi-type schematic is substantially redrawn, Figure 8 adds scheduling diagrams, and Figure 6 gains a third series and shared legend. Table 2 is substantially expanded and reorganized, and Table 1 is resized with additional rows. Earlier Figures 3–5 are retained with changed numbering and placement.

R1.justification: v3 adds references on random-feature GNNs, bandit-based multi-task training and MCTS, replaces the Bertsekas book reference and removes the t-SNE reference. The broad positioning against specialized and routing-focused models remains unchanged; many other reference edits concern bibliographic metadata.

T1.justification: The tail-recursive multi-task formulation and mixed-attention equations remain unchanged. Expanded explanations of bisimulation, low-rank projections and type combinations do not introduce new proofs or substantive mathematical revisions.

improvement.justification: Additional comparators, broader size-generalization evidence and the frozen-backbone control strengthen validation, while architectural disclosures improve clarity. These are useful, bounded gains over v2's existing empirical case. Unexplained numerical revisions and the conflict between Section 4's all-greedy statement and Table 2's COMPASS exception limit the improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GOAL research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds baseline comparisons, further size-generalization results and a frozen-backbone control.

before.justification: v2 reports original experiments on eight training tasks, transfer to eight further tasks, architectural ablations and size generalization.

title: GOAL: A Generalist Combinatorial Optimization Agent Learner

C1.justification: The central claims about diverse function calls, complex instructions, benchmark scale, and the model–human performance gap are retained. v3 broadens the opening framing to task automation through Python and adds BigCodeBench-Hard as an available contribution in the conclusion.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations: low lexical overlap suggests limited contamination; Hard ranking differences may reflect domain imbalance and overfitting to easy tasks; and inconsistent CoT gains motivate discouraging prompt customization for official evaluation. It also argues for Hard's greater user relevance through reported SEAL-Coding agreement and removes v1's explicit CPU-efficiency limitation.

D1.justification: v3 documents the Hard retrieval model and thresholds, adds a concrete mocked-network unit-test example, reports a hosted execution sandbox, and replaces separate generation/sanitization commands with an integrated evaluation command. The main artifact reference advances to v0.2.0/post3, although the appended supplement still lists v0.1.0. Existing hardware and dependency specifications are retained.

E1.justification: v3 adds empirical analysis of the Stack Overflow archive and StarCoderData Python corpus for contamination and query alignment. The main coverage remains 1,140 Python tasks across seven domains. Hard selects existing tasks rather than introducing another programming language or task domain.

E2.justification: The comparator rosters in v1 Tables 6–7 are retained in v3 Tables 7–8. Additional comparisons in v3 Figure 11 include Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro/Flash, and Phi-3 Medium. Table 9 also compares zero-shot chain-of-thought with plain prompting for GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro.

E3.justification: v3 adds substantial evaluation procedures: embedding-based Hard subset selection, difficulty filtering, rankings averaged across Complete and Instruct, 10-/13-gram contamination checks, and controlled prompting comparisons. The original greedy and five-sample stochastic evaluation settings remain unchanged. The Hard solve-rate threshold is inconsistently documented between Figure 8 and the prose.

E4.justification: New analyses examine lexical contamination, how restricting evaluation to Hard changes model rankings and their reported alignment with SEAL-Coding, and sensitivity to zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting. The existing domain analyses, calibration study, and ten qualitative examples are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the same five-sample stochastic-generation disclosure and discussion of execution variability below 0.6%. v3 adds no repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests; its statement about no significant CoT advantage does not document a statistical test.

E6.justification: The original performance tables retain their numerical values, but v3 adds substantial results in Figure 11 and Tables 4 and 9. Table 9 reports GPT-4o calibrated Pass@1 changing from 29.1% to 34.5% with CoT on Hard-Complete, versus 61.1% to 59.4% on Full-Complete. These are new within-setting prompting comparisons, not improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The original three-stage construction pipeline and Complete-to-Instruct transformation remain unchanged. v3 Appendix F adds a subset-construction procedure using sentence embeddings, Stack Overflow query matching, and difficulty filters for BigCodeBench-Hard; v1 Appendix D.2 only proposed a future Mini subset.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and the section sequence remain intact. Changes include rewriting the opening motivation, revising terminology and citation style, expanding appendix organization, and shortening evaluation-tool instructions. The appended standalone supplement repeats existing datacard, construction, and timeline material rather than supplying a rewritten scientific narrative.

P2.justification: v3 adds the Hard workflow, paired query/task screenshots, ranking scatterplot, contamination table, and CoT table. It also changes the document template, typography, headers, and placement of retained displays, and appends separately numbered, line-numbered supplementary pages. Existing performance figures and tables largely retain their contents.

R1.justification: New Appendix E substantially expands positioning across encoder-only, encoder-decoder, and decoder-only code models, multilingual and object-oriented benchmarks, and repository-level evaluation. Added discussions include CodeBERT, PLBART, CodeT5, ClassEval, CodeScope, and OpenCodeInterpreter; Appendix F explicitly relates Hard construction to MixEval.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theoretical guarantees, formal assumptions, propositions, or proofs. The additions concern empirical selection and evaluation procedures rather than new mathematical analysis.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's planned small subset and untested contamination concerns, v3 provides a concrete Hard construction procedure, additional validity evidence, and a useful prompting comparison while retaining the original results. These gains are limited by contradictory Hard filtering descriptions, disagreement between the contamination prose and Table 4 about the omitted n-gram setting, and duplicated supplementary material with unresolved references.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BigCodeBench and provide readable main texts, results, figures, and appendices. The separately numbered supplement appended to v3 largely repeats documentation that can be matched to v1.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds contamination measurements, BigCodeBench-Hard evaluations, and plain-versus-chain-of-thought prompting results.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 60 LLMs, benchmark statistics, qualitative analyses, and a human evaluation with 32 of 33 sampled tasks solved.

title: BigCodeBench: Benchmarking Code Generation with Diverse Function Calls and Complex Instructions

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same benchmark contributions and central claims about complex instruction following, diverse tool use, and remaining model limitations. Additional appendix evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive discussion of future contamination, limited annotator expertise and library diversity, and API-maintenance challenges. Appendix P qualifies the realism of structured instructions and acknowledges ambiguity from rephrasing; Appendix O explains NaturalCodeBench's closer alignment with Instruct.

D1.justification: Appendix P supplies the rephrasing prompt and generator settings, while Appendix N adds concrete visualization-test code. The cited artifact release changes from v0.2.0.post3 to v0.2.4, and dataset-hosting guidance shifts toward Hugging Face. These disclosures do not establish changes to the retained experiments.

E1.justification: The correlation analysis adds MBPP+ and NaturalCodeBench's Python-English coverage. Appendix P adds evaluation under less structured, potentially underspecified instructions derived from BigCodeBench-Hard. The underlying benchmark's language, domains, and original tasks are retained.

E2.justification: Table 10 adds evaluated models Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, and GPT-4o-mini-2024-07-18 alongside the previously evaluated GPT-4o. Comparator membership in the retained main evaluations and chain-of-thought comparison is unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix P introduces an original-versus-rephrased evaluation, using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct to rewrite natural-language instructions at temperature 0.2, with a reported top_k of 0.95. The existing zero-shot greedy and five-sample random-generation protocols remain unchanged; the latter parameter's labeling is unclear.

E4.justification: Appendix P adds a four-model sensitivity study testing performance under casually rephrased instructions. Appendix O extends the analysis of agreement with other benchmarks. Existing chain-of-thought, domain-level, contamination, and qualitative analyses are retained.

E5.justification: There is no change to repeated-run, seed, or uncertainty-reporting practices. The additional results use point estimates without introducing confidence intervals, significance tests, or new uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Table 10 adds original/rephrased scores, including 27.7/8.8 for Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct and 25.0/12.8 for GPT-4o. Table 9 adds MBPP+ and NaturalCodeBench correlations. The original detailed model scores and HumanEval+/LiveCodeBench correlation values are unchanged; the new prompt-condition results are not cross-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction, Complete-to-Instruct conversion, testing, and calibration procedures remain unchanged. Prompt rephrasing is an additional evaluation condition; BigCodeBench-Evolved in Appendix G.4 is a future maintenance proposal rather than a revision to the current method.

P1.justification: v4 makes localized language corrections and clarifies calibrated Pass@1. It moves the benchmark-comparison section into Appendix O, adds appendix subsections, and removes the duplicated supplementary attachment while retaining its substantive construction guidance. Author affiliations and publication headers also change.

P2.justification: v3 Table 3 becomes the expanded v4 Table 9, with two additional benchmark rows. v4 adds Table 10 and visualization-test and rephrasing listings. Existing figures and main evaluation-table designs are retained, with limited layout and pagination changes.

R1.justification: v4 adds citations to SciCode, NaturalCodeBench, and two studies of Python API evolution or deprecation. These support localized discussion of benchmark coverage and maintenance; the principal research positioning and related-work sections remain stable.

T1.justification: Existing benchmark definitions and scoring mathematics are retained. The added empirical analyses and maintenance discussion introduce no new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: v4 modestly strengthens support for benchmark alignment and improves transparency through additional correlations, visualization-test documentation, and explicit coverage and contamination limitations. The rephrasing study is informative but limited: its example removes requirements, so the score drops cannot isolate sensitivity to wording. With the core benchmark and existing evidence retained, these additions support a limited overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BigCodeBench and provide readable main text, figures, tables, and appendices. Relocated sections and v3's largely duplicated supplementary attachment can be matched reliably to v4.

after.justification: v4 retains these empirical results and adds benchmark correlations and a four-model evaluation of rephrased instructions.

before.justification: v3 reports original model evaluations, tool-use analyses, contamination measurements, and human validation, including 32 successful solutions among 33 sampled tasks.

title: BigCodeBench: Benchmarking Code Generation with Diverse Function Calls and Complex Instructions

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central claims of efficient exact unlearning, parameter isolation, and improved deletion capability. The introduction replaces its specific claim of an optimal graph-matching selection algorithm with a contribution comprising several sequence-selection approaches, modestly revising the contribution framing.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes random-sequence retention theory from practical cyclic selection and leaves cyclic optimality and joint BMS diversity/score optimality open. It removes v1's dedicated limitation concerning expensive high-budget, large-model offline training, although the general offline-training tradeoff remains elsewhere. Interpretations of retained benchmark and ablation results largely persist.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds cyclic-selection pseudocode and weighted-matching implementation details, and corrects model reinsertion in deletion pseudocode from set difference to union. It acknowledges unspecified corner-case selection heuristics. Hardware, optimizer, training precision, and Table 2 hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The vision, GLUE/SuperGLUE, instruction-tuning, and LLM evaluation datasets remain unchanged. v2 adds evaluated sequence-selection scenarios with nonuniform, Dirichlet-sampled deletion priors in Section 4.3 and Appendix C.3; v1 discusses known priors but does not report these experiments.

E2.justification: Figure 6 adds ProtoSISA and full retraining alongside SISA. The new nonuniform-prior panels in Figure 8 compare BMS with Conditional Sampling, as identified by their legends, although nearby prose calls it random sampling. Appendix Figure 15 adds Sorted Cyclic Rotation. These substantially expand the deletion and sequence-selection comparisons.

E3.justification: Sequence evaluation changes from average minimum edit distance to reported average edit distance and adds deletion-prior scores, an L=5 budget sweep through 120, and nonuniform-prior tests. A new CIFAR-10 protocol measures cumulative checkpoint-switching and retraining time over 1,000 deletion requests. The existing fine-tuning hyperparameters in Table 2 are unchanged.

E4.justification: The single BMS diversity comparison expands into cyclic-rotation budget sensitivity and prior-aware sequence-quality analyses. Appendix C.3 additionally compares BMS with sorted cyclic rotation, examining score differences despite equal diversity. Existing slice-deletion, layer-allocation, sequential-training, training-time, and storage analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly reports averaging over ten Dirichlet-sampled deletion priors for the new sequence-selection analyses. v1 provides no corresponding repetition count. Existing parenthetical uncertainty values in Table 1 and uncertainty displays in retained plots remain unchanged; no increase in repetitions for those experiments is established.

E6.justification: The LLM scores in Table 1 and storage/deletion-rate values in Table 3 are unchanged. v2 adds comparator curves, cyclic-rotation and prior-aware selection findings, and deletion-time results. Figure 9 newly reports cumulative deletion time lower by factors of 2.8 versus SISA and 25 versus full retraining after 1,000 requests.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 replaces uniform-prior BMS selection with iterative cyclic rotation. For nonuniform priors and B <= L, conditional sampling gives way to score-weighted BMS using Hungarian matching and highest-score sequence selection; conditional sampling remains for larger budgets. The underlying sequential LoRA training remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section order and much of the prose are retained. v2 edits the introduction and background, integrates the roadmap into the introduction, adds a worked workflow example, moves design choices to Appendix C.2, and reorders appendix proofs. These are localized editorial and structural changes alongside the substantive additions.

P2.justification: Figures 3 and 4 are redrawn for cyclic rotation and weighted matching, and Figure 8 expands from one plot to three panels. New displays cover deletion time, cyclic-selection trees, and sorted-rotation comparisons. The conditional-sampling diagram moves to Appendix Figure 11. The document also adopts new headers, heading styles, table-caption placement, and extensive figure reflow.

R1.justification: v2 adds related work including Park, Zhang, Lucki, and Xu (2024), plus Kuhn and Tomizawa for weighted matching, while removing the Cormen, Gibbons, and Hopcroft-Karp references. The overall positioning around SISA and the approximate/exact unlearning distinction remains stable.

T1.justification: Section 3.4 generalizes the deletion-rate bound from B >= L to O(mL log(m min(B,L))). The retention proof replaces B'(1-k/L)^r with 1-[1-(1-k/L)^r]^B', changes the budget cap from binomial(L,k) to L!/(L-k)!, and introduces explicit random-sequence and uniform-prior assumptions. v2 also defines a prior-dependent sequence score; the existing BMS diversity lemma is relocated and adapted.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens empirical support for practical efficiency through additional deletion comparisons and direct deletion-time measurements, and more clearly qualifies the theory's applicability. These gains are tempered by unspecified cyclic-selection heuristics, the remaining gap between retention theory and practical cyclic selection, and removal of the explicit high-budget training-cost limitation. The evidence supports a positive but limited overall quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same S3T research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds deletion-time measurements and evaluations of cyclic rotation and prior-aware sequence selection.

before.justification: v1 reports original vision, language-understanding, instruction-tuning, deletion-performance, and ablation experiments in Section 4 and Appendix C.

title: Towards Scalable Exact Machine Unlearning Using Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions and claims concerning PEFT parameter isolation, budgeted diverse sequence training, improved deletion capabilities, and performance retention.

C2.justification: New Appendix D explicitly discusses expensive training for larger models and high budgets, and motivates sample-efficient PEFT for small modular components. v3 also interprets the new non-uniform-prior results as greater deletion capacity. The malicious-deletion caveat already appeared in v2.

D1.justification: v3 adds an implementation repository address and a reproducibility statement reporting supplementary code submission. It also specifies hours for Figure 9's deletion time and explains ProtoSISA's weighted logit combination. Existing hardware, optimizer, and training hyperparameters are unchanged.

E1.justification: All benchmark datasets remain. v3 extends deletion-rate evaluation to requests sampled from non-uniform priors (Figure 15 center); v2 used such priors for sequence-selection evaluations while its deletion-rate experiments used uniform requests.

E2.justification: The comparator methods remain unchanged, including SISA, ProtoSISA, full training/retraining, sequential PEFT training, and the sequence-sampling alternatives. The new ProtoSISA analysis sweeps parameters of an existing baseline.

E3.justification: New Appendix C.3 protocols vary budget with m=5 and L=32 under non-uniform deletion, sweep ProtoSISA weights 0.9, 0.5, and 0.3, and test ensemble sizes 1–10 using ViT-base on CIFAR-100 with m=5 and L=4. Existing protocols and Table 2 hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix C.3 adds focused analyses of budget sensitivity under non-uniform deletion, ProtoSISA mixing-weight sensitivity, and accuracy versus sequence-ensemble size (Figures 15–16). Existing deletion, layer-allocation, sequence-selection, training-time, and storage analyses remain.

E5.justification: Table 1's parenthetical uncertainty entries and the ten-prior averaging used for sequence-selection comparisons are retained. New plots continue existing reporting practices; no new run counts, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are specified.

E6.justification: v3 adds non-uniform deletion-rate results, small benefits from lower ProtoSISA weights after many deletions, and ensemble accuracy that initially increases and then plateaus around 90.6–90.7% (Figures 15–16). Existing benchmark and storage results remain unchanged. These are additional results under specified settings, not revisions establishing same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: v3 adds an experimental inference variant that ensembles models trained on different sequences within a shard (Appendix C.3, Figure 16). v2 describes selecting one best-performing model per shard before ensembling across shards. The default training, sequence-selection, and deletion algorithms remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 makes limited grammatical edits, adds reproducibility and ethics statements and a limitations appendix, reorders the storage discussion, and updates publication and author-contact text. The main narrative and section organization remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds shard labels to Figure 1, expands Figure 15 from one plot to three, and introduces Figure 16. It moves Table 2's caption above the table, relocates Table 3, and adjusts spacing and pagination while retaining the other displays.

R1.justification: The cited works are unchanged, as is S3T's positioning relative to SISA, approximate unlearning, and complementary partitioning or adapter approaches.

T1.justification: Definition 1, Lemmas 1–3, sequence-scoring equations, and Appendix A proofs retain the same mathematical content. Edits to proof prose are grammatical.

improvement.justification: The new ProtoSISA sensitivity and ensemble-size tests help assess previously untested choices, while explicit limitations and implementation access information improve practical usefulness. These are limited gains over a stable paper. The non-uniform-prior analysis is less conclusive: its comparison with Figure 6 uses different slice counts, 32 versus 64, and its highly variable curve weakly supports the stated gradual budget trend.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same S3T research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated storage-cost and broader-impact material.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds experiments on non-uniform deletion priors, ProtoSISA weight sensitivity, and ensembling models trained on different slice sequences.

before.justification: v2 reports original fine-tuning, deletion, and simulation results across vision and language tasks, including Table 1, Figures 5–9, and Appendix C.3.

title: Towards Scalable Exact Machine Unlearning Using Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims about theoretical novelty, expert specialization, balanced routing, early termination, and forgetting/generalization behavior.

C2.justification: Section 3.2 newly states that extending the theoretical analysis to top-k routing is outside scope. Section 5.2 suggests that top-k routing might reduce forgetting while weakening positive knowledge transfer, so generalization need not improve. These are limited new scope qualifications and interpretations.

D1.justification: Section 3.3 newly makes explicit that locality-loss computation only needs the selected expert's term because other experts' model changes are zero. This is an implementation clarification; Appendix A's hardware, hyperparameters, data processing, and execution times remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same synthetic regression tasks and MNIST tasks involving digits 1, 4, and 7. Appendix A retains the same task-cluster scenarios; no additional coverage is evaluated.

E2.justification: The single-expert comparison and the same multi-expert configurations with and without termination remain in Figures 2–3. Newly cited works in v2 are not added as evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: Section 6 and Appendix A retain the same data generation, metrics, expert counts, and training procedures. The MNIST experiment still uses 100 training and 1000 testing samples per round, with SGD at learning rate 0.2 for 600 epochs.

E4.justification: The early-termination comparisons and Appendix A's threshold-sensitivity and load-balancing analyses are unchanged. The new top-k discussion contains no additional ablation, robustness test, or case study.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging 100 repetitions for Figure 5. Repeated-run disclosures and statistical reporting remain unchanged, with no added confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed information.

E6.justification: Figures 2–5 retain identical plotted results, including forgetting and generalization curves and expert-routing records. Their empirical findings are unchanged; the top-k paragraph offers possibilities rather than new observed results.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, noisy top-1 routing, expert updates, locality and auxiliary losses, and early termination are unchanged. v2 explicitly names top-1 routing and discusses a hypothetical top-k extension without revising the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: Localized additions in Sections 3–6 clarify routing terminology, loss computation, expert grouping, and possible top-k behavior. The overall section organization and most prose, including the abstract, introduction, conclusion, and appendices, are retained.

P2.justification: Figures 1–5 retain their visual content, but surrounding text and equations reflow. Figures 2–3 move from page 9 to page 10, with adjusted spacing and reference placement; there are no added or redrawn result displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds references [44], Yang et al.'s M6-T, and [47], an Evron et al. 2023 entry. These support expanded top-1 motivation and a new statement comparing experimental breadth with earlier theoretical studies. The existing related-work discussion and central positioning remain intact.

T1.justification: The formal definitions, assumptions, propositions, theorems, and proofs in Appendices B–J are unchanged. The added top-k discussion supplies qualitative intuition without a new derivation or formal guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 improves clarity by explicitly identifying the top-1 theoretical scope and explaining the efficient locality-loss computation. The new top-k tradeoff discussion is tentative and lacks additional validation. These modest explanatory gains leave the underlying method, proofs, and empirical evidence unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, Theory on Mixture-of-Experts in Continual Learning. The main text, equations, figures, and Appendices A–J are readable and support reliable comparison; the appendix content is unchanged apart from pagination.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results, including the main experiments and supplementary experiments in Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic linear-regression and MNIST neural-network experiments in Figures 2–3, plus termination-threshold and load-balancing experiments in Appendix A, Figures 4–5.

title: Theory on Mixture-of-Experts in Continual Learning

C1.justification: The central claims remain expert specialization, balanced routing, necessary gate-update termination, and forgetting/generalization benefits. The conclusion's added statement that more experts need not improve performance already appeared in v2's abstract and introduction.

C2.justification: The explicit restriction 0<σ₀<1 narrows the stated applicability of the analysis. Otherwise, interpretations of specialization, gate collapse, load balancing, expert count, and the top-k routing tradeoff remain substantively unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds substantial reproducibility information for the new experiments, including class subsets, sample counts, ResNet-18 initialization, Adam settings, batch size, weight decay, and learning-rate scheduling. Hardware reporting changes from macOS/Intel graphics to Red Hat Linux/Xeon/V100; the earlier execution-time estimates are removed.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from synthetic regression and MNIST to selected natural-image classes: four CIFAR-10 classes, six CIFAR-100 classes, and six Tiny ImageNet classes. MNIST remains in Appendix A.4 rather than being removed.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparisons remain single-expert learning and MoE configurations with and without early termination. Existing experiments retain their comparator membership; the added benchmarks introduce no new comparison method.

E3.justification: Added image experiments introduce ResNet-18, Adam, five epochs per round, new sample budgets, 300–350 rounds, and accuracy metrics. Retained MNIST is redescribed as N=60 tasks in K=3 clusters instead of N=3, without establishing a rerun; synthetic N=7 is corrected to 6. Some new settings remain ambiguous: Appendix A.5 states N=350, whereas Figure 6 states N=6.

E4.justification: V3 substantially extends tests of early termination and expert count to natural-image tasks, using paired termination/no-termination curves and accuracy comparisons in Figures 3–4 and 6–7 and Tables 1–2. The existing synthetic threshold and load-balancing analyses are retained as Figures 8–9.

E5.justification: Both versions report 100 repetitions for the synthetic threshold experiment, shown in v2 Figure 5 and v3 Figure 9. V3 introduces no new repeated-run counts, seed reporting, confidence intervals, or uncertainty estimates for the added experiments.

E6.justification: V3 adds natural-image learning curves and average incremental accuracy results. Table 1 reports CIFAR-100 accuracy of 32.9% for M=10 versus 9.1% without early termination; Table 2 reports Tiny ImageNet accuracy of 37.6% for M=8 versus 10.5% without termination. These are new benchmark results; the retained synthetic and MNIST curves are unchanged.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same routing rule, expert updates, locality and auxiliary losses, and early-termination mechanism. ResNet-18 is introduced as a backbone for added experiments, without changing the proposed MoE procedure.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact, with localized rewriting and corrections. Appendix A gains dataset-specific subsections, MNIST moves there, and v3 adds acknowledgments and updates author affiliations and conference text.

P2.justification: V3 adds natural-image error, forgetting, and accuracy plots plus two accuracy tables, substantially expanding the empirical presentation. V2 Figure 3 moves to v3 Figure 5, and Figures 4–5 become Figures 8–9. The ICLR template also changes headers, author layout, typography, and algorithm placement.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds discussion of statistical MoE theory and Bayesian task-free continual learning, including Nguyen and Chamroukhi and Lee et al. Additional references support linear-model generalization and sparse routing. These are limited expansions within the retained research positioning.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 restricts σ₀ from σ₀>0 to 0<σ₀<1. Appendix E.7 also changes the Lemma 13 proof bound from the norm of θ(T2)−θ(T1+1) to the norm of θ(T2). The principal theorem statements and remaining derivations are retained.

improvement.justification: The added ResNet-18 experiments on selected natural-image classes strengthen support for extending the linear-model insights beyond MNIST, while accuracy tables make early-termination comparisons clearer. The overall gain is limited by conflicting task counts in appendix text and captions, absent uncertainty estimates for the new results, and removal of runtime information; the central theoretical contribution remains largely unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, figures, equations, and Appendices A–J are readable and matchable, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains those experiments and adds original CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet results, including accuracy comparisons.

before.justification: V2 reports original synthetic and MNIST experiments, including early-termination comparisons and termination-threshold/load-balancing analyses.

title: Theory on Mixture-of-Experts in Continual Learning

C1.justification: The headline claims change from removing at least 90% of second-moment entries and saving 45–50% memory to removing at least 99.9% and saving 50%. Claimed LLM effectiveness expands from 125M–7B to 39M–13B. The central structural contribution is also revised: Value/MLP blocks previously described as dense wholes are replaced by neuron-level partitions, with token-level embedding/output partitions.

C2.justification: V6 replaces the whole-block and sparse-embedding rationale with token/neuron-level Hessian interpretations and a shared-backpropagation-error explanation for averaging. It adds qualifications about unclear Value structure, training-length-dependent partition choices, untested non-Transformer architectures, baseline tuning and uncertain generalization of the GPT-2 loss-spike finding (Sections 2.3–2.4 and Appendices B–C).

D1.justification: V6 replaces the TinyLlama implementation description with Torchtitan and adds scaling architecture/training tables, runtime information, synthetic-data and matrix-generation code, Hessian ordering instructions and the optimizer.wv_names switch. V1's CommonCrawl preprocessing/split instructions and GaLore configuration are removed. These materially change reproducibility documentation; the Adam-mini repository link itself is retained.

E1.justification: Llama pre-training changes from explicitly processed CommonCrawl 2019-30 data to C4. V6 also adds synthetic binary classification data for the MLP Hessian experiment. OpenWebText, UltraFeedback/MT-Bench, ImageNet, CelebA and OGBN-arxiv tasks remain; the changes are limited within the retained application domains.

E2.justification: V6 adds LAMB to the GPT-2-125M comparison, Adafactor-Zhai-version to Llama comparisons, and Lion evaluations in Appendix C.5. GaLore disappears from the GPT-2-125M comparison, while GaLore and SM3 disappear from the trajectory comparison. These are substantive comparator changes, verified in the corresponding plot legends.

The Transformer Hessian study changes from four layers at initialization to one layer at 1% of training. The reported LoRA learning rate changes from 5e-6 to 2e-5. These are protocol revisions, without independently establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V6 adds MLP Hessian tracking throughout training, controlled matrix-density/preconditioning experiments, scaling analyses, detailed Adafactor/Lion sensitivity sweeps and an AdamW epsilon/loss-spike analysis. V1's layer-by-layer initialization Hessians and exceptional diagonal-block case study are removed or superseded. The trajectory comparison and LoRA analysis already existed in v1, although their reported comparisons are revised.

E5.justification: V6 Appendix E.2 specifies 100 Xavier initializations per matrix and 40 sampled angle configurations per dimension/condition-number pair, averaging results for Figure 5. This adds repeated-sampling estimation for a new diagnostic. It does not establish additional training seeds; the shared-seed trajectory design remains, and neither version provides systematic confidence intervals.

E6.justification: V6 adds scaling results, including 1B-model perplexities of 12.452 for AdamW and 12.372 for Adam-mini after 26.21B tokens (Table 5). Adam-mini's calculated Llama 2-7B optimizer memory changes from 28.04 to 26.96 GB (Table 1). Several training and trajectory curves change, and GPT-2-770M results disappear. MT-Bench and non-LLM table scores remain unchanged; revised experimental conditions preclude interpreting changed curves as same-setting gains.

M1.justification: V1 partitions Query/Key by head, otherwise generally uses whole parameter tensors, and retains coordinate-wise second moments for embedding/output layers. V6 Algorithms 1–3 instead partition embedding/output layers by token and Value/attention-projection/MLP matrices by output neuron, with a whole-Value option for short runs. This substantially changes learning-rate assignments and optimizer storage.

P1.justification: V6 extensively rewrites the abstract and method narrative, organizes motivation into explicit case studies, and revises the conclusion. Related work, the complete algorithm and non-LLM experiments move into appendices, which are reorganized from A–B into A–E. This substantially changes the document's narrative and organization.

P2.justification: V6 redraws Figure 2, replaces and expands Hessian displays, combines GPT-2 panels, and adds scaling, tuning and instability plots. Memory/throughput tables gain rows and subtables, and new configuration tables appear. Algorithms and LoRA/non-LLM displays are relocated or regrouped, alongside a changed page template and caption styling.

R1.justification: V6 Appendix A adds substantive comparisons with BAGM and NovoGrad, acknowledging earlier block/layer-wise adaptivity and distinguishing Adam-mini's Hessian-based partitions. It also distinguishes LAMB, discusses the relevance and limits of Das et al.'s preconditioning bounds, and substantially expands Hessian-related research positioning. These changes go beyond moving related work or updating citation style.

T1.justification: V6 adds an explicit cross-entropy Hessian expression for a one-hidden-layer network and its assumptions (Equation 1), plus mathematical definitions of matrix density and preconditioning effectiveness (Equation 3). These extend the mathematical reasoning beyond v1's qualitative discussion. The original quadratic construction remains, and no new convergence theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: V6 substantially strengthens validation: the 26.21B-token Llama 2-1B run and scaling study test sustained training, while explicit Adafactor/Lion sweeps address v1's limited baseline-tuning evidence. Revised partition instructions and BAGM/NovoGrad comparisons clarify reproducibility and novelty. These gains outweigh the removed comparisons. A reporting weakness remains: v6's new blanket claim of identical AdamW hyperparameters conflicts with the different ReMax learning rates in Appendix E.1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Adam-mini, with identifiable corresponding methods and experiments. All pages, including appendices, equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: V6 reports original empirical results, including retained training experiments and additional scaling-law studies, Hessian diagnostics and optimizer comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original optimization simulations, Transformer Hessian analyses, language-model training and alignment experiments, and vision and graph results.

title: Adam-mini: Use Fewer Learning Rates To Gain More

The added experiments support these existing contributions without redefining their scope.

Appendix D.8 adds arguments about limited transferability of Lion tuning and Adam-mini's interpretability. These refine explanations and qualifications while retaining the main interpretation.

D1.justification: Appendix F adds implementation references and learning rates for Swin, DiT-XL-2, and DC-AE-Diffusion. Appendix D.8 documents revised Lion search grids, and the CIFAR-100 configuration replaces the synthetic-data setup and generator. General-form pseudocode appears in the main text, while the MT-Bench table moves to the appendix. These substantially change the displayed evidence.

before.justification: v6 reports original optimization experiments, LLM pre-training and alignment results, throughput measurements, and vision and graph experiments, including appendix results.

title: Adam-mini: Use Fewer Learning Rates To Gain More

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and discussion retain the central claims that LLMs assume excessive human rationality and that their inverse inferences closely track human inferences. No main contribution is added or strengthened.

C2.justification: Interpretations involving training data, shared heuristics, and alignment with behavior versus expectations remain unchanged. Section 5 retains the same limitations concerning generalization, sampling, simulation methods, and missing direct human-prediction comparisons.

title: Solving Token Gradient Conflict in Mixture-of-Experts for Large Vision-Language Model
