title: Iterative Nash Policy Optimization: Aligning LLMs with General Preferences via No-Regret Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about learning a Nash policy, avoiding expected-win-rate estimation, convergence guarantees, and empirical advantages.

C2.justification: Section 3.4 adds the tentative explanation that avoiding expected-win-rate estimation may prevent performance degradation from estimation errors. This extends v3's discussion of estimation difficulty and cost without experimentally testing that mechanism.

D1.justification: Implementation settings and access information are unchanged, including Appendix B's learning-rate schedule, warm-up ratio, batch size, parameter search, and regularization rule. The embedded model, data, and repository links also remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use AlpacaEval 2.0, Arena-Hard, MT-Bench, IFEval, GPQA, MMLU, HellaSwag, TruthfulQA, and GSM8K. The training-data coverage and Appendix B evaluations are unchanged.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in Tables 1–5 is unchanged, including iterative DPO and SPPO. Section 3.4 discusses Nash-MD and DNO/DNO-Prct without adding them to the reported experiments.

E3.justification: Both versions retain three training iterations, eight sampled responses per prompt, the same preference-selection procedures, model configurations, benchmark sample counts, judges, and evaluation metrics.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 and Table 3 retain the same KL-regularization ablation under reward-model and preference-model feedback. No robustness tests, sensitivity analyses, or case studies are added or removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for the experiments. Statistical reporting is unchanged.

E6.justification: All numerical entries and reported experimental findings in Tables 1–5 are unchanged. For example, INPO (PM) retains 42.6 on AlpacaEval 2.0, 37.8 on Arena-Hard, and 8.43 on MT-Bench in Table 1.

M1.justification: The OMD update, population loss, sampling procedure, and Algorithm 1 are unchanged. New Section 3.4 explains existing methodological differences without modifying INPO.

P1.justification: v4 replaces the short closing comparison in Section 3.3 with a dedicated Section 3.4 Discussion and repairs the LLaMA-3 citation. The surrounding narrative and appendix organization remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: The added discussion causes limited layout reflow: Table 1 now precedes the Settings paragraph, and Table 3 follows rather than precedes the Section 4.3 heading. Table designs, captions, Algorithm 1, and appendix displays are unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 3.4 expands the comparison with Nash-MD, DNO, and SPPO, including their practical approximations and DNO-Prct's relationship to online DPO. v4 also adds Dubey et al. (2024), The Llama 3 Herd of Models, replacing v3's unresolved citation.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, Assumption A, regret and convergence guarantees, loss-equivalence results, and Appendix A proofs are unchanged. Section 3.4 adds conceptual discussion without new formal results.

improvement.justification: The new discussion makes the practical distinctions from Nash-MD, DNO/DNO-Prct, and SPPO clearer, and the repaired LLaMA-3 citation improves attribution. These are useful but limited gains; the method, proofs, experimental evidence, and reproducibility information remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same INPO study. Their complete main text, equations, Algorithm 1, Tables 1–5, and Appendices A–B are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains the original benchmark evaluations, ablations, and Appendix B experiments reported in Tables 1–5.

before.justification: v3 reports original INPO benchmark evaluations and KL-regularization ablations in Section 4, plus experiments starting from LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct in Appendix B.

title: Iterative Nash Policy Optimization: Aligning LLMs with General Preferences via No-Regret Learning

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from versatile local/mechanistic interpretation with clinical and human-study benefits to automated, fine-grained circuit discovery. V1's twofold speedup over path patching and user-trust claims are replaced by claims about recovery of manual circuits, hours-to-seconds runtime relative to ACDC, performance against random circuits and matching full-model faithfulness with fewer nodes.

C2.justification: Clinical hierarchy and human-trust interpretations are removed. V2 explains negative/supporting heads and ablation effects, and explicitly describes CD-T as combining direct and indirect effects rather than isolating direct effects. New limitations concern relevance-score scale and sign, heuristic tuning and limited human-understandable interpretation. Appendix A also qualifies the Greater-than reference comparison because all MLPs are retained.

D1.justification: V1's fine-tuning recipe, anonymized clinical examples and survey instructions are replaced by pretrained-model identifiers, corrupted-input distributions and explicit circuit/reference head lists. V2 specifies A100 hardware for its experiments. The code-access statement changes from code available in supplementary material to a promised future Python package; actual availability cannot be verified from the supplied PDFs.

E1.justification: The pathology/Gleason classification, SST-2 sentiment and AGNews topic experiments disappear, including their human evaluation. V2 instead evaluates indirect object identification, numerical Greater-than completion and Python Docstring completion. This replaces clinical and local-explanation coverage with language/code circuit-discovery tasks.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates path patching for circuit discovery and LIME, SHAP and Integrated Gradients in human experiments. V2 replaces these comparisons with ACDC optimized for KL divergence, EAP and manual-circuit references; random circuits remain comparators. ACDC participates in Figure 1 but is explicitly excluded from Figure 2. EAP-IG is discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: BERT-based experiments are replaced by GPT2-small and attn-only-4l protocols. V2 uses separate circuit-discovery and evaluation samples, task-specific corrupted inputs, and correctly answered examples only for Docstring. It introduces manual-circuit ROC-AUC sweeps over selection percentiles 90–99 and coarse-node comparisons. Faithfulness changes from v1's average true-class logit ratio to baseline-adjusted differences of dataset-average task scores.

E4.justification: V1's pathology word-cluster analyses, phrase-attribution cases and reported sensitivity to N are removed. V2 adds mean-versus-zero ablation comparisons, faithfulness-versus-circuit-size analyses and comparisons against random circuits of varying sizes. Appendix A adds IOI relevance heatmaps examining negative, backup and other functional heads, including disagreements with the manual analysis.

E5.justification: V1 averages random-baseline faithfulness over ten random seeds. V2 introduces a reference-distribution analysis estimating the probability that CD-T circuits are more faithful than random circuits across sizes, framed as circuit hypothesis testing (Section 5.2.2). It reports ten repetitions without confidence intervals. This changes the statistical procedure; it does not establish an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: V1's pathology results, including 46.0% versus 41.9% faithfulness, and its phrase/human-study findings disappear. V2 reports approximately 97% average manual-circuit ROC AUC, new runtime and size–faithfulness curves, and appendix results such as Docstring CD-T task score 3.235 and correct-guess rate 0.57. These are results under replacement tasks and protocols, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: V1 decomposes attention values while explicitly leaving attention weights undecomposed. V2 decomposes queries, keys, attention probabilities and outputs (Eqs. 6–15). Circuit discovery also replaces fixed top-N selection with revised relevance scoring, layer normalization, heuristic selection, pruning and performance-based stopping. V1's word2vec/PCA/k-means circuit-interpretation pipeline is removed.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, method exposition and conclusions are extensively rewritten around automated circuit discovery. V2 adds a standalone definitions section, reorganizes the methodological explanation and replaces the multipurpose appendix with task-specific experimental documentation. The title and author list also change.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. Pathology circuit/word-cluster diagrams, phrase tables, survey bars and attribution visualizations are replaced by runtime–ROC and random-circuit plots, three faithfulness curves, appendix relevance heatmaps and task-result tables. Algorithm 1 is also substantially reformatted to display the revised procedure.

R1.justification: The local-attribution-centered review is substantially replaced by discussion of causal patching and automated circuit discovery. New positioning covers ACDC, EAP/EAP-IG, sparse-autoencoder methods and circuit hypothesis testing, including Conmy, Syed, Hanna, Marks, O'Neill and Shi. CD-T is now positioned primarily against approximation, training and granularity limitations of circuit-discovery methods.

T1.justification: The attention decomposition is mathematically revised from fixed-weight value sums to decompositions through attention products and softmax. The relevance functional changes from average absolute relevant activation in v1 Eq. 1 to summed relevant/irrelevant L1-norm ratios in v2 Eq. 16. V2 also formalizes tasks and changes the mathematical definition of faithfulness. These are substantive definitions and equations, although no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: Standard-task comparisons, automated baselines, size curves and ablations strengthen v1's narrow circuit-discovery validation. The net gain is tempered by lost clinical/human coverage and the change from supplementary-code availability to a future release promise. New reporting problems also limit confidence: q*=0.8 is described as '80% more faithful,' while Appendix A.1.2 reports an ablated Greater-than score of -2.095 despite defining a probability-difference metric bounded by -1 and 1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CD-T and its use for circuit discovery, despite substantial changes to the title, method and experiments. Both main texts and complete appendices are readable, and their equations, tables and figures support comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original CD-T evaluations on IOI, Greater-than and Docstring, including benchmark curves in Figures 1–2 and circuit analyses and numerical results in Appendix A.

before.justification: V1 reports original pathology circuit experiments, phrase-attribution results and an eleven-participant human study, including Tables 1–5 and Figure 2.

title: Efficient Automated Circuit Discovery in Transformers using Contextual Decomposition

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims about efficient fine-grained discovery, transformer compatibility, 97% average ROC AUC, superiority to random circuits, and full-model faithfulness with fewer nodes. The added code-availability statement concerns reproducibility.

C2.justification: Appendix B.1 adds qualifications about finding universally suitable selection heuristics and possible numerical instability. The limitation that circuit discovery does not automatically produce an interpretation moves into Section 3.3.1; concerns about interpretable score scales remain in Appendix A.

D1.justification: V2 promises a future package; v3 states that implementation and reproduction code are available and supplies a repository link. V3 also documents handling of opposite-sign decomposition constituents and explains input averaging. These disclosures do not establish that the experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same IOI, Greater-than, and Docstring tasks, including the same corrupted-input scenarios. No dataset, domain, or task coverage is added or removed.

E2.justification: Figure 1 retains ACDC and EAP comparisons. Figure 2 retains EAP, random circuits, and manual references, with ACDC still omitted. Appendix A's manual-circuit comparisons are unchanged; EAP-IG remains discussed but unevaluated.

E3.justification: The models, task-specific discovery and evaluation sample counts, metrics, ablation distributions, and 90–99 percentile sweep remain unchanged. V3's general recommendation to average 10–100 inputs adds guidance without revising the experiments' stated protocols.

E4.justification: The mean-versus-zero ablation comparison, circuit-size analysis, random-circuit tests, and Appendix A's IOI heatmaps and circuit case studies are retained. Appendix B adds methodological discussion without a new ablation or robustness experiment.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten random-circuit repetitions and the same runtime averaging across threshold sweeps. Neither adds seeds, confidence intervals, or uncertainty estimates. The new input-averaging guidance does not describe additional experimental runs.

E6.justification: Figures 1–2 and Appendix A's numerical results are unchanged. V3 adds brief qualitative observations that averaging 10–100 inputs typically yields stable performance (Section 3.3.1) and that contribution distributions vary substantially (Appendix B.1), without new quantitative evaluations.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 changes the stated pruning scope from newly selected nodes S to the accumulated circuit C, with repeated removal passes until C stops changing. The decomposition equations and relevance metric remain unchanged. Layerwise normalization is retained in Appendix B.1 rather than removed.

P1.justification: The standalone circuit-definition section moves into Section 3.3.1, the algorithm explanation is revised, the limitations discussion is condensed, and Appendix B is added. Most introductory, experimental, and Appendix A prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: Algorithm 1 expands into a nested-loop display, conference headers are added, and text reflows around the reorganized sections and new appendix. Figures 1–2, appendix heatmaps, and result-table structures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The reference lists and substantive positioning relative to contextual decomposition, activation patching, and SAE methods are unchanged. Section 2.2 elaborates the manual effort required by earlier approaches without materially changing the research positioning.

T1.justification: New Appendix B.2 adds complexity reasoning: decomposition costs comparable to a forward pass, memory below three times a forward pass, and linear scaling with input count and node granularity. The underlying decomposition equations remain unchanged; no new correctness proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: The repository pointer, expanded pruning description, and Appendix B's implementation and complexity details modestly improve reproducibility and clarity. Quantitative validation is unchanged, and some details remain underspecified, including the constituent chosen for zeroing in the stabilization rule, so the overall gain is limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CD-T research. Their text, equations, algorithms, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison, including the new Appendix B in v3.

after.justification: V3 retains these original empirical results in Figures 1–2 and Appendix A.

before.justification: V2 reports original CD-T experiments on IOI, Greater-than, and Docstring, including runtime, circuit recovery, faithfulness, and appendix circuit analyses.

title: Efficient Automated Circuit Discovery in Transformers using Contextual Decomposition

C1.justification: The central claim that min-p improves the creativity–coherence balance, especially at high temperatures, is retained. v2 adds an explicit claim of human preference and identifies practical parameter guidelines as a contribution in the introduction.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning scaling to larger models, the accuracy–diversity frontier, parameter sensitivity and practical efficiency relative to eta/epsilon sampling. Appendix A adds specific limitations about hyperparameter selection and evaluating pre-generated rather than interactive outputs, alongside new connections between uncertainty and chain-of-thought reasoning.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands documentation of tested hyperparameters and selection rationale, human-study procedures, A100 runtime observations, and inference-engine integrations. It retains the implementation code and adds an anonymous repository address. However, v1's identification of Claude as the AlpacaEval judge and its explicit Exact Match reporting statement disappear.

E1.justification: GPQA, GSM8K and AlpacaEval Creative Writing remain the benchmark coverage. v2 adds a small creative-story study using the prompt 'Write me a creative story?' and English-fluent regular LLM users. Larger models and self-consistency extend evaluation settings rather than benchmark domains.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 adds top-k, eta and epsilon sampling to the GPQA/GSM8K comparisons, which previously evaluated min-p against top-p and unrestricted sampling. Table 3b also adds epsilon sampling to the creative-writing comparison. Mirostat was already evaluated in v1 Table 3.

E3.justification: v2 adds Mistral Large 123B evaluations, GSM8K self-consistency with an embedding-based entropy measure, and a Llama 3 70B human-study protocol using three outputs per configuration and 1–10 ratings. It also reports additional temperature settings. The existing 5-shot GPQA and 8-shot GSM8K prompting are retained.

E4.justification: v2 Figure 2 introduces an accuracy–diversity frontier and parameter-sensitivity analysis; Appendix B.2 adds runtime and high-temperature failure analysis for eta/epsilon sampling. The original case studies and temperature plots remain. The newly titled AlpacaEval ablation mostly repackages v1 Table 3, while omitting its weaker min-p configurations at temperature 1.5.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates without corresponding uncertainty estimates or formal significance tests. v2 Table 4 introduces mean±SD human ratings, and Section 6 reports a paired t-test with p < 0.05. Benchmark seed counts and repeated-run uncertainty remain unspecified.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial baseline, larger-model, accuracy–diversity and human-rating results. For example, Table 3a newly reports Mistral Large GPQA accuracy of 22.77% for min-p versus 2.01% for both top-p settings at temperature 3. Original plots survive in Appendix C.3, but Table 6 omits v1's temperature-1.5 min-p results with win rates 48.13% and 42.09%.

M1.justification: The threshold pbase × pmax, token filtering and renormalized sampling remain equivalent. The MinPLogitsWarper implementation in v1 Appendix A is retained in v2 Appendix B. Self-consistency is introduced as an evaluation procedure without changing the min-p algorithm.

P1.justification: The title and much of the prose are rewritten. Related work moves near the beginning, the separate background section is absorbed into other sections, methodology expands into several subsections, and experiments and results are reorganized. Human evaluation, reproducibility and ethics statements are added, and limitations move to Appendix A.

P2.justification: The main document changes from two columns to one. Figure 1 is rearranged into a grid, the case-study tables are merged, and original benchmark plots move to the appendix. New benchmark summaries, human-rating tables and an accuracy–diversity plot substantially change the presentation. Figure 1's revised caption incorrectly identifies several retained panels.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning around computationally costly entropy-based methods and connects min-p to risk-based parameter calibration, self-consistency and uncertainty-guided reasoning. It adds relevant work such as Zhou et al. and Wang et al., while dropping v1's dedicated discussions of locally typical sampling and contrastive decoding.

T1.justification: The defining mathematics of min-p remains equivalent, and neither version provides theorems or proofs. v1's background decoding formulas are condensed into prose. v2's threshold example explains the existing rule, while its entropy measure is an evaluation addition without a formal derivation.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly identifies its single-model scope and lack of human evaluation as limitations. v2 substantially addresses these through larger-model results and direct human assessments of quality and diversity, reinforced by the new accuracy–diversity analysis and broader baseline comparisons. These additions strengthen evidence for the central claim. The single-prompt human study, omitted weaker AlpacaEval configurations, incomplete experimental details and Figure 1 caption errors qualify—but do not outweigh—the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same min-p sampling method and share identifiable experiments, implementation code and figures. Their main text and appendices are readable and support comparison despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark experiments, a GSM8K accuracy–diversity analysis, larger-model evaluations and a human study with 54 retained responses.

before.justification: v1 reports original Mistral 7B experiments on GPQA and GSM8K across sampling parameters and temperatures, including results in Figures 2–5.

title: Turning Up the Heat: Min-p Sampling for Creative and Coherent LLM Outputs

C1.justification: The central claims about dynamic truncation, high-temperature quality/diversity, and human preference remain. The introduction explicitly broadens the experimental contribution to multiple model families and sizes and extends the practical-impact claim to advanced reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1.

C2.justification: V3 newly diagnoses limitations of the original human study, including sampling-order differences and participants overlooking incoherence. It adds explanations for low-temperature convergence, possible problems with combined samplers, and the diversity cost of higher min-p thresholds, plus an argument against universally optimal greedy decoding. Appendix A.5 also acknowledges false positives behind the earlier adoption estimates.

D1.justification: V3 substantially expands reproducibility documentation: it identifies benchmark inference frameworks and details the original survey's recruitment, compensation, presentation, filtering, and data processing. New evaluations include schemas, constraint libraries, prompts, parameter grids, judge instructions, and logging information. These disclosures extend far beyond v2's implementation listing and general experimental descriptions, although some new study details remain incomplete.

E1.justification: The principal reasoning and creative-writing tasks are retained. Appendix C.3 adds three creative-writing prompts requiring schema-constrained outputs, extending coverage to structured generation. The added Llama models concern experimental configurations; cited EQ-Bench, DeepSeek-R1, and agent-training work do not establish additional original task evaluations.

E2.justification: V3 substantially broadens reported comparisons: Table 7 adds greedy and configurations labeled tfs, quad, and dynatemp to AlpacaEval comparisons; Table 12 evaluates combined top-p/top-k sampling. Table 4 newly reports standard-sampling controls for the original human study, alongside the retained min-p and top-p results.

E3.justification: New benchmark settings cover Llama 3.2 1B/3B and Llama 3.1 8B/70B. The second human study changes the inference engine and reported temperature/truncation ordering, thresholds, recruitment, story presentation, and rating instructions. Appendix C.3 introduces structured generation, randomized blind comparisons, and five judge-rated metrics. These are additional protocols, not evidence that the retained benchmark experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V3 adds substantial analyses of low-temperature behavior, combined top-p/top-k sampling, higher min-p thresholds, and greedy decoding comparisons (Tables 10–14). Tables 17–18 analyze temperature and configuration effects in constrained writing. The original entropy/Pareto analysis remains, while v2's full benchmark sweep plots are omitted.

E5.justification: Human-evaluation reporting changes from mean ± SD to mean ± standard error, with condition-specific paired-test annotations. Tables 2–3 newly state approximate standard errors of 1–1.5 percentage points and mark results accordingly. Table 7 identifies a seed1337 configuration, but neither version establishes a general repeated-run protocol or an increase in run counts.

E6.justification: Tables 2–3 and the original min-p/top-p human means remain unchanged, but v3 adds extensive model, control, ablation, and evaluation results. Under the new human-study protocol, Table 15 reports temperature-3 quality scores of 5.80 for min-p=0.1 versus 1.23 for top-p=0.9. AlpacaEval metric assignments also change: v2 Table 6 reports 58.12/56.54 for win rate/LC win rate at min-p=0.1, temperature 1.5; v3 Table 7 reports 56.54/58.12. This reversal does not establish a performance gain.

M1.justification: The core min-p equations and implementation remain unchanged. Appendix D.2 introduces an exploratory min-z variant with a median-centered logit selection rule; it is not incorporated into the reported min-p experiments.

P1.justification: V3 reorganizes the appendices into implementation, benchmark results, additional evaluations, and applications/future work, moving the original limitations discussion to D.2. It extensively documents the existing human study and revises the evaluation narrative and resource discussion. Much of the core method prose remains recognizable.

P2.justification: V3 retains Figures 1–2 but removes v2 Figures 3–6. It redesigns the human-evaluation table to include controls and statistical annotations, expands the AlpacaEval table with configuration identifiers and output lengths, and adds numerous benchmark, analysis, and evaluation tables. Conference formatting also changes headings, headers, and the author block.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands substantially through connections to Top-Nσ as a successor method, independent replications, greedy-decoding studies, adaptive decoding, reinforcement-learning exploration, and DeepSeek-R1 deployment. These relationships are developed in the reproducibility statement and Appendix D, beyond the largely retained traditional-sampler review. Two earlier Shwartz-Ziv information-theory references are removed.

T1.justification: The original min-p mathematical definitions are retained. Appendix D.2 adds explicit threshold and selection-set definitions for Top-Nσ and the proposed min-z variant. No new theorem, proof, or formal guarantee for min-p is supplied.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens validation through additional model families and sizes, broader comparisons, and a second human study addressing the reported temperature/truncation-order problem. Detailed protocols and correction of misleading adoption estimates improve transparency. Important reporting problems remain: Table 14 conflicts with underlying benchmark tables, and the second study's sample size is unspecified. Nevertheless, the gains in empirical validation and methodological accountability constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same min-p sampling work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains original experiments and adds Llama benchmark results, a second human evaluation, and a structured creative-writing evaluation using an LLM judge.

before.justification: V2 reports original GPQA and GSM8K experiments, a self-consistency analysis, and a human evaluation with 54 retained respondents.

title: Turning Up the Heat: Min-p Sampling for Creative and Coherent LLM Outputs

C1.justification: The introduction modestly narrows the human-evaluation contribution to showing 'instances where' evaluators prefer min-p. The central claims about the method, high-temperature quality and diversity, generalization across models, and community adoption remain substantively intact.

C2.justification: Section 6 newly emphasizes that diversity ratings concern one fixed triplet per condition and do not measure variation across other possible triplets. Appendix C.2 distinguishes relative high-temperature robustness from optimal absolute quality. Sections 3.4 and A.5 also qualify framework popularity as evidence of availability and potential impact rather than direct usage.

D1.justification: Section 5.2.3 and Table 7 newly identify openchat-3.5-0106, GPT-4 Turbo judging with chain-of-thought prompting, and the fixed temperature-1 standard-sampling baseline. Section 5.2.2 specifies 20 configurations per method for Figure 2. Appendix A.5 supplies the supplementary search query. The implementation code and project access remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions cover GPQA, GSM8K CoT and self-consistency, AlpacaEval creative writing, human story evaluation, and constrained creative generation. No new model-evaluation task or input scenario is established. The expanded adoption survey concerns the same open-source ecosystem.

E2.justification: Comparator membership remains unchanged in the corresponding experiments, including temperature-only, top-k, top-p, epsilon, eta, Mirostat, and the additional configurations in Table 7. Despite v5's new explanatory note, Table 7's extra sampling configurations were already included in v3.

E3.justification: Appendix A.5 adds a supplementary adoption-assessment procedure using a specified code-search query and manual inspection, beyond the retained curated integration survey. The LLM evaluation protocols are not demonstrably changed: newly identified judges, controls, and configuration counts document existing evaluations rather than establish reruns.

E4.justification: Appendix A.5 adds corroborating analysis of adoption beyond the curated frameworks, reporting over 13,000 matching code files and manual inspection of their relevance. The temperature and threshold ablations, combined-sampler tests, case studies, second human evaluation, and structured-generation analyses already appeared in v3.

E5.justification: Table 7 changes from point estimates alone to reporting 95% confidence intervals for both win-rate measures and per-configuration counts labeled '# runs'. This substantially expands uncertainty reporting for the creative-writing comparison without establishing additional independent replications. Table 4 also changes its italicized significance criterion from p>0.05 to p<0.05, without explaining a reanalysis.

E6.justification: Several creative-writing entries change. In Table 7, temp150_topp_80 changes from 20.00% to 24.21% win rate and from 43.05% to 17.65% length-controlled win rate; other high-temperature top-p scores and output lengths also change. Table 3b's top-p score changes from 50.07 to 50.43. Table 6 updates reported framework stars from 575,800 to 668,000. Most benchmark and human-study results remain unchanged; the PDFs do not explain the experimental basis of the revised scores.

M1.justification: The relative probability threshold, token filtering, renormalized sampling, and Appendix A.1 implementation remain unchanged. The second human study's inference-engine adjustment and Appendix D.2's proposed min-z extension were already present in v3.

P1.justification: v5 extensively condenses and rewrites the abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations, experimental narrative, and human-evaluation discussion. It standardizes terminology and folds the separate resource-availability subsection into Section 3.4. These are substantial editorial changes despite largely stable scientific content; some malformed prose remains.

P2.justification: The existing figures and tables are retained, with several relocated and captions rewritten. Table 6 expands and removes its framework-group headings; Table 7 widens its presentation to include confidence intervals, counts, and an explanatory note. The underlying Figure 1 and Figure 2 graphics remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The bibliography contains the same works, and the substantive positioning against prior sampling methods is retained. The added main-text citation to Tajwar et al. refers to work already cited and discussed in v3's Appendix D.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4 corrects the complementary-threshold expression from 'Top-p-1' to '1-top-p'. This is a limited mathematical correction; the worked example, core sampling equations, and Appendix D.2 mathematics remain unchanged, with no new proof or theorem.

improvement.justification: v5 improves transparency through Table 7's uncertainty and count reporting, clearer evaluation details, and explicit limits on the human diversity judgments. These gains are tempered by unexplained score revisions and a new traceability problem: Table 3b's top-p score of 50.43 matches Table 7's p=0.98 row, while its caption still specifies p=0.9 or 0.95. The significance-legend reversal is also unexplained. Overall, reporting improves modestly while the method and most supporting evidence remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same min-p sampling work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D support reliable comparison; no material reading gaps remain.

after.justification: v5 retains these original benchmark, human-study, and structured-generation results, with some revised results and additional statistical reporting.

before.justification: v3 reports original GPQA and GSM8K experiments, human evaluations, and an explicitly original structured creative-writing evaluation in Appendix C.3.

title: Turning Up the Heat: Min-p Sampling for Creative and Coherent LLM Outputs

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same claims about novelty, quality-diversity benefits, high-temperature performance, cross-model applicability, human preference, and community adoption.

C2.justification: Interpretations of confidence-sensitive filtering, accuracy-diversity tradeoffs, computational behavior, and human-study limitations are retained. Appendix D.2 preserves the same applicability boundaries and future-research qualifications.

D1.justification: Implementation code, hyperparameter-selection guidance, hardware/runtime disclosures, survey and judge procedures, and project-access information remain unchanged. Splitting the code listing across pages adds no technical information.

E1.justification: Both versions retain GPQA, GSM8K including self-consistency, AlpacaEval creative writing, human story evaluations, and constrained creative generation in Appendix C.3. EQ-Bench results were already discussed in v5.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged across corresponding experiments, including top-p, top-k, temperature-only, epsilon/eta sampling, Mirostat, and appendix sampler variants. Newly cited contrastive decoding is discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: Prompting, model configurations, temperature grids, metrics, judges, and survey designs are retained. The switch to vLLM and other refinements described in Appendix C.2 already appeared in v5.

E4.justification: The temperature and threshold sweeps, combined-sampler tests, token case studies, accuracy-diversity analysis, and supplementary evaluations are unchanged. No ablation or robustness analysis is added or removed.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the same confidence intervals, standard errors, significance conventions, paired-test description, and seed/run information. There is no new uncertainty-reporting practice or reported increase in repetitions.

E6.justification: Matched numerical results and qualitative findings are unchanged throughout the main text and appendices. For example, Table 2 retains GPQA accuracy of 26.34% for min-p and 6.47% for top-p at temperature 2.0.

M1.justification: The threshold pbase times pmax, token filtering, renormalization, sampling procedure, and temperature ordering are unchanged. Appendix A.1 retains the same implementation; the new contrastive-decoding discussion does not modify min-p.

P1.justification: v7 adds one related-work paragraph, renames 'Computational Efficiency' to 'Simplicity,' repairs the unresolved EQ-Bench citation, and adjusts citation labels and bibliography formatting. The overall narrative and section organization remain intact.

P2.justification: Text reflow changes placement around existing figures and tables, and Appendix A.1's code listing now spans pages 16-17. Figures, table structures, axes, legends, and captions are retained; pages 20-34 are visually identical.

title: On the Expressive Power of Sparse Geometric MPNNs

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes language inequality and GPT-3/GPT-4 differences in dominant moral justifications. v2 removes the justification claims and foregrounds generally weak human alignment across 19 models. It also redefines the inequality question around high- versus low-resource languages and concludes that systematic disadvantage is not demonstrated, rather than treating cross-language differences themselves as inequality.

C2.justification: Interpretations of utilitarianism/fairness shifts and language-specific comprehension failures give way to explanations involving preference diversity, influential moral dimensions, and speaker-count correlations. v2 newly argues that procedural generation avoids training exposure when interpreting those correlations. It also expands discussion of dimension-dependent refusals and the limits of treating trolley-task alignment as real-world moral competence.

D1.justification: v2 adds open-model checkpoint identifiers and VRAM requirements, five exact paraphrases, dataset statistics, translation-checking information, and details of demographic-source collection and first-language weighting. Conversely, v1's explicit system-role prompt and full response transcripts disappear. The code/data link is retained. Some documentation remains inconsistent, including the vignette total and model identifiers.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same trolley-problem domain, six moral dimensions, random-character scenarios, and Moral Machine human reference data. Appendix B.1 contains the same 107 language codes in both versions; v1's references to 106 do not establish narrower coverage. Paraphrases test the retained task within existing languages.

E2.justification: v1 Table 4 compares nine GPT variants; v2 Figure 2 compares 19 models, adding Llama, Gemma, Mistral, Phi, Qwen, and GPT-4o Mini. Older GPT variants and GPT-3.5 disappear from the reported preference comparisons, although GPT-3.5 remains in v2's API documentation table.

E3.justification: v2 introduces global speaker-weighted model scoring, language-sensitivity measurement, four-cluster analysis, and a five-paraphrase evaluation on 14 languages using Llama 3 8B and 70B. The latter adds agreement, kappa, F1, and accuracy metrics. The underlying L2 distance and zero-temperature decoding were already present in v1.

E4.justification: v1's character-level preference analysis, reason decomposition, answer-eligibility analysis, order-consistency results, and extended response case studies are removed. v2 adds model-specific language clustering, analyses of dimensions associated with misalignment, speaker-count correlations, and paraphrase robustness tests. These substantially replace the questions investigated by the supplementary analyses.

E5.justification: v1 mainly reports descriptive frequencies without inferential uncertainty assessment. v2 adds Pearson correlations with significance reporting for moral dimensions and speaker counts, including coefficients and p-values for all 19 models in Table 10. It also newly states that generation uses a fixed random seed. Neither version establishes repeated-run uncertainty estimates or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: v1's reason-distribution results, including GPT-4's 52.72% utilitarianism and 41.85% fairness, disappear. v2 newly reports three Llama models with global misalignment below 0.6, near-zero speaker-count correlations, and paraphrase results of 75.9% four-of-five agreement, 78% F1, and 81% accuracy. Its world map evaluates Llama 3.1 70B instead of GPT-4, so this is a replacement result rather than a same-model improvement.

M1.justification: The core MULTITP construction and prompting approach remains: controlled trolley scenarios, automatic translation, and forced-choice completion. The prompt called token-forcing in v2 already appears in v1 Section 4.3. New scoring and analysis procedures change evaluation rather than establish a new model or inference method.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, dataset exposition, and conclusions are extensively rewritten. The results narrative becomes five research questions with separate methods and findings, replacing the moral-tendencies/meta-behaviors organization. The appendices are substantially reorganized, and the extended multilingual-example appendix is removed.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a single-column conference format. Reason-decomposition charts and capability histograms are replaced by ranked bars, violin plots, radar plots, and cluster boxplots, with several new tables. Figure 1 is reformatted, and the world map moves to the appendix with a different model, scale, and legend.

R1.justification: v2 substantially reframes the study around pluralistic alignment and psychological evaluation, explicitly distinguishes it from Takemoto's Moral Machine LLM study, and expands Table 1 with MoCa, GlobalOpinionQA, OffTheRails, and PRISM. It also recognizes controlled variation in MoralExceptQA, qualifying v1's stronger contrast with prior datasets. Literature supporting the removed moral-reason categories is dropped.

T1.justification: v2 Section 5.3 introduces a formal definition of cross-language sensitivity using dispersion of language-specific preferences. The displayed L2 misalignment equation otherwise formalizes the distance already described in v1 Appendix D. Neither version contains substantial theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical basis for general claims about LLM alignment: v1's GPT-centered comparisons and descriptive language examples are supplemented or replaced by comparisons across multiple model families, explicit speaker-count tests, and quantified prompt robustness. These address important weaknesses in generality and evidential support, while checkpoint documentation improves reproducibility. The loss of detailed rationale analyses is a meaningful tradeoff. Dataset/model documentation inconsistencies remain, and null correlations do not prove equal alignment, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger evaluation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the MULTITP study, despite the changed title and substantially revised analyses. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of 19 LLMs, language clustering, correlation analyses, and paraphrase robustness results in Section 5 and Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLM preference measurements, reason classifications, and language-specific capability and consistency results in Sections 5–6 and Appendices D–E.

title: Language Model Alignment in Multilingual Trolley Problems

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same dataset contribution and principal findings: most evaluated LLMs align poorly with human trolley preferences, while alignment does not clearly favor high-resource languages. The added appendix evidence does not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: v2 already cautioned against high-stakes deployment and treating trolley problems as comprehensive moral assessments. v5 adds an explicit descriptive-versus-normative distinction in Section 3.1 and the Ethics Statement: matching culturally specific human preferences may be undesirable, and alignment should avoid perpetuating harmful biases. It also interprets the new checks as supporting translation quality and option-order robustness.

D1.justification: v5 supplies translation-annotation instructions, task duration and cost, clarifies greedy decoding, and updates the advertised code/data repository from moralmachine to multiTP. Existing model identifiers, VRAM requirements and approximate API budget remain. The brief sentence about extracting binary choices through post-processing is removed, without evidence of a procedural change.

E1.justification: The core 107-language trolley benchmark and six moral dimensions are unchanged. Translation-validation coverage expands from an unspecified manual check in several major languages to human assessment of 44 languages, including low-resource languages, and automatic back-translation checks across languages. The regional analyses reuse existing geographic coverage.

E2.justification: The same 19 LLMs participate in the overall alignment and language-sensitivity comparisons. Additional analyses use models already evaluated in v2; no new comparator or competing translation method is introduced.

E3.justification: v5 substantially extends the validation protocols: five-point human ratings of 25 translation pairs per response, 169 responses across 44 languages, and back-translation evaluation using embedding cosine similarity. It also introduces regional grouping and an option-order consistency metric. Existing benchmark settings and paraphrase protocols remain unchanged; presenting both option orders was already documented in v2.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained paraphrase and language-clustering analyses, v5 adds human and automatic translation validation, tests the relationship between misalignment and language sensitivity, examines regional preference differences, and quantifies option-order robustness. These address additional validity and robustness questions rather than merely relocating the earlier appendix.

E5.justification: The new translation audit reports per-language means, standard deviations and annotation counts in Table 7, and adds a Spearman correlation analysis. Existing fixed-seed information and Pearson p-value reporting are retained. Neither PDF comparison establishes an increase in repeated model runs.

E6.justification: The main rankings, Table 3 sensitivity scores, speaker-count correlations and paraphrase results are retained. New results include 88.6% of 44 audited languages scoring at least 3/5, a back-translation similarity histogram, and a misalignment–sensitivity correlation of 0.43 with p = 0.07. Table 13 adds option-order consistency ranging from 87.1% for GPT-3 to 99.5% for GPT-4o Mini. Regional plots and Table 14's Llama-family preference entries further expand the empirical record.

M1.justification: The vignette-generation procedure, token-forced completions, presentation of both option orders and preference computation remain unchanged. Section 3.2 now lists translation as a third adaptation, but translation into 107 languages was already part of v2.

P1.justification: Changes include localized language corrections, revised author/affiliation and header text, expanded prompt explanations, and renaming Appendix B. Reproducibility and ethics statements move after the references, while the earlier results appendix becomes Appendix E. The main section order and five-question narrative remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v5 substantially expands the displays with a translation-quality table and histogram, a combined misalignment/sensitivity table, option-consistency and Llama-preference tables, and three regional multipanel figures. Existing clustering plots and the world map are retained and renumbered; main-text figures are relocated, and several table headings and captions are refined.

R1.justification: v5 adds supporting references on translation evaluation (Lavie; Goto), positional effects (Liu), and the risks of reflecting human preferences (Bommasani; Ethayarajh and Jurafsky; Santurkar). Section 2 and the central positioning relative to earlier moral-alignment benchmarks remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The preference-vector definitions, L2 misalignment metric and language-sensitivity formula are unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the added empirical validation does not introduce substantive mathematical theory.

improvement.justification: v5 strengthens the evidence for translation fidelity and option-order robustness, and clarifies why matching human preferences is not necessarily ethically desirable. These are useful improvements to validation and interpretation. Their impact is limited by the translation audit's partial coverage and several single-response languages; its stated standard-deviation range also conflicts with Table 7. The additions improve transparency without fully resolving the study's validation limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MultiTP study, retaining its multilingual trolley problems, six moral dimensions and 19-model evaluation. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v5 retains those original evaluations and adds translation-quality results, option-order consistency, regional analyses and further model comparisons in Appendices D–E.

before.justification: v2 reports original LLM evaluations, including misalignment rankings, language clustering, speaker-count correlations and paraphrase-consistency results in Section 5 and Appendix D.

title: Language Model Alignment in Multilingual Trolley Problems

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about MULTITP, multilingual moral alignment, widespread model–human misalignment, and the absence of a strong high-resource-language advantage. The count corrections and additional experiment do not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: Section 6 now interprets the uncensoring experiments as improving measured human alignment and reducing refusals, while acknowledging that refusals persist. Appendix F additionally identifies stronger effectiveness for Llama 3.1 8B. Existing qualifications about descriptive human preferences, trolley-problem scope, and language-to-country mapping remain unchanged.

The new uncensoring study cites its methodological source but supplies no additional implementation settings, modified-model identifiers, or reproduction instructions.

E5.justification: The fixed-seed statement, existing significance reporting, and translation-score variability reporting are unchanged. The new uncensoring results introduce no repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or other uncertainty-estimation procedures.

The gain is limited by sparse implementation details, persistent refusals, unexplained vignette-count revisions, and Figure 2's incompletely updated caption and accompanying results text.

after.justification: V6 retains those empirical results and adds original comparisons of four uncensored model variants with their original counterparts in Section 6 and Appendix F.

before.justification: V5 reports original evaluations of 19 LLMs, translation-quality assessments, and multilingual and robustness analyses in Section 5 and Appendices D–E.

title: OpenVid-1M: A Large-Scale High-Quality Dataset for Text-to-video Generation

C1.justification: The dataset and MVDiT contributions persist, but v3's introduction makes superiority on video restoration an explicit third contribution. This substantially extends the claimed usefulness beyond v2's text-to-video-focused contributions. The motivation also shifts from manageable dataset size toward maintaining million-scale coverage with better videos and captions.

C2.justification: The central quality and alignment interpretations remain. v3 adds explanations of caching redundancy and restoration benefits, and acknowledges caption hallucinations and remaining motion-description weaknesses. Its limitations remove the explicit inability to model long-duration dynamics and add a hypothesis that more high-quality training data could improve physical realism.

D1.justification: v3 Table 1 adds GPU counts and processing times; Appendix A.1 details scoring, three cascaded cut detectors, and human-guided filtering thresholds; Section 6.1 expands staged-resolution training documentation. Conversely, v2's hosting, CC-BY-4.0 licensing, maintenance discussion, and frozen-encoder statement disappear. These are documentation changes, not evidence that access or encoder training actually changed.

E1.justification: v3 extends evaluation beyond text-to-video generation to arbitrary-resolution video restoration, including a low-resolution UDM10 example in Figure 7, and adds direct human assessment of caption quality. Existing generation coverage remains; Panda-50M-HD is a resolution-selected subset of previously used data.

E2.justification: Relative to v2 Table 2, v3 Table 3 adds CogVideoX-5B and replaces OpenSoraPlan-V1.1 with V1.2 in the quantitative comparison; V1.1 remains in qualitative figures. The restoration experiment introduces Upscale-A-Video as a comparator. The earlier qualitative comparison against Gen2 is removed.
