after.justification: v3 retains the original SpikeLLM experiments in Section 5 and Appendix A, including repeated-training comparisons and additional quantization benchmarks.

before.justification: v2 reports original SpikeLLM accuracy, perplexity, efficiency, and ablation results in Section 5, with additional experiments in Appendix A.

title: SpikeLLM: Scaling up Spiking Neural Network to Large Language Models via Saliency-based Spiking

C1.justification: The introduction replaces BatchNorm-induced myopia as a principal theoretical contribution with a general TD stability analysis. The headline Hanabi comparison against R2D2 is also withdrawn in favor of MAPPO-focused discussion. The central proposal of fast, regularized Q-learning without target networks or replay remains.

C2.justification: v1 explains BatchNorm failures through myopia and short effective horizons. v2 instead emphasizes the gap between naive BatchNorm and practical CrossQ modifications, acknowledges beneficial input normalization, and calls for further theoretical analysis. It also clarifies why online PQN remains off-policy and interprets the new highly random sampling experiment accordingly.

D1.justification: v2 adds a reproducibility statement directing readers to an anonymous repository instead of v1's named public repository. It removes the Craftax MLP hyperparameter table while retaining the MLP results. Hardware, optimizer information, pseudocode, and the remaining hyperparameter values are largely unchanged.

E1.justification: The same benchmark coverage is retained: Atari, MinAtar, Craftax, Hanabi, Smax, Overcooked, classic control, Baird's counterexample, and DeepSea. DeepSea and the Dopamine Atari configuration already appear in v1's appendix. The new high-exploration experiment uses existing Atari-10 tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds BatchNorm and CrossQ-style PQN variants to the Atari comparisons in Figures 5a and 12. Removing v1 Table 4 eliminates the detailed Hanabi score comparison with R2D2-VDN, although the R2D2 resource comparison remains in Table 2.

E3.justification: The new Atari experiment collects data with randomness decreasing from 100% to 70% (v2 Figure 13). Normalization experiments introduce additional controls, and the reported Craftax recurrent module changes from GRU to LSTM. Retained benchmark budgets and hyperparameter tables otherwise remain substantially unchanged; these revisions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands the analysis of the central normalization mechanism: Atari ablations add BatchNorm and CrossQ-style modifications, while Craftax explicitly compares three normalization choices with and without input normalization. Figure 13 additionally tests learning under highly off-policy sampling. Existing Baird, DeepSea, lambda, and replay-buffer analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Removing v1 Table 4 removes explicit Hanabi numerical uncertainty entries, including PQN-VDN's 24.37±0.04. Both versions retain the stated practice of 10 seeds generally and 3 for ALE, along with shaded learning curves. No increase in repeated runs or new statistical procedure is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds normalization-variant results and shows a learned policy outperforming its highly random behavior policy. It removes the detailed Hanabi mean, maximum, and training-time entries from v1 Table 4. The ALE summary in Table 3 and all 57 per-game score pairs in v1 Table 11/v2 Table 9 are unchanged.

M1.justification: The reported Craftax recurrent architecture changes from a GRU in v1 Appendix F to an LSTM in v2 Appendix D. Algorithms 1–2, Q(lambda), and VDN integration remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish whether the architecture revision reflects rerunning experiments or correcting the description.

P1.justification: The theoretical narrative is reorganized around TD stability, LayerNorm stabilization, and a revised BatchNorm discussion. Related work and experimental interpretations are extensively rewritten; preliminary sections are reordered, appendices reorganized, a reproducibility section added, and the broader-impact section removed.

P2.justification: v2 adopts ICLR formatting, merges the separate Craftax and multi-agent figures, expands normalization panels and per-game Atari plots, and adds the high-exploration figure. It also removes the Hanabi results and Craftax MLP hyperparameter tables and substantially rearranges appendix displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds substantial positioning against Yue et al.'s LayerNorm analysis, expands distinctions from asynchronous Q-learning and CrossQ, and adds references supporting its theoretical assumptions and Retrace discussion. The detailed PQL and large-batch discussion in v1 Appendix B.4 disappears. These changes extend beyond citation-format updates.

T1.justification: v2 removes the BatchNorm-myopia theorem and proof, adds a mean-square TD convergence theorem and Markov-sampling analysis, and introduces explicit Robbins–Monro, compactness, Lipschitz, and geometric-ergodicity assumptions. It also revises the LayerNorm stability theorem and analyzed critic: v1 applies ReLU after LayerNorm, whereas v2 applies LayerNorm after a general Lipschitz activation. Appendix B contains substantive new and rewritten derivations.

improvement.justification: The added normalization controls and highly off-policy test strengthen empirical diagnosis, and the BatchNorm discussion becomes more qualified. However, the new Appendix B.1 proof does not justify its inference from vanishing weighted-average error in Eq. (11) to iterate convergence. Removing detailed Hanabi comparisons and uncertainty, plus Craftax MLP settings, also reduces transparency. These material benefits and unresolved theoretical and reporting costs prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PQN research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including material relocated or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark results and reports additional normalization comparisons and an experiment with highly random data collection in Section 5 and Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original RL experiments, benchmark comparisons, and ablations in Section 5 and Appendix G, including Atari, Craftax, and multi-agent results.

title: Simplifying Deep Temporal Difference Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion narrow the practical claim from eliminating replay buffers to eliminating large replay buffers. v3 explicitly distinguishes the buffer-free theoretical result from practical PQN’s small trajectory buffer. The central claims of simplicity, competitive performance and substantial training-speed advantages remain.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly states that convergence to a TD fixed point does not imply zero value-function error and clarifies PQN’s focus on simulator-based parallel-world problems. It interprets the new parallelism results as showing that multiple environments improve efficiency without being essential for learning. The earlier limitation concerning the absence of prioritised replay is removed.

D1.justification: v3 replaces the anonymous repository reference with a stated public GitHub repository and explicitly describes the I*T trajectory buffer and minibatch sampling. Hardware, optimiser and hyperparameter Tables 4–8 are retained. However, Algorithm 1 line 14 introduces a positive squared-error gradient step where v2’s Algorithm 2 used descent, creating a reproducibility inconsistency.

E1.justification: The evaluated environments and tasks are retained, including MinAtar, DeepSea, classic control, Atari, Craftax, SMAX, Overcooked, Hanabi and Baird’s counterexample. The new MinAtar parallelism sweep changes configurations within existing task coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding benchmark comparisons retain the same baseline algorithms, including PPO, DDQN, prioritised DDQN, Rainbow, CleanRL-DQN and the existing MARL baselines. The additional higher-L2 Baird curve varies regularisation strength within an existing ablation rather than introducing a distinct baseline algorithm.

E3.justification: The new MinAtar sweep varies parallel environments from 1 to 512, adjusting minibatches and epochs to control gradient steps and batch size, with learning-rate adjustments where necessary. Table 3 revises reported PPO/PQN update counts at 200M frames from 700k to 780k and Rainbow’s from 50M to 12.5M; these reporting revisions do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds a systematic test of the central parallelism design choice: aggregate and per-game sample-efficiency and time-efficiency analyses across four MinAtar tasks and nine environment counts (Figures 6e and 10–12). It also adds a stronger-L2 setting to the Baird ablation. These substantially extend evidence about when parallelism and regularisation help.

E5.justification: Both versions report 10 seeds generally and 3 seeds for ALE, with existing IQM summaries and shaded variability plots retained. The added experiments do not introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice or an explicit increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: New MinAtar curves show learning with one environment and improved aggregate sample and time efficiency with greater parallelism; Baird gains a higher-L2 result. Section 5.2 also reduces the reported gradient-update comparison from over 50 times to over 16 times. Main benchmark scores, including Tables 3 and 9, remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Equation (9) changes the regularised TD update from penalising only final-layer weights to also penalising the hidden-layer matrix, with an explicit eta > 1 condition. The practical lambda-return, minibatch and multi-epoch procedure already appeared in v2’s Algorithm 2; its appearance in v3’s Algorithm 1 is largely expanded documentation and relocation.

P1.justification: Sections 3–4 and the proof appendix receive substantial explanatory rewriting, including geometric intuition, proof roadmaps and a reorganised algorithm description. The practical algorithm moves from Appendix C into the main text, duplicate regularisation-related-work material is consolidated, and subsequent appendices are reorganised.

P2.justification: v3 adds the geometric stability diagram and MinAtar parallelism plots, expands the main result and ablation figures, and revises Figure 1’s labels and caption. Baird’s plot gains a curve and revised vertical scaling and is also displayed in the main text. Other benchmark graphics and table structures are largely retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds Boyd and Vandenberghe, Kolter, and Liu et al. (2020), while removing Lee et al. (2019). It explicitly positions the practical lambda-return procedure as a parallelised version of Daley and Amato’s approach, already cited in v2, and narrows the claimed normalisation analysis to LayerNorm when discussing CrossQ.

T1.justification: Section 3 and Appendix B substantially revise the mathematical foundation. v3 replaces the earlier Lipschitz activation specification with C2 pre/post-normalisation activations and bounded second derivatives, revises width-dependent bounds and the regularisation conditions, and uses the symmetric Jacobian part in Theorem 1’s eigenvalue argument. It also corrects LayerNorm derivatives and adds derivations of the stability decomposition and recursive lambda-returns.

improvement.justification: v3 improves precision through revised regularisation conditions and mathematical corrections, more accurate buffer and update-count claims, and controlled evidence about parallelism. These strengthen explanation and support without changing the main benchmark conclusions. The gains are tempered by the newly incorrect gradient sign in Algorithm 1, which weakens reproducibility and prevents an unqualified substantial improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PQN research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial theoretical revisions and reorganisation.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds results on parallelism in MinAtar and stronger regularisation in Baird’s counterexample.

before.justification: v2 reports original experiments on Baird’s counterexample, Atari, Craftax, MinAtar and several multi-agent environments, including ablations and appendix results.

title: Simplifying Deep Temporal Difference Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions: stability through LayerNorm and regularisation, and efficient parallel Q-learning without target networks or a large replay buffer.

C2.justification: Interpretations and qualifications remain unchanged, including regularisation’s effect on fixed points, difficult exploration games, and reduced sample efficiency under the alternative sticky-action ALE configuration.

D1.justification: The code-access information, hardware specifications, RAdam implementation details, network descriptions and Appendix E hyperparameter values are retained.

E1.justification: Both retain Baird’s counterexample, DeepSea, classic control, MinAtar, Atari, Craftax, SMAX, Overcooked and Hanabi. Removing detailed MinAtar ablation plots does not remove its games from evaluation.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is retained. In particular, v3 Figure 16 and v6 Figure 14 both show PQN, CrossQ, PQN with BatchNorm and PPO; CrossQ is not a newly added baseline.

E3.justification: The stated budgets, evaluation procedures, architectures and hyperparameters in Appendices C and E are unchanged. Figure 10 retains the same controlled MinAtar parallelisation comparison. Revised plots do not document a protocol change.

E4.justification: v6 removes v3 Figures 11–12, which disaggregate the parallel-environment ablation into sample- and time-efficiency curves for four MinAtar games. Aggregate evidence remains in Figures 6e and 10, so this reduces diagnostic detail without removing the overall analysis.

E5.justification: Both state that results use 10 seeds, except ALE results using 3 seeds, and retain shaded uncertainty displays. No change to the stated statistical estimation or uncertainty-reporting procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: The per-game MinAtar ablation result entries disappear. Displayed traces and bands also change in the redrawn Atari-10 figure and the Craftax replay-buffer panel, without an explanation establishing reruns. Headline numerical tables remain unchanged, including Table 3’s PQN 400M-frame median of 245 and 40 above-human games.

M1.justification: The regularised Q-network, parallel sampling, recursive λ-return targets and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged, as do the RNN and multi-agent adaptations.

P1.justification: Edits are limited to notation and wording corrections, the attribution sentence in Appendix B.4, and updated figure references. The section structure and substantive narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: Two MinAtar figures are removed. The Atari-10 raster-panel collection becomes a consolidated vector figure with reordered panels and a shared legend. Other appendix figures and hyperparameter tables are repositioned, with limited additional plot-formatting changes.

R1.justification: Appendix B.4 newly identifies Daley and Amato (2019, Appendix D) as the original source of the repeated and adapted λ-return derivation. That work was already cited elsewhere; the broader related-work discussion is unchanged.

T1.justification: The assumptions, stability theorems, proofs and λ-return derivation are retained. Policy/distribution notation and the description of the optimal-policy set are clarified; Appendix B.4 adds attribution without changing its mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: Explicit attribution in Appendix B.4 and a more readable Atari-10 figure improve clarity. However, v6 removes per-game MinAtar diagnostic evidence and changes some appendix curve traces without explaining the revisions. With the main theory, protocols and headline findings retained, these mixed effects do not establish a reliable net improvement or deterioration.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PQN research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–E are available and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated appendix content.

after.justification: v6 retains original PQN training results, benchmark comparisons and ablations in Section 5 and Appendix D.

before.justification: v3 reports original PQN experiments, including Baird’s counterexample, Atari, Craftax and multi-agent evaluations, with additional empirical results in Appendix D.

title: Simplifying Deep Temporal Difference Learning

C1.justification: v2 removes explicit new-paradigm and first-to-outperform novelty claims, qualifies the homomorphism conclusion as a possibility, and adds introductory claims about scaling and prompt robustness. The central claims of effective language-based recommendation, zero-shot transfer, and intention awareness remain.

C2.justification: v2's limitations explicitly acknowledge the absence of a theoretical guarantee, replacing v1's unresolved online-deployment limitation; the broader-impact discussion of attacked representations is also removed. The explanation for KAR/RLMRec trailing AlphaRec changes from language representations providing most of their benefit to their supposedly naive fusion design.

D1.justification: v2 supplies construction details for its new tests, including the random-letter perturbation and 19-negative candidate sets. Existing embedding extraction, model dimensions, hardware, optimizer, hyperparameter grids, query generation, and code access information are retained. Steam processing and the LLMRank model configuration are not adequately specified.

E1.justification: v2 adds Steam as a zero-shot evaluation population in Appendix D.2.3 and evaluates noisy item-title inputs in Section 3.2. The original six datasets remain; Industrial becoming Industrial & Scientific is a renaming, not added coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds an evaluated LLMRank comparator in Appendix D.2.3, Table 8. The comparator sets in the retained general recommendation, full-ranking zero-shot, and intention-capture comparisons remain unchanged. LLMRank's underlying work was already cited in v1, but was not evaluated there.

E3.justification: Added evaluations use Llama2 sizes of 7B, 13B, and 70B, titles with 5–10 random letters appended, and a separate LLMRank protocol with one positive plus 19 negative candidates and NDCG@1/5/10/20. These supplement the retained protocols; the documented 4:3:3 splits, filtering, and main training hyperparameters are unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends the investigation of encoded collaborative signals through controlled model-size scaling and prompt-noise robustness tests (Figure 2 and Table 2). Conversely, v1's shuffled-representation control testing the feature-encoding explanation is removed (Appendix B.3, Table 6). Existing component ablations, embedding visualizations, training-data analyses, and intention case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the same significance statements and markings in the main comparison tables. Neither supplies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or error bars; v2's added experiments introduce no new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds scaling and noise findings and LLMRank comparison results; Table 8 reports MovieLens-1M NDCG@1 of 0.3919 for AlphaRec versus 0.2485 for LLMRank under sampled ranking. The shuffled-control results disappear. Retained main-table raw scores are unchanged, but Table 3 fails to reorder its improvement percentages with the datasets, incorrectly assigning Movies & TV Recall improvement 6.79% instead of v1's 9.12%.

M1.justification: Equation (1) changes the stated user initialization: v1 averages MLP-transformed historical item embeddings, whereas v2 applies the MLP to their average language embedding. These procedures are not equivalent for a nonlinear MLP. Graph propagation and InfoNCE remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish whether the equation revision reflects an implementation change or a documentation correction.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. v2 introduces a separate Preliminary section and reorganizes the narrative around uncovering signals, building AlphaRec, and exploring representation potentials. Research questions and appendix organization are revised, alongside terminology and citation-style changes.

P2.justification: v2 adds the scaling figure and noise/LLMRank tables, removes the paradigm-comparison and shuffled-control tables, redraws Figure 1, swaps the convergence/ablation panels, and reorders dataset columns. Displays are extensively relocated within a different document template, although most existing experimental plots are reused.

R1.justification: v2 situates AlphaRec within existing LM-based representation generators and reduces v1's explicit novelty positioning. It adds relevant context such as Pazzani and Billsus on content-based recommendation and Harte et al. on language-model initialization. Appendix A's main research taxonomy remains substantially intact.

T1.justification: Equation (1) substantively revises the mathematical definition of the initial user representation by exchanging averaging and nonlinear projection. This exceeds a notation change. No theorem, proof, formal guarantee, or new derivation is added.

improvement.justification: The added scaling/noise analyses and direct LLMRank comparison provide useful evidence beyond v1, while the explicit theoretical limitation better qualifies the homomorphism claim. The gain is limited by removal of the shuffled-representation control, newly misaligned Table 3 percentages, sparse Steam evaluation details, and the unexplained user-initialization revision.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AlphaRec research despite the changed title and organization. All 25 pages of each version, including equations, figures, tables, references, and appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds model-size, prompt-noise, and LLMRank comparison results.

before.justification: v1 reports original recommendation experiments, linear-mapping evaluations, ablations, zero-shot results, and user-intention analyses in the main text and appendices.

title: Language Representations Can be What Recommenders Need: Findings and Potentials

C1.justification: Both versions claim possible homomorphism between language and behavior spaces, effective recommendation without ID embeddings, good initialization, zero-shot transfer, and intention awareness. The conclusion's replacement of 'fast convergence' with 'good initialization' repeats a contribution already stated in v2's abstract and Section 5.1.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations concerning inconsistent gains from feature replacement, possible noise in generated profiles, and narrower encoder performance gaps within AlphaRec. It interprets recent-data performance as evidence of preference understanding rather than memorization. Section 6 newly acknowledges the shared MLP's limited personalization and the impracticality of fixed intention queries.

D1.justification: Appendix C.5 newly discloses the representation adaptation used for the reported RLMRec baseline. Table 16 adds embedding-extraction time and monetary costs per 10,000 items. Existing hardware and hyperparameter details remain, but v3 removes v2's code-availability footnote and repository link; this establishes removal of access information, not withdrawal of the code itself.

E1.justification: Appendix C.6 adds Amazon Electronics 2023, extending evaluation to another product domain and recent interactions. Existing datasets, including Steam in the LLMRank comparison, and the recommendation, zero-shot, and intention-capture tasks remain.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds XSimGCL_t, which replaces ID embeddings with language representations, and untrained EMB-KNN. Table 4 adds VQ-Rec to the zero-shot comparison. These introduce substantive feature-replacement and no-training controls plus a stronger transfer baseline. New Table 8 also evaluates a generated-profile version of RLMRec against the retained implementation.

E3.justification: New experiments vary the language encoder within AlphaRec, compare RLMRec representation constructions, and restrict Amazon Electronics 2023 to interactions after 2022. Existing splits, ranking metrics, negative sampling, stopping rules, and default hyperparameters are retained. The newly documented RLMRec adaptation does not establish that the earlier experiment was changed or rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices C.4–C.6 add analyses of encoder dependence, the effect of generated profiles on RLMRec, and possible pretraining leakage through evaluation on recent data. XSimGCL_t and EMB-KNN provide additional controls for the importance of model design and training. Existing component ablations, prompt-noise tests, t-SNE analyses, and intention case studies remain.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the p-value << 0.05 statements in Tables 3–4. Neither supplies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or a specified significance-testing procedure. The added results do not introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Previously reported scores remain unchanged, but v3 substantially expands the results with new comparators, encoder substitutions, profile-based RLMRec, and Electronics evaluation. New Table 9 reports Recall 0.0687 for AlphaRec versus 0.0633 for RLMRec. In Table 4, VQ-Rec becomes the strongest zero-shot comparator, with Industrial & Scientific Recall 0.0645 versus AlphaRec's retained 0.0913. These are added findings, not same-setting improvements to AlphaRec.

M1.justification: The linear mapping procedure and AlphaRec's frozen language representations, two-layer MLP, graph convolution, InfoNCE objective, cosine scoring, and intention interpolation remain unchanged. Additional encoder evaluations do not introduce a new proposed procedure.

P1.justification: v3 makes local paragraph revisions, expands the limitations, adds acknowledgments and appendix subsections, and updates the publication header. The baseline-exclusion rationale and component-ablation explanation move into the appendix. The main narrative and section organization remain largely unchanged.

P2.justification: Tables 3–4 gain comparator rows, and v3 adds Tables 7–9 and 16. Existing tables are renumbered and several figures and tables move within the layout. The original figures retain their visual content, with no substantive redrawing or redesign.

R1.justification: New Appendix B.3 positions the study as complementary to approaches that use LLMs to interpret behavioral embeddings, discussing Tennenholtz et al. and Lei et al. Additional citations appear in the introduction and related work, including Fang et al. The overall research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: The task formulation, linear mapping mathematics, and Equations 1–4 are retained. No formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or substantive derivations are added. Both versions acknowledge the lack of a theoretical guarantee.

improvement.justification: The encoder and profile controls, stronger zero-shot comparator, and explicit personalization limitations make the empirical support more convincing and its boundaries clearer. The recent-data evaluation adds useful evidence but does not establish freedom from pretraining leakage. These gains are tempered by removal of the code-access link and retention of Table 4's already inconsistent improvement percentages despite adding VQ-Rec.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AlphaRec study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–E support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds encoder comparisons, a RLMRec profile ablation, and Amazon Electronics 2023 results.

before.justification: v2 reports original recommendation experiments, including linear mapping, AlphaRec comparisons, zero-shot transfer, intention capture, and appendix ablations.

title: Language Representations Can be What Recommenders Need: Findings and Potentials

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on random rewiring, graph-tailored attention, and the connection between message passing and sparse Transformers. v3 adds a novel efficient encoding contribution, D-RRWP, and makes the combination of encoding, rewiring, and attention central in the abstract and conclusion. The broad state-of-the-art performance claim remains.

C2.justification: v1 partly attributes performance to narrow, deep models and inductive bias on small datasets. v3 instead develops component-specific interpretations concerning D-RRWP efficiency, regular rewiring, attention alternatives, and the limited influence of minor design choices. Section 5.1 newly acknowledges that scalability on extremely large graphs has not been thoroughly evaluated; the nondeterministic-output limitation remains.

D1.justification: Both versions already provide detailed hyperparameter and timing tables. v3 updates encoding, hardware, compilation, and checkpointing information; discloses PyTorch Geometric implementations and ablation adjustments; and corrects pseudocode loop endpoints. It omits explicit 1cycle schedule naming and RAM/VRAM capacity rows. Both versions still promise a future GitHub release without providing access.

E1.justification: All eight original benchmark datasets remain, and v3 adds COCO-SP evaluation in Table 2. This extends the existing superpixel node-classification coverage to another image corpus. The new PascalVOC-SP ablations use a dataset already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 add NeuralWalker, while Table 2 removes GatedGCN+RWSE. More substantially, v3 adds direct component comparisons against GAT, GatedGCN, and Transformer attention, plus LapPE encoding alternatives, in Tables 4 and 6. These substantially expand the comparisons testing the proposed components.

E3.justification: Retained benchmark settings change: CLUSTER training decreases from 100 to 50 epochs, PascalVOC-SP from 600 to 500, and PATTERN/CLUSTER rewiring degree from 15 to 6. Their edge-removal rates increase from 0.3 to 0.5. New ablations introduce parameter-budget matching, padded LapPE controls, and optimization adjustments. Table 2 also adopts externally retuned LRGB baseline configurations.

E4.justification: v1 provides ZINC component-removal ablations and a regular-graph degree sweep. v3 substantially expands these into encoding and attention replacement studies, regular versus non-regular rewiring, fully connected controls, optimizer replacement, and corresponding PascalVOC-SP analyses. Tables 3–6 additionally examine runtime, peak memory, and D-RRWP storage requirements.

E5.justification: Table 1 raises reported training-run counts from 8 to 16 for ZINC and from 6 to 8 for other GNN benchmarks. ZINC rewiring-variance estimation changes from 30 to 100 test evaluations, and Figure 4 adds standard-error bars. Mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting remains, but v1's four-run preprocessing-time uncertainty is omitted in v3.

E6.justification: Numerous results are replaced under revised models and settings: ZINC MAE changes from 0.046 to 0.047, CIFAR10 accuracy from 82.471 to 83.750, and PATTERN accuracy from 90.997 to 89.177. COCO-SP MacroF1 of 0.4752 and extensive ablation/resource results are added. These are not controlled version-to-version gains. v3's claimed fifth-place Peptides-func ranking conflicts with Table 2, which lists eleven higher means.

M1.justification: Section 3 introduces D-RRWP, a truncated-eigendecomposition alternative to exact RRWP. It also concatenates forward and reverse RRWP edge encodings, replaces PN-V with batch normalization, removes degree-scaled attention, and includes the receiving node in attention neighborhoods. These change preprocessing and layer computations. Edge flipping and random edge removal were already present.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and related-work section are extensively rewritten, and GRASS's expanded name changes. Methods explanations are reorganized, random-rewiring theory moves into Appendix A, and experiments gain separate benchmarking and ablation subsections. The conclusion gains dedicated limitations and reproducibility subsections, and the appendices are reorganized.

P2.justification: The architecture overview is redrawn and moved from the appendix into the main text. v3 adds a simplified attention diagram and an ablation chart, updates the detailed attention diagram, and substantially restructures ablation tables to display controls and resource costs. Benchmark tables gain comparator rows and a COCO-SP column, while appendix tables are regrouped.

R1.justification: The core relationship to RRWP/GRIT, GPS, Exphormer, and BigBird remains. v3 more explicitly credits existing random rewiring and locates novelty in the component combination and D-RRWP. It adds NeuralWalker, the LRGB reassessment, and decomposition/implementation references while pruning earlier background citations. The extensive prose rewrite exceeds the change in underlying research positioning.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 adds the D-RRWP derivation: a symmetric normalized transition matrix, truncated eigenpairs, approximate matrix powers, time/storage bounds, and an argument for setting walk length equal to the number of eigenpairs. The earlier random-regular-graph arguments largely move to Appendix A.1; the diameter bound is additionally qualified as asymptotic and applying to almost every such graph.

improvement.justification: v1 claims advantages for graph-tailored attention but provides only limited component ablations on ZINC. v3's alternative-attention, encoding, and rewiring comparisons on ZINC and PascalVOC-SP substantially strengthen evidence for its design choices. D-RRWP gains mathematical explanation and an empirical storage/accuracy comparison, and stronger LRGB baselines improve evaluation credibility. Explicitly acknowledging untested large-graph scalability also improves qualification of the claims. These gains outweigh the incorrect Peptides-func ranking and loss of preprocessing-time uncertainty reporting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GRASS research framework, despite the changed title and substantive revisions. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching and comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original GRASS results on nine benchmark datasets, expanded ZINC and PascalVOC-SP ablations, stochastic-output variance measurements, and computational and storage results.

before.justification: v1 reports original GRASS results on eight benchmark datasets, ZINC ablations, stochastic-output variance measurements, and computational timings in the main text and appendices.

title: Greener GRASS: Enhancing GNNs with Encoding, Rewiring, and Attention

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims about combining encoding, rewiring and additive attention. The highlighted 20.3% ZINC MAE reduction is unchanged; the additional experiments do not redefine the main contribution.

C2.justification: v4 qualifies D-RRWP's applicability by acknowledging weaker performance on Peptides-struct. It interprets the new rewiring control as evidence that resampling, alongside regularity, matters for performance. Section 5.1 also clarifies deterministic-output handling through an input-graph hash.

D1.justification: Section 5.2 replaces a promised future code release with a stated repository location. Appendix F newly specifies GLU activation in task-head hidden layers and supplies roman-empire hyperparameters. These improve documentation without establishing changes to the existing implementation.

E1.justification: v4 Appendix C adds evaluation on roman-empire, extending coverage to a single heterophilic graph. All nine previously evaluated benchmark datasets remain.

E2.justification: The new roman-empire comparison includes NAGphormer and Polynormer, which were absent from v3's comparisons, and reports GAT (-sep). Comparator membership in the existing benchmark tables remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v4 adds a ZINC control that rewires once before training instead of every epoch. Its new roman-empire configuration uses 2,075,730 parameters, 24 attention layers, 4,000 epochs and batch size one (Table 13). Previously reported benchmark settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 4 adds a controlled test of whether repeatedly resampling added edges matters, complementing the existing tests of edge count and regularity. Previous encoding, attention and other design ablations are retained.

E4.justification: Figure S3 supplies detailed evidence for the low-variance-PC denoising check already described in v2 Section 4.1. E5.justification: Neither version adds or revises repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty-estimation procedures. Existing uncertainty displays are retained, and the new supplementary results introduce no additional statistical reporting practice.

E6.justification: Results in Figures 1–7 and S1–S2 are retained. Figure S3 adds denoising curves supporting the earlier observation. Figure S5 newly reports CKA equivalence with centered-cosine RSA, largely independent relationships with other RSA variants, and non-equivalence between cosine- and correlation-based RSA.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1 and C.1 revise the written ridge-similarity optimization target: regularization affects coefficient fitting but no longer contributes directly to the resulting score. An implementation change is not established. The overall Adam-based framework remains; Appendix C.3's explicit absolute-error loss documents the existing joint-optimization procedure.

P1.justification: Local revisions clarify score interpretation, PC thresholds, perturbations and joint optimization, alongside paragraph consolidation and expanded appendix descriptions. The title, overall section order and most prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v3 adds Figures S3–S5: denoising evidence, an explanation of joint-score boundary estimation, and RSA comparisons. Figure 5 receives clearer axis and color-bar labels. Existing principal figures and the overall document layout are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds the RSA reference by Kriegeskorte et al. (2008a) and Williams (2024), and removes Cloos et al. (2024). Section 2 sharpens the positioning around interpreting intermediate similarity scores, contrasting this with invariance properties at maximum similarity.

T1.justification: The regression-score definition is corrected by separating penalized coefficient estimation from residual-based R2 in Sections 3.1 and C.1. The CKA/NBS perturbation derivation and assumptions in Appendix C.2 remain unchanged; removing 'Proof' from its heading does not remove the derivation.

improvement.justification: Detailed preprocessing information, explicit joint-optimization instructions, revised regression-score mathematics and Figures S3–S5 make the work easier to scrutinize and reproduce. The gains supplement an otherwise stable paper. Some ambiguity remains: B.1's PCA preprocessing is not reconciled with B.2's statement that scores precede dimensionality reduction, and S5 leaves its reference dataset unspecified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, framework, datasets and principal analyses. All pages, figures, equations and Appendices A–C are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and additionally reports RSA relationship results in Figure S5 and detailed denoising evidence in Figure S3.

before.justification: v2 reports original synthetic-data optimization experiments, trained-RNN comparisons and analyses of neural recordings, including Figures 2–7 and S1–S2.

title: Differentiable Optimization of Similarity Scores Between Models and Brains

C1.justification: The contribution expands from depth-wise Transformer Alignment and trajectory regularity to coupling across both tokens and depth. The abstract and contributions also newly claim that coupling correlates more strongly with benchmark performance than parameter budget, model depth, or embedding dimension. These are substantive extensions of the central claims.

C2.justification: The in-context-learning discussion changes from claiming that coupling could only emerge through joint problem-solving to presenting a gradient-update analogy. v2 makes the exponential-growth explanation more explicitly conditional and adds layer normalization as a possible explanation for untrained singular-value scaling. The limitation concerning uncontrolled differences between independently trained models is retained.

D1.justification: Table 1 adds positional-encoding information and additional Pythia specifications, and corrects the Neo 2.7B and Pythia 6.9B parameter-unit entries. New captions disclose checkpoint selections, layer windows, and prompt counts. GPU, batching, quantization, and claimed supplementary-code information are retained; the smaller Jacobian prompt subset remains unspecified.

E1.justification: The six leaderboard datasets are retained. v2 Figure 19 additionally uses WikiText-2 prompts for representation and logit-entropy measurements, adding general-text input coverage within the existing language-model analysis.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 25 adds explicit comparisons of coupling with parameter count, layer count, and embedding dimension as predictors of benchmark performance. These competing reference predictors were not evaluated in the corresponding correlation analysis in v1.

E3.justification: v2 adds Pythia checkpoint evaluations, normalized coupling with a layer-separation restriction, 11-layer measurement windows, and K=25/50/75/100 sensitivity settings. Expodistance also changes from growth rates of layer increments relative to the initial increment to adjacent representation-norm ratios (v1 Section 3.4 versus v2 Section 3.3). The original growth plot is nevertheless reused, so the PDFs do not establish that its measurements were recomputed under the revised definition.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of training-time emergence, sensitivity to the number of singular vectors, associations with model properties and positional encoding, and depth-resolved norms, linearity, spacing, and logit entropy (Figures 2, 4, 19–22, 25–29). E5.justification: The existing median and interquartile-range reporting is retained. New checkpoint plots, including Figures 4 and 21, display mean curves with extrema or range information. Neither version supplies repeated-run counts or significance tests; the added bands describe variability rather than establishing uncertainty across independent training runs.

E6.justification: The headline R²=0.7214 and reported mean LSS values of 4.25 trained versus 6.54 untrained remain. v2 adds cross-token and checkpoint results; Figure 25 reports benchmark R² values of 0.3254, 0.3547, and 0.3614 for depth, embedding dimension, and parameter count. Figure 26 adds R² values from 0.7331 at K=25 to 0.6933 at K=100. v1 Figure 3's fine-tuned-inclusive correlation panel is omitted.

M1.justification: v1 analyzes a token's self-Jacobian across layers. v2 Section 3.1 generalizes this to input-output token-pair Jacobians and introduces coupling analyses with matching input/output tokens, fixed input tokens, and fixed output tokens. This substantially extends the analytical procedure beyond renaming alignment.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and contribution narrative are substantially rewritten around transformer block coupling and explicit research questions. Evaluation is separated from Methods, while PCA methodology and the ResNet comparison move into the appendices. The changes substantially reorganize the presentation beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds a coupling schematic, token-interaction heatmaps, checkpoint curves, and numerous diagnostic panels. The correlation display changes from two panels to one and moves forward; LSS is reordered and duplicated in the appendix. Existing spectral figures are enlarged and rearranged, and Table 1 gains a positional-encoding column.

R1.justification: The existing dynamical-systems and Residual Alignment foundations remain. v2 sharpens the distinction through transformer-specific token interactions and adds references to Su et al., Sarfati et al., and Wu and Papyan, while removing the introductory Brown et al. and Devlin et al. references.

T1.justification: v2 extends the mathematical definitions to token-pair coupling, introduces normalized mis-coupling, and revises the exponential-rate definition. Section 7 adds a short gradient-update argument linking coupling to in-context learning. The SVD framework and appendix linear-ODE derivation remain substantially unchanged, with no new theorem or substantial proof development.

improvement.justification: v1 supports training emergence mainly through randomly initialized versus final-model comparisons. v2 directly examines Pythia checkpoints, tests singular-vector-count sensitivity, and establishes a distinct cross-token extension through several interaction cases. These substantially strengthen the empirical foundation and contribution. The unreconciled expodistance definition and reused plot, together with removal of the fine-tuned-inclusive correlation panel, weaken reporting but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Jacobian and hidden-trajectory study, despite the changed title and expanded scope. Their main text, equations, figures, model table, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical measurements and adds cross-token coupling, training-checkpoint analyses, and supplementary representation and sensitivity results (Section 5 and Appendix A.6).

before.justification: v1 reports original measurements of Jacobian alignment, trajectory linearity, exponential growth, and singular-value scaling in trained and randomly initialized LLMs (Section 4 and Appendix A.4).

title: Transformer Block Coupling and its Correlation with Generalization in LLMs

C1.justification: The central claims about coupling, its correlation with generalization, and trajectory regularity remain. v3 adds adjacent-layer locality emerging through training to the contribution statement, refining the coupling claim without replacing the paper's central thesis.

C2.justification: v3 adds a subspace interpretation, an argument that stronger coupling complicates optimization, and an interpretation connecting stochastic depth to coupling. Table 2 claims implications for merging, pruning, projection, permutation and early exiting. Exponential growth is also qualified from occurring across all considered LLMs to occurring in the vast majority of trajectories; the heterogeneous-pretraining limitation remains.

D1.justification: Appendix A.7 supplies the new ViT experiment's architecture, hyperparameter grids, Adam learning rate, 500-epoch schedule, warmup, mixup, batch size, GPUs and training time. E1.justification: v3 adds CIFAR10 image classification, substantially extending the language-focused coverage of v2. E5.justification: v3 adds regression p-values for the full model sample and restricted subsets in Table 4, including 1.56×10^-6 for the full sample. Figure 5(b) also supplies uncertainty intervals for untrained expodistance, whereas v2's Figure 18 showed points without intervals. Existing LSS median/IQR reporting continues; no repeated-seed protocol is introduced.

E6.justification: The main correlation plot is revised from R²=0.7214 to 0.75, with changed plotted coupling values and model membership; this is not a same-setting performance gain. New ViT results report R² values of 0.35, 0.48, 0.74 and 0.83 at stochastic-depth rates 0, 0.05, 0.1 and 0.3. Additional findings include model-dependent CoT effects and perturbation responses. M1.justification: The Jacobian/SVD coupling procedure and LSS/expodistance measurements are retained. Although v3 simplifies the top-K notation in Section 3.1, Section 5.4 and Appendix A.6 still refer to truncated calculations. The ViT experiments apply the existing analysis rather than introduce a new proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction, methods explanation, discussion and related work undergo substantial rewriting. Token-wise coupling is reorganized into self/context categories, linearity and exponential-growth results are combined, and the limitations and conclusion are condensed. These changes materially reshape the narrative beyond accommodating new experiments.

P2.justification: v3 rebuilds Figure 1 as a five-panel overview, adds axes and colorbars to enlarged coupling displays, and combines/restyles regularity plots. It adds Tables 2–4 and multiple experimental figures, while moving several earlier main-text figures into the appendix and regrouping existing appendix panels. These are substantial visual and layout changes.

R1.justification: v3 substantially broadens positioning through generalization bounds, dynamical isometry, subspace models, compression and early exiting, particularly in Sections 5.4–6.2 and Table 2. It adds associated references such as Arora, Pennington, Ashkboos and Gromov. The earlier information-processing subsection and its associated references are removed.

T1.justification: v2's continuous-ODE motivation is replaced and expanded with finite-depth matrix products and spectral derivations. v3's Appendix A.5 derives conditions yielding ED=0 and LSS=1, while Section 6.2 adds a gradient-based optimization argument. Appendix A.6 also introduces computational-complexity analysis. These are substantive mathematical additions beyond notation changes.

improvement.justification: v2's central generalization evidence relied primarily on heterogeneous pretrained LLMs. v3 adds fixed-architecture ViT training experiments and restricted-model correlation checks, providing substantial controlled and size-restricted support for the central relationship. Detailed training instructions and clearer comparative figures improve reproducibility and assessment. The new compression and early-exit explanations in Table 2 exceed the experiments presented, and LLM causality remains unresolved, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the stronger empirical foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same transformer block coupling study. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original LLM analyses and adds results from training 64 vision transformers, alongside new prompt and perturbation experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original measurements of Jacobian coupling, hidden trajectories and training dynamics across LLMs, including extensive appendix experiments.

title: Transformer Block Coupling and its Correlation with Generalization in LLMs

C1.justification: The core claims about coupling, its association with generalization, and trajectory regularity remain. v4 explicitly extends the abstract, contribution summary, and conclusion to ViTs and their training-time emergence of coupling. ViT experiments already appeared in v3, so this is a limited broadening of the headline contribution.

C2.justification: v4 replaces the suggestion that coupling explains stochastic-depth regularization with an interpretation emphasizing a structural property shared by LLMs and ViTs, including training-data coupling versus test accuracy. It removes v3's specific limitations concerning expensive LLM training and heterogeneous pretraining setups. Most subspace and optimization interpretations survive through relocation from Section 6.2 to Appendix A.4.

D1.justification: v4 adds a specific source-code repository address where v3 only mentions supplementary code. It updates the ViT hyperparameters and reported training time from approximately two to six hours; most LLM hardware, batching, and quantization information remains. However, the retained multi-weight-decay sweep in v4 Figure 7 loses its matching 64-model training description when Appendix A.7 is rewritten.

E1.justification: The Easy2Hard-Bench difficulty and prompt-length experiment in v3 Figure 9 disappears. The six leaderboard datasets, WikiText-2, CIFAR-10, and the chain-of-thought and embedding-perturbation scenarios remain. E2.justification: The comparisons against model depth, embedding dimension, and parameter count remain, as do trained-versus-untrained comparisons. E5.justification: Both versions report regression R-squared/p-values and use medians with interquartile ranges for trajectory measurements. E6.justification: Figure 1 changes from R-squared 0.75 and p = 1.56e-6 to 0.80 and p = 9.99e-10 under a revised metric and model sample. Table 1 changes Pythia-12B's score from 58.9 to 38.82 and swaps the Gemma-1.1 7B/2B scores. These are revised results, not controlled performance gains.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 adds the matrix B = (V'_K)^T J U'_K to extend the analysis to alignment between left and right singular vectors. The underlying block-Jacobian construction and SVD procedure remain unchanged; the substantial coupling-metric revision is assessed separately below.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and selected explanations are edited, a dedicated ViT results subsection is added, and the significance discussion moves into Appendix A.4. The limitations section disappears, acknowledgments are added, and the header changes to ICLR 2025 publication status. The overall narrative and most explanatory prose remain recognizable.

P2.justification: The central correlation plots are redrawn with revised axes and model labels, and a substantially different ViT Figure 6 is placed in the main text. Table 1 expands, Tables 3–4 disappear, and several appendix displays are removed or reduced. Retained heatmaps and trajectory plots are extensively rearranged and resized; image matching confirms that many are redisplayed rather than new results.

The substantive positioning relative to residual alignment, neural ODEs, in-context learning, and neural collapse remains.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 replaces off-diagonal mis-coupling, ||A - Diag(A)||_F, and its A-normalized variant with ||A_K - S_K||_F/||s_K||_p, typically using p = 1, and defines coupling as 1 minus this quantity. This changes the central mathematical definition substantially. The exponential-growth derivation largely retains assumptions already present in v3 Appendix A.5. However, v4 Appendix A.4 changes the growth/decay criterion from the sign of s_j to whether s_j exceeds 1, despite retaining the factor (1 + s_j)^l.

improvement.justification: Broader LLM correlations, new ViT training trajectories, and an explicit code address improve empirical reach and accessibility. However, v3's subgroup/difficulty checks and specific cross-model limitations disappear. The retained ViT sweep no longer has matching training documentation, and Appendix A.4 introduces a growth/decay threshold inconsistent with its displayed dynamics. Higher correlations use changed metrics or settings. These benefits and losses do not establish a reliable net improvement or deterioration.

after.justification: v4 retains original LLM measurements and reports revised cross-model correlations and ViT coupling/accuracy measurements across training checkpoints.

before.justification: v3 reports original Jacobian-coupling measurements, trajectory analyses, training-checkpoint observations, and CIFAR-10 experiments with trained ViTs.

title: Transformer Block Coupling and its Correlation with Generalization in LLMs

Decoder-free learning and prospective scalability cease to be headline contributions, although their experiment and exploratory claims remain in Appendix D.3.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes distortion's conflict with reconstruction; v2 emphasizes its conflict with prior alignment. v2 adds explanations connecting cosine regularization to latent expressiveness and GMG debiasing to gradient stability. The joint-regularization interpretation disappears, while the decoder-free limitation favoring DST remains. Broad GMG-dominance wording needs qualification because some new encoder rows favor DST.

D1.justification: Algorithm 1 and Appendix E substantially expand implementation disclosure: cost-dependent entropy scaling, epsilon scale 0.1, mean-based normalization, uniform coupling initialization and implementation code. Appendix C.2 specifies the stability procedure. Existing VAE architecture and hardware details remain. New encoder experiments extend configurations of these methods. Newly cited related works do not become additional evaluated baselines.

E4.justification: v2 adds a substantial stability investigation comparing encoder and decoder gradients across all four datasets (Figures 3–4). Table 1 extends encoder ablations from cosine to squared and scaled squared distances. Conversely, the joint encoder–decoder ablations in v1 Table 4 are removed. The decoder-free analysis is retained in Appendix D.3.

E6.justification: Most previously reported decoder and decoder-free scores are retained. v2 adds encoder distance-cost results and gradient-alignment findings, with a particularly clear decoder-alignment advantage on DSprites. The Shapes3D beta-VAE decoder GMG entry with squared-distance costs changes from 72.0 ±12.5 to 72.0 ±8.5. Joint encoder–decoder result rows are removed.

M1.justification: The proposed method remains distortion minus Gromov-Wasserstein cost, incorporated into VAE objectives through encoder or decoder regularization. The same geometric cost families remain, with IR/SIR/CR renamed L2-squared/ScL2-squared/Cos. New pseudocode and implementation details do not establish an underlying algorithm change.

P1.justification: The title is shortened and substantial portions of the introduction, background, method exposition and experimental narrative are rewritten. Duplicated introductory material is removed, contributions are enumerated, and experiments are organized around explicit questions. Proofs and appendices are reorganized, decoder-free learning moves to Appendix D.3, and a reproducibility section is added.

P2.justification: v2 adds a GMG schematic, Algorithm 1 and two gradient-stability figures. The original synthetic figure becomes Figure 2 with a revised caption. Table 1 integrates existing encoder results and new configurations; Table 2 removes the duplicated Shapes3D display. Ablation tables are reduced, the decoder-free table moves to the appendix, and typography, headers and page layout change throughout.

R1.justification: v2 acknowledges concurrent GMG work by Sotiropoulou and Alvarez-Melis and distinguishes its disentanglement application and theoretical investigation. It expands geometric/topological related work, including Hahm, Moor and Balabin, and discusses flexibility relative to neural GW approaches. Some background OT citations, including Genevay and Pooladian, are removed.

T1.justification: The central weak-convexity theorem and most derivations remain (v1 Theorem 3.7; v2 Theorem 3.5). v2 makes admissible-kernel assumptions explicit, qualifies the GM/GW optimality-gap interpretation, and adds zero-gap sufficiency and cost-rescaling proofs in B.1–B.2. improvement.justification: v2 makes the existing contribution easier to understand and assess through clearer exposition, explicit concurrent-work positioning, solver details and relevant encoder/stability analyses. P1.justification: The distortion material moves from v2 Section 3.1 into v3 Section 2.3, with corresponding subsection and theorem renumbering. P2.justification: The appendix gains a two-panel entropy/performance and iteration plot, two latent-traversal image grids, higher-resolution hyperparameter and results tables, and a solver pseudocode display. (2023), including its cost conditions and dependence on dimensions and fourth moments.

improvement.justification: v3 modestly strengthens empirical validation and usability through entropy-sensitivity and convergence checks, higher-resolution evaluation, latent visualizations, and additional solver and code-access information. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Gromov-Monge Gap research and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–E. Retained material can be matched across restructuring and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds entropy-sensitivity experiments, higher-resolution Shapes3D results, and latent-traversal visualizations.

before.justification: v2 reports original synthetic transport experiments, disentanglement results on four image datasets, gradient-stability analyses, and decoder-free experiments.

title: Disentangled Representation Learning with the Gromov-Monge Gap

C1.justification: The central claims about confounded model comparisons, fine-tuning adjustment, and emergence remain. Section 7 modestly narrows the emergence conclusion: v1 says adjustment removes unpredictability and discontinuity, whereas v2 says it greatly reduces unpredictability and makes capabilities predictable at smaller scales.

C2.justification: Section 4.1 newly emphasizes that base-model performance may not predict performance after adaptation. Appendix F explains instruction/chat trends through benchmark-containing instruction data and a shift from preference-oriented to benchmark-oriented post-training. Appendix B now supports saturation indirectly through performance equalization after removing the dedicated saturation analysis.
