These additions substantially broaden the models compared before and after adjustment.

E3.justification: Section 3.1 changes its reported design from randomly partitioning older models into treatment/control groups to comparing original models with fine-tuned copies, restricting treatment to models with at least 7×10^21 pretraining FLOPs. New protocols include a five-value learning-rate sweep and September 2023/January 2024 cutoffs. The final displayed GSM8K emergence checkpoint also changes from 1.6 million to 320,000 training examples.

E4.justification: New Appendix A.3 tests whether hyperparameter selection favors older models, while Appendix C.1 tests sensitivity to the temporal cutoff. Conversely, v1 Appendix B.3 and Figure 13, which directly examine late-training saturation, are removed. The existing language-based split and model-discrimination analyses are retained under new appendix numbering.

E5.justification: Both versions report regression standard errors and mark statistical significance at p<0.05. The causal tables retain the same uncertainty reporting, and new experiments use existing conventions. No new repeated-run counts, seed disclosures, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are introduced.

E6.justification: With the expanded model cohort, Figure 1's unadjusted MMLU/GSM8K recency gaps change from 0.068/0.168 to 0.073/0.191. Figure 3 reports different estimates under its revised control design. New Figure 19 reports instruction/chat gaps of 0.063/0.154 unadjusted and -0.001/0.027 adjusted. Robustness results are added and saturation results removed; these are not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The proposed adjustment remains full-parameter fine-tuning on the same sufficient task-relevant data before evaluation. The main datasets and three-epoch procedure are retained. Changes to the controlled validation experiment and hyperparameter sensitivity tests concern evaluation rather than a new method component.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution summary, experimental explanations, and discussion undergo broad paragraph-level rewriting. Robustness material is reorganized from Appendix B into a dedicated Appendix C, and the later appendices receive a revised organization. The main seven-section outline remains, but exposition and appendix navigation change substantially.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is redesigned from six panels to four. The original emergence Figures 8–9 are regrouped by benchmark into v2 Figures 8 and 18, moving GSM8K to the appendix. New sensitivity, cutoff, and instruction/chat figures and a model table are added; the saturation figure is removed. Several retained figures also receive axis-label and layout refinements.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds an adaptation-before-evaluation subsection connecting the proposal to prior arguments for controlling adaptation resources. It expands the distinction from data contamination and acknowledges closely related emergence findings by Snell et al. and evaluation recommendations by Gu et al. These additions substantially develop the methodological positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(6), the causal graph, piecewise log-linear specification, and direct/mediated-effect derivations are retained. The hard-intervention interpretation still requires saturation. Its empirical justification changes, but the formal assumption and mathematical analysis do not.

improvement.justification: The learning-rate and temporal-cutoff checks address concrete alternative explanations, while instruction/chat evaluations strengthen applicability beyond base models. Clearer data descriptions and prior-work positioning also help. However, removing v1 Appendix B.3's direct saturation evidence leaves the causal intervention assumption less directly supported. The added validation provides a net improvement, tempered by that loss.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study and proposed evaluation adjustment. Their main text, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds learning-rate sensitivity, alternative temporal cutoffs, and instruction/chat-model evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, fine-tuning interventions, regression analyses, and emergence experiments, with additional results in the appendices.

title: Training on the Test Task Confounds Evaluation and Emergence

C1.justification: Section 1.1 adds an explicit contribution concerning changes in individual-model rankings on MMLU and GSM8K, extending the earlier emphasis on model-family comparisons. The central claims about confounded evaluation, emergence, and the fine-tuning remedy remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 interprets test-task training as a potentially primary mechanism behind improved compute efficiency and adds the accessibility benefits of smaller, extensively pretrained models. It also supplies a concrete data-filtering example for the existing data-quality interpretation. The stated limitations and causal qualifications are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix A retains the same model repositories, optimizer and learning-rate settings, precision, batch/context sizes, hardware, and GPU-hour estimates. Code and fine-tuned-model access information is unchanged.

E1.justification: Training sources and evaluated tasks are retained, including MMLU, GSM8K, ARC, HellaSwag, and the five additional benchmarks in Appendix D. The new ranking analyses reuse existing MMLU and GSM8K evaluations.

E2.justification: The model lists, control/treatment comparisons, and Pythia–Llama 2–Qwen 1.5 family comparison are unchanged. Newly cited research is discussed without adding evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 adds mean and maximum rank displacement as evaluation measures for the existing before/after fine-tuning comparisons. Existing benchmark metrics, shot counts, model cohorts, training budgets, and appendix evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds a focused analysis of how adjustment changes individual-model rankings, in Section 4.2 and Appendix E. Existing hyperparameter, temporal-cutoff, language-mixture, task-format, and emergence analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 reports significance and standard errors without specifying model-family clustering. v3 Section 2.2 explicitly states that significance calculations use clustered standard errors with each model family as a group. This newly documents the estimation procedure; it does not establish that the estimator or number of runs changed.

E6.justification: v3 newly reports average/maximum rank shifts of 7.7/21 places for GSM8K and 4.8/16 for MMLU, supported by Figures 7 and 18. Previously reported benchmark results, regression summaries, and appendix findings are retained.

M1.justification: Both versions propose the same adjustment: fine-tune each compared model on the same sufficient task-relevant data before evaluation. The fine-tuning procedure and model components are unchanged.

P1.justification: The revision makes localized grammar and wording corrections, inserts Section 4.2 on model rankings, renumbers the progress subsection, and broadens Appendix E's heading. The overall narrative and section organization are retained.

P2.justification: v3 adds ranking diagrams in Figures 7 and 18 and changes the treatment-group color in Figure 3. Existing figures and tables are retained, with limited resizing, relocation, reflow, and renumbering.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to Hardt (2024), Ruan et al. (2024), Rogers and Luccioni (2024), and Gadre et al. (2024), connecting the work to rankings, observational scaling, and emergence debates. These are targeted positioning additions.

T1.justification: The regression formulation in Equation 1 and the causal assumptions, structural equations, and derivations in Appendix B remain unchanged. Edits to their explanatory wording do not alter the mathematics.

improvement.justification: The ranking analyses make the consequences for model selection explicit, while the clustered-standard-error disclosure improves statistical transparency. Targeted editing and related-work additions also improve clarity and context. These are useful, limited gains: the underlying method, experimental coverage, principal results, and causal assumptions remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A-F support reliable comparison, including matching content across figure renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results and adds quantitative analyses of changes in model rankings on GSM8K and MMLU.

before.justification: v2 reports original fine-tuning and benchmark evaluations of 56 base models, additional results for 36 instruction/chat models, and robustness and causal analyses.

title: Training on the Test Task Confounds Evaluation and Emergence

C1.justification: V1 foregrounds a 4.3% LongBench improvement over InfLLM and human-like event segmentation. V2 broadens the main claims to performance across five base LLMs and two benchmarks, superiority over RAG and full-context inference, and successful retrieval across 10 million tokens. The underlying human-memory contribution remains.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations attributing advantages over RAG to layer-specific retrieval and advantages over full-context inference to reduced attention dilution. Appendix A.2 discusses retriever-capacity bottlenecks and pipeline complexity, while Appendix C.2 explains growing memory and retrieval-time costs and offloading tradeoffs. Existing cognitive interpretations and contiguity qualifications largely remain.

D1.justification: V2 supplies explicit backbone identifiers, RAG construction settings, Hugging Face integration details and offloading/parallelisation procedures. Appendix C.2 newly documents four-GPU nodes with 32GB per GPU, CPU-memory requirements, timing methodology and API use for full-context results. V1 provides substantially less implementation and hardware information.

E1.justification: V2 retains LongBench, PG-19 and the human podcasts, while adding six ∞-Bench tasks covering code debugging, mathematical finding, long-book multiple-choice questions and KV/passkey/number retrieval. Figure 1 also adds an extended passkey-retrieval scenario reaching 10 million tokens.

E2.justification: V1's downstream comparison uses InfLLM. V2 retains it and adds RAG pipelines using all-mpnet-base-v2 and NV-Embed-v2 in Table 8, plus full-context inference alongside NV-Embed-v2 RAG in Table 9. These introduce substantially different comparator families.

E3.justification: Alongside the retained 4K+2K evaluation, v2 adds LLaMA-3/3.1 configurations with 4K+4K contexts and Phi-3/3.5 configurations with 1K+3K contexts. New experiments introduce a 300-word, top-five-chunk RAG protocol and timing measurements over 100 chunks of 512 tokens. These do not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 extends component ablations across additional models and ∞-Bench, adds a layer-specific retrieval case study in Figure 5, and extends human-segmentation comparisons to Mistral and LLaMA-3 in Figures 7–8. Runtime profiling and Figure 9's configuration comparisons add further analyses. V1's sensitivity plots remain as Figures 10–11.

E5.justification: V2 Figure 5 adds box-and-whisker summaries of retrieval-ratio variability across more than 500 chunks. Existing PG-19 plus/minus statistics and human-data plot bands are retained. Neither version reports a repeated-seed protocol or confidence intervals for downstream benchmark performance.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive benchmark, comparator, model and efficiency results. Corresponding original LongBench entries also change: the S variant's PassageRetrieval score changes from 85.42 in v1 Table 1 to 82.67 in v2 Table 3, while InfLLM remains 64.00. The configuration selection behind these revisions is unexplained. PG-19 Table 2 values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The surprise-based segmentation, boundary refinement and two-buffer retrieval algorithm remain. Appendix C.2 introduces execution adaptations for very long sequences: disk-backed LRU memory management, optional CPU offloading of representative tokens and layer parallelisation across GPUs.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the method and related-work prose remain. V2 revises the abstract and experimental framing, condenses the discussion and conclusion, and reorganises the supplemental material into thematic appendices with a contents list. These are focused editorial and organisational revisions.

P2.justification: V2 redesigns the main performance table around task groups and multiple models, and adds comparison, diagnostic, ablation and resource displays. It introduces the opening radar/scalability figure and redraws a subset of the human results for the main text. Original figures are preserved elsewhere, including v1 Figures 3–5 as v2 Figures 6, 10–11.

R1.justification: The existing long-context and episodic-memory reviews, including novelty relative to InfLLM, largely remain. V2 adds focused positioning against RAG and references covering NV-Embed, all-mpnet-base-v2, MTEB, RAG enhancements and ∞-Bench. Publication-status updates to existing citations do not introduce new works.

T1.justification: Section 3.4 revises the stated total retrieved-event count from k = ks + kc + 2 to k = ks + kc. The graph-based definitions, complexity argument and two k-NN/softmax approximation lemmas otherwise remain unchanged; the original complexity analysis and proof move to Appendices C.1 and E.1.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow downstream validation and largely theoretical efficiency discussion through broader model and benchmark testing, RAG/full-context comparisons, extreme-length retrieval evidence and concrete resource measurements. Implementation details also improve reproducibility. Reporting inconsistencies qualify this gain: Section 4.1's 30.5%/11.5% RAG improvements do not reconcile with Table 9, and Table 4's LLaMA-3 ∞-Bench results contradict uniformly superior performance. These issues limit claim reliability but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EM-LLM work. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations across models and benchmarks, RAG/full-context comparisons, retrieval diagnostics and runtime measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original LongBench evaluations, PG-19 segmentation comparisons, analyses against human event boundaries and component ablations.

title: Human-inspired Episodic Memory for Infinite Context LLMs

C1.justification: V3 narrows the biological framing from human-like to human-inspired; Appendix E.1 explicitly supports this qualification by acknowledging missing evidence of actual human-like episodic processing. The introduction also updates the refinement-complexity claim. The central architectural contributions and headline empirical claims remain.

C2.justification: New Appendix E substantially qualifies the human-memory analogy, identifying non-parametric storage, missing nested events and consolidation, limited multimodal integration, and absent direct mechanistic validation. V3 also discusses the lack of refinement-convergence guarantees, hypothesizes why RAG-S underperforms, and explains the limited scope of the buffer-size study.

D1.justification: V3 adds a code-repository link and substantial parameter-selection documentation in Appendix D.1: model-specific gamma choices, their selection using LongBench, one neighboring event on either side, the selected contiguity ratio of 0.3, and token-budget interpretation. These disclose existing experimental choices; hardware and offloading information was already present.

E1.justification: Both versions use LongBench, ∞-Bench, PG-19, and the same human-annotated podcast material. New experiments use retained LongBench tasks. V2 already shows retrieval across approximately 10 million tokens in Figure 1; v3's revised maximum-length statement does not establish additional coverage.

E2.justification: Table 9 adds RAG-S, using NV-Embed-v2 with EM-LLM's surprise-based segmentation, to the LLaMA-3.1 comparison. Results are provided for LongBench only. InfLLM, the original RAG configurations, full-context models, and segmentation comparators are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include dynamically retrieving surprise-segmented RAG chunks to a 1500-word budget and varying Mistral's retrieved buffer across 1K, 2K, 4K, and 6K tokens with 4K local tokens. Appendix D.3 also stratifies results by example length. Existing benchmark settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V3 adds targeted investigations of surprise segmentation within RAG and retrieval-budget sensitivity on four LongBench tasks, including analysis by context length. Existing segmentation and contiguity ablations are retained: v2 Figures 9–11 correspond to v3 Figures 11–13.

E5.justification: Appendix A.1 newly reports two-tailed z-tests, stating benchmark-level significance at p < 0.05 with a reported Phi-3.5 LongBench exception of p = 0.23. It acknowledges that most individual-task improvements are not significant. No additional seed or repeated-run information is supplied.

E6.justification: Previously reported table scores are retained. Additions include RAG-S's LongBench average of 25.89 in Table 9 and retrieval-buffer results in Table 12; QMSum scores are 23.24, 23.68, 24.47, and 24.30 for 1K, 2K, 4K, and 6K retrieved tokens. These are additional comparisons, not version-to-version performance gains.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.4 and Algorithm 1 retain the same surprise segmentation, graph refinement, and similarity/contiguity retrieval procedure. Corrected threshold notation and explanations of single-pass refinement clarify the existing method. Discussed neural and multimodal extensions are not implemented additions.

P1.justification: V3 substantially expands structured exposition through parameter-selection guidance and a five-part discussion appendix. It rewrites the introduction around labeled Contributions and Performance paragraphs, changes human-like terminology to human-inspired, and reorganizes appendices C–F. The main section sequence remains intact.

P2.justification: V3 adds complexity Figures 9–10 and buffer-analysis Figure 14/Table 12, expands Table 9 with RAG-S, and adds task categories to Table 3. Existing figures are retained with relocation, renumbering, and limited caption or legend edits; the overall visual format remains similar.

R1.justification: Appendix E substantially expands positioning against differentiable and associative memory approaches, including SEM, Hopfield networks, Neural Turing Machines, differentiable neural computers, and MERLIN. It newly relates refinement to Louvain and adds multimodal connections. The Newman fast-community-detection citation supporting the old complexity argument is removed.

T1.justification: Appendix C.1 replaces the O(kn) refinement derivation with chunk-based accounting yielding O(nm + n^2/k), bounded by O(nm). New Appendix C.2 separately derives attention and retrieval costs, including the growing retrieval term. The existing k-NN/softmax approximation proof moves from E.1 to F.1 unchanged.

improvement.justification: V3 improves reproducibility and assessment through parameter disclosures, a code link, targeted additional experiments, and clearer computational-cost accounting. Its explicit human-inspired qualification makes the biological interpretation more defensible. These are useful gains, although the new empirical evidence is limited and Appendix A.1's significance-testing procedure remains underspecified; the core experimental findings are unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EM-LLM, with matching authors, architecture, benchmarks, and retained results. The main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: V3 retains these original results and adds surprise-segmented RAG results and retrieval-buffer-size experiments in Table 9 and Appendix D.3.

before.justification: V2 reports original LongBench and ∞-Bench experiments, PG-19 segmentation measurements, human-annotation analyses, and component ablations.

title: Human-inspired Episodic Memory for Infinite Context LLMs

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction move from empirical and heuristic support for joint decoding to explicit claims of theoretical perplexity improvement and bounded approximation error. They also broaden the stated empirical contribution to downstream effectiveness and models up to 70B parameters, while retaining the central quality-and-efficiency objective.

C2.justification: v2 interprets its new bounds as convergence toward exact joint decoding and discusses limited gains and memory costs from multiple-draft extensions. It adds verification-overhead explanations for SpecInfer/Spectr performance. v1's explicit warning that improved perplexity may not improve downstream effectiveness is removed with Section 8, although a shorter well-trained-model qualification remains.

D1.justification: v2 supplies hyperparameters for SpecInfer and the added datasets and revises the batch-study hardware description. However, its dataset-statistics table removes the test-input-count column. Existing code access, power-measurement instructions, and most configuration details are retained; the new fine-tuning experiments lack detailed training recipes.

E1.justification: v2 retains ChatGPT-Prompt, ChatAlpaca, and CNN/DailyMail and adds Spider text-to-SQL and MT-Bench evaluation. These introduce substantive task coverage, including structured query generation and math, coding, reasoning, and other conversational tasks.

E2.justification: SpecInfer, unsuccessful because of memory limits in v1, becomes an evaluated comparator in v2 Tables 4 and 9. The main benchmark table drops the greedy comparator, although it remains in other comparisons. The block-efficiency comparison also expands from speculative decoding versus the proposed method to all five methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds OPT-30B and Llama-2-Chat-70B configurations, downstream scoring, fine-tuning controls, and a GPT-3.5 experiment selecting among ten outputs generated at temperature 2. Block efficiency measures generated tokens rather than just accepted draft tokens. Section 4 also changes the reported batch-study hardware from two 24GB A10 GPUs to one 48GB L40 while retaining identical results; this establishes a reporting change, not a confirmed rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a perplexity-versus-execution-accuracy analysis, top-k/top-p sensitivity tests, and comparisons of no fine-tuning, draft-only fine-tuning, and fine-tuning both models (Table 1 and Appendix C.2–C.3). The original beam-count and acceptance-threshold analyses remain, while block-efficiency analysis expands.

E5.justification: Both versions report four experimental repetitions and standard deviations. v2 additionally states that MT-Bench deviations include variation across tasks, and Table 9 reports means and deviations across datasets. These extend statistical reporting without establishing an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Shared benchmark entries in v1 Table 2 and v2 Table 4 are unchanged, but v2 adds substantial comparator, benchmark, larger-model, and downstream results. Table 6 newly reports MTAD/speculative Spider accuracy of 13.0/11.5 and MT-Bench averages of 2.68/2.58, with several category declines. Expanded-coverage speed and energy ratios become 1.42×/1.54× versus 1.49×/1.62×; these are aggregate changes. Section 5.1 also changes the comparator for the claimed 21.2% perplexity reduction from BiLD to speculative decoding.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 is identical after normalizing the method name. Both versions use auxiliary-model beam drafting, joint-likelihood verification, longest-prefix acceptance, and an additional target-model token. v1 already documents stochastic top-k/top-p sampling; v2's terminology and expanded explanation do not establish a procedural change.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and introduction are substantially rewritten, including an explicit contribution list. Sampling terminology and the preliminaries are revised throughout. The appendices are reorganized around proofs and additional experiments, and the limitations-and-impact section is removed.

P2.justification: The main benchmark table is restructured with added datasets and SpecInfer, removing greedy and speed-up rows. The per-dataset acceptance bar chart is replaced by an aggregate block-efficiency table. v2 adds multiple downstream and appendix tables, expands the hyperparameter table, and relocates the retained threshold plot; Figures 1 and 2 remain substantially unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds EAGLE/MEDUSA positioning as complementary drafting approaches, citations for decoding evaluation, Spider, and MT-Bench, and removes the de Vries energy-footprint reference. The broader positioning against speculative and non-autoregressive decoding remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: v1 Appendix F offers a heuristic score-function argument. v2 replaces it with asymptotic perplexity analysis, a greedy-decoding comparison, approximation-error and acceptance-length bounds, and proofs in Appendix A (Theorem 3.2 through Theorem 3.6). The energy decomposition remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens empirical support through downstream metrics, SpecInfer comparisons, larger models, and fine-tuning controls. However, its central new guarantees have unresolved reasoning gaps: Appendix A.2 compares fixed prefixes without addressing the differing histories acknowledged in v1 Appendix F, and Theorem 3.6 omits the algorithm's finite draft-length cap. Removing the explicit downstream-performance limitation and test-count reporting also reduces transparency. The empirical gains and concerns about the stronger theoretical claims prevent a reliable net quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, with MJGD/MJSD renamed MTJD/MTAD. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds downstream evaluations, larger-model results, and sampling and fine-tuning analyses, including Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original decoding benchmarks, energy measurements, and beam-count and acceptance-threshold experiments in Sections 3–5.

title: Optimized Multi-Token Joint Decoding With Auxiliary Model for LLM Inference

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution summary replace the headline 21.2% perplexity reduction with a 25% downstream-performance improvement. The central joint-decoding, bounded-approximation, and energy-efficiency contributions remain, as do the reported 1.42× speedup and 1.54× energy-reduction headlines.

C2.justification: v3 explains why lossless methods can generate different sequences even with a fixed seed and acknowledges energy variation across L40 machine nodes (Section 5.2 and Appendix C.8). It removes the earlier explanation of good perplexity at threshold zero. Most existing mechanism explanations and applicability qualifications remain.

D1.justification: v3 removes v2 Table 13's selected hyperparameters for each method/model/dataset and Appendix E's matched-input rule for perplexity evaluation. It instead supplies MTAD search ranges, explicitly reports temperature 1, and adds node-matching and licensing information. The reported code link changes from an anonymous repository to the named MTAD repository. Losing exact selected configurations materially reduces reproducibility detail.

E1.justification: v3 adds HumanEval coding evaluation alongside the five existing datasets. Spider and MT-Bench were already evaluated, while ChatGPT-Prompts, ChatAlpaca, and CNN/DailyMail remain in Appendix C; their relocation is not lost coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds MCSS and typical decoding to the four existing speculative baselines in Table 5. Its downstream comparison also includes BiLD, Spectr, and SpecInfer, whereas v2 Table 6 compared downstream performance only against vanilla speculative decoding. SpD is the renamed existing speculative baseline.

E3.justification: v3 adds evaluations with Llama-3.1-8B targets and Llama-3.2-1B drafts, including Instruct variants, a four-token MTJD comparison, and HumanEval pass@1. E4.justification: v3 adds acceptance-length measurements across thresholds for Llama-3 variants (Table 10), broader perplexity–quality analysis (Figure 4), and grouped energy–speed analysis (Figure 5). Existing beam-count, threshold, top-k/top-p, and fine-tuning analyses remain, mostly relocated within Appendix C.

E5.justification: v3 removes v2's explicit four-run description and the explanation that MT-Bench standard deviations also include task variation. Legacy uncertainty values remain in the appendices, but new main Tables 4–5 provide point estimates without run counts or uncertainty. The PDFs do not establish a reduction in actual repetitions.

E6.justification: v3 Tables 4–5 add substantial MTJD and MTAD results under new model settings; for example, Table 5 reports HumanEval pass@1 of 38.4 for MTAD versus 32.9 for SpD with Llama-3-Instruct. Table 10 adds threshold-dependent acceptance lengths. Matched older benchmark and ablation values are retained, so these additions are not same-setting improvements over v2.

M1.justification: The MTJD formulation and MTAD procedure remain unchanged: auxiliary beam sampling, joint-likelihood verification, acceptance of the longest qualifying prefix, and an additional target-model token. Algorithm 1 is unchanged; the new model evaluations do not introduce a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: Prose is edited throughout the abstract, preliminaries, methodology, and energy discussion. Section 5 is reorganized around separate MTJD and MTAD evaluations, while the original benchmark discussion and ablations move into a reorganized Appendix C. Terminology, affiliations, and acknowledgments also change.

P2.justification: v3 introduces main Tables 4–5, supplementary Table 10, and Figures 4–5; relocates v2 Tables 4–7 and Figure 3 into the appendices; and removes the selected-hyperparameter table. Retained displays are resized or reformatted, and the document adopts an ICLR conference layout. These changes substantially reorganize the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for HumanEval, Llama-3, and MCSS, and briefly positions MCSS as extending SpecInfer through sampling without replacement in Section 6. The broader positioning against single-token decoding and alongside complementary draft-model improvements remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The MTJD definition, perplexity and approximation bounds, energy decomposition, and Appendix A proofs are retained. Equation 2's rewritten summation indexing and Equation 5's formatting do not substantively change the mathematics.

improvement.justification: v3 Tables 4–5 extend direct MTJD quality tests and broaden MTAD's downstream comparisons beyond v2's SpD-only comparison, strengthening empirical support for the central quality claim. Gains are tempered by deleted run-count and selected-configuration information and missing uncertainty for new main results. Numerical reporting also needs correction: Table 5 implies approximately 7.2% mean relative speed improvement over MCSS, versus the 17.2% claimed in Section 5.2.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MTJD/MTAD research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, pseudocode, and Appendices A–G support comparison, including matching material relocated in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds Llama-3 evaluations, HumanEval results, and supplementary analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original decoding experiments, downstream evaluations, energy measurements, and ablations using GPT-3.5, Llama-2, and OPT models.

title: Optimized Multi-Token Joint Decoding With Auxiliary Model for LLM Inference

C1.justification: Both versions claim a benchmark covering nonlinear and tabular optimization, a reverse Socratic synthesis method, and improved small-model performance through ReSocratic-29k fine-tuning. The renamed benchmark and shortened abstract do not materially change these contributions or their scope.

C2.justification: v2 removes v1's explanation of anomalous nonlinear-table SFT performance through train-test mismatch and its specific limitation concerning insufficiently diverse seed scenarios. It emphasizes dataset diversity, adds an intermediate-reasoning explanation for reverse synthesis, and interprets NL4OPT-E results as showing that benchmark is comparatively easy. D1.justification: v2 newly supplies the SFT system/user/assistant template. It removes the dataset datasheets and licensing/maintenance disclosures, including annotator-background information, and omits the BERT model and pooling details used for the retained t-SNE visualization. Core prompts, synthesis settings, hardware, and training hyperparameters remain. The repository disclosure moves to the abstract; it is not a newly announced release.
