The appendix prompts are substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: The title, benchmark terminology, and scenario/demonstration terminology change throughout. The abstract, introduction, related work, and method exposition receive substantial editing. Dataset statistics and selected analyses move into expanded experimental subsections, while the appendix contents page, datasheets, and limitations sections disappear. This substantially reorganizes the narrative.

P2.justification: Figures 1-3 are substantially redrawn, including a clearer evaluation workflow. Separate dataset-statistics figures become combined percentage plots, and t-SNE panels are rearranged and relocated. Tables reorder columns and rows; Table 1 adds dataset sizes and drops its MAMO row. v2 also adds Table 5 and the implicit/explicit example figure, while removing two diagnostic figures.

R1.justification: v2 removes the generic LLM survey and associated citations, adds formal-reasoning work such as TRIGO, MUSTARD, and Lean 4 autoformalization, and revises its characterization of ORLM. Appendix A expands positioning against NL4OPT and implicit-number benchmarks. These are focused revisions within the retained optimization-modeling and reverse-synthesis positioning.

T1.justification: The optimization formulations and end-to-end evaluation equations are retained, and neither version develops theorems or proofs. The removed mean-cosine expression documents the discarded empirical diagnostic rather than a distinct theoretical contribution.

improvement.justification: The additional NL4OPT-E and Self-Instruct comparisons and clearer workflow figures are useful. However, the main accuracy evidence is unchanged, while v2 removes the specific distribution-mismatch analysis and limitation, along with provenance and licensing documentation. It also introduces unexplained distribution changes: Figure 4's synthetic question-length percentages total 98.3%, whereas v1's corresponding counts reconcile with its dataset total. These losses in transparency and numerical consistency outweigh the limited evidential and presentation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same optimization benchmark and ReSocratic synthesis work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison; E-OPT is renamed OPTIBENCH, and relocated content can be matched.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds Self-Instruct results in Table 4 and NL4OPT-E evaluations in Appendix A, Table 5.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLM evaluations, fine-tuning experiments, ablations, synthetic-data accuracy measurements, and appendix analyses.

title: OptiBench Meets ReSocratic: Measure and Improve LLMs for Optimization Modeling

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same central claims: a 605-question benchmark covering linear, nonlinear, and tabular optimization; reverse Socratic data synthesis; and improved open-model performance through ReSocratic-29K fine-tuning. The additional evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v4 substantially expands interpretation beyond v2's difficulty-by-data-type discussion. Appendix B attributes failures to mathematical reasoning and solver-specific coding limitations, and interprets runtime comparisons as locating the main bottleneck in correctness rather than execution efficiency. It also presents problem expansion as a possible basis for future self-improvement. Appendix C.3 explains back-translation as largely extracting the demonstration's natural-language content.

D1.justification: v4 newly specifies annotator qualifications, a six-person team, four independent annotations per question, and adjudication procedures in Appendix D.1. It supplies exact reasoning-first and LLM-judge prompts in Appendix E. Existing training hardware, hyperparameters, data formats, and synthesis prompts are retained or relocated. Conversely, v2's project code/data link and contest access links are removed; this does not establish that the resources themselves became unavailable.

E1.justification: OptiBench, NL4OPT-E, and ReSocratic-29K retain their existing coverage. v4 Appendix B.5 adds a limited problem-expansion scenario: DeepSeek-V2.5 must enlarge an existing optimization problem's variables and constraints, with ten expanded samples evaluated by humans. No additional benchmark or application domain is evaluated.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds evaluated comparisons with Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Qwen2-7B-Instruct, DeepSeek-V2.5, GPT-4o-mini, and GPT-4o. Its few-shot block drops Llama-3-70B, DeepSeek-V2, GPT-3.5-Turbo, and GPT-4; the latter two retain aggregate results in Table 9. v4 also introduces reasoning-first prompting comparisons and human-written code as a runtime comparator. The Self-Instruct and Evol-Instruct synthesis comparisons remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The original answer-accuracy evaluation and fine-tuning settings remain stable. New protocols include DeepSeek-V2.5 judging mathematical formulations, a separate formulation-to-code accuracy measure, reasoning-first prompting, Pass@5 through Pass@30 at temperature 0.7, and runtime comparisons restricted to correctly solved instances. Separate human assessments validate judge agreement, expanded problems, and back-translations.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained filter and step-question ablations, v4 adds substantial diagnostic evidence: formulation-versus-coding error analysis and two coding-error cases, prompting sensitivity, multiple-attempt performance, generated-code efficiency, and problem-expansion feasibility in Appendix B. Appendix C.3 separately checks back-translation fidelity. These investigate failure sources and component reliability absent from v2.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, uncertainty across replicated experiments, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v4's Pass@k results vary the candidate-generation budget rather than estimate run-to-run uncertainty. Its human assessments report raw agreement or correctness counts, retaining the point-estimate reporting practice already used for synthetic-data accuracy in v2.

E6.justification: v4 adds numerous results, including GPT-4o accuracy of 66.1% zero-shot and 69.4% few-shot in Table 2, making it the strongest reported overall comparator. New findings include lower accuracy with reasoning-first prompting, increasing Pass@k, 19/20 human-judge agreement, 9/10 valid problem expansions, and 20/20 correct back-translations. Shared SFT results remain 30.6% and 51.1%, and Tables 3-5 retain their numerical results.

M1.justification: The proposed three-stage ReSocratic pipeline, rule and similarity filters, question/code translation, and supervised fine-tuning procedure remain unchanged. The original synthesis and evaluation prompts are retained. Additional reasoning-first and problem-expansion experiments are presented as supplementary studies rather than revisions to the synthesis pipeline.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and the principal section order remain unchanged. v4 shortens the main annotation description, moves the training-message format to Appendix C.4, and reorganizes the appendices around a new experimental section. It also makes limited wording edits and updates affiliations, conference headers, and acknowledgments.

P2.justification: Table 2 is expanded and its comparator rows reorganized. Six new tables, Tables 6-11, present error decomposition, prompting comparisons, Pass@k, and runtime results, substantially extending the displayed evidence. Figures 1-8 are retained, with several figures and tables relocated or resized within the revised layout.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds Chen and Lampouras (2023) and Xie et al. (2023), distinguishing ReSocratic's stepwise reverse construction from back-translation-based augmentation. References also add Gose, Scholle, Mistral, and Qwen2 sources. These are focused additions; the broader positioning against existing optimization benchmarks and forward synthesis remains stable.

T1.justification: The formal evaluation construction and existing mathematical formulations are retained. Neither version develops a theoretical analysis with theorems or proofs. The additional optimization formulations in v4 serve as empirical examples and prompt demonstrations rather than new theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v4 makes benchmark performance more interpretable through formulation-versus-coding diagnostics, broader baseline comparisons, and targeted human checks that were absent from v2. These benefits are limited by small audit samples and incomplete integration: Section 5.3 still calls GPT-4 strongest despite Table 2 favoring GPT-4o. Removing the code/data access link also weakens reproducibility guidance. The added evidence supports a net improvement, while the central synthesis and fine-tuning evidence remains unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OptiBench benchmark, ReSocratic synthesis method, and ReSocratic-29K dataset. Their complete main texts, appendices, tables, figures, and mathematical content support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds model evaluations, error analysis, prompting experiments, Pass@k results, runtime comparisons, and human assessments in Appendices B and C.

before.justification: v2 reports original model evaluations, supervised fine-tuning results, synthesis ablations, and forward-versus-reverse synthesis comparisons in Tables 2-4, plus NL4OPT-E evaluations in Appendix A.

title: OptiBench Meets ReSocratic: Measure and Improve LLMs for Optimization Modeling

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion expand the contribution from accurate non-uniform quantization and inference acceleration to compatibility across quantization formats and scalable grid learning. Compatibility with existing inference kernels and quantization up to 405B become central claims.

C2.justification: v2 questions whether perplexity represents downstream accuracy and attributes non-uniform grids' lower loss errors to greater placement freedom. The central outlier-preservation explanation remains. v1's specific limitations concerning truthfulness, fairness, interpretability and adversarial robustness are removed.

D1.justification: v2 documents the affine search granularity, GPU thread/block assignment, expanded hardware specifications and baseline reproduction details, including checkpoint provenance, OmniQuant training settings and GPTQ activation ordering. These materially improve implementation documentation. The earlier worked bits-per-weight calculation, inference implementation discussion and artifact-license list disappear.

E1.justification: v2 adds LAMBADA, MMLU, HellaSwag and instruction-following evaluation on MT-Bench, substantially broadening task requirements. WikiText-2, C4, ARC, PIQA, WinoGrande and SQuAD remain; the BERT/SQuAD experiment moves to Appendix A.1.

E2.justification: The zero-shot comparisons drop QUIP and introduce GPTQ and SqueezeLLM while retaining OmniQuant. Grouped GPTQ/AWQ rows disappear from the perplexity comparison, while SqueezeLLM gains C4 comparisons beyond its earlier WikiText-2 evaluation. The OBQ comparison for BERT remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 reports p = 4 throughout instead of v1's bit-dependent 2.5/3/3.5 defaults. It adds Llama-3 and Mistral configurations up to 405B, grouped affine evaluations and GPT-4o judging. Quantization measurements use L40s or dual RTX 8000 GPUs instead of V100 hardware. The C4 calibration and perplexity sequence procedures are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled initialization comparisons in Table 11 and fused-kernel on/off experiments in Table 5. Sensitivity and layerwise loss-error analyses now cover both grid types and additional models. v1's uninformed-grid comparison is retained conceptually through the p = 0 rows in v2 Table 10.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed values, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new MT-Bench win/tie/loss counts and win rates are point results, without an accompanying uncertainty analysis.

E6.justification: v2 adds affine, MT-Bench, 123B/405B and resource results, while removing the decoding-latency results and LLaMA-1-30B/65B entries. Non-uniform 3-bit Llama-2-7B WikiText-2 perplexity changes from 6.30 to 6.19 under revised settings; BERT F1 scores remain identical. New Tables 1/8 contain GPTQ averages excluding ARC-E, and Table 8 repeats several non-uniform result rows across 7B/13B models.

M1.justification: v1 learns non-uniform grids using k-means++ initialization. v2 adds loss-aware affine-grid optimization over scaling factors and zero-points, with a fused search kernel, and introduces uniformly spaced initialization for non-uniform clustering. Algorithms 1 and 2 now support both grid types.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around versatility and scalability. Background and methodology are reorganized by grid type, experiments emphasize accuracy and quantization resources, and BERT evaluation and error-accumulation discussion move into the appendices.

P2.justification: The paper changes from two-column to single-column formatting. Separate motivation figures become a combined histogram/grid comparison, loss-error plots gain affine/non-uniform traces, and tables are reorganized by grid type. Perplexity and BERT tables move to appendices; MT-Bench graphics and resource tables are added.

R1.justification: Research positioning shifts substantially toward framework compatibility and quantization resource costs. v2 adds substantive discussion of AQLM, Student Float, LLM-QAT, Marlin, LUT-GEMM and llama.cpp, and expands discussion of QUIP#. Earlier FlashAttention, KV-cache quantization and NOMAD-attention references disappear.

T1.justification: v2 adds formal definitions for uniformly spaced initialization and the constrained affine-grid optimization in Equation 7. The Taylor approximation, OBQ loss-error derivation and Hessian updates remain substantively unchanged. The existing error-accumulation argument moves to Appendix B; no new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2's controlled initialization/kernel studies, broader task evaluation and baseline reproduction details make the method better supported and easier to assess. However, inconsistent GPTQ averaging in Tables 1/8 inflates headline comparisons, and unexplained duplicated 7B/13B rows weaken confidence in some added results. Removal of the limitations discussion and direct inference measurements also reduces transparency. These drawbacks substantially temper the benefits, leaving a limited net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LeanQuant by the same authors. The complete main texts and appendices, including equations, algorithms, figures and tables, support reliable comparison despite substantial revision and relocation.

after.justification: v2 reports original affine and non-uniform quantization results, large-model evaluations, MT-Bench judgments, resource measurements and ablations, alongside retained BERT results.

before.justification: v1 reports original LeanQuant perplexity, zero-shot accuracy, BERT/SQuAD results, ablations and efficiency measurements in Tables 1–8 and Figure 3.

title: LeanQuant: Accurate and Scalable Large Language Model Quantization with Loss-error-aware Grid

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: loss-error-aware affine and non-uniform grids, accurate and compatible quantization, and scalability to Llama-3.1-405B using two 48GB GPUs in approximately 21 hours. Added experiments support these existing claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: V3 explains uniformly spaced initialization through the tendency of random or k-means++ initialization to undersample extreme weights. Section 3.2.2 and Appendix B newly discuss excessive range shrinkage, poor representation of extremes and the rationale for bit-dependent shrinkage limits. The existing interpretation of loss-error reduction and iterative grid robustness is retained.

D1.justification: V3 adds a LeanQuant code-access URL, explicit shrinkage settings, and documentation of a dedicated non-uniform CUDA inference kernel and exllamav2 affine kernels. Appendix J specifies hardware and workloads for the new timings. Existing calibration, baseline reproduction and quantization hardware instructions are largely unchanged.

E1.justification: The represented datasets and language tasks remain C4, WikiText2, the existing zero-shot benchmarks, MT-Bench and SQuAD. Additional model variants and comparisons reuse this coverage. The revised allocation of benchmarks to the 405B model and new timing workloads change evaluation settings rather than introduce a new data domain or language task.

E2.justification: V3 adds QuaRot-RTN and QuaRot-GPTQ comparisons in Table 8, extending evaluation to rotation-based quantization. AWQ participates in the new grouped zero-shot comparisons in Table 9, whereas v2 reports it in the perplexity comparison. GPTQ is also added to the memory comparison in Table 4. Existing baselines are retained.

E3.justification: Appendix J introduces inference profiling on an A100-40GB GPU, measuring decoding throughput and prefill latency with 4096-token workloads and batch sizes 1, 4 and 16. New evaluations include grouped quantization, Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct and non-uniform quantization of the largest models. Table 3 replaces the 405B PIQA column with broader LAMBADA/MMLU evaluation, changing its average's composition. The affine search bounds are also revised.

E4.justification: V3 Table 12 adds an inference-efficiency analysis across batch sizes and decoding/prefill phases, exposing batch-dependent differences between LeanQuant and SqueezeLLM. The existing p sensitivity study, initialization ablation, fused-grid-learning-kernel ablation and loss-error plots are retained. The renamed robustness appendix largely restates v2's error-accumulation discussion.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. Existing point-estimate and MT-Bench win-rate reporting is retained, and the new experiments do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: V3 adds large-model non-uniform results, QuaRot and grouped comparisons, GPTQ memory measurements and inference timings. Existing values also change: Table 1's affine 3-bit Llama-2-7B average changes from 52.84 to 50.42, and 2-bit Mistral-7B from 40.18 to 34.43. The LLaMA-7B non-uniform rows are revised in v2 Table 8 versus v3 Table 10, including LeanQuant's 4.05-bit average from 58.87 to 53.36. These are reported revisions; the changed search specification and 405B task mix preclude interpreting all differences as same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The specified affine search changes from enumerating endpoints through T/2-1 to a bit-dependent bound t: 0.2T, 0.3T and 0.4T for 4-, 3- and 2-bit quantization (Equation 7 and Appendix B). Algorithm 1 also corrects the error-buffer index from j-1 to j-i. The underlying weighted grid learning and GPTQ/OBQ integrations remain.

P1.justification: V3 extensively rewrites the quantization background and grid-learning explanations, relocates the p discussion and inverse-Hessian update, and reorganizes the appendices around added explanatory, shrinkage, inference and related-work sections. Publication headers, affiliations and acknowledgements also change. The explanatory restructuring extends beyond ordinary copyediting.

P2.justification: V3 adds the grid illustration in Figure 3 and new QuaRot, grouped-quantization and inference tables. Tables 2-4 gain rows or columns, and the 405B table is substantially restructured. Table 11 redisplays the memory comparison in transposed form. Existing loss-error and MT-Bench figures are retained with resizing, relocation or renumbering.

R1.justification: New Appendix M substantially expands the short related-work discussion into calibration-based versus calibration-free quantization, quantization-aware training, broader LLM efficiency techniques, and uniform versus non-uniform quantization. New cited works include QuaRot, SpQR, BitNet, OneBit, NUPES, Mr.BiQ and KV-cache compression methods. This broadens research positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Equation 7 revises the formally defined affine feasible set, and Equation 8 introduces its bit-dependent bound. The main loss approximation and quantization derivations remain unchanged. The inverse-Hessian removal identity moves from v2 Equation 4 to v3 Equation 9; it is not a new derivation or proof.

improvement.justification: V3 improves clarity and reproducibility through the explicit shrinkage specification, corrected pseudocode index, grid explanations and code-access information. New baseline comparisons and inference measurements provide useful evidence beyond v2's already extensive evaluation. The gain remains limited: several accuracy revisions lack an explanation of whether they reflect corrections or reruns, and the changed 405B task mix prevents direct comparison of averages. These limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the added documentation and evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LeanQuant and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices. Retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains original experiments and adds quantization comparisons, large-model results and inference-efficiency measurements.

before.justification: V2 reports original LLM quantization evaluations, efficiency measurements, ablations, MT-Bench comparisons and BERT quantization experiments on SQuAD.

title: LeanQuant: Accurate and Scalable Large Language Model Quantization with Loss-error-aware Grid

C1.justification: The abstract newly emphasizes Markovian agents as a new general category motivated by limitations of prior work. The introduction adds a novelty claim about abstracting limited cognitive abilities and recency bias in steering. The central objective, existence, and algorithmic contribution claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds a behavioral rationale for Markovian agents and explains how insufficient exploration can confuse avaricious and normal agents, harming subsequent steering. Appendix G.4 qualifies the SIAR-MPC comparison through its necessary adaptation. The existing limitations discussion is unchanged and relocated from Appendix A to H.

D1.justification: V2 documents FETE-RE construction, adds an avarice-scaling rule, and includes an explicit pointer to supplementary running instructions. V1's statement about random initialization when training exploitation policies is no longer stated. The new scaling rule assigns both beta^n values to the same condition, pi^n(A) <= 0.5, leaving the intended implementation ambiguous. Repository, hardware, and timing disclosures remain.

E1.justification: Section 6.2 replaces the large-model scenario of intrinsically rewarded, opportunistic agents that accelerate learning with larger action-value differences. The replacement uses agents with no intrinsic rewards whose learning slows under high incentive payments, with the mediator rewarded for unanimous action A. The other game environments remain.

E2.justification: Figure 3 adds FETE-RE to the final steering-gap and cost comparisons, which previously included only FETE and Oracle. Random exploration already appeared in the identification comparison. FETE-RE is explicitly an adaptation of SIAR-MPC using MLE and RL, rather than an evaluation of its original implementation.

E3.justification: The revised large-model evaluation changes the candidate class from 4^10 to 3^10, Umax from 2.0 to 1.0, and the evaluated realizations from four to three. Figure 3 changes whole-model identification probability to agent-type identification accuracy and plots steering gap divided by N. The 500-step total horizon and 30-step exploration budget remain.

E4.justification: The FETE versus FETE-RE comparison extends the exploration analysis to downstream steering gaps and costs, holding the identification and exploitation approach fixed. Previously, learned and random exploration were compared only through identification success. The existing beta-sensitivity analyses in Figures 5–6 remain unchanged.

E5.justification: The reported five-seed averaging, 95% confidence intervals, and two-sigma error-bar practices are retained, including for the revised large-model evaluation. No new statistical testing or increased run count is reported.

E6.justification: Figure 3 replaces results for fA–fD with results for f1–f3 under different agent dynamics and metrics, and adds FETE-RE outcomes. The new comparison shows larger steering gaps for FETE-RE, most visibly for f2. These are replacement results, not comparable-setting performance gains. The small-model table and Figures 1, 2, 5, and 6 retain their results.

M1.justification: Objective (1), belief-state steering, FETE, and Algorithms 3–4 retain their procedures. The posterior-based exploration objective numbered (13) in v2 already appears unnumbered in v1 Appendix H.3.2. The revised agent dynamics belong to the experimental environment.

P1.justification: The introduction and closest-related-work discussion are substantially rewritten around behavioral motivation and comparative novelty. Opponent-shaping and episodic/non-episodic RL discussions move into the appendix, limitations move to the final appendix, and new comparison and reproducibility subsections reorganize the explanatory narrative.

P2.justification: V1's overview Table 1 is removed, while the retained empirical table is relocated and renumbered. Figure 3 is redrawn with three model groups, an additional comparator, and revised axes and caption. Other figures remain, alongside document-wide changes to title, headings, and preprint headers.

R1.justification: The introduction adds behavioral literature on bounded rationality and recency bias. Sections 1.1 and 5.2 and Appendices B.2 and G.4 substantially expand positioning against Zhang et al. (2023) and Canyakmaz et al. (2024), distinguishing information assumptions, incentive representations, exploration, identification, and exploitation.

T1.justification: The formal problem definitions, Assumptions A–D, Proposition 3.3, existence results, and PMD, MLE, and POMDP arguments are retained. Matching the renumbered appendices reveals no substantive change to their proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens empirical support for strategic exploration by testing its downstream effects against FETE-RE, and clarifies the relationship to prior steering work. The gain is limited: the experiment replaces an existing scenario, the comparator adapts SIAR-MPC, and the contradictory scaling rule weakens reproducibility. With the theory and other experiments retained, the added controlled comparison supports a modest net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching objectives, algorithms, and theoretical results. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix G retain original steering experiments and report a revised large-model experiment involving avaricious agents.

before.justification: Section 6 and Appendix H report original simulations on normal-form and grid-world Stag Hunt, Matching Pennies, and multi-agent cooperative games.

title: Learning to Steer Markovian Agents under Model Uncertainty

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the central claims about the non-episodic steering objective, existence guarantees, belief-state and FETE algorithms, and empirical effectiveness. Appendix H's extensions do not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix H replaces the dedicated limitations and societal-impact discussion with substantive applicability arguments for non-tabular games, infinite model classes, finite-memory dynamics, and neural models, including scalability qualifications. Its explicit steering-cost limitations disappear, although Section 5.2 retains the FETE caveat. New Remark C.1 interprets Pareto optimality through wasteful constant reward increases.

D1.justification: Appendix G's implementation, hyperparameter, hardware, and runtime information is unchanged. The reproducibility statement now contains the same repository link already disclosed in v2's first-page footnote; this does not establish newly available code or data.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same Stag Hunt, Matching Pennies, and ten-agent cooperative scenarios. The broader settings introduced in Appendix H are discussed mathematically, without additional training or evaluation.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain unsteered agents, model-specific steering strategies, Oracle, and FETE-RE, the adaptation of SIAR-MPC. Newly cited RND and Bootstrapped DQN are suggested alternatives, not evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: Section 6 and Appendix G retain the same initialization grids, training settings, model configurations, and evaluation metrics, including the 30-step exploration and 470-step exploitation design. No new evaluation protocol is reported.

E4.justification: The steering-gap/cost sensitivity analyses in Figures 5–6, policy trajectories, and strategic-versus-random exploration analysis in Figure 3 are retained unchanged. Appendix H adds theoretical discussion rather than new empirical ablations or robustness tests.

E5.justification: The same five-seed averaging, 95% confidence reporting, and two-sigma error-bar descriptions remain in Section 6 and Appendix G. No run-count, seed, or statistical-estimation changes are reported.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the experimental plots preserve their values and findings. For example, the belief strategy under f0.7 retains success probability 0.87 ± 0.05 and steering cost 10.5 ± 0.4. The embedded figure graphics also match.

M1.justification: Objective (1), Procedures 1–2, and evaluated implementations remain unchanged. New Appendix H proposes adaptations using parameterized linear-quadratic steering, finite model covers, augmented states for finite-memory agents, and neural dynamics models. These are extension prescriptions rather than replacements of the evaluated algorithms.

P1.justification: There are localized rewrites of the related-work comparison, explanatory clarifications in Sections 3–5, a new Remark C.1, and replacement of Appendix H. The main narrative structure and most prose remain unchanged, while the header changes from preprint to ICLR 2025 publication.

P2.justification: The same figures and tables remain, with resized Figure 1, reflowed captions and algorithm formatting, removal of Figure 2's panel labels, and relocation of Figure 5 and Table 2. These are display and placement changes rather than new results.

R1.justification: Section 1.1 removes the characterization of Canyakmaz et al. as using only potentially suboptimal history-independent steering, and Section 5.2 narrows its comparison to exploration and model estimation. Appendix H adds five references concerning linear-quadratic control and scalable exploration; the broader related-work treatment remains intact.

T1.justification: Appendix H substantially extends the mathematical scope through linear-quadratic parameterization, finite-memory state augmentation, and a total-variation covering argument with terminal-goal error bounded by T ε0 ηmax and cumulative-cost error by T² ε0 max ηcost. Appendix E also corrects Example 4.4's proof by explicitly conditioning its separation argument on fMLE differing from f. The principal numbered theorems remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: The proof correction and explicit approximation and finite-memory arguments add useful substance. However, new Appendix H contains inconsistent linear-quadratic reward equations, substituting Theta for Xi in the second agent's modified reward, and does not establish the total-variation covering condition needed for its neural-model extension. It also replaces the dedicated cost-limitations discussion. These mixed gains and losses leave the net effect on rigor and explanatory quality uncertain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same steering framework and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Content can be reliably matched across pagination and layout changes.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and their reported outcomes in Section 6 and Appendix G.

before.justification: v2 reports original steering experiments on normal-form and grid-world Stag Hunt, a ten-agent cooperative game, and Matching Pennies, including appendix results.

title: Learning to Steer Markovian Agents under Model Uncertainty

C1.justification: v4 expands the headline claims to SOTA performance on six of seven datasets, training-free portability across LLMs, applicability to associated graph/document collections, and smaller-model reasoning comparable to GPT-3.5. It explicitly positions bidirectional KG×Text coupling as the contribution. v1 emphasizes accurate, interpretable graph-guided reasoning demonstrated on four datasets.

C2.justification: v4 adds interpretations concerning knowledge exposure, backbone capability, single-hop versus multi-hop tasks, and the respective roles of triples and documents. Appendix B.1 introduces substantive limitations involving missing knowledge, retrieval failures, misunderstood questions and exact-match false negatives. However, the new context-length explanation contradicts Figure 3b: LLM scores increase while reranker scores decrease overall.

D1.justification: v4 supplies pseudocode, full pruning/reasoning prompts, the Azure entity-linking implementation, explicit W=D=3 and K=10 settings, and financial-dataset construction procedures and statistics. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing that newly disclosed defaults changed. v1's GPU configuration and 256-token generation-limit disclosures are dropped.

E1.justification: v4 adds Creak, Zero-Shot RE and ToG-FinQA, expanding coverage to additional fact verification, slot filling and Chinese financial multi-hop QA. ToG-FinQA contains 97 questions. The earlier HotpotQA evaluation is now identified as AdvHotpotQA, a challenging subset; the PDFs do not establish whether this reflects a different underlying sample.

E2.justification: v4 adds explicit text-based Vanilla RAG and CoT-SC comparisons, evaluates GraphRAG on ToG-FinQA, and fills previously absent CoK comparisons on WebQSP and QALD-10-en. v1's Vanilla prompting corresponds to v4's Direct reasoning and is retained, rather than newly introduced.

E3.justification: FEVER changes from v1's blanket two-shot prompting to three-/six-shot demonstrations with an initial self-consistency step. Backbone experiments replace the reported Llama-2 configuration with Llama-3-8B, Qwen2-7B and GPT-4o. New experiments introduce retrieval-tool, context-count, width/depth and self-consistency-threshold comparisons, plus a manual analysis of 50 sampled outputs.

E4.justification: The original TP/RC/query-feedback ablation survives as Appendix B.2, Table 6. v4 substantially extends analysis with backbone comparisons, pruning-tool and context-count tests, width/depth sensitivity, self-consistency thresholds, measured runtime, evidence-source attribution, error categorization and additional QA cases (Sections 4.5–4.7; Appendices B and D).

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v4's self-consistency experiments concern inference behavior, while its runtime averages and manual-category percentages are additional results rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v4 adds extensive financial, backbone and diagnostic results and removes the Llama-2 result rows. Direct WebQSP changes from 74.55 to 65.9. Main FEVER results become 63.1/59.7 under revised prompting; the earlier 58.54 remains rounded to 58.5 in the appendix ablation. HotpotQA 40.91 versus AdvHotpotQA 42.9 is not an established same-setting gain. Proposed-method WebQSP/QALD scores only change rounding.

M1.justification: The core pruning, retrieval and reasoning loop remains. However, v1 scores chunks against a query containing the question, clue query and triple; v4 Equation 5 instead attaches a verbalized triple to the scored context. v4 also introduces a self-consistency prepass setting (Section 4.3; Appendix B.4). These are limited procedural revisions within the retained framework.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and method exposition are extensively rewritten and reorganized. v4 standardizes the ToG-2 name, changes the title, separates graph search, context retrieval and reasoning explanations, adds a conclusion and thematic appendices, and relocates the original component ablation.

P2.justification: The ACM two-column presentation becomes a single-column preprint. Both principal diagrams are redrawn, including a new loose-coupling hybrid panel in Figure 1. Performance tables are expanded and regrouped, the retained ablation moves to the appendix, and new sensitivity plots, runtime/error tables, case diagrams and prompt tables substantially change the presentation.

R1.justification: Related work is reorganized around text-based, KG-based and hybrid RAG. Added discussion of GraphRAG and HybridRAG supports a substantive positioning change toward mutually improving graph and text retrieval through tight coupling. Additional references cover Self-RAG, self-consistency, context filtering and the expanded datasets.

T1.justification: v4 Section 4.6 adds explicit LLM-call bounds: 2D+1 for combined pruning, WD+D+1 for separate pruning, and 2WD+D+1 for ToG. This extends v1's asymptotic pruning-cost argument. Most other added equations formalize existing search and weighted scoring; neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses important evidential gaps in v1 through explicit text-RAG and hybrid comparisons, financial-domain evaluation, controlled design studies, measured runtime and manual error analysis. Pseudocode, prompts and dataset documentation also make the framework substantially easier to assess. Reporting problems remain, notably Figure 3b's contradictory interpretation and the abstract's Llama-2 claim after its supporting result rows were removed, but these do not outweigh the substantial gains in experimental support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Think-on-Graph 2.0 framework. All six pages of v1 and 22 pages of v4 are readable, including figures, tables, equations and v4's Appendices A–E. v1 contains no appendix.

after.justification: v4 reports original benchmark results, a newly constructed financial QA evaluation, sensitivity experiments, runtime measurements and manual analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark and component-ablation results for ToG2.0, including GPT-3.5 and Llama-2 experiments in Tables 1–2.

title: Think-on-Graph 2.0: Deep and Faithful Large Language Model Reasoning with Knowledge-guided Retrieval Augmented Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same central claims: tightly coupled KG–text retrieval, deep and faithful reasoning, training-free compatibility with different LLMs, leading performance on six of seven datasets, and improvements for smaller models.

C2.justification: v6 substantially extends the applicability and failure discussion. It explains Creak errors through output-format failures, excessive caution, and annotation mismatch; argues that high pruning thresholds discard potentially useful relations; and discusses why severe graph incompleteness harms reasoning and broader, shallower exploration partially compensates. These extend v4's more general retrieval and evaluation limitations.

D1.justification: The abstract adds a source-code repository link. v6 also specifies the 0.2 relation-pruning cutoff followed by top-W selection, clarifies the relation-pruning ablation, and documents configurations for the new runtime comparison, including CoK's rationale-update setting and NaiveRAG's corpus and BM25/BGE-Reranker pipeline.

E1.justification: The established QA, fact-verification, and Chinese financial QA coverage is retained. Appendix B.7 adds a distinct degraded-retrieval scenario: HotpotQA questions evaluated while retaining only 30%, 50%, or 80% of discovered graph entities and relations.

E2.justification: v4's runtime comparison evaluates ToG-2 against ToG. v6 adds CoK and NaiveRAG to the efficiency comparison in Table 9. The comparator sets in the main benchmark tables remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Section 4.3 changes the reported exploration temperature from 0.4 to 0, with reasoning remaining at 0; the PDFs do not establish that retained results were rerun. New protocols include a 50-example Creak audit, a three-threshold sweep, a 100-question graph-deletion experiment with alternative width/depth settings, and total-runtime/API-call comparisons.

E4.justification: v6 substantially expands analysis beyond the retained component, backbone, retrieval-tool, and self-consistency studies. It adds Creak answer-source analysis and three failure cases, relation-pruning threshold sensitivity, graph-incompleteness robustness with an exploration adjustment, and broader efficiency analysis in Appendix B.

E5.justification: v4 contains no significance testing. v6 introduces pairwise t-tests comparing ToG-2 with CoK and ToG on WebQSP, Zero-Shot-RE, QALD-10-en, and Creak, reporting p-value thresholds in Table 12. It explains why other comparisons cannot be tested, but adds no repeated-run counts, seeds, or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Main Tables 1–3 retain their numerical results. Figure 3b reverses the method assignments: at context count 10, v4 assigns 37 to LLM and 34 to BGE-Reranker, while v6 assigns 34 and 37 respectively. New Tables 6 and 9–12 add substantial results on answer sources, efficiency, thresholds, graph completeness, and significance. For example, Table 11 reports 43% EM with full graph retention, 23% with 30% retention, and 29% after adjusting exploration.

M1.justification: Section 3, Equations 1–7, Algorithm 1, and the appendix prompts retain the same retrieval and reasoning procedure. The newly specified pruning threshold documents existing low-score filtering. Revised call accounting includes query rewriting already described in v4.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section structure remain intact. Changes include local grammar and citation formatting, an author-affiliation edit, terminology corrections, and additional appendix subsections. The added scientific material does not entail extensive rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: The appendix gains dedicated tables for Creak answer types, total runtime/API calls, pruning thresholds, graph completeness, and significance. Figure 3 is redrawn, including the reversed legend assignments in panel b. Several captions are clarified or corrected, and existing appendix displays are relocated and renumbered; the other original figures are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 and the reference list retain the same works and substantive positioning relative to text-based, KG-based, and hybrid RAG. Citation-format corrections do not change the research positioning.

T1.justification: Section 4.6 revises the combined-pruning LLM-call bound from 2D + 1 to 2D + (D - 1) + 1. Appendix B.4 explains the additional query-rewriting term. This changes the quantitative cost reasoning; the method equations and other mathematical content remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v6 provides useful additional scrutiny through incomplete-graph and threshold experiments, Creak failure analysis, and broader runtime comparisons. Figure 3b's revised assignments align the plot with its discussion, while revised call accounting and added implementation information improve clarity. The net gain is limited by the 100-question robustness sample, sparse significance-test documentation, and the unexplained relationship between the temperature revision and unchanged main results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ToG-2 research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–E are readable and support reliable matching despite the expanded appendix in v6.

after.justification: v6 retains these original experiments and adds Creak case analysis, pruning-threshold experiments, incomplete-graph evaluations, runtime comparisons, and significance tests.

before.justification: v4 reports original ToG-2 benchmark results, component and backbone ablations, runtime measurements, and manual analyses in Section 4 and the appendices.

title: Think-on-Graph 2.0: Deep and Faithful Large Language Model Reasoning with Knowledge-guided Retrieval Augmented Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims about tightly coupled retrieval, deep and faithful reasoning, training-free compatibility and performance. The abstract's claim of SOTA performance on six of seven datasets is unchanged.

C2.justification: Interpretations concerning contextual versus triple-based reasoning, efficiency and backbone capabilities are retained. Appendix B preserves the same qualifications about incomplete knowledge, retrieval bottlenecks, Creak errors, excessive caution and exact-match evaluation.

D1.justification: Implementation settings, model descriptions, entity-linking information, ToG-FinQA construction details and Appendix E prompts are unchanged. The source-code URL is identical, with no new technical or resource-access disclosure.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate WebQSP, AdvHotpotQA, QALD-10-en, FEVER, Creak, Zero-Shot RE and ToG-FinQA. The incomplete-graph scenarios in Appendix B are also retained, with no changes to dataset, domain or task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains Direct, CoT, CoT-SC, Vanilla RAG, ToG and CoK; Table 2 retains the same financial-QA comparators, including GraphRAG. Comparator membership in the backbone, pruning-tool and runtime analyses also matches. The added citations introduce no evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Metrics, full-Wikipedia/Wikidata retrieval, backbone models, demonstration settings and appendix sampling procedures are unchanged. Section 4.3 retains temperature 0, width and depth of 3, and K = 10.

E4.justification: The backbone, pruning-tool and width/depth ablations in Section 4.5 are unchanged. Appendix B retains the component, threshold, self-consistency, graph-completeness, runtime and error analyses; Appendix D retains the same case studies.

E5.justification: Appendix B.8 retains the same pairwise t-test procedure and Table 12 significance reporting, including the limitation concerning unavailable baseline outputs. No repeated-run, seed or uncertainty-reporting information is added or revised.

E6.justification: The numerical results and qualitative findings match throughout. For example, Table 1 retains ToG-2's 42.9% EM on AdvHotpotQA and 93.5% accuracy on Creak, while Table 2 retains 34.0% on ToG-FinQA. Appendix results and plotted values are also unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Appendix A retain the same initialization, relation pruning, context retrieval, entity scoring, iterative reasoning and stopping procedures. The prompts in Appendix E are also unchanged.

P1.justification: v7 replaces the preprint heading with an ICLR 2025 publication notice, adds corresponding-author markers for Chengjin Xu and Jiaxin Mao, and updates citations, including replacing the introduction's unresolved '(?)'. Section order and substantive prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: The conference running header and citation additions produce limited spacing, line-wrap and page-break changes, including bibliography reflow. Figures 1–8 and Tables 1–19 retain their content, captions and visual designs.

R1.justification: v7 adds Kahneman (2011), two Li et al. works on KG entity typing and completion, and Qiu et al. (2024) on RAG decoding. These supplement existing background without revising the paper's positioning. CoK remains the same cited work, now labeled Li et al. (2024c).

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(7), their mathematical definitions and scoring rules, and the LLM-call-count expressions remain unchanged. No formal assumption, theorem, proof or mathematical correction is introduced.

improvement.justification: v7 repairs the introduction's unresolved citation with Kahneman (2011) and adds three further references for existing KG and RAG background. This modestly improves citation completeness and traceability. The methods, empirical evidence, reproducibility information and limitations remain unchanged, so the overall gain is limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ToG-2 study. The complete main text and Appendices A–E are readable and align across versions, including figures, tables, equations and prompts.

after.justification: v7 retains these original empirical results in Section 4 and Appendix B, including ToG-FinQA evaluations. Their retention from v6 does not change their status as original results.

before.justification: v6 reports original ToG-2 benchmark results, ablations, runtime measurements, manual analyses and graph-completeness experiments in Section 4 and Appendix B, including results on the authors' ToG-FinQA dataset.

title: Think-on-Graph 2.0: Deep and Faithful Large Language Model Reasoning with Knowledge-guided Retrieval Augmented Generation

C1.justification: V1 largely equates linear decodability with disentanglement when tasks span the latent space. V2 separates this claim from orthogonal disentanglement, adding a stronger task-number condition for the latter. Its abstract and contributions also introduce transformer disentanglement at Ntask >= D as a principal finding.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations connecting transformer generalization to orthogonality and interpreting noise-CDF/activation mismatch as geometric distortion. It explicitly places multiplicative boundaries outside the theorem's coverage, while removing v1's explanations of multiplicative-only failure and inadequate boundary coverage. The factorization assumption and lack of standard ML benchmarks remain acknowledged limitations.

D1.justification: V2 supplies GPT-specific architecture and training details, decoder-angle and Jacobian-analysis procedures, and an explicit one-layer RNN/LSTM setting in Table S1. Most existing RNN hyperparameters remain unchanged. V1's NeuroGym implementation statement and approximate ten-minute laptop-CPU training-time disclosure are removed.

E1.justification: The synthetic evidence-aggregation domain and linear, nonlinear and free-reaction-time task families remain. V2 adds anisotropic Gaussian, temporally correlated AR(1) and Gumbel noise scenarios (Appendix A.8), while removing v1's scenario with classification boundaries restricted to two quadrants.

E2.justification: GPT-2 joins the architecture comparison containing leaky RNNs, non-leaky RNNs and LSTMs (v1 Figure 1g; v2 Figure 3b), and is compared against RNNs across input dimensionalities in Figure 5b. This substantially expands the comparative architecture evidence. The context-dependent RNN comparison is retained in Appendix A.7.

E3.justification: V2 extends evaluation beyond decoding r2 and trajectory visualization to pairwise decoder angles and Jacobian eigenspectra (Appendices A.3 and A.6). The new GPT experiments use 20,000 training batches, versus the retained 100,000-batch RNN setting. The existing quadrant-based cross-validation protocol remains unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds direct orthogonality measurements, local dynamical-stability analysis, GPT activation analysis and tests of alternative noise assumptions. It removes the standalone multiplicative-task failure analysis and the restricted-boundary analysis from v1. Interleaved learning, correlated inputs and free-reaction-time analyses are retained, largely through relocation.

E5.justification: Both versions describe five trained networks, five decoder fits per held-out quadrant, and reporting of the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles. V2 applies the same practice to decoder-angle measurements. No increased repetition count or new confidence-interval or significance-testing procedure is reported.

E6.justification: V2 adds GPT performance and geometry results, stability spectra, and noise-robustness medians: r2 = 0.96 for anisotropic noise and 0.95 for AR(1) and Gumbel noise (Appendix A.8). Removed results include multiplicative-only r2 = 0.71 and restricted-boundary median r2 = 0.80, with lower quartile 0.62. The changed main training objective prevents interpreting revised plots as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: V2 changes the main fixed-reaction-time classifier from MSE/tanh with ±1 targets to cross-entropy/sigmoid with 0/1 targets. It also introduces a continuous-input GPT-2 implementation without tokenization or positional encodings (Section 4; Appendix A.5). The earlier MSE/tanh formulation remains in the free-reaction-time comparison.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten. Problem formulation and methods become separate sections, the experiment narrative is reorganized around generalization and representational geometry, and nonlinear/free-reaction-time material moves into Appendix A. The discussion is extensively reorganized and the separate conclusion disappears.

P2.justification: V1 Figure 1 is redistributed across v2 Figures 1–3, the free-reaction-time figure moves to Figure S4, and the former supplementary activation figure becomes an expanded RNN/GPT comparison in Figure 4. New angle, spectral and CDF-approximation displays are added; multiplicative-only and restricted-boundary panels are removed.

R1.justification: V2 adds positioning against Roeder et al.'s linear-identifiability work, adopts definitions from Ostojic and Fusi, and adds references supporting noise and manifold arguments. Some broad foundation-model citations are removed. The central relationship to Johnston and Fusi's multi-task representation work remains.

T1.justification: V2 adds explicit representation definitions, sigmoid Corollary B.8, orthogonality Corollary B.9, and general-noise extensions including anisotropic Gaussian Lemma B.10. The main theorem distinguishes decodability at Ntask >= D from orthogonality at Ntask >> D. These materially extend v1's Gaussian/tanh development, although the new inverse-CDF reconstruction in Appendix B.4 has an internal sign inconsistency.

improvement.justification: Direct angle measurements and stability analyses address gaps in v1's empirical support, while GPT and noise experiments broaden the evidence. However, v2 removes informative failure analyses and introduces inconsistencies in its expanded theory: Equation 25 contains an extra C-transpose factor, and Appendix B.4's inverse-CDF step has the opposite sign implied by its preceding equation. These empirical gains and losses in completeness and theoretical reliability leave the net quality change unclear.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same multi-task evidence-aggregation framework, with matching core experiments and theoretical results. The main text, figures, table and Appendices A–C are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds GPT-2 comparisons, decoder-angle measurements, dynamical analyses and noise-robustness results.

before.justification: V1 reports original RNN/LSTM experiments, OOD decoding results, attractor analyses and task variants in the main text and appendices.

title: Disentangling Representations through Multi-task Learning

C1.justification: The abstract explicitly qualifies the guarantees as applying to affine boundaries in latent space and reframes the contribution as linking multi-task competence to world models. The introduction emphasizes independence from the training paradigm. The principal disentanglement, noise, continuous-attractor and transformer claims remain.

C2.justification: Appendix A.14 substantially expands the biological interpretation: competence need not require simultaneous behavioral actions or simultaneous external supervision, because previously learned tasks can continue constraining representations. Additional discussion connects this account to replay, interprets distillation as transferring world models, and explains sparsity through representational capacity. Existing factorization and benchmark limitations are retained in the expanded Appendix A.15.

D1.justification: v3 adds an explicit code-repository link and reproducibility statement, and clarifies that the fixation input is concatenated with encoded observations. Existing hyperparameters and GPT-2 implementation details are retained. The PDFs establish added access information, not independently verified repository availability.

E1.justification: Appendix A.5 adds an input scenario using quadratic observation-map nonlinearities, extending evaluation beyond the original ReLU mapping. The synthetic latent distributions and existing classification, interleaved-learning and reaction-time tasks are retained.

E2.justification: Matched comparisons retain RNNs, non-leaky RNNs, LSTMs, GPT-2 and the context-dependent computation comparison. No comparator is added to or removed from these experiments; the new sparsity analysis reuses existing recurrent architectures.

E3.justification: The new sparsity analysis samples 1,000 ground-truth vectors per network, computes a response-sparseness score for each neuron and averages across neurons. Existing decoder splits, training budgets, transformer configurations and Table S1 settings are unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds a ReLU-versus-quadratic observation-map robustness test and a systematic sparsity analysis across task count, latent dimensionality and recurrent architecture. These refine existing robustness and sparsity claims; the earlier noise, correlation, interleaving and reaction-time analyses remain.

E5.justification: The new reproducibility statement explicitly says the experiments are seeded. Five networks per configuration, repeated decoder fits and percentile reporting were already documented in v2 Appendices A.2–A.3; there is no documented increase in repetitions.

E6.justification: New Figure S1 reports virtually identical OOD generalization for quadratic and ReLU observation maps. New Figure S6 reports approximately 90% sparsity for RNNs and non-leaky RNNs, lower sparsity for LSTMs, and decreasing RNN sparsity with increasing latent dimensionality. Existing main results, including median OOD/ID r-squared values of 0.96/0.97, are retained.

M1.justification: The multi-task classification procedure, trained architectures, objectives and linear probing method remain unchanged. The quadratic encoder experiment varies the fixed observation-generating map to test robustness; it does not introduce a new learning algorithm.

P1.justification: v3 revises the abstract and theoretical exposition, adds a proof roadmap, reproducibility and author-contribution statements, and moves the limitations discussion into Appendix A.15. Terminology and citations are edited, but most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: v3 adds Figures S1 and S6, annotates and relocates Figure 2, and redisplays the Gaussian-CDF approximation plot with a revised legend. It adopts conference headers and typography and adjusts captions and figure placement. The main empirical figures and hyperparameter table retain their displays.

R1.justification: v3 adds references concerning activation-dependent geometry, multi-task disentanglement, information theory, sparsity and biological memory/replay. These support targeted contextual expansions; the central positioning relative to Johnston and Fusi, Lachapelle and other prior disentanglement work remains.

T1.justification: Theorems B.5–B.6 replace the earlier mutual-information/entropy argument with explicit reconstruction and sufficient-statistic reasoning, while B.4–B.5 explicitly require Ntask >= D. New Corollary B.7 specifies assumptions and an approximate O(1/sqrt(Ntask)) recovery-rate assertion for suboptimal classifiers. v3 also corrects the tanh approximation statement and the extra transpose factor in the sigmoid reconstruction formula. These substantively revise the theoretical support.

improvement.justification: The revised reconstruction proofs remove v2's unsupported mutual-information/entropy equality and correct mathematical expressions. The targeted robustness and sparsity analyses strengthen existing claims, while code and seed disclosures improve auditability. These are useful but bounded gains: the main empirical findings remain unchanged, and the new recovery-rate assertion in Corollary B.7 lacks a detailed error-propagation derivation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Disentangling Representations through Multi-task Learning. The complete main texts, appendices, equations, figures and tables are readable and support matching retained, revised and added material.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds results on quadratic observation-map nonlinearities and quantitative sparsity in Appendices A.5 and A.12.

before.justification: v2 reports original experiments with RNNs, LSTMs and GPT-2, including generalization scores, representation geometry and robustness analyses in Section 5 and the appendices.

title: Disentangling Representations through Multi-task Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion expand the headline contribution from NeRF editing to model-agnostic editing with claimed state-of-the-art results on both NeRF and 3DGS. The earlier priority claim about adopting decreasing timesteps for general 3D editing is dropped. The central diffusion-sampling and FreeU contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive applicability and failure explanations: inherited IP2P prompt-following failures, improvement through detailed prompts, and segmentation/projection mismatch attributed to GE/DGE errors (Appendices C.2 and F.1). It also interprets the alternative-weight results as robustness to the precise coefficient choice, extending v1's discussion of the identity/editability trade-off.

D1.justification: v2 newly reports an official code repository, 3DGS implementation recipes, the complete evaluation prompt list and survey details including vigilance filtering, shared camera trajectories and randomized options. Existing NeRF and guidance details move to Appendix B. However, v1's timestep range [0.2, 0.9] and statement about retaining FreeU's original skip-feature scaling settings disappear.

E1.justification: Both versions report eight scenes and 40 prompt pairs from IN2N/PDS data. Figure 15 adds a limited input-condition scenario comparing simple and detailed prompts alongside the corresponding 2D-IP2P failure. The larger 3DGS evaluation primarily changes model configurations within the retained scene-editing coverage.

E2.justification: The NeRF comparison retains IN2N and PDS. The new 3DGS comparison evaluates GaussianEditor with DDS and IN2N guidance, plus DGE (Table 2 and Figure 8). These are substantial additions to the evaluated comparator set; DGE was only cited in v1.

E3.justification: Appendix B.2 introduces separate Nerfstudio/splatfacto and Threestudio 3DGS protocols, with method-specific training budgets and densification settings. The reported user-study sample changes from 50 to 100 participants, and the prompt-alignment question drops its quality requirement. These are reported protocol revisions; unchanged preference percentages do not establish that the study was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds quantitative FreeU ablations, alternative-weight sensitivity tests, additional FreeU examples and an IP2P/prompt-specificity failure analysis. It removes v1's controlled 500-iteration random-versus-decreasing-timestep comparison for DreamCatalyst. Appendix C.1 instead tests PDS with decreasing timesteps, answering a different question.

E5.justification: Both versions retain Figure 5's linear-regression trend lines with 95% confidence bands. v2 adds no repeated-run counts, seed information, uncertainty estimates for the tabulated scores or significance tests. The participant-count revision concerns study sample size rather than uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises retained NeRF scores: PDS CLIP directional similarity changes from 0.174 to 0.161, while the fast mode changes from 0.158 to 0.165, reversing their order. v2 adds 3DGS, weighting-variant, quantitative FreeU and failure-case results. NeRF timings and user-preference percentages remain unchanged. The score revisions are unexplained and cannot be treated as demonstrated method improvements.

M1.justification: The default identity-regularized DDS objective, decreasing timesteps, FreeU and IP2P guidance are retained. v2 adds two alternative DDS weighting functions and a GaussianEditor-integrated variant with a densification cutoff (Section 3.3 and Appendix B.2), extending the procedure without replacing its core.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and methodological narrative are extensively rewritten and reorganized. SDEdit preliminaries, text guidance and implementation details move into appendices; the preliminary and experimental subsections are restructured. New appendix organization and an ethics statement further change the document's narrative structure.

P2.justification: v2 adds 3DGS and FreeU result tables, a full prompt table, comparison grids, survey screenshots and a limitations figure. Figure 2 gains weighting curves; Figure 6 replaces the FreeU examples and removes the timestep-ablation row. Existing displays are also relocated and resized, substantially changing the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 substantially develops positioning against model-specific GaussianEditor/DGE approaches and explicitly distinguishes its interpretation from DreamSampler's source–target equality assumption. It adds citations including DDS, GaussianEditor, 3DGS, Threestudio and DreamGaussian, while removing InstructHumans and the associated discussion of earlier decreasing-timestep editing.

T1.justification: v2 explicitly defines the DDIM noise coefficient from the schedule and changes the stated PDS noise-scale factor from beta_t to 1-alpha_t in Section 2. It also defines two additional weighting functions. The central DDS/SDEdit derivation is retained, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation and reproducibility beyond v1's NeRF-only comparisons and qualitative component ablations. The 3DGS evaluations, quantitative FreeU and weighting tests, detailed prompts and implementation information, and illustrated IP2P limitation make the method more assessable. Unexplained score and participant-count revisions, removal of the original scheduling ablation, and lost setting disclosures are weaknesses, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DreamCatalyst with the same authors and core framework. All 13 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v2 are readable, including equations, tables and figures. v1 ends with references; v2 includes appendices A–F.

after.justification: v2 retains original NeRF results and reports additional 3DGS comparisons, quantitative ablations and qualitative analyses in Section 4 and the appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original NeRF editing comparisons, quantitative metrics, human preferences and qualitative ablations in Section 4.

title: DreamCatalyst: Fast and High-Quality 3D Editing via Controlling Editability and Identity Preservation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions: the DDS–SDEdit interpretation, controllable weighting, FreeU integration and fast, high-quality editing across NeRF and 3DGS. The approximately 23-fold and eightfold speedup claims are unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 explains why FreeU can worsen PDS identity preservation and why its effect depends on the underlying method (Appendix D.2). Appendix F.2 also qualifies the existing weighting discussion with occasional background saturation attributed to excessive editability at small timesteps. The previous IP2P limitation is retained.

D1.justification: The new reproducibility statement explicitly says the previously linked repository provides setup information and datasets as well as source code. The added PDS experiment documents b = 1.1. Appendix B's existing implementation and hardware details remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish a new resource release.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate eight scenes with 40 source/target prompt pairs across NeRF and 3DGS, with the same user-study coverage. The added appendix comparisons use existing scene types and editing tasks.

E2.justification: v3 adds PDS with FreeU as an evaluated comparison variant in Table 5 and Figure 13. The established NeRF and 3DGS comparator sets remain unchanged; Figure 7 supplies additional illustrations from the already compared PDS method.

E3.justification: The new convergence evaluation measures CLIP directional similarity and visual outputs at intermediate optimization iterations (Figures 12 and 14). The added PDS control uses FreeU with b = 1.1. Existing benchmark budgets, metrics, implementation settings and user-study procedures remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v2's weighting-function and FreeU sensitivity studies, v3 adds convergence diagnostics against IN2N and PDS and a controlled examination of FreeU on PDS (Appendix D, Table 5, Figures 12–14). These substantially extend the analyses testing optimization efficiency and whether FreeU alone explains the advantages.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same 95% confidence intervals around fitted regression lines in Figure 5. v3 adds no seed counts, repeated-run information, significance tests or uncertainty estimates for the new ablation and convergence results.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their numerical values. New Table 5 reports PDS with FreeU at 0.162 CLIP directional similarity, 0.668 image similarity and 5.413 aesthetic score, versus 0.161, 0.687 and 5.437 without FreeU. Additional figures report convergence trajectories and qualitative comparisons; these are added findings, not improved DreamCatalyst scores between versions.

M1.justification: The weighted DDS objective, identity regularizer, weighting functions, decreasing timestep schedule, IP2P backbone and FreeU integration are unchanged. The added explanations and PDS experiments do not modify DreamCatalyst's procedure.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized wording edits, expands explanations in Section 3, adds acknowledgements and a reproducibility statement, and inserts an additional quantitative-evaluation appendix. Most prose and the main narrative structure are retained. New Appendix C.2 incorrectly describes a skull edit where Figure 7 shows a mustache.

P2.justification: v3 adds Figures 7 and 12–14 and Table 5, clarifies FreeU condition labels in Table 4 and Figure 11, and adjusts table sizing and emphasis. Existing illustrations are retained, with appendix displays relocated or renumbered; equation highlighting and citation colors also change.

R1.justification: The reference lists contain the same works, and the relationships to DDS, PDS, DreamSampler and FreeU remain substantively unchanged. The added comparisons reinforce the existing positioning.

T1.justification: The DDS–SDEdit derivation, mathematical objectives, weighting definitions and design conditions are retained. Several equations become inline or are renumbered. Removing v2's explicit chain-rule gradient display, Equation 19, leaves the objective and stated Jacobian omission unchanged and does not revise the mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: The convergence comparisons and PDS-with-FreeU control strengthen evidence for the existing efficiency and component claims, while the expanded artifact discussion improves interpretation. These are useful additions to an otherwise stable method and benchmark evaluation. The new skull/mustache mismatch in Appendix C.2 and Figure 7 is a small reporting defect that does not outweigh the added validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DreamCatalyst and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices. Corresponding content can be matched despite renumbering and added supplementary evaluations.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds convergence comparisons and experiments applying FreeU to PDS.

before.justification: v2 reports original NeRF and 3DGS experiments, component ablations and a 100-participant user study in Section 4 and the appendices.

title: DreamCatalyst: Fast and High-Quality 3D Editing via Controlling Editability and Identity Preservation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: a stochastic-map framework, necessary and sufficient conditions for preserving estimator consistency, and analysis of statistical and computational concerns. The revised motivation and emphasis on representation learning do not change these core claims.

C2.justification: Section 4 adds explanations connecting normalization operations to noninjective encoding and discusses stochastic decoding as a possible approach to unfamiliar symbols. Section 7 newly acknowledges that effective computation of exact tokenizers remains unaddressed. These refine practical implications and limitations within the retained theoretical scope.

D1.justification: No implementation, experimental hyperparameters, hardware specifications, training times, or code/data release information for this work is added or revised. The new references to tokenizer software and preprocessing operations support conceptual discussion rather than reproducibility instructions.

E1.justification: Neither version trains or evaluates on datasets or benchmarks. The constructed alphabet and tokenization examples are retained; newly cited empirical studies do not constitute additional task coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates comparison methods against a proposed implementation. BPE, WordPiece, and Unigram remain theoretical illustrations, while additional cited methods serve the literature discussion.

E3.justification: Neither version specifies an original experimental evaluation protocol. No splits, evaluation metrics, training budgets, model configurations, or testing procedures are added or revised.

E4.justification: The inconsistency, ambiguity, and uncomputability examples in Examples 4.1, 4.2, and 5.1 are retained. Neither version contains empirical ablations, robustness tests, or error analyses; the added normalization discussion is conceptual.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates. The mathematical treatment of estimator consistency is not empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: There are no original empirical result entries in either version. Figure 1 retains the reference probabilities (0.2, 0.4, 0.4), encoded probabilities (0.2, 0, 0.8), and decoded probabilities (0, 0.2, 0.8). The other worked examples retain their findings.

M1.justification: Both versions retain the tokenizer as a pair of stochastic encoder and decoder maps and the same distribution-mapping framework. The revised formal properties and proofs do not introduce a new tokenization algorithm, architecture, objective, or inference procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten, and the historical opening and Saussure epigraph are removed. Sections 4–5 gain topical paragraph headings, expanded explanations, and more explicit encoder/decoder terminology.
