P2.justification: v3 redesigns the title and author block, adds running Preprint headers and rules, changes heading typography, and adjusts spacing and figure placement relative to the text. Figure 1 and the existing commutative diagrams remain; no new tables or substantive graphical displays are introduced.

R1.justification: v3 replaces the extensive historical-linguistic positioning around Plato, Saussure, and Chomsky with a substantially expanded contemporary NLP context. It adds discussion and citations covering token-free models, empirical tokenizer studies, open-vocabulary approaches, and marginalization methods. Section 4 replaces the detailed Cao and Rimell discussion with a broader set of related approaches.

T1.justification: v3 makes substantive repairs to the mathematical foundation: Lemma 3.1 corrects the sign in its Fatou argument, and Lemma 3.2 restores a limit and replaces an equality with the required inequality. Section 2 adds definitions of stochastic-map support, injectivity, and surjectivity. New Proposition 3.2 proves decoder determinism on the encoder's support, qualifying v1's unrestricted assertion. Theorem 3.1 itself is unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 improves mathematical reliability through the corrections to Lemmas 3.1–3.2 and the qualified determinism proof in Proposition 3.2. Its focused introduction and explicit computational limitation also improve clarity. The gains remain limited: the central theorem and examples are unchanged, and Definition 4.1 still asserts decoder determinism more broadly than Proposition 3.2 establishes.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same tokenization framework and provide readable text, equations, proofs, diagrams, and worked examples. Both end with references; neither contains an appendix. The material supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 remains a theoretical paper. Its added proposition and expanded discussion do not introduce original empirical results, and Section 7 continues to describe experimental investigation as future work.

before.justification: v1 presents mathematical definitions, proofs, and constructed examples in Sections 3–5. Empirical findings are attributed to prior work; no original experiments, simulations, or data analyses are reported.

title: The Foundations of Tokenization: Statistical and Computational Concerns

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the unified stochastic-map framework and necessary-and-sufficient consistency guarantee. The supporting computational contribution changes from tractability and boundedness through finite decomposition to finiteness and sequentiality through bounded variation.

C2.justification: V4 qualifies the cited practical impact of spurious ambiguity as occurring mostly on strongly out-of-domain evaluation sets and adds a linguistic-segmentation prerequisite for modeling linguistic ambiguity. It also removes v3's explicit limitations concerning structural questions, vocabulary choice, effective computation, interpretability, and potential empirical investigation. These alter qualifications while retaining the central interpretations of inconsistency and ambiguity.

D1.justification: No implementation recipe, experimental hyperparameters, hardware information, or work-specific code/data access is added or removed. The new appendix definitions are mathematical specifications, not reproducibility information for an implementation.

E1.justification: Neither version trains or evaluates on datasets or tasks. Added discussion of linguistic segmentation and character-level language models does not introduce evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version reports evaluated baselines. BPE, WordPiece, and Unigram remain examples in theoretical discussion, rather than participants in experimental comparisons.

E3.justification: Neither version specifies an empirical evaluation protocol. V4's new string-distance definition supports its mathematical analysis; it is not an evaluation metric used in an experiment.

E4.justification: No ablations, robustness tests, or empirical supplementary analyses are introduced. V3's ambiguity and uncomputability examples are retained as Examples 8.1 and 8.2 in v4, rather than added analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or empirical uncertainty estimates. Discussion of estimator consistency is theoretical.

E6.justification: Figure 1 retains the same illustrative distributions: (0.2, 0.4, 0.4), encoded as (0.2, 0, 0.8) and decoded as (0, 0.2, 0.8). No experimental result entries are added or revised; the new mathematical result is assessed under T1.

M1.justification: The tokenizer remains a pair of stochastic encoder and decoder maps. V4 revises mathematical characterizations of tokenizers without introducing or changing an implemented tokenization algorithm, training procedure, or inference method.

P1.justification: The main exposition is substantially reorganized: existing proofs move to Appendix 8.1 and two worked examples to Appendix 8.2. Section 5 is rewritten around sequentiality, preliminary explanations and terminology are revised, and the limitations section is removed. These changes materially alter the narrative structure despite preserving much of the underlying content.

P2.justification: V4 introduces systematic green/violet mathematical notation, reformats Figure 1 from a vertically stacked display into a side-by-side arrangement, and adds an identity arrow to the main commutative diagram. The overall single-column format remains, with no new experimental tables or plots.

R1.justification: V4 adds connections to Berstel and Choffrut's transduction theory, Lehmann and Casella's estimation text, linguistic-tokenization studies, and work by Giulianelli et al. and Vieira et al. These broaden the supporting literature and connect the framework to follow-up character-level modeling while retaining its overall foundational positioning.

T1.justification: Section 5 replaces finite-type maps and bounded tokenizers in Definitions 5.3–5.4 with a prefix-based string distance and bounded variation. V4 adds Proposition 5.2, proving that multiplicativity implies bounded variation, invokes Choffrut's subsequentiality criterion, and adds sequential/subsequential transducer definitions in Appendix 8.3. This substantially revises the computational theory. The central consistency theorem and its existing supporting proofs are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: V4 develops Section 5 more fully through bounded variation, the proved Proposition 5.2, and explicit transducer definitions. Collecting existing proofs and examples in the appendix also streamlines the main argument without removing their support. These provide a modest gain in theoretical development and readability, although deleting v3's limitations section weakens transparency about unresolved questions and constrains the overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with the same authors, framework, and central consistency theorem. All pages are readable, including v4's Appendix 8. V3 contains its proofs in the main text and has no separate appendix.

after.justification: V4 remains theoretical, including its appendix. The added proposition, proof, and transducer definitions do not constitute empirical results.

before.justification: V3 presents mathematical results and constructed examples, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes. Empirical findings are attributed to cited research.

title: The Foundations of Tokenization: Statistical and Computational Concerns

The central claims about tense generalization, weaker future-tense attacks and the feasibility of targeted fine-tuning remain.

C2.justification: Section 5 newly qualifies automated jailbreak scores: some successful judgments concern generic or dual-use answers that may not satisfy the cited policy definition or help an attacker substantially. It proposes that reasoning can act as an implicit output filter and argues for evaluating answer usefulness. Section 3 also adds a hypothesis linking similar GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini ASRs to similar alignment methods.

D1.justification: Additional technical disclosure is limited to the 100-restart AdvBench configuration and the o1 API/input-filter context. Sampling temperature, fine-tuning details, appendix prompt texts and code/artifact access remain unchanged. The appendix table labeled as a future-tense prompt still contains past-tense instructions in both versions.

E6.justification: Existing results in Tables 1, 3 and 4 are retained. M1.justification: The GPT-3.5 Turbo reformulation procedure, repeated sampling, success criterion and refusal fine-tuning approach remain unchanged. Additional target models and a larger attack budget do not introduce a new method component.

P1.justification: v3 inserts a reasoning-model section and contribution bullet, updates model lists and results paragraphs, and makes small terminology and language edits. The original narrative and section sequence otherwise remain, with related work and discussion renumbered.

P2.justification: v3 adds Table 5 and Figure 4, expands Tables 1 and 3, enlarges Figure 2 from six to eight panels, and redraws Figure 3 with additional series and revised colors and legend. Prompt tables are reformatted, and Table 4's caption moves above the unchanged results.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for Claude-3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o mini, the o1 system card and the OpenAI Model Spec. It also positions the attack as competitive with Andriushchenko et al. (2024) through the added AdvBench comparison. The existing related-work discussion is substantially retained.

improvement.justification: Additional conventional-model tests and the new o1 analysis strengthen empirical support, while Section 5's distinction between automated success and answer usefulness improves interpretation. The gain is limited: usefulness remains qualitatively assessed, the AdvBench comparison is briefly documented, and Appendix A's future-tense prompt mismatch remains unresolved.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with matching authors, methodology and retained experiments. All 15 pages of v1 and 17 pages of v3, including figures, tables, equations and Appendix A, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds results for four target models, a separate AdvBench evaluation, and measurements of o1 input-filter blocking.

before.justification: v1 reports original jailbreak evaluations on six models, past-versus-future comparisons, and fine-tuning experiments measuring attack success and overrefusals.

title: Does Refusal Training in LLMs Generalize to the Past Tense?

C2.justification: The proposed generalization mechanisms, failure explanations, overrefusal tradeoff and qualifications about reasoning-model answer usefulness remain unchanged. Adding 'specifically' in Section 4 and a training-set cross-reference in Section 6 clarifies existing interpretations.

M1.justification: The reformulation procedure, auxiliary model, multiple-attempt strategy and fine-tuning approach remain unchanged. Adding 'Instruct' to three target-model names clarifies documentation without establishing a method or model substitution.

P1.justification: v4 adds a short Section 4 introduction, clarifies wording and a cross-reference in Section 6, and updates publication and funding text. Most prose and the section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: Document-wide ICLR retypesetting changes margins, typography, display sizes and float placement. Figures 2–3 now share a page, Figure 4 moves alongside the opening reasoning-model discussion, and Appendix Tables 10–12 share one page. Display content is retained.

R1.justification: v4 adds Wei et al. (2022) for chain-of-thought reasoning, Jain et al. (2023) for defenses and Ousidhoum et al. (2021) for toxicity probing. These supply limited additional attribution without changing the broader research positioning.

T1.justification: Section 2 retains the same token-sequence model, binary judge definition and constrained attack objective. No formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs are added or revised.

improvement.justification: Explicit Instruct variant names and three relevant citations modestly improve reproducibility and attribution. The scientific evidence remains unchanged, and the extensive reformatting provides no additional support for the claims. Table 10's future-tense caption paired with a past-tense prompt remains unresolved, limiting the documentation improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching methods, experiments, figures and Appendix A. Text extraction and visual inspection support comparison of all material despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v4 retains these original experimental results, including quantitative attack success rates, fine-tuning outcomes and reasoning-model examples.

before.justification: v3 reports original jailbreak evaluations, fine-tuning and overrefusal experiments, and reasoning-model evaluations in Sections 3–5, Tables 1 and 3–5, and Figures 1–4.

title: Does Refusal Training in LLMs Generalize to the Past Tense?

C1.justification: Both versions claim that patch-level training followed by token-level adaptation can halve training costs while maintaining comparable performance across 370M–2.7B models. The revised information-density framing does not change the central contribution or empirical claim.

C2.justification: Section 3.7 explicitly discusses the loss of within-patch token order and interprets the new ablation as showing that lower patch loss need not improve final token performance. The neuron-activation discussion also expands its interpretation toward unused model capacity. Existing scalability qualifications remain.

D1.justification: v2 documents the new ablation's input and output mapping dimensions, token-level output construction, removal of extra parameters during transfer, and experimental settings. The main implementation recipe, optimizer settings, tokenizer and source-code access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the Pile, WikiText-103, the same six zero-shot benchmarks, GPT4 Alpaca and MT-Bench. The 60B-token multi-epoch experiment already appears in v1; the new architecture ablation introduces no dataset, domain or task coverage.

E2.justification: New Table 5 compares the original patch-training architecture against three internal alternatives: +InputMap, +OutputMap and +Both. The comparator sets in the existing benchmark experiments remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Section 3.7 adds an architecture comparison using 90B training tokens, a 370M-parameter model, batch size 512K and lambda = 1/2, evaluating both patch-level and final token-level perplexity. Existing benchmark protocols, including the 60B-token, six-epoch experiment, are unchanged.

E4.justification: The new architecture ablation tests whether learned input and output mappings improve patch modeling and subsequent transfer. It complements the retained context-length, scaling, patch-size, training-fraction and neuron-activation analyses; the multi-epoch results are reorganized rather than newly added.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without experimental run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new architecture table introduces no uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 5 adds patch perplexities of 159.17, 146.93, 99.48 and 86.50, and final token perplexities of 11.46, 11.63, 11.50 and 12.33, respectively for Transformer, +InputMap, +OutputMap and +Both. These show better patch fitting but worse final token performance for the alternatives. Existing tables and result figures retain their findings and values.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure retains averaged token embeddings, a shared prediction head, next-patch training and subsequent token-level adaptation. v2 tests additional mapping layers as architectural alternatives but explicitly retains the original method.

P1.justification: v2 revises the abstract and introductory motivation around compute and information density, promotes existing multi-epoch material into Section 3.3, and edits the discussion and conclusion. The overall section structure and most method and experimental exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 5 and relocates existing displays as the text reflows: Figures 6–7 move from page 7 to page 8, and Figure 8 moves from page 8 to page 9. The eight existing figures and Tables 1–4 are retained without substantive redesign.

R1.justification: v2 adds Anagnostidis et al., Beyer et al., Muennighoff et al. and Nawrot et al., while removing four introductory references. Related work expands connections to changing visual patch sizes and resolution. Positioning against model growth shifts from potential joint application toward preserving the full parameter set.

T1.justification: The patch-embedding definition, training loss and cost-reduction expression remain unchanged. v2's introductory C ≈ 6ND formula provides standard compute-accounting motivation rather than a substantive theoretical development; no new proof or formal guarantee is introduced.

improvement.justification: The new architecture ablation supplies evidence for a previously largely qualitative design rationale: adding both mappings lowers patch perplexity from 159.17 to 86.50 but worsens final token perplexity from 11.46 to 12.33. Expanded related-work context also helps. These are limited gains; the main evaluations remain unchanged, and stronger claims about preserving full model capabilities receive no new comparison against model-growth methods.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same patch-level training work. All pages, equations, tables and figures support comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix; both end with references.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds an architecture ablation in Section 3.7 and Table 5.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-model training experiments, benchmark evaluations, instruction-following results and sensitivity analyses in Section 3.

title: Beyond Next Token Prediction: Patch-Level Training for Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contribution and claim: patch-level training followed by token-level adaptation approximately halves training compute while maintaining performance for 370M–2.7B models. The expanded title and additional supporting experiments do not redefine that claim.

C2.justification: Sections 2 and 3.7 newly interpret an unchanged input or output interface as an anchor for representation transfer. Appendix B qualifies theoretical savings with data-loading and synchronization overhead. Appendix D adds the interpretation that tokenizer compression affects suitable patch size. Appendix C connects its new control to the existing long-range-dependency hypothesis.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds implementation pseudocode for embedding aggregation, position IDs, shifted labels/logits, and loss averaging. Appendix B supplies eight-A100 hardware and local batch, block-length, and accumulation settings for its measurements. Appendix D documents tokenizer-specific configurations. These supplement the already detailed setup; the source-code access information is unchanged.

E1.justification: Training and evaluation retain the Pile, WikiText-103, six zero-shot benchmarks, Alpaca instruction tuning, and MT-Bench. Appendix D changes tokenization of the existing data, without adding a dataset, domain, or task. Mixup changes the training procedure rather than coverage.

E2.justification: Figure 9 adds Mixup K=4 as a comparator alongside patch-level initialization and training without initialization. Existing comparator sets remain. Table 5's InputMap/OutputMap become InputProj/OutputProj with identical results, so these are renamed comparators.

E3.justification: Tables 3–4 switch the reported scaling metric from perplexity to cross-entropy loss. New supplementary protocols include throughput comparisons with gradient accumulation adjusted to preserve batch size, and LLaMA3 tokenization with a 128,000-word vocabulary, approximately 300B training tokens, and a 75B-token patch-size study. The original main experimental settings are retained.

E4.justification: Appendices B–D substantially extend the supplementary analyses: measured throughput tests practical efficiency and synchronization overhead; mixup tests whether consecutive-token grouping matters; and tokenizer experiments test sensitivity to compression rate, including K=2 versus K=4. These address practical validity and design choices beyond the retained scaling, architecture, patch-size, and activation analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance-testing procedures. The added experiments retain point estimates and single displayed trajectories.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial empirical evidence. Table 6 reports 247.1K baseline tokens/second versus 933.5K and 864.2K for two patch configurations, yielding 3.78× and 3.50× speedups. Under the new LLaMA3-tokenizer setting, Table 7 reports baseline/patch perplexities of 15.48/15.32 and average accuracies of 42.8/42.9. Figures 9–11 add mixup and tokenizer findings. Tables 1, 2, and 5 retain their values; Tables 3–4 express existing scaling results as log losses, not improved performance.

M1.justification: The main method retains consecutive-token embedding averaging, single-head next-patch prediction, and subsequent token-level training. Appendix C introduces an experimental mixup variant that instead groups corresponding tokens from randomly selected training samples. This is a limited alternative aggregation procedure; the new pseudocode and projection terminology clarify the existing main method.

P1.justification: The title gains 'Beyond Next Token Prediction,' conference-publication headers replace 'Preprint,' and several method and interpretation paragraphs receive local edits. Appendices A–D extend the document, while the main section order and most prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds a substantial supplementary display set: throughput Table 6, tokenizer comparison Table 7, loss-trajectory Figures 9–11, and a boxed pseudocode listing. Existing Figures 1–8 remain, while Tables 3–4 receive metric-caption changes and Table 5 receives renamed labels. The expansion adds new visual evidence without redesigning the main paper.

R1.justification: v3 adds Shao et al. (2019, 2020, 2023) to the non-autoregressive training-objective discussion, plus Dubey et al. (2024) and Zhang et al. (2018) for LLaMA3 and mixup. The positioning relative to model growth, multi-token prediction, and patch-level models remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The compute relationship, patch-embedding definition, and training objective remain mathematically equivalent; changing pθ to P is notation. Appendix B substitutes measured speed into the existing cost accounting. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens practical credibility through measured throughput and an explicit distinction between theoretical 0.5× cost and approximately 0.523× estimated runtime in Appendix B. Mixup and tokenizer controls add useful validation, and pseudocode improves reproducibility. These are focused improvements to an already developed empirical paper: the main results remain unchanged, the added model-quality experiments concern 370M models, and uncertainty reporting is still absent.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same patch-level training work. All pages, equations, tables, and figures are readable. v2 ends with references; v3 adds Appendices A–D. The title change and additions do not prevent reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains the original experiments and adds throughput measurements, a mixup comparison, and tokenizer experiments in its appendices.

before.justification: Section 3 reports original language-model training results, downstream evaluations, scaling experiments, and ablations.

title: Beyond Next Token Prediction: Patch-Level Training for Large Language Models

title: BRIGHT: A Realistic and Challenging Benchmark for Reasoning-Intensive Retrieval

The central claims about benchmark novelty, retrieval difficulty, reasoning-enhanced queries, and resistance to document contamination remain.

C2.justification: New Appendix D categorizes the required reasoning as deductive, analogical, causal, or analytical and explains these categories through existing examples. This adds substantive interpretation of the benchmark's demands. The QA-evaluation caveats and limitations concerning subjective relevance and unaddressed modalities are retained.

D1.justification: v4 supplies direct GitHub code and Hugging Face dataset links and replaces the reproducibility section's Drive link with the project website. Hardware, model checkpoints, context limits, and training hyperparameters remain unchanged. Passage-splitting and false-negative guidance is relocated rather than newly disclosed.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 12 datasets and 1,384 queries, with unchanged dataset statistics in Table 1. The long-context and downstream QA tasks also remain; additional metrics and model conditions do not introduce new data or task coverage.

E2.justification: The theorem-based downstream comparison expands from none/random/oracle contexts in v2 Table 48 to include Qwen retrieval in v4 Table 47. The main set of 13 retrieval models and the MiniLM, Gemini, and GPT-4 reranking comparators remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Table 46 substantially revises the reported QA evaluation: five criteria covering accuracy, relevance, comprehensiveness, clarity, and objectivity are replaced by reference-content coverage with ten-point anchors and a REASON/SCORE format. v4 also adds Precision@10 and Recall@10 and removes the separate GPT-4 generation condition for StackExchange QA. These are evaluation changes, not evidence of improved performance under identical conditions.

E4.justification: The downstream document-source analysis adds actual Qwen retrieval for theorem-based QA, testing whether oracle-context benefits extend to an available retriever. The separate GPT-4 StackExchange QA replication disappears. The leakage-training, reranking, and long-context analyses remain.

E5.justification: The five-seed averaging and standard-deviation reporting for theorem-based QA are retained from v2 Table 48 in v4 Table 47, including the same practice for the added Qwen row. Annotation-agreement reporting and statistical-significance statements are unchanged; no new uncertainty-estimation procedure is documented.

E6.justification: Many retrieval values change in Tables 2 and 34–39; for example, Qwen's Table 2 average changes from 24.3 to 22.5. Table 4 replaces closed-book/Qwen/oracle QA averages of 57.7/64.3/74.9 with 77.7/79.6/81.8 under revised grading. Precision/recall results and Qwen theorem-QA results are added, while the separate GPT-4 StackExchange QA results are removed.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction, reasoning-enhanced query generation, reranking procedures, and GritLM continued-training objectives are retained. The revised QA judging prompt changes evaluation rather than the retrieval method.

P1.justification: v4 adds contents and acknowledgments, revises subsection titles and cross-references, relocates StackExchange construction guidance, and rewrites Section 5.2. Most prose and the main narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: Figure 1 replaces its keyword-retrieval example, Figure 3 and Tables 3–4 change placement, and the QA prompt display expands. v4 removes the GPT-4 StackExchange QA table, adds two precision/recall tables, and extends the theorem-QA table with a Qwen row. The overall visual design remains similar.

R1.justification: New Appendix I expands the comparison with the already-cited RAR-b, distinguishing dataset construction, document characteristics, and practical objectives. The bibliography and broader related-work discussion remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The formal retrieval-task definitions and mathematical filtering criteria remain unchanged. Neither version adds original theorems or proofs; the new reasoning taxonomy is explanatory rather than a formal theoretical development.

improvement.justification: v4 adds useful retrieval metrics, a practical Qwen QA comparison, and clearer reasoning and related-work explanations. However, it changes QA grading and removes the GPT-4 replication, while Table 46 substitutes {predicted_answer} for the problem. The PDFs do not establish whether this is a documentation error or an evaluation defect. Headline/table inconsistencies also persist: v2 states 22.1 against Table 2's 24.3, while v4 states 24.3 against 22.5. These tradeoffs prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BRIGHT benchmark and provide readable main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices. Moved and renumbered material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical evaluations and adds precision/recall results and a Qwen retrieval condition for downstream theorem-based QA.

before.justification: v2 reports original retrieval evaluations, downstream QA experiments, reranking experiments, and continued-training and long-context analyses.

title: BRIGHT: A Realistic and Challenging Benchmark for Reasoning-Intensive Retrieval

C1.justification: V1's headline claims emphasize outperforming GPT-4o by up to 11% and achieving up to 3.4-fold efficiency gains. V2 instead emphasizes up to 13% superiority over open-source LMMs, processing 10,000 images on one 40GB A100, and a new RetVQA state of the art. The RetVQA claim is unsupported by the supplied comparison: v2 reports 67.6 while omitting v1's MI-BART result of 76.5.

C2.justification: V1 attributes MIRAGE's multi-needle advantage over Gemini to multi-image training; v2 instead emphasizes unresolved cross-image reasoning weaknesses relative to Gemini. V2 adds training-data hypotheses for oracle and positional failures and qualifies caption aggregation as query-unaware. It removes the discussion of query-aware retrieval preventing efficient LSH/k-nearest-neighbor indexing. The COCO, template, and societal limitations largely move unchanged to Appendix C.

D1.justification: V2 Appendix B adds API snapshot identifiers, checkpoint links, evaluation and caption-aggregation prompts, and detector-baseline implementation details. Training and inference hardware disclosures also change. Conversely, v2 omits v1's explicit retrieval threshold, one-epoch count, dataset-license statement, and LLaVA-image exclusion statement. Documentation remains inconsistent: Section 4.2 describes about 600K instruction samples while Figure 5 retains a 1.2M training set, and Table B.1 labels a CLIP checkpoint link as OWLv2. The existing project URL is relocated, not newly introduced.

E1.justification: Reported pretraining coverage expands from Share-GPT captioning data to a mixture also including CC3M/12M, LAION-400M, and COCO, substantially broadening the training sources (v1 Section 3.2; v2 Section 4.2). The principal evaluation tasks remain VHs, RetVQA, and single-image QA. VizWiz disappears from the main model comparison but remains in the compression experiment, so its coverage is not wholly removed.

E2.justification: V2 adds an OWLv2 detector oracle and evaluates Qwen2-VL, Phi-3 Vision, InternVL2, mPLUG-Owl3, LongVILA, and Idefics3 on VHs, while dropping standalone LLaVA and Claude-3 Opus from that comparison. Caption aggregation changes from LLaVA plus Llama3 to Qwen2-VL plus Llama-v3.1, and CLIP plus LLaVA gains an end-to-end VHs accuracy comparison. V2 Table 1 also omits MI-BART and Qwen-VL-Chat from v1's conventional-benchmark comparison.

E3.justification: V1 uses the 100-question VHs_small subset throughout its main VHs evaluation; v2 uses the full dataset for haystacks of at most 100 images and the small subset for larger haystacks. Single-needle dataset size changes from 880 to 1,000 questions, and multi-needle construction changes from two–five relevant images to two–three. V2 also adds a controlled one/two/three-needle oracle experiment and reports training on 16 rather than eight A100 GPUs.

E4.justification: V2 extends the existing oracle comparisons by separately examining performance with one, two, and three relevant images in Figure 3(A), and expands positional-bias testing to newer models. Appendix A adds object-frequency analysis, and Table C.1 identifies Idefics3's answer-format failures. The compression ablation and retrieval/runtime analysis are retained from v1 rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions use bootstrapped averages. V1 gives a general 3–4% standard-deviation range and specifies 75 observations per bootstrap sample; v2 reports condition-specific standard deviations and graphical error bars but omits that resample-size detail. This refines uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in independent runs or seeds.

E6.justification: The revised MIRAGE results include RetVQA 70.8 to 67.6, VQAv2 70.0 to 76.6, and MM-Vet 25.8 to 33.4 (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 1). VHs results are extensively replaced under changed model and evaluation conditions—for example, single-needle N=100 changes from 55% to 61.99%, which is not a matched-setting gain. V2 adds many result entries and removes multi-needle N=10,000 results. It also places v1's GPT-4 VQAv2/TextVQA values under GPT-4o without explanation; the compression-ablation values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: V1 uses a Vicuna backbone and a single-layer MLP retriever operating on pooled query/image features; v2 uses Llama-v3.1-8B and several transformer blocks for retrieval. V2 also introduces pretraining data annealing and changes the relevant-image-only training phase from 75% to 60%. The CLIP encoder, 32-token Q-Former, and joint next-token/binary-cross-entropy objectives remain.

P1.justification: The title changes from 'Answering Harder Questions About Sets of Images' to 'A Vision-Centric Needle-In-A-Haystack Benchmark.' The abstract, introduction, and substantial portions of the main narrative are rewritten around three model failure modes. Benchmark evaluation becomes a separate section, limitations move to the appendix, and the appendices are reorganized and expanded.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the main VHs tables with line plots and places expanded numerical tables in the appendix, redraws the positional heatmaps, and adds dataset examples, an object-frequency chart, prompt/checkpoint displays, and positional line plots. Its model figure combines the revised architecture with the training-distribution chart previously in v1's appendix. The compression table and retrieval/runtime figure are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning against contemporary multimodal and video haystack benchmarks, contrasting their synthetic or out-of-distribution needles and shorter contexts with VHs's natural-image construction. It also discusses newer long-context architectures and adds references supporting modern baselines, pretraining sources, and benchmark-reliability arguments. Most earlier MIQA and retrieval-augmented-generation related work remains.

T1.justification: The retrieval formulation, minimal relevant-image subset, and Equation (1) are retained. Neither version provides substantive theoretical guarantees or proofs, and the revised architectural explanations do not introduce new mathematical results.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens the central benchmark evaluation: larger samples and explicit uncertainty improve assessability, while the detector control and needle-count oracle analysis better distinguish retrieval from cross-image reasoning failures. Broader contemporary comparisons and implementation documentation also improve usefulness. These gains are limited by important new problems, especially the RetVQA state-of-the-art claim despite the omitted, stronger MI-BART result, and unreconciled training-set counts. Overall, the benchmark evidence improves, but the revision does not establish a substantial overall quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the Visual Haystacks benchmark and MIRAGE framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite extensive revision and a changed title.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark evaluations and diagnostic experiments in Figures 2–4, Tables 1–2, and appendix Tables C.1–C.2, including results for the revised MIRAGE model.

before.justification: V1 reports original VHs evaluations, MIRAGE results on RetVQA and single-image benchmarks, positional-bias experiments, and compression and retrieval analyses.

title: Visual Haystacks: A Vision-Centric Needle-In-A-Haystack Benchmark

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and Section 7 retain the principal benchmark, scalability, and performance claims. However, the new Section 5 conclusion claims faster runtimes than CLIP. This strengthens the efficiency claim beyond v2 and conflicts with the retained Figure 6 and text stating that CLIP is faster.

C2.justification: v3 explains that some multi-needle questions can be answered using one suitable image, whereas others require all relevant images, qualifying their relative difficulty. Section 5 adds a token-compression explanation for selected single-image performance deficits and a fairness argument for single-model comparisons. Existing COCO scope, bias, and generalization limitations remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix A provides separate MIRAGE and VHs repository addresses, stated licenses, and LLaVA/POPE code provenance; v2 already advertised availability through the project page. Table 1 newly identifies the sources of single-image baseline scores. These are documentation additions, not evidence of changed training or newly available resources.

E1.justification: v3 adds MME and SEED-Bench evaluations in Table 1, modestly broadening conventional single-image QA coverage. The training datasets, VHs tasks, RetVQA, and previous single-image benchmarks remain. The new multi-needle breakdown analyzes existing question types rather than introducing another task.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds GPT-4o and Gemini v1.5 Pro to the reported POPE comparison, replacing their v2 dashes with 87.2 and 88.2. v3 identifies single-image baseline scores as externally sourced. The comparator sets in the retained VHs and compression experiments are unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix C.4 introduces category-conditioned evaluation: accuracy across haystack sizes is reported separately for ANY-Yes/ALL-No and ANY-No/ALL-Yes questions, alongside aggregate and single-needle results. The existing VHs sample-selection rules, zero-shot setting, model configurations, and training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Figure C.2 examines two GPT-4o/Gemini failure cases involving small or non-salient objects. Appendix C.4 and Figure C.3 investigate why multi-needle accuracy can exceed single-needle accuracy. The compression ablation is retained from v2 Table 2 as v3 Table C.2, not newly added.

E5.justification: Both versions describe bootstrapped averages with standard-deviation error bars. The uncertainty values in v2 Tables C.1–C.2 match v3 Tables C.3–C.4. No new run counts, seed disclosures, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are documented.

E6.justification: Table 1 newly reports MIRAGE scores of 1437.9 on MME and 59.0 on SEED, together with additional baseline entries. Figures C.2–C.3 add qualitative outcomes and question-category performance curves. Previously reported VHs, RetVQA, single-image QA, and compression-ablation values are retained.

M1.justification: Sections 4.1–4.2 retain the frozen CLIP encoder, 32-query Q-Former, relevance retriever, Llama-v3.1 backbone, losses, and two-stage training. The new description of MIRAGE as an end-to-end single-model architecture clarifies the existing procedure.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized rewrites in Sections 4–6, adds a results-summary paragraph and code-release appendix, and reorganizes appendix subsections. The compression discussion moves out of the main text. The overall narrative remains stable, while headers change from under review to ICLR 2025 publication.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains MME and SEED columns and changes row ordering. The compression table moves to Appendix C, and new Figures C.2–C.3 display failure cases and subgroup curves. Existing figures are retained, with limited resizing, caption edits, and appendix reflow.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds comparisons with CompBench, MANTIS, and MUIRBench, emphasizing VHs's scale and diagnostic focus, and adds an xT citation. MME and SEED-Bench references accompany the expanded evaluation. The established relationship to retrieval-based QA and long-context models remains largely intact.

T1.justification: The image-encoding and relevance formulation in Equation 1 is unchanged. No formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations are added. The ANY/ALL discussion provides a conceptual interpretation of empirical difficulty.

improvement.justification: Compared with v2's aggregate multi-needle results, v3's category breakdown gives a more informative account of retrieval and integration difficulty. Added benchmark results, baseline-source disclosure, and explicit code-access information also improve assessment and reproducibility. These are incremental gains. A countervailing defect is the new Section 5 runtime claim contradicting Figure 6; it limits, but does not outweigh, the additions' overall value.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Visual Haystacks benchmark and MIRAGE framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison. Rotated tables are readable, and relocated material can be matched.

after.justification: v3 retains those original empirical results and adds MIRAGE evaluations on MME and SEED-Bench, qualitative failure cases, and a multi-needle question-category analysis.

before.justification: v2 reports original VHs evaluations, MIRAGE benchmark results, retrieval/runtime comparisons, and compression ablations in Figures 2–6, Tables 1–2, and the appendices.

title: Visual Haystacks: A Vision-Centric Needle-In-A-Haystack Benchmark

C1.justification: v1 claims approximately GPT-4-Turbo-level long-context performance and that direct long-context use beats RAG on 32K tasks. v2 claims superiority over GPT-4-Turbo, Qwen2 and Llama3.1 on beyond-100K and short-context RAG benchmarks, and that sufficiently large retrieval sets outperform direct context on both 32K and 128K tasks. Public release of research resources also becomes an explicit contribution.

C2.justification: The practical interpretation of 32K retrieval changes from an accuracy sacrifice for efficiency to an accuracy advantage with sufficient retrieved text. v2 emphasizes robustness to chunk size rather than v1's preference for larger chunks, identifies passkey retrieval as an easier diagnostic, and newly attributes weak summarization to insufficient summarization SFT data.

D1.justification: v2 newly announces released model weights, training data and evaluation setup, and supplies a project access address, materially expanding documented reproducibility access beyond v1's recipe and source-dataset links. It also specifies the needle texts and passkey question. Core training hyperparameters remain unchanged; the external resources themselves were not inspected.

E1.justification: The training datasets and four InfiniteBench, six 32K and nine ChatRAG evaluation tasks remain unchanged. Synthetic coverage expands from v1's single generically described needle test to separately reported natural-language fact and numeric-passkey scenarios in v2 Figures 1 and 3; v1 does not specify its exact needle.

E2.justification: v2 adds Llama3.1-8B-Instruct and Llama3.1-70B-Instruct across all three benchmark groups and as needle/passkey comparators. Kimi-Chat disappears from the InfiniteBench comparison. GPT-4-1106 preview loses its Table 2 row, although its aggregate result remains quoted in Section 5.2.

E3.justification: v2 adds 8B model configurations and changes the selected ChatQA-2 retrieval setting for the beyond-100K comparison from top-5 to top-30 chunks (v1 Table 6 versus v2 Table 5). Main benchmark metrics, dataset exclusions and default top-5 retrieval with 1200-token chunks remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds a controlled comparison of natural-language needle and numeric-passkey difficulty across ChatQA 2 and Llama3.1. Chunk-size and retrieval-budget ablations already existed in v1 Tables 1 and 5; v2 revises their presentation and evidence in Figure 2, omitting the previous 32K top-30 endpoint.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The additional heatmaps show performance across test conditions, not statistical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: In Tables 2-4, reported ChatQA-2-70B averages change from 34.11 to 41.04 on InfiniteBench, 47.37 to 48.15 on 32K tasks, and 54.81 to 56.30 on ChatRAG. Qwen2's InfiniteBench average changes from 34.88 to 39.77. v2 adds 8B/Llama3.1 results and reverses the reported 32K RAG-versus-full-context trend. The beyond-100K RAG comparison also changes retrieval budgets, so its higher score is not a same-setting gain.

M1.justification: The documented method retains the same context-extension recipe, RoPE adjustment, three-stage instruction tuning, synthetic NarrativeQA construction and E5-mistral retrieval. The added 8B configuration does not introduce a different algorithm or training procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract and contribution statements are rewritten, three existing method sections become subsections of Method, and RAG-versus-long-context analysis becomes a standalone section. Context-length terminology and author text also change. Most underlying technical exposition remains closely matched.

P2.justification: v2 adds an illustrated overview table, replaces the earlier retrieval-ablation tables with Figure 2, expands the main needle figure into four panels, and adds four appendix passkey panels. Benchmark tables are expanded and regrouped, alongside a changed document template. These substantially alter the paper's visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 discusses concurrent Llama3.1 models and positions ChatQA 2's released training data and reproduction recipe against Qwen2/Llama3.1's open-weight availability. The broader related-work survey and bibliography are substantially retained.

T1.justification: Neither version presents new formal theory or proofs. The descriptive RoPE discussion and method reasoning are retained without substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: v2 makes the evaluation more informative through Llama3.1 comparisons, 8B results and explicit fact-versus-passkey diagnostics, while newly documenting resource access. The benefit is limited by unreconciled evidence: Figure 2 places the full-context reference near 47.9 whereas Table 3 reports 48.15, and substantial score revisions lack corresponding explanations in the largely unchanged training recipe. The added comparisons improve usefulness, but the higher reported scores alone do not establish stronger paper quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ChatQA 2 and provide readable methods, experiments, tables and figures. All pages were inspected, including v2's new Appendix A; v1 ends with references and has no appendix. The material supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original ChatQA-2-70B and 8B evaluations, retrieval analyses and comparative needle/passkey experiments, including Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 reports original ChatQA-2-70B benchmark results, retrieval ablations and a Needle in a Haystack evaluation.

title: ChatQA 2: Bridging the Gap to Proprietary LLMs in Long Context and RAG Capabilities

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: a reproducible 128K ChatQA 2 recipe, competitive ultra-long and short-context RAG performance, and benefits from retrieving sufficient context. New experiments support or qualify these claims without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: v3 explains task-dependent retriever and training-stage trade-offs and attributes the new model's lower MT-Bench score to missing preference alignment. It narrows the earlier blanket statement that RAG underperforms full context, describes the 32K RAG advantage as marginal, and removes the inference that the retained 100K results demonstrate difficulty reasoning over long contexts.

D1.justification: Appendix C/Table 10 newly documents sample counts and epochs for 15 Stage 2 datasets, substantially expanding training transparency. Section 3.2 adds NarrativeQA provenance, sentence-preserving summary-insertion details, and a dataset link. New experiments disclose the 2B-token budget and 1.6M-example data size, while v2's 128K first-stage data-size statement is removed. These disclosures do not establish changes to the original training.

E1.justification: Table 8 extends evaluation beyond long-context understanding and RAG to coding, general knowledge, conversational quality, and mathematics through HumanEval, MMLU, MT-Bench, and GSM8K. Appendix A adds InfiniteBench retrieval evaluations, including key-value retrieval. Passkey retrieval was already tested in v2; newly listed Stage 2 training datasets are disclosures rather than established coverage changes.

E2.justification: Tables 1–5 retain their comparator sets. v3 adds evaluated NV-emb-v2, all-in-one-stage training, and EOS/BOS separator alternatives in Table 6, Table 7, and Figure 4. Section 5.2 also drops the prose-only GPT4-1106 preview comparison, which was absent from Table 2 in both versions.

E3.justification: v3 adds distinct experimental designs: single-stage training of the 8B base using blended instruction data, a model trained with a new 1.6M-example SFT dataset, and separator comparisons after 2B training tokens. Table 8 specifies zero-shot GSM8K evaluation. These supplement the unchanged original benchmark protocols and default top-5, 1200-token retrieval setting.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained chunk-size/top-k analysis, Section 5.5 tests retriever sensitivity, three-stage versus single-stage training, and expanded SFT data. Appendix B adds direct NIAH evidence comparing document separators, supporting a preference asserted without a corresponding controlled figure in v2. These substantially expand investigation of the recipe's design choices.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. New results retain point-estimate reporting. Appendix C's epoch counts describe training exposure, not repeated experimental trials.

E6.justification: Tables 1–5 and the original plots retain their results, but Tables 6–9 and Figure 4 add substantial findings. Table 7 reports short-context scores of 52.50 versus 48.55 for three-stage versus single-stage training; Table 9 reports key-value retrieval scores of 91 versus 89 for ChatQA-2-70B and GPT-4-Turbo. Table 8 concerns a differently trained model, not revised original scores. The prose-only GPT4-1106 preview score of 28.23 is removed.

M1.justification: The proposed context-extension procedure, three-stage instruction tuning, and E5-mistral RAG pipeline remain unchanged. Expanded NarrativeQA construction and retrieval explanations do not establish a changed algorithm. Alternative retrievers, training stages, and separators are evaluated as controls; the larger SFT dataset changes an experimental training setting.

P1.justification: v3 makes targeted abstract and introduction edits, expands the retrieval and NarrativeQA explanations, and adds Section 5.5 and Appendices B–C within the retained narrative structure. Conference headers are added. Some cross-references become incorrect, including the passkey reference to Figure 4 and the training comparison reference to Table 10.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 6–10 and the two-panel separator heatmap in Figure 4, substantially expanding the displayed evidence. Existing tables are repacked and relocated, and Figure 2 is resized without changing its findings. New caption errors include Table 8 naming a 70B model despite its 8B column heading and Table 10 describing a training comparison instead of dataset statistics.

R1.justification: v3 adds explicit references for NarrativeQA, SCROLLS, LongBench, and The Llama 3 Herd of Models, while removing the RULER reference and its associated motivation sentence. The overall positioning relative to long-context LLMs, ChatQA, and RAG remains stable.

T1.justification: Neither version supplies formal theoretical results or proofs. Added descriptions of embedding retrieval and data construction introduce no substantive mathematical definitions, assumptions, or derivations.

improvement.justification: The new retriever, training-stage, and separator ablations provide empirical checks of choices asserted in v2, while Appendix C improves training transparency and broader evaluations reveal capability trade-offs. These are useful gains, but the new 1.6M-example dataset remains underspecified and new model-size, caption, and cross-reference inconsistencies hinder interpretation. The evidence supports a limited overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ChatQA 2, with matching methods and identifiable corresponding experiments. All main-text and appendix material is readable. Local caption and cross-reference inconsistencies in v3 do not prevent a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds retriever and training ablations, broader capability evaluations, and separator experiments in Section 5.5 and the appendices.

before.justification: v2 reports original ChatQA 2 benchmark evaluations, needle/passkey retrieval tests, and retrieval chunk-size analyses in Tables 1–5 and Figures 1–3.

title: ChatQA 2: Bridging the Gap to Proprietary LLMs in Long Context and RAG Capabilities

C1.justification: v2 adds a headline claim that its quantitative survey reveals a growing capability gap in interpretability research. It also presents the intervention-graph architecture as an explicit contribution centered on separating experiments from deployment and improving reproducibility, alongside NNsight and NDIF. v1 primarily presents the library and service; their original access and flexibility claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of the research gap and remote-service costs, and explicitly limits current co-tenancy to sequential execution in its appendices. v1's graph-optimization and high-level-abstraction limitation discussions disappear, while the closed-model restriction remains. Section 4 also introduces a runtime-benefit claim for larger models that is not supported by Table 2's request latencies.

D1.justification: Appendices B–D substantially expand documentation of Ray routing, model sharding, distributed tensor handling, memory management, protocols and benchmark implementation. Additional examples cover LoRA training, gradient manipulation and remote probing; Appendix A documents survey curation. Conversely, v1's NNsight 0.2 syntax note and specific NDIF early-access eligibility/application instructions are omitted.

E1.justification: v2 adds a research-usage analysis covering 184 papers and evaluates standard remote inference, remote interventions and concurrent-user workloads. Attribution-patching timing evaluation disappears, although example code remains. IOI is newly identified as benchmark data; v1's unnamed 32-example batch does not establish whether the underlying dataset changed.

E2.justification: Petals becomes an evaluated comparator in Figure 6c, having appeared only in related work in v1. v2 also introduces direct HPC-versus-NDIF comparisons. The local baukit, pyvene and TransformerLens comparison remains, with TransformerLens now participating in the Gemma comparison where v1 reported missing results.

E3.justification: Table 1 changes from eight A100 GPUs with CUDA 12.4 to four H100 GPUs with CUDA 12.3, and replaces Llama3-70B with Llama-3.1-8B; both versions specify 32-example batches. New protocols measure setup time, sweep OPT model sizes, compare private Petals/NDIF deployments, and test concurrent requests over 30-second windows. The survey adds paper-selection and MMLU-imputation procedures.

E4.justification: v2 adds workload stress testing with 1–100 concurrent users in Appendix D.2, examining response-time growth and variability. Figure 6 analyzes setup and communication costs across OPT sizes. Appendix A additionally compares research-model and released-model size distributions. These analyses extend substantially beyond v1's library runtime comparison.

E5.justification: v1 already reports values with ± notation but provides no sample count or interval definition. v2 Figure 6 specifies n=128 and discusses 95% confidence intervals; Figure 10 reports medians, quartiles and extrema. These improve statistical documentation without establishing increased repetitions of the earlier experiments.

E6.justification: Table 1 contains replacement timings under changed hardware/model settings: for example, NNsight's Gemma activation-patching time changes from 0.337 to 0.227 seconds. Attribution timings disappear, while setup, remote-service, survey and load-testing results are added. v2 Table 2 reports OPT-66B HPC/NDIF setup times of 23.697/0.423 seconds but request times of 1.889/2.739 seconds, distinguishing setup savings from request latency.

M1.justification: The core tracing, intervention graphs, Envoy/Proxy access and sessions remain. The reported serving procedure changes: v1 Section 3 says multiple users can be batched, whereas v2 Appendices B.2/D.2 specify queued execution with one forward pass per user and defer shared batching to future work. The PDFs do not establish whether implementation changed or the earlier description was corrected.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and the tutorial-oriented main text is reorganized around a survey, formal framework, evaluation and discussion. Much implementation material moves into Appendix B, with expanded examples in Appendix C. Separate ecosystem and limitations sections disappear, and ethics and reproducibility statements are added.

P2.justification: v2 adds survey plots, formal graph and infrastructure diagrams, a side-by-side code comparison, benchmark plots, a load-testing plot and three appendix tables. Table 1 replaces its attribution-patching block with setup times. The remote-pipeline diagram is substantially expanded, while v1's Envoy diagram is retained as v2 Figure 9.

R1.justification: The main positioning against Garçon, Petals and local intervention libraries remains. v2 extends it with S-LoRA, dLoRA and Punica, distinguishing their adapter-serving scope from general interventions, and adds sources supporting the survey and distributed implementation. Some background citations disappear. Publication updates to existing works such as Petals do not constitute new related work.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.1 adds formal computation/intervention-graph definitions, getter/setter edges and an acyclicity condition. Appendix E supplies a constructive equivalence argument between multiple-output and single-output apply nodes. v1 describes graph implementation without these mathematical definitions or derivations.

improvement.justification: Explicit repository pointers, a fuller architecture diagram in the main text, and clearer access and remote-training explanations make v4 easier to understand and use. title: NNsight and NDIF: Democratizing Access to Open-Weight Foundation Model Internals

D1.justification: V2 adds selected hyperparameters in Table 9, baseline implementation and checkpoint links in Appendix A, explicit identification of Mazes training maps, and detailed hardware and sampling settings in Appendix L. E5.justification: Table 3 retains the same evaluation seed counts. T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, including the evaluation metrics in Equations 1–9, are unchanged. No theoretical assumptions, derivations, or proofs are added or revised.

before.justification: v2 reports original MAPF and lifelong MAPF benchmark evaluations, alongside environment-speed and scalability experiments in Appendix L.

title: POGEMA: A Benchmark Platform for Cooperative Multi-Agent Pathfinding

C1.justification: v1's broad claim that smaller models memorize while larger models generalize becomes a task-dependent account: factual QA relies more on memorization, while translation and harder MMLU tasks rely more on generalization. Emergence and instruction-tuning contributions are dropped. Explaining LLM probabilities better than ∞-gram becomes a central claim.

C2.justification: v2 introduces explanations involving transferable translation skills, rare-knowledge retrieval and reasoning complexity, and interprets checkpoint influence as complementary causal evidence. These substantially revise v1's emergence and instruction-tuning interpretations. Appendix A additionally identifies checkpoint availability as a constraint, while retaining the limitations concerning older models and pair-filtering quality.

D1.justification: v2 supplies previously missing cosine-filter thresholds, explains the division between WIMBD and ∞-gram searches and zero-probability handling, and lists MMLU task groups. It promises code upon acceptance rather than documenting an available release. Hardware and dataset-access disclosures are largely retained, and the checkpoint schedule remains unspecified.

E1.justification: v1 analyzes Pythia/Pile and OLMo/Dolma and reports searching Tulu; v2's substantive corpus analyses focus on Pythia/Pile, although Tulu's license entry remains. WMT, TriviaQA and MMLU are retained. Appendix Figure 11 adds auxiliary pair-detection evaluations using FLAN-family texts spanning NLI, summarization, sentiment and other tasks, without identifying exact constituent datasets.

E2.justification: v2 introduces an evaluated ∞-gram language-model comparator for the central distributional analysis, absent from v1. The output-only n-gram control remains in the influence analysis. Appendix E additionally reports unsuccessful LLM-based and NER-based alternatives to semantic pair identification, although those alternatives are incompletely specified.

Distributional evaluation changes from R² to Spearman correlation; the redesigned influence experiment specifies checkpoint aggregation and 50 retrieved documents per example.

E4.justification: v2 adds knowledge-versus-reasoning MMLU analyses, comparisons across n-gram lengths, a contamination check using overlaps longer than 14 tokens, unsuccessful pair-detection alternatives, and aggregate translation-alignment histograms. The OLMo instruction-tuning analysis disappears. Earlier illustrative examples and the WMT novel-pair chart are retained rather than newly introduced.

Appendix Figures 10–11 add error bars. v1 provides R² fits and some fit annotations but no comparable significance-reporting scheme. v2 does not explain the appendix error bars or provide repeated-run and seed counts.

E6.justification: Central results are replaced under changed estimators: v1's R² curves and OLMo comparisons of 0.42 versus 0.51 give way to task-dependent Spearman correlations and checkpoint-influence results. v2 also adds MMLU accuracy curves and appendix findings. WMT and TriviaQA performance curves and WMT novelty counts are retained; the new correlations should not be interpreted as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: v2 replaces v1's sequence-level count-product approximation and regression analysis with conditional pair probabilities and Spearman correlations against reference-output probabilities. It also replaces count-weighted gradient cosine similarity with gradient dot products accumulated across checkpoints. These change the analytical procedures beyond renaming the existing pair table.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition and conclusions are extensively rewritten around distributional memorization and task-gram models. Influence analysis moves after the distributional results, related work moves from the appendix into the main text, and task-specific interpretive subsections reorganize the narrative. These exceed changes caused solely by added experiments.

The retained novelty chart joins the new four-panel Figure 3, while the separate WMT performance-versus-size panel disappears. Example tables are reformatted, and appendix Figures 9–12 add new displays.

These are substantive mathematical revisions, although neither version supplies a theorem-and-proof development.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central analysis through explicit conditional definitions, an evaluated ∞-gram comparator, significance reporting and knowledge-versus-reasoning analyses. These support a more differentiated account than v1's broad scaling conclusions. Loss of OLMo/Dolma coverage reduces generality, and reporting defects remain: Section 5 states five-gram TriviaQA correlation exceeds 0.35 although Figure 3 stays below 0.25, and appendix error bars are undefined. Nevertheless, the methodological clarification and stronger comparative evidence constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same investigation of LLM capabilities through task-relevant pretraining n-grams. Their text, equations, figures and appendices are readable, allowing retained material to be matched despite substantial methodological and structural revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original task evaluations, distributional correlations and training-influence analyses in Sections 4–6, plus pair-identification and generation analyses in the appendices.

E6.justification: v3 adds GSM8K/OLMo performance and ranking-distance results, threshold-dependent correlations, and prompt-comparison outcomes, while removing the pair-detection diagnostics. improvement.justification: GSM8K and OLMo/Dolma extend support for the reasoning claims beyond the original tasks and model family, while the threshold ablation tests an important methodological choice. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same task-gram and distributional-memorization study. Their main text, equations, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching material moved between sections.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds GSM8K, OLMo/Dolma analyses, threshold-sensitivity results, and prompt-optimization experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original Pythia/Pile experiments on WMT, TriviaQA, and MMLU, including memorization correlations, training-influence estimates, and appendix analyses.

title: Generalization v.s. Memorization: Tracing Language Models’ Capabilities Back to Pretraining Data

C2.justification: The explanations involving translation transfer, factual recall, rare knowledge, reasoning, and training influence remain substantively unchanged. Appendix A retains the same limitations concerning models, corpus search, and n-gram filtering.
