title: Generalization v.s. Memorization: Tracing Language Models’ Capabilities Back to Pretraining Data

C1.justification: v1 claims demonstrated 400K context extension and leaves faster execution and 1M scaling to future work. v2 claims achieved million-token scaling, a 128-fold extension to 4M, and efficient execution without additional overhead. It also explicitly conditions infinite context on sufficient memory. The 4M headline attribution to LLaMA3.2 conflicts with Section 3.3 and Figure 4, which assign that result to Qwen2-1B.

C2.justification: v2 adds a substantive applicability limitation: poor performance on synthetic key-value retrieval, despite success on natural-context tasks. Section 4.3 and Appendix B propose disrupted cache coherence and positional ambiguity as explanations. Section 4.1 also explains semantic-fragmentation, local-context and selection-budget tradeoffs. These substantially qualify v1's predominantly favorable interpretation of position-agnostic selection.

D1.justification: Beyond revised cache settings, v2 documents the Triton operator-fusion implementation and profiling with real inference Q/K inputs on an A800-80GB GPU, a 48-core CPU and 256GB RAM. Appendix B.1 describes extracting Q/K states before and after positional embedding, reshaping them and applying t-SNE. These add implementation and analysis procedures absent from v1's evaluation settings and future optimization plan.

E1.justification: v2 adds InfiniteBench's English multiple-choice, question-answering and summarization tasks, RULER synthetic retrieval evaluations, and PG19 examples for cache analysis in Appendix B. These materially expand the evaluated data and input types beyond the retained LongBench, L-Eval and needle-retrieval coverage.

E2.justification: InfLLM changes from a cited method in v1 to an evaluated comparator on InfiniteBench and RULER in v2 Tables 1 and 3. v2 also compares the fused kernel against its PyTorch implementation. Full-attention and StreamingLLM comparisons remain, while v1's paired Dynamic NTK multi-needle comparison is no longer reported in the corresponding v2 retrieval experiment.

E3.justification: v1 uses model-dependent cache budgets; v2 standardizes local length to 4096 and k' to 127, replacing LLaMA3's k'=96 and most other models' local length 8192/k'=256. The benchmark roster adds LLaMA3.1/3.2 and 70B/72B models while dropping LLaMA2 and InternLM2 variants. Main needle tests change from four to eight A100s and extend their length ranges. New protocols include 32K/64K/128K InfiniteBench tests, 8K/16K RULER tests and controlled attention-budget ablations.

E4.justification: v1's correct/wrong attention-distribution case study is retained as v2 Figure 8. v2 additionally tests chunk size, span size, top-k and local-window sensitivity in Table 2, examines runtime and memory scaling, and investigates synthetic-retrieval failures through cache visualizations. Appendix B expands these diagnostics across natural and synthetic texts, layers, positional encodings and models.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for its experimental results. The added tables and efficiency plots continue reporting point estimates without statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: Retained results are revised: LLaMA3's LongBench average changes from 35.07 for LongCache in v1 Table 2 to 35.03 for ReAttention in v2 Table 4, under changed cache settings. v2 adds extensive InfiniteBench, efficiency, ablation and longer-retrieval measurements. New negative findings include ReAttention's RULER MultiKey3 scores of 78.00 at 8K and 15.00 at 16K in Table 3. These are revised or newly reported outcomes, not evidence of a uniform same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: The selection, voting, neighboring-span extraction and positional-reassignment procedure in Sections 2.1–2.2 remains unchanged. However, v2 implements a fused Triton kernel for attention-score computation and top-k selection, replacing separate PyTorch operations and intermediate-memory transfers; v1 leaves GPU optimization as future work. This is a limited execution adaptation rather than a new selection algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and contribution statements are substantially rewritten around three conditions for infinite context and an attention-before-attention explanation. The discussion becomes three subsections, detailed benchmark reporting moves into Appendix A, and Appendix B introduces a separate diagnostic narrative. The method name, title, author information and citation style also change.

P2.justification: v1's two-part cache-operation diagram is replaced by a higher-level architecture diagram. Its separate benchmark tables become regrouped results in v2 Appendix Table 4 with main-text summary plots. v2 adds efficiency charts, ablation and RULER tables, and multiple t-SNE figures, while redesigning the retrieval panels. The existing attention maps are retained and relocated from Figure 4 to Figure 8.

R1.justification: The main positioning against full-attention extrapolation and sparse retrieval methods remains. v2 sharpens its distinctions from InfLLM and LongHeads, adds RetrievalAttention and references supporting the new evaluations and analyses, and removes the xPos/parallel-context-window/NBCE discussion. This refines the existing research positioning rather than replacing it.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(3) retain the same mathematical operations, with only notation clarification. v2's three conditions for infinite context and its manifold-based discussion are conceptual arguments and empirical interpretations; they introduce no formal definitions, theorems, proofs or derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1: efficiency was previously future work, the closely related InfLLM lacked direct comparison, and hyperparameter sensitivity and synthetic-retrieval failures were unexplored. Measured efficiency, controlled ablations, additional comparisons and explicit failure analysis substantially strengthen practical validation and clarify applicability. The inconsistent attribution of the 4M result and the unproven causal interpretation of t-SNE plots weaken specific claims, but the broader evidential gains support a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same cache-selection approach, renamed from LongCache to ReAttention. Their text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. All 11 pages of v1 and 18 pages of v2 were inspected, including v2's Appendices A–B; v1 has no appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark and retrieval results, efficiency measurements, hyperparameter ablations, RULER experiments and appendix cache-visualization analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original LongBench, L-Eval, single- and multi-needle retrieval experiments, together with attention-distribution case studies.

title: ReAttention: Training-Free Infinite Context with Finite Attention Scope

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the claims of training-free unbounded context under sufficient memory, performance comparable to full attention, retrieval over millions of tokens, and efficient Triton implementation. Added evidence does not materially redefine these claims.

C2.justification: Appendix C newly distinguishes latency at identical batch sizes from throughput under memory-capacity constraints and interprets larger feasible batches as an efficiency benefit. Existing explanations of position-agnostic retrieval and limitations on synthetic, incoherent text remain unchanged.

D1.justification: V3 adds prefilling and decoding pseudocode, a project-code access pointer in the abstract, and batch-size/generation-length details for efficiency evaluation. This substantially expands implementation documentation. However, Algorithm 1 resets the cache inside the chunk loop, and both algorithms use global/local slices inconsistent with Section 2, limiting their reproducibility value.

E1.justification: Both versions use LongBench, L-Eval, InfiniteBench, single/multiple-needle retrieval, RULER, and the same natural-text cache-analysis examples. New task-category breakdowns and efficiency measurements do not establish additional dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: V3 adds InfLLM to LongBench comparisons for three LLaMA models in Table 1 and StreamingLLM to their InfiniteBench comparisons in Table 2. DynamicNTK remains in the stated protocol despite losing its separate table label. Other comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: Appendix C adds throughput evaluation with 1024 generated tokens and batch sizes selected to utilize available GPU memory across 32K–256K contexts. V3 also omits the native-8K LongBench/L-Eval configuration reported in v2. The retained benchmark truncation, NTK scaling factor, and ReAttention hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix C extends efficiency analysis by examining whether memory savings support larger batches and higher throughput. Existing hyperparameter ablations, attention case studies, RULER failure analysis, and t-SNE analyses are retained, including the material moved from Appendix B to E.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random-seed protocols, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates for the evaluated results.

E6.justification: V3 substantially expands reported results through task-category LongBench scores, added comparator scores, and throughput measurements, while matched existing scores remain unchanged. Table 2 newly shows StreamingLLM averaging 15.71 versus ReAttention's 15.36 for LLaMA3.2, qualifying its superiority caption. Table 7 reports 43.380 versus 40.595 tokens/s at 32K using batches 8 and 2, respectively, rather than demonstrating a same-batch speedup. V2's native-8K benchmark row is removed, and language-group summaries are replaced by task-category summaries.

M1.justification: Sections 2.1–2.2 retain position-agnostic top-k selection, voting, neighboring-span extraction, global/local cache retention, and positional embedding after selection. Appendix A newly documents prefilling and decoding; its inconsistencies do not establish an actual algorithm redesign.

P1.justification: V3 makes limited prose refinements, updates author affiliations and publication headers, adds acknowledgements, and reorganizes the appendices around pseudocode, effectiveness, efficiency, related work, and cache analysis. The main section sequence and most explanatory text remain intact.

P2.justification: Benchmark presentation is substantially reorganized: v2's six-panel overview disappears, v3 adds a main-text LongBench table, and the detailed benchmark table replaces language columns with task categories. InfiniteBench gains comparator rows, and two algorithm blocks plus TTFT/throughput tables are added. Other analytical figures are largely retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: New Appendix D substantially expands positioning within token eviction and cache compression, covering DCP, Scissorhands, SnapKV, DuoAttention, PyramidKV, PyramidInfer, Gemfilter, LongGen, VATP, and InfiniPot. It explicitly relates ReAttention's context extrapolation to these cache-selection approaches; these citations are not additional evaluated baselines.

T1.justification: Equations 1–3 and the three motivating conditions remain unchanged. Neither the added pseudocode nor the expanded discussion introduces a new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: Additional comparators, task-level results, throughput evidence, code-access information, and related-work discussion strengthen the paper's assessment and context. However, the new pseudocode contradicts the retained cache procedure, and Table 5 duplicates the LLaMA3.2-3B label on the block matching v2's 70B results. These newly introduced reproducibility and attribution problems make the net quality benefit uncertain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReAttention work and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. V2 Appendices A and B correspond to v3 Appendices B and E, allowing retained material to be distinguished from additions.

after.justification: V3 retains these original empirical results and adds comparator results and throughput measurements.

before.justification: V2 reports original benchmark evaluations, needle-retrieval experiments, efficiency measurements, hyperparameter ablations, and cache visualizations.

title: ReAttention: Training-Free Infinite Context with Finite Attention Scope

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about foundation-model performance, downstream compute trade-offs, and the benefits of combining foundation models with object-centric representations.

C2.justification: Section 4.1 adds a qualification to the usefulness of several models on CLEVR and CLEVRTex: their performance barely exceeds prediction from questions alone. Existing limitations concerning synthetic data and differing foundation-model pretraining remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendices B–D retain the same implementation details, hyperparameters, preprocessing instructions, and resource information. No dedicated architecture or training details are added for the revised synthetic baseline.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate CLEVR6, CLEVRTex, Multi-dSprites, and the same filtered VQA-v2 subset. VQA and object-property prediction task coverage is unchanged.

E2.justification: Section 3.2 and Figures 2 and 15 replace the synthetic datasets' majority-class baseline with a trained question-only predictor. VQA-v2 already used a question-only baseline in v1. The representation-model comparator set is unchanged.

E3.justification: Synthetic evaluations now control for prediction from question text through a learned question-only model, rather than constant majority-class prediction. Splits, preprocessing, metrics, and the retained models' training budgets and size configurations are unchanged.

E4.justification: The question-only comparison extends the assessment of performance without visual input to the synthetic datasets. Existing property-prediction correlations, upstream-metric analyses, model-size and data-size sweeps, question-category analyses, and extended VAE training experiments remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the same seed-count disclosures, 95% confidence-interval reporting, and correlation significance practices. No increase in repeated runs or new uncertainty-estimation procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Figure 15 replaces the 26.8% majority-class baseline at every Multi-dSprites size with question-only accuracies of 55.4%, 56.1%, 55.9%, and 57.2% for 40k, 80k, 160k, and 320k images, respectively. Figure 2 also updates synthetic baseline bars. These are different comparators, not same-model performance gains; representation-model results in Tables 7–13 and the VQA-v2 results are unchanged.

M1.justification: The representation-learning framework, text encoder, representation formatting, downstream transformer, and training objectives are unchanged. The revision concerns a comparison baseline rather than the study's main method.

P1.justification: There are localized revisions to the baseline description, synthetic-results discussion, real-world-results paragraph, and acknowledgments. The section structure and overall narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: Local spacing and text wrapping change around the results discussion, and the expanded bibliography reflows. All figure and table structures are retained; the updated baseline bars do not introduce new chart designs.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds citations to Dittadi and Winther's LAVAE and Daniel and Tamar's work on deep latent particles, expanding the bibliography from 96 to 98 references. The research positioning otherwise remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation of representations and downstream prediction is unchanged. Neither version adds or revises theoretical propositions, proofs, or formal assumptions.

improvement.justification: Replacing majority-class prediction with question-only baselines makes the synthetic comparisons more informative about the contribution of visual representations. Section 4.1 appropriately acknowledges that several models barely outperform text alone. This strengthens the evaluation modestly, while the main results remain unchanged and baseline-specific implementation details are not expanded.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same empirical study. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, and Appendices A–E are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and reports revised synthetic-dataset baseline results in Figures 2 and 15.

before.justification: v1 reports original VQA and object-property prediction experiments, including model comparisons and supplementary analyses in Appendix E.

title: Exploring the Effectiveness of Object-Centric Representations in Visual Question Answering: Comparative Insights with Foundation Models

C1.justification: The claimed empirical scope narrows from over 800 models in the abstract and 852 in the introduction to over 600 and 640. The central contributions concerning foundation-model trade-offs, object-centric representations and their combination remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly discusses DINOSAURv2's CLEVR shortfall and tentatively attributes it to hyperparameter sensitivity. It extends the representation-explicitness interpretation to Multi-dSprites and qualifies the property-prediction correlation as holding for most properties. The earlier explanation of Slot Attention's T-20 decline disappears.

D1.justification: Table 5 and Appendix A.1 revise DINOSAURv2's dataset-specific training and decoder settings. The previously stated VQA-v2 learning rate for T-20 is removed. A new reproducibility statement directs readers to implementation, dataset and metric details, without documenting a new code or data release.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate CLEVR6, CLEVRTex, Multi-dSprites and the same filtered VQA-v2 task. Property prediction, question categories and represented data domains are retained.

E2.justification: The same 15 upstream representation methods and question-only baseline are retained, with the same dataset-specific comparator exclusions. Removing a downstream depth configuration changes the experimental settings, not the comparator methods.

E3.justification: The systematic downstream depth grid changes from 2/5/15/20 layers to 2/5/15, with the stated model count falling from 852 to 640. Table 5 changes DINOSAURv2 training on CLEVR and Multi-dSprites from 500k to 250k steps and decoder hidden width from 512 to 1024. These are explicit setting revisions; the PDFs do not establish whether they reflect reruns or corrections. The separate T-20 comparison in Figure 8 remains.

E4.justification: Figures 3 and 14 lose the T-20 endpoint, removing the evidence and discussion of performance saturation beyond T-15 and Slot Attention's CLEVR deterioration. v3 additionally reports qualitative DINOSAURv2 hyperparameter sensitivity, without a quantified sweep. The other supplementary analysis questions remain.

E5.justification: Both versions retain three-seed reporting for applicable models, one seed for foundation models, 95% confidence intervals and the same correlation-significance reporting practices. Revised numerical correlations and error bars do not introduce a new statistical procedure.

E6.justification: Revisions concentrate on DINOSAURv2 and derived analyses. Its reported T-15 accuracy changes from 87.0% to 94.3% on CLEVR and from 92.0% to 94.4% on Multi-dSprites-320k, now slightly exceeding DINOv2's unchanged 94.2% there (Tables 7 and 12). These accompany changed settings, not demonstrated same-setting gains. Figures 7/16 revise error reductions and identify CLIP rather than STEVE as the largest-gain case; question-category correlations also change. CLEVRTex and VQA-v2 table results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The representation extraction, T5 embeddings, representation conversion, transformer classifier and training objectives remain unchanged. DINOSAURv2 retains the same construction; its decoder-width adjustment is a model-size setting covered under E3.

P1.justification: There are localized rewrites of the motivation, limitations and results discussion, plus terminology and typo corrections. The former Broader Impact appendix moves to an Ethics Statement, a Reproducibility Statement is added, and appendices B–E become A–D. The main narrative structure remains intact.

P2.justification: Figures 3 and 14 change their axes and displayed depth configurations, Table 5 expands its dataset columns, and Figure 16 moves to the following page. Figure sizing, legends and surrounding layout receive limited adjustments. The same 27 figures and 13 tables are retained.

R1.justification: The bibliography and related-work section retain the same works. Section 4.1 adds a limited positioning link by explicitly describing CNN/MultiCNN underperformance as consistent with Yoon et al. [32]; there is no broader novelty or literature revision.

T1.justification: The mathematical specification of representations, downstream classification and property prediction is retained. Neither version adds or removes formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or substantive derivations.

improvement.justification: v3 improves CLIP's error-reduction reporting: Figure 7 now shows roughly 49%, consistent with Tables 9 and 12, and adds useful sensitivity qualifications. However, it removes the scaling endpoint exposing Slot Attention's deterioration and leaves inconsistent DINOSAURv2 reporting: Table 7 gives 94.3% on CLEVR while unchanged Figure 11 retains scores around 87%. Tables 9–11 also revise overall scores without changing category scores. These benefits and unresolved empirical inconsistencies prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both complete, readable 34-page PDFs describe the same study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison, including matching the renumbered appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical evaluations and reports revised results in Section 4 and Appendix D, including Tables 7–13.

before.justification: v2 reports original VQA experiments, property-prediction evaluations and scaling analyses in Section 4 and Appendix E, including Tables 7–13.

title: Exploring the Effectiveness of Object-Centric Representations in Visual Question Answering: Comparative Insights with Foundation Models

C1.justification: The stated empirical contribution expands from 640 downstream models on three synthetic and one real-world dataset to 684 models on three synthetic and two real-world datasets. The central claims about foundation-model competitiveness, object-centric computational advantages, and weak global VAE representations remain.

C2.justification: v4 qualifies cross-category consistency with the GQA exception and proposes greater reliance on linguistic cues as an explanation for Logical and Compare questions (Section 4.2). Section 3.6 removes v3's discussion of independent synthetic object properties and its explicit disclaimer about optimizing VQA performance, while retaining the unequal-pretraining caveat.

D1.justification: Appendices A–B document GQA training schedules, splits, seven slots, preprocessing, and reuse of VQA-v2 architecture settings. Acknowledgments add JUPITER/JUWELS computing resources, while the A100 footnote drops the 40GB memory specification. Most existing implementation and reproducibility information is retained.

E1.justification: v4 adds balanced GQA while retaining all four earlier datasets. Its five question categories and 1,834 answers substantially broaden real-world reasoning coverage beyond v3's VQA-v2 subset restricted to yes/no and numerical answers (Section 3.3; Appendix B; Table 6).

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the retained experiments. The new GQA evaluation reuses the six foundation models, ResNet SA, STEVE, DINOSAURv2, and question-only baseline already evaluated on VQA-v2; no new comparison method is introduced.

E3.justification: The added GQA experiment introduces balanced train/testdev evaluation, its own splits, and downstream training for 900k steps with batch size 32 and learning rate 0.0001 (Appendices A.3 and B; Table 6). Existing synthetic and VQA-v2 protocols and metrics are retained.

E4.justification: v4 extends the downstream-capacity and computational-cost analyses to GQA and adds GQA question-category difficulty and rank-correlation analyses (Figures 4, 14, 17, and 28). These extend existing analytical questions; the property-prediction, upstream-metric, training-size, and VAE investigations remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report three seeds and 95% confidence intervals where available, with one seed for foundation models, and retain the same STEVE seed-selection disclosure. GQA follows these practices. Some plotted interval values change, but no revised statistical procedure or increased run count is reported.

E6.justification: v4 adds a substantial GQA result suite, including T-15 accuracies of 51.3% for DINOv2 and 51.1% for DINOSAURv2 (Table 14), plus scaling and category findings. Figures 3 and 14 also revise DINOSAURv2's T-15 curves: approximately 94.3% to 95.8% on CLEVR and 94.4% to 93.8% on Multi-dSprites. Tables 7–13 remain unchanged, leaving unexplained plot/table discrepancies.

M1.justification: The representation models, frozen T5 encoder, representation conversions, transformer classifier, and training objectives remain unchanged. GQA reuses the real-world model adaptations already described for VQA-v2; it does not introduce a new method component.

P1.justification: The abstract, limitations, real-world discussion, and conclusion receive localized rewrites, with added GQA explanations and expanded acknowledgments. Citations switch to author-year format, but the main section sequence and Appendix A–D organization are preserved.

P2.justification: Figure 4 expands into three panels; Figures 9, 14, and 17 gain GQA panels; Figure 28 and Table 14 are added; and Table 6 gains a GQA row. The ICLR template changes title styling, headers, and placement, while most existing graphics and table structures are retained.

R1.justification: v4 adds Hudson and Manning's GQA reference, Liu et al. (2022) for the linguistic-cue interpretation, and a Jülich computing-resource reference. The related-work argument and positioning remain substantially unchanged; most other reference edits concern style or bibliographic metadata.

T1.justification: The mathematical descriptions of representation reshaping, projection, classification, and property-prediction matching are retained. Neither version adds theoretical propositions, proofs, or new formal assumptions.

improvement.justification: GQA strengthens the study by testing broader real-world reasoning than v3's restricted VQA-v2 subset, and its capacity and category analyses expose a useful exception to cross-question consistency. This provides a limited net improvement. The benefit is tempered by unreconciled DINOSAURv2 discrepancies between revised Figures 3/14 and retained Tables 7/12, and by the still broadly worded cross-category takeaway.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same representation-learning study. Their main text, figures, tables, mathematical descriptions, and Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across layout changes.

after.justification: v4 retains the original empirical study and adds GQA experiments, including accuracy, computational-cost, model-size, and question-category results.

before.justification: v3 reports original VQA experiments on three synthetic datasets and VQA-v2, together with property-prediction and supplementary analyses. Results appear throughout Section 4 and Appendix D.

title: Exploring the Effectiveness of Object-Centric Representations in Visual Question Answering: Comparative Insights with Foundation Models

C1.justification: The core contribution remains contrastive variational inference using self-generated soft labels. V2 makes stable, mass-covering objectives and lower forward KL more explicit in its headline claims, and its conclusion specifically emphasizes advantages on complex posterior geometries requiring flexible density estimators.

C2.justification: V2 substantially develops the explanation of low-alpha failures through log-ratio variability, label degeneracy, and dimensionality. It also explains restricted-support recovery failures, qualifies that the control variate need not reduce variance everywhere, and connects small-K degradation to gradient noise. These extend v1's shorter leakage and variance discussions with substantive applicability limits.

D1.justification: V2 newly states the linear-regression priors and documents the toy model and parameter controls; its FlowJax citation changes from version 12.3.0 to 14.0.0. Conversely, v1's learning rate of 1e-3 and eight-layer SLCP flow specification disappear. These omissions do not establish changed settings. The implementation and reproduction-code links remain the same.

E1.justification: The four main inference tasks remain unchanged. Appendix A.3 adds a Gaussian mean-inference toy task for gradient diagnostics, extending coverage beyond v1's experiments.

E2.justification: ELBO and SNIS-fKL remain the evaluated baselines in corresponding benchmark comparisons. The added benchmark analyses reuse these comparators, and the new gradient diagnostic compares against the existing SNIS-fKL baseline. SNIS-fKL-LV is identified with SoftCVI alpha = 1, rather than evaluated as a separate additional comparator.

E3.justification: The common training budget changes from 100,000 to 50,000 optimization steps. V2 adds K = 2 evaluations and controlled gradient sweeps in dimensions 1 and 50. The stated GARCH conditioning inputs also change from alpha1 and alpha2 to alpha0 and alpha1, although the PDFs do not establish whether this correction reflects an implementation change.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's leakage illustration and posterior marginals, v2 adds gradient signal-to-noise diagnostics, tests of posterior-based negative distributions, sensitivity to K = 2 versus K = 8, and posterior visualizations for six SLCP runs (Appendices A.3–A.5). These substantially expand the investigation of mechanisms, sensitivity, and failure behavior.

E5.justification: The stated number of independent seeded runs increases from 20 to 50. Both versions already display variation through boxplots. V2 additionally describes estimating gradient means and element-wise standard deviations across random seeds in Appendix A.3, without specifying that diagnostic's seed count.

E6.justification: V1 describes SoftCVI alpha = 1 and SNIS-fKL as performing similarly; v2 reports advantages for SoftCVI on most tasks and frequent poor SLCP mode approximation by SNIS-fKL. Performance, runtime, and marginal plots change, and new diagnostic and sensitivity results are added. Because the training budget changes, these are revised results rather than demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: V2 proposes an explicit SNIS-fKL-LV loss with a mean-log-q control-variate term (Section 3.2, Equation 15). This is a limited auxiliary objective addition: it is gradient-equivalent to the existing SoftCVI alpha = 1 case, while Algorithm 1 and the main SoftCVI loss remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction, negative-distribution discussion, results, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Related work moves before the experiments, the expanded SNIS-fKL comparison moves from Appendix C into the main text, and Appendices A–C are reorganized into A.1–A.5. This materially changes the explanatory sequence.

P2.justification: Figure 1 changes its calibration display from actual coverage to actual-minus-nominal coverage with a zero reference line. V2 adds gradient, alternative-negative-distribution, small-K, and six-run SLCP figures. The existing runtime and marginal displays are retained as Figures 5 and 8 with revised layouts and axes, rather than constituting wholly new analyses.

R1.justification: V2 adds references including Chehab et al. on negative-distribution choice, Rainforth et al. on gradient SNR, and Blei et al. on variational inference, while removing references such as Rossi et al. and Wan et al. It sharpens the relationship to SNIS-fKL and other soft-label contrastive methods, retaining the central positioning between variational inference and contrastive learning.

T1.justification: V2 extends v1's Appendix C comparison by deriving the normalization-term gradient, establishing equality of expected gradients with SNIS-fKL, and identifying the control variate and inverse-K variance behavior (Section 3.2 and Appendix A.2). Appendix A.4 adds reasoning for posterior-based negative distributions. The original zero-gradient-at-optimum proof is retained as Appendix A.1.

improvement.justification: V2 turns v1's brief SNIS-fKL comparison into a substantially better-supported account of the method's gradient behavior. The derivations in Section 3.2 and Appendix A.2, combined with gradient diagnostics and sensitivity experiments, explain both advantages and failure conditions. These gains strengthen the paper beyond its changed performance scores. Omitting the learning rate and flow depth weakens reproducibility, but this limited loss is outweighed by the stronger theoretical and empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SoftCVI by the same authors. Their main texts, equations, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across the reorganization.

after.justification: V2 reports original 50-run main comparisons and additional gradient diagnostics, negative-distribution experiments, small-K tests, and SLCP case studies.

before.justification: V1 reports original 20-run comparisons on Eight Schools, linear regression, SLCP, and GARCH, including performance, posterior marginals, and runtime results.

title: SoftCVI: Contrastive variational inference with self-generated soft labels

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution paragraph, and conclusion retain the central claims: contrastively derived variational objectives, self-generated soft labels, zero gradient variance at exact approximation, and frequent calibration and forward-KL benefits. The additional applications do not redefine these principal claims.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands applicability qualifications. It explains that model-parameter learning requires an additional objective and attributes the neural experiment's limited SoftCVI advantage to Gaussian posterior misspecification. It also discusses why predictive likelihood/calibration need not establish posterior accuracy, selection bias from validation procedures, and architecture-dependent runtime costs.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.7 supplies substantial model specifications, including eight-schools and GARCH priors, SLCP covariance construction, and reference-sampling details. v3 also discloses the four-layer SLCP flow and implementation settings for the added applications. The implementation package/link changes from softcvi to pyrox. Newly disclosed settings do not establish changes to the original implementations.

E1.justification: Alongside the retained Bayesian benchmarks and Gaussian diagnostic task, v3 adds MNIST generative-model training and synthetic nonlinear regression with Bayesian neural additive models. These extend coverage to image generation and neural-network posteriors with 1,500 or 3,000 parameters.

E2.justification: ELBO and SNIS-fKL remain the comparison methods in the matched benchmark experiments. The new neural additive-model study uses these same comparators, and the VAE example uses ELBO. Newly discussed adversarial methods are not evaluated as baselines.

E3.justification: The original benchmarks retain their documented 50,000-step, K = 8 protocol and metrics. Added protocols include VAE training for 100,000 steps with batch size 1; neural-model widths 50/100, 300/150/1,000 training/validation/test samples, validation-based stopping, and predictive metrics; and a K = 2–64 sweep. These are additional protocols, not established changes to the original experiments.

E4.justification: v3 extends the existing K = 2 versus K = 8 investigation into a sample-count sweep measuring posterior fit and computational cost (Figure 7). Table 1 also compares neural-network widths. The original SNR, alternative-negative-distribution, and multimodal-posterior analyses remain.

E5.justification: Appendix A.5 newly specifies ten networks initialized with different seeds, and Table 1 reports values with ± terms, although their statistical meaning is unspecified. The original 50-run benchmark count remains. The replacement runtime curves no longer display the run-to-run spread shown by v2's timing boxplots.

E6.justification: v3 adds VAE manifolds, neural additive-model predictions and metrics, and accuracy/runtime curves across K, alongside small updates to Figure 1's plotted summaries. In new Table 1, width-50 ELBO achieves test log-likelihood -2.392 ± 0.005 versus -2.424 ± 0.007 for SoftCVI with alpha = 0.75. These are new-setting results, not performance changes relative to v2.

M1.justification: The core SoftCVI algorithm is retained. New Appendix A.4 introduces a limited extension for jointly learning model parameters: an additional ELBO-derived model loss trains the decoder and prior while SoftCVI trains the encoder, reusing proposal samples (Equations 28–29).

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the soft-label explanation and selected related-work passages, streamlines main-text task descriptions with a new detailed appendix, and adds acknowledgments and affiliation edits. The main section order and most existing exposition remain stable.

P2.justification: The ICLR format changes typography, headers, spacing, and figure placement throughout. v3 adds VAE and neural-component figures and Table 1, and replaces the fixed-K timing boxplots with accuracy/runtime curves. Other appendix displays are retained and renumbered, including v2 Figures 4 and 6 becoming v3 Figures 6 and 8.

R1.justification: Section 3.3 adds a focused comparison with adversarial variational methods using separate classifiers. v3 also adds chi-divergence and neural-model references while removing some generic contrastive-learning examples. The broader positioning between variational inference and contrastive estimation remains intact.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 explicitly adds the assumption that the variational family contains the true posterior and specifies optimality over all proposal sample sets, equivalently the expected objective. This tightens the posterior-recovery statement. The existing appendix proofs remain; the rewritten control-variate gradient formula is mathematically equivalent.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves the evidence about SoftCVI's applicability and limits. The high-dimensional neural study tests a setting absent from v2 and transparently reports little advantage over SNIS-fKL, connecting this outcome to posterior misspecification. The expanded K analysis establishes practical accuracy/cost tradeoffs, while Appendix A.7 improves reproducibility. M1.justification: Appendix E revises the specified attack templates, including contextual prompting, command-channel requirements and semantic-rephrasing constraints. R1.justification: The Cangelosi and Schlesinger (2018) citation and bibliography entry are removed. The related-work discussion and positioning against existing embodied-system and jailbreak research otherwise remain substantively unchanged.

T1.justification: Definitions 1–2, Equations 1–2, attack formulas, mitigation mathematics and complexity arguments are retained. Section 2.2 explicitly states the action-unsafe condition already underlying the attack objective; this clarifies the existing focus without adding a formal result.

improvement.justification: The expanded ethics discussion and more explicit prompts add useful detail. However, v5 introduces expert-access claims inconsistent with its retained ordinary-user threat model, changes prompts without explaining their relationship to retained results, and leaves replication access ambiguous. These reduce coherence and reproducibility, while the underlying empirical contribution remains preserved.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BadRobot and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures and Appendices A–J. Corresponding material can be reliably matched despite title edits and pagination changes.

after.justification: v5 retains these original experimental outcomes in Sections 4–5 and the appendices, including Tables 1–3 and Figures A1–A2.

before.justification: v4 reports original digital, simulator and physical-robot experiments, including attack success rates, harmfulness scores and mitigation evaluations.

title: BadRobot: Jailbreaking Embodied LLM Agents in the Physical World

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the central claims: generalization across distribution and environment-space changes using compact causal world models and three-step, low-cost adaptation. CoinRun and the additional experiments broaden supporting evidence without redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: New Appendix A.4 explicitly identifies nonlinear transition-factor identifiability as unresolved and explains why transition invertibility is problematic. Appendix D.5 qualifies Atari changes as often involving latent dynamics rather than new observable entities, interpreting added variables through reconstruction interventions. These materially refine applicability and mechanism claims; the existing nonstationarity and search-cost limitations remain.

D1.justification: v3 fills important implementation gaps: the prediction threshold equals the source task's final loss, expansion ranges are listed, and expansion-penalty and regularization coefficients are specified. It also adds A100 hardware and training-time information, explicit Atari mode/difficulty options, and CoinRun and six-action CartPole settings. These disclosures substantially improve reproducibility.

E1.justification: v3 adds CoinRun transfer from easier levels to harder levels containing new enemies. It also adds CartPole Task 4, expanding the available actions from two force directions to six direction/magnitude combinations. The original simulation, CartPole shift/friction scenarios and five Atari games remain.

E2.justification: The retained comparisons preserve their comparator sets: DQN, Dreamer and AdaRL for simulation/CartPole, and Random, SPR, Dreamer, AdaRL and EfficientZero in the Atari score table. CoinRun and the new reconstruction comparisons reuse existing comparator groups.

Ablation reporting changes from separate environment curves and a Pong-only comparison to normalized aggregate evaluations. Atari target-task plots now span 400k rather than 100k; the PDFs do not establish whether this reflects changed training budgets or step-count conventions.

New analyses examine nonlinear change-factor recovery (Figure 4), structural-mask evolution (Figure 9), and reconstructions after deactivating newly added variables (Figure 12). CoinRun and Atari reconstruction comparisons substantially extend v1's CartPole analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging five runs and retain uncertainty values in their score tables. v3 adds shaded variability bands to previously unshaded simulation and CartPole learning curves. The bands' statistical meaning is unspecified, and no increase in run count is reported.

E6.justification: v3 adds CoinRun, CartPole Task 4 and representation-analysis results, and revises Atari learning curves. Table 1 changes DQN's CartPole Task 1–3 means from 44.2/61.8/39.8 to 102.8/65.6/107.4; the other methods' corresponding scores remain unchanged. Atari Table 2 retains every numerical result, so the revision does not establish improved Atari final performance.

M1.justification: The three-step CSR procedure and self-adaptive expansion controller remain. Section 3.3 replaces six separately weighted sparsity penalties with one shared regularization coefficient; v3 also relaxes the stated cross-task constancy of structural masks. These are limited formulation changes, while the newly specified threshold and layer-expansion details primarily improve documentation.

P1.justification: The six-section main narrative remains, with targeted rewrites of the abstract, motivating examples and method explanations. Algorithm 1 moves into a dedicated appendix, experimental details gain a hyperparameter subsection, and citations switch to author–year style. P2.justification: v3 replaces the Portal 2 illustrations with CoinRun, redraws the framework diagram and substantially restructures Figure 3. Tables gain task columns, expansion ranges and settings; new recovery and reconstruction figures are added. T1.justification: Section 2.3 and Appendix A substantially revise the identifiability theory. Theorem 1 now uses a noisy joint observation–reward mapping with a new deconvolution argument. Theorem 2 is restricted to linear additive transitions with rank and initial-state assumptions, replacing the earlier inversion argument with Jacobian derivations and Proposition 1. Theorem 3 also changes its observation requirements.

improvement.justification: CoinRun, explicit action-expansion evaluation and added-variable interventions address gaps in v1's empirical support, while documented thresholds and hyperparameters improve reproducibility. The expanded theory therefore cannot be treated as a demonstrated correctness improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CSR research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds CoinRun experiments, CartPole action expansion, nonlinear change-factor recovery and representation analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation, CartPole and Atari experiments, including comparative scores, learning curves, ablations and reconstruction results.

Appendices C and E add prospective applications involving other policy learners, goal misalignment and continual or domain-agnostic RL. E3.justification: The added Appendix D.4 diagnostic specifies a controlled Pong sequence of (mode, difficulty) pairs: (0,0), (0,1), (1,1), (1,0), and measures prediction errors and adaptation-mode selections. Existing benchmark protocols remain unchanged. Newly disclosed detection-step budgets belong to implementation documentation and do not establish revised budgets.

E4.justification: Figure 14 and Appendix D.4 add a focused analysis of whether prediction error and the selected adaptation mechanism correspond to environmental changes across the four environment families. Existing causal-structure ablations, expansion-strategy comparisons and latent-variable removal analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions state that results are averaged over five runs and retain the same tabulated uncertainty values and shaded learning curves. No new seed information, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty-estimation procedure is reported.

E6.justification: The added Figure 14 reports new diagnostic results, including Pong prediction errors of 0.2, 0.15, 1.77 and 0.09 across its four tasks, plus adaptation-mode selections. Existing performance and expansion results in Tables 1–3 and retained learning curves are unchanged; these additions do not show improved benchmark performance over v3.

M1.justification: Section 3 changes the reward contribution in the stated reconstruction objective from p_phi(r_t | ...) to log p_phi(r_t | ...). This is a limited loss-formula correction; the three-step CSR framework remains intact. Expanded pseudocode chiefly documents existing operations and does not establish that the implementation or experiments changed.

P1.justification: Section 4 is reframed around three explicit questions, introductory environment descriptions move to Appendix D.3, and the appendices gain clearer subdivisions and a future-directions section. Local wording, affiliations, publication headers and acknowledgments also change. Most main-text prose and its section order are retained.

P2.justification: v4 adds the causal-graph illustration in Figure 5 and diagnostic plots in Figure 14, expands and reformats Algorithm 1, and adds highlighting to the reconstruction comparison now numbered Figure 13. Captions gain emphasized takeaways, and appendix displays move. Existing benchmark plots and table structures are largely retained.

R1.justification: v4 adds implementation and future-direction references, including Ng et al. (2022), Di Langosco et al. (2022) and Khetarpal et al. (2022), and removes the Hafner et al. (2019) reference. Section 5 and the principal positioning against methods assuming fixed environment spaces remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definition of the reconstruction objective in Section 3 is corrected by inserting a logarithm on the reward probability. The identifiability definitions, assumptions, Theorems 1–3, Proposition 1, Corollary 1 and Appendix A proofs otherwise remain unchanged apart from notation and equation numbering.

improvement.justification: v4 improves the paper through more actionable implementation documentation, a corrected reconstruction objective, clearer explanations and direct diagnostic evidence for adaptation decisions in Figure 14. These targeted gains strengthen clarity and reproducibility. The central performance evidence and identifiability arguments remain unchanged, while the newly discussed broader applications remain prospective.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CSR research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v4 retains these original empirical results and adds prediction-error and adaptation-mode diagnostics in Appendix D.4 and Figure 14.

before.justification: v3 reports original simulations and experiments on CartPole, CoinRun and five Atari games, including performance comparisons, ablations and reconstruction analyses.

title: Towards Generalizable Reinforcement Learning via Causality-Guided Self-Adaptive Representations

C1.justification: The principal contributions remain walk-profile expressivity, Multi-q Mag-PE, and stable complex PE processing. The introduction adds a specific approximately half-walk-length recovery requirement and explicitly claims the first basis-invariant, stable architecture for complex eigenvectors. These sharpen retained contributions without replacing the paper's central objective.

C2.justification: v1's brief computational-overhead limitation becomes an expanded expressivity–cost discussion supported by runtime evidence. v2 additionally discusses robustness and ill-conditioning of q selection, dimensionality and scalability tradeoffs against directly using walk-profile features, and the probabilistic interpretation and motivation of normalization. These materially broaden the explanations and applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: Appendices D–E document timing measurement procedures, evaluated configurations, random-q sampling, and minimum separation; Table 17 adds graph-size statistics. Tables 11–14 correct HLS target headings from Gain/BW to DSP/LUT. The existing hyperparameter tables, hardware disclosure, and code-access link are largely retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate directed random graphs and DAGs, sorting networks, two-stage Open Circuit Benchmark amplifiers, and HLS graphs on the same task families. Normalizing the walk-profile target changes the retained evaluation protocol. The new biological motif examples do not introduce an evaluated domain.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain the same Laplacian, SVD where previously evaluated, and fixed/tuned single-q Magnetic Laplacian comparators, together with the same PE processors and backbone alternatives. Appendix E studies a random-q configuration of the proposed method; no baseline family is added or removed.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 changes the walk-profile prediction target from counts to normalized bidirectional random-walk probabilities, substantially changing what its RMSE measures. New protocols evaluate runtime across numbers of potentials and uniformly sampled q vectors with minimum separation. Existing dataset splits, benchmark architectures, and training budgets are otherwise retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds preprocessing, training, and inference cost analyses versus the number of potentials, plus random-versus-evenly-spaced q sensitivity experiments across the existing tasks. Appendix F also reports failure to fit distances above 10 when reducing the number of potentials to 10. These extend v1's single-q tuning and PE-processing comparisons substantially.

E5.justification: Appendix D newly specifies timing averages over 10 epochs, and Appendix E states that each training seed receives a newly sampled q vector. Existing benchmark seed counts and ± reporting remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish an increase in independent repetitions.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces both walk-profile result columns following normalization; for example, Multi-q/SPE DAG RMSE changes from 0.430±0.052 to 0.002±0.000, which is not a same-target performance gain. New runtime and random-q results substantially expand the evidence. Sorting results remain unchanged; Table 3 corrects SAT(bidirected-GIN)+Lap/SPE phase-margin RMSE from 1.044±0.021 to 1.046±0.021.

M1.justification: The multi-q eigendecomposition, concatenation, and complex SPE architecture remain intact. However, the weighted-graph construction changes: v1 Appendix A multiplies edge weights by exp(±i2πq), whereas v2 Section 3 makes the phase depend on the difference between opposing edge weights. This revises the weighted extension without establishing a change to the benchmark architectures.

P1.justification: The abstract, substantial introduction passages, contribution descriptions, and walk-profile exposition are rewritten around bidirectional motifs. Limitations move from the conclusion into Section 4.3, the conclusion is revised, and the document gains a runtime subsection and Appendices D–G. This constitutes substantial narrative and structural revision.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document template and typography, replaces Figure 1's critical-path example with a feed-forward loop, and updates the walk-profile panels of old Figure 4/new Figure 5. It adds runtime Figure 4, Tables 15–18, and Figure 9, combining new random-q evidence with redisplayed benchmark results.

R1.justification: v2 adds Mangan and Alon's feed-forward-loop reference while removing Chen and Du's critical-path reference and Chung's spectral-graph-theory reference. It also explicitly positions complex stable PE processing as a first contribution. The related-work coverage otherwise remains substantially the same; the citation-style conversion is presentational.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.1 changes its adjacency domain from complex to real matrices and receives a replacement counterexample using adjacency spectra. Theorem 4.2 reduces the stated sufficient number of potentials from L+1 to ceil(L/2)+1 using conjugate symmetry, with a changed potential interval and substantially revised proof. Appendix A.2 explicitly adds a no-reciprocal-edge assumption, and Appendix G defines normalized walk profiles.

improvement.justification: The runtime and random-q analyses make practical cost and sensitivity more assessable, while Appendix G explains the revised normalized target. These provide useful empirical and explanatory gains. However, the strengthened theory remains imperfectly aligned with its statements: Appendix A.1 explicitly analyzes Aq instead of the stated normalized Lq encoding, and Appendix A.2 introduces an assumption absent from Theorem 4.2. These gaps limit the overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Multi-q Magnetic Laplacian PE study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark results, replaces the walk-profile results under a normalized target, and adds runtime and random-q experiments in Section 5.4 and Appendices D–E.

before.justification: v1 reports original distance-prediction, sorting-network satisfiability, and circuit-property experiments in Tables 1–3, with additional single-q sensitivity results in Appendix C.

title: What Are Good Positional Encodings for Directed Graphs?

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements and conclusion retain the same claims about walk profiles, existing PE limitations, Multi-q expressiveness and stable complex-eigenvector processing.

C2.justification: New Appendix F interprets its comparison as showing that a strong SAT backbone cannot fully compensate for older PEs' distance-representation limitations. Existing computational-cost limitations and discussion of directly using walk profiles remain unchanged, with the latter moved from Appendix F to G.

D1.justification: The added distance comparison specifies SAT with a bidirectional GIN encoder and SPE processing, providing limited configuration information. Existing implementation tables, hardware and training-time disclosures, and the code link are unchanged. No dedicated hyperparameter table accompanies the new comparison.

E1.justification: Both versions cover synthetic directed and acyclic graphs, sorting networks, Open Circuit Benchmark and high-level synthesis. The new Appendix F evaluates already covered DAG distance and walk-profile tasks using another backbone.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds a no-PE comparator for each of four backbones: undirected GIN, bidirected GIN and their SAT variants. The previously evaluated PE comparators remain present.

E3.justification: Appendix F adds a reported DAG distance evaluation using SAT with a bidirectional GIN encoder and SPE processing. The original MLP-based distance experiment remains, and existing splits, metrics, budgets and hyperparameter tables are unchanged.

E4.justification: The added no-PE controls test the benefit of including positional encodings. Appendix F also examines whether a stronger graph-transformer backbone addresses older encodings' distance-prediction limitations. Existing q-selection, generalization and runtime analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Table 3 replaces overall-best dagger annotations with stars indicating that the best result exceeds the runner-up by one standard deviation. This adds a comparison based on reported variability. Existing seed counts and uncertainty reporting remain unchanged; no formal significance test is added.

E6.justification: Existing numerical results and plotted findings are retained. Table 3 adds 20 no-PE results, including bidirected-GIN Gain RMSE of 0.386±0.008. Table 19 adds SAT-labelled results, but all 12 mean-and-uncertainty pairs exactly match Table 1's corresponding DAG SPE entries despite the different stated backbone; whether these represent independent results is unclear.

M1.justification: The Multi-q Magnetic Laplacian construction and complex-domain stable PE processing in Section 4 are unchanged. The added SAT evaluation uses the existing encodings without revising the proposed method.

P1.justification: v3 updates the publication header, makes limited wording and equation-typography corrections, and inserts a short Appendix F, renumbering the former F–G as G–H. Most prose and the main narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: Table 3 gains no-PE rows and revised highlighting, and Table 19 is added. Figures 1–2 are reduced in size, while Table 2, Figure 3 and Table 3 move within the main text. Existing figure content and plotted curves are unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 and the bibliography add Qitong Wang et al.'s Directed graph transformers as prior work using singular-vector positional encodings. The broader related-work discussion and novelty positioning remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The walk-profile definitions, Theorems 4.1–4.2, Appendix A proofs and normalized-walk-profile definition are retained. Removing stray braces in Equations 3–4 is a typographical correction without a change to the mathematics.

improvement.justification: Table 3's no-PE controls make the contribution of positional encodings easier to assess, while its revised annotations give context about winning margins relative to variability. These provide a limited improvement to the retained evaluation. The added SAT study carries uncertain additional evidential value because Table 19 exactly repeats Table 1's SPE results under a different stated architecture.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Existing material can be matched across the layout changes and appendix renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and additionally reports no-PE controls in Table 3 and a SAT distance-prediction comparison in Appendix F.

before.justification: v2 reports original distance-prediction, sorting-network satisfiability and circuit-property experiments in Section 5, with additional experimental results in the appendices.

title: What Are Good Positional Encodings for Directed Graphs?

C1.justification: The central channel-pruning novelty and memory-saving claims remain. v2 extends the headline empirical comparison to quantization and adds claims of 2.8-fold peak-memory reduction and up to fivefold batch capacity for ThinK combined with KIVI. Its contribution paragraph narrows the stated linear savings from both computation and memory to memory.

C2.justification: v2 removes v1 Section 3.3's argument that masked-query decoding should require less computation than zero-filling, and emphasizes the batch-capacity implications of the new KIVI measurements. Existing qualifications about aggressive pruning, small cache budgets, and value-cache pruning on Mistral remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C.1 and Figure 7 newly document KIVI integration, including prefill ordering and residual-buffer handling. v2 also specifies the synthetic workload lengths and quantization precisions. It omits v1's zero-filling/FlashAttention implementation discussion and changes the hardware disclosure from one A100 to A100 GPUs without specifying their count.

E1.justification: LongBench and Needle-in-a-Haystack coverage remains unchanged. v2 Section 4.4 adds synthetic batched-generation workloads for peak-memory evaluation, providing a limited additional test scenario. The additional LLaMA backbones are changes in experimental configuration.

E2.justification: v2 extends the evaluated comparator families beyond token eviction by adding KIVI: Table 4 compares KIVI with KIVI plus ThinK, and Figure 3b includes 2-bit and 4-bit KIVI configurations. KIVI was cited but not experimentally compared in v1. H2O, SnapKV, and the magnitude-pruning comparisons remain.

The magnitude-plot attribution also changes from LLaMA3-8B in v1 Figure 2 to LLaMA-2-7B in v2 Figure 4; this does not establish that the plot was regenerated.

E4.justification: v2 adds a batch-size sensitivity analysis of peak memory for KIVI with and without ThinK at two precisions, shown in Figure 3b. The recent-size, equal-memory, joint key/value-pruning, and retrieval-depth analyses are retained; their relocation or renumbering does not constitute new analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests for its experiments. v2 continues the same point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: All original table values are retained. v2 adds 70B results, including LongBench averages of 46.27 for SnapKV and 46.45 with ThinK at pruning ratio 0.4 and cache size 512. New Table 4 reports 31.92 for KIVI versus 31.77 with ThinK, while Figure 3b adds peak-memory curves. These are newly reported comparisons under additional configurations.

M1.justification: The channel-selection objective, query-dependent score, observation window, and value-pruning rule remain unchanged. v2 Appendix C.1 adds a KIVI-specific inference procedure: pruning before quantization during prefill and pruning/quantizing accumulated decoding keys when the residual buffer reaches G tokens. The masked-query implementation illustrated in v2 was already described in v1.

P1.justification: v2 extensively edits the abstract, introduction, experimental discussion, related work, and conclusion. It removes the contents page, replaces 'End Note and Future Direction' with 'Conclusion', and reorganizes supporting material into Appendices A–D. These are substantial editorial and structural changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a substantially different, more compact layout. It expands Table 2 with 70B blocks, adds the KIVI table and workflow diagram, combines the existing equal-memory plot with a new memory-scaling panel, and redraws the decoding diagram. Magnitude plots, SVD plots, retrieval heatmaps, and the joint-pruning table move to appendices.
