The principal positioning as channel pruning complementary to eviction and quantization remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The pruning optimization, channel scores, selection constraints, SVD energy formula, and value-pruning equations are mathematically unchanged. The SVD formula and value-pruning formulation move to v2 Appendices A and D. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 asserted compatibility with quantization without experimentally validating it. v2 supplies the KIVI accuracy comparison, peak-memory measurements across batch sizes, and an implementation description, substantially strengthening the practical compression claim. The 70B results also strengthen evidence beyond the original smaller models. Denser tables and incomplete KIVI configuration details limit readability and reproducibility, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ThinK, the same query-driven KV-cache channel-pruning work. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and the equations, tables, and figures can be matched across the reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds LLaMA-3-70B results, KIVI comparisons, and synthetic-workload peak-memory measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original LongBench and Needle-in-a-Haystack experiments, channel-pruning ablations, and comparisons under equal cache-memory budgets.

title: ThinK: Thinner Key Cache by Query-Driven Pruning

C1.justification: The central contribution and channel-pruning claims remain. The abstract clarifies batch-size capacity as increasing from 4× with KIVI alone to 5× with THINK, while the conclusion now qualifies efficiency by acknowledging increased time to first token.

C2.justification: v3 explains the tradeoff between channel-importance computation increasing prefilling latency and reduced memory traffic improving decoding. Section 4.4 and Appendix D newly connect harder value-cache pruning to more uniform channel magnitudes. The conclusion explicitly identifies timing overhead and further value-cache pruning research as limitations.

D1.justification: v3 adds a THINK code-availability statement and repository address. Appendix F supplies batch size 300 for the new timing experiments. Existing A100 hardware disclosures, pooling and observation-window settings, and Appendix C's quantization implementation are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same LongBench tasks, Needle-in-a-Haystack tests, and synthetic workload with input/output lengths of 160/338. The added experiments change compression configurations and measurements within existing coverage.

E2.justification: Table 12 adds an evaluated comparison family: Palu on Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 and ASVD on LLaMA-2-7B-Chat. Existing H2O, SnapKV, KIVI, and norm-based comparisons remain. Eigen Attention is newly cited but is not an evaluated baseline in that table.

E3.justification: v3 substantially extends evaluation beyond accuracy and memory: Appendix F introduces TTFT, TPOT, and throughput measurements, specifying batch size 300 for timing. Appendix E adds full-cache controls without companion compression. Appendix G introduces purportedly matched-compression comparisons, although its 'compressed by 80%' wording conflicts with the stated 20% total-cache reduction for THINK(0.4), leaving exact matching unclear.

E4.justification: Appendix E tests whether THINK remains effective without token eviction or quantization, varying channel pruning from 40% to 60% on two existing models. This adds a focused control and sensitivity analysis. Existing recent-size, equal-memory, retrieval-depth, and joint key/value analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added tables continue reporting point estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1–8 and the existing figures retain their results; Tables 9–12 add substantial new outcomes. Table 9 reports LLaMA-3 standalone averages of 41.86 for vanilla and 42.27/42.25 at 40%/50% pruning. Table 10 reports KIVI TPOT of 0.27 versus 0.25/0.24 ms/token with THINK, alongside TTFT of 7.0 versus 10.4/10.2 ms. Table 11 adds throughput results, and Table 12 adds SVD-comparator scores.

M1.justification: The query-driven channel scores, greedy selection, recent-token preservation, masking procedure, KIVI integration, and value-cache pruning equations remain unchanged. Expanded implementation explanations and experiments on vanilla models do not introduce a different method.

P1.justification: v3 makes targeted abstract, implementation, results-discussion, and conclusion edits. Section 6 becomes 'Conclusion and Limitations,' Appendix D expands, Appendices E–G are appended, and the header changes to ICLR 2025 publication status. The main narrative and section order remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 9–12 and adjusts appendix placement: Figures 4 and 5 share a page, Figure 6 moves to the following page, and Table 8 shares space with Table 9. All seven existing figure graphics and the structures of Tables 1–8 are retained.

R1.justification: Appendix G adds targeted positioning against Palu, ASVD, and Eigen Attention, contrasting direct online pruning with calibrated low-rank decomposition and cache reconstruction. Two Lu et al. papers are also newly cited. The established positioning against eviction, quantization, and structured pruning remains.

T1.justification: The pruning optimization, channel-selection criteria, Equations 1–4, and Appendix A's SVD energy definition are unchanged. No new formal assumption, theorem, proof, or derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: Standalone controls in Table 9 and measured latency/throughput tradeoffs in Tables 10–11 strengthen practical validation beyond v2's memory measurements. Explicit limitations and code-access information improve transparency. These gains are bounded: Appendix G's inconsistent compression wording weakens confidence in its claimed matched comparisons, while the central method and earlier evidence remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe THINK, with matching methods, equations, experiments, and shared appendices. Text extraction and visual inspection support comparison of the complete documents, including v3's added Appendices E–G.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds standalone pruning experiments, latency and throughput measurements, and SVD-method comparisons.

before.justification: v2 reports original LongBench and Needle-in-a-Haystack evaluations, memory measurements, pruning ablations, and cache analyses in the main text and appendices.

title: ThinK: Thinner Key Cache by Query-Driven Pruning

C1.justification: The abstract, principal contributions and claimed 4.4-point average CIFAR-10 robustness advantage remain unchanged. Section 6 newly makes an explicit claim about potential real-time applications, supported by the added latency discussion.

C2.justification: The revision adds qualifications about fine-tuning overhead and when that cost may be worthwhile. It also explains possible training collapse for alternative bridges and RDC's applicability constraints. The computational discussion shifts from relative FLOP overhead toward measured latency and parameter costs, while retaining the original robustness interpretations.

D1.justification: The abstract replaces a promised future code release with a stated public repository link. The timing benchmark supplies hardware and batch-size information. Existing optimizer, EMA, software versions, training batch sizes and fine-tuning settings are retained; repository accessibility was not independently checked.

E1.justification: Section 5.3 and Appendix E.4 extend evaluation to patch-like and diffusion-based black-box threats: NCF, PI-FGSM, Diff-Attack and Diff-PGD on ImageNet-100. This substantially broadens the tested perturbation scenarios beyond the previously evaluated norm-bounded threats; the four datasets remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds BPDA as a comparator for the proposed attack-evaluation procedure. Existing defense comparator sets are retained; the new ImageNet-100 threat comparison reuses Liu et al., Debenedetti et al. and DiffPure from the earlier ImageNet-100 evaluation.

E3.justification: Table A10 introduces wall-clock evaluation using batch size 1 on one NVIDIA 3090 GPU, comparing 1–5 and 100 reverse sampling steps. Existing training budgets, attack bounds, sampling procedures and PGD/EOT settings are retained. Detailed budgets for the new black-box attacks are not specified.

E4.justification: Appendix E.4 adds a substantive generalization study across four previously untested black-box attacks. Appendix F also extends the computational-cost analysis with measured latency versus sampling steps. The original reverse-step, noise-generation and classifier-transfer ablations remain.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three adaptive-attack runs on 512 sampled test images and report means with standard deviations, sometimes omitting deviations. No increased run count, new uncertainty-estimation procedure or significance testing is documented.

E6.justification: New findings include BPDA's 81.40±0.16% DiffPure robustness, Table A8's ADBM accuracies of 33.9/42.7/42.8/72.4% under the four new threats, and Table A10's latency measurements. Corresponding pre-existing benchmark scores are unchanged. The earlier 39/18-GFLOP costs and 46.2% overhead estimate are removed.

M1.justification: The bridge construction, training objective, classifier-assisted adversarial-noise generation, fixed within-step randomness and inference procedure remain unchanged. Section 4.2 expands their explanation without introducing a new method component.

P1.justification: Most original prose and the main section sequence remain. Changes comprise localized explanations, expanded related-work and limitations passages, updated affiliations and citation style, an acknowledgment, and appendix reorganization with inference cost becoming a separate appendix.

P2.justification: The paper adopts the ICLR template and headers, lightly revises the two schematics, adds a BPDA row and two new tables, and reformats or relocates existing tables. The earlier classifier-transfer Table A8 becomes Table A9 without changing its results.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix A substantially expand positioning against diffusion bridges, including Bortoli, Zhou, Zheng and Liu, and explain distinctions from robust diffusion classifiers. Section 4.2 additionally discusses AToP. These additions address the relationship to closely related approaches rather than merely updating citations.

T1.justification: Theorem 1's proof changes the sampling endpoint from τ0=1 to τ0=0, explicitly distinguishes discrete and continuous time grids, and expands the one-step DDIM substitution (v1 Appendix B.2; v2 Appendix C.2). The theorem statements, bounds and other derivations are retained.

improvement.justification: The new threat evaluations and measured latency strengthen evidence for generalization and practicality; related-work distinctions, the proof endpoint correction and code disclosure also help. These are useful incremental gains. Sparse settings for the new attacks, removal of explicit relative FLOP overhead, and the unexplained 0.010-second two-step Tiny-ImageNet timing in Table A10 limit the improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ADBM research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices support comparison despite formatting changes and appendix renumbering.

after.justification: The original empirical results are retained, with additional ImageNet-100 attack evaluations and measured inference times in Tables A8 and A10.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix D report original robustness experiments, ablations and classifier-transfer results across four image datasets.

title: ADBM: Adversarial Diffusion Bridge Model for Reliable Adversarial Purification

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions and claims concerning ADBM, reliable adaptive evaluation, theoretical guarantees, acceleration and robustness against unseen threats.

C2.justification: The explanations of purification behavior, attack effectiveness and classifier transfer are unchanged. Section 6 and Appendices F–G retain the same computational limitations, applicability discussion and potential adverse impacts.

D1.justification: Implementation details, optimizer settings, batch sizes, software versions, GPU configuration and timing disclosures remain unchanged. The code, dataset and checkpoint access links also have identical destinations.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate SVHN, CIFAR-10, Tiny-ImageNet and ImageNet-100 under the same white-box, black-box, norm-bounded and additional unseen attack scenarios. No dataset or task coverage changes.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain the same adversarial-training and purification baselines, including DiffPure and its compared variants. The attack comparisons in Section 3 and Appendix E.1 also retain their comparator sets.

E3.justification: Sections 3 and 5 and Appendices D–E retain the same architectures, training budgets, attack bounds, sample sizes and evaluation procedures, including the principal 200-step PGD evaluation with 20 EOT samples and five-step DDIM purification.

E4.justification: The forward/reverse-step analyses, adversarial-noise-generation ablations, alternative-attack evaluations and transfer to new classifiers are unchanged. Tables 2, 5–6, A1–A3 and A9 contain the same analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report three adaptive-attack repetitions and mean accuracies with standard deviations, with some deviations omitted for readability. Section 3 and Appendix D.2 contain unchanged reporting practices.

E6.justification: All numerical results and reported empirical findings in Tables 1–6 and A1–A10 are unchanged. For example, Table 3 retains average robust accuracies of 53.5% for ADBM and 49.1% for DiffPure.

M1.justification: The bridge coefficient, training loss, classifier-assisted adversarial-noise generation and inference procedure in Sections 4.1–4.3 are unchanged. The appendix corrections repair derivations without changing the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: The arXiv version/date stamp and one in-text citation year are updated. Several bibliography entries receive publication, page-range and style updates, while the prose, terminology and section organization remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Reference entries on page 12 are reordered and reflowed, and the corrected appendix equations produce small local spacing changes. Figures 1–2 and all main-text and appendix tables retain their structure, captions and placement.

R1.justification: No cited work is added or removed, and research positioning is unchanged. The Li, Chen and Hu backbone-robustness citation changes from its 2023 preprint to its 2025 journal publication; other reference edits supply publication details for existing works.

T1.justification: Appendix C.1, Eq. (19), replaces (alpha_t - bar_alpha_t)/(1 - bar_alpha_t) and the corresponding product factors with their reciprocals. Appendix C.2, Eq. (29), removes an extra (1 - bar_alpha_T)/bar_alpha_T multiplier from the expected squared residual. These correct intermediate mathematical steps; the final bridge coefficient, theorem statements and final bounds remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: The corrections to Eqs. (19) and (29) remove local algebraic inconsistencies in the bridge derivation and Theorem 1 proof, improving the mathematical presentation. Updated reference details provide a smaller editorial benefit. The gains are limited because the method, theorem conclusions, empirical evidence and limitations are otherwise unchanged.

A1.justification: Both complete, readable 23-page PDFs describe ADBM and contain the same main sections and Appendices A–G. Text comparison and rendered-page inspection support comparison of the equations, figures, tables and appendices without material gaps.

after.justification: v4 retains the original ADBM experiments, ablations, supplementary evaluations and timing measurements in Section 5 and Appendices E–F.

before.justification: v2 reports original ADBM robustness experiments and ablations in Section 5, with additional benchmark, classifier-transfer and inference-time results in Appendices E–F.

title: ADBM: Adversarial Diffusion Bridge Model for Reliable Adversarial Purification

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: TAR provides substantial tamper-resistance while preserving benign capabilities and demonstrates that progress on open-weight safeguards is tractable.

C2.justification: Appendix D.5 interprets the new refusal-training trajectories as evidence that TAR can satisfy complex resistance objectives and potentially accommodate other useful objectives. The existing limitations, capability tradeoffs, and discussion of unsuccessful defenses remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 makes the test-time Retain corpus explicit and distinguishes it from the mixed training corpus in Appendix F.1. Hardware, implementation optimizations, dataset-construction details, and code/model access information otherwise remain unchanged after appendix renumbering.

E1.justification: Coverage remains WMDP biosecurity, chemical security and cybersecurity, MMLU, HarmBench/MT-Bench refusal evaluation, and benign economics fine-tuning. The new DPO analysis uses the existing refusal task; the retain-data specification is revised within retained evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: The comparator sets in Tables 1, 2, 11, and 12 and the baseline descriptions are unchanged. However, v3 adds Rosati et al.'s Immunization work and says the 'latter two works' were covered by its comparisons, without an identifiable Immunization setup or result. Whether an additional comparator was actually evaluated is unresolved.

E3.justification: v3 adds average DPO win-rate tracking during refusal training. Appendix F.1 also explicitly specifies Pile-bio Retain data for test-time evaluation, whereas v1 Appendix E.1 referred to the mixed training Retain corpus defined in D.2. This revises the reported setup; the PDFs do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix D.5 and Figure 7 add an analysis of whether refusal preference persists along training-time attack trajectories. The existing benign fine-tuning, targeted patching, inner-loop-length, component-ablation, and loss-weight analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Existing averaging practices remain unchanged, and the new DPO trajectory supplies no uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Existing tabular results are unchanged, including TAR's 63.9% average post-attack HarmBench ASR in Tables 2 and 11. New Figure 7 reports increasing refusal win-rates during training and final inner-loop trajectories that flatten near 1.0.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, the two-stage safeguarding procedure, training objectives, and implementation of TAR remain unchanged. DPO-based refusal training was already present in v1; its new diagnostic does not introduce a method component.

P1.justification: v3 adds an Author Contributions appendix, moves targeted patching before the inner-loop-length analysis, and makes limited paragraph and terminology revisions. Most main-text and appendix prose is retained.

P2.justification: v3 adds the DPO trajectory Figure 7; v1's chemical/cybersecurity heatmaps become Figure 8 with unchanged content. Figure 3's caption specifies the training duration, and appendix figures and tables are locally repositioned and reflowed.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to Immunization against Harmful Fine-tuning Attacks, Targeted Latent Adversarial Training, and Shadow Alignment. Section 2 also revises its characterization of Vaccine and qualifies the evaluation coverage and robustness of concurrent defenses.

T1.justification: The threat-model assumptions, tamper-resistance definitions, Equations 1–3, and appendix loss formulations are retained. No theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is added or revised.

improvement.justification: The new refusal-training diagnostic fills a narrow explanatory gap in v1, while the added prior-work coverage and more explicit evaluation documentation improve completeness. The gains are limited: benchmark evidence and substantive limitations remain unchanged, and the asserted Immunization comparison remains insufficiently documented.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TAR research. The full main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results and adds a refusal-training diagnostic in Appendix D.5 and Figure 7.

before.justification: v1 reports original safeguard evaluations, red-teaming results, benign fine-tuning experiments, and ablations in Section 5 and the appendices.

title: Tamper-Resistant Safeguards for Open-Weight LLMs

C1.justification: The abstract narrows resistance from thousands to hundreds of fine-tuning steps. The introduction replaces robustness against 28 adversaries, including 5,000-step attacks, with 26 adversaries and hundreds of steps. This substantially narrows the central robustness claim while retaining the proposed method and its claimed advantage over prior safeguards.

C2.justification: V4 explains contamination and shuffling-related vulnerabilities, emphasizes sensitivity to adversary distributions, and explicitly excludes input-space robustness from its optimization goal. Appendix A newly discusses low post-attack benign performance and the resulting risks for legitimate fine-tuning with contaminated data. Appendix D.4 shifts the initial safeguard's interpreted benefit toward pre-attack restriction rather than the large post-attack robustness benefit reported in v3.

D1.justification: New Appendix C.1 documents the sampler's seed override and the data-cleaning/retraining correction. Training configuration descriptions are updated, and Appendix D.1 newly identifies the benign fine-tuning optimizer. Existing hardware, distributed-training and memory-management details, and code/model access information remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: The main datasets and tasks remain unchanged. However, Appendix D.1 replaces cybersecurity with chemical security in the benign fine-tuning evaluation, including the corresponding WMDP forget-subject check. Biosecurity and the economics adaptation task remain, making this a limited change in that experiment's domain coverage.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain Max Entropy, Min Posterior, LLMU, RMU, MLAC-AR, and SOPHON-AR for knowledge restriction, and Refusal Trained, R2D2, RepNoise, and RR for refusal. Newly cited Booster and Lisa are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix C.1 reports retain-data cleaning, retraining, and correction of overlapping train/test shuffling orders. Table 9 replaces the main 1,000-step attacks with 500-step attacks and removes the two 5,000-step biosecurity attacks. Section 5.1 and Table 7 revise the chemical loss weight and chemical/cyber training adversaries. Appendix D.1 changes benign fine-tuning from 800 steps with batch size 64 to two epochs with batch size 32. These are substantive reported setting changes, despite C.1's general statement that hyperparameters were unchanged.

E4.justification: V4 adds a five-seed shuffling-sensitivity study in Figure 5 and entropy diagnostics in Figure 6, materially revising the evidence about robustness and convergence. It removes the ablation isolating the retain loss's squared-distance term from Table 5. The existing inner-loop-length and DPO analyses remain; the earlier generalization analysis is moved and extended rather than entirely new.

E5.justification: V3 does not report seed replication counts. V4 explicitly reports averaging three different-seed attack replicates for the main knowledge-restriction results and displays five separate seeded trajectories in Figure 5. This substantially changes replication and variability reporting, although confidence intervals and significance tests are still absent. V3's undisclosed run count does not establish that it used only one run.

E6.justification: Knowledge-restriction results change throughout Table 1, Tables 3–6 and 12, and the heatmaps. TAR's average post-attack accuracies change from 31.3/27.6/29.5 to 35.2/27.1/28.6 for biosecurity/chemical security/cybersecurity under revised conditions, not directly comparable performance gains or losses. Table 5 changes the no-initial-safeguard result from 46.9 to 35.5, versus full TAR's 31.3 and 35.2 respectively. Refusal results in Tables 2 and 11 remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the two-stage TAR procedure remain unchanged: initial safeguarding followed by first-order adversarial training, using entropy or DPO objectives and a retain loss. Data cleaning, sampler corrections, and revised training configurations do not introduce a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: Most prose and the overall section hierarchy remain intact. V4 adds the implementation-update subsection, revises robustness and limitations passages, moves the generalization discussion from Section 5.3 into Appendix D.3, and expands the acknowledgements. These are focused edits and reorganizations.

P2.justification: V4 consolidates v3's Figures 4 and 8 into a three-domain Figure 4, revises heatmap scales and labels, adds the seed-sensitivity figure, and relocates the generalization plot with an added entropy trace. Table 5 loses one ablation row. The overall document format and most other display structures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V4 adds Booster and Lisa to the concurrent-defense literature and cites Qi et al.'s On Evaluating the Durability of Safeguards for Open-Weight LLMs when acknowledging and corroborating vulnerabilities in the earlier release. The broader related-work structure and existing references are retained.

T1.justification: The mathematical objectives, first-order approximation, Random Mapping formulation, and baseline loss definitions remain unchanged. The added entropy and convergence discussion interprets empirical trajectories; it introduces no new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: V4 addresses important validity deficiencies: Appendix C.1 reports correcting retain-data contamination and train/test shuffling overlap, while repeated-seed results and Figure 5 expose limitations obscured by v3's stronger claims. Narrowing the headline robustness claim and documenting practical fine-tuning limitations substantially improve credibility and calibration. The shorter main attack horizon and removed retain-loss ablation reduce evidential scope, and some reporting inconsistencies remain, but these costs are outweighed by the correction of central evaluation flaws.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TAR research. Their main text, algorithms, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–G support reliable comparison, including matching content across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V4 retains original empirical experiments, reports revised knowledge-restriction results, and adds an original analysis of sensitivity to dataloader shuffling seeds.

before.justification: V3 reports original safeguarding experiments on WMDP/MMLU and HarmBench/MT-Bench, plus benign fine-tuning, targeted patching, and component ablations.

title: Tamper-Resistant Safeguards for Open-Weight LLMs

C1.justification: The central contributions remain a fast, data-driven simulator and released RL agents. The introduction replaces 95% goal-reaching on 100 scenes in two hours with 1,000 scenes in 15 hours, while the abstract replaces broadly 'generally capable' agents with the more specific claim of navigating thousands of scenarios.

C2.justification: V2 explains how scene density affects usable CASPS and suggests selecting denser scenes. It adds a mechanism explanation for LiDAR's speed advantage. New Section 4.3 interprets the previously reported approximately 2% unreachable goals as an approximately 98% success ceiling caused by mislabeled road edges.

D1.justification: V2 adds memory-allocation, termination, agent-removal, road-edge handling, nanobind/Gymnasium interface, and Stable Baselines implementation details. Appendix A updates the release from v0.1 to v0.2.0 and the total-compute bound from under 24 to under 2 GPU-days. Appendix C replaces its code link with an anonymization placeholder, although the public link remains elsewhere.

E1.justification: Both versions use WOMD for driving simulation and goal-reaching tasks. Larger training subsets change sample counts, while the added sensor-speed experiment compares simulator configurations within the existing dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: The throughput comparison retains original Nocturne, Nocturne parallelized through PufferLib on 16 CPU cores, and Waymax. The ten-scene training comparison still uses Nocturne, and Table 1 retains the same simulator membership.

E3.justification: Section 3.2 changes the reported training subset for released agents from 500 to 1,000 scenes. V2 adds a radial-filter/LiDAR throughput sweep and a controllable-agent analysis over 512 scenarios. The ten-scene comparison and its Table 2 hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds an observation-modality speed comparison across GPU types and parallel-environment counts in Figure 4, plus a controllable-agent distribution in Figure 3. The existing scenario-count scaling analysis and appendix collision/off-road curves are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions average the training comparison across three seeds and list the same seeds, 42, 12, and 67, in Table 2. The added histogram describes variation between scenes; it does not introduce a new uncertainty-estimation procedure for experimental performance.

E6.justification: The central throughput curves are revised, and Waymax's reported memory-limited parallelism changes from 32 to 16 environments. V2 adds the approximately threefold LiDAR speedup and agent-distribution results. Reported training throughput changes from 20 to 30 million steps/hour, released-agent success from 97% to 95%, and Nocturne training speedup from 25–40x to 30–40x. These revisions do not establish same-setting performance gains; the principal training and scenario-scaling plots are retained.

M1.justification: The Madrona/BVH/road-decimation design, bicycle dynamics, observation modes, rewards, and IPPO approach are retained. Added descriptions of memory allocation and episode termination do not establish that the underlying procedure changed between versions.

P1.justification: The overall section sequence and most prose are retained. V2 makes localized rewrites, adds feature-description paragraphs and Section 4.3, renames Appendix B, removes the acknowledgments/funding section, and switches to author-year citations.

P2.justification: V2 adds a four-scenario illustration and a sensor-throughput figure, and expands the main throughput display from two panels to three with an agent-count histogram. It corrects the swapped ASPS/CASPS caption descriptions, relabels the observation diagram, reformats Table 1, and resizes the unchanged appendix curves into separated panels with added labels.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations for Gymnasium, nanobind, and Stable Baselines, and qualifies its comparison with Waymax by acknowledging the absence of reactive IDM agents. The broader related-work coverage and positioning remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The bicycle-model equations and assumptions in Section 3.2 and Appendix B, and the ASPS formula, are unchanged. Describing Ak as a set rather than a number clarifies notation without changing the metric. No substantive theory or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: V2 makes the speed claims easier to assess through direct sensor comparisons, corrected ASPS/CASPS descriptions, and evidence about controllable-agent counts. Added implementation details also improve clarity. The gains remain limited: the main learning evidence is retained, and the new 1,000-scene/15-hour claim is not reconciled with the retained 1,024-scene/about-200-minute result.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GPUDrive, with matching simulator design, experiments, and Appendices A–D. Their text, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix D retain original simulation and training results and add sensor-throughput measurements and an analysis of controllable-agent counts.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix D report original simulator-throughput measurements, reinforcement-learning performance, scenario-scaling results, and collision and off-road outcomes.

title: GPUDrive: Data-driven, multi-agent driving simulation at 1 million FPS

C1.justification: The introduction expands the released-software contribution from one basic policy-gradient training loop to two training loops. The central claims about million-step throughput, goal-reaching agents and training across thousands of scenarios remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: The conclusion removes specific caveats about training-hyperparameter and reset-overhead bottlenecks, while adding future directions involving multiple datasets and more realistic agents. Section 3.2 replaces the late-appearing-agent explanation with a rationale for filtering trivial goals. The limitations concerning unreachable goals and imperfect driving performance remain.

D1.justification: v3 adds Dockerfile availability, a single-file reproduction workflow taking approximately 16 hours on an A100, and access information for preprocessed WOMD JSON data through Hugging Face. It updates the reproducibility release from v0.2.0 to v0.4.0 and specifies the existing nontrivial-agent initialization threshold as more than two meters from the goal.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate WOMD driving scenarios, retaining the 10-scenario comparison and larger scene collections. NuPlan and NuScenes appear only as proposed future extensions in v3. New scene illustrations and initialization details do not establish additional evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: Figure 3 retains Waymax, original Nocturne and Nocturne parallelized across 16 CPUs; Figure 5 retains Nocturne as the training comparator. PufferLib replaces GPUDrive's training implementation rather than introducing another evaluated baseline.

Appendix A revises the stated RL hardware from RTX 8000/A100 to RTX 4080/A100. The matched 10-scenario protocol and Table 2 hyperparameters remain unchanged; these disclosures do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The observation-modality speed analysis, scene-count scaling analysis and failure discussion are retained. Appendix D's goal-reaching, vehicle-collision and off-road plots reuse the same images, renumbered from Figure 7 to Figure 8 and enlarged. No new ablation or robustness experiment is reported.

E5.justification: Figure 5 adds shaded uncertainty bands to learning curves and removes the completion-time bar chart with error bars. Both versions report three-seed averages and list seeds 42, 12 and 67 in Table 2. The statistical meaning of the new bands is unspecified.

E6.justification: Section 4.2 revises the reported training speedup over Nocturne from 30–40x to 200–300x and the time to solve 10 scenarios from under 15 minutes to under 3 minutes. Figure 5 is revised, and v3 newly reports 200K–500K controlled agent steps per second for PufferLib PPO. These results concern a changed implementation and reported hardware, not an isolated same-setting simulator improvement.

P1.justification: The abstract, initialization discussion and concluding future-work passage receive localized rewrites. v3 adds reproducibility, ethics and acknowledgment sections and reorganizes Appendix A. Most of the original exposition and section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: v3 adds a six-panel simulator-state/agent-view overview, replaces the original scene illustrations, and substantially redesigns Figure 5, including a logarithmic-time learning-curve panel instead of completion-time bars. It relocates the sensor illustration to Appendix A, enlarges Appendix D's plots, updates plotting styles and adopts the conference layout.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to Isaac Gym, Panerati et al.'s quadcopter environment, Gigastep and nuScenes. These modestly extend the surrounding literature and future-work context; the positioning against driving simulators and the comparison in Table 1 remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The ASPS definition, simplified dynamics equation and Appendix B bicycle-model equations and assumptions are unchanged. Numbering the ASPS equation introduces no mathematical revision, and neither version adds theoretical proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 provides clearer reproduction and data-access instructions, specifies agent-selection details, and makes learning variability and simulator observations easier to inspect. These offer a modest overall quality gain. The revised training results use a different implementation, the uncertainty bands remain undefined, and specific training/reset bottleneck caveats disappear without a corresponding diagnostic analysis, limiting the strength of the improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GPUDrive with the same authors, simulator design and experimental framework. The complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original simulator and learning experiments, revises the end-to-end training results in Figure 5, and includes the supplementary driving outcomes in Appendix D.

before.justification: v2 reports original simulator-throughput measurements, reinforcement-learning comparisons and scene-scaling results in Section 4, with goal-reaching, collision and off-road outcomes in Appendix D.

title: GPUDrive: Data-driven, multi-agent driving simulation at 1 million FPS

C1.justification: v2's abstract explicitly claims hallucination reduction without compromising LVLMs' general ability, extending the earlier emphasis on faithful, high-quality text and efficiency. The central SID/CT2S contribution and the critique of holistic input disturbances remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–7 retain the same mathematical content, including attention scoring, contrastive decoding, the additive alternative, and CHAIR definitions. Moving the metric definitions to Appendix A.3 adds no theory. Neither version presents formal theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: The added general-capability evaluations and actual DoLa comparisons modestly strengthen validation beyond v1's hallucination-focused evidence. Clearer organization, explicit manual-setting limitations, and the corrected Shikra SHR display also help. These benefits outweigh limited losses from removing standalone Beam Search controls and dataset-access links, although the inconsistent 7B/8B description remains. The new capability results cover only one backbone, so the overall gain is limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Self-Introspective Decoding (SID). All 32 pages of v1 and 23 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable. Equations, experiments, tables, and figures can be matched despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original SID experiments and reports additional MME/MMBench evaluations and DoLa comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original SID evaluations on POPE, CHAIR, GPT-assisted assessments, efficiency measurements, and ablations, alongside some baseline results attributed to prior work.

title: Self-Introspective Decoding: Alleviating Hallucinations for Large Vision-Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's three contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: contextual token-level hallucination amplification and subtraction, improved faithfulness while preserving general ability, and reduced contrastive-decoding cost. Additional experiments support these existing claims without redefining the contribution.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly discusses residual fine-detail hallucinations in the existing case studies and tentatively attributes them to visual-encoder limitations in Appendix A.6. It also explains InstructBLIP's visualization limitation and adds interpretations of AVISC and VDGD behavior. The main explanation of SID remains unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 provides VDGD's detailed prompt and reimplementation description, identifies backbones for the new LURE/HA-DPO comparisons, and clarifies that Table 6 measures whole-dataset inference time. The anonymous code pointer is removed, while the GitHub address already present in v2 is retained.

E1.justification: v3 adds MathVista, MMVet, and MMMU, extending evaluation to visual mathematics, integrated multimodal capabilities, and multidisciplinary knowledge and reasoning. LLaVA-Bench-in-the-Wild, previously used for qualitative captioning cases, also receives a formal question-answering evaluation in Appendix A.5 and Table 8.

E2.justification: v3 adds evaluated comparisons with LURE and HA-DPO in Table 10, AVISC in Table 13, and VDGD in Table 15. LURE and HA-DPO were previously cited but not experimentally compared; v3 also evaluates their combinations with SID and VCD. Existing main-text comparators remain.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce MathVista test-mini, the 24-image/60-question LLaVA-Bench evaluation, and MMVet's LLM-based scoring. Table 10 adds MiniGPT-4 13B and comparisons combining decoding with auxiliary-network or instruction-tuned systems under greedy decoding. These expand the evaluation design; existing CHAIR/POPE protocols and SID defaults are retained.

E4.justification: v3 extends the plausibility-constraint ablation from POPE to CHAIR and MME in Table 11, tests SID's complementarity with LURE and HA-DPO in Table 10, and adds object/attribute MME breakdowns in Table 9. Earlier layer, pruning, hyperparameter, larger-backbone, and sampling-strategy analyses remain.

E5.justification: Table 5 gains uncertainty values using ± notation, and new Table 11 explicitly reports averages over three runs with three random seeds. v2 already included three-run averages and ± reporting elsewhere. v3 does not define Table 5's uncertainty statistic, and the PDFs do not establish an increase in run counts.

E6.justification: New Tables 8–11 and 15, plus AVISC rows in Table 13, substantially expand reported findings. Most existing results are retained, but Table 5 revises SID's MME score from 1520.2 to 1520.4 and MMBench from 65.1 to 65.0. New Table 15 reports VDGD above SID on MMBench, 65.2 versus 65.0, while SID performs better on its hallucination metrics.

M1.justification: Both versions use CT2S to preserve low-attention vision tokens after early decoder layers and contrast the resulting logits. The scoring rule, decoding equations, and default layer/pruning settings remain unchanged. Applying SID alongside LURE and HA-DPO does not document an alteration to SID itself.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence are largely retained. Changes include localized wording corrections, author and affiliation updates, acknowledgements, expanded discussion and future work, and a new Appendix A.5 that shifts the subsequent appendix numbering.

P2.justification: v3 adds five appendix tables and expands v2 Table 9 into v3 Table 13. Table 5 is reformatted for uncertainty reporting, table captions generally move above their tables, and appendix prompts and cases are packed into shared pages. Figures 1–15 are retained with relocation, resizing, and small label corrections.

R1.justification: v3 adds positioning against AVISC and VDGD, citations for new benchmarks and potential auxiliary detectors, and background references on multimodal learning, federation, and trustworthiness. The main related-work taxonomy and novelty claim remain stable. The Zhao citation's year change refers to the same work.

T1.justification: Equations 1–7 retain the same substantive definitions and reasoning, including contrastive decoding, plausibility constraints, attention scoring, the visual-enhancement alternative, and CHAIR metrics. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens an already extensive evaluation with reasoning benchmarks, broader competitors, and additional constraint and compatibility tests. Its discussion of remaining hallucinations also improves balance. Reporting remains imperfect: Table 5's ± values are undefined, and Tables 5 and 10 give unexplained different SID MME scores, 1520.4 and 1525.3. The additions provide a useful but qualified overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SID research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated figures and renumbered appendix analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds reasoning-benchmark evaluations, additional baseline comparisons, and supplementary analyses in Appendices A.5–A.7.

before.justification: v2 reports original SID experiments across multiple LVLMs, including hallucination benchmarks, general-capability evaluations, efficiency measurements, and ablations.

title: Self-Introspective Decoding: Alleviating Hallucinations for Large Vision-Language Models

C1.justification: The central dataset and automated-annotation contributions remain. v2 extends the headline SOTA claim from two benchmarks to all three using the newly displayed averages, highlights benefits across other model families, and revises the source-count claim from over 90 to over 30.

C2.justification: v2 adds a qualification that classification-based open-question baselines may overestimate generalizability and explains how multiple ROIs support global diagnosis. Conversely, deleting Appendix G removes the explicit warning that generated descriptions may remain inaccurate despite metadata and retrieved knowledge. These change qualifications and interpretation within the retained framework.

D1.justification: Deleting v1 Appendix G removes the preprocessing-code link, collection dates, raw-data release policy, intended licensing, and maintenance/access disclosures. The dataset homepage, source tables, expert-model mapping, and prompt templates remain. v2 additionally specifies initial pretraining on 600K PMC-15M image-text pairs; this is newly disclosed detail rather than evidence that the existing training procedure changed.

E1.justification: Appendix A retains the same source datasets and sample counts, and evaluation still uses VQA-RAD, SLAKE, and PathVQA. The change from over 90 to over 30 sources and the corrected main-text sample total do not establish changed data coverage; the latter already appeared in v1's appendix.

However, v2 Table 4 substantially expands the controlled with/without-pretraining comparison to MiniCPM-V-2.6-8B, InternVL2-8B, and PubMedCLIP. PubMedCLIP previously appeared only as a literature baseline, not in this controlled comparison.

E3.justification: Section 3.3 replaces the described 50-sample SLAKE/MIMIC-CXR GPT-4V alignment study with a random 200-sample evaluation using both medical experts and GPT-4V, with scores normalized to 0–1. VQA reporting also introduces average accuracy across open and closed questions. These revise evaluation design and aggregation; three-epoch VQA fine-tuning remains stated.

E4.justification: The pretraining ablation expands from one model to additional MLLMs and a CLIP model, substantially strengthening the investigation of transfer across architectures. The qualitative coarse-caption, ROI, and retrieval ablations remain, while the ROCO comparison example is removed. The added global-context illustration reuses an existing example rather than supplying an independent case.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results in Table 4 and replaces dataset-specific alignment scores of 8.2/10 and 8.9/10 with expert and LLM averages of 0.85 and 0.86 under the revised evaluation. LLaVA-Med baseline entries change, including VQA-RAD open/closed scores from 55.5/66.5 to 61.5/84.2, without establishing identical experimental conditions. The proposed model's open/closed VQA scores remain unchanged; its stated PathVQA pretraining gain is corrected from 13.25% to 8.3%.

M1.justification: The metadata integration, expert ROI localization, top-eight knowledge retrieval, and hierarchical generation prompt remain substantively unchanged. LLaVA-MedCaptioner/LLaVA-Med++ are renamed LLaVA-Medcap/LLaVA-Tri; LLaMA3 and multiscale feature extraction were already described in v1, including Appendix B. No new algorithmic component is established.

P1.justification: There is extensive rewriting of the introduction, related work, data-format explanation, generation description, and dataset-analysis narrative. Section 4 is reorganized into model alignment and broader pretraining evaluation, terminology and model names are revised throughout, and the datasheet section is removed.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the quality table, adds average columns and a separate ablation table, merges the word-count chart into the statistical overview, and redraws the disease word cloud. Several examples move into the appendix, and an existing alignment example is displayed again to explain global context. The ROCO panel and relative-word-count bar chart are removed, although the latter's 3.6% finding remains in prose.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting InternVL and MiniCPM-V and removes works including PaLM-E, the ISIC examples, and Datasheets for Datasets. The principal positioning against report-dependent medical datasets and existing medical multimodal models remains. The author–year citation conversion is a presentation change.

improvement.justification: Expert assessment in Table 2 and broader controlled pretraining experiments in Table 4 strengthen evidence for annotation quality and dataset utility beyond v1's GPT-only quality assessment and single-model ablation. The PathVQA gain correction also improves accuracy. These benefits provide a limited net improvement, tempered by removal of useful datasheet documentation and the annotation-error caveat, together with sparse details about the new expert evaluation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MedTrinity-25M. Their complete main texts and appendices, including figures, tables, and graphical prompt templates, support reliable comparison. Renamed models and relocated material can be matched.

after.justification: v2 retains original VQA results and reports additional model-pretraining comparisons and expert evaluation of generated annotations.

before.justification: v1 reports original VQA experiments with and without MedTrinity-25M pretraining, GPT-4V annotation-alignment evaluations, and dataset analyses.

title: MedTrinity-25M: A Large-scale Multimodal Dataset with Multigranular Annotations for Medicine

C1.justification: The dataset and automated-pipeline contributions, broad applicability claims, and claim of state-of-the-art performance on all three VQA benchmarks remain. Revised headline accuracies change the reported evidence without changing these central claims' stated scope.

C2.justification: The interpretation that multigranular alignment benefits medical models remains unchanged. Table 3 rewords the existing warning about classification-based open-answer evaluation and training-test answer overlap, without introducing a distinct limitation or mechanism explanation.

D1.justification: Section 4.1 revises the documented fine-tuning duration and explicitly attributes the 15-epoch setting to following LLaVA-Med. Data-processing instructions, expert-model lists, prompt templates, and dataset access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same MedTrinity-25M sources and coverage, documented in Appendix A, and evaluate on VQA-RAD, SLAKE, and PathVQA. No datasets, tasks, populations, or test scenarios are added or removed.

E2.justification: Table 3 retains all nine comparators and their benchmark participation. Table 4 also retains the same model comparisons. Separating non-MLLM and MLLM rows changes presentation, not comparator membership.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the reported fine-tuning budget from 3 to 15 epochs on each of the three VQA datasets, adding that this follows LLaVA-Med. This fivefold budget revision substantially changes the stated conditions of the central experiments; the PDFs do not establish whether experiments were rerun or the description was corrected.

E4.justification: Table 4 revises the evidence for the existing alignment ablation by replacing both aligned and unaligned LLaVA-Tri results. The ablation question, other model comparisons, qualitative component analyses, and appendix studies remain unchanged; no new ablation or robustness test is introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports new repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The parenthesized additions in Table 4 remain performance gains, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Reported LLaVA-Tri averages change from 81.6/87.8/82.8 to 75.0/87.8/65.3 on VQA-RAD/SLAKE/PathVQA. Table 4's corresponding alignment gains change from 10.8/6.1/8.3 to 2.0/5.0/1.6 points. PathVQA open accuracy now ties LLaVA-Med at 37.9. Baseline component scores remain unchanged, while Table 3 removes average entries. These are substantial replacement results under a changed reported budget, not established same-setting performance declines.

M1.justification: The annotation pipeline, retrieval and ROI components, LLaVA-Medcap generation procedure, and LLaVA-Tri architecture remain unchanged. The revised downstream training duration is an experimental-setting change.

P1.justification: There are localized wording changes in the training-protocol passage and Table 3 caption, together with the updated version stamp. The title, section organization, broader narrative, and appendix text remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Table 3 is reorganized into non-MLLM and MLLM blocks, introduces Ref columns, removes Average columns and asterisk markers, and moves its rewritten caption below the table. Nearby content shifts slightly; all figures and appendix layouts are unchanged.

R1.justification: The related-work section and bibliography are unchanged. Regrouping existing comparators does not add prior work or revise the dataset and pipeline's novelty positioning.

T1.justification: No mathematical definitions, formal assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs are added, removed, or revised. The methodological descriptions and appendices retain the same content.

improvement.justification: Table 3 makes the existing distinction between classification-based reference scores and MLLM results more explicit, modestly improving comparison clarity. Removing average columns reduces convenience, but the component scores remain available. The changed training budget and replacement results do not themselves establish stronger empirical quality; the supported improvement is limited to reporting and presentation.

A1.justification: Both complete, readable 25-page PDFs describe the same MedTrinity-25M and LLaVA-Tri work. Text and rendered-page comparisons support reliable matching throughout, including Tables 1-6, Figures 1-14, and Appendices A-F.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical studies, including revised LLaVA-Tri results in Tables 3-4.

before.justification: v2 reports original VQA experiments, alignment ablations, expert and LLM annotation evaluations, and a caption comparison in Appendix B.

title: MedTrinity-25M: A Large-scale Multimodal Dataset with Multigranular Annotations for Medicine

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: success-rate-based adaptive exploration and exploitation, efficient learning-free KDE-RFF reward construction, and improved sample efficiency and convergence stability. Rewriting and the emphasis on 'extremely sparse' rewards do not establish a different core contribution.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of the comparative visitation patterns, including explanations for SASR's exploration and the narrower behavior of SAC and NoisyNet. It replaces v1's unresolved reward-implies-completion limitation with the segmentation discussion in Section 4.2.2. Dense-reward applicability and retention-rate limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix G adds task objectives, initial conditions, target randomization, and episode limits; Appendix C identifies the timing hardware. Conversely, v3 removes the SASR source-code link and the statement identifying CleanRL or original-author implementations for baselines. Existing network structures, hyperparameter values, and general computing-resource information remain.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same seven MuJoCo tasks, two robotic tasks, and MountainCar. The new visitation and timing analyses use retained tasks; Appendix G documents existing task configurations without establishing additional coverage.

E2.justification: The eight baselines in Table 1 are unchanged. v3 adds NoisyNet to the MountainCar exploration comparison alongside ReLara, #Explo, and SAC, and introduces a timing comparison against SASR without RFF and backbone SAC.

E3.justification: New evaluation procedures measure MountainCar visitation densities over four consecutive 25,000-step windows and compare training time across six retained tasks on an RTX A6000. Existing return comparisons and hyperparameter settings are retained; Appendix G's newly documented episode limits do not establish changed experimental settings.

E4.justification: v3 adds substantive tests of two central design rationales: comparative exploration dynamics in Figure 5 and computational efficiency with versus without RFF in Appendix C. Figure 4 also adds estimated success-rate profiles to the AntStand case study. The five original component and sensitivity ablations remain.

E5.justification: Section 5 changes unspecified 'multiple instances' with different seeds to an explicit ten instances per setting. This discloses the run count without establishing an increase in runs. Existing mean and standard-error reporting is retained.

E6.justification: Table 1 and all five original ablation tables match numerically across versions. v3 nevertheless adds distinct efficiency results and comparative exploration findings: Table 3 reports faster training with RFF on all six tested tasks, including RobotReach at 7.07 versus 11.12 hours without RFF, while Figure 5 reports differing visitation dynamics across five methods.

M1.justification: The Beta-sampling, KDE-RFF, and SAC pipeline and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. However, Section 4.2.2 adds reward-delimited subsequences with maximum-step success/failure labeling for rewards that do not indicate task completion, extending beyond v1's explicit completion-reward premise. The PDFs do not establish a procedure change in the retained experiments.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations, and experimental discussion undergo extensive rewriting and condensation. 'Hidden value' becomes 'inherent value,' Section 4.2 gains dedicated complexity and implementation subsections, and the appendices are reorganized around the added timing and task documentation.

P2.justification: v1 Figures 5–9 are consolidated into v3 Figure 6(a–e), with resized plots and revised axes and legends. v3 adds a visitation-density figure and timing table, redraws Figure 4 with estimated-rate overlays, and relocates figures and appendix tables.

R1.justification: v3 expands exploration references, including count-based methods by Lobel, Machado, and others, distributional RND by Yang, and NoisyNet. It removes the imitation-learning paragraph and associated citations. The broad reward-shaping taxonomy and positioning relative to ReLara remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A, Table 2 substantively revises the Gaussian kernel/spectral-density pair, adding an explicit exponential and bandwidth-dependent expressions. The remaining RFF and complexity derivations are retained. The revised table's bandwidth dependence is inconsistent with the main-text formulas in Equations 7 and 9.

improvement.justification: The direct RFF timing comparison and comparative exploration analysis strengthen evidence for central efficiency and exploration claims, while explicit run counts and task configurations improve assessability. These provide a limited overall gain over the retained performance evidence. Benefits are tempered by removal of code-access and baseline implementation information and inconsistencies in the revised Gaussian formulas.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SASR, the same reward-shaping research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across revisions.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds comparative state-visitation analyses and training-time measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on ten tasks, including baseline comparisons, episodic returns with standard errors, and five ablation studies.

title: Highly Efficient Self-Adaptive Reward Shaping for Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The introductory contribution statement now explicitly claims exploration through both reward perturbations and higher rewards for unvisited states; v3 emphasized stochastic reward-driven policy diversification. The central claims about autonomous shaping, computational efficiency, sample efficiency, and convergence stability remain.

C2.justification: V3 stresses randomly rewarding arbitrary states, whereas v4 explains an implicit novelty preference: failed visited states lose success probability while unvisited states retain Beta(1,1). V4 also discusses dimensionality and distribution mismatches as disadvantages of adding actions to KDE inputs. The dense-reward and retention-rate limitations are retained.

D1.justification: V4 adds a source-code access link, explicitly defines the linear reward-scaling function, and supplies task state dimensions in Table 14, including 84×84 Atari inputs. It also documents the added tasks' reward conditions and episode limits. Existing architecture, default hyperparameter, hardware, and RFF timing disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: V4 adds RobotSlide, RobotPickPlace, and five Atari games: Pitfall, Frogger, Montezuma's Revenge, Solaris, and Freeway. AntSpeed, AntVeryFar, and WalkerKeep disappear from both the main evaluation and task appendix. The new manipulation objectives and image-based Atari domain substantially change coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 and Figure 3 retain the eight previous baselines and add DRND-online and GFA-RFE, materially expanding the main comparative evaluation. RND also joins the MountainCar exploration-density comparison in Figure 5; its presence in v3's main benchmark did not previously extend to that analysis.

E3.justification: V3 describes Table 1 as summarizing returns throughout training; v4 specifies evaluation of final models over 100 episodes. New experiments introduce SASR-normalized maximum-memory and training-time metrics, plus task-specific horizons such as ten million training steps for Pitfall and Montezuma. Shared network and hyperparameter defaults remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V4 adds a six-task state-only versus state-action reward ablation, comparative runtime and memory analyses, and RND to the exploration-density case study. The previous bandwidth sensitivity analysis remains in Appendix A.5 and Table 11 despite losing its main-text plot. The original RFF timing ablation is retained as Table 5.

E5.justification: Both versions specify ten instances with different random seeds and report means with standard errors. V4's 100-episode final-model evaluation changes the testing protocol, but no different uncertainty estimator, increased training-run count, confidence-interval procedure, or significance test is specified. Changed error values alone are result changes.

E6.justification: Main comparison and retained ablation values are extensively replaced, alongside new task, comparator, and resource results. For example, Table 1's SASR AntStand entry changes from 39.12±2.86 to 94.9±0.0 under the revised evaluation summary, not a demonstrated same-setting gain. New Montezuma results report DRND-online at 6828.5 versus SASR at 6737.9.

M1.justification: The core SASR procedure, Algorithm 1, losses, and network architectures remain unchanged. New Appendix A.4 proposes optional procedures for automatically selecting kernel bandwidth and RFF dimension. These are limited procedural additions, not documented replacements for the fixed settings used in the experiments.

P1.justification: V4 copyedits and condenses passages, swaps the implementation and complexity subsections, moves the bandwidth discussion into the appendix, and regroups appendices under A.1–A.7. Author and acknowledgement text also changes. These are localized editorial and organizational revisions within the retained narrative.

P2.justification: The ICLR template changes typography and page layout throughout. Figures 2–3 reorganize and expand the task panels; Table 1 is transposed to task rows; Figure 5 gains an RND row; and Figure 6 introduces the state-action comparison while removing the bandwidth panel. New resource, ablation, and state-dimension tables substantially revise the displays.

R1.justification: V4 adds several references, including Mahankali et al. (2024), Zhang et al. (2024), and Wilcox (2011), while removing the multitask reward-agent preprint and Ma et al. (2023). The intrinsic-motivation versus inherent-value taxonomy and principal comparison with ReLara remain substantially intact.

T1.justification: The existing RFF and computational-complexity derivations are retained. Appendix A.4 adds Silverman's bandwidth formula, the dimension prescription M = O(epsilon^-2 log(N/delta)), and a kernel-approximation norm criterion. These are limited mathematical additions without a new convergence or optimality proof.

improvement.justification: V3's efficiency evidence chiefly compared SASR with its RFF ablation and SAC; v4 adds direct runtime and memory comparisons against reward-shaping competitors, addressing an important gap behind the efficiency claim. Added competitive baselines, visual Atari tests, and the state-action ablation substantially strengthen validation, while the code link improves reproducibility documentation. Three control tasks are lost, and the changed evaluation summary prevents interpreting higher scores as method improvements, but the net gain in relevant empirical support is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SASR research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support matching retained, relocated, and revised material.

after.justification: V4 reports original experiments on fourteen tasks, including Atari games, together with ablations, exploration analyses, and comparative runtime and memory measurements.

before.justification: V3 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments on ten tasks, exploration case studies, component ablations, and training-time measurements.

title: Highly Efficient Self-Adaptive Reward Shaping for Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The central claim of efficient feedback-conditioned diffusion control remains. v2 explicitly adds theoretical derivation and acceleration compatible with DDIM to its stated contributions, while dropping v1's assertion that the method introduces no extra hyperparameters. These extend the existing contribution rather than redefine the research objective.

C2.justification: v2 explains diffusion's advantage through horizon-wide objective-guided optimization, adds interpretations of obstacle-shift generalization and independent DDIM acceleration, and discusses sample-specific fluid sensitivity in Appendix G. The offline-training and physical-prior limitations largely retain their meaning after relocation to Appendix I.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, explicit RDM thresholds, DDIM step counts and eta settings, model horizons, and random-obstacle movement rules. Conversely, it removes substantial local reproduction information: Gaussian data-generation distributions, exact obstacle/exit coordinate tables, smoke-accounting procedures, and the explicit 2D guidance intensity. This is a substantial mixed revision of reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: The two physical domains and FO/PO settings remain, but v2 adds evaluation on randomly shifted internal obstacles. It removes the sparse-time and linearly decreasing Burgers target scenarios and narrows fluid-control corruption coverage from four probabilities to p=0.1. These substantially change the tested requirements and environments.

E2.justification: Aggregate comparisons retain the same baseline families. However, the fluid case studies expand from CL-DiffPhyCon-only examples in v1 Figure 8 to explicit comparisons with BC, BPPO, RDM, and DiffPhyCon in v2 Figures 4 and 9–12. The DiffPhyCon-9 to DiffPhyCon-14 change principally concerns experimental settings.

E3.justification: v2 reports 50 fluid test samples per map setting, versus v1's 500 test trajectories, and changes timing hardware from A100 to A6000. Fluid scores become a minimized failure objective rather than a maximized success fraction. DiffPhyCon suffixes are described as replanning intervals, with the 2D interval 9 replaced by 14. DDIM introduces 30/75-step evaluations. Retained 1D FO timings are rescaled by 60/50 from minutes to per-sample seconds, rather than demonstrating faster execution.

E4.justification: v1's target-form analysis and random-control-probability sweep disappear. v2 adds obstacle-shift generalization testing and DDIM accuracy/runtime comparisons. Fluid case studies now compare methods on individual samples and include poor outcomes, such as the DDIM failure in Figure 10, substantially revising the supplementary evidence.

E5.justification: v2 Appendix G newly states that each method performs stably on individual samples through multiple evaluations. This adds qualitative repeated-evaluation information, but supplies no counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or numerical variability estimates. It does not establish an increase in runs.

E6.justification: Most retained Burgers objective values are unchanged, but CL-DiffPhyCon's PO value changes from 0.0092 to 0.0090. New DDIM rows include FO objective 0.0112 at 0.7585 seconds. The fluid results are replaced by FM/RM comparisons, with CL-DiffPhyCon objectives 0.3371/0.3485. These are new reported results under revised settings, not directly comparable improvements over v1's success fractions. Target-form and corruption-sweep result entries are removed.

M1.justification: v2 adds DDIM sampling to both synchronous initialization and asynchronous control generation (Section 4.4). The underlying two-model procedure, feedback conditioning, and shifting noisy horizon remain. The extensive SDE reformulation does not establish a replacement of the base algorithm.

P1.justification: Background and method exposition are extensively rewritten around SDEs and initializing/transition distributions. Experimental questions and discussion are reorganized, and the numbered appendix becomes topic-specific Appendices A–I, with limitations moved there. These are substantial narrative and structural changes beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 adds a comparative sampling schematic and redraws the method overview. Main tables combine objectives and runtimes; the timing bar chart is replaced by tabulated reporting. New comparative trajectory panels, DDIM rows, sample-level objective labels, and hatched unobserved regions substantially revise the figures and tables across both main text and appendices.

R1.justification: v2 adds focused positioning against Rolling Diffusion and discusses the already-cited AR-Diffusion as related asynchronous generation, distinguishing environmental interaction and distribution-derived construction. It also adds DDIM, SDE, and inverse-problem references. The broader positioning against classical control, reinforcement learning, and diffusion control remains.

T1.justification: v1's brief decomposition and transition proposition are substantially expanded into an augmented-distribution theorem, asynchronous marginal and closed-loop propositions, and SDE/Tweedie/VP-DDPM derivations in v2 Sections 3–4 and Appendices A–C. This goes beyond notation changes. The new formulation also introduces an inconsistency between its Gaussian covariance and the noise multiplier used in training.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful DDIM efficiency and obstacle-shift evidence and clearer comparative figures, but removes robustness analyses and substantial data-generation detail. Its expanded theoretical foundation also introduces an unresolved inconsistency: unlike v1's standard-deviation noise scaling, v2 Section 4.2 multiplies standard Gaussian noise by s(t)^2 sigma(t)^2, while Appendix A Equation 23 specifies that quantity as the covariance. The PDFs do not establish whether this affects only exposition or implementation. These benefits and unresolved harms prevent a reliable net quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CL-DiffPhyCon for the same two physical-control domains. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: v2 retains original control experiments and reports additional DDIM and random-obstacle-map results, including numerical comparisons and appendix visualizations.

before.justification: v1 reports original Burgers and incompressible-fluid simulations, control objectives, inference timings, and trajectory visualizations in the main text and appendices.

title: CL-DiffPhyCon: Closed-loop Diffusion Control of Complex Physical Systems

C1.justification: The main contributions remain theoretically motivated asynchronous closed-loop diffusion control, reduced sampling cost, compatibility with DDIM, and strong physical-control performance. The expanded experiments support these existing claims without materially redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly acknowledges the absence of optimization-performance bounds under guided sampling, replacing v2’s future-work discussion of incorporating PDE priors. improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's small TDEC deletion sets by testing structured author-profile removal on additional model families and cumulative effects of sequential deletion. improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the connection between the method and its supporting evidence: Proposition 1 now treats rectangular features, MLP controls test the need for downstream graph processing, and runtime and ESNR analyses expose practical and interpretive limits. after.justification: V3 retains those original experiments and adds runtime measurements, MLP comparisons and edge signal-to-noise ratio analyses.

before.justification: V2 reports original synthetic and real-world node-classification experiments, spectral-clustering results, ablations and simulations in its main text and appendices.

improvement.justification: v4 improves mathematical clarity and internal consistency by correcting the parameter bounds in Proposition 1 and the summation index and terminology in Appendix A.3. after.justification: v4 retains these original empirical results in Section 3 and the appendices, including benchmark performance, runtime measurements, ablations, and simulations.

before.justification: v3 reports original synthetic and real-world node-classification experiments in Section 3, plus runtime measurements, ablations, clustering experiments, and simulations in the appendices.

title: Joint Graph Rewiring and Feature Denoising via Spectral Resonance

The rewritten contributions emphasize explicit policy parameterization without materially changing these claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds boundary concentration as a possible explanation for TAWAC performance and skewness as an explanation for Beta's Mountain Car performance. Its limitations remove the proposed large-scale initialization/annealing remedy and add the dimensional difficulty of exact boundary projection. The offline failure of light-tailed policies remains acknowledged.

These disclosures do not by themselves establish implementation changes.

E6.justification: Offline boxplots, aggregate comparisons and learning curves are revised across algorithms. For example, Figure 18's InAC Student's t curve on Hopper-medium-expert ends around 85–90 in v1 versus 60–65 in v2, alongside a changed reported learning rate. improvement.justification: V2 makes the study easier to follow and implement through clearer algorithm integration, consolidated online comparisons and fuller clipping and hyperparameter documentation. after.justification: V2 reports original online and offline evaluations in Section 5 and Appendix E, including revised results and an added boundary-density analysis.

improvement.justification: v3 adds useful sensitivity and sampling-cost evidence plus a code-access pointer, while retaining the core experimental results.
