title: Agent Security Bench (ASB): Formalizing and Benchmarking Attacks and Defenses in LLM-based Agents

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same substantive claims: efficient spatial control through conditional decoding, competitive image quality and consistency, and arbitrary-resolution generation. The appendix extensions do not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly discusses spatial controls overriding conflicting text prompts and presents reduced control strength as mitigation. Section 4.3 newly attributes encoder-performance differences to pretraining-data alignment. Earlier limitations concerning portability and simultaneous multiple controls remain.

D1.justification: Section 4.2 newly specifies height/width sampling in increments of 16 and a rotary-position-encoding maximum length of 2304, elaborating the existing resolution range and token cap. Appendix A.2 supplies control-dropping probability, grayscale-grid construction, and the new fine-tuning budget. Hardware disclosures and the promised code-release status are unchanged.

E1.justification: The original datasets and control modalities are retained. V2 adds limited scenarios involving synthetic resolution maps without spatial-content guidance and prompts conflicting with depth or edge controls (Figures 8–9). The source of approximately 1M training pairs for the new resolution experiment is unspecified.

E2.justification: New Table 9 evaluates OmniGen and Lumina-mGPT on ADE20K segmentation and MultiGen-20M canny, HED, and depth tasks. Lumina-mGPT was previously cited but not quantitatively evaluated. Existing ControlVAR and diffusion-model comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: New experiments include fine-tuning LlamaGen-XL on approximately 1M text-image pairs for 30k steps, a six-value alpha sweep from 1 to 0, and failure-case comparisons at alpha 1 and 0.4. Existing benchmark settings remain unchanged; the expanded multi-resolution recipe documents previously unspecified details.

E4.justification: V2 adds qualitative control-strength sensitivity examples in Figure 7 and text-versus-spatial-control failure cases in Figure 9, including comparisons with ControlNet v1.1 and ControlNet++. These focused analyses supplement the unchanged encoder, fusion, training-strategy, and decoding-versus-prefilling ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V2's added comparisons continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice; its alpha sweep is a sensitivity experiment.

E6.justification: Tables 1–8 retain their values. Table 9 adds baseline scores while repeating ControlAR's earlier scores; for example, OmniGen reports segmentation mIoU 44.23 versus ControlAR's 39.95, and HED SSIM 82.37 versus 85.63. Figures 7–9 add qualitative outcomes. Section 3.3 replaces the 361M-parameter ControlNet++ comparison with an approximately 0.05T-MAC overhead report at 512×512.

M1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds localized adaptations: skipping control fusion with 50% probability during training and scaling control tokens by alpha during inference; and supplying synthetic grayscale grids for resolution control without a content-bearing spatial image. The core encoder, conditional-decoding architecture, and loss remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are largely retained, with localized revisions to the equation explanation, resolution recipe, and encoder interpretation. The appendix gains experimental exploration and failure discussion sections. Sections A.3 and A.4 duplicate the limitations paragraph, introducing some editorial redundancy.

P2.justification: V2 adds Table 9 and Figures 7–9 for new comparisons, control-strength examples, synthetic resolution maps, and failures. Original appendix Figures 7–13 are retained as Figures 10–16. Existing main figures and table designs remain substantially unchanged, with localized page reflow.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations to ControlVideo and OmniGen and expands discussion of the already-cited Lumina-mGPT through direct evaluation and a contrast between resolution-conditioning approaches. The broader positioning as an efficient framework for controllable next-token image generation remains intact.

T1.justification: Equation 4 is recast from a conditional-probability factorization into a layerwise projection-and-addition expression. The projection, addition, and one-position shift were already described in v1 Sections 3.2–3.3. This reformulation introduces no substantive new mathematical assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

improvement.justification: Table 9 provides useful contemporary comparison, while the new failure cases make the tradeoff between text adherence and spatial consistency more transparent. Added resolution-training details improve reproducibility. These gains are limited by mostly qualitative validation of the new adaptations and duplicated appendix discussion; the main benchmark evidence remains unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ControlAR and retain matching core methods, benchmarks, and original appendix examples. All 23 pages of v1 and 25 pages of v2, including equations, tables, figures, and appendices, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds comparative measurements in Table 9 and qualitative experiments on control strength, resolution-only conditioning, and failure cases.

before.justification: Sections 4.2–4.3 report original image-generation benchmarks, ablations, efficiency measurements, and generated examples, with additional results in the appendix.

title: ControlAR: Controllable Image Generation with Autoregressive Models

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same claims about efficient spatial control of autoregressive generation, competitive performance against diffusion methods, and arbitrary-resolution generation.

C2.justification: The explanations of encoder and fusion performance are unchanged. Appendices A.3–A.4 retain the same limitations concerning model portability, simultaneous control images, and conflicts between text prompts and spatial controls.

D1.justification: Implementation and reproducibility information remains identical, including preprocessing, hyperparameters, batch sizes, GPU hours, and the eight A100 80GB GPUs. Both abstracts retain the same repository link and statement that code, models, and a demo will soon be available.

E1.justification: Both versions use ImageNet-1K, ADE20K, COCOStuff, and MultiGen-20M for the same class-to-image and text-to-image control tasks. Arbitrary-resolution generation and the appendix test scenarios are also retained unchanged.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is identical: ControlVAR in Table 1; GLIGEN, T2I-Adapter, Uni-ControlNet, UniControl, ControlNet, and ControlNet++ in Tables 2–3; and OmniGen and Lumina-mGPT in Appendix Table 9. The conditional-prefilling comparison is also unchanged.

E3.justification: The 256×256 C2I and 512×512 T2I evaluations, multi-resolution sampling, metrics, model configurations, dataset splits, and training settings match throughout Sections 4.1–4.2 and Appendices A.1–A.2.

E4.justification: Tables 4–6 retain the same encoder, fusion, and training-strategy ablations. The decoding/prefilling comparison, resolution analysis, control-strength examples, and prompt-control failure cases in Figures 2 and 6–9 are unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions use the same point-estimate reporting without reported repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Table 1 retains the caveat that ControlVAR FID values are estimated from histograms.

E6.justification: All numerical results, plotted trends, and qualitative examples match. For example, ControlAR's canny F1 score remains 37.08 in Table 2 and its COCOStuff FID remains 14.51 in Table 3. Appendix Table 9 and Figures 7–16 are also unchanged.

M1.justification: The control encoder, conditional decoding, token fusion, and MR-ControlAR procedure in Section 3 are unchanged. Appendix A.2 already contains the control-strength adjustment and grayscale resolution-control procedures in v2.

P1.justification: The running header changes from 'Preprint.' to 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025', and the arXiv version/date stamp is updated. Two superscript footnote markers before the introduction are removed; the remaining wording and section structure are unchanged.

P2.justification: The header and arXiv stamp displays change, and removing the page 2 footnote markers slightly reflows the opening paragraph. All nine tables and sixteen figures retain identical formatting and placement; page bodies from pages 3–25 are visually identical.

R1.justification: The cited works and research positioning are unchanged, including Section 2's distinction from ControlVAR's next-scale prediction. The discussion of OmniGen and Lumina-mGPT in Appendix A.2 already appears in v2.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(4), covering autoregressive factorization, the training objective, and conditional decoding, are identical. Neither the main text nor the appendices introduce revised mathematical reasoning or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 updates publication metadata and provides a small typographic cleanup. The scientific content, empirical evidence, reproducibility information, and limitations remain unchanged throughout the main text and appendices, so these edits produce no meaningful net difference in overall paper quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same ControlAR work with 25 readable pages, including the main text, Appendices A.1–A.5, equations, nine tables, and sixteen figures. No material gaps prevent comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains the original ControlAR experimental results in Section 4 and Appendix A.2, including quantitative benchmark measurements and qualitative generation examples.

before.justification: v2 reports original ControlAR generation experiments and ablations in Section 4, together with additional comparisons, control-strength experiments, and resolution-generation results in Appendix A.2.

title: ControlAR: Controllable Image Generation with Autoregressive Models

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same novelty and capability claims concerning explainable forgery detection/localization, MMTD-Set, domain tags and performance across manipulation types. The FFAA discussion contextualizes these existing contributions.

C2.justification: Interpretations concerning domain conflicts, decoupled training, SAM's semantic capabilities and robustness are unchanged. Appendix A.1 retains the same limitations for identity switching and full-face generation, along with the same proposed future work.

D1.justification: The LLaVA-v1.5-13B configuration, LoRA settings, hardware, learning rates, batch sizes and training epochs remain unchanged. Both versions retain the same repository link, dataset-construction instructions and full appendix prompts.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same PhotoShop benchmarks, FFHQ/FaceApp DeepFake data and COCO-derived AIGC-Editing data. Table 7 and Appendix A.2 retain the same training and evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged within Tables 1–4 and the qualitative comparisons. The newly cited FFAA is discussed as related work but is not added to any reported experimental comparison.

E3.justification: The versions retain the same splits, dataset counts, model configurations, training schedules, ACC/F1/IoU/CSS metrics and 0.5 threshold. The JPEG/Gaussian degradation settings and ablation procedures also remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Both contain the same DTG-removal and LLM-removal ablations, JPEG/Gaussian robustness study, answer word clouds and qualitative examples. Tables 5–6, Figure 5 and Appendix A.3–A.5 provide unchanged analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or formal significance tests. The same point estimates and training curves are retained.

E6.justification: Tables 1–6, Figure 5 and appendix examples retain the same results. For example, FakeShield's IMD2020 ACC/F1 remains 0.83/0.90 in Table 1, and its DSO CSS remains 0.8873 in Table 3. Relocated figures preserve their findings.

M1.justification: Sections 3.2–3.5 retain the same domain-tag-guided detection module, tamper comprehension module, SAM localization, LoRA training and loss functions. The notation edits and redrawn dataset-construction diagram do not change the procedure.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized prose additions about FFAA, adjusts notation and figure-reference wording, updates bibliography metadata, adds an affiliation and removes the submission header. The section hierarchy and most prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn into three tampering-category rows and its caption clarifies Au/Tp terminology. Figure 4 moves from page 9 to 10, while Table 5 and Figure 5 move from page 10 to 9. Other displays are retained with limited caption and page-layout changes.

R1.justification: v3 adds Huang et al. (2024), FFAA, and discusses its relationship to FakeShield's GPT-assisted dataset construction, tampering coverage and localization in Sections 2.2 and 3.1. A footnote credits its influence on Figure 2's design. Other reference changes update metadata for existing citations.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5 preserve the same forward computations and training objectives. Added function notation such as Gdt(·) is cosmetic; no mathematical assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs are added or revised.

improvement.justification: v3 improves attribution and research positioning by acknowledging FFAA, explaining the relationship between the works and crediting Figure 2's design inspiration. The reorganized diagram also clarifies the construction workflow. These are modest benefits: the methods, experimental evidence, reproducibility information and appendix limitations remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FakeShield study and contain complete, readable methods, equations, tables, figures and appendices. Text comparison and visual inspection support a reliable comparison, including all appendix pages.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experimental results and appendix analyses. Results retained from v1 still constitute original empirical outcomes of the work.

before.justification: v1 reports original detection, localization and explanation results in Tables 1–4, robustness and ablation results in Tables 5–6 and Figure 5, and qualitative analyses in the appendix.

title: FakeShield: Explainable Image Forgery Detection and Localization via Multi-modal Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's four contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about explainable forgery detection, MMTD-Set, domain-tag guidance, decoupled localization, and broad tampering coverage. New experiments support these existing claims without redefining the principal contribution.

C2.justification: Appendix A.3 newly explains implicit error correction through training on potentially inaccurate detector descriptions and attributes the unsuccessful explicit correction variant to possible interference between text and mask optimization. A.4 interprets the unseen-generator results as generalization evidence. The limitations concerning identity switching and full-face generation remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Section 4.1 removes the previously disclosed batch sizes of 24 and 48 while retaining hardware, LoRA settings, learning rates, and epoch counts. New appendix passages document correction supervision, input combinations, and the generators and sample count used for additional testing. The existing repository link moves into the abstract without establishing a change in resource availability.

E1.justification: v4 adds Seq-DeepFake evaluation and tests images produced by previously unseen ControlNet and SDXL inpainting generators (Table 2 and Appendix A.4). It also adds DeepFake localization evaluation. These materially broaden the tested manipulation sources and generalization scenarios. DFFD is the existing FaceApp/FFHQ coverage under a clearer label, not another newly added dataset.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds Exposing and RECCE alongside CADDM and HiFi-DeepFake, including comparisons on the retained DFFD data. The general detection, localization, and explanation comparator sets remain unchanged. The new generator experiments reuse MVSS-Net, CAT-Net, and HiFi-Net rather than introducing further comparison methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include correction-supervised and alternative-input controls in Appendix A.3, plus testing on 2,000 newly constructed tampered images from unseen generators in A.4. Section 4.2 specifies retraining Exposing and RECCE. Existing metrics, thresholds, learning rates, and training epoch counts remain unchanged; omitted batch sizes do not establish an actual training-setting change.

E4.justification: Appendix A.3 adds controlled studies asking whether explicit correction of detector descriptions improves localization and which instruction, image, domain-tag, and description inputs are effective. Appendix A.4 adds unseen-generator generalization tests, and Table 6 extends the domain-tag ablation to IMD2020. These substantially expand the evidence probing the architecture and generalization beyond v3's retained ablations and JPEG/noise tests.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty bars for the experimental results. The added tables continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include Seq-DeepFake ACC/F1 of 0.84/0.91, DeepFake localization IoU/F1 of 0.14/0.22, and Tables 8–10's ablation and unseen-generator results. ControlNet and SDXL detection accuracy is 0.99, but ControlNet pixel-level F1 is 0.24 versus HiFi-Net's 0.28. DeepFake dialogue examples gain IoUs and one revised response. Existing benchmark values are largely retained; Table 2's original DFFD entries merely round to two decimals. The learning curve also revises plotted epoch positions.

M1.justification: FakeShield retains the same domain-tag generator, decoupled detection and localization modules, TCM/SAM pipeline, LoRA adaptation, and loss components. Appendix A.3 tests correction and input variants as ablations; it does not replace the proposed method. The Figure 3 input correction agrees with the tokenized input already specified in v3's Equation 3.

P1.justification: The revision tightens several methodology and results paragraphs, clarifies notation and captions, and updates affiliations, acknowledgments, and conference headers. Two appendix subsections are inserted and later subsections renumbered. The overall narrative, main section order, and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redesigned to show dataset sources and reference inputs explicitly. v4 adds a main-text dialogue example, extends the localization comparison with a DeepFake column, expands Tables 2, 4, and 6, and adds Tables 8–10. DeepFake dialogue examples gain masks and IoU labels, and the learning curve is redrawn. These materially expand the visual presentation; most remaining appendix figures are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v4 broadens related-work citations covering copy-move detection, inpainting forensics, and image immunization, and adds references supporting the new baselines and datasets. Section 3.1 cites Huang et al. as methodological inspiration while removing the explicit concurrent-work distinction and old Figure 2 layout acknowledgment. The main novelty positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5 retain the same functional mappings and loss components. Changes clarify prediction versus ground-truth notation, rename the text target, and rearrange equation layout. No substantive mathematical assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs are added or removed.

improvement.justification: v4 provides stronger empirical support through additional DeepFake competitors, unseen-generator tests, and targeted architectural ablations, while documenting previously unreported DeepFake localization outcomes. The benefit is limited by sparse descriptions of the new evaluation setups and removal of both batch sizes. Table 10 also qualifies the generalization narrative: FakeShield does not lead ControlNet pixel-level F1. The added evidence yields a useful but limited overall quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FakeShield framework and MMTD-Set. The complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, figures, prompts, and examples, support reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds DeepFake comparisons, localization results, and appendix ablation and generalization experiments in Tables 8–10.

before.justification: v3 reports original detection, localization, explanation, robustness, and ablation results in Tables 1–6 and accompanying figures and appendix examples.

title: FakeShield: Explainable Image Forgery Detection and Localization via Multi-modal Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same claims about efficient characterization of molecular interactions, symmetry properties, and superior performance on three benchmarks. Additional experiments support these existing claims without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix C adds interpretations concerning robustness to moderate coarsening and loss-weight variation, while acknowledging performance drops at extreme choices. Existing explanations of molecular interactions, generalization, and component behavior remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability statement and a project repository address in the abstract, providing access information absent from v1. Appendix B retains the existing implementation and training details. Repository availability or contents cannot be verified from the PDFs alone.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same gene regulatory, EGFR drug-sensitivity, and GPCR activation tasks. The added sensitivity tests reuse these datasets. GPCR atom selection changes preprocessing within retained coverage, rather than adding a dataset or task.

E2.justification: v2 adds the Transformer-based GraphTrans comparator to Tables 1, 2, and 4 and the scalability comparisons in Figure 4. Existing comparators remain. The newly cited DSR method is not evaluated as a baseline.

E3.justification: Section 4.3 changes the stated GPCR selection from Cα atoms to backbone atoms. Appendix C introduces coarsening levels of 100, 50, 30, 10, and 5 and loss-weight sweeps over 10, 1, 0.1, and 0.01. Existing cross-validation and training budgets remain unchanged; the revised atom-selection statement does not itself establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's scalability tests, component ablations, and qualitative analyses, v2 adds systematic sensitivity studies of coarsening on both EGFR and GPCR and of all three loss weights. Appendix C and Tables 5–8 substantially expand evidence about dependence on parameter choices.

E5.justification: v1's Tables 1–4 report point estimates; v2 adds ± uncertainty entries throughout these tables and the new sensitivity tables. This substantially expands uncertainty reporting. The five-run statement and five-fold procedure are retained, without a documented increase in runs or an explicit definition of the ± statistic.

E6.justification: v2 adds GraphTrans and sensitivity results and revises existing scores. In Table 2, Cα-dihedral accuracy changes from 61.333% to 63.73%, and Deep Signature recall from 22.0% to 21.27%. Table 4 replaces GPCR results, including Deep Signature's 64.200% accuracy and 41.3% recall with 58.00% and 43.30%. Changed atom selection prevents treating this as a same-setting performance decline. Section 4.3 still quotes the old values.

M1.justification: Sections 3.2–3.4 retain the spectral clustering, log-signature extraction, LSTM, classifier, and three-term training objective. GraphTrans is an added comparator; the parameter sweeps test existing components.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized related-work and introductory wording edits, adds acknowledgments and Appendix C, and introduces the conference-publication header. The main section order and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Tables 1, 2, and 4 accommodate GraphTrans, existing tables add uncertainty entries and display recall on a percentage scale, and Figure 4 adds GraphTrans curves and legends. Four compact sensitivity tables are added. Other figures and the overall visual organization are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds Sun et al. (2023), DSR, and briefly positions its implicit protein-surface representation relative to interatomic pathway modeling. The remaining research positioning is substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 and Appendix A retain the same symmetry arguments, assumptions, and time-reparameterization theorem and proof. Equation 10 corrects a misplaced parenthesis without substantively changing the mathematical definition or reasoning.

improvement.justification: The added Transformer comparison and parameter sweeps provide useful checks of comparative performance and dependence on parameter choices that v1 lacked. Uncertainty entries and code-access information also improve transparency. These gains are limited by undefined ± notation and unreconciled prose: Section 4.3 still reports 64.200% GPCR accuracy despite Table 4 reporting 58.00%. Overall, empirical scrutiny improves, but reporting inconsistencies prevent a stronger assessment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Deep Signature research. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–B can be matched reliably; v2 additionally contains Appendix C. No material reading gaps remain.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and reports additional GraphTrans comparisons and parameter-sensitivity experiments in Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments on gene regulatory, EGFR, and GPCR dynamics, together with scalability tests, ablations, and molecular case analyses.

title: Deep Signature: Characterization of Large-Scale Molecular Dynamics

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions and claims concerning efficient dynamics characterization, symmetry properties and superior performance on three benchmarks.

C2.justification: Interpretations concerning class imbalance, nonlinear dynamics, feature generalization, structural fidelity and interpretability remain unchanged. Appendix C retains the same qualifications about extreme coarsening levels and loss weights.

D1.justification: Implementation and reproducibility information in Section 3.4 and Appendix B is unchanged, including pooling sizes, hidden dimensions, optimizers, batch sizes, simulation settings and software references. Code and data access information also matches.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same gene regulatory classification, EGFR drug-sensitivity prediction and GPCR state classification tasks. Figure 4 retains the same trajectory-duration and system-size coverage.

E2.justification: Figure 4 removes GraphTrans from both scalability comparisons, retaining Head, Tail, Head & Tail and GraphLSTM against Deep Signature. GraphTrans remains in Tables 1, 2 and 4; their comparator membership is unchanged.

E3.justification: The temporal five-fold validation procedure, independent testing, dataset sizes, model configurations, training settings and evaluation metrics remain unchanged in Sections 3.4–4 and Appendix B. Expressing recall as percentages does not change the metric.

E4.justification: The scalability analysis in Figure 4 loses GraphTrans evidence concerning sensitivity to trajectory duration and system size. The loss ablation, structural and feature analyses, interpretability examples and Appendix C parameter-sensitivity analyses remain unchanged.

E5.justification: The five-run averaging statement, repeated validation procedure and tabulated plus/minus uncertainty reporting are unchanged. Neither version adds different seed information, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Section 4.2 corrects EGFR recall from 0.220 to 21.27%. Section 4.3 corrects Deep Signature's GPCR accuracy/recall from 64.200%/0.413 to 58.00%/43.30%, and GraphLSTM's from 53.333%/0.360 to 53.47%/38.13%. These changes align the prose with unchanged Tables 2 and 4, rather than documenting new performance outcomes. Figure 4 also removes GraphTrans results; retained curves and table values are unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same spectral clustering, log-signature transform, LSTM and classifier, with unchanged clustering, temporal consistency and classification losses. The architectures in Appendix B also match.

P1.justification: Edits are limited to numerical presentation and nearby wording in Sections 4.2–4.3, including percentage-form recall and consistent two-decimal accuracy formatting. The arXiv version/date stamp changes; section organization and the surrounding narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 4 is redrawn without GraphTrans curves or legend entries, adds horizontal-axis labels T and N, and makes small sizing and styling adjustments. Other figures and table structures remain unchanged, with only local text reflow.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion, cited works and positioning relative to molecular representations, coarse-graining methods and previous signature-based approaches are unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and derivations in Section 3 and the translation, rotation, permutation and time-reparameterization arguments in Appendix A are unchanged, including Theorem 1.

improvement.justification: v3 resolves text–table contradictions in Sections 4.2–4.3, particularly the GPCR accuracy reported as 64.200% despite Table 4 showing 58.00%. This improves reporting reliability. Removing GraphTrans from Figure 4 reduces the completeness of scalability comparisons, but its main benchmark results remain available; the numerical corrections provide a modest net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Deep Signature research. All 19 pages in each, including equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–C, support reliable comparison through text extraction and visual inspection.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experimental results in Section 4 and Appendix C, including classification comparisons and component and parameter analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original classification experiments on gene regulatory, EGFR and GPCR dynamics, with scalability studies, ablations and additional sensitivity results in Appendix C.

title: Deep Signature: Characterization of Large-Scale Molecular Dynamics

C1.justification: The introduction reframes AuroraCap from a claimed state-of-the-art video captioning model to a video-understanding base model with improved captioning performance. The central claims concerning token efficiency, the VDC benchmark and VDCscore remain intact.

C2.justification: Section S1 newly argues that sparse frames and image-trained CLIP features make strong temporal merging undesirable. Section S9 suggests CLIP misses fine-grained caption errors and interprets additional QA pairs as improving robustness. Table 2 also qualifies the unusually low cited GPT-4V scores; existing OCR limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Sections S17-S18 supply previously omitted answer-extraction and correctness-evaluation prompts. v2 also specifies the GPT-4o usage period and explains randomized, model-blinded Elo comparisons in S15. Direct code/model access information is added, while resource wording changes from already available to future release; actual availability cannot be established from the PDFs.

E1.justification: Section S2 adds actual evaluation on MovieChat-1K and EgoSchema, substantially extending coverage to long-form video understanding. MovieChat-1K was only discussed as related work in v1. Existing training datasets, captioning benchmarks and other evaluations are retained.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds InstructBLIP-7B and InstructBLIP-13B. New long-video comparisons include previously unevaluated comparators such as TimeChat, mPLUG-Owl and VideoLLAMA2, while Section S9 adds CLIP similarity as a metric comparator. Existing principal comparison sets are retained.

E3.justification: Supplementary evaluations introduce ROUGE answer matching, CLIP scoring, and controls using 5 and 10 QA pairs alongside the existing 20-pair setup. New MovieChat-1K results distinguish breakpoint and global evaluation. Previously reported training hyperparameters, decoding settings and benchmark sample counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Sections S2, S3 and S9 substantially expand validation through an EgoSchema token-retention ablation, alternative answer-matching analysis, CLIP-versus-human correlation, and QA-count sensitivity. These examine long-sequence robustness and metric design choices beyond v1's retained token-merging, slowfast, efficiency, training and backbone analyses.

E5.justification: No new repeated-run counts, seeds, significance tests or uncertainty-estimation procedures are reported. Added correlation plots follow the existing reporting approach. Elo parameters, including the reported 2,778 matches, are unchanged.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include AuroraCap's MovieChat-1K breakpoint/global scores of 52.6/59.7 and EgoSchema accuracy of 46.0, plus human correlations of 0.74 for ROUGE answer matching and 0.39 for CLIP. Added InstructBLIP-7B achieves 118.2 NoCaps CIDEr versus AuroraCap's retained 111.4. Existing AuroraCap main-table and appendix ablation values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Section S3 adds an evaluated VDCscore variant that uses ROUGE for final answer matching instead of LLM judgment. AuroraCap's architecture, frame-wise token merging, three-stage training and default VDCscore procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence remain intact. Changes include localized copyediting, numeric citation style, revised author/header information, expanded supplementary explanations, and limited reordering within the ablation discussion. The appendices are reorganized from lettered sections into S1-S18.

P2.justification: Document-wide retypesetting changes page geometry, title and abstract styling, headers, table headings, and figure/table sizing and placement. New displays include Figures S1-S4, Figure S15 and Table S1. Existing visualizations and case-study images are largely retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to EgoSchema, OmniCorpus and MM-Ego. Section S1 expands positioning against Chat-UniVi's temporal token handling and distinguishes VDCscore evaluation from LLaVA-Hound-DPO's preference-data construction. Most related-work coverage is retained.

T1.justification: The token-size-adjusted attention equation and per-layer merging formula are unchanged; v1 Equation 2 becomes v2 Equation S1. No new mathematical assumptions, proofs or derivations accompany the additional empirical metric analyses.

improvement.justification: The new long-video and metric analyses broaden evidential support, while the missing evaluation prompts and clearer Elo procedure improve reproducibility. The gain is limited by sparse settings for the new long-video experiments and misleading best-score bolding in Table 2, which overlooks the added InstructBLIP NoCaps results. Overall, the additions provide a useful incremental improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AuroraCap, VDC and VDCscore. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and matchable despite reformatting, renumbering and supplementary additions.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds long-video evaluations and further analyses of the proposed evaluation metric.

before.justification: v1 reports original AuroraCap captioning and question-answering results, token-merging and training ablations, and comparisons with human Elo judgments.

title: AuroraCap: Efficient, Performant Video Detailed Captioning and a New Benchmark

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: efficient AuroraCap captioning, the VDC benchmark, and QA-based VDCscore with stronger human alignment. The evaluator substitution does not introduce a new headline claim.

C2.justification: Interpretations of token redundancy, temporal complexity, instruction-following failures, and OCR limitations remain unchanged. v4 adds no explanation or qualification concerning the evaluator substitution.

D1.justification: Evaluator identification changes throughout Section 3.2.1 and S12/S17/S18, and the footnote specifying the September 2024 GPT-4o version is removed. Appendix response labels become generic LLM labels. Training details, hardware information, prompts, and resource-access links otherwise remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Training datasets, evaluation benchmarks, VDC coverage, and appendix test scenarios are unchanged. Section 3.1.2 still specifies GPT-4o for benchmark caption construction; generic LLM labels in S11 do not establish regenerated data.

title: PAD: Personalized Alignment of LLMs at Decoding-time

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central contributions: importance sampling toward an ideal token-reward distribution, three contrastive-model weight estimators, and improved alignment and summarization. Rewritten contribution bullets and the expanded conclusion largely restate these claims rather than redefine their scientific scope.

C2.justification: The added appendices substantially expand interpretation and limitations: computational tradeoffs, annotation-noise resilience, degradation with very wide clipping bounds, unavailable ground-truth token weights, limitations of GPT-4 token selection, applicability to diverse preference data, and positional bias attributed to contrastive DPO training. These go beyond v1's existing discussion of prompt-distribution mismatch and imperfect weight estimation.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a new GPT-4 token-identification prompt, parameter-sweep ranges, computational-budget descriptions and the positional-decay coefficient lambda = 0.995. Existing optimizer, hardware and contrastive-training details remain. These are useful additional disclosures, without a comprehensive revision of reproducibility information.

E1.justification: Appendix J adds UltraFeedback preference data, described as including general dialogue, reasoning, mathematics and multi-turn conversations. The existing PKU-SafeRLHF, Anthropic-HH, TL;DR and evaluation datasets remain. This broadens data coverage within the retained preference-alignment task and MT-bench evaluation framework.

E2.justification: The comparator memberships in Tables 1–2 and Figure 3 remain unchanged. Added appendix experiments reuse existing comparison methods. Table 7's DPO (reversed) matches the DPO-Negative procedure already described as a comparison in v1 Section 7.4; its new numerical results do not establish a different baseline method.

E3.justification: V2 adds several evaluation designs: three-epoch DPO versus one-epoch TIS-DPO for a stated computational-budget comparison; 20% preference-label swaps; sweeps over weight parameters and clipping bounds; and GPT-4 token-identification evaluation using average weight and rank percentile. Appendix J additionally uses Llama3-8B and reports turn-specific MT-bench scores. These supplement the unchanged original settings.

E4.justification: V1's weight ablations, reward trajectories and qualitative case studies are retained. Appendices F–I and K add computational-budget controls, annotation-noise robustness, hyperparameter sensitivity, quantitative agreement with GPT-4 token selections, positional-weight analysis and a decay intervention. These substantially expand investigation of the method's reliability and mechanism.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or formal significance tests. V2's added tables continue reporting point estimates. The revised theoretical concentration bound is not experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and Figure 3 retain their results, while Tables 3–8 and Figure 8 add substantial new evidence. For example, Table 4 reports 65.2% safety for DPO and 93.2% for TIS-DPO(D) under 20% annotation noise; Table 8 reports 96.7% without positional decay and 97.9% with it. These are newly reported comparisons, not changed scores for the retained main experiments.

M1.justification: The main TIS-DPO objective and three contrastive-model construction methods remain unchanged. Appendix K.2 introduces and evaluates an additional procedure multiplying each token's estimated weight by a position-dependent decay factor, lambda^(N−1). This is a limited methodological extension.

P1.justification: V2 condenses contribution bullets, adds section introductions, expands the conclusion and introduces acknowledgements and conference-header information. The main section order and most retained prose remain stable. The added scientific appendices do not constitute a wholesale rewrite of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: V2 adds six appendix tables, the two-panel positional-weight Figure 8 and a boxed token-evaluation prompt. Conference formatting also changes typography, link colors and placement of retained tables and figures. Together these substantially expand and revise the presentation of evidence; Figures 1–7 remain represented.

R1.justification: V2 adds the UltraFeedback citation to Cui et al. and removes Hoeffding's reference and two Liu et al. references concerning watermarking and misinformation. Its positioning relative to DPO, TDPO and contrastive alignment remains substantially unchanged. Consolidating the duplicate TDPO preprint and conference references is bibliographic cleanup.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 and Appendix A.2 are substantively revised. V1 uses two Hoeffding bounds combined through a union bound with a chosen deviation parameter. V2 replaces this with a McDiarmid bound explicitly involving the expected winning–losing reward gap and bounded token-reward changes, supported by a new derivation. The remaining principal derivations are retained.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, the noise, sensitivity and token-consistency experiments provide useful additional scrutiny of practical reliability. Reporting issues limit the gains: Appendix F's cost-equivalence argument is not reconciled with Appendix B.2's three-epoch SFT setup, and Figure 8 shows negative mean 'weights' without explaining their relationship to Equation 19's positive weights. The revision improves empirical examination, but these ambiguities prevent a stronger overall quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TIS-DPO work. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison, including v2's added Appendices F–K.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds experiments on computational budgets, annotation noise, hyperparameters, token-weight consistency, UltraFeedback and positional weight decay.

before.justification: V1 reports original alignment and summarization experiments, ablations, training curves and token-weight case studies in Section 7 and Appendix D.

title: TIS-DPO: Token-level Importance Sampling for Direct Preference Optimization With Estimated Weights

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same claims about optimal token-reward distributions, importance sampling, three contrastive estimators, and alignment and summarization improvements. The added code statement does not revise the scientific contributions.

C2.justification: The explanations concerning prompt/data-distribution mismatch, contrastive-model effectiveness, computational overhead, missing ground-truth token weights, and positional bias are retained. No substantive interpretation or limitation is added or removed.

D1.justification: The v3 abstract newly states that code is available and supplies the TIS-DPO GitHub address; v2 lacks this implementation-access pointer. Hardware, hyperparameters, training details, and evaluation prompts otherwise match.

E1.justification: Both versions use PKU-SafeRLHF, Anthropic-HH, TL;DR, and UltraFeedback. The AdvBench/JailbreakBench, Alpaca, and MT-bench evaluation coverage and the appendix test scenarios are also retained.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains DPO, PPO, IPO, TDPO, and KTO. The RLCD comparison in Table 2, SFT comparison in Figure 3, and reversed-DPO comparison in Table 7 are also unchanged.

E3.justification: Model configurations, evaluation metrics and prompts, training hyperparameters, and testing procedures match. The equivalent-compute comparison, 20% annotation-noise condition, sensitivity ranges, and decay setting in the appendices are unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 7.5 and Appendices D, F–I, and K retain the same weight and eta ablations, training analysis, case studies, compute comparison, noise test, sensitivity study, token-consistency evaluation, and positional-bias analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed or repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Point-estimate reporting and the absence of experimental uncertainty estimates remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Tables 1–8 and the plotted and qualitative findings retain the same results. For example, TIS-DPO(D)'s LLaMA2-7B PKU-SafeRLHF safety rate remains 96.7%, and its UltraFeedback win rate remains 69.2%.

M1.justification: The TIS-DPO objective, weight estimation, clamping, and three contrastive-model construction methods remain unchanged. The position-dependent weight decay in Appendix K was already present in v2.

P1.justification: The abstract gains a short code-availability sentence, and the arXiv version/date text updates. The remaining prose and section organization are retained, without extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v3 adjusts equation sizing, compacts Tables 1–2, slightly resizes Figure 3, and changes citation and cross-reference colors to blue. Paragraphs and acknowledgments reflow across pages; no figure or table is added or removed.

R1.justification: Section 2 and the bibliography retain the same cited works and positioning relative to DPO, TDPO, token-aware data construction, and importance sampling. Reference reflow and hyperlink formatting do not change research positioning.

T1.justification: Theorems 1–2, Definition 1, mathematical objectives, and Appendix A proofs are unchanged. The differences in equation size and delimiter rendering are typesetting changes.

improvement.justification: v3 adds a direct implementation-access pointer absent from v2, modestly improving practical usability. Presentation refinements are limited, and the scientific evidence, proofs, and limitations remain unchanged. The PDFs establish improved access information but do not verify the repository's contents.

A1.justification: Both complete 30-page PDFs describe the same TIS-DPO work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–K are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains the original experiments and results in Section 7 and the appendices, including benchmark comparisons, ablations, and robustness analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original alignment and summarization experiments in Section 7, plus computational-budget, robustness, sensitivity, token-weight, and UltraFeedback results in the appendices.

title: TIS-DPO: Token-level Importance Sampling for Direct Preference Optimization With Estimated Weights

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the three-stage explanation, dominance claim and parallel bypasses. Section 6 adds an explicit priority claim that this is the first work to unify fragmented empirical conclusions, strengthening the stated novelty of the retained contribution.

C2.justification: V2 substantially develops the circuit's applicability boundary: induction can harm prediction when the correct label is absent, while demonstrations can help through other dynamics. Section 6 expressly qualifies generalization to these cases. V2 also interprets copying as general pretrained behavior and discusses future control through forerunner-token design.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.7 explicitly describes zeroing designated connections and matching random controls within the same layers, supported by Figure 10. Appendix G supplies diagnostic-selection rules and the counterexample prompt. Existing quantization, prompt templates and the promise to release code after acceptance are retained.

E1.justification: The six sentence-classification datasets remain. Appendix G adds targeted evaluation of contexts omitting the correct query label and a small occupation-classification case using Geoffrey Hinton and Michael Jordan, extending the represented scenarios and input types.

E2.justification: Figure 19 adds a random baseline to the new comparison between attention-derived predictions and model outputs. Existing ablation and decoding comparator sets are retained. The newly discussed gradient-descent and Bayesian explanations are not added experimental baselines.

E3.justification: New supplementary protocols measure length-normalized preceding-token attention and Jensen–Shannon divergence, selecting the five lowest-divergence heads per layer. Appendix G also filters contexts by correct-label absence. Existing default sampling, model settings and ablation-layer fractions remain unchanged; Appendix A.7 chiefly clarifies the existing intervention.

E4.justification: Appendix D newly tests whether copying differs between label and non-label positions. Appendix G adds explanatory-fidelity comparisons, circuit ablations when the correct label is absent, and a counterexample where demonstrations help despite weak induction activity. These substantially extend the tests of the circuit's mechanism and applicability.

E5.justification: Random-ablation controls in Table 1 and v1 Table 6/v2 Table 8 change from single reported values to mean ± standard deviation. Repetition counts and seeds remain unspecified, so the PDFs establish new uncertainty reporting but not an explicit increase in runs.

E6.justification: Original target-ablation scores remain, but control values change: Table 1's 75% demonstration-encoding control moves from -4.65 to -3.29 ± 1.87. New Table 6 reports +22.95 and +29.26 percentage points from full Step 3 ablation under missing-label conditions for Llama 3 8B and Falcon 7B. Copying distributions, divergence results and occupation-label probabilities are also added. These are new-condition findings, not cross-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The three inference stages, head-identification criteria and decoding/bypass procedures remain unchanged. 'Summarize' becomes 'Input Text Encode.' The new copying and output-divergence measures diagnose the existing circuit rather than modify its operation.

P1.justification: V2 makes local wording corrections, renames Step 1 and clarifies attention-arrow notation. It expands the discussion, inserts appendix sections, and moves the reproducibility, authorship and acknowledgment statements before the references. The main narrative and most existing prose remain recognizable.

P2.justification: V2 adds an ablation schematic, copying and divergence distribution plots, counterexample heatmaps, and two result tables (Figures 10, 15, 19, 20; Tables 6–7). Tables 1 and 8 are widened and reformatted for uncertainty reporting. Earlier plots are retained, with caption, placement and numbering changes.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds specific contrasts with gradient-descent, kernel-regression, Bayesian and earlier induction-circuit explanations. Appendix G challenges Wang et al.'s label-anchor interpretation and introduces Xiao et al.'s attention-sink work. Most other reference edits add URLs or update metadata; Xie's 2021 and 2022 entries describe the same work.

T1.justification: Appendices D and G.1 introduce mathematical definitions for normalized copy magnitude and an attention-derived label distribution, Equations 15–17. The earlier kernel-alignment derivation, centroid rules and hidden-space argument are retained. No new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: The missing-label ablations and explicit counterexample improve scrutiny of the explanation and motivate a clearer applicability limit. Appendix A.7 and control standard deviations improve transparency. These gains are tempered by unspecified repetition counts and reporting errors, including Table 6's duplicated Llama 3 Step 2/Step 3 connection label.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same three-step ICL circuit study. All 31 pages of v1 and 37 pages of v2, including appendices, equations, tables and figures, support comparison. Retained content can be matched across renaming, relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds token-copying comparisons, missing-correct-label experiments and a named-person classification counterexample.

before.justification: V1 reports original representation measurements, attention-head analyses, classification and ablation results on Llama and Falcon models, plus Pythia pretraining-checkpoint experiments.

title: Revisiting In-context Learning Inference Circuit in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same claims: a three-stage explanation of ICL, empirical evidence for its operations, explanations of observed phenomena, and a dominant circuit accompanied by bypass mechanisms.

C2.justification: Interpretations of label denoising, prediction bias, demonstration saturation and pre-training remain unchanged. Section 6 and Appendix G retain the same limitations concerning circuit granularity, classification-only coverage and generalization to in-weight learning.

D1.justification: The Reproducibility Statement replaces v2's promise to release code after acceptance with a specific official implementation repository, hc495/ICL_Circuit. The implementation and experimental details in Appendix A remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same six classification datasets, the TEE control comparison and the same appendix scenarios, including prompts without the query's ground-truth label in the demonstrations.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged: zero-shot and random prediction references, random-connection ablations, LM-head versus centroid decoding, and contextual calibration remain in their corresponding comparisons.

E3.justification: Section 2.2 and Appendix A retain the same models, default four demonstrations, 512 test examples per dataset, 256-example centroid training, metrics, quantization settings and ablation procedures.

E4.justification: The circuit and shortcut ablations, delimiter sensitivity tests, pre-training analysis, direct-decoding investigations and in-weight-learning counterexample are retained. Appendices B–H introduce no new or revised analyses.

E5.justification: Uncertainty reporting remains unchanged, including mean and standard deviation for random-ablation controls in Tables 1 and 8. Neither version adds or revises run counts, seeds or statistical estimation procedures relative to the other.

E6.justification: Matched numerical results, plotted findings and qualitative observations are unchanged throughout the main text and appendices. For example, Table 3 retains 66.19% accuracy for full LM-head inference and 84.27% for Layer34 centroid inference, with the latter's 2.38× speed.

M1.justification: The three-stage circuit—input text encoding, semantics merging, and feature retrieval and copying—is unchanged. The bypass mechanisms and early-exit centroid decoding procedure are also retained.

P1.justification: v3 makes small wording edits in Section 4.1, revises the author-contribution statement, adds reviewer acknowledgments and changes the header from under review to published. The section structure and scientific narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: There are small spacing and page-break adjustments, altered equation layout in Appendix A.4, and a blue-to-black change to the appendix title. Figures and tables retain their content, with only limited placement and formatting changes.

R1.justification: The cited works and research positioning are unchanged, including comparisons with induction-circuit explanations, implicit gradient descent, kernel regression and Bayesian inference in Sections 2.1 and 6.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and derivations, including head overlap, kernel alignment, centroid classification and the appendix attention-based analysis, are unchanged. Equation typesetting adjustments in Appendix A do not alter the mathematics.

improvement.justification: The concrete implementation link in v3 replaces a future-release promise and improves the paper's reproducibility information. Scientific evidence, claims and limitations remain unchanged, so the gain is limited. The supplied PDFs do not establish the linked repository's completeness or usability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable 37-page versions of the same paper, with corresponding main sections, figures, tables, equations and Appendices A–H. No material gaps prevent comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and results, including the main circuit ablations, pre-training measurements and appendix investigations of in-weight learning.

before.justification: v2 reports original hidden-state measurements, attention-head analyses and intervention experiments, including circuit ablations in Table 1 and additional empirical analyses in Appendices B–H.

title: Revisiting In-context Learning Inference Circuit in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the central claims: up to 10× faster SNF training, preserved generalization at moderate scaling, richer high-frequency representations and better conditioning. The added experiments support these existing contributions without redefining their central novelty.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the previously open question about other architectures with specific applicability boundaries: GaussNet and Sinc NF can fit faster while generalization worsens, and WIRE can deteriorate. It adds interpretations concerning Hessian outliers, learning-rate-dependent scale selection and extended-training generalization. The PDE discussion acknowledges unavailable ground truth beyond the initial time.

D1.justification: New Appendices F.1–F.3 disclose tuning grids and layerwise learning-rate compensation for existing analyses. Further additions document baseline settings, NeRF network sizes and codebase, and scheduled long-training learning rates. Conversely, v1's reproducibility statement promising public code is removed without replacement project-code access instructions.

E1.justification: v2 adds novel-view synthesis on NeRF-synthetic Lego and Drums, plus Gaussian-pulse wave-equation reconstruction and temporal extrapolation from initial observations (Appendices F.6–F.7). The original image, occupancy, spherical, audio and neural-dataset tasks remain.

E2.justification: Table 1 expands from seven to nine baselines by adding MFN and Sinc NF across the original domains. These methods also enter the qualitative comparisons, while Xavier panels disappear from the image, audio and spherical examples despite its retained quantitative row. MFN additionally enters the replacement long-training comparison.

E3.justification: New protocols include two NeRF resolutions with 300/600-epoch budgets, a 40,000-step PDE experiment, and batch-size and learning-rate sweeps. The earlier longer-training comparison is replaced by a scheduled 5,000-step Kodak study. The stated spherical-data learning rate changes from 1e-4 to 1e-5; the PDFs do not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained spectral, gradient-decoupling and conditioning analyses, v2 adds Hessian eigenspectrum snapshots, mini-batch sensitivity, scaling tests with other activations, and learning-rate dependence of the optimal scale (Figures 11 and 13–15). The earlier multi-domain continuation analysis is replaced by substantially longer Kodak train/test curves in Figure 23.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five seeds and mean/standard-deviation reporting for the principal data-fitting experiments. Added Table 1 baseline rows follow this practice. No changed run count, new confidence-interval procedure or significance test is documented.

E6.justification: Existing Table 1 entries and Table 3 remain unchanged, but v2 adds baseline scores, diagnostic curves and new task outcomes. Examples include 28.17 dB for WS on 800×800 Lego after 300 epochs and initial-time PDE MSE of 2.8e-5. v1's longer-budget Table 4 is removed; the replacement Kodak study reports peak test PSNR of 37.45 dB under its different training protocol.

M1.justification: The initialization rule in Eq. (3), including leaving output-layer weights unscaled, remains unchanged. The new NeRF application introduces a limited adaptation: WS applies only to the volume-density network, leaving the color network outside the scaling procedure (Appendix F.6).

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order remain largely intact. Changes include targeted related-work and conclusion rewrites, publication-header and affiliation updates, acknowledgments, theorem renumbering, and reorganized appendices. Most expansion consists of new scientific material rather than extensive rewriting of retained content.

P2.justification: Figure 1 replaces target-PSNR training-step bars with multi-method learning curves. Table 1 gains baseline rows, qualitative grids are rearranged, and new Hessian, sensitivity, NeRF and PDE displays are added. The earlier long-training table disappears, while a NeRF table and extended train/test plots provide different comparisons.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds discussion of sinusoidal activations beyond neural fields, including generative models, low-rank learning and compression. The new kernel and Hessian analyses substantially expand connections to Gaussian kernels, spectral conditioning and periodically activated networks. MFN and Sinc NF also broaden the comparison-related literature; the central training-efficiency positioning remains.

T1.justification: New Appendix C.3 develops a two-layer eNTK decomposition and conditional Gaussian-kernel/eigenvalue arguments relating scaling to conditioning (Eqs. 52–56), incorporating an explicitly attributed theorem. Appendix B.1 also restores omitted W^(3) factors in Eqs. (31)–(32). The original distribution-preservation and harmonic results otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central speed/generalization claim through additional baselines, mini-batch and learning-rate tests, training-to-saturation curves and held-out-view evaluation. Newly disclosed tuning procedures also improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh the loss of the earlier multi-domain long-training table and code-release promise. The new theoretical argument remains conditional, and PDE extrapolation lacks later-time ground-truth validation, so those additions provide more limited support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, core initialization rule and retained experiments. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial appendix expansion and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds baseline evaluations, sensitivity analyses, novel-view synthesis experiments and wave-equation reconstruction results.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction experiments across several modalities, optimization analyses, and neural-dataset construction and classification results in Tables 1 and 3.

title: Fast Training of Sinusoidal Neural Fields via Scaling Initialization

C1.justification: Both retain the claims of up to tenfold training acceleration, effectiveness across data domains, improved high-frequency representation and better-conditioned optimization. The scope of the claimed contributions is unchanged.

C2.justification: Both retain the speed–generalization interpretation, frequency and conditioning explanations, downstream-classification tradeoffs and qualifications concerning other activations. Section 6 still acknowledges the limited architectural scope and absence of an explicit convergence bound.

D1.justification: v3 adds an abstract statement that code is available, linked to the project repository effl-lab/Fast-Neural-Fields; v2 lacks this project-code link. This adds access information, while implementation descriptions, hyperparameters and hardware disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use Kodak/DIV2K images, Lucy occupancy data, ERA5, Bach audio, MNIST/CIFAR-10 neural datasets, Lego/Drums NeRF scenes and wave-equation reconstruction. No dataset, task or test scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the same nine baselines, including SIREN initialization, NFSL, WIRE and Sinc NF. Comparator membership also matches within the neural-dataset, NeRF and appendix qualitative comparisons.

E3.justification: Splits, preprocessing, sample sizes, metrics, model sizes and training budgets match throughout Section 5 and Appendix F. Both NeRF resolution/epoch combinations and the extended-training protocol are retained.

E4.justification: Both retain the initial-function versus gradient ablation, spectral and eigenvalue analyses, scaling-factor sensitivity, mini-batch experiments, other-activation comparisons and extended-training analysis. Their tested questions and supporting evidence are unchanged.

E5.justification: Both Table 1 captions and Appendix F.4 specify five random seeds and reporting means and standard deviations. Uncertainty reporting in the appendix tables also matches; no statistical procedure or run-count information changes.

E6.justification: Numerical entries, plotted results and qualitative reconstructions match throughout. For example, weight scaling retains Kodak PSNR 42.83±0.35 in Table 1 and Lego test PSNR 28.17 for the 800×800, 300-epoch setting in Table 4.

M1.justification: The architecture and weight-scaling procedure remain unchanged: initialized weights are multiplied by alpha except in the final layer. Equations (1)–(3), training objectives and task-specific adaptations match.

P1.justification: v3 removes the stray word Another at the end of Section 4.2 and changes many Appendix references to Section. Several references and proof headings now say Theorem despite retained Proposition/Lemma statement labels. The narrative and section organization otherwise remain stable.

P2.justification: All 23 figures and four tables retain their graphics, structures and placement. Changes are limited to local text reflow and caption references, notably Appendix F.1 becoming Section F.1 in Figure 2 and Lemma 5 becoming Theorem 5 in Figure 8.

R1.justification: The cited works, bibliography and research positioning match. Comparisons with SIREN initialization, NFSL, meta-learning and initialization-scale research are substantively unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical statements, assumptions, equations and proofs remain unchanged, including Appendices A–C. Several references and proof headings change from Proposition or Lemma to Theorem, but the corresponding statement labels and mathematical content are retained.

improvement.justification: The new abstract code link improves implementation discoverability, providing a modest documentation benefit over v2. The inconsistent theorem references introduce a small editorial regression, but the numbered statements remain identifiable. Overall, the access improvement is limited and practical; the scientific evidence and conclusions are unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, Fast Training of Sinusoidal Neural Fields via Scaling Initialization. Their complete main texts and Appendices A–F, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results, including the quantitative comparisons in Tables 1, 3 and 4 and the appendix analyses and reconstructions.

before.justification: v2 reports original neural-field experiments in Section 5 and additional neural-dataset, NeRF and differential-equation results in Appendix F.

title: Fast Training of Sinusoidal Neural Fields via Scaling Initialization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same substantive claims about unified long-context forecasting, TimeAttention, benchmark performance and pre-training transferability.

C2.justification: Interpretations concerning causality, normalization and context saturation are unchanged. Appendix E retains the same limitations involving iterative-generation errors, output-length flexibility and computational complexity.

R1.justification: Section 2, the cited works and the bibliography are unchanged. The positioning relative to earlier forecasting models and claimed novelty remain the same.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and equations in Section 3 and Appendix A's derivations of FLOPs, parameter counts and memory requirements are unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 provides small copyedits, updated author contact domains and a clearer EPF label in Table 8. after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments, including forecasting results in Tables 1–6 and 11 and performance variability in Table 9.

before.justification: v1 reports original Timer-XL forecasting, pre-training, ablation and efficiency experiments in Section 4, with additional empirical results in the appendices.

title: Timer-XL: Long-Context Transformers for Unified Time Series Forecasting

C1.justification: The central unified-forecasting and TimeAttention contributions remain. The introduction adds an explicit claim of outperforming advanced zero-shot models at comparable model and pre-training scales, while the abstract recasts Timer-XL as a promising foundation-model architecture.

C2.justification: Section E.4 adds explanations involving selective attention versus attention to noisy context and mismatched normalization statistics during autoregression. The earlier inference that decoder-only models better accommodate the embeddings, based on the Moirai comparison, is removed. The limitations paragraph is retained.

D1.justification: Table 10 adds LOTSA training hyperparameters and Moirai configurations, Section E.2 identifies checkpoint-based evaluation, and Table 12 provides a model-checkpoint access link. Section 3.2 clarifies per-head variable biases. Existing implementation documentation largely remains, and the LOTSA training duration is unspecified.

E1.justification: Sections 4.4 and E.2 add LOTSA as a substantial pre-training collection alongside UTSD and ERA5-Large, including aggregated UTSD+LOTSA training. Downstream task families remain stable; the additional ETT result blocks concern datasets already listed in v2 Table 8.

Tables 2–4 and 11 also reassign the former Moirai entries to UniTST while retaining their matched scores; the PDFs do not explain whether these were recomputed.

E3.justification: v3 adds LOTSA training configurations and a multi-horizon zero-shot protocol using official checkpoints, each model's maximum input length, and exclusions for pre-training overlap. Additional protocols include ERA5 one-day forecasting across daily-to-yearly lookbacks and 672-to-96 normalization comparisons. Existing supervised splits and settings are largely retained.

E4.justification: New analyses examine prediction quality through showcases (Figures 9–10), encoder-versus-decoder attention behavior (Figure 11), ERA5 context-length sensitivity (Table 14), and normalization dependence on three conventional benchmarks (Table 15). The original embedding ablation is retained as Table 13, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same three-random-seed standard deviations in Table 9. v3 introduces no additional uncertainty-estimation practice, significance testing or repeated-run disclosure.

C1.justification: v1 asserts that the n^(-3/4) second-order rate cannot generally be improved and attributes a matching lower bound to prior work. v2 replaces this with a best-known-rate claim and removes the lower-bound assertion. D1.justification: v2 supplies an experimental recipe, including the sample-size grid and step-size selection, and adds a code-repository link in Appendix E. v1 contains no experimental implementation or code-access information.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on one scalar synthetic problem, f(theta)=theta^2+cos(theta), with additive standard Gaussian gradient noise. v1 has no empirical evaluation; the new coverage is limited to this illustrative problem.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically evaluates external comparison algorithms. Figure 1 in v2 compares error components of the same Richardson–Romberg estimator; cited methods such as Root-SGD are not experimental baselines.

E3.justification: The new experiment uses n=250×2^k for k=0,...,14 and gamma=1/sqrt(n). It evaluates squared errors with and without the leading noise term and rescales them by n and n^(3/2), respectively. These are newly introduced protocols, not revised settings for an earlier experiment.

E4.justification: v2 adds a diagnostic that removes the analytically identified leading stochastic term and examines the residual's scaling with sample size. Figure 1 tests the predicted second-order rate; v1 contains no corresponding empirical analysis.

E5.justification: Section 5 and Appendix E newly report averaging over 320 independent runs. Neither version reports empirical confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars. This is first reporting for a new experiment, not an increase in previously reported runs.

E6.justification: Figure 1 adds empirical trends consistent with approximately n^(-1) full MSE and n^(-3/2) leading-term-removed MSE, with roughly stable rescaled curves. v1 reports no empirical results, so these are new findings rather than same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: Both versions use SGD chains with shared noise and step sizes gamma and 2gamma, average iterates n+1 through 2n, and combine them using Richardson–Romberg extrapolation. Changes to theorem conditions do not introduce a different algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 edits the abstract, introduction, discussions, and conclusion, clarifies root-MSE terminology, and moves Markov-coupling definitions to Appendix A. It adds numerical-results and acknowledgements sections and extends the appendices, while retaining the main theoretical narrative and proof organization.

P2.justification: v2 adds the two-panel Figure 1, compacts the author and affiliation block, and reflows equations and page layouts. Neither version contains result tables; most existing mathematical displays retain their presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including Ruppert, Yu et al., Vlatakis-Gkaragkounis et al., and Kwon et al., and removes Bach and Moulines (2013). It revises the characterization of Root-SGD and changes the rate attributed to Moulines and Bach (2011) in Section 2 from delta=1/12 to delta=1/6.

T1.justification: Theorems 6 and 9 add step-size restrictions involving 2/(11L) and p/(4×3^p L), with corresponding corollary conditions. v2 corrects Taylor integral remainders, revises bias constants and leading coefficients, extends the fourth-moment coupling lemma to higher moments, and supplies an arbitrary-initial-distribution argument in Lemma 24. These substantially revise the formal guarantees and supporting proofs, although the principal convergence rates remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 improves claim calibration, adds an illustrative numerical check and code-access information, and expands several proofs. However, its newly stated Lemma 13(b) bounds an inverse-matrix norm by 1/2, which fails already for scalar H*=1: the inverse is 1/(2-gamma)>1/2 for admissible positive gamma. This bound is used in deriving the revised bias constants. The benefits therefore coexist with a new correctness concern in the central theory, preventing a reliable net-quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SGD–Richardson–Romberg analysis. The main text, equations, proofs, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including v2's added experiment.

after.justification: Section 5 and Figure 1 report an original synthetic optimization experiment, averaged over 320 independent runs, with settings in Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 presents theoretical results and proofs but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

D1.justification: The added experiments document learning rates, momentum, epoch budgets, sample counts, and the CNN input adaptation. They specify dataset-dependent learning rates and momentum, selected by grid search for test accuracy. The original experiments' stated settings are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses examine important applicability boundaries: Boston regression tests an underparameterized setting where SGC is unlikely, while CIFAR10 logistic regression compares parameterization regimes and finds no acceleration despite positive RACOGA. These extend the questions tested beyond the retained batch-size, trajectory, and curvature analyses.

E5.justification: Existing ten-run or ten-initialization averages and the five-initialization RACOGA analysis are retained. Added benchmark convergence curves also average ten initializations.
