Figure 1 also updates trajectories and histograms while retaining its principal trend. Original neural-network accuracies remain unchanged, including SNAG's 88.73% on SPHERE and 70.88% on CIFAR10 in v1 Table 1/v2 Table 2.

M1.justification: The principal SNAG recurrence and experimental implementations are retained. Appendix F introduces a diminishing-step regime, s_n = 1/[2L(K)(n+1)], with corresponding coupling parameters for convergence without SGC. This is a limited procedural extension of the previously constant-step formulation.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section organization remain intact. Local revisions include the title, introduction, contribution ordering, an explicit explanation of almost-sure notation, and explanatory subheadings in Section 5.1. New appendix sections expand the document, but do not amount to extensive rewriting of retained material.

This substantially extends the theoretical analysis. The original SGC convergence and RACOGA results are retained; their appendix moves and renumbering do not constitute new results.

improvement.justification: v2 broadens empirical support, includes useful non-acceleration cases, and clarifies attribution. However, its new Theorem 9 introduces a substantive theoretical problem: the strongly convex proof invokes Lemma 4's requirement s <= 1/L, but the prescribed s = mu/[16(L(K)-mu)^2] need not satisfy it, and the theorem states no corresponding restriction. This unresolved gap in a newly added guarantee prevents a confident net quality judgment despite the empirical and explanatory benefits.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RACOGA/SGC analysis of momentum acceleration. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across renumbering, including v1 Appendices F–H becoming v2 Appendices G–I.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds Boston housing regression, four additional image datasets, and CIFAR10 logistic-regression experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic linear-regression experiments, SPHERE and CIFAR10 neural-network results, and appendix analyses of batch size, optimizer comparisons, and RACOGA.

Because v2 uses it to connect the blockwise theorem to Theorem 3.5, the empirical benefits coexist with a new gap in the central theoretical argument, leaving net quality uncertain.

The PDFs establish a narrower reported performance gap, but do not establish whether the replacement improves result validity, leaving the overall quality direction uncertain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Drama research and contain 28 inspectable pages, including equations, figures, tables and Appendices A.1–A.8. Textual and visual comparison establishes localized differences without material reading gaps.

after.justification: v4 retains these original empirical results, with one revised Transformer result in the grid-world comparison.

before.justification: v3 reports original Atari100k evaluations, grid-world prediction experiments, ablations and appendix timing results.

title: Drama: Mamba-Enabled Model-Based Reinforcement Learning Is Sample and Parameter Efficient

C1.justification: The abstract narrows the online-planning claim from superior FAS to comparable FAS. The introduction adds an explicit claim of outperforming GPM. The central contributions—sequence generation at low decision frequencies, model-based training with model-free control, and FAS—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations for SAC's Swimmer advantage and GPM's weak sequence generalization, plus discussion of delay handling and hardware constraints in Section 2 and Appendix A.3. Future work qualifies infinite-horizon control as near-infinite control in noiseless settings with corrections. Existing modeling-error limitations and latent-space interpretations are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds an official SRL repository link, and the new comparisons document plan-length choices and selected TempoRL maximum sequence lengths. Existing network sizes, optimization parameters, hardware specifications and environment-budget tables are retained. The PDFs establish the new access information, not the repository's availability or contents.

E1.justification: V3 adds Pendulum-v1, expanding the benchmark suite from ten to eleven continuous-control environments. This is distinct from the InvertedPendulum and InvertedDoublePendulum environments already evaluated in v1. The stochastic-timestep scenario and latent Walker2d evaluation were already present.

E2.justification: V3 adds GPM as a direct comparator in four environments (Figure 4) and randomized SAC, SAC-R, in Appendix A.10. TempoRL, already compared with latent SRL on Walker2d in v1, receives a broader seven-environment evaluation in Table 7. The latter reports rewards and sequence lengths rather than a matched FAS comparison.

E3.justification: V3 trains SAC at J = 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16, enabling comparisons beyond v1's baseline trained at the default timestep. It also introduces randomized frame-skipping during SAC training, specifies GPM plan-length choices and adds TempoRL maximum-length tuning. The original SRL update schedule, common hyperparameters and stochastic-timestep evaluation procedure remain.

E4.justification: The SAC timestep sweep and randomized frame-skipping analysis test whether adapting baseline training closes the frequency-robustness gap. These add substantial controls absent from v1. Existing stochastic-timestep correlations and latent-space analyses are retained; the additional matched-J learning-curve figures primarily redisplay the expanded comparisons.

E5.justification: The main FAS tables retain five-trial means and standard deviations, and frequency plots retain standard-error reporting. V3 Table 7 newly specifies averaging TempoRL results over ten seeds. This adds experiment-specific seed information without establishing an increase in runs for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Numerous retained FAS entries change: Hopper SRL-16 changes from 0.44 ± 0.04 in v1 Table 2 to 0.57 ± 0.02 in v3 Table 3, while Lunar Lander SRL-16 changes from 0.89 ± 0.05 to 0.84 ± 0.03. New comparator results substantially expand the evidence and reveal stronger SAC performance on Swimmer. These are reported revisions, not verified improvements under identical experimental conditions.

M1.justification: Equation 5 corrects the documented actor-loss summation endpoint from J to J−1, matching the stated J-action sequence. The GRU actor, dynamics model, critics, Algorithm 1 and latent-space extension otherwise remain unchanged. This correction does not establish that the implementation changed.

P1.justification: V3 revises the motivation, delay discussion, experimental narrative and future-work prose, merges the macro-action and action-repetition subsections, and adds appendix headings. The main section order and much of the method, neuroscience and existing appendix exposition remain intact; these are targeted revisions rather than a wholesale narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn, the combined FAS table becomes separate SAC and SRL tables, and learning and frequency plots are separated and expanded. V3 adds GPM and randomized-SAC displays and matched-J curve panels, while relocating existing illustrations and appendix material. Presentation changes are substantial, although several appendix pages become sparse and some comparison panels are very small.

R1.justification: V3 substantially expands positioning around temporally correlated exploration, including GPM, TLA and related exploration methods. It connects the evaluation to Dulac-Arnold's real-world RL challenges and discusses hardware acceleration and software optimization alternatives. The MPC distinction also shifts from requiring an already accurate model to requiring model access during deployment.

T1.justification: Equation 5 removes an extra terminal loss term by changing the summation endpoint from J to J−1; the accompanying sequence range is corrected accordingly. This resolves a mathematical inconsistency with the stated sequence length. Other substantive equations, including the latent temporal-consistency objective, are retained; neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially addresses an important weakness in v1: the main SAC baseline was trained at the default timestep. SAC-J and SAC-R controls test whether training adaptation explains SRL's advantage, while GPM supplies a close sequence-generating comparator. The Swimmer exception and moderated online-planning claim make the conclusions more informative. Unexplained FAS revisions and inconsistently updated illustrations, such as the Hopper curves in v3 Figures 2 and 9, remain drawbacks, but the stronger comparative evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SRL work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and renumbering.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds experiments involving GPM, multiple SAC training timesteps, randomized frame-skipping and broader TempoRL evaluation.

before.justification: V1 reports original continuous-control experiments, FAS comparisons, stochastic-timestep evaluations and a latent-space Walker2d experiment in its appendix.

title: Overcoming Slow Decision Frequencies in Continuous Control: Model-Based Sequence Reinforcement Learning for Model-Free Control

C1.justification: The abstract removes the claim that SRL replicates basal-ganglia action chunking. The central claims about model-based training, model-free sequence control, FAS, and comparative performance remain; biological inspiration is still discussed elsewhere.

C2.justification: v4 removes the hypothesis explaining GPM's limitations through disrupted sequence consistency and the future-work expectation of near-infinite-horizon control in noiseless environments. Existing modeling-error explanations and practical limitations remain. The neuroscience discussion is relocated, not deleted.

D1.justification: The new Section 5 overview explicitly identifies OpenAI Gym's MuJoCo implementation as the experimental platform, clarifying an existing setup without establishing a software change. Appendix hyperparameters, architectures, hardware, and repository information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The same 11 continuous-control tasks, four-environment GPM comparison, stochastic-timestep scenarios, and Walker2d latent-state experiment remain. No dataset, domain, or task scenario is added.

E2.justification: SAC, GPM, model-based online planning, TempoRL, and randomized SAC retain their roles in the corresponding comparisons. Removing standalone plots does not remove these comparators from the retained evaluations.

E3.justification: Training sequence lengths, actor update frequencies, FAS evaluation, uniformly sampled stochastic timesteps, and environment-specific budgets remain unchanged. The new experimental overview does not establish any protocol change.

E4.justification: Removing v3 Figure 5 eliminates the detailed Humanoid comparison of SRL and online-planning sensitivity to action-sequence length; Table 4 retains only their aggregate FAS comparison. Stochastic-timestep validation, latent-state analysis, and randomized frame-skipping analysis remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions retain five-trial reporting for SAC/SRL, the same standard-deviation and standard-error conventions, and ten-seed TempoRL results. No repeated-run or uncertainty-estimation practice changes.

E6.justification: v4 removes the standalone Hopper and Humanoid results in v3 Figures 2 and 5. The Hopper curves differ numerically from the retained appendix curves, so their removal is not merely deduplication; the Humanoid online-planning curve is also absent. Tables 2-4 and 7 and the retained plot images are unchanged.

M1.justification: The GRU actor, model-assisted policy training, critic training, and inference procedure remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 and the latent-state extension are also retained.

P1.justification: v4 adds an experiments overview and appendix contents, promotes Hyperparameters to a numbered subsection, moves Neural Basis for Sequence Learning from Section 6 to Appendix A.9, and trims introductory and discussion passages. Most prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: v4 removes main-text Figures 2, 3, and 5, shrinks Figure 1, and repositions tables and appendix figures. The removed Ant scatterplot survives in the appendix. Retained graphics and table structures are largely unchanged.

R1.justification: v4 adds Brockman et al. (2016), OpenAI Gym. The repaired OpenAI et al. (2019) citation refers to an already included work, and the relocated neuroscience discussion retains its references. Broader research positioning is substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations (1)-(7), including the training losses and latent-space formulation, remain unchanged. No theorem, proof, derivation, or formal assumption is added or revised.

improvement.justification: v4 modestly improves navigation and claim precision through the appendix contents, experimental overview, and removal of the abstract's biological-replication claim. The unchanged tables preserve central empirical support, although deleting distinct Hopper and Humanoid curves sacrifices result detail and limits the overall benefit.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SRL research. Their full text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v4 retains original experimental results in Tables 2-4 and 7, the GPM comparison, and the experimental appendix figures.

before.justification: v3 reports original continuous-control experiments, FAS comparisons, stochastic-timestep evaluations, and appendix results for latent SRL, randomized frame-skipping, and TempoRL.

title: Overcoming Slow Decision Frequencies in Continuous Control: Model-Based Sequence Reinforcement Learning for Model-Free Control

C1.justification: The abstract and three contribution statements retain the same benchmark, annotation-pipeline and evaluation claims. The conclusion preserves the identified industrial-knowledge and multi-image weaknesses and potential of enhancement methods. Its added statement about needing extensive data reiterates a point already made in v1's introduction.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation through explanations of CoT instability, visual dependence, missed detections versus false alarms, and contrasting human perception with GPT-4o's object knowledge. Appendix A.5 newly acknowledges that annotators may lack the originating industry's specialized expertise. Appendix A.7 also introduces an overstatement that humans outperform models on every metric, which Table 8 does not support.

D1.justification: v1 already disclosed 26 reviewers and over 200 working hours. Appendix A.5 adds reviewer expertise, preliminary program filtering, item-level review, the filtering interface, annotation cues and exclusion of erroneous questions. v2 also specifies Claude's API snapshot and describes the new prompting procedures. These are additional disclosures; the PDFs do not establish a revised dataset-construction process. The code/data access link is unchanged.

E1.justification: The four source datasets, 8,366 images, 39,672 questions and seven subtasks remain unchanged. Appendix A.4 adds a no-vision evaluation condition, extending testing to unavailable visual input. The human study samples existing benchmark examples rather than introducing another industrial dataset or task.

E2.justification: Table 2 extends the model-only comparison to expert and ordinary human reference groups and adds Claude-3.5-Sonnet, while retaining all previous MLLMs. The human references materially broaden the comparison underlying the industrial-inspector research question. Figure 6 also adds a GT-text comparison condition. LLaVA-OnVision becoming LLaVA-OneVision is a name correction.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include 177 randomly sampled examples assessed by three experts and five ordinary participants, structured CoT comparisons, and vision-removal controls. Appendix A.7 adds recall, precision and F1 with anomalies designated positive. These substantially extend the evaluation protocol; the original 1-shot settings and balanced anomaly-discrimination accuracy remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds systematic CoT and visual-dependence ablations, question/option vocabulary analysis, precision-recall error diagnostics, and the GT-text control. Appendix B adds human-versus-GPT-4o cases and expands the earlier cable-response example. These substantially broaden benchmark validation and failure analysis. Earlier in-context-learning results and caption/domain-knowledge cases are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports model-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new human sample and participant counts describe study design, without adding uncertainty estimates or repeated-run reporting.

E6.justification: All retained Table 2 scores and Tables 3–5 remain numerically unchanged. New results include Claude's 68.36% average and human averages of 86.65% and 78.69% on the sampled study. Table 6 adds CoT comparisons of 69.59% to 65.82% for InternVL2-40B and 70.75% to 72.29% for 76B. Tables 7–8 and Figure 6 add vision-removal, precision/recall/F1 and GT-text results. These are additional outcomes under specified conditions, not revisions demonstrating same-setting improvement between versions.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction pipeline and principal boost methods remain intact. v2 adds structured CoT prompting involving object identification, image comparison and defect judgment, organized into two response stages (Appendix A.3), and extends expert inputs to textual descriptions of ground-truth defect location and size (Section 4.4). v1 already used a brief analysis prompt in one qualitative example.

P1.justification: v2 makes local wording corrections and condenses parts of Sections 4.1 and 4.3, while preserving the main narrative and section sequence. The appendix gains dedicated analysis subsections and moves case studies from A.3 to Appendix B. Most retained prose is unchanged, so the added scientific material does not constitute extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: The visual presentation expands substantially: Figure 1 substitutes a human curve for MiniCPM, Table 2 adds and regroups rows, and new Tables 6–8 and Figures 8–10 display ablations, filtering tools, word clouds and precision-recall results. The earlier response case is expanded with colored comparative responses, two cases are added, and older caption/domain-knowledge figures are relocated and compacted into Figures 14–17.

R1.justification: v2 adds MathVista, Chu et al.'s CoT survey and Chen et al.'s evaluation study. It also strengthens criticism of Seed-Bench and CompBench from lacking industrial images to involving fictional tasks without realistic references. These are limited additions to the existing related-work framing.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theorems, proofs or mathematical derivations. The additional standard evaluation metrics and positive-class convention in Appendix A.7 do not introduce substantive mathematical theory.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens benchmark validation and transparency through visual-dependence controls, error-profile metrics and clearer annotation-review documentation while preserving the original results. The net improvement is limited by the preliminary human study: only 177 examples are sampled, uncertainty is unreported, and model scores on that same subset are not clearly provided. The new claim of human superiority on every metric also contradicts Table 8, which reports higher recall for LLaVA-1.5 and higher precision for SPHINX.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MMAD benchmark, dataset construction pipeline and evaluation framework. Their complete main texts, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds human evaluation, Claude-3.5-Sonnet results, CoT and vision-removal experiments, and additional performance diagnostics.

before.justification: v1 reports original MLLM evaluations, template and model-scaling experiments, RAG and expert-agent comparisons, and appendix experiments on in-context learning.

title: MMAD: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal Large Language Models in Industrial Anomaly Detection

C1.justification: The title and abstract remove the explicit 'first-ever' assertion. This softens the headline novelty claim only: the introduction, contribution bullets and conclusion still describe MMAD as the first benchmark, and its substantive scope and performance claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 removes the explanation that additional normal images help traditional detectors estimate the normal distribution and avoid misclassifying noise. The interpretations of MLLM performance saturation, possible information overload and insufficient instruction-tuning coverage remain, as do the appendix limitations.

D1.justification: Implementation guidance, API identifiers, quantization statements, prompting information and human-filtering details are retained. The code/data link has the same destination despite different line wrapping; no new reproducibility information is supplied.

E1.justification: Both versions use MVTec AD, MVTec LOCO AD, VisA and GoodsAD, covering the same seven subtasks, 8,366 images and 39,672 questions. The evaluation scenarios are retained; newly cited datasets are not incorporated into the experiments.

E2.justification: Comparator membership remains identical across the corresponding main and appendix experiments. This includes the commercial and open-source MLLMs, human comparisons, and AnomalyCLIP, PatchCore and ground-truth experts in Figure 6. Newly cited methods are not newly evaluated.

E3.justification: The default 1-shot, 0-shot, retrieved-template, few-shot and in-context settings are unchanged, as are model configurations, API versions, option handling and evaluation metrics. The human evaluation still uses 177 examples and eight participants.

E4.justification: Both retain the template, model-size and normal-image-count analyses, RAG and expert comparisons, and appendix in-context, CoT, vision-disable, error analyses and case studies. Section 4.3 shortens the discussion without adding or removing an analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same point-estimate results without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. Parenthesized performance differences remain differences rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Numerical results and plotted findings are unchanged throughout the main text and appendices. For example, Table 2 retains GPT-4o's 74.92% average and InternVL2-76B's 70.75%; the RAG, expert-agent and supplementary results also match.

M1.justification: The GPT-4V annotation pipeline, template retrieval, RAG procedure and visual expert-agent method in Sections 3.3–3.4 are unchanged. No algorithmic component or model adaptation is added or revised.

P1.justification: The title and abstract receive limited wording edits, and the final analysis paragraph in Section 4.3 is condensed. Headers change from 'Preprint copy' to the ICLR 2025 publication statement. Section order and appendix prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 are modestly enlarged and repositioned, and spacing and page breaks change elsewhere. The conclusion now fits entirely on page 10 instead of continuing onto page 11. All figure and table content is retained; appendix page bodies are visually identical.

R1.justification: Sections 1–2 add citations to ADer, M3DM-NR, Real-IAD and SoftPatch+, while removing Roth et al. (2022). These are limited updates to the industrial-anomaly-detection context; the broader research positioning remains substantially the same.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theoretical results or proofs. The existing task definitions, retrieval description and evaluation-metric explanations are unchanged.

improvement.justification: The citation refresh, condensed discussion and modest layout adjustments provide limited editorial benefits, while removing one background explanation slightly reduces detail. The novelty assertion remains elsewhere despite the softer title and abstract. With the methods, empirical evidence, appendices and reproducibility information unchanged, overall paper quality is essentially the same.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable, complete 23-page versions of MMAD, with corresponding main sections, figures, tables and Appendices A–B. Text and visual inspection support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains the original model and human evaluations, RAG and expert-agent experiments, and appendix analyses, including their reported outcomes.

before.justification: v2 reports original model evaluations, a human evaluation using 177 examples, performance-enhancement experiments and supplementary analyses in Appendix A.

title: MMAD: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal Large Language Models in Industrial Anomaly Detection

C1.justification: The introduction's empirical contribution changes from visual control 'while being safe during learning' to 'incurring significantly fewer constraint violations.' This narrows that safety claim; the central algorithmic and theoretical contributions, abstract, and conclusion remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly limits the practical safety requirement to after a controlled or supervised warm-up period. The new appendix discussion attributes ACTSAFE's exploration advantage to a more confined state-action space and acknowledges that OPAX recovers performance with additional exploration.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2 newly specifies a 750K-parameter policy and replaces the anonymous implementation link with a named GitHub repository link. The new appendix comparison also explicitly states ACTSAFE's 1M-step Cartpole exploration budget. These additions improve documentation without demonstrating a model-size change.

E1.justification: Both versions cover the same GP tasks, dense and sparse SAFETY-GYM tasks, POINT and DOGGO robots, RWRL Cartpole, dynamics shifts, and HUMANOIDBENCH POLE. Figure 12 uses the existing CARTPOLESWINGUPSPARSE task.

E2.justification: Figure 12 adds OPAX to the RWRL CARTPOLESWINGUPSPARSE comparison, with two exploration budgets. V1 already evaluated OPAX on GP tasks and HUMANOIDBENCH, but not in this comparison. Existing comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: Section 5.2 replaces the stated initialization from 200K offline random-policy steps with a 200K-step warm-up, explicitly shared across baselines and allowing initially unpenalized safety violations. Figure 12 adds comparisons using 1M and 1.25M exploration steps. These are reported protocol revisions and additions; they do not establish that all retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds a focused analysis of whether restricting exploration to safe policies helps sparse-reward learning, including whether additional OPAX exploration removes its performance deficit. Existing pessimism, LBSGD, and distribution-shift analyses remain.

E5.justification: Figure 4 changes from reporting the median and standard error across 5 seeds to the mean and standard error across 10 seeds. Appendix B.2 retains its default of 5 seeds and median reporting unless otherwise specified, so this is a localized reporting change.

E6.justification: Figure 4's learning curves change, including a smaller final ACTSAFE–LAMBDA reward gap on PUSHBOX, under revised aggregation and initialization reporting. New Figure 12 shows OPAX failing to learn a successful policy with 1M exploration steps but recovering with 1.25M, while violating constraints at both budgets. These are revised and additional results, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2, the exploration and safety objectives, and the GP/RSSM implementations remain substantively unchanged. The newly stated policy parameter count documents the implementation without establishing an architectural change.

P1.justification: V2 makes limited wording corrections, updates the publication header, expands related-work and warm-up explanations, and adds an Appendix C subsection. The main section organization and most prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: V2 adds Figure 12, rearranges the GP bar charts and Figure 6 into side-by-side panels, and adds warm-up shading and revised axes or reference lines to several plots. Figures 2 and 3 exchange numbering; their underlying experiment types are retained. Table 1 remains substantively unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds discussion and citations for safety-critic and recovery approaches by Srinivasan, Thananjeyan, and Bharadhwaj. References to offline-learning work by Kidambi, Matsushima, and Feng are removed with the revised initialization discussion. The overall research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: The assumptions, safe-set definitions, Theorem 4.8, and Appendix A derivations and proofs are substantively identical. Differences are formatting and whitespace.

improvement.justification: The OPAX budget comparison gives a more informative test of sparse-reward exploration, including a control showing recovery with additional exploration. Clearer warm-up assumptions and a narrower empirical safety contribution improve transparency, while Figure 4 reports more seeds. These are limited gains in support and clarity; the method and theory remain unchanged, and the revised curves do not establish like-for-like performance improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ACTSAFE and contain readable main text, equations, figures, Table 1, and Appendices A–C. The retained material and additions support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds an ACTSAFE–OPAX comparison with different exploration budgets in Appendix C, Figure 12.

before.justification: V1 reports original GP control experiments and evaluations on SAFETY-GYM, RWRL, and HUMANOIDBENCH, including appendix ablations and distribution-shift experiments.

title: ActSafe: Active Exploration with Safety Constraints for Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about safe exploration, finite-sample near-optimality under assumptions, scalability to visual control, and empirical performance.

C2.justification: The explanations of conservatism versus reward, initial calibration requirements, LBSGD's unmet unbiasedness assumption, and simulator-fidelity/pessimism tradeoffs are unchanged in Section 5 and Appendix C.

D1.justification: Implementation details, reward and cost definitions, model size, ensemble and planner descriptions, and the code-access statement are unchanged. The added funding acknowledgment supplies no new reproducibility information.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same Pendulum/Cartpole tasks, dense and sparse Safety-Gym tasks, RWRL Cartpole, DOGGO, shifted-dynamics scenarios, and HumanoidBench POLE task. Appendix coverage is unchanged.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain their comparator sets, including OPAX, LAMBDA, CPO, BSRP-LAG, GREEDY, UNIFORM, OPTIMISTIC, and the same ActSafe ablation variants. The deleted citation in Section 4.3 does not remove an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Section 5 and Appendices B-C retain the same metrics, training budgets, episode lengths, 200K-step visual-control warm-up, 50-episode evaluation procedure, and dynamics-shift protocols.

E4.justification: The pessimism ablation in Figure 3, optimizer ablation in Figure 9, dynamics-shift analysis in Figure 10, and OPAX exploration-budget comparison in Figure 12 are unchanged.

E5.justification: Figure 4 still reports means and standard errors over 10 seeds. Appendix B.2 retains five seeds by default and median/standard-error reporting. No repeated-run or uncertainty-reporting practice changes.

E6.justification: The experimental plots and accompanying findings in Section 5 and Appendix C are identical. No numerical results, rankings, trends, or qualitative outcomes are added, removed, or revised.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1-2, the exploration and exploitation objectives, pessimistic safety constraints, and GP/RSSM implementations are unchanged. The correction to Assumption 4.5 does not alter the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: v3 corrects 'n-the' and 'Furterhmore', restores a missing closing brace in Assumption 4.5, and adds an ELSA/EU funding acknowledgment for Bhavya Sukhija. Section order and the overall narrative remain unchanged.

P2.justification: All 12 figures and Table 1 retain their content, design, and placement. The expanded acknowledgment shifts and compresses reference spacing on page 11; other visual edits are limited to local text reflow and the updated arXiv margin stamp.

R1.justification: Section 4.3 removes Sukhija et al. (2023), GoSafeOpt, from the examples credited with a similar safe-set relaxation, retaining Berkenkamp et al. (2021) and Baumann et al. (2021). GoSafeOpt remains cited elsewhere and in the bibliography; broader positioning is unchanged.

T1.justification: Assumption 4.5 changes the kernel bound from k(s,s) <= sigma_max for states s in S to k(z,z) <= sigma_max for state-action pairs z in Z. This corrects the formal domain to match Definition 4.4. Theorem 4.8 and all Appendix A proofs remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 improves mathematical precision by correcting Assumption 4.5's kernel-bound domain to the state-action space already used by the dynamics model. Local typographical repairs add clarity. These are limited improvements: the methods, empirical evidence, main claims, and appendix proofs remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete 25-page versions of the same ActSafe paper, including Appendices A-C. Text and rendered-page inspection support direct comparison of the equations, figures, tables, and appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and their reported outcomes, including GP control, visual control, and HumanoidBench evaluations.

before.justification: v2 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments in Section 5 and Appendix C, including reward, safety-cost, ablation, and dynamics-shift results.

title: ActSafe: Active Exploration with Safety Constraints for Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The introduction's contribution list and the conclusion retain the same claims about off-policy episodic learning, Transformer sequence-value estimation, sample efficiency, and performance across 53 tasks. The abstract edits do not materially change these claims.

C2.justification: Section 5.3 adds the interpretation that varying segment lengths regularizes critic training by exposing the V-function to Q-targets over different action horizons. The limitations concerning within-episode changes and POMDPs remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository hyperlink and a reproducibility statement covering implementations, environments, and trained models. Appendices A.1–A.2 disclose Cholesky-based sampling, TRPL projection details, and behavior-policy or EMA reference choices. These expand documentation; the existing hyperparameter tables are unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 50 Meta-World tasks, Hopper Jump, and dense- and sparse-reward Box Pushing. The individual Meta-World plots in v2 disclose results within existing coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparators remain TCE, BBRL, PPO, GTrXL trained with PPO, gSDE, SAC, and PINK. The critic-target variants in Figure 5 and Table 1 are also unchanged.

E3.justification: Figure 4c–d extends TOP-ERL's reported training/evaluation horizon from approximately 14 million interactions in v1 to 40 million in v2. The task definitions, evaluation metrics, and hyperparameter Tables 4–7 remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish whether runs were continued or repeated.

E4.justification: Appendix B.4 and Figure 7 add a concrete Box Pushing trajectory example contrasting an unconditioned new trajectory with five segments initialized at the old trajectory's states. The performance ablations, segmentation sensitivity experiment, and action-correlation analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify eight random seeds, interquartile means, and 95% stratified bootstrap confidence intervals. The additional curves do not introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice or an increased seed count.

E6.justification: Figures 8–9 add individual learning curves for all 50 Meta-World tasks and their baselines, substantially expanding the reported results beyond the existing aggregate. Figure 4 also revises and extends TOP-ERL's Box Pushing curves to approximately 40 million interactions. Table 1 and the aggregate Meta-World and Hopper Jump curves remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The Transformer critic, N-step targets, policy objective, ProDMP initialization, TRPL, and random segmentation remain unchanged. Appendices A.1–A.2 explain retained components and reference-policy options without establishing a change to the implemented algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized prose corrections, clarifies Section 4 headings, expands Appendix A into three subsections, and adds Appendix B.4 plus acknowledgments, ethics, and reproducibility statements. The main narrative structure remains intact. Appendix A.1 introduces incorrect section and equation references.

P2.justification: The new trajectory Figure 7 and two figures containing 50 individual task panels substantially expand the visual presentation. Figure 4 is relocated, retained appendix figures are renumbered, and hyperparameter tables receive increased vertical spacing.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Agrawal et al. (2019) and Schulman et al. (2015) in the TRPL discussion. Section 4 more explicitly distinguishes inherited trajectory-generation and stabilization techniques from the proposed critic and update mechanisms, while retaining the original research positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds explicit constrained optimization definitions for the per-state mean and covariance projections in Eq. (11). Appendix B.3 removes v1's final xi-based trajectory expansion and coefficient definitions while retaining the underlying initial-condition solution. The core objectives and ODE mathematics remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 improves transparency through individual Meta-World results and longer Box Pushing curves, and improves reproducibility documentation through fuller explanations of policy training and TRPL plus a code link. These are useful additions to an otherwise stable method and evaluation. title: TOP-ERL: Transformer-based Off-Policy Episodic Reinforcement Learning

after.justification: v4 retains these original simulation results and supplementary analyses, including benchmark learning curves, critic-update comparisons, and action-correlation visualizations.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds True/False evaluations, additional models, and analyses separating changed from unchanged objects, including Tables 5–7.

Existing training settings and the stated 1,000/9,000 calibration/test split are unchanged.

Appendix C and Figure 13 test whether majority aggregation restores coverage concentration lost through partitioning. P1.justification: Localized rewrites clarify the background, desiderata, majority threshold, and discussion, including a main-text proof sketch. A new statistical-efficiency appendix is inserted, shifting existing Appendices C–E to D–F. The main section sequence and overall narrative remain.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 9, 10, and 13 and reflows the appendices. The earlier Figures 9–11 are retained as Figures 11, 12, and 14. Existing plots and the main document's visual style are preserved.

R1.justification: The bibliography is unchanged, but Section 2 sharpens the distinction between pointwise reliability and prior conformal-coverage guarantees. Theorem 6 replaces tau with the majority threshold tau-hat(alpha). These are localized mathematical revisions, although v2 leaves the quantile-level versus integer-index convention unclear.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds CIFAR100 results, partition-count sensitivity results, and a repeated empirical-coverage study.

No new reliability theorem replaces the retained certificates.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens the paper through focused pretraining evidence, a clearer account of partitioning limitations, correction of the finite-sample quantile formula, and improved reproduction and access information. The revision provides a modest net improvement without substantially resolving the retained method's limitations.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical evaluations and adds experiments comparing pretrained and randomly initialized classifiers in Appendix B, Figure 11.

title: Dualformer: Controllable Fast and Slow Thinking by Learning with Randomized Reasoning Traces

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about fast one-step high-resolution segmentation, edge-assisted detail and determinism, and state-of-the-art DIS performance. Wording changes do not materially alter their scope.

C2.justification: Section 5.3 changes the explanation for inferior multi-step denoising: v1 attributes it to prediction variance from inconsistent training distributions, whereas v2 attributes it to stochastic variations amplified across denoising steps and their conflict with deterministic segmentation. No new experiment tests this revised explanation.

D1.justification: The abstract replaces a generic promise of future code availability with a specific DiffDIS repository hyperlink, while still describing release prospectively. Section 5.1 updates the documented batch size to 4; the other implementation and hardware details remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions train on the same DIS5K coverage and evaluate on DIS-VD and DIS-TE1–4. Replaced illustrative examples do not establish an additional task, domain, or test scenario.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains the same eleven comparators, including MVANet, BiRefNet, and GenPercept. The pretrained-model comparisons in Table 4, DBIAgeo comparison in Table 5, and qualitative comparator set in Figure 6 also remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 changes the reported training batch size from 2 to 4. The splits, metrics, 1024 × 1024 resolution, optimizer, learning rate, and 90-epoch limit remain unchanged. Both versions already binarize predictions; v2 adds a rationale. The PDFs do not establish whether experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The existing ablation questions and configurations are retained, but their evidence changes. In Table 3, the reported incremental maximum F-measure benefit of DBIA changes from 0.015 to 0.005, while CutMix changes from no increase to a 0.011 increase. No new ablation family or robustness test is introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Revised point estimates do not change the uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 2–5 substantially revise the central comparative and ablation evidence. Table 2 changes overall maximum F-measure from 0.921 to 0.911 for DiffDIS and 0.916 to 0.908 for MVANet. On DIS-TE4, DiffDIS's lead reverses: 0.916 versus 0.911 becomes 0.909 versus 0.912. Table 4 changes training-from-scratch maximum F-measure from 0.747 to 0.682 and one-step SDV2.1 from 0.890 to 0.853. Selected predictions in Figure 6 also change. These are revised reports; the batch-size change prevents treating them as established same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The VAE latent representation, SD-Turbo initialization, one-step denoising, auxiliary edge prediction, batch-discriminative embeddings, DBIA, and scale-wise conditional injection remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–2 retain the same procedures.

P1.justification: The introduction's challenge and strategy paragraphs are streamlined, and the DBIA and scale-wise injection explanations receive localized edits. The section hierarchy and overall narrative remain the same.

P2.justification: Figure 1 replaces one illustrated image-mask example, and Figure 6 updates selected displayed predictions while preserving its comparison grid. Table 2 explicitly labels the aggregate as DIS-TE(1–4). Spacing changes fit the abstract onto the first page and produce limited reflow; the main diagrams and table structures are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2.1 adds references on mixed-scale and open-vocabulary camouflaged segmentation and context-dependent segmentation, while removing Le et al. (2019). Section 4.2 replaces Cheng et al. (2020) with Zhao et al. (2022) for edge-related work. These are localized literature updates; the principal research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: Equations 1–6, their mathematical assumptions, and the one-step denoising derivation retain the same content. Equation 4 moves across a page boundary, but no definition, derivation, or proof is substantively revised.

improvement.justification: v2 modestly improves documentation and table consistency through a concrete code destination, clearer aggregate labeling, and a corrected MVANet overall weighted F-measure: 0.855 becomes 0.861, matching the mean of the unchanged equal-sized test subsets. The gains are limited: other score revisions remain unexplained, and v2 introduces a small mismatch between the corresponding SD-Turbo baseline maximum F-measures in Tables 3 and 4, 0.882 versus 0.883.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DiffDIS research. All pages, equations, tables, and figures support comparison; both documents end with references and contain no separate appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical studies and reports revised numerical results and qualitative predictions.

before.justification: v1 reports original DIS5K segmentation experiments, VAE reconstruction results, component and denoising ablations, and qualitative predictions in Tables 1–5 and Figures 1, 4, and 6.

title: High-Precision Dichotomous Image Segmentation via Probing Diffusion Capacity

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain identical claims about segmentation accuracy, rapid one-step inference, detail preservation, and improved determinism.

C2.justification: Interpretations of edge-assisted determinism, SD-Turbo initialization, and multi-step stochasticity are unchanged. No substantive limitations or applicability qualifications are added or removed.

D1.justification: Implementation details, hardware, optimization settings, and preprocessing instructions are identical. Both retain the same future code-release statement and repository hyperlink.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same DIS5K training, validation, and four test subsets. No dataset, task, domain, or test scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains the same 11 baselines, including GenPercept, MVANet, and BiRefNet. The qualitative comparison and DBIA interaction comparison also retain their comparator sets.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 retains identical splits, five metrics, 1024×1024 inputs, training settings, and evaluation binarization. The denoising configurations and DIS-VD ablation protocol are also unchanged.

E4.justification: The VAE reconstruction analysis, edge/DBIA visualization, component ablations, pretrained-weight and denoising-step comparisons, and interaction ablation remain identical in Tables 1 and 3–5 and Figure 4.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Statistical and uncertainty-reporting practices are unchanged.

E6.justification: All numerical entries and qualitative results are identical. For example, Table 2 reports DiffDIS DIS-VD maximum F-measure of 0.908 and MAE of 0.029 in both versions.

M1.justification: Sections 3–4 and Algorithms 1–2 are unchanged, including one-step denoising, joint mask/edge prediction, batch-discriminative embeddings, DBIA, and scale-wise conditional injection.

P1.justification: v3 adds the running text 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025' and updates the arXiv version/date stamp. Body wording, terminology, and section organization remain identical.

P2.justification: The added publication header and updated first-page margin stamp make small visual changes. Figures 1–6, Tables 1–5, captions, placement, and body layout are unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2, citations, and the complete reference list are unchanged, as is the positioning relative to segmentation and diffusion research.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(6), including the one-step denoising derivation, training objective, and mutual attention formulation, are unchanged. No assumptions, proofs, or mathematical corrections are introduced.

improvement.justification: The revisions identify conference publication and update version markings. Scientific content, empirical evidence, explanations, reproducibility information, and body presentation are identical, establishing no meaningful overall quality difference.

A1.justification: Both complete, readable 14-page PDFs describe the same DiffDIS research. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. Both end with references; neither contains an appendix.

after.justification: v3 retains the same original benchmark results, ablations, and qualitative comparisons.

before.justification: v2 reports original DIS5K benchmark results, component and denoising ablations, and qualitative segmentation comparisons in Section 5.

title: High-Precision Dichotomous Image Segmentation via Probing Diffusion Capacity

C1.justification: The introduction retains the same three contributions: sharing unaggregated prompts, personalized attention-based prompt mixtures, and empirical superiority across nine datasets. Although the abstract and conclusion are shortened, the central novelty, applicability, and comparative-performance claims remain.

C2.justification: Appendix A adds explanations linking prompt provenance and KNN selection to privacy risk, local gating to noise tolerance, gate aggregation to reduced personalization, additional experts to diminishing returns, and large feature dimensions to overparameterization. It also interprets attention weights as expert contributions and claims every expert is indispensable, an inference stronger than the visualization alone establishes.

D1.justification: Table 5 newly documents dataset training/test sizes and class counts; the appendix supplies configurations, gate sizes, and attention-averaging procedures for its added studies. v3 also provides a repository link and states code availability, replacing v1's promised public release upon acceptance. Existing backbone, optimizer, learning-rate, and epoch details are retained; repository availability was not independently checked.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same five CLIP classification datasets, CIFAR10/100, DomainNet, and Office-Caltech10 with the same label- and feature-shift coverage. The added privacy and architectural studies vary procedures and configurations within these retained tasks and datasets.

E2.justification: The comparator sets in the original benchmark tables remain unchanged. Appendix Table 7 newly evaluates linear-projection gating with three and ten experts and an aggregated attention gate against the proposed local attention gate. The additional related-work citations do not introduce evaluated benchmark baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix A adds privacy experiments with epsilon 25/50 and delta 0.05, gate-aggregation controls, expert-count sweeps on DomainNet and CIFAR10, and pooled feature dimensions from 32 to 1024. Separately, Section 5.1 corrects CIFAR's stated client count from 10 to 100, agreeing with v1's existing caption and discussion; this does not establish rerunning the original experiments.

E4.justification: v1 analyzes shot count and the local-logit coefficient. v3 retains those analyses and adds privacy-noise robustness, attention versus linear gating, local versus aggregated gating, sensitivity to expert count and feature dimension, and attention-contribution visualizations. These substantially expand tests of architectural choices and operating conditions.

E5.justification: Section 5.2 in both versions specifies means and standard deviations over three runs with different seeds. The added tables continue this reporting practice without announcing additional runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: The original benchmark values and Figures 3–4 are retained, including the renumbered CIFAR and DomainNet tables. Appendix A adds substantial results: Table 7 reports Flowers102 accuracy of 69.64±4.57 for ten-expert linear gating versus 98.41±0.04 for local attention gating; Table 6 reports 98.36±0.12 for private pFedMoAP at epsilon 25. Further results cover expert count, feature dimension, and attention contributions.

M1.justification: The core pFedMoAP architecture, objectives, expert selection, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Appendix A.2 adds an evaluated differential-privacy adaptation that clips prompt gradients and adds noise to uploaded prompts, introducing limited training and communication operations.

P1.justification: The abstract and conclusion are condensed, several related-work and evaluation passages are edited, and Appendix A introduces four organized subsections. The main section sequence and most explanatory prose, including the method exposition, remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 5–9, an expert-count curve in Figure 5, and six contribution charts in Figure 6. The original figures remain; the CIFAR and DomainNet tables exchange numbering, DomainNet moves beside Office-Caltech10, and best-score bolding and associated caption statements are removed from the original tables.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to Cai et al., Deng et al., FedTP, and Pan et al. in its research context, plus Collins et al. and Dwork for appendix discussions. These modestly broaden coverage of personalization, prompt-learning theory, and privacy while preserving the original positioning around unaggregated prompt sharing.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, objectives, and derivations in Equations 1–11 remain unchanged. The added privacy experiments and citation to a theoretical federated-learning framework introduce no new formal definition, theorem, proof, or mathematical guarantee.

improvement.justification: v1's central arguments for attention-based and locally maintained gating lacked direct experimental controls. v3's Table 7 tests both choices, while Tables 8–9 examine dependence on expert count and feature dimension, substantially strengthening validation of the design. Dataset statistics and stated code access also improve reproducibility. Privacy guarantees remain under-specified, and attention weights do not prove expert indispensability, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger evidence supporting the central architecture.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same pFedMoAP research. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison. v1 ends after the references; v3 adds a readable Appendix A.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds measured privacy, gating-network, expert-count, feature-dimension, and attention-contribution results in Appendix A.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original experiments across nine datasets, including comparative accuracies in Tables 1–4 and ablations in Figures 3–4.

title: Mixture of Experts Made Personalized: Federated Prompt Learning for Vision-Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion retain identical claims about sharing lightweight prompts, personalized attention-based gating, and effectiveness under heterogeneous federated settings.

C2.justification: Interpretations of gating behavior, privacy, expert-count saturation, and feature-dimension tradeoffs are unchanged, as are the stated limitations. The new NIH/NSF policy disclaimer does not alter scientific interpretations or applicability.

D1.justification: Implementation details, hyperparameters, dataset setup, code-access information, and the Bridges-2 computing-resource disclosure are unchanged. The added NIH contract is funding information rather than a technical or reproducibility detail.

E1.justification: Section 5.1 and Appendix A retain the same nine image-classification datasets and the same few-shot, label-shift, combined feature/label-shift, and differential-privacy scenarios.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in every corresponding experiment. Table 1 retains ZS-CLIP, CoOp, PromptFL, adapted FL methods, pFedPrompt, and FedOTP; the other main and appendix comparisons also retain their original rows.

E3.justification: Section 5 and Appendix A preserve the same data partitions, client counts, participation rates, CLIP backbones, training budgets, accuracy metric, and differential-privacy settings.

E4.justification: The shot-count and local-logit-weight studies in Section 5.3 are unchanged. Appendix A retains identical analyses of differential privacy, gating architecture and aggregation, expert count, feature dimension, and expert contributions.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations over three runs with different seeds in Section 5.2. Uncertainty reporting in the main and appendix results is unchanged.

E6.justification: All result entries and plotted findings in Tables 1–4 and 6–9 and Figures 3–6 are unchanged. For example, Table 1 retains Flowers102 accuracy of 98.41±0.04 for pFedMoAP with λ=0.5.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Algorithm 1 retain the same prompt-expert pool, KNN expert selection, attention-based gating, training procedure, and combination of local and MoE logits.

P1.justification: Page 12 changes the funding wording to 'supported in part,' adds NIH contract 1OT2OD037972-01, and adds an NIH/NSF policy disclaimer. Page 1 updates the arXiv version/date stamp; research prose and section organization are unchanged.

P2.justification: The expanded acknowledgments cause local text reflow and tighter vertical spacing on page 12. Figures, tables, captions, and appendix layouts are unchanged; all pages other than 1 and 12 render identically.

R1.justification: Section 2, citations throughout the paper, and the reference list are unchanged. No prior work is added or removed, and the research positioning remains identical.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(11), objective definitions, prompt/MoE formulations, and attention mathematics are identical. No formal assumptions, derivations, or proofs are added or revised.

improvement.justification: v4 expands the funding acknowledgment and adds an agency-policy disclaimer, with minor local layout changes. These administrative updates leave the scientific content, empirical evidence, clarity of the research exposition, and reproducibility information unchanged, including Appendix A, so overall paper quality does not meaningfully change.

A1.justification: Both complete, readable 20-page PDFs describe pFedMoAP and contain the same main sections and Appendix A. Text and rendered-page comparisons support reliable comparison of the equations, figures, tables, and appendices.

after.justification: v4 retains these original benchmark results, differential-privacy experiments, and ablations in the main text and Appendix A.

before.justification: v3 reports original image-classification experiments across nine datasets, with benchmark results in Tables 1–4 and additional privacy experiments and ablations in Appendix A.

title: Mixture of Experts Made Personalized: Federated Prompt Learning for Vision-Language Models

C1.justification: Both versions claim input-driven surrogate modeling with automatically reduced latent dimensionality, continuous propagation of variational parameters, stochastic stabilization, and Koopman approximation. The expanded benchmark examples and condensed conclusion change supporting evidence and emphasis without redefining these central contributions.

C2.justification: v1's discussion emphasizes real-data inference requirements, unresolved uncertainty-quantification applications, and numerical stability. v3 replaces this with comparative accuracy, automation, speed, and applicability arguments, and removes explicit dynamic-variance training caveats from Section 3.4. It also adds interpretations connecting fewer function evaluations to speed and masking results to persistent dimensionality reduction.

D1.justification: A.5.6–A.5.10 add dataset construction settings, MuJoCo filtering, PyKoopman implementation information, DMD rank searches, and radial-basis-function tuning. Small Grid and Water Hammer models or datasets are stated to be available on request. A.5.4 newly documents final-stage dopri5 training and adaptive batch step-size control; the main code-access link remains unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds controlled robot dynamics from MuJoCo Ant, pressure-wave dynamics from Water Hammer, and three-dimensional airflow from Small Grid (Sections 4.3, 5.3, and A.5.6–A.5.8). These substantially broaden the evaluated domains beyond the retained thermal examples and analytic Koopman system.

E2.justification: Table 2 introduces evaluated eDMDc and DMDc comparisons for linear surrogates. Table 1 adds zero-β B-NODE controls and changes comparator membership on retained tasks, including SS-NODE on heat flow and input-conditioned Latent NODE on the power plant. These extend v1's heat-flow TBR/Latent ODE and power-plant SS-NODE comparisons.

E3.justification: New benchmark protocols specify variance-normalized RMSE, with power-plant outputs evaluated in the nonlinear benchmark and states in the linear benchmark (A.5.9–A.5.10); retained plots use mean normalization. Added experiments introduce MuJoCo sequence/feature filtering, DMD rank and observable searches, and masking/retraining and sensitivity controls. These are new evaluation designs, not demonstrated changes to existing accuracy experiments.

E4.justification: A.6.1 newly tests masking low-KL channels in linear and nonlinear B-NODEs, followed by training with β set to zero. This differs from the retained static VAE masking analysis in A.3.3. A.6.2 adds sensitivity tests covering network depth and width, activations, decoder controls, latent capacity, solver tolerances, and β.

E5.justification: No new repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. The existing latent-distribution variability visualization remains, while the added benchmark and sensitivity tables report point estimates without run-level uncertainty.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2, Table 4, and Figure A.10 add substantial results. For example, Table 2 reports power-plant RMSE 0.20 for both B-NODE β=0.01 with 25 states and eDMDc with 45 states. Figure 6b replaces B-NODE CPU timing of 4.1 seconds with 0.5 seconds and SS-NODE GPU timing of 15.5 seconds with 68 seconds; the expanded solver and batch descriptions prevent treating these as established same-setting performance comparisons.

M1.justification: The encoders, Gaussian latent distributions, continuous propagation of variational parameters, stochastic training, ELBO objective, and linear Koopman variants remain unchanged. The new masking and architectural variations are supplementary experiments, rather than revisions to the proposed core procedure.

P1.justification: Localized rewrites expand the motivation and KL-channel explanation, standardize SS-NODE terminology, replace the discussion/future-work text, and condense the conclusion. Benchmark subsections are added, but the overall background–method–applications progression and most existing method and appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds four tables and Figures A.8–A.10. Figure 6b is redesigned with an additional CPU comparison, speedup factors, and ODE-evaluation counts. Several retained figures are relocated or resized, and plot annotations are revised. This substantially expands and reorganizes the presentation of evidence.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting PyKoopman, Gymnasium/Minari, and the Water Hammer example, while removing the Koopman VAE discussion and citation and the hybrid-modeling reference to Thummerer and Mikelsons. The broader positioning relative to Neural ODEs, DVAEs, model reduction, and Koopman theory remains substantially intact.

T1.justification: The probabilistic factorizations, ELBO derivations, KL decomposition, and Koopman equations are retained. The Gaussian KL formula newly displayed in Section 2.2 already appears in v1 Appendix A.3.1. Expanded explanations of independence and fixed priors do not establish a substantive change to the existing mathematical formulation.

improvement.justification: Table 2 supplies the DMD comparisons explicitly left for future work in v1, while Table 1 broadens comparative validation across distinct dynamics. The new B-NODE masking and sensitivity experiments directly strengthen evidence for the central dimensionality-reduction claim. Removing useful stability and real-data caveats weakens qualification, and timing comparisons require care, but the improved comparative and diagnostic evidence substantially strengthens the paper overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Balanced Neural ODE research, retaining matching methods, case studies, and appendix derivations. Text extraction and visual inspection covered both complete documents, including figures, tables, and appendices, without material reading gaps.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds nonlinear and linear surrogate benchmarks, B-NODE masking experiments, and hyperparameter sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original VAE and B-NODE experiments, including heat-flow reconstruction and generalization, power-plant accuracy and runtime, Koopman approximation, and appendix latent-channel analyses.

title: Balanced Neural ODEs: nonlinear model order reduction and Koopman operator approximations

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same claims about dimensional reduction, continuous propagation of variational parameters, time-varying inputs, robustness and Koopman approximation.

C2.justification: The accuracy–dimensionality tradeoff, proposed explanation of dynamic variance, short-horizon MPC applicability and broader interpretations remain unchanged. No substantive limitation or qualification is added.

D1.justification: Implementation, hyperparameter, hardware, configuration-file and FMU disclosures are unchanged. V4 replaces the reproducibility statement's first-page pointer with the same repository URL already supplied in v3's first-page footnote; this adds no resource or access condition.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same thermal-network VAE example, stratified heat flow, power plant, analytic Koopman example, Small Grid, Water Hammer and MuJoCo Ant data. No training or evaluation scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged: SS-NODE and Latent NODE in Table 1, TBR in Figure 4, eDMDc for Power Plant and DMDc for Small Grid in Table 2, and the physical-simulation baseline in Figure 6b.

E3.justification: The same splits, sample selection, normalization, metrics, model configurations, solvers and training schedules are reported. Experimental settings in Appendices A.3.2 and A.5 are retained despite early-appendix reflow.

E4.justification: The step-input generalization test, VAE latent-channel and threshold analyses, B-NODE masking experiment and SHF hyperparameter sensitivity analysis are unchanged, including Figures 4b, A.3–A.4, A.10 and Table 4.

E5.justification: Sampling disclosures, the uncertainty representation in Figure 6a and statistical reporting remain unchanged. No repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures are added or revised.

E6.justification: Benchmark values, computation times, rankings and appendix findings are unchanged. For example, Table 1 reports SHF RMSE 0.02 with five states for B-NODE with beta 0.01 in both versions.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Appendix A.4 retain the same B-NODE architecture, variational dynamics, noise injection, training objective, inference procedure and linear Koopman adaptations.

P1.justification: V4 changes the running header from under review to published at ICLR 2025, revises the XRG affiliation, adds acknowledgments and funding information, and lightly rewrites the reproducibility statement. The scientific narrative and section ordering remain intact.

P2.justification: The author block and references reflow, the appendix opening moves from page 14 to page 15, and Figure A.2 moves from page 16 to page 17. Existing figures and tables retain their content and design; these are limited layout changes.

R1.justification: The bibliography and positioning relative to VAEs, Latent ODEs, model order reduction and Koopman methods are unchanged. References crossing page boundaries are retained works, not additions or removals.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, assumptions and derivations are retained, including the ELBO derivations in A.3.1 and A.4.1 and KL-divergence derivation in A.4.4. Equation 24 moves across a page boundary without mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: V4 adds attribution and funding information and repeats an existing repository link directly in the reproducibility statement. These limited editorial benefits do not materially change the methods, evidence, arguments or practical reproducibility, while the accompanying reflow introduces no substantial quality loss.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Balanced Neural ODEs research. All 30 pages, including Appendix A.1–A.6, are readable and support comparison of text, equations, tables and figures after matching reflowed content.

after.justification: V4 retains these original empirical results, including the surrogate-model benchmarks, computation-time measurements and appendix experiments.

before.justification: V3 reports original simulation and model-evaluation results in Sections 4–5, including benchmark Tables 1–2, plus latent-channel analyses and hyperparameter experiments in the appendix.

title: Balanced Neural ODEs: nonlinear model order reduction and Koopman operator approximations

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction narrow the novelty claim from the first unified model to the first diffusion-based unified model. The central claims about two-phase unification and improved generation and prediction remain, while the conclusion retains the broader original novelty wording.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of conditional-evaluation failures from invalid molecules receiving plausible predicted properties, distinctions from denoising pre-training, and comparability limits arising from different bond-inference rules. It also removes v1's explicit qualification that comparing error upper bounds may not reflect actual performance. The original mechanism interpretations largely remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix C consolidates hyperparameters and adds nucleation-time selection guidance, dataset-specific configuration details, and hardware/runtime disclosures: approximately seven days on one A100 for QM9 and 6.5 days on four A100s for GEOM-Drugs. The conflicting GEOM-Drugs settings limit the reproducibility benefit.

E1.justification: V2 adds property-conditioned molecular generation across six QM9 properties, extending the original unconditional generation and property prediction tasks. The new Frad comparison also includes pre-training on 3.4 million PCQMv2 molecules. UniGEM's original QM9 and GEOM-Drugs coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The original comparator sets remain. Table 7 adds EquiFM, GFMDiff, and GeoBFN to generation comparisons; Table 8 evaluates conditional EDM; Table 9 adds Uni-MOL and Frad with EGNN and TorchMD-NET backbones. These substantially broaden the reported comparisons.

E3.justification: New protocols include conditional-generation evaluation using average MAE, molecular stability, and stable-molecule MAE, plus an EGNN-matched Frad comparison. Appendix C also reports four GEOM-Drugs layers and batches of 32 per GPU, versus v1's nine layers and batch 64. V2's main text retains the earlier settings, creating a reporting conflict rather than establishing that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The original loss, sampling, and nucleation-time ablations remain. V2 adds a shared-layer sensitivity study at depths 1, 3, and 5, an EGNN-matched Frad representation analysis, and illustrative generation trajectories in Figure 5. These are focused additions to the existing analyses.

E5.justification: Table 1 retains the same parenthetical quantities. V2 adds no repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or new uncertainty-reporting practice; its additional tables report point estimates.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1–6 retain their scores. New results include 93.7% molecular stability for the BFN variant in Table 7, guided-generation LUMO MAE of 0.592 versus conditional EDM's 0.606 in Table 8, and Frad comparisons in Table 9. These expand the findings substantially; they are not same-setting improvements over v1's UniGEM results.

M1.justification: The original two-phase architecture and losses remain. Appendix B.1 adds a variant replacing EDM coordinate generation with BFN, while B.2 introduces conditional sampling with a property-loss gradient using the existing prediction head. These substantially extend the generation and inference procedures.

P1.justification: V2 condenses Section 2.2, moves property-prediction results into their corresponding subsection, and inserts supplementary-experiment and hyperparameter appendices before the retained material. It also updates affiliations, publication headers, and acknowledgements. Most prose and the main narrative structure remain unchanged.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the empirical displays with a generation-trajectory figure and Tables 7–10 covering new comparisons, conditional generation, and hyperparameters. Tables 2–3 gain baseline shading and annotated gains, and Table 3 becomes full-width. Existing schematics remain; the former Figure 5 becomes Figure 6.

R1.justification: V2 expands positioning relative to denoising pre-training and generators using different bond representations and evaluation rules. Most related work is retained. The GeoBFN reference to Song et al. (2023) disappears, with unresolved citation marks replacing it; several new positioning passages also contain unresolved citations.

T1.justification: The existing analyses receive substantive corrections: generation bounds replace q(yT) with q(y0) in prior-error terms and replace second-moment factors with their square roots. Appendix G.3 revises the KL decomposition using a conditional distribution, and F.3 adds the parameter-independent constant linking denoising and score losses. No new theoretical framework is introduced.

improvement.justification: Appendices B.1–B.3 provide useful additional evidence for generator adaptability, conditional use, and representation learning, while Appendix C improves practical documentation. These strengthen the paper beyond v1's retained core results. The net gain is limited by inconsistent GEOM-Drugs settings, incompletely specified conditional sampling, and newly unresolved citations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UniGEM, with matching core methods, experiments, and theoretical analyses. All 22 pages of v1 and 25 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable. Relocated material, equations, tables, and figures can be reliably matched.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds experiments on BFN-based generation, property-conditioned generation, denoising pre-training comparisons, and shared-layer sensitivity.

before.justification: V1 reports original molecular generation and property prediction experiments on QM9 and GEOM-Drugs, error comparisons, and ablations in Tables 1–6 and Figure 2.

title: UniGEM: A Unified Approach to Generation and Property Prediction for Molecules

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same claims about unified generation and prediction, the two-phase design, improved performance, and potential broader applicability.

C2.justification: The added related-work discussion reiterates the existing rationale for generating coordinates and predicting atom types. Interpretations of results, conditional-evaluation caveats, and limitations on comparisons with alternative molecular generators were already present in v2.

D1.justification: v3 adds a page-1 footnote announcing public code release and providing a repository address; v2 lacks this access disclosure. Implementation, hyperparameter, hardware, and training-time information otherwise remains unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions cover QM9 molecular generation and six-property prediction, GEOM-Drugs generation, and QM9 property-conditioned generation. No dataset, task, or test scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged throughout the reported experiments, including GeoBFN, EquiFM, and GFMDiff in Table 7 and conditional EDM in Table 8. Newly discussed discrete-flow references are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Data splits, model configurations, training budgets, 10,000-molecule evaluation samples, and metrics remain unchanged. Table 8 adds physical-unit labels without changing the reported values or evaluation procedure.

E4.justification: The predictive-loss, sampling/branching, nucleation-time, and shared-layer analyses are retained unchanged in Section 3.2, Figure 2, and Appendix C. No new robustness analysis or case study appears.
