title: Counterfactual Generative Modeling with Variational Causal Inference

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: a counterfactual variational formulation, supervision without observed counterfactuals, latent disentanglement, robust marginal estimation, and empirical advantages.

C2.justification: The explanations of training stability, metric limitations, fairness, unobserved confounding, and relations among treatments remain substantively unchanged. The added causal-hierarchy labels and main-text remarks about surrogate metrics restate distinctions already present in v2.

D1.justification: Appendices J–M retain the same architecture, embeddings, gradient-detaching options, hyperparameters, preprocessing, and hardware information. The code-access information and link target are unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same four datasets and intervention scenarios. Digit-intervention examples already appear in v2 Figure 13; the additional references to them in v3 introduce no new coverage.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged: Table 1 retains AE, CEVAE, GANITE, and CPA; Table 2 retains DEAR, Diff-SCM, CHVAE, MED, and SAE. The ablation variants and Appendix N comparison methods are also retained.

E3.justification: Data splits, preprocessing, model configurations, training schedules, intervention sampling, and evaluation procedures remain unchanged in Appendix M. Replacing 'MSE' with 'error' in some prose and captions does not change the metrics shown in tables and plots.

E4.justification: Section 3.2 extends the ablation account with a qualitative report that counterfactual supervision also improves early optimization on single-cell datasets. No corresponding new curves or detailed analysis are supplied; Figures 3 and 10 and the Appendix N analyses are otherwise unchanged.

E5.justification: The existing five-independent-run reporting, standard errors, and variability plots are retained. No run counts, uncertainty-reporting practices, or statistical procedures are added or revised.

E6.justification: v3 newly reports that the early-training benefit of counterfactual supervision also occurs on single-cell datasets when measured by mean R2. Numerical tables and plotted or sampled outcomes are unchanged; for example, Table 2 retains VCI's mixed-intervention image MSE of 0.36 × 10^-2.

M1.justification: The VCI objective, counterfactual supervision, latent-divergence regularization, robust marginal estimator, and model architectures are unchanged. Revised notation and explanations do not alter the procedures.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized wording and paragraph edits, adds a 'Semi-autoencoding' signpost, supplies explicit pointers to assumptions and Figure 13, and corrects a theorem cross-reference. The overall narrative and section organization remain intact.

P2.justification: Table 3 moves from above Appendix A into the related-work section and is reformatted. Existing Appendix D formulas become numbered displays, several captions are revised, and surrounding material reflows. All figures and tables are retained.

R1.justification: The reference list, related-work comparison, and substantive positioning remain unchanged. The Melistas citation moves from Appendix N.4 to Section 3.2, while the added Pearl citation accompanies an existing interventional-versus-counterfactual distinction.

T1.justification: The assumptions, definitions, mathematical results, and proofs retain their substance. Appendix D turns existing inline formulas into Equations 11–13, expectation notation is standardized, and Corollary 3's erroneous reference to Theorem 3 is corrected to Theorem 2.

improvement.justification: v3 modestly improves readability and navigation through clearer assumption references, correction of Corollary 3's theorem reference, better placement of Table 3, and more readable displayed formulas. The scientific content and quantitative evidence remain essentially stable. The new single-cell training observation lacks additional numerical support, so it provides only a limited evidential gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same research work, with readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete Appendices A–N. The material supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results in Section 3 and Appendix N, including benchmark comparisons, marginal-estimator evaluations, and disentanglement analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original experiments on Sciplex, Marson, Morpho-MNIST, and CelebA-HQ, including quantitative comparisons, ablations, and generated examples.

title: Counterfactual Generative Modeling with Variational Causal Inference

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: a generalized iterative preference framework, overconfident labeling as a source of rewarding bias, and cross-iteration consistency regularization to improve self-rewarding. Additional experiments support these claims without materially redefining their scope.

C2.justification: New discussion explains label smoothing versus loss scaling, the rarity of near-zero consistency, model-level uncertainty, and averaging as variance reduction. Appendices A and C.6 explicitly discuss computational costs and the need for initial alignment. Longer-term stability and ensemble comparisons receive substantive interpretations. The arena discussion also newly mentions GPT-4o as an opponent, although Figure 3 still shows it only as judge.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies five sampled responses per prompt, comparator hyperparameter grids, ensemble learning rates and weighted-DPO checkpoint selection. Conversely, it removes the NVIDIA A6000 hardware statement and explicit GPT-4o provenance of curated preference labels. The code link and principal optimizer, learning-rate and epoch disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use OpenAssistant, ARC-Easy/Challenge, OpenBookQA, SIQA and GSM8K, plus curated preference-ranking data and RewardBench. The added larger and initially unaligned models are configurations evaluated on retained tasks, without new datasets, domains or input scenarios.

E2.justification: v3 substantially expands evaluated comparators. Table 1 adds SRLM + KL and CREAM w/o RC; Tables 6, 8 and 12 add weighted-DPO SRLM, Ensemble-Worst, Ensemble-Mean, Distilled DPO and P-CREAM comparisons. Original SRLM, Oracle and P-SRLM comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols extend training from M3 through M6, evaluate Llama-2-13B and non-chat Llama-3-8B, and introduce regularization grids and three-model ensembles trained with different learning rates. Appendix C.2 also specifies checkpoint selection for weighted-DPO experiments. The original benchmark settings remain; newly specifying five responses per prompt is disclosure, not evidence of a changed sampling budget.

E4.justification: v3 adds targeted tests of adaptive versus fixed consistency, simple loss weighting, ensemble rewards, thresholded versus per-example regularization, and prompt-based regularization. It also examines M4–M6 stability, consistency distributions, model size and initial alignment. The original date-arithmetic case study in Section 4.3.4 and Table 5 is removed rather than relocated.

E5.justification: The existing plus/minus reporting in Table 2 is unchanged. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. New consistency-score distributions in Table 7 describe an additional analysis, without introducing a new uncertainty-estimation procedure for benchmark performance.

E6.justification: Original benchmark scores and Figures 3–5 are retained, and v1 Table 6 reappears as v3 Table 13. Extensive new results include CREAM's average peaking at 83.65 at M4 and declining to 82.73 at M6, versus SRLM's 68.59 at M6 (Table 5). New M3 comparisons report 57.46 versus 49.33 on Llama-2-13B and 42.67 versus 35.55 with initially unaligned Llama-3. These are added settings, not improvements to the original scores.

M1.justification: The default algorithm, intrinsic rewards and consistency-weighted normal/reversed DPO objective remain unchanged. Appendix C adds limited procedural variants: threshold-dependent regularization, per-example consistency weights and prompt-rewarding P-CREAM. The corrected worst-response selection formula agrees with v1's existing best/worst-response description.

P1.justification: The introduction and experimental discussion are edited and condensed, the case-study subsection is removed, and appendices are reorganized into Limitations, Proofs and subdivided Additional Results. The main five-section narrative and method exposition remain largely intact. The publication header changes from Preprint to ICLR 2025.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains comparator rows and an Average column and is substantially resized. Eight new appendix tables appear as Tables 5–12; the original case-study table is removed, while v1 Table 6 becomes Table 13. Existing figures are retained, but experiment-page table placement, sizing and text flow are substantially rearranged.

R1.justification: Section 2 and Appendix C.4 substantially expand positioning against reward hacking, reward-model ensembles and robust preference optimization, including Coste, Eisenstein, Rame, Zhang and Fisch. New distillation references support that discussion. Two peripheral vision-language references are removed. The revision develops substantive distinctions about preference regularization, conservatism and ensemble costs.

T1.justification: The original theorems, lemmas and proofs are retained, with Appendix A becoming B. Equations 3.11–3.12 correct worst-response selection from argmin to argmax. Appendices C.2 and C.4 add gradient/equal-ratio analysis, a zero-loss self-distillation minimizer argument and mathematical comparisons of regularization objectives; these supplement the existing theoretical framework.

improvement.justification: Table 1 and Appendix C substantially strengthen validation by testing adaptive consistency against simpler regularization and weighting alternatives, examining later-iteration degradation, and probing model-size and initial-alignment dependence. These address important gaps in v1, while explicit limitations clarify applicability. Lost hardware and label-provenance details and unsupported GPT-4o-opponent wording are drawbacks; run-based uncertainty also remains unreported. The targeted validation gains outweigh these narrower weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CREAM research, with matching authors, core algorithm and original experiments. Text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and can be matched across the expanded and reorganized material.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds comparator, longer-training, model-configuration and regularization experiments in Section 4 and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original Llama-2/Llama-3 benchmark experiments, preference-ranking evaluations, consistency analyses and ablations in Section 4 and Appendix B.

title: CREAM: Consistency Regularized Self-Rewarding Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: a generalized iterative preference-tuning framework and consistency regularization to mitigate rewarding bias and improve alignment.

C2.justification: The mechanism explanations, applicability qualifications, and Appendix A limitations are retained. The arena correction changes the attributed empirical comparison, while leaving its interpretation as evidence of improvement across iterations unchanged.

D1.justification: The implementation details, hyperparameters, data preparation descriptions, and code-access link are unchanged. Appendix text flowing onto different pages adds no reproducibility information.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same Open Assistant training data, ARC-Easy/Challenge, OpenBookQA, SIQA, GSM8K, RewardBench, curated preference data, and arena evaluation. No task or test scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: The actual comparator sets remain unchanged, including SRLM, Oracle, SRLM + KL, ensemble methods, and Distilled DPO. Removing GPT-4o from the arena discussion does not remove an evaluated comparator: Figure 3 identifies it as the judge in both versions.

E3.justification: The data construction, model configurations, training budgets, decoding procedures, and evaluation metrics are unchanged. The appendix experiments retain their original settings, including extended iterations and larger or initially unaligned models.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 and Appendix C retain the same analyses of rewarding, consistency measurements, extended training, weighted DPO, ensembles, data-specific consistency, model applicability, and prompt rewarding.

E5.justification: Table 2 retains the same plus/minus reporting, and statistical reporting elsewhere is unchanged. Neither version adds repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests relative to the other.

E6.justification: Section 4.2 removes the reported qualitative finding that CREAM's win and tie rates improve against GPT-4o, retaining that finding only for Oracle. All numerical table and figure results remain unchanged; for example, Table 1 retains the Llama-3 CREAM M3 average of 83.37.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Algorithm 1 retain the same intrinsic rewarding, cross-iteration ranking consistency, and consistency-weighted DPO/reversed-DPO training procedure. The appendix variants are also unchanged.

P1.justification: v5 makes a localized wording correction to the arena paragraph, replaces malformed iteration arrows in Appendix C.6, and updates the arXiv version/date stamp. The section organization and narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: v5 standardizes CREAM typography in several passages, captions, and table labels, with small spacing adjustments and appendix text reflow. All five figures and thirteen tables are retained without substantive display restructuring.

R1.justification: The cited works and research positioning are unchanged, including Section 2 and Appendix C.4's discussion of ensemble methods and robust preference optimization.

T1.justification: The definitions, objectives, theorems, lemmas, and Appendix B proofs are unchanged, as are the mathematical analyses in Appendix C. Correcting iteration arrows in Appendix C.6 is typographical.

improvement.justification: v5 corrects Section 4.2's unsupported statement about improvement against GPT-4o: Figure 3 consistently identifies GPT-4o as the judge, while Oracle is an opponent. This improves agreement between the narrative and evidence. Minor typographical fixes also help readability; the methods, experiments, numerical results, and proofs otherwise remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CREAM research work. Their complete main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–C support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v5 retains these original experiments, including downstream benchmark scores, arena comparisons, reward-ranking evaluations, and appendix ablations.

before.justification: v3 reports original CREAM and baseline experiments on Llama-2 and Llama-3 in Section 4, with additional experiments and analyses in Appendix C.

title: CREAM: Consistency Regularized Self-Rewarding Language Models

C1.justification: Both versions claim automatic discovery and measurement of well-defined, differentiating, user-aligned vibes, alignment with human-discovered traits, approximately 80% model identification and 61% preference prediction, and applicability across the same three application domains.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 adds explicit task-dependent preference interpretations and qualifies them as preliminary evidence without individual-level comparisons. It also softens the explanation of lower STEM accuracy to a suspicion. However, its new statement that formality positively correlates with writing preference contradicts Figure 3’s negative writing coefficient.

D1.justification: v4 adds a VibeCheck code-repository link in the abstract and a Chatbot Arena dataset-access link in Section 5.2; v1 describes obtaining those battles from maintainers. The implementation descriptions, prompts and hyperparameter tables are otherwise retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use HC3, Chatbot Arena overall/STEM/writing, CNN/DailyMail, correctly answered MATH problems with chain-of-thought responses, and COCO/ShareGPT-4V captions. No new dataset, task or test population is introduced.

E2.justification: The predefined-vibe baseline and one- versus three-iteration VibeCheck comparisons remain identical in v1 Table 3 and v4 Table 2. The models compared within each application also remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Figure 1 changes its illustrated model-identity accuracy criterion for a differentiating vibe from greater than 70% to greater than 55%. The experimental splits, judges, budgets and operational filtering thresholds in Sections 4–5 and Appendix A remain unchanged; this does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The iteration comparison, qualitative examples and judge-error cases are retained. v4 Figure 3 juxtaposes STEM/writing results already displayed separately in v1; the accompanying interpretation does not establish a new ablation or robustness experiment.

E5.justification: v1 Tables 7–14 and 16 report per-vibe model-matching and preference-regression p-values. v4 removes these tables, and its replacement figures omit both sets of p-values, despite Section 5 still promising them. Neither version supplies repeated-run uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Headline accuracies remain unchanged, but v4 removes the model-matching coefficient entries from v1 Tables 7–16. Figure 17 newly reports COCO per-vibe Cohen’s kappa and changes displayed preference results: Contextual Storytelling has coefficient -13.514 in v1 Table 15 but a positive bar in v4. These are reporting changes, not demonstrated performance gains.

M1.justification: The discovery, clustering/reduction, two-judge validation, position swapping, filtering and error-driven iteration procedures remain unchanged in Section 4 and Appendix D. The shortened main-text discovery prompt is an explanatory paraphrase.

P1.justification: v4 copyedits and tightens the prose, reorganizes the experimental overview and limitations, expands captions, and moves the example appendix. The main narrative structure and most methodological and technical-appendix text remain intact.

P2.justification: v4 redraws the overview and vibe displays, introducing colored low/high descriptions and signed bars. It consolidates the Arena accuracy table, adds joint STEM/writing and MATH displays of existing results, replaces detailed numerical appendix tables with compact figures, and relocates examples and the predefined-vibe list.

R1.justification: v4 adds the Lin et al. (2014) Microsoft COCO reference and associated citations. The existing related-work coverage and positioning of VibeCheck relative to earlier approaches otherwise remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions of vibe scores, separability and regression-based evaluation remain unchanged. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: Clearer displays and new code/data pointers improve usability, but removing numerical regression tables and coefficient p-values weakens scrutiny of the central preference associations. The new discussion also misstates the direction of writing preference for formality relative to Figure 3. With the principal experiments unchanged, these losses in evidential transparency and interpretive accuracy produce a modest net decline.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VibeCheck. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables and figures support comparison, including matching material across substantial display changes and relocation.

after.justification: v4 retains these original experiments and their quantitative and qualitative outcomes in Sections 5–6 and the appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original vibe discovery, model-matching and preference-prediction experiments on HC3, Chatbot Arena, summarization, mathematics and captioning.

title: VibeCheck: Discover and Quantify Qualitative Differences in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions and application claims, including the stated 80% model-identity and 61% preference-prediction accuracies.

C2.justification: Appendix B drops the quoted RLHF explanations and strengthens the HC3 description from ChatGPT expressing less emotion to not expressing emotions. The principal interpretations and limitations in Sections 5–7 remain unchanged, including the summarization discussion despite the reversed coefficient signs.

D1.justification: Appendix B replaces exact HC3 gold-standard descriptions with abridged summaries, reducing the reference-label detail available for checking human alignment. Implementation prompts, hyperparameters, dataset statistics, and code/data access information are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate HC3, Chatbot Arena overall/STEM/writing, CNN/DailyMail summarization, MATH reasoning, and COCO captioning using ShareGPT-4V captions. No dataset, task, or test scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains the Predefined Vibes baseline and the same one- and three-iteration VibeCheck comparisons. The evaluated model pairings in Table 4 and predefined axes in Appendix C are unchanged.

E3.justification: Train/test counts, hyperparameters, metrics, preference-label generation, and filtering procedures are unchanged, including the MATH restriction to mutually correct answers. The shortened HC3 descriptions do not establish a changed evaluation protocol.

E4.justification: The iteration comparison, STEM-versus-writing analysis, judge-failure examples in Appendix F, and qualitative examples in Appendix H are retained. Removing the main-text summarization plot does not remove its analysis, which remains in Appendix G.

E5.justification: The regression/p-value discussion and statistical reporting practices are unchanged. Neither version adds repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or new uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: The CNN/DailyMail preference-coefficient profile reverses direction between v4 Figure 15 and v6 Figure 14 under unchanged axis definitions: conclusion strength, example specificity, and viewpoint coverage switch from negative to positive, while emotional tone switches from positive to negative. This substantially changes the reported preference associations, although accuracy results remain unchanged. The STEM caption also corrects nine discovered vibes to seven, matching the retained seven rows.

M1.justification: Sections 3–4 and Appendix D retain the same discovery, reduction, judge-based validation, filtering, logistic prediction, and error-driven iteration procedures. No algorithm or model component changes.

P1.justification: Appendix B is condensed and rewritten, acknowledgments become a shorter unnumbered paragraph, and conference headers and small caption edits are introduced. The main scientific narrative and section organization remain largely unchanged.

P2.justification: v6 removes the main-text top-five summarization display while retaining the full appendix plot, places the math plot beside its discussion, enlarges and reflows Table 6, and adjusts figure spacing and captions. These are limited presentation changes rather than a wholesale redesign.

R1.justification: The cited works and research positioning in Section 2 and Appendix E are unchanged. The Chiquier et al. and GLUE reference edits update publication metadata rather than introduce different works.

T1.justification: Section 3 retains the same formal vibe definition, separability formula, and prediction formulations. No mathematical assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs are added or revised.

improvement.justification: The corrected STEM count and more readable Table 6 improve clarity. However, the unexplained summarization coefficient reversal leaves Section 6.1 unreconciled with the newly negative emotional-tone coefficient, and Appendix B loses exact reference detail while strengthening an emotion claim. The PDFs do not establish whether the coefficient reversal corrects an error or introduces one, preventing a reliable judgment of the net quality change.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VibeCheck research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete Appendices A–H support comparison, including matching content across figure removals and renumbering.

after.justification: v6 retains these original empirical evaluations in Table 2, Section 6, and Appendix G.

before.justification: v4 reports original VibeCheck evaluations, including model-matching and preference-prediction results in Table 2, application results in Section 6, and per-vibe results in Appendix G.

title: VibeCheck: Discover and Quantify Qualitative Differences in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same scientific contributions and claims about discovering, quantifying, and interpreting model vibes. The abstract's resource-access update does not change these claims.

C2.justification: The revised Arena motivation foregrounds the benchmark–preference discrepancy already discussed in v6. The interpretation that qualitative traits may explain user preferences, task-specific explanations, and limitations in Section 7 and Appendix F remain unchanged.

D1.justification: The abstract replaces the direct VibeCheck GitHub code pointer with bench-mark.org and explicitly advertises a vibe visualizer alongside the code. This changes documented access information; implementation details and prompts remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish the website's functionality.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate HC3, Chatbot Arena overall and its STEM/Writing subsets, CNN/DailyMail, MATH, and COCO captions. The revised MMLU background discussion introduces no evaluated dataset or scenario.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains the same Predefined Vibes comparator and VibeCheck iteration variants, and Table 4 retains every evaluated model pair. Removing Claude-3-Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 from the background paragraph does not remove evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: Evaluation metrics, preference judges, data splits in Table 3, and hyperparameters in Table 5 are unchanged. The Section 6 description of cached HELM predictions and 1,000 COCO images moves across a page boundary without changing the protocol.

E4.justification: The iteration comparison in Table 2, task-specific analysis in Figure 3, judge-error examples in Appendix F, and illustrative cases in Appendix H are retained unchanged.

E5.justification: No run counts, seeds, uncertainty intervals, or significance procedures are added or revised. References to regression p-values and the limitation concerning run-to-run variability remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Section 5.2 replaces the background statement that Llama-3-70b outperforms Claude-3-Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 on MMLU with a statement that GPT-4 and Claude 3 Opus outperform Llama on conventional benchmarks despite similar Arena preferences. This changes a contextual ranking comparison involving different model pairs. VibeCheck's own results are unchanged, including Table 2's three-iteration overall accuracies of 80.34% for model matching and 59.34% for preference prediction.

M1.justification: Sections 3–4 and Appendix D retain the same discovery, vibe reduction, judge scoring, filtering, logistic regression, and iterative refinement procedures. No algorithmic component changes.

P1.justification: v7 repairs the awkward evaluation-description sentence in Section 5, trims the opening of Section 5.1, and condenses the background and setup paragraphs in Section 5.2. Section organization and the remaining narrative are preserved.

P2.justification: Spacing and text reflow shift existing tables, figures, and example panels within pages 6–10. Figure 2 moves upward, allowing the Section 6 opening paragraph to fit on page 7, and spacing around Table 2 changes. Display content, captions, and appendix layouts remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The cited works and positioning relative to earlier research in Section 2 and Appendix E are unchanged. The Llama 3 model-card reference receives only a punctuation correction.

T1.justification: The vibe-score definition, separability equation, and classifier-based definitions in Sections 3–4 are identical. No assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs are added or revised.

improvement.justification: v7 makes the Arena motivation more direct, improves a few awkward passages, and adds explicit visualizer access information. These are limited readability and documentation gains, with the experimental evidence and limitations preserved. The PDFs do not establish improved empirical support or verify the advertised website's functionality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same VibeCheck paper, with 29 readable pages and complete Appendices A–H. Text comparison and rendered-page inspection support a reliable comparison; all appendix pages are identical.

after.justification: v7 retains these original evaluations and their reported outcomes in Table 2, Section 6, and Appendix G.

before.justification: v6 reports original VibeCheck evaluations, including model-matching and preference-prediction results in Table 2 and analyses of summarization, mathematical reasoning, and captioning in Section 6 and Appendix G.

title: VibeCheck: Discover and Quantify Qualitative Differences in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract expands its claim of consistent superiority over DPO from three publicly available LLMs to five, retaining four math datasets. The stated contributions and conclusion are otherwise unchanged, so this is a limited expansion of claimed empirical scope.

C2.justification: V2 interprets BBH improvements as transferred long-chain reasoning and stable MMLU performance as preserved knowledge. Appendix C adds explanations involving chosen-response likelihood decline, absolute ranking positions, semantic similarity versus token overlap, and the beta/forgetting trade-off. These substantially extend interpretation while retaining the original forgetting and reward-imbalance limitations.

D1.justification: Appendix B supplies exact BBH and MMLU prompts, while Appendix C specifies the new DPO pair constructions and TPO beta settings. Existing data-generation prompts, hardware, optimizer, learning rate and code-access information remain. This is a limited expansion of reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: V2 adds BBH multi-step reasoning and MMLU multiple-choice evaluations to the retained four math and two coding datasets (Section 4.1, Table 2). This substantially broadens out-of-distribution task coverage. The mathematical preference-training corpus remains unchanged.

E2.justification: SFT becomes an evaluated comparator in Tables 1-2. Appendix C.2/Table 5 adds custom DPO* and DPO+ baselines constructed from top-versus-other and adjacent ranked preferences, respectively. Table 6 additionally compares Pointwise SoftMax, Pairwise Logistic and Listwise MLE against LambdaLoss. These are substantive additions to the evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 backbones, BBH step-by-step and MMLU multiple-choice prompting, preference-pair construction controls, and a beta sweep over 0.5, 0.1 and 0.01. These expand the evaluation design; the original pass@1 metric and stated one-epoch training recipe are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds analyses of preference-data use, alternative ranking losses, statistical validation of Adaptive Step Reward, two reward-margin case studies and beta sensitivity. Conversely, v1's MATH difficulty and problem-type breakdowns in Appendix A.2 are removed. The original component ablations and preference-list analyses remain.

E5.justification: Appendix C.4/Table 7 newly reports 20 independent experiments for each TPO/without-Adaptive-Step-Reward condition, performance means with standard errors, independent t-tests, exact p-values and significance markers. V1 reports variability in reward distributions but no corresponding repeated-run uncertainty or significance analysis of model performance.

E6.justification: Original numerical results in Tables 1-3 and Figure 3 are retained, but substantial new results cover SFT, additional backbones, BBH/MMLU, DPO variants, ranking losses, repeated-run estimates and beta settings. For example, new BBH results give Qwen2-7B TPO 69.62 versus DPO 65.58. These are added comparisons, not version-to-version performance gains. The earlier MATH subgroup results are removed.

M1.justification: Equation (10) changes the stated reward calculation: the semantic-similarity weight now multiplies the entire difference between step log-ratios, whereas v1 weights only the first term. This is a limited correction within Adaptive Step Reward; the other components and Algorithm 1 remain. The PDFs do not establish whether the implementation changed.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and the section sequence remain. V2 removes two introductory method-summary paragraphs, moves Algorithm 1 to Appendix A, reorganizes the appendix into algorithms, prompts, experiments and related literature, updates affiliations and conference headers, and adds acknowledgments. The retained narrative is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: Tables 1-2 gain SFT rows, and Table 2 gains grouped reasoning columns. V2 adds six appendix tables, a four-panel reward-margin Figure 4 and two case-study boxes, while removing v1's two MATH breakdown tables and relocating Algorithm 1. Figures 1-3 remain unchanged. This substantially changes the presentation of evidence.

R1.justification: New Appendix D and Table 9 explicitly position TPO against S-DPO, Rose-DPO and ODPO through their objectives and treatment of negative preferences, ranking positions and weighting. Additional ranking-loss, LambdaLoss and preference-optimization literature supports the expanded discussion. These related methods are not reported as direct empirical baselines.

T1.justification: Equation (10)'s revised weighting makes identical shared steps contribute zero, resolving the inconsistency between v1's printed formula and its stated cancellation property. V2 also explicitly explains that cancellation. The other core mathematical definitions and derivations remain, without a new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: The stronger preference-data controls, alternative-loss and beta comparisons, and 20-run significance tests substantially strengthen validation of TPO's central components, especially the previously unquantified small Adaptive Step Reward gains. Additional backbones and reasoning tasks improve assessment of generality, and Equation (10) is corrected. These benefits outweigh the loss of MATH subgroup detail and a flawed new Case 1, whose supposedly correct responses incorrectly calculate (5+3i)(5-3i) as 16.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TPO research and are readable throughout, including equations, figures, tables and appendices. Retained content can be reliably matched despite appendix restructuring.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix C retain original evaluations and add reasoning benchmarks, model backbones, comparison methods, sensitivity experiments and repeated-run statistical results.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix A.2 report original math and coding evaluations, component ablations, preference-list analyses and detailed MATH results.

title: TPO: Aligning Large Language Models with Multi-branch & Multi-step Preference Trees

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions and claims about learning from preference trees, outperforming DPO on in-distribution tasks and potential out-of-distribution generalization.

C2.justification: The interpretations and limitations are unchanged, including catastrophic forgetting as an explanation for HumanEval declines, imbalanced reward distributions, semantic similarity versus token overlap, and the beta trade-off.

D1.justification: The repository link, implementation libraries, hardware, hyperparameters, data-generation instructions and Appendix B prompts are unchanged. No technical or reproducibility information is added or removed.

E1.justification: The training data and evaluation coverage remain identical: MATH, SVAMP, ASDiv, GSM-Plus, HumanEval, MBPP, BBH and MMLU. No dataset, task or test scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain the same SFT, DPO, DeepSeekMath-7B-RL and GPT baselines. Appendix C.2 also retains both DPO* and DPO+ in Table 5.

E3.justification: The model configurations, ten trajectories per training problem, one-epoch training budget, evaluation prompts and pass@1 metric are unchanged. The supplementary experiments retain their original settings.

The introduction's experimental contribution changes from protein structure generation to multimodal protein generation, while Section 9 replaces FrameFlow-focused improvement claims with state-of-the-art claims for MultiFlow jump variants. This expands the empirical claim without redefining the framework.

C2.justification: Appendix E adds substantive interpretations connecting transport versus jumps to probability-path suitability and explaining discretization sensitivity through large Lipschitz constants and repeated small movements. Appendix A further explains the regularity restrictions and why matching marginals can suffice without full time reversal. Appendix I interprets alternative losses as improving training stability.

D1.justification: Appendix G.4 changes the implementation/checkpoint source from FrameFlow to MultiFlow and newly specifies model size, NFE usage and reliance on default configurations. Appendix I documents loss-mixture weights and its sampler. Most image implementation details remain in Appendix F, although the explicit joint-model output-channel count is omitted from the revised main text.

E1.justification: Protein evaluation expands from structure generation to joint structure–sequence generation, alongside a retained structure-only task. This directly tests multimodal generation. CIFAR-10, ImageNet32 and the checkerboard distribution were already evaluated in v1; their additional analyses do not constitute new datasets.

E2.justification: The protein comparison changes from FrameDiff and FrameFlow to FrameFlow, RFdiffusion, FoldFlow, Protpardelle, ProteinGenerator and MultiFlow; FrameDiff disappears from the reported comparison. The expanded checkerboard comparison also adds flow under the mixture path. The image benchmark comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix G.4 changes protein evaluation from 690 samples across lengths 60–128 to 400 samples at lengths 70, 100, 200 and 300, and changes rotation discretization from 1024 to 2056 bins. V2 adds designability reporting and separate multimodal/unimodal comparisons. New experiments introduce 5–500 NFE sweeps and flow-only loss comparisons using dopri5. Protein sampling remains at 100 steps.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's trajectory illustrations and image-sampler comparison, Appendix E systematically examines probability-path/process combinations and sensitivity to sampling NFEs, including mixture-path flow failures. Appendix I adds CIFAR-10 ablations of Bregman loss choices and their training dynamics. These substantially expand analysis of design choices and numerical sensitivity.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. V2's additional generated-sample counts and training curves do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Image FIDs are unchanged between v1 Table 3 and v2 Table 2. The protein results are replaced under different models and protocols, with new multimodal and designability entries; v2 reports multimodal diversity of 0.48 for jumps versus 0.38 for MultiFlow. Appendix I newly reports flow-only FID 2.62 for MSE versus 2.54 for a modified Bregman loss. These are new comparisons, not direct v1-to-v2 performance gains.

M1.justification: The general GM recipe remains, but its concrete models expand substantially. Section 9 replaces the FrameFlow-based structure model with a MultiFlow-based joint structure–sequence model. Appendix E introduces a mixture-path flow and a three-component superposition; Appendix I implements cosh- and exponential-based Bregman training losses.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much existing prose remain. V2 standardizes capitalization and measure notation, clarifies explanations, reorders image/protein experiments, reorganizes Appendix E and removes the acknowledgments. Much of the appendix expansion comprises new scientific content rather than rewriting existing exposition.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the protein montage, expands the protein comparison into multimodal/unimodal columns, and adds the systematic model table, full protein table, checkerboard comparison/NFE panels and loss-training plot. Some checkerboard displays expand existing Figure 2 material. The original manifold illustration is retained as Figure 9 rather than newly added.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning against prior jump-based generation through a new Appendix H.7 covering piecewise-deterministic models, Lévy-process models and trans-dimensional jump diffusion. It also adds a substantive Blackout Diffusion discussion and citations supporting new theoretical and protein comparisons. MultiFlow was already discussed in v1; its empirical comparator role is new.

T1.justification: V2 adds formal strong/weak time-reversal definitions and a general KFE criterion in Appendix A.4. Appendix E adds several path-specific derivations and an impossibility argument for a zero-drift diffusion generating the CondOT path. It also restores missing B-function terms in the Bregman sufficiency proof. These changes extend mathematical substance beyond the retained core propositions and revised notation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the framework's distinctive multimodal and loss-flexibility claims through actual co-design experiments and loss ablations. Its systematic path/process study explains practical failure conditions, while expanded prior-work discussion improves positioning. The gains concern evidential and explanatory quality, not comparable cross-version score improvements. Limitations remain: uncertainty is unreported, and Table 5 shows lower designability for jump variants despite higher diversity, making the blanket claim of best results in all categories too strong.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Generator Matching research, retaining the core framework, propositions and image experiments. Their full texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports image and protein experiments, expanded checkerboard analyses in Appendix E, and original CIFAR-10 loss-function experiments in Appendix I.

before.justification: V1 reports original image and protein generation experiments in Section 9, Tables 2–3, and checkerboard simulations in Figure 2.

title: Generator Matching: Generative modeling with arbitrary Markov processes

C1.justification: The central claims about unification, generator and loss characterization, jump models, superpositions, and multimodal modeling remain intact. The revised abstract and contribution list describe the same capabilities and empirical applications.

C2.justification: The Section 2 remark broadens stated conditioning applicability from the specific start/end-point case to more general latent variables. This is a limited applicability clarification; experimental interpretations and substantive limitations otherwise remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Implementation, sampling, hyperparameter, and loss details in Appendices F, G, and I are unchanged, as are the pretrained-model and repository access information. New acknowledgments provide contributor credit without new reproducibility instructions.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate CIFAR10, ImageNet32 with blurred faces, unimodal and multimodal protein generation, and synthetic checkerboard distributions. The new main-text pointers to Appendices E and I refer to existing experiments.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains DDPM, VP-SDE, EDM, and the same flow/jump comparisons. Tables 3 and 5 retain the same protein baselines, including FoldFlow and MultiFlow. Appendix I retains the same loss-function comparisons.

E3.justification: Evaluation settings and metrics are unchanged, including image sampler comparisons, the protein protocol with 100 NFEs and 400 samples in Appendix G.4, checkerboard NFE sweeps, and Appendix I's dopri5 evaluation.

E4.justification: The sampler comparisons, probability-path and discretization analyses in Appendix E, and alternative-loss study in Appendix I already appear in v2. Section 9 adds a pointer to these analyses, without new ablations or robustness evidence.

E5.justification: The same point estimates and training curves are reported. v3 introduces no run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, significance tests, or changed uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: Numerical results and plotted findings are unchanged. For example, Table 2 retains mixed Jump + Flow FIDs of 2.36 on CIFAR10 and 3.33 on ImageNet32; Appendix I retains the 2.62 versus 2.54 loss-comparison result.

M1.justification: The generator constructions, conditional training objectives, jump models, superpositions, multimodal composition, and Algorithms 1–2 are retained. The rewritten sampling explanation introduces no procedural change.

P1.justification: v3 revises portions of the abstract, contribution list, and probability-path explanation, tightens prose, adds appendix-study pointers and acknowledgments, and updates the publication header. The overall section and appendix organization is retained.

P2.justification: Table 1 expands the diffusion-parameter entry into explicit matrix dimensions and a positive-semidefinite label. Typographic emphasis, headers, and reference pagination change slightly. Figures, empirical table structures, and appendix body layouts are retained.

R1.justification: The bibliography contains the same works. Section 8 and Appendix H retain the same relationships to diffusion, flow matching, stochastic interpolants, and prior Markov generative models; wording edits do not substantively reposition the work.

T1.justification: Theorems, propositions, assumptions, and appendix proofs are unchanged. Equation (1) expresses the same marginal distribution through hierarchical sampling. Table 1 spells out positive semidefiniteness already defined in Theorem 1, rather than changing the constraint.

improvement.justification: v3 modestly improves clarity through the sampling and endpoint explanations in Section 2, explicit diffusion notation in Table 1, and pointers to existing appendix experiments in Section 9. These improve accessibility and navigation; methods, proofs, empirical evidence, and reproducibility information remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Generator Matching work and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices A–I. Full-text and rendered-page comparisons support reliable matching; appendix content is unchanged.

after.justification: v3 retains the original image, protein, checkerboard, and alternative-loss results, including Tables 2, 3, and 5 and Figure 10.

before.justification: v2 reports original image and protein generation results, checkerboard experiments in Appendix E, and alternative-loss experiments in Appendix I.

title: Generator Matching: Generative modeling with arbitrary Markov processes

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the central claims of latent-feature-hierarchy recovery, novel tree decoding, efficient computation, and classification advantages. The introduction's Wasserstein-versus-TWD wording reflects the existing identity for tree ground metrics.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of density normalization under nonuniform sampling, the distinction between initial and transport ground metrics, and single-linkage suitability in hyperbolic space. Appendix E.3.6 interprets the new controls as supporting hierarchy learning, but its broad superiority statement overlooks Table 1's CLASSIC exception: WMD scores 97.2 versus 96.9 for the proposed method.

D1.justification: Appendix D.1 adds explicit Word2Vec/Gene2Vec setup information, identifies Google News pretraining, supplies embedding/data access links, and specifies baseline ground metrics and subclass construction. Hardware, hyperparameter grids, selected settings, and the diffusion-landmark implementation remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The datasets remain, including MNIST, but Appendix D.1 and Table 2 redefine both biological classification targets: Zeisel changes from 7 cell types to 47 subclasses, and CBMC from 13 types to 56 subclasses. These finer targets materially change the reported task requirements.

E2.justification: Table 6 adds direct Euclidean and cosine feature-space classification baselines. Existing TWD, WMD/GMD, and ED/OT-ED comparators remain. Changes from names ending in '-TW' to '-TWD' are renamings.

E3.justification: Appendix D.1 now reports divisive biclustering to generate classification subclasses, replacing the previously stated cell-type labels. Appendix E.3.6 also introduces cosine-ground-cost WMD/GMD evaluations and direct-distance controls. The 70/30 splits and kNN settings remain; the PDFs do not establish whether the relabeled cell experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix E.3.6 examines whether baseline ground-metric choice and classification without Wasserstein transport explain performance differences. This extends the existing initial-metric ablation; earlier tree-construction, embedding, curvature, noise, and non-hierarchical-data analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-run evaluations and mean/standard-deviation results. The added tables follow the existing uncertainty-reporting practice; no new seed information, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedure appears.

E6.justification: Tables 5–6 add numerical results, including cosine-cost WMD at 93.5±0.3 on CLASSIC and GMD at 86.9±0.5 on Zeisel. Retained tables and plots preserve their values, including v1 Table 5 becoming v2 Table 7. Unchanged cell scores cannot establish equivalent performance under the revised classification targets.

M1.justification: The multi-scale hyperbolic diffusion embedding, HD-LCA construction, binary tree decoding, and TWD formula remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–3 retain the same procedures; expanded assumptions and experimental descriptions do not establish an algorithm change.

P1.justification: Parts of the introduction, problem formulation, and related-work discussion are rewritten; Appendix D.1 expands, and E.3.6 and F.5 are added. Diffusion-convergence discussion moves into Appendix A.2. The overall organization and most existing exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 5–6, renumbers the previous Table 5 as Table 7, and relocates existing appendix displays. Figure 2 updates comparator labels, Algorithms 1–2 use more compact formatting, and Table 1's caption expands. Existing empirical plots retain their graphical data.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting manifold assumptions and diffusion normalization, plus Fakcharoenphol et al. (2003) in the new single-linkage discussion, and removes Luecken and Theis (2019). Positioning against Euclidean-ground-metric TWD methods is elaborated while the central novelty distinction remains.

T1.justification: Theorems 1–2 and their proofs replace explicit 1/sqrt(2) and 1 bounds with unspecified positive constants. Section 4.1 introduces a complete, simply connected, negatively curved manifold formulation, and Section 4.4 explicitly conditions recovery on heat-kernel convergence. Theorem C.1 is also restated using d_T^(2alpha), materially revising the formal guarantees.

improvement.justification: The added ground-metric controls and direct-distance baselines address specific gaps in evaluating the empirical advantage, while clearer assumptions and data provenance improve transparency. The gain is limited: quantitative guarantees become weaker, revised cell labels accompany unexplained identical scores, and Appendix E.3.6 overgeneralizes superiority despite the retained CLASSIC WMD exception.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same tree-Wasserstein method and contain readable text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–F. Reported task revisions are identifiable and do not prevent comparison of the documents.

after.justification: Original experiments are retained, and Appendix E.3.6 adds cosine-cost WMD/GMD and direct-distance classification results.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix E report original synthetic, classification, runtime, and ablation experiments, alongside explicitly attributed baseline results.

title: Tree-Wasserstein Distance for High Dimensional Data with a Latent Feature Hierarchy

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about latent-feature hierarchy recovery, hyperbolic tree decoding, computational efficiency, and empirical advantages.

C2.justification: Mechanism explanations and limitations remain unchanged, including the probability-simplex restriction and qualifications concerning non-hierarchical data. The added main-text applicability remark summarizes the existing Appendix E.4 discussion.

D1.justification: v3 adds a Reproducibility Statement with a code-repository link and a pointer to Appendix D. The implementation settings and hardware information were already documented in v2; the PDFs do not establish the linked code's completeness.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate synthetic hierarchical data, BBCSPORT, TWITTER, CLASSIC, AMAZON, Zeisel, CBMC, and MNIST. The later main-text reference to non-hierarchical applications points to the existing Appendix E.4 experiment.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged throughout the main and appendix experiments, including TWD and graph/clustering methods, WMD/GMD, alternative hyperbolic embeddings, and ED/OT-ED comparisons.

E3.justification: Section 5 and Appendix D retain the same sample sizes, 70/30 splits, preprocessing, kNN settings, and parameter searches. Appendix evaluation procedures are also unchanged.

E4.justification: Both retain the toy recovery and runtime analyses, initial-distance and tree-construction ablations, alternative embeddings, curvature sensitivity, Gaussian-noise robustness, and non-hierarchical MNIST evaluation. No analysis is added or removed.

E5.justification: The five-run information and mean/standard-deviation reporting remain unchanged in Section 5 and Appendix D.1. The figures retain the same uncertainty displays.

E6.justification: All 46 numerical result rows across Tables 1 and 3–7 match, and the result figures retain their graphical content. For example, Table 1 reports the same proposed-method accuracies of 99.8±0.1 on synthetic data and 89.1±0.4 on Zeisel.

M1.justification: The diffusion embedding, HD-LCA construction, binary-tree decoding, and TWD computation are unchanged. Algorithms 1–3 retain their procedures; Algorithm 2's function-name edit is cosmetic.

P1.justification: v3 adds Ethics and Reproducibility Statements, expands affiliations and acknowledgments, numbers appendix remarks, and makes limited prose edits. Most wording and the scientific section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: The manuscript is retypeset throughout in ICLR format, changing text width, typography, headers, display sizes, and figure/table placement. All ten figures and seven tables are retained; Figure 7 moves from page 32 to 33 and Table 7 from page 37 to 38 without content changes.

R1.justification: Appendices A.2 and B add background citations to Lin et al. (2024), Lin et al. (2025), and Mendelman and Talmon (2025). These modestly extend the literature coverage without changing the paper's central positioning.

T1.justification: Section 3 revises the formal tree setup from m vertices with an m-by-m weight matrix to a vertex set V with m leaves and a |V|-by-|V| matrix, distinguishing leaves from all vertices. The TWD formula, main propositions and theorems, and Appendix C proofs remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 modestly improves clarity and reproducibility documentation through the corrected vertex-versus-leaf setup in Section 3 and the new code-access statement. Added references provide limited contextual benefit. The extensive reformatting leaves the methods, proofs, and empirical evidence essentially unchanged, so the overall gain is limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. All 38 pages in each version, including Appendices A–F, equations, ten figures, and seven tables, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains the original experiments and results in Section 5 and the appendices, alongside explicitly attributed baseline scores.

before.justification: v2 reports original synthetic-data experiments, document and cell classification results, and appendix robustness and MNIST evaluations. Some baseline scores are explicitly attributed to earlier work.

title: Tree-Wasserstein Distance for High Dimensional Data with a Latent Feature Hierarchy

C1.justification: The central claim that CBS scales primarily with data size remains. The introduction narrows the claimed literature gap from lacking a formal CBS definition to lacking a formalism relating model and data sizes. It also replaces the compute-for-speed trade-off wording with an assertion of greater parallelism without FLOPs-efficiency loss.

C2.justification: The scheduling takeaway changes from outperforming cosine at large batches to competitive performance. v3 explains disabling weight decay through its limited CBS effect and explicitly attributes width/depth-associated CBS growth to increased data. The conclusion removes the earlier future-work qualifications concerning heterogeneous data and extreme model/data ratios.

D1.justification: v3 discloses cosine duration multipliers, schedule-free beta1 choices, the PyTorch weight-decay implementation, and scipy.optimize.fsolve usage. Table 3 better explains defaults and selective sweeps. These disclosures do not by themselves establish changes to existing experiments; hardware and code-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions study autoregressive language-model pre-training on C4, retaining the context-length and under-/over-training investigations. The added weight-decay and threshold checks introduce no new dataset, domain, or task.

E2.justification: Cosine, WSD, and schedule-free optimization remain the evaluated scheduler comparators against Constant+EWA, including in the corresponding appendix panels. Newly cited works are not added empirical baselines.

E3.justification: v3 adds weight-decay sweeps at learning rates 0.01 and 0.00316 and evaluates CBS using 10% and 50% overhead thresholds alongside 20%. Its scheduler comparison ends at batch size 4096 rather than 8192. Principal model settings, target-loss selection, and validation procedures remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix A adds an ablation testing whether disabling weight decay affects CBS, and Appendix E adds sensitivity to the overhead threshold. Scheduler analyses are revised, while the existing context-length, width/depth, momentum, warmup, and EWA analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix D retains the same evaluation-set variance measurements and sample counts. Neither version adds training-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance testing.

E6.justification: v3 reports overhead-sensitivity exponents of 0.48 and 0.44 for 10% and 50% thresholds, and little CBS effect from weight decay. Scheduler curves are replaced, and the batch-8192 comparison is removed. The principal CBS fits and Tables 6–7 remain unchanged; the revised curves do not establish a controlled performance gain.

M1.justification: The architectures, Adam-based training, constant-learning-rate plus EWA procedure, and principal CBS estimation approach remain unchanged. Weight decay remains disabled for the principal experiments; its new evaluation is an ablation.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially reorganized into empirical takeaways and theoretical implications. Section 4.2 now presents the detailed risk theorem and corollary previously in Appendix G. Experimental-design explanations, scheduling discussion, the conclusion, and several appendix passages are also rewritten.

P2.justification: Former Figures 1 and 6 become a six-panel Figure 1 with reordered control panels. Figure 2 is redrawn as one panel, appendix scheduler plots are redrawn, context/width figures are reordered, and a weight-decay figure is added. Several Figure 1 references retain the old middle/right ordering.

R1.justification: v3 adds a substantive comparison with concurrent Filatov et al. (2024), distinguishing model-scale coverage and theoretical support. It also adds references concerning EWA optimization, scheduler connections, weight decay, and parallelism, while retaining the overall research positioning.

T1.justification: The formal results and Appendix G proofs are retained, with theorem and corollary statements moved into Section 4.2. However, new informal Corollary 1 asserts 0 < c < 1/2 in the variance-dominated regime. This is not generally implied by the retained exponent 1-a/min{b,2a+1}, which can exceed 1/2.

improvement.justification: The added weight-decay and threshold-sensitivity checks modestly strengthen empirical support, while clearer tuning and fitting details improve reproducibility. These gains are limited by incorrect Figure 1 panel references, the new inconsistent informal exponent bound, and removed scope qualifications. The principal findings and formal proofs remain stable, supporting a limited overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CBS scaling study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–G are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and reports additional weight-decay and CBS-threshold sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original C4 language-model training experiments, fitted CBS scaling laws, scheduler comparisons, and optimization ablations.

title: How Does Critical Batch Size Scale in Pre-training?

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions: CBS scales primarily with data size, depends weakly on model size, and can be studied using constant learning rates with EWA.

C2.justification: The explanation following Corollary 2 now correctly associates variance-dominated behavior and the corresponding batch-size tradeoff with b > a. Empirical interpretations and existing applicability qualifications remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Implementation details, hyperparameter tables, evaluation instructions, A100 hardware disclosure, OLMo framework information and the code-access link are retained. Added citations provide context without changing reproducibility instructions.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same C4 language-modeling coverage and experimental scenarios. No datasets, tasks or evaluated domains are added or removed.

E2.justification: The scheduler comparisons retain cosine, WSD and schedule-free optimization in Figures 2 and 9. The added Adam convergence citation does not introduce an evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: Target-loss selection, the 20% CBS overhead criterion, training budgets, validation cadence and hyperparameter grids remain identical. Tables 1–5 retain the same settings despite relocation.

E4.justification: The context-length, width/depth, warmup, EWA, weight-decay, Adam and small-batch analyses are retained. Repositioning the appendix figures introduces no new ablation or supplementary analysis.

E5.justification: Uncertainty-reporting practices are unchanged, including Appendix D's variance estimates for different validation-set sizes. No run-count, seed, confidence-interval or significance-testing information is added or revised.

E6.justification: The reported losses, optimization-step curves, CBS scaling fits and forecasts are unchanged, including the appendix results and Tables 6–7. Moved figures retain their original plotted content.

M1.justification: The model architectures, Adam training procedure, constant learning rate with exponential weight averaging, and CBS measurement procedure are unchanged.

P1.justification: There are localized punctuation, capitalization, tense and caption-wording edits, plus brief additions connecting experimental choices to prior work. Section ordering and the overall narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: The appendix layout is consolidated: Figure 8 moves to page 20, Figure 12 is placed beside text, Figures 13–14 share page 23, and Tables 2–3 share page 25. Figures and tables retain their content and numbering.

R1.justification: v4 adds Zhang et al. (2022), Adam can converge without any modification on update rules. Appendices A and D also explicitly connect existing warmup and hyperparameter choices to Porian et al. (2024); the broader research positioning remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 corrects the condition in the variance-dominated discussion from b < a to b > a, resolving a mathematical inconsistency with Corollary 2. The formal theorem and corollary statements and Appendix G proofs are unchanged.

improvement.justification: v4 fixes the misleading b < a condition in Section 4.2, bringing the explanation into agreement with Corollary 2 and its existing proof. Added attribution improves context for experimental choices, and appendix consolidation preserves the evidence. These are limited improvements; the methods, empirical support and central claims remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same critical-batch-size study. The complete main texts, figures, tables and Appendices A–G are readable and matchable; v4's shorter length reflects layout consolidation rather than missing material.

after.justification: v4 retains these original empirical results in the main text and appendices, including experiments with models ranging from 85M to 1.2B parameters.

before.justification: v3 reports original C4 language-model training experiments, critical-batch-size scaling results, scheduler comparisons and hyperparameter ablations.

title: How Does Critical Batch Size Scale in Pre-training?

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion strengthen the central claim from generalized stationarity, with ordinary KKT guarantees restricted to smooth squared norms, to ordinary KKT limit points for every algorithm norm. The stated empirical contribution also expands from Adam connections to Adam and Shampoo.

C2.justification: V2 adds an interpretation of Shampoo's spectral-margin behavior and removes v1's stated open question about extending ordinary KKT guarantees to arbitrary norms. It expands the applications discussion to Shampoo and language-model training. The caution that late-stage margins alone do not explain teacher–student generalization remains.

D1.justification: Appendix D documents the new Shampoo experiment's frozen output layer, initialization scale of 0.01, and learning rates of 0.01, 10, and 20 for Adam, GD, and Shampoo respectively. Section 4.3 identifies the implementation through Novik (2020). Details for retained experiments are unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate sparse-teacher Gaussian classification and binary MNIST classification, retaining the 3-versus-6 and 2-versus-7 digit experiments. The added Shampoo experiment uses MNIST with a different model configuration, without introducing a documented new task or domain.

E2.justification: Section 4.3 and Figure 3 add an evaluated Shampoo comparison against Adam and GD. Shampoo was previously discussed theoretically but not experimentally compared. Comparator membership in the retained experiments is unchanged.

E3.justification: The new Shampoo comparison uses a width-128 network with its second layer frozen, no momentum, optimizer-specific learning rates, and spectral-margin evaluation. These are settings for an added experiment; the teacher–student and Adam protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 adds a focused case study testing Shampoo's predicted spectral bias through loss, spectral-margin, and l1-margin trajectories. The existing initialization sensitivity, optimizer-switching, and Adam precision/momentum analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The 20-seed teacher–student reporting and three-seed Adam comparison remain unchanged. No new uncertainty-estimation convention, significance test, or repeated-run count is specified for the Shampoo experiment.

E6.justification: New Figure 3 reports that Shampoo finishes with a larger spectral margin than GD and Adam, alongside additional loss and l1-margin trajectories. The existing experimental plots retain their contents. These are new results under a frozen-second-layer setting, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The steepest-descent and steepest-flow procedures in Equations 1 and 3 are unchanged. Shampoo already appeared in Appendix C.2; v2 expands its description and evaluates it without introducing a new optimizer.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution narrative, Section 3.2, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around direct KKT stationarity. Bregman definitions and supporting derivations are consolidated in Appendix B, the principal proof is reorganized, and a separate Shampoo subsection is introduced.

P2.justification: V2 adds the three-panel Shampoo Figure 3. Existing experimental graphics are resized or relocated without changing their plotted contents; the Bregman illustration becomes Figure 4, and the two appendix experiment figures are arranged together as Figures 5 and 6.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to Cai et al. (2024), Jordan et al. (2024), and Novik (2020), and explicitly contrasts its theorem with the earlier version. It expands the connection to modular-norm optimization and removes the smoothness-specific Kakade and Shalev-Shwartz references, while retaining the broader related-work framework.

T1.justification: V2 replaces v1's generalized-KKT theorem and smooth-squared-norm KKT corollary with an ordinary-KKT theorem for arbitrary norms, using a revised approximate-KKT construction in Appendix A. It also corrects Lemma A.7's soft-margin bound and adds Corollary A.8 on soft/hard-margin convergence. The Bregman analysis is largely retained in Appendix B.

improvement.justification: V2 adds useful Shampoo evidence, corrects the soft-margin bound, and targets v1's explicit arbitrary-norm KKT limitation. However, the revised proof of Theorem A.16, around Equation 61, infers convergence of selected subgradients from membership in the limiting subdifferential; that implication need not hold at nonsmooth points and is not justified in the PDF. Because this step supports the principal claimed advance, the stronger theorem and clearer presentation do not establish a reliable net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. Their main text, equations, figures, references, and Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: The original experiments remain, and Section 4.3 adds an MNIST comparison of Shampoo, Adam, and gradient descent.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix D report original teacher–student and MNIST experiments, including margin trajectories, test accuracies, and optimizer-switching results.

title: Flavors of Margin: Implicit Bias of Steepest Descent in Homogeneous Neural Networks

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims of increasing algorithm-dependent margins and directional convergence to KKT points for arbitrary norms, together with connections to Adam and Shampoo. The proof changes support these existing claims.

C2.justification: Section 3.2 now explicitly distinguishes arbitrary-norm asymptotic stationarity from finite-time approximate-KKT guarantees requiring smooth squared norms. It also clarifies that normalized limit points are proportional to KKT points. The empirical interpretations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix D preserves the implementation framework, hyperparameters, sampling details, initialization rules, early stopping, and plotting conventions. The normalization explanation in Appendix C.1 restates the existing sign-gradient relationship rather than disclosing a different implementation.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate sparse Gaussian teacher–student classification and MNIST digit-pair classification, including the appendix experiment on digits 2 and 7. No dataset, task, or test scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged: GD, CD, and SD in teacher–student experiments; GD, SD, and Adam variants in the Adam experiments; and GD, Adam, and Shampoo in the spectral-margin comparison.

E3.justification: Section 4 and Appendix D retain the same sample counts, architectures, learning rates, initialization scales, losses, training budgets, and stopping procedures. Moving experimental details and figures does not alter the protocols.

E4.justification: The initialization-scale analysis, switching from GD to CD or SD after separation, Adam precision/momentum comparisons, and additional digit-pair experiment are retained. No empirical ablation or supplementary analysis is added or removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report 20 seeds for the teacher–student experiment and three seeds for Figure 2, with unchanged averaging, plotted uncertainty, and descriptions of seed-dependent sampling and initialization.

E6.justification: The empirical plots and reported findings are unchanged. Figures 1–3 match across versions, and v2 Figures 5–6 correspond to v3 Figures 4–5 with the same results; the removed v2 Figure 4 is a conceptual illustration.

Appendix B retains the Bregman bound, incorporates the existing complementarity estimate, and adds Proposition B.7, Corollary B.8, and Remark B.9 on finite-time guarantees for smooth squared norms. The general proximity-measure optimization in v2 Appendix B.1 is removed.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses a central proof gap: v2 Equation (61) assumes convergence of selected norm subgradients from membership in the limiting subdifferential, which is insufficient for nonsmooth norms. The revised Theorem A.16 instead uses closed-graph subsequence arguments and bounded multipliers, substantially strengthening support for the paper's arbitrary-norm claim. The finite-time limitations are also clearer. New Equation (79) appears to omit a square in its strong-convexity bound, but this local auxiliary defect does not outweigh the repair to the central proof.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, Flavors of Margin. Their main text, equations, figures, references, and Appendices A–D are readable and support a complete comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and their empirical results in Section 4 and Appendix D.

before.justification: v2 reports original teacher–student and MNIST experiments measuring margins, losses, and generalization under several optimizers, including additional appendix results.

title: Flavors of Margin: Implicit Bias of Steepest Descent in Homogeneous Neural Networks

The principal TS-roots and sample-average contributions remain; linear scaling and breaking dimensionality's curse were already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly qualifies the MES application: TS-roots supplies optimized posterior samples but does not optimize the MES acquisition function itself. Appendix D additionally interprets successful-start ranks as largely independent of iteration and dimension, motivating smaller set sizes. Existing mechanism explanations and the unresolved choice of the sample-average control parameter remain.

D1.justification: Appendix H newly discloses n_o = 500, and Appendix C.2 specifies recursive subdivision above polynomial degree 100. Appendix G supplies truss loads, material constants, variable bounds, normalization constants, and objective weights. The main code link, hardware descriptions, and other retained experimental settings are unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds one ten-variable structural-design problem: minimizing a weighted combination of cross-sectional area and displacement for a ten-bar truss (Appendix G, Figure 2(f)). The existing synthetic functions and dimensions remain.

Existing main-experiment settings, including n_e = 250 and n_x = 200, remain. Newly reporting n_o = 500 does not establish a change to those existing experiments.
