This directly investigates minimum useful set sizes and supports smaller-budget recommendations, whereas v1 left subset-size effects to future work. The existing sample-average sensitivity study is retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report medians and interquartile ranges from 20 runs for the main benchmark and sample-average studies, and ten runs for MES. No revised repetition counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance procedures are reported. The new start-rank histograms describe diagnostic outcomes rather than uncertainty in performance estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial result sets: truss optimization curves favoring TS-roots in Figure 2(f), successful-start rank distributions in Figure 7, and grid/LHS comparisons in Figures 10–11 showing stronger high-dimensional acquisition optimization and runtime performance. These are additional findings, not demonstrated improvements over v1 under identical settings.

M1.justification: Equation (4) changes exploitation-point ranking from posterior-mean values in v1 to posterior-sample values in v2, also specified in Appendix D. The remaining rootfinding and sample-average procedures are retained. Algorithm 1's comment still says posterior mean, leaving an implementation ambiguity despite the documented rule change.

P1.justification: The existing sample-average derivation moves from Results into a standalone Section 4. The abstract and pathwise-conditioning background are expanded, and method wording and appendix organization are refined. Most existing prose and the overall argumentative structure remain.

P2.justification: Figure 2 gains a sixth panel, and v2 adds the multi-panel starting-rank diagnostic, truss schematic, and two initialization-comparison figures. R1.justification: v2 adds references to entropy search, Wilson et al.'s pathwise-conditioning work, and Hoffman and Ribak's Gaussian-field conditioning work. These are limited positioning additions; most reference changes are formatting.

T1.justification: Appendix C.5 adds a conditional whole-algorithm complexity derivation combining posterior evaluation, gradient optimization, and minimum-selection costs, concluding O(dn + dθ) under fixed-budget assumptions. The existing local-minimum proposition and proof, counting formulas, rootfinding theorem, and sample-average derivation remain.

improvement.justification: The truss experiment, grid/LHS comparisons, and starting-point diagnostics strengthen support for the existing contribution, while added settings and cost analysis improve transparency. The gain is limited by the empirical best-multistart reference underlying the small-set optimality claims and the conflicting posterior-mean comment in Algorithm 1. The core theoretical foundations and existing results remain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TS-roots research. Their main texts, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison across the reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds truss optimization, starting-point diagnostics, and comparisons with grid and Latin hypercube initialization.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark optimization, inner-loop comparisons, MES experiments, and sample-average sensitivity results in the main text and appendices.

E6.justification: Figures 2-7 and 9-13 retain the same plotted results, and their associated numerical statements, rankings and empirical findings are unchanged. No result entries are added or removed.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized wording revisions in Section 3.1 and Appendix C.1, adds an appendix cross-reference and acknowledgments, and updates the arXiv stamp. The broader narrative and section order are unchanged.

P2.justification: Acknowledgments occupy previously blank space on page 12. Expanded Appendix C.1 text moves part of the eigenfunction formula onto page 22 and shifts subsequent material. Figures and captions are retained without redesign.

R1.justification: Section 5 and all 53 references are unchanged. The added acknowledgments provide credits and funding information without changing research positioning.

The benefit is limited because the consequences for the unchanged posterior-sampling and sample-average arguments are not examined; the empirical evidence remains identical.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TS-roots research. All 33 pages, including Appendices A-I, are available and readable; text, equations, algorithms and figures support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains the original benchmark, truss, inner-loop optimization, MES and sensitivity results reported in v2.

before.justification: Section 6 and Appendices D/I report original optimization experiments on benchmark functions and a ten-bar truss, including comparator and sensitivity results.

title: Optimizing Posterior Samples for Bayesian Optimization via Rootfinding

D1.justification: Appendix K specifies blending settings and scheduling, Appendix M documents frequency extraction and top-20-word prompting, and Appendix O identifies a 40GB A100 and the scope of timing measurements. The code link changes from Rare2Frequent to Rare-to-Frequent; availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark scores are retained, while Table 4 and Tables 15–18 add substantial results. Within the new four-step comparison, FLUX/R2F-FLUX property scores are 72.5/78.7, but complex scores are 73.7/68.7. LAION mapping variants score below standard R2F, and newly reported diffusion times are 20.60 seconds for R2F versus 72.37 for R2F+.

M1.justification: The standard R2F and R2F+ procedures remain unchanged. Appendix K introduces a four-step FLUX-schnell adaptation that replaces alternating guidance with text-embedding blending during selected early steps, followed by rare-prompt-only sampling. This adapts an existing ablation component into an accelerated variant.

P1.justification: Localized rewrites explain acceleration, IterComp comparisons and new appendix references, and the header becomes 'Preprint, Under review.' Appendices K–P extend the document without substantially reorganizing the existing narrative or Appendices A–J.

P2.justification: v2 expands Table 4, adds Tables 15–18 and Figures 16–17, reformats Table 13, and resizes several illustrations. Figure 10 relabels the unchanged imagery from 'star-shaped panda' to 'star-shaped spaceship.' The established visual organization is retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting image-quality assessment and prospective applications, including ImageReward, SpatialVLM, visual instruction tuning and speech/audio/music generation. Section 2 and the central positioning against existing compositional and LLM-grounded diffusion approaches remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.1, its assumptions and the complete Appendix A proof are unchanged. Appendix O adds a simple, empirically motivated runtime derivation for R2F+: N(T+1)+(T+10), combining per-object generation and masking with final guided generation.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens practical validation through additional backbone and acceleration tests, mapping and guidance diagnostics, and quantitative R2F+ quality/cost evidence. These address limited gaps in an already extensive evaluation. Undefined ± statistics and an optimistic acceleration interpretation despite the complex-category decline limit the gains, but the added evidence and computational transparency provide a clear net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same R2F/R2F+ work. Text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, including the retained Appendices A–J and newly added K–P in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds IterComp results, accelerated FLUX experiments, guidance diagnostics, image-quality measurements and GPU profiling.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-generation experiments on RareBench, DVMP and T2I-CompBench, with automatic and human evaluations, ablations and qualitative analyses.

title: Rare-to-Frequent: Unlocking Compositional Generation Power of Diffusion Models on Rare Concepts with LLM Guidance

C1.justification: Both claim training-free improvement of rare-concept composition, compatibility across backbones and LLMs, the R2F+ extension, and RareBench. The headline improvement of up to 28.1 percentage points is retained.

C2.justification: Interpretations and applicability limits remain unchanged, including explanations of frequent-concept guidance, automatic-evaluation failures, and R2F+ failures with overlapping or small bounding boxes. Appendix application discussions are also retained.

D1.justification: Implementation settings, LLM instructions, pseudocode, hardware, and resource measurements are unchanged. The abstract replaces the displayed repository URL with 'link', but its hyperlink points to the same repository.

E1.justification: RareBench, DVMP, and T2I-CompBench coverage is unchanged, including their single-object and multi-object scenarios. The LAION-based analyses and ImageNet-class diagnostic also remain.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the benchmark, backbone, guidance, and paraphrasing comparisons. Newly cited GenArtist is discussed as related work, not added as an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Both retain the same dataset sizes, default 50 sampling steps, four-step FLUX experiment, evaluation metrics, scoring rubrics, and ten human evaluators. No experimental setting is revised.

E4.justification: The guidance and stopping-point ablations, backbone/LLM comparisons, paraphrasing analysis, and appendix studies remain unchanged. These include evaluation-metric failures, R2F+ failure cases, and LAION-assisted concept mapping.

E5.justification: Both specify default seed 42, show eight-seed qualitative examples in Appendix G, and report the same uncertainty notation in Table 17. No repetition counts or statistical reporting practices change.

E6.justification: Numerical results and qualitative examples are retained throughout. For example, Table 2 still reports R2F property scores of 89.4 for GPT evaluation and 86.3 for human evaluation; appendix Tables 15–18 also remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Both retain the same LLM concept mapping, adaptive alternating guidance, R2F+ region-control procedure, and four-step FLUX adaptation in Appendix K. No algorithmic component changes.

P1.justification: v3 makes limited wording edits, removes author email addresses, and changes the header from under review to publication at ICLR 2025. The section sequence and overall narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: Spacing, diagram sizing, and page flow are adjusted. Table 4 and Figure 7 move from page 9 to page 8, while their content is retained; no substantive figure or table redesign occurs.

R1.justification: v3 adds Parashar et al. on neglected tails, Liang et al. on diffusion factorization/composition, and Wang et al.'s GenArtist. These locally extend the motivation, theoretical context, and related-work citations without redefining the research positioning.

T1.justification: The Gaussian assumptions, Theorem 3.1, mathematical definitions, and Appendix A proof are unchanged. Adding a Liang et al. citation to the Gaussian setup does not revise its mathematical substance.

improvement.justification: The added citations modestly improve attribution and scholarly context, especially around the Gaussian motivation and LLM-based image editing. The methods, empirical evidence, proofs, and limitations remain unchanged, so the overall gain is limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Rare-to-Frequent research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–P are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experimental results, including benchmark comparisons, human evaluations, and supplementary analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original R2F and R2F+ experiments on RareBench, DVMP, and T2I-CompBench, including human evaluations, ablations, and appendix analyses.

title: Rare-to-Frequent: Unlocking Compositional Generation Power of Diffusion Models on Rare Concepts with LLM Guidance

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statement substantially narrow the convergence claims: the large-batch O(1/T) guarantee is removed, and PL convergence is explicitly to a neighborhood of the optimum. The method's central flexibility claim remains. Abstract CIFAR-100 advantages change from 21.4%/12.2% to 18.2%/7.4%, reflecting stronger comparators rather than changed LASER-VFL scores.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations linking Combinatorial's behavior to training-data scarcity for larger feature subsets, discusses task-sampling variance growing with client count, and explicitly states the MCAR boundary. Appendix A.2 argues that adjusted representation models preserve aggregation expressivity. These substantially expand interpretation beyond the retained dropout-like regularization explanation.

D1.justification: The abstract adds a code-availability link. Appendix D newly identifies the MLP, LSTM, and ResNet18 model choices, explains PlugVFL's zero-filled missing representations and per-party dropout adaptation, and reports runtimes. These improve documentation, although detailed training hyperparameters and hardware remain unspecified.

E1.justification: All five datasets and prediction tasks are retained. Appendix E adds a CIFAR-10 scenario with heterogeneous, Beta-distributed missingness probabilities across feature blocks, including independently sampled training and inference probabilities. This is a limited extension of input-condition coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Combinatorial and an adapted PlugVFL across all five datasets, substantially strengthening the comparator set. Combinatorial was previously only a conceptual alternative, while the work underlying PlugVFL was cited but not evaluated. Existing baselines retain their dataset participation.

E3.justification: The primary four-client missingness grid and metrics remain unchanged. Added protocols measure accuracy and runtime across two to eight clients at missingness probability 0.1, and compare Beta(2,2) block probabilities against a fixed 0.5 control. Combinatorial is omitted at eight clients because of resource constraints.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's missingness grid, v2 adds dedicated scalability and runtime analysis in Figure 2 and nonuniform-missingness robustness tests in Appendix E. These provide substantial new examinations of the method's efficiency and sensitivity to heterogeneous feature availability.

E5.justification: Both versions report Table 1 means and standard deviations over five seeds. The new Table 3 follows the same practice. No changed run count, confidence-interval procedure, or significance-testing method is stated.

E6.justification: All retained Table 1 scores are unchanged, but new comparator results alter rankings: with complete HAPT training data and inference missingness 0.5, PlugVFL scores 90.3 ± 1.3 versus LASER-VFL's retained 87.0 ± 1.2. Figure 2, Appendix D runtimes, and Table 3 add substantial scaling, cost, and nonuniform-missingness findings.

M1.justification: The shared representation and fusion models, averaging aggregation, weighted objective, task-sampling procedure, and training/inference algorithms remain equivalent. Revised notation and the aggregation explanation in Appendix A.2 do not establish a changed architecture or procedure.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites clarify the objective and task-sampling exposition, revise notation and terminology, and expand and reorganize the appendices. The main section sequence and much of the introductory and concluding prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds the two-panel scalability/runtime Figure 2, the LASER-VFL forward-pass diagram in Figure 3, and the nonuniform-missingness Table 3. Table 1 gains comparator rows and revised best-score emphasis. Figure 1 is relocated and its preview explicitly labeled MIMIC-IV.

R1.justification: V2 adds Ganguli et al. and supporting references for missingness mechanisms and model architectures, fixes the unresolved FedSVD citation, and expands closest-work comparisons in Appendix A.1. The central research positioning remains. Sun's updated PlugVFL reference corresponds to work already cited in v1.

T1.justification: Section 4 and the proofs replace the single variance bound sigma^2/B with separate mini-batch and task-sampling bounds, producing sigma_b^2 + K sigma_s^2 terms in both theorems. Large-batch O(1/T) and full-batch exact-convergence statements disappear. V2 also explicitly assumes missingness completely at random and adds an aggregation-equivalence derivation in Appendix A.2.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for effectiveness and efficiency through relevant additional baselines, measured scaling, and heterogeneous-missingness tests that v1 lacked. Separate task-sampling variance accounting and narrower convergence claims improve theoretical qualification; implementation disclosures improve transparency. Some Section 5 wording overstates Combinatorial's dominance relative to Table 1, and training details remain limited, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LASER-VFL work. Their text, algorithms, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison; retained appendix content can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds baseline evaluations, client-count/runtime experiments, and nonuniform-missingness experiments in Figure 2 and Appendix E.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on HAPT, Credit, MIMIC-IV, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, including Table 1 results across training and inference missingness conditions.

The abstract updates numerical illustrations from 18.2% and 7.4% to 19.3% and 9.5%, without changing the scope of these central claims.

C2.justification: Section 5 qualifies Combinatorial's low-missingness advantage from outperforming 'all' baselines to 'most,' specifies when PlugVFL trails Combinatorial or Ensemble, and includes PlugVFL in the explanation of scalability through representation reuse. The task-sampling regularization interpretation and applicability assumptions remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix D retains the same VFedTrans components, PlugVFL adaptation, MIMIC-IV processing description, metric formulas, model families, and runtime information. after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and reports revised measurements in Table 1, Figure 2, and Appendix E.

title: Vertical Federated Learning with Missing Features During Training and Inference

C1.justification: The principal claims about reasons without recourse, responsive feature highlighting, and flagging potentially fixed predictions remain. v2 adds an explicit contribution concerning information missing from explanations and strengthens the conclusion that explainability mandates need clearer requirements for explanation content and construction.

C2.justification: Section 5 adds a substantive distinction between a feature admitting recourse and an explanation providing enough information to attain it. It explains failures caused by nonmonotonic responses and counterintuitive directions, and discusses supplying thresholds or imposing model constraints. v2 also introduces potential applications in content moderation and criminal justice; the earlier individual-feasibility and causal-assumption limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds algorithm pseudocode, detailed optimization and sampling routines, the enumeration setting epsilon_min=0.5, preprocessing explanations, feature-partition mappings, and continuous-case actionability specifications. Code links change from responsiveness-public to reachml. Conversely, v1's illustrative enumeration cost of roughly one hour and 18.8 GB is removed.

E1.justification: Empirical coverage remains loan repayment and recourse on heloc, german, and givemecredit. The continuous-feature givemecredit case uses the existing population and task; its changed representation and diagnostic criteria constitute protocol and supplementary-analysis changes rather than additional dataset or task coverage.

For heloc/LR, Table 3's no-recourse rate changes from 19.1% to 22.2%, while Table 4's wholly unresponsive LIME explanations change from 82.0% to 92.7%. RF results also change. M1.justification: The central responsiveness score is retained. C2.justification: Section 4.2 newly states that supplied generation concept labels are unnecessary because ACS could provide concept scores. This expands the stated applicability beyond the documented label-supervised experiments, without reporting a corresponding evaluation. The principal result interpretations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Section 3.1 newly identifies the similarity function as cosine cubed, and Section 4.1 explicitly describes generation-layer dimensions. Existing prompting instructions, regularization constants, timing results, and code access information are retained.

E3.justification: Appendices A.1 and B.1 introduce Gemma2-2B classification and Llama2-13B/Mistral-7B generation configurations. Previously reported sample caps, metrics, and the 100-token steering procedure remain unchanged. These are additional model settings, not documented revisions to the original experiments.

E4.justification: Table 7 extends the sparse-final-layer comparison to Gemma2-2B, and Appendix B.4 adds a toxicity-steering case in Figure 16. Existing ACC/adversarial ablations and unlearning analyses are retained; Figure 15 redisplays the existing generation examples.

E5.justification: Both versions report three independent worker evaluations per human-study question. v2 adds no model-run counts, seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical tests, including for its new backbone results.

E6.justification: Tables 7 and 12 substantially expand concrete results across three additional backbones, covering classification accuracy and generation accuracy, steerability, and perplexity. Table 5 also changes Llama3-based CB-LLM's DBpedia steerability from 0.58 to 0.76 without explaining the revision. Other main-table results and the existing GPT2 results are retained.

M1.justification: The five-step classification pipeline and the generation architecture with adversarial disentanglement retain the same procedures and objectives. Naming the cosine-cubed similarity and specifying layer dimensions clarify the method; they do not establish an algorithm change.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract and portions of the introduction, expands the generation-module explanation, and standardizes CB-LLMs terminology. It moves the MTurk appendix from A.1 to A.7, while retaining the main classification-then-generation organization.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 3 receive visual revisions, and Figure 15 is redrawn around the same generated examples. Tables 7 and 12 and Figure 16 are added. Most existing appendix displays are retained with relocation, renumbering, or sizing changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds Classification with Conceptual Safeguards, Discover-then-Name, and VLG-CBM. Section 2 briefly discusses VLG-CBM's faithfulness and Number of Effective Concepts metric. The overall positioning against existing text bottleneck models remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(9) retain their mathematical substance. Explicit layer dimensions and revised weight notation restate the existing architecture; no new theorem, proof, substantive assumption, or derivation appears.

improvement.justification: The additional backbone comparisons provide useful evidence of portability beyond v1's tested models, while the explicit similarity choice and revised diagrams improve clarity. The gains are limited by sparse documentation and absent uncertainty estimates for the added experiments. The unexplained DBpedia score revision does not itself establish a performance improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CB-LLM research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–B are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds backbone comparisons in Tables 7 and 12 and another toxicity-steering example.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, human-evaluation, generation, concept-unlearning, and toxicity-steering results in Sections 3–4 and the appendices.

title: Concept Bottleneck Large Language Models

E5.justification: The added METRA sensitivity study explicitly reports means and standard deviations over two seeds. The existing ten-seed main comparisons and five-seed CSF scaling study retain their reporting; no change to their run counts is stated.

E6.justification: Figure 11 adds learning curves showing broadly similar Ant coverage across the tested METRA hyperparameters. Appendix C.6 newly reports that neither CSF nor METRA achieved consistently stable MiniHack performance. Existing benchmark curves, numerical findings, and rankings are retained.

M1.justification: CSF's contrastive representation objective, intrinsic reward, successor-feature critic, and policy updates remain unchanged in Section 5 and Algorithm 1. The MiniHack report does not document a new method component or procedural adaptation.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized edits and condensation in Sections 6–7, adds a reproducibility statement and conference headers, and inserts two appendix subsections. The broader narrative and section organization are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds the three-panel Figure 11 and adjusts the surrounding appendix layout. The existing trajectory visualization becomes Figure 12 and is repositioned, while other changes concern figure sizing, captions, spacing, and headers.

R1.justification: v2 adds Samvelyan et al. (2021) for MiniHack. The related-work discussion and positioning relative to MISL, contrastive learning, successor features, and METRA otherwise remain substantively unchanged.

T1.justification: The propositions, assumptions, corollary, and appendix derivations remain substantively unchanged. Appendix A.4 changes the notation for the same variational distribution from qπ to q̃ without changing the argument.

improvement.justification: The added METRA sensitivity checks provide useful evidence about the hyperparameters removed by CSF, and the MiniHack failure report makes applicability limits more transparent. These are modest gains: the sensitivity study uses only two seeds, and MiniHack lacks quantitative results and detailed settings. The core method, theory, and established benchmark evidence remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CSF/METRA study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–C are readable and can be matched reliably, including renumbered and relocated material.

after.justification: The original empirical results are retained, with additional METRA sensitivity experiments and a qualitative report of unsuccessful MiniHack experiments.

before.justification: Section 6 and Appendices B–C report original reinforcement-learning experiments, including exploration, goal reaching, hierarchical control, representation analyses, and ablations.

title: Can a MISL Fly? Analysis and Ingredients for Mutual Information Skill Learning

E3.justification: Training budgets, model and skill dimensions, goal sampling, evaluation metrics, and hierarchical-controller procedures are unchanged. Both retain the 50-goal evaluation, staying-time-fraction metric, and settings in Tables 1–3.

E4.justification: Section 6 and Appendix C retain the same representation checks, contrastive-loss and information-bottleneck ablations, critic-parameterization tests, hyperparameter sensitivities, trajectory visualizations, and MiniHack failure analysis.

M1.justification: Section 5 and Algorithm 1 retain the same representation objective, intrinsic reward, successor-feature critic, and policy updates. Correcting the policy symbol in the algorithm summary aligns the prose with the existing procedure.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized grammar, punctuation, and terminology edits throughout the main text and appendices, corrects the policy notation, explains parameter symbols, and expands the wording of the Appendix C.4 heading. The section organization and narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 reformats the author block, colors citations and cross-references, and makes modest spacing and placement changes, including moving Corollary 1 onto the preceding page. All figures and tables are retained with unchanged data displays.

R1.justification: The cited works and research positioning are unchanged, including the distinctions from METRA, CIC, and VISR and connections to contrastive learning and successor features.

T1.justification: Corollary 1 now states that METRA approximates the contrastive lower bound on mutual information, whereas v2 said it approximates mutual information itself. This corrects the formal assertion to match its existing displayed relation; the supporting derivations and appendix proofs remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 improves precision by correcting Corollary 1's claim about what is approximated and aligning the policy notation with Algorithm 1. Copyediting also improves readability. These are limited gains because the method, supporting derivations, empirical evidence, and reproducibility information remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CSF/METRA research and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–C. The complete material supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results, including benchmark learning curves, representation measurements, ablations, and the MiniHack failure report.

before.justification: v2 reports original representation analyses, skill-learning benchmark results, ablations, sensitivity studies, and failed MiniHack experiments in Section 6 and Appendices B–C.

title: Can a MISL Fly? Analysis and Ingredients for Mutual Information Skill Learning

title: The Utility and Complexity of In- and Out-of-Distribution Machine Unlearning

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about dimension-independent in-distribution deletion capacity, separation from differential privacy, worst-case out-of-distribution failure, and robust training with near-linear complexity.

C2.justification: The explanations involving initialization error, robust training, and retain-set interpolation error are unchanged. Section 5's added zero-capacity clause makes explicit the already-stated worst-case failure to unlearn even one sample, without introducing a new limitation or interpretation.

D1.justification: Figure 1a changes 'Alg. 1 w/ SGD' to 'Alg. 1', removing the explicit optimizer identification for that experiment. Appendix F's implementation settings otherwise remain unchanged, and no replacement optimizer is documented.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate synthetic linear regression with in-distribution and label-shifted out-of-distribution forget data, plus out-of-distribution unlearning on California Housing. No dataset or test scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: Figure 1a still compares Algorithm 1 against DP-SGD. Figure 1b and Figure 2 still compare Algorithms 1 and 2. The analytical comparison methods in the tables also remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The captions and Appendix F retain the same sample sizes, forget fractions, label-shift construction, unlearning budgets, optimization budgets, and evaluation metrics. No revised experimental protocol is documented.

E4.justification: The dimensionality study and convergence comparisons across forget-set sizes are retained, including the California Housing validation. No ablation, robustness test, or supplementary analysis is added or removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The uncertainty-reporting practice is unchanged; revisions to theoretical sub-Gaussian bounds belong to T1.

E6.justification: Table 2 corrects Algorithm 1's non-Lipschitz out-of-distribution computational deletion capacity from 'Unbounded' to '0'. This changes a reported theoretical result entry. The empirical curve values and findings in Figures 1 and 2 remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1 and 2 retain the same optimization procedures, output perturbation, and robust trimmed-mean training. Removing the SGD qualifier from Figure 1a does not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: v3 adds a first-page correction notice, expands acknowledgments, and revises local proof explanations and a sentence in Section 5. The overall narrative and section organization remain intact.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion, cited works, and novelty positioning remain unchanged. References moving between pages 10–12 are retained entries, not additions or removals.

T1.justification: Proposition 1 and Appendix B receive a localized proof correction: population-risk bounds now use distance decompositions around the population minimizer, replacing an invalid smoothness step at empirical minimizers. Lemma 4 becomes a squared-distance bound and drops its smoothness assumption. Equations (4)–(6) revise constants and replace ln(n) with ln(n+1); Appendix C adjusts corresponding coefficients. The main theorem scopes and asymptotic rates remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 repairs the invalid smoothness argument supporting Proposition 1 and corrects Table 2's misleading capacity entry, improving mathematical reliability. The correction remains incomplete: Appendix E, page 25, still applies Proposition 1 with the old coefficients. Figure 1a also loses its explicit SGD identification. These changes provide a clear but limited net improvement.

after.justification: v3 retains the original synthetic-data experiments in Figure 1 and California Housing experiments in Appendix F, Figure 2.

before.justification: v2 reports original linear-regression experiments on synthetic data in Figure 1 and California Housing data in Appendix F, Figure 2.

title: BaB-ND: Long-Horizon Motion Planning with Branch-and-Bound and Neural Dynamics

C1.justification: Both versions claim superior human-difficulty prediction, category-specific percept enhancement, and improved learning across the same three domains, retaining the 33–72% accuracy-margin gains and 20–23% training-time reductions. v2 emphasizes unmodified held-out testing, already documented in v1.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the checkpoint results as suggesting that classification accuracy matters less than robustness for difficulty prediction, while acknowledging that early-checkpoint enhancements were not tested with humans. It also connects central perturbation concentration to changes around image subjects. Existing clinical-bias, homogenization, and hallucination limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix S1 adds task-specific fine-tuning learning rates, batch sizes, attack-step settings, and heat-map construction details. The reproducibility statement changes from promising future code release to stating that code is provided, although both PDFs already contain the same repository link.

E1.justification: Both versions use ImageNet animal categorization, iNaturalist moth images, HAM10000 dermoscopy, and MHIST histology. The added analyses reuse existing data and task coverage; no new domain, population, or task is evaluated.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is retained: c-score, prediction depth, adversarial robustness, the six guide-model configurations, CLAHE/MSRCR/Lightroom controls, cross-entropy enhancement, and ET/DS ablations. The new checkpoint analysis varies training progress within an existing model.
